secs.head: AI Tea Lounge: Sipping Knowledge in AI Domains
secs.body: Knowledge, served in short sips. Notes on AI, machine learning, software engineering and the business around them. Each page is short enough to finish before your tea goes cold.

secs.head: ☕ What's brewing
secs.body: aCupOfTea is a personal knowledge base built during day-to-day work in data science and engineering. It collects: - Concepts : the ideas behind ML, deep learning, statistics and generative AI. - Engineering : clean code, design patterns, version control, parallel programming and systems. - Problems and projects : reusable problem write-ups and the projects that solved them. - Business context : how the technical work connects to real decisions. It is written for practitioners who want the core of a topic quickly, and for anyone who likes to learn something new on a coffee break.

secs.head: 🗺️ How to read it
secs.body: - On the website: use the sidebar. It is generated from the folder structure, so it always matches the repo. - On GitHub: every folder has a README.md that lists its pages. - Projects marked ↗ are separate repositories, linked as git submodules. Clone with git clone --recursive to get them locally. <details <summary <b Repository layout</b </summary </details

secs.head: 🤝 Pull up a chair
secs.body: Contributions are welcome: a correction, a clearer explanation or a whole new topic. 1. Branch from dev and keep one topic per branch. 2. Put the page where it belongs. SPEC.md describes the structure, and folder and page names use kebab-case . 3. Open a pull request against dev . The step-by-step guide, with the script that creates a page and the checks to run, is in CONTRIBUTING.md. Found something off but no time to fix it? Open an issue. That helps too.

secs.head: Start here
secs.body: Pick a cup: follow a path, grab a quick read, or start with the basics.

secs.head: Learning paths
secs.body: Read each path in order; every step builds on the one before.

secs.head: Generative AI · 6 steps · 58 min
secs.body: 1. Compute-Bound vs Memory-Bandwidth-Bound — Why a 3x faster GPU can give you 1.6x - arithmetic intensity, the ridge point and the roofline, explained with a pizza kitchen and two lines of arithmetic. (intermediate · 9 min) 2. LLM Inference on the Roofline — Why your chatbot reads a novel-length prompt in a blink but types its answer like a tired intern - prefill, decode, batching and the KV cache on the roofline. (intermediate · 9 min) 3. Sizing a 70B Model with a Pencil — A live whiteboard walk-through - Llama 2 70B on 8xH100, from "does it fit?" to the exact token-rate ceilings at batch 1 and batch 64, using only a datasheet. (intermediate · 9 min) 4. Optimizations, Mapped to the Roofline — Five proposals in one meeting, one roofline to judge them - batching, PagedAttention, quantization, tensor parallelism, FlashAttention, speculative decoding, disaggregation, and how to measure. (intermediate · 12 min) 5. 2:4 Sparsity: Half the Weights, Not Half the Time — How NVIDIA's 2:4 structured sparsity works, what it really saves (44% of weight bytes, not 50%), and why its doubled TFLOPS help prefill while decode only feels the byte savings. (intermediate · 9 min) 6. Sparsity vs Quantization: Who Pays, and Who Wins — What it costs to prune an LLM to 2:4, how much accuracy goes with it, how it compares with FP8 and 4-bit quantization, and why the usual order is quantize first, sparsify second. (intermediate · 10 min)

secs.head: Systems and HPC · 18 steps · 160 min
secs.body: 1. Containers 101 — Containers from the ground up: what happens at boot, kernel and user space, virtual machines, then namespaces, cgroups and Linux containers. (8 min) 2. Kubernetes in Five Nouns, Explained Like You Just Inherited the Cluster — The five Kubernetes nouns (node, pod, namespace, event, API server) explained through HPC analogies, for someone who just inherited a cluster. (advanced · 8 min) 3. Build a Two-Node Kubernetes Lab on Your Laptop (and Survive the DNS Pothole) — Build a two-VM Kubernetes lab on your laptop with Vagrant, libvirt and k3s, and dodge the DNS and network potholes. (intermediate · 7 min) 4. Fake GPUs in Kubernetes: Learn GPU Scheduling Without Owning a GPU — Patch a node with a fake nvidia.com/gpu counter to learn GPU scheduling without owning a GPU. (intermediate · 6 min) 5. Broken Pods: A Rogues' Gallery (and the One Command That Catches Them All) — How to recognise CrashLoop, OOMKilled, ImagePull and Pending pods by reading status, events and previous logs. (intermediate · 6 min) 6. Booked Is Not Busy: GPU Allocation vs Utilization — The scheduler knows who has booked the GPUs, not whether they’re busy, so use kubectl for the first question and DCGM-style telemetry for the second. (intermediate · 7 min) 7. The Cluster That Passed Every Test Except the One That Mattered — Even when traditional monitoring tools show all GPUs and networks operating normally, subtle bottlenecks—like a single slow GPU or a degraded network link—can silently drag down the performance of an (intermediate · 10 min) 8. Isolating GPU Workloads: Taints, Labels and the Device Plugin — How the NVIDIA device plugin exposes GPUs to pods, why taints alone don't dedicate GPU nodes, and why distributed training needs all-or-nothing scheduling. (intermediate · 9 min) 9. The Job Execution Journey: From kubectl apply to the First All-Reduce — From kubectl apply to the first NCCL all-reduce of an 8-GPU job, via the API server, Kueue, operators, scheduler, device plugin, runtime and Multus. (intermediate · 13 min) 10. Draining a GPU Node With a Three-Day Run on It — Why kubectl drain means the opposite of Slurm's drain, how the SIGTERM-to-SIGKILL clock works, five ways a long training run dies anyway, and a runbook that keeps the checkpoint. (intermediate · 10 min) 11. The Pod Killed With Memory to Spare — Why a training pod is OOMKilled on a node with memory free: three killers, per-container limits, working set, /dev/shm, QoS and a spike no dashboard caught. (intermediate · 11 min) 12. k3s vs kubeadm: Furnished Flat or Empty Unit? — k3s and kubeadm deliver the same conformant Kubernetes; what each installs, how upgrades and HA differ, and how to choose for a lab, edge box or GPU cluster. (intermediate · 9 min) 13. Your kubeconfig Is a House Key — What a kubeconfig holds, how kubectl picks one, why a leaked certificate can't be revoked, and how to issue each person a short-lived key instead of sharing yours. (intermediate · 8 min) 14. RBAC: The Error Message Writes the Rule for You — Read a Forbidden error as the rule you need, build a read-only user in two commands, and see RBAC's guardrails and why the binding is the off switch for a certificate. (intermediate · 9 min) 15. Polite API Server Monitoring: Leave Your Number, Don't Knock Every Second — Why polling the API server every second hurts, measured on a lab: 20 lists vs 1 list and a watch, what a list costs in bytes, the priority lane monitors share, and five habits for a polite monitor. (intermediate · 10 min) 16. Kubernetes at HPC Scale: The Front Desk Meets a 100,000-Task Array — What changes when a cluster gets big and the work looks like an HPC job array: the published limits, where the pressure lands, and how to turn an array into one Indexed Job. (intermediate · 10 min) 17. kubectl Troubleshooting Cheat Sheet: Five Questions, in Order — A kubectl cheat sheet for a pod or Job that won't work: where is it, what does it say, what did the cluster say, why did it die, and how to look inside. Commands from the Kubernetes reference. (intermediate · 9 min) 18. Singularity — Singularity (rootless containers for HPC): installing it, building SIF images, converting from Docker, bind mounts and definition-file variables. (10 min)

secs.head: Deep Learning · 3 steps · 39 min
secs.body: 1. Deep Learning Basics — Neurons, loss and cost, and the common activation functions, explained from first principles. (beginner · 30 min) 2. Sequence Models — How models handle ordered data like text, from RNNs and LSTMs to transformers and LLMs. (intermediate · 6 min) 3. Encoder-Decoder for Machine Translation — The encoder-decoder idea behind neural machine translation, with a basic seq2seq model. (intermediate · 3 min)

secs.head: Systems and HPC · 3 steps · 28 min
secs.body: 1. Four Ways to Ask Slurm for Mixed GPUs — Typed GRES, constraint operators, heterogeneous jobs and heterogeneous steps - what each one actually allocates, and the one-character constraint that mixes GPU types by accident. (intermediate · 9 min) 2. Why Mixed-GPU Training Disappoints — Why 8 H100s plus 8 A100s train like 16 A100s, which H100 features the A100s switch off, and what co-scheduling a heterogeneous job costs you in the queue. (intermediate · 9 min) 3. Where Heterogeneous Jobs Shine — The workloads where mixing GPU types in one Slurm job is exactly right, how admins should label and guard a multi-generation cluster, a decision table, and the interview answer. (intermediate · 10 min)

secs.head: Systems and HPC · 6 steps · 64 min
secs.body: 1. How GPU Memory Fails, and Why You Can See It Coming — How ECC, row remapping and error containment work on NVIDIA GPUs, why memory errors repeat and cluster, and the error ladder that makes failure predictable. (intermediate · 11 min) 2. Reading the GPU's Vital Signs — The telemetry concepts behind GPU failure prediction - counters, gauges and events, volatile versus persistent, in-band versus out-of-band - and the ways each one misleads. (intermediate · 9 min) 3. From Signals to Decisions — How to design GPU failure rules - state, event and trend rules, personal baselines, persistence, noise floors and action tiers - and the traps that make rules silently fail. (advanced · 10 min) 4. Acting Without Making It Worse — The principles of safe automated response to GPU failure predictions - reversibility, drain semantics, blast radius, drain budgets, staged rollout and rollback. (advanced · 9 min) 5. Is the Prediction Any Good? — How to judge GPU failure predictions - base rates, precision, recall, lead time, horizons, label quality, leakage and drift - and when a learned model is worth it. (advanced · 10 min) 6. Runbook: Deploying GPU Failure Prediction End to End — The hands-on companion to the series - counters file, node checks, tested Prometheus rules, Alertmanager routing, a guarded Slurm drain hook and a backtest, step by step. (advanced · 15 min)

secs.head: Systems and HPC · 6 steps · 58 min
secs.body: 1. How Linux Reclaims Memory: Cache, Swap and the Two Kinds of Stall — Why free memory near zero is normal, which pages the kernel can drop for free and which need swap, how kswapd and direct reclaim differ, and why the second one is where programs stall. (intermediate · 9 min) 2. Pressure Stall Information: Measuring Time Lost, Not Bytes Left — How to read /proc/pressure/memory, why the share of time tasks spend stalled is a better alarm than free bytes, and how to get woken by the kernel the moment a threshold is crossed. (intermediate · 8 min) 3. The OOM Killer: Who Gets Thrown Overboard, and Why So Late — How the kernel decides when it is out of memory and whom to kill, how oom score adj shields or sacrifices a process, and why userspace killers like systemd-oomd act earlier than the kernel. (intermediate · 9 min) 4. cgroup v2 Memory Control: The Levers Between Doing Nothing and Killing — The memory files of a cgroup v2 group, from protection (min, low) to throttling (high) to the hard cap (max), plus the active levers: reclaim, freeze and kill, and why they need privilege. (intermediate · 12 min) 5. Memory Locking: Keeping a Rescuer in RAM with mlockall — Why a program that rescues a machine under memory pressure must pin its own pages in RAM, what mlockall does, why the 8 MiB limit exists, and why root gets the real lock - explained with a tow truck. (intermediate · 12 min) 6. Making a Rescuer Survive: CPU, Protection and a Checklist — Beyond memory locking, what keeps an emergency program running under load - real-time priority, an OOM shield, restart and watchdog - and one checklist that ties all six pages together. (intermediate · 8 min)

secs.head: Image Processing · 9 steps · 66 min
secs.body: 1. Images Are Just Matrices — A pixel is a number in a grid - sampling, quantization, bit depth, coordinates and neighbours, and why 200 + 100 can equal 44. (beginner · 7 min) 2. Geometric Transforms and Interpolation — Moving the whole map - affine transforms in homogeneous coordinates, why you must map backwards, and nearest, bilinear and bicubic interpolation with a bilinear example worked by hand. (intermediate · 7 min) 3. Intensity Transforms and Histograms — Rescue a dark image with one formula - negatives, log, gamma and histogram equalization, with the CDF worked out by hand on a tiny image. (beginner · 7 min) 4. Spatial Filtering — Kernels, correlation versus convolution, padding and separability - blurring explained as a neighbourhood vote, with the mean and median compared on one noisy pixel. (beginner · 7 min) 5. Edges and Sharpening — Derivatives as differences between neighbours - gradient, Sobel, Laplacian and unsharp masking, plus a one-line example that shows exactly where sharpening halos come from. (beginner · 7 min) 6. The Fourier Transform for Images — What the 2D DFT really says - an image as a sum of waves, magnitude versus phase, a 4-point DFT done by hand, and the convolution theorem that turns sliding windows into multiplication. (intermediate · 8 min) 7. Frequency Filtering and Aliasing — Low-pass, high-pass and notch filters as masks on the spectrum, why the ideal filter rings, and how sampling too coarsely creates moire - with the Nyquist rule worked on one number. (intermediate · 7 min) 8. Noise and Restoration — The degradation model g = h f + n, common noise types, why inverse filtering explodes, and how the Wiener filter gives up gracefully - with PSNR to score the result. (intermediate · 7 min) 9. Wavelets and Multiresolution Processing — Seeing an image at several scales at once - pyramids, a Haar wavelet transform by hand, the four 2D subbands, and why mostly-zero detail makes denoising and compression work. (intermediate · 9 min)

secs.head: Systems and HPC · 3 steps · 21 min
secs.body: 1. Keep the Job on One Switch: Topology-Aware Placement in Slurm — How Slurm places multi-node jobs with and without a topology plugin - topology/tree, --switches, topology/block that refuses to straddle, the 25.05 topology.yaml, and a fatal block config. (intermediate · 7 min) 2. Launching Distributed Training on Slurm: srun, torchrun, and the Rank Contract — Why a 2-node training job can run on one node, the environment PyTorch needs from Slurm, launching with srun or torchrun, and the double-launch trap - tested with PyTorch 2.15 on Slurm 23.11. (intermediate · 6 min) 3. Containers on Slurm with Pyxis and Enroot — Running Slurm job steps in containers with Pyxis and Enroot - the node that silently ran outside the container, read-only images, mounts, node-local paths, named containers, and the PyTorch env hook. (intermediate · 8 min)

secs.head: Systems and HPC · 8 steps · 60 min
secs.body: 1. Not Twins, Not Even Cousins: OpenMP, MPI and Open MPI — OpenMP and Open MPI differ by one space and share almost nothing. Three names, three jobs - an API for threads, a standard for messages, and one program that implements the second. (beginner · 6 min) 2. Two Tribes, One Problem: Where OpenMP and MPI Came From — The 1990s story - shared-memory vendors each had their own directives, distributed-memory users each had their own message libraries, and two committees fixed it from opposite sides. (beginner · 6 min) 3. Cooks and Kitchens: Threads, Ranks and the One Mental Model — Run one tiny program of each kind and watch the difference - OpenMP threads sharing one memory (and a data race), MPI ranks with separate memory (and a reduction) - on a real 4-core machine. (beginner · 7 min) 4. Know It on Sight: Reading OpenMP and MPI Code, Builds and Job Scripts — A field guide to recognizing OpenMP, MPI or both in 30 seconds - the include lines, the pragmas, the function prefixes, the compile commands, the launch lines and the environment variables. (beginner · 7 min) 5. Kitchens With Cooks: Hybrid MPI+OpenMP and the Binding Trap — Why big jobs use MPI across nodes and OpenMP inside them, and the default - Open MPI pinning each rank to one core - that makes your threads queue on a single CPU. Tested, with the fix. (intermediate · 7 min) 6. Two Tickets About the Future: OpenMP 6, MPI 5 and What Never Expires — OpenMP 6.0 and MPI 5.0 are out. Do you have to rewrite everything? Two Monday tickets, the new GPU annex and the standard delivery box, and the ideas that will outlive every version number. (beginner · 9 min) 7. Who Starts the Ranks? OpenMP and MPI Under Slurm — How Slurm launches MPI ranks and OpenMP threads - srun direct launch, mpirun inside an allocation, PMIx as the address book, and how ntasks and cpus-per-task decide the binding trap from part 5. (intermediate · 9 min) 8. No Login Node, No Hostfile: OpenMP and MPI on Kubernetes — How an MPIJob turns pods into an MPI cluster - launcher, workers, headless Service, SSH keys, hostfile - and which three numbers keep the binding trap away. (intermediate · 9 min)

secs.head: Systems and HPC · 2 steps · 17 min
secs.body: 1. Parallel Filesystems: Why 10,000 GPUs Can Starve on a Full Disk — How Lustre-style parallel filesystems split metadata from data, why millions of small files starve GPUs, how striping works, and why checkpoints - not datasets - set your storage peak. (intermediate · 9 min) 2. RDMA, InfiniBand and GPUDirect: Taking the CPU Out of the Way — Why AI clusters use RDMA fabrics (InfiniBand or RoCE), what kernel bypass and zero-copy mean, and how GPUDirect RDMA and GPUDirect Storage move data straight into GPU memory. (intermediate · 8 min)

secs.head: Deep Learning · 2 steps · 7 min
secs.body: 1. PyTorch 101 — Notes for starting with PyTorch: where to learn, data type precision, GPU properties, the training loop, making predictions, and saving and loading models. (6 min) 2. PyTorch DDP — A short pointer page on PyTorch Distributed Data Parallel: a recommended distributed training tutorial and a related read on the Python GIL. (1 min)

secs.head: Systems and HPC · 5 steps · 40 min
secs.body: 1. Reading the Reason Column: Why Is My Slurm Job Pending? — What Slurm's common pending reasons mean, which ones fix themselves and which never will, what users can fix without an admin, and a small triage script tested against each reason. (beginner · 7 min) 2. Slurm Multi-Tenancy: Who Stores the Rules, Who Enforces Them — How slurmctld, slurmd, slurmdbd and sacctmgr split the work of multi-tenant accounting, why limits you set can silently do nothing, and how associations, TRES limits, QOS and fairshare fit together. (intermediate · 9 min) 3. The Guest List: Setting Up QOS Preemption Without Starting a War — A step-by-step setup of QOS-based requeue preemption (slurm.conf, sacctmgr, who may use what), a drill that proves it works, and the quiet ways it goes wrong. (intermediate · 9 min) 4. Who Goes First: Slurm's Priority Number, Taken Apart — How Slurm's multifactor priority is computed from age, fairshare and QOS weights, why every weight defaults to zero, how Fair Tree turns usage into a rank, and reading sprio and sshare. (intermediate · 8 min) 5. Limits That Wait Forever: QOS and Account Limits in Practice — How Slurm QOS and account GPU limits behave on a real queue - the job that never runs, the second QOS that slips past a cap, partition QOS, DenyOnLimit, and live usage via assoc mgr. (intermediate · 7 min)

secs.head: Systems and HPC · 2 steps · 21 min
secs.body: 1. Schedulers: The Traffic Controller Nobody Thanks Until It Breaks — What a cluster scheduler does, how it differs from the OS scheduler, the scheduler landscape, the concepts they share, and the Slurm architecture at a glance. (beginner · 10 min) 2. The Tale of a Slurm Job Script: Submission Is a Commitment, Not a Promise — Why editing a script after sbatch changes nothing, where Slurm keeps the frozen copy, what stays live, how to read the script back, and how to keep runs traceable. (intermediate · 11 min)

secs.head: Statistics · 15 steps · 153 min
secs.body: 1. Stir the Pot First: Population, Sample, and Why We Guess — Why a sip judges a pot of tea only if you stir it: population versus sample, four ways to draw a sample, the poll that asked 2.4 million and still erred. (beginner · 11 min) 2. Mira's Notebook: What Kind of Data Is This, and How Do You Count It? — Why you cannot average a blend name: the four kinds of data, and how to turn raw numbers into honest category, ungrouped and grouped frequency tables. (beginner · 13 min) 3. Draw It Before You Describe It: Three Pictures of the Same Fifty Days — Why a table of counts glazes eyes and a picture does not: the histogram, frequency polygon and ogive built from one table, and the mistakes that make them lie. (beginner · 11 min) 4. The Number on the Tin: Mean, Median and Mode — Why a perfectly computed average can describe nobody: "typical" is ambiguous, and mean, median and mode are three honest answers to three different questions. Look at the picture first. (beginner · 12 min) 5. How Far From the Middle? One Question Behind Every Summary Number — Mean, median and mode are one question asked with three rulers: how much should a long walk hurt? Spread is what is left over. Variance, SD, IQR and the n-1 mystery fall out of that. (beginner · 11 min) 6. Where Do You Stand? Percentiles, Z-Scores and the Box Plot — A score means nothing without its crowd. Two rulers give it a position: rank (percentile) and distance in spreads (z-score). The box plot is just the ogive read at four landmarks. (beginner · 10 min) 7. Counting the Ways: Probability as a Share of the List — Probability is the share of the equally likely ways. So "or" adds, "and" multiplies, and "at least one" is 1 minus none, because of what each does to the list of ways. (beginner · 9 min) 8. The Test That Was 99% Accurate: Conditional Probability and Bayes' Rule — Conditional probability is "shrink the crowd to those who match, then count again". Bayes' rule is that count read the other way; a tree of whole tins shows why a 99% test is often wrong. (beginner · 9 min) 9. What to Expect: Random Variables and Expected Value — A random variable is a number attached to each way things could turn out. Expected value and variance are the mean and the leftover walk of earlier parts, weighted by probability instead of frequency. (beginner · 9 min) 10. Coins and Calls: Binomial and Poisson as Recipes — A named distribution is a recipe for who gets how much probability. Binomial fits "how many yeses in n tries", Poisson fits "how many events in a window". Know the question and the assumptions. (intermediate · 9 min) 11. The Bell Curve: Probability as Area, and One Ruler for Every Bell — Many small nudges add up to a bell. For continuous data probability is area, and the z-score makes every bell the same bell, so one table serves all of them, until the data are not a bell. (intermediate · 9 min) 12. Why Averages Behave: The Sip You Could Take a Thousand Times — An average is itself random: every sample gives a different one. Their spread shrinks as sigma over root n, and whatever the crowd looks like, sample averages pile into a bell. Bias is not cured. (intermediate · 10 min) 13. How Sure Are You? Confidence Intervals — A confidence interval is an honest "about this, give or take": the estimate plus or minus a margin built from the standard error. The 95% describes the method, not one interval. (intermediate · 9 min) 14. The Courtroom for Numbers: Could Plain Luck Do This? — A hypothesis test asks one question: could plain luck have produced a difference this big? Shuffle the labels and count. What the p-value is, what it is not, and how testing twenty things fools you. (intermediate · 10 min) 15. Two Things Moving Together: Correlation and the Line — Correlation is the average product of paired z-scores, a number about straight-line togetherness only. The regression line is least squared walking applied to a line. Graph first, always. (intermediate · 11 min)

secs.head: Systems and HPC · 6 steps · 49 min
secs.body: 1. The Cluster That Worked Perfectly and Remembered Nothing: a Two-Minute Slurm Smoke Test — A six-check, two-minute Slurm smoke test (MUNGE, controller, nodes, srun, sbatch, sacct) as one script with three outcomes, tested against four injected failures and a busy cluster. (beginner · 9 min) 2. Measure Twice, Reconfigure Once: Smoke-Testing a slurm.conf Change — What a bad slurm.conf does (typo, partition naming a missing node) and the dry runs that catch it first: a snapshot diff, sbatch --test-only and a canary partition. (intermediate · 8 min) 3. The Morning After the Upgrade: Smoke Tests for the Change You Cannot Undo — What to check around a Slurm upgrade: a backup proven by restoring it, versions on every node, a before/after snapshot, the control-plane smoke test, and why downgrading is not supported. (intermediate · 8 min) 4. Does the Rulebook Still Work? Smoke-Testing QOS, Submit Rules and Preemption — A two-stage smoke test for QOS, submit rules and preemption: routing and refusals with no resources, then a real eviction and requeue, with a full script and its output. (intermediate · 7 min) 5. Back From the Repair Shop: Is This Node Fit to Return to Service? — Why idle does not mean a node is healthy, what Slurm does when hardware and slurm.conf disagree (and how config overrides hides it), and a reservation fence for a probe job. (intermediate · 8 min) 6. When Smoke Becomes a Fire Drill: SchedMD's Test Suite, ReFrame and the Baseline Rule — What SchedMD's test suite and ReFrame do, how both were run against a live test cluster, and why results only mean something against a baseline taken before the change. (advanced · 9 min)

secs.head: Devops · 6 steps · 53 min
secs.body: 1. The Laptop That Ran Ansible 2.16: An Install You Can Trust — A pinned Ansible install per project, which Python the control machine and the nodes need, ansible.cfg, SSH host keys, and the errors you hit on the first runs. (beginner · 10 min) 2. Four Nodes Said "Too Many Open Files": Inventories and Ad-Hoc Commands — Inventory groups and ranges, group vars with overrides, targeting patterns, ad-hoc commands across the cluster, the node that was down, and checking a change in a fresh login. secs.head: aCupOfTea Repository Specification
secs.body: Status: Active Scope: Repository organization and information architecture Content modification: Out of scope unless explicitly requested Related infra: Docsify site deployed from main via .github/workflows/deploy-docs.yml — see §13, §16, §26, §27

secs.head: 1. Purpose
secs.body: aCupOfTea is a personal knowledge repository covering AI, machine learning, software engineering, programming, business context, and applied projects. It is intended to function as a long-term, searchable knowledge system — increasingly served as a browsable Docsify site , not just a folder tree read on GitHub. Two goals guide every structural decision: 1. Share knowledge. Pages are written from real experience and read like a short blog: a reader (first of all the author, coming back to recall something) should find a page, finish it in a coffee break, and find the next related page. The rendered site, including on a phone, is the primary reading surface. 2. Make adding knowledge easy. A new page should take one command or one markdown file, with navigation, indexes and search updating without hand-editing (§27). When a proposal does not serve one of these goals, prefer not doing it (§25). This spec defines how information is organized . It does not define the technical correctness of any individual document's content.

secs.head: 2. Design Principles
secs.body: The repository MUST prioritize, in no particular order: clear information architecture, discoverability, consistent naming, low directory complexity, separation of concerns, a single source of truth per artifact, project isolation, long-term scalability, Git-friendly changes, human-and-AI maintainability, and a coherent Docsify navigation experience.

secs.head: 3. Primary Content Types
secs.body: Type Purpose --- --- Concept Explains an idea, theory, principle, or technique Technology Describes a tool, framework, library, or platform Engineering Software/system engineering practice Problem A reusable problem formulation Project A concrete implementation addressing a defined problem Experiment Exploratory or temporary investigation Business Business-domain or product knowledge Reference Lookup-oriented material Decision A recorded decision and its rationale Every substantive artifact SHOULD have exactly one canonical location, classified by its primary purpose .

secs.head: 4. Conceptual Repository Model
secs.body: This is the target conceptual architecture, not a mandate to migrate everything immediately. Migration is incremental and evidence-based (§19). Current top-level layout (the implementation today): Folder Holds Target equivalent --- --- --- fields/ subject knowledge, plus some technology notes ( libraries-frameworks-containers/ ) and infra topics ( benchmarks/ , schedulers/ , system-administration/ ) knowledge/ , technologies/ programming/ programming and software-engineering practice engineering/ problems/ reusable problem formulations and interview problems problems/ projects/ projects (mostly git submodules) projects/ experiments/ exploratory notebooks/codebases experiments/ business/ business-domain knowledge business/ tips/ quick tips and lookups references/ journal/ dated notes —

secs.head: 5–13 Content Type Rules
secs.body: Knowledge — organized by subject, not by the project it was originally learned from. Engineering — reusable practices; don't bury generally-useful engineering knowledge inside one project. Technologies — organized around a specific tool/library. NOT a dumping ground for every file that happens to import it; primary subject still determines placement. Problems — reusable problem formulations independent of any single implementation. Projects — first-class artifacts with their own objective, implementation, dependencies, results, and docs. Never relocated into a technology folder just because it uses that technology. Experiments — lightweight, exploratory; promotable to projects/ once they mature. Business — business models, KPIs, stakeholders, AI opportunities, domain constraints — separated from implementation detail. References — cheat sheets, terminology, external links; never a substitute for organizing real knowledge. Decisions — durable architecture/methodology calls: context, decision, reason, alternatives considered, consequences.

secs.head: 13. Repository Root & Docsify Infrastructure
secs.body: The root SHOULD contain only genuinely repository-wide files: .nojekyll is not committed: the deploy workflow creates it in the published copy. Do not treat the Docsify infra files as clutter to be moved — they are load-bearing for the hosted site. Do not place temporary notes, experiments, or project-specific docs at the root.

secs.head: 14. Naming Convention
secs.body: New directories and .md pages SHOULD use lowercase-kebab-case ( deep-learning , used-car-price-estimation ). Code, notebook, and data files keep their own conventions (Python modules can't be kebab-case; scripts and notebooks reference data by filename), and README.md keeps its name. Avoid camelCase , PascalCase , mixed naming, misspellings, unexplained abbreviations. Existing names are only renamed when the benefit clearly outweighs migration cost and link breakage.

secs.head: 15. Directory Depth
secs.body: Hierarchy MUST communicate meaningful distinctions. Avoid nesting like knowledge/machine-learning/algorithms/supervised/classification/concepts/... when each level holds almost nothing. Prefer a shallow structure plus a README.md index once a folder needs one — the generated sidebar picks it up automatically (§16).

secs.head: 16. Index Files & Docsify Navigation
secs.body: Two navigation layers exist and both must stay accurate: 1. README.md indexes inside a folder — description, subcategories, links, related projects/technologies. Should not duplicate large amounts of underlying content. 2. .docs/ sidebar.md — the navigation tree for the rendered Docsify site. It is generated from the file tree by .docs/gen sidebar.sh , and CI regenerates it on every push to main . It MUST NOT be hand-edited; regenerate and commit it in the same change as any move/rename/new section so the repo matches what's published. - Inside a folder the README comes first, then pages with an order (front matter, §26) by that number, then the rest alphabetically; Previous/Next follow the sidebar. - A page's label is the text after the last hyphen of its H1 (the whole H1 if it has none). A sidebar label in front matter overrides it without editing the heading. - A folder's group name is the text before the last hyphen of its README.md H1, and the group heading links to that README (the README is not repeated as a child entry; the chevron folds the group). A sidebar group in that README overrides it; use it when sibling folders would share a name. - An additive Explore section (Start here, Domains, Tags) comes from the metadata layer (§26); the folder tree below it is untouched. Folder README.md indexes SHOULD list their pages in a File Description table under Contents , the format new page.py updates automatically (§27). Converging the remaining list-style indexes is tracked in issue 77. Search ( .docs/search.js ) indexes the pages listed in the generated sidebar, so any page reachable from the sidebar is searchable with no extra step. On the deployed site the text comes from one prebuilt file, .docs/search-index.json , which stage site.py writes into the published copy (never committed); a local preview has no such file, so the search reads every page instead and gives the same results. The sidebar governs what's reachable on the site; the folder README.md governs what's understandable when browsing the raw repo. Keep README indexes in sync with the folder contents. Link style: internal links MUST be root-absolute ( /fields/benchmarks/hpl.md ), which resolve on both GitHub and Docsify ( relativePath: false ). Relative ./ / ../ links break on the site.

secs.head: 17. Canonical Location & Duplicate Prevention
secs.body: Every substantive artifact has one canonical location. If it's relevant from multiple angles, prefer canonical document + cross-reference over copies. Never duplicate knowledge into multiple categories just to make it independently discoverable — link to it from the relevant README indexes.

secs.head: 18. Projects vs. Knowledge
secs.body: Answers --- --- Knowledge "What is this?" Problem "What are we solving?" Technology "What tool implements it?" Project "What did we build?" Experiment "What did we investigate?" Decision "Why this approach?" This distinction MUST guide all future placement decisions.

secs.head: 19. Migration Rules
secs.body: Structural migrations MUST: preserve file content · prefer git mv · preserve project boundaries · update internal references (including absolute self-repo GitHub URLs) AND regenerate the sidebar/navbar · check for broken links · avoid unnecessary renames · avoid deleting substantive material · stay reviewable · be incremental rather than one giant restructure. Changes flow feature branch → dev → main : each feature is developed on its own branch cut from dev and merged into dev by PR. main MUST only be updated by a dev → main PR, because every push to main redeploys the published site.

secs.head: 20. Ambiguous Content
secs.body: If classification is unclear: do not silently guess. Record the ambiguity, list the plausible classifications, and let a human decide.

secs.head: 21. Content Preservation
secs.body: During organization-only work: content = immutable, structure = mutable. Agents may reorganize; agents must not rewrite substantive content unless explicitly instructed.

secs.head: 22. Validation Requirements
secs.body: Before considering a structural change complete, verify:

secs.head: 23. Scalability Rule
secs.body: The taxonomy MUST remain usable if the repository grows by an order of magnitude. Don't create categories solely for today's contents; prefer stable conceptual categories over highly specific one-off folders.

secs.head: 24. Source of Truth
secs.body: When architectural ambiguity exists, priority is: SPEC.md defines the intended architecture. CLAUDE.md defines operational behavior for AI agents. The repository (including its Docsify navigation) is the implementation of both.

secs.head: 25. Change Philosophy
secs.body: The goal is not a "perfect" directory tree — it's a structure that is understandable, predictable, searchable, maintainable, scalable, and renders correctly as a Docsify site. Structural simplicity beats theoretical purity.

secs.head: 26. Metadata Layer
secs.body: Content type, location and navigation are unchanged; metadata is an overlay that lets one page be discovered under several domains/tags and linked to related pages. Markdown + YAML front matter is the only source of truth; there is no database or service. - Optional: pages without front matter remain valid and keep working; coverage grows incrementally (§19, §23). - Identity: a page that participates in relations needs an explicit, repo-unique, kebab-case id . Ids are independent of the path, so moving a file does not break relations. The path-derived fallback id is read-only and is never a relation target. Any id collision (explicit vs explicit, or explicit vs fallback) is an error. - Reader aids: optional summary (one line, max 200 chars) and level (beginner, intermediate, advanced) are authored; reading time is computed. They drive the Explore lists and a generated Start here page (learning paths from prerequisite chains, quick reads, beginner picks). Prerequisites must be acyclic. - Vocabulary: type (one value, or a list of at most two with the main one first) ∈ the kinds defined in taxonomy.yaml (concept, guide, reference, note, problem, project, experiment to start with; a new kind is added there with a one-line definition); status ∈ draft, stable, deprecated; relation types are exactly related and prerequisites ; domains and tags are defined in .docs/metadata/taxonomy.yaml . A tag needs 2+ pages or must name a concrete technology, and a page carries at most 5 tags. Domain overlap rules (deep-learning vs machine-learning, generative-ai with natural-language-processing) are in CLAUDE.md §21. - Location: schema, taxonomy, tools and generated data live under .docs/ (served by GitHub Pages), so the root allowlist (§13) is unchanged. - Generated, deterministic: .docs/generated/ holds objects.json , domains.json , tags.json , relationships.json (with reverse links), related.json and the Explore pages. The sidebar gains an additive Explore section (Start here, Domains, Tags); the folder tree is untouched. - Submodules are never written into and are skipped by the tools; relations may not target their content. - Link previews: the staged copy also holds a share page per content page at its folder address (title and summary as Open Graph tags, then a redirect to the / page), so a shared link previews that page; summary in front matter feeds the description, else the first paragraph is used. - Deployment: the published site is a staging copy with front matter stripped and a "Read first / See also / Read next" strip under the title; repository sources are never rewritten. - Reading order: optional order (whole number from 1 up, unique within a folder) is a page's position in its folder: it drives the generated sidebar, the Previous/Next buttons, the "Read next" strip and Start here paths. A prerequisite in the same folder should have a smaller number. - Partial front matter, sidebar label and sidebar group : every field is optional (defaults: title = first H1, type = note, status = stable); id only for pages in relations. sidebar label overrides a page's sidebar label without editing its heading; sidebar group (folder README.md only) overrides the folder's group name. Labels must be unique within a folder and groups among sibling folders. A page with only these fields is not indexed and gets no domain. See CLAUDE.md §21 for the contributor how-to.

secs.head: 27. Adding New Knowledge
secs.body: Finishing any change: python3 .docs/tools/check all.py --fix runs the validation suite (front matter, links, tests) and regenerates the indexes, sidebar and navbar; CI runs the same script without --fix on every PR to dev / main and push to dev , so a stale generated file or a broken rule blocks the merge. Adding a page MUST stay a small, repeatable step for a solo author or an outside contributor: - Entry point: cupctl <verb <action ( .docs/tools/cupctl.py , run cupctl alone to list the commands) wraps every script below; it adds no rules of its own. - Preferred: python3 .docs/tools/new page.py ( cupctl page new ). It asks for a title, optional summary, folder, type, domains (suggested from the folder), tags, level, prerequisites and related pages, then creates the kebab-case file with front matter and a short outline, adds the page to the folder's README.md table, and regenerates the sidebar and navbar. It suggests the closest existing folders, warns about similar existing pages (§17), never overwrites a file, and never creates a folder without confirmation (§15). New tags are added to taxonomy.yaml only after confirmation (§26). Reading time is never entered: the site computes it from the text, and new page.py --check PAGE shows it together with what is still missing. - In the browser: new page.py --gui serves the same questions, the hand-written-page flow and the page doctor.py list (similar problems grouped under one heading) as a form on 127.0.0.1 only ( page gui.py , page gui.html ); it runs new page.py with options, so the rules are the same. - Changing metadata later: new page.py --update PAGE changes the summary, kind, subjects, tags, level or relations of a page that has front matter, keeping every other field and the page text. - A page written by hand: python3 .docs/tools/new page.py --adopt PAGE adds the front matter and index link to an existing page without changing its text, and, for a page with partial front matter, keeps it and adds only the missing fields. - Without the script: create a kebab-case .md file with one H1 , add it to the folder's README.md index, and regenerate the sidebar. Front matter stays optional. - Code files and notebooks ( .py , .ipynb , ...) linked from a page open as readable pages on the site: stage site.py writes name.py.md / name.ipynb.md in the published copy ( code pages.py ), so link them root-absolute like pages and nothing else is needed. - Images for new pages SHOULD be committed next to the page (for example images/ in the same folder) rather than linked from other sites, which can disappear. Moving existing linked images into the repo is tracked in issue 82. - Contributor steps live in .github/CONTRIBUTING.md ; changes go through a feature branch and a PR into dev (CLAUDE.md §11).

label: The HPC Benchmarking Landscape: A Field Guide
title: The HPC Benchmarking Landscape: A Field Guide
desc: One node. Five different questions. Five different tools. This is the map that ties OSU , STREAM/BabelStream , HPL , NCC

secs.head: The HPC Benchmarking Landscape: A Field Guide
secs.body: One node. Five different questions. Five different tools. This is the map that ties OSU , STREAM/BabelStream , HPL , NCCL , and the execution/affinity layer together — plus the benchmarks that haven't come up yet but will, the moment you validate your next node.

secs.head: Why one benchmark is never enough
secs.body: Every HPC node is really four separate subsystems wearing a single hostname: A single "the node feels slow" complaint could be caused by any one of these — or, more often, by a misconfiguration between two of them (wrong rank placement, wrong NUMA binding, wrong buffer type). Running one benchmark and declaring victory is how regressions slip through acceptance testing. Running the right sequence of benchmarks is how you actually localize the fault before you touch a support ticket. ---

secs.head: The mental map
secs.body: The single most important idea in this whole map: compute, memory, and communication are orthogonal. A win in one tells you nothing about the others. A GPU that aces BabelStream can still fail NCCL. A node that aces OSU over CPU buffers can still choke the moment you switch to GPU-aware MPI. Test them separately, on purpose. ---

secs.head: The core five — quick index
secs.body: Benchmark One-line job Full write-up --- --- --- --- 1 OSU Micro-Benchmarks MPI point-to-point & collective latency/bandwidth over the network (see OSU deep-dive) 2 STREAM / BabelStream / stream-gpu-test Raw memory bandwidth — CPU RAM or GPU HBM, before any real compute happens stream-benchmarks-blog.md 3 HPL / HPL-GPU Dense linear algebra compute throughput — the TOP500 number hpl-benchmarks-blog.md 4 NCCL / nccl-tests GPU-native collective communication — NVLink, NVSwitch, GPUDirect RDMA nccl-benchmarks-blog.md 5 Parallel Execution & Affinity Not a benchmark itself — the placement/binding discipline that makes the other four trustworthy parallel-execution-affinity-blog.md Plus the standalone Intel vs. Netlib HPL comparison — a worked example of why "same binary category, different vendor build" numbers aren't directly comparable without controlling for problem size. ( hpl-cpu-comparison-blog.md ) ---

secs.head: The benchmarks we haven't covered yet
secs.body: The five above get you most of the way through H200-class node validation — but the broader HPC benchmarking world is bigger. Here's what else exists, organized by the same compute/memory/communication/storage split, so you know what to reach for when OSU, HPL, STREAM, and NCCL don't answer the question in front of you.

secs.head: Compute-adjacent
secs.body: Benchmark What it tests When you'd reach for it --- --- --- HPCG (High Performance Conjugate Gradient) Sparse linear algebra — deliberately memory-bandwidth-bound , unlike HPL's compute-bound dense math TOP500's companion list; a much more "realistic application" proxy than HPL MLPerf (Training / Inference / HPC) End-to-end ML workload throughput on real model architectures (BERT, ResNet, GPT-style) Validating a GPU cluster's actual deep-learning throughput, not just raw FLOPS SPEC CPU / SPEC HPC General-purpose CPU throughput across a broad workload suite Comparing CPU generations/vendors outside of pure linear algebra Graph500 Breadth-first search / graph traversal performance Irregular-memory-access workloads — very different stress profile than dense HPL

secs.head: Memory & storage adjacent
secs.body: Benchmark What it tests When you'd reach for it --- --- --- Intel MLC (Memory Latency Checker) Fine-grained memory latency and bandwidth, per NUMA domain, per access pattern Diagnosing exactly where in the NUMA topology a memory bottleneck lives — more granular than STREAM IOR / IOzone / mdtest Parallel filesystem I/O throughput and metadata performance Validating Lustre/Weka/GPFS storage — the layer STREAM and OSU don't touch at all fio Block-device-level I/O benchmarking Isolating storage hardware from the parallel filesystem layer above it

secs.head: Communication-adjacent
secs.body: Benchmark What it tests When you'd reach for it --- --- --- GPCNeT (Global Performance and Congestion Network Test) Network congestion and "noisy neighbor" interference under concurrent load Multi-tenant cluster fabrics — does one job's traffic pattern degrade another job's? iperf3 / netperf Raw TCP/UDP throughput, no MPI or RDMA involved Baseline Ethernet sanity check before layering RoCE/MPI complexity on top ib send bw / ib read bw / perftest suite Raw InfiniBand verbs-level bandwidth and latency — below MPI entirely Isolating "is the fabric itself fine" from "is my MPI stack configured correctly" — the layer underneath OSU [!TIP] When OSU gives you a bad number, perftest (ib send bw etc.) is often your next move — it strips MPI out of the equation entirely and talks to the verbs layer directly. If perftest looks great but OSU looks bad, the problem is definitely in your MPI stack, not the fabric. ---

secs.body: Putting the whole map into a single run order — this is roughly the sequence I'd actually execute on a fresh H200 node before signing off on it: Steps 1–6 are diagnostic. Step 8 is the number that actually matters to your users — but it's meaningless to debug directly if you skipped 1–6, because a slow training run could be caused by any of the five layers above it, and step 8 alone won't tell you which one. ---
