It then prints the username and text of each tweet. 3- Data extraction from a public dataset using Pandas: This script uses Pandas to read a public CSV dataset and prints the first few rows of the data. Please note that these are just basic examples, and there are many more advanced techniques and tools available for ODI and OSINT. Additionally, it's important to ensure that any data collection and analysis activities comply with relevant laws and regulations, such as GDPR and CCPA.

secs.head: Advanced Techniques
secs.body: There are numerous advanced techniques and tools available for ODI and OSINT, constantly evolving to adapt to new challenges and opportunities. Here are some examples: ODI (Organizational Data Intelligence): Example Details -- -- Predictive Analytics Uses statistical models, machine learning algorithms, and data mining techniques to forecast future trends, behaviors, and outcomes. This enables organizations to proactively address potential issues, optimize processes, and identify new business opportunities. Prescriptive Analytics Goes beyond predictive analytics by suggesting specific actions based on the predicted outcomes. It uses advanced algorithms, such as optimization and simulation modeling, to recommend the best possible solutions to complex problems. Real-Time Analytics Enables organizations to analyze and act upon data as it is generated, allowing for instant responses to changing conditions. Use cases include fraud detection, recommendation engines, and real-time personalization. Text Analytics Also known as natural language processing (NLP), this technique allows for the analysis of unstructured data found in texts, emails, social media posts, and other forms of human communication. It helps organizations extract insights, sentiment, and entities from vast amounts of textual data. Graph Analytics Used to analyze relationships between data entities, graph analytics is particularly useful for detecting patterns, networks, and anomalies in large datasets. Common use cases include fraud detection, recommendation systems, and cybersecurity threat detection. Machine Learning Automation Automates the machine learning process, allowing organizations to quickly deploy and manage models at scale. This enables data scientists to focus on higher-level tasks while automating repetitive tasks such as feature engineering and hyperparameter tuning. Cloud-Based Analytics Leverages cloud computing resources to store, process, and analyze massive datasets. Cloud-based analytics platforms offer scalability, flexibility, and cost savings compared to traditional on-premises solutions. Explainable AI (XAI) Focuses on making machine learning models transparent and interpretable. XAI techniques help organizations understand why a particular decision was made, which improves trust in AI systems and supports ethical considerations. IoT Analytics Deals with the analysis of data generated by Internet of Things (IoT) devices, such as sensors, cameras, and smart appliances. IoT analytics enables organizations to derive insights from sensor data, optimize operations, and improve product development. Edge Analytics Performs data processing and analysis closer to the source of the data, reducing latency and bandwidth requirements. Edge analytics is particularly useful for applications that require real-time processing, such as autonomous vehicles, drones, or smart cities. OSINT (Open-Source Intelligence): Example Details -- -- Social Media Monitoring Analyzes publicly available social media data to identify trends, sentiments, and key influencers. Organizations can use this information to assess brand reputation, track competitors, and identify emerging threats. Online News Monitoring Tracks online news articles, blogs, and forums to stay informed about recent developments, events, and opinions related to a specific topic or industry. Public Records Search Utilizes public records databases, such as property records, court filings, and criminal records, to gather information about individuals, companies, or assets. People Search Engines Finds and aggregates information about people from various online sources, including social media profiles, professional networking sites, and public records. Domain Name Analysis Analyzes domain name registration data, DNS records, and website content to identify ownership, hosting, and infrastructure information. This can help organizations investigate cyberthreats, monitor brand infringement, and perform due diligence checks. IP Address Geolocation Maps IP addresses to geographic locations, providing insight into the physical location of servers, routers, or other networked devices. This information can be useful for cybersecurity threat assessment, asset tracking, and supply chain risk management. Open-Source Intelligence Tools Utilizes software tools like Maltego, OSINT Framework, or Shodan to streamline and automate OSINT data collection and analysis. These tools provide features like data visualization, entity recognition, and link analysis. Dark Web Monitoring Explores dark web marketplaces, forums, and chat rooms to identify potential security threats, such as stolen data, malware, or illegal activities. Organizations can use this information to anticipate and mitigate risks.

secs.head: Data Privacy and protection
secs.body: There are several relevant laws and regulations related to data privacy and protection, some of which are mentioned below: Law & Regulation Details -- -- General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) The GDPR is a comprehensive data protection law in the European Union (EU) that went into effect on May 25, 2018. It sets forth strict rules for the collection, storage, use, and sharing of personal data of EU residents. Organizations that violate the GDPR can face hefty fines, up to €20 million or 4% of their global annual turnover, whichever is greater. California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) The CCPA is a data privacy law in the United States that went into effect on January 1, 2020. It grants California residents certain rights, such as the right to know what personal information is being collected, the right to access their personal information, and the right to request deletion of their personal information. Organizations that violate the CCPA can face fines up to $7,500 per intentional violation. Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) HIPAA is a federal law in the United States that sets national standards for protecting the privacy and security of individually identifiable health information. It applies to health plans, healthcare clearinghouses, and healthcare providers who transmit health information electronically. Violators of HIPAA can face civil penalties ranging from $100 to $50,000 per violation. Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) PCI DSS is a set of security standards designed to ensure that companies that handle credit card information maintain a secure environment. It applies to any organization that stores, processes, or transmits credit card data. Non-compliance with PCI DSS can result in fines, penalty fees, and even the revocation of the right to process credit card transactions. Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) SOX is a federal law in the United States that regulates the disclosure of financial information by publicly traded companies. It requires companies to establish and maintain internal controls over financial reporting, including the protection of sensitive financial data. Violations of SOX can result in criminal and civil penalties, including fines and imprisonment. Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLBA) GLBA is a federal law in the United States that sets privacy standards for financial institutions. It requires financial institutions to explain their information-sharing practices to their customers and to safeguard sensitive customer data. Violations of GLBA can result in civil penalties up to $100,000 per violation. Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) FERPA is a federal law in the United States that protects the privacy of student education records. It applies to educational agencies and institutions that receive funding from the Department of Education. Violations of FERPA can result in the loss of federal funding and legal action by affected students. Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) COPPA is a federal law in the United States that regulates the collection of personal information from children under the age of 13. It requires websites and online services directed to children to obtain parental consent before collecting, using, or disclosing personal information from children. Violations of COPPA can result in civil penalties up to $42,530 per violation. Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA) ECPA is a federal law in the United States that prohibits the interception or disclosure of electronic communications without the consent of the parties involved. It applies to email, instant messaging, and other forms of electronic communication. Violations of ECPA can result in criminal and civil penalties. Video Privacy Protection Act (VPPA) VPPA is a federal law in the United States that governs the handling of video tape rental and sale records. It requires video service providers to obtain consumer consent before disclosing personally identifiable information. Violations of VPPA can result in civil penalties up to $42,530 per violation. These are just a few examples of the many laws and regulations related to data privacy and protection. It's important for organizations to be aware of the laws that apply to them and to implement appropriate measures to comply with these regulations.

secs.head: Probability & Statistics, One Sip at a Time
secs.body: Most people do not struggle with statistics because the formulas are hard. They struggle because the ideas arrive before the reason for them. Why divide by n − 1 ? Why does a p-value not mean what it sounds like? Why is a 99% accurate test often wrong? This series goes the other way. Every page starts with something that goes wrong for a small, invented tea shop, and the idea shows up as the fix. The formulas come last, when you already know what they are for.

secs.head: Feeling lost? Start here
secs.body: If the series feels like too many numbers, too many graphs and too many steps, hold on to three ideas. Everything else is built from them. 1. A summary is a stand-in for a crowd. Mean, median and mode are not rival formulas. They are one question, how much should a long walk hurt? , asked three ways. Spread is how badly the stand-in still misses. (Part 5) 2. Graphs are one table seen three ways. The histogram shows how much lives where. The ogive shows how many are at or below. The box plot is the ogive keeping only its landmarks. Look first, with the histogram. (Part 6) 3. A value has no meaning without its crowd. Ask "better than what?", then place it with a rank (percentile) or a distance (z-score). Then keep The Map of Leaf & Kettle open as a reference. It lays every idea in the series out as rooms of one shop (nine downstairs, nine upstairs for chance), so you recall a room instead of a formula.

secs.head: How each page is built
secs.body: 1. A scene. Mira, who runs a tea shop called Leaf & Kettle, runs into a problem. 2. The wrong instinct. What most of us would do, and why it fails. 3. One mental model. The idea that repairs the story. 4. The mechanics. Definitions, formulas and worked tables, with numbers you can check by hand. 5. Check yourself. A few questions, with answers at the bottom. 6. Back to the story. The page returns to the opening scene and resolves it with what you have just learned, usually by handing the next question to the next page. 7. A cheat sheet you can read in thirty seconds before you need it.

secs.head: The pots on the shelf
secs.body: Page The question it answers Status --- --- --- --- 1 Stir the Pot First Why can a small, well-chosen sample beat a huge careless one? Written 2 Mira's Notebook What kind of data is this, and how do I count it honestly? Written 3 Draw It Before You Describe It Which picture answers which question: histogram, polygon or ogive? Written 4 The Number on the Tin What does "typical" mean: mean, median or mode? Written 5 How Far From the Middle? Why are there three middles and so many spreads? Variance, SD, IQR and the mystery of n − 1 Written 6 Where Do You Stand? How does one value find its place in a crowd? Percentiles, z-scores and the box plot Written 7 Counting the Ways What is a probability, and why do "or" and "and" add and multiply? Written 8 The Test That Was 99% Accurate Why is an accurate test so often wrong? Conditional probability and Bayes' rule Written 9 What to Expect What does "expected" mean? Random variables, expected value and variance Written 10 Coins and Calls Which recipe fits which question? The binomial and Poisson distributions Written 11 The Bell Curve Where does the bell come from, and what is probability as area? The normal distribution Written 12 Why Averages Behave Why does an average wobble less than a single value? Sampling distributions and the central limit theorem Written 13 How Sure Are You? How do you say "about this, give or take"? Confidence intervals and the bootstrap Written 14 The Courtroom for Numbers Could plain luck have done this? Hypothesis tests, p-values and how they get misused Written 15 Two Things Moving Together Do two columns rise and fall together, and what does that not prove? Correlation and regression Written Ref The Map of Leaf & Kettle Every idea so far as a memory palace, a decision chart and a definitions sheet Grows with the series The order is deliberate. Pages 1 to 6 are about describing what you have : where the data came from, what kind it is, what it looks like, where its middle is, how spread out it is, and where one value sits within it. Pages 7 to 11 build the language of chance : counting the ways, updating on evidence, what to expect, the common distributions and the bell curve. Pages 12 to 14 join the two: using a sample to make an honest statement about something you cannot fully see. Page 15 puts two columns side by side. Each chance page reuses an idea from the first half (the expected value is the mean again, the z-score finally meets the bell), so there is less new to memorize than the list suggests.

secs.head: Conventions
secs.body: - Characters are invented. The numbers in the stories are chosen so you can do the arithmetic yourself. - Where a story borrows a real event, the sources are listed at the bottom of that page. - x̄ is a sample mean, μ is a population mean, n is a sample size, N is a population size, f is a frequency and M is a class midpoint. - The same small data sets come back from page to page, so a table you met earlier may turn out to have a surprise in it later.

label: Stir the pot first
title: Stir the Pot First: Population, Sample, and Why We Guess
desc: Part 1 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. The tea shop and its customers are invented. The 1936 poll in

secs.head: Stir the Pot First: Population, Sample, and Why We Guess
secs.body: Part 1 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. The tea shop and its customers are invented. The 1936 poll in the middle of the page is real, and its sources are listed at the end. By the end you will see why a sip can speak for a whole pot, and that the four famous sampling methods are one idea asked two ways.

secs.head: Prologue: the Saturday morning poll
secs.body: Mira runs Leaf & Kettle, a tea shop with 4,000 customers on its loyalty list. She has developed a new smoky blend, and before she orders 500 kilos of it she wants to know whether her customers will like it. On Saturday morning she asks the first 30 people through the door to try a cup. Twenty-seven say they love it. That is 90%. She places the big order. By March, most of the smoky blend is still on the shelf. Her arithmetic was fine: 27 out of 30 really is 90%. The mistake came before any arithmetic, in who got asked . Early Saturday visitors come on purpose and like trying new things. They are not a small copy of her 4,000 customers, only of the kind of person who shows up early on Saturdays. ☕ Try it before you scroll. Mira's friend says: "Fine, so ask 3,000 people next time, not 30." Would that fix it? Hint: who would the 3,000 be, if she asked the same way?

secs.head: The idea in one minute
secs.body: A sample is a promise about a crowd: "these few people look like all of them." Whether the promise holds depends on how you chose the few, not on how many you chose. - Ask 3,000 early-Saturday visitors and you are 3,000 times as sure about the wrong crowd. - Ask 40 picked so every kind of customer had a fair chance, and you can speak for all 4,000. That is the whole page. The rest names the parts and shows ways to keep the promise when you cannot stir the whole pot.

secs.head: Three words, and why we sip at all
secs.body: Word Meaning In Mira's story --- --- --- Population The complete group you want to know about All 4,000 loyalty-card customers Sample The part of it you actually observe The 30 people she asked Statistic vs parameter A number from a sample, versus the true number for the whole population 90% of her 30, versus the real share among all 4,000 The parameter is what you want and cannot see; the statistic is what you have. Statistics is saying something honest about the first using the second. One more word hides in every survey: the sampling frame , the actual list you draw from. Mira's frame was "whoever walks in on Saturday morning", her population "everyone on the loyalty list". The sample can only speak for the frame. Why not ask everyone (a census )? Often you cannot: it costs too much, it destroys the thing (you cannot taste the whole pot and still have a pot), or the answers change before you finish. So you sip. The question is when the sip is trustworthy.

secs.head: How you chose, not how many
secs.body: Tasting the top of an unstirred pot tells you about the top of the pot, where the tea is weakest. A sip is fair only if every part of the pot had a fair chance of reaching the spoon. Stirring is what randomness does in sampling. A sample can miss for two reasons. Bad luck shrinks as you ask more people. Bias (the method leans one way every time, like "only early Saturday visitors") does not shrink at all: more people only make the wrong answer look more convincing. So the real question of sampling is: how do I choose fairly when I cannot stir the whole pot? The four classic methods are four answers.

secs.head: Four ways to choose fairly, from two questions
secs.body: Mira wants n = 40 from N = 4,000 . Two questions give the four methods. One worry, "is this fair?", answered four ways. No groups: chance or pattern. - Simple random. Number the customers 1 to 4,000 and let a random number generator pick 40. Every customer, and every possible group of 40, has the same chance. The pot, properly stirred. It needs a full list. - Systematic. A shortcut for the same stirring: step k = N / n = 4,000 / 40 = 100 , random start (say 37), then every 100th customer: 37, 137, 237, up to 3,937. That is 40 customers. The trap is a rhythm in the list. If rows alternate between her two shops and k is even, every pick lands on the same shop (I checked: all 40 picks starting at 37 are odd rows). The pattern replaces the chance, so check that the list has no rhythm that matches k . Groups: every group or some groups. - Stratified: every group, some people. Split the crowd into groups that differ in ways that matter, then draw at random inside each. Mira's customers are 1,600 students, 1,400 office workers and 1,000 retirees, and she draws in proportion ( n h = n × N h / N ): 16, 14 and 10. Every kind of person is guaranteed a seat, which pays off when groups really differ. - Cluster: some groups, every person. Split the crowd into natural groups that each look like a mini-crowd, such as neighborhoods (40 of about 100 people each), pick a few at random and survey everyone inside them: 4 neighborhoods, 400 people. Cheap when no full list exists. The price: neighbors resemble each other, so 400 people from 4 neighborhoods tell you less than 400 drawn from everywhere. Stratified and cluster are the pair students mix up. Stratified groups differ from each other (students versus retirees) and you do it for precision; cluster groups resemble each other (each neighborhood is a mini-crowd) and you do it for cost. ☕ Try it before you scroll. Which method would you pick to survey every child in a country's schools with no list of children, only a list of schools? Hint: you have groups, but you cannot visit them all.

secs.head: The poll that asked 2.4 million people
secs.body: If you believe that more data fixes everything, the 1936 US presidential election is a cold shower. The magazine Literary Digest mailed about 10 million questionnaires to automobile and telephone owners, and about 2.4 million came back (sources give 2.27 to 2.38 million). It had called every winner from 1920 to 1932, and now predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt by about 57% to 43%. Roosevelt won with about 61% of the vote, in a landslide. Enormous sample, badly wrong answer, for the two reasons above: - The frame did not match the population. In the middle of the Great Depression, owning a car or a telephone leaned toward the better off, who leaned toward Landon. - Who answered was not random either. Only about a quarter of the questionnaires came back, and the people who answered were not like those who did not. A study cited in the arXiv paper below (Squire, 1988) found the two together produced the error. Meanwhile George Gallup polled about 50,000 people using a "scientific sample" built to include the right proportion of voters from each economic group (in the spirit of stratification), and predicted Roosevelt's win. Mira's lesson, a million times larger: a huge biased sample is just a more confident way of being wrong.

secs.head: Two jobs for statistics
secs.body: Descriptive statistics summarizes the numbers in front of you: Mira's 30 ratings have an average and a spread, and nothing is a guess. Inferential statistics speaks about the people you did not ask, so it comes with uncertainty: a confidence interval gives a range, and a hypothesis test asks "is this gap real, or luck in who I asked?" The second job is only honest when the sample was drawn fairly, which is why it starts here.

secs.head: Check yourself
secs.body: Answers are below the cheat sheet. 1. A school has 900 students in 30 classes of 30. The principal picks 3 classes at random and surveys every student in them. Which method? 2. A list holds 1,200 employees sorted by ID. You pick a random number between 1 and 40, then take every 40th employee after it. Which method, and how large is the sample? 3. A company has 600 men and 400 women, and you want a sample of 50 that mirrors that mix. How many of each? 4. Which sample would you trust more to estimate the opinion of all voters: 10,000 volunteers who answered an online poll, or 400 people chosen at random from the voter list? Why? 5. Mira sorts her customers into three age groups and asks 10 people from each group. Is that stratified sampling? What detail would you check?

secs.head: Back to the story
secs.body: Mira still has the unsold smoky blend on her shelf, and she is not going to make the same mistake twice. This time she works from the loyalty list and draws a stratified sample of 40: 16 students, 14 office workers and 10 retirees, each picked at random from its own list. Twenty-two of the 40 say they would buy the smoky blend. That is 55%, far below the 90% she celebrated in the doorway, and much closer to how the blend actually sold. She orders 100 kilos instead of 500. The 55% is a statistic ; the true share is a parameter she will never see. Takeaway: a sample is a promise about a crowd, and what keeps the promise is how you chose, not how many. The difference between the two Saturdays was never the arithmetic. It was the stirring. But 55% from 40 people is still a number, and numbers come in kinds. Is "smoky: yes or no" the same sort of thing as "score out of 100" or "number of cups per week"? It is not, and the kind decides which tools are allowed. Next cup: Data Types and Frequency Tables.

secs.head: Answers
secs.body: 1. Cluster sampling. The classes are the clusters, and every student in the chosen classes is surveyed. 2. Systematic sampling , with 1,200 / 40 = 30 employees in the sample. 3. Stratified, proportional: 60% of 50 is 30 men , and 40% of 50 is 20 women . 4. The 400 random people. Volunteers choose themselves, and size does not fix that (1936 again). The 400 have a wider margin of error, but it is the honest kind that shrinks with size. 5. Yes, it is stratified (every group, some people from each). Check whether 10 per group matches each group's size: equal samples from unequal groups over-represent the small ones unless you reweight. And each 10 should be drawn at random. Pauses: 3,000 asked the same way are the same early-Saturday crowd, so no fix. Schools but no child list: cluster , pick some schools and survey every child in them.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Why do polls fail? (arXiv 2107.14166): the mailing to automobile and telephone owners, 2,376,523 returns of 10 million, the roughly 25% return rate, Gallup's 50,000, Squire (1988). Fetched and read. - The poll that changed polling: selection bias and the 1936 US election (Pivotal Research): the 57% to 43% prediction and over 2.27 million returns. It gives Roosevelt 62% and a subscriber-list source, which differ from the others; this page uses "about 61%" and the arXiv list description. Fetched and read. - Roosevelt's smashing of Landon in the 1936 presidential election (Brewminate): Roosevelt's 60.8%, the Digest's 57.1% for Landon. Fetched and read. - Two sources of the earlier version (Emory Math Center, Mathspace) could not be retrieved on rework, so nothing here relies on them. - The numbers in the story (16, 14, 10; the 40 systematic picks from 37 to 3,937; 30; 30 and 20; 55%) were recomputed with Python 3.14.4. The customers and shop are invented.

label: Data types and frequency tables
title: Mira's Notebook: What Kind of Data Is This, and How Do You Count It?
desc: Part 2 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It continues from Stir the Pot First: Mira has a properly dra

secs.head: Mira's Notebook: What Kind of Data Is This, and How Do You Count It?
secs.body: Part 2 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It continues from Stir the Pot First: Mira has a properly drawn sample and a notebook full of answers. By the end you will know what you are allowed to ask of any column before you compute, and how to count it without losing its shape. All people and numbers are invented, and every table can be checked by hand.

secs.head: The idea in one minute
secs.body: - The kind of data decides which questions make sense. Can two values be told apart (nominal), ordered (ordinal) or measured apart (numbers)? Each step allows more arithmetic. - A frequency table is counting without losing the shape. Tally how often each value appears, and the crowd's outline stays visible. - A grouped table is drawers for values. When values are too many, sort them into equal drawers. The drawers must touch, because measured values have no gaps between them. That one fact explains class boundaries.

secs.head: Prologue: the average blend
secs.body: Mira's sample is in. She types her notebook into a spreadsheet, five columns for each of 20 customers: Customer ID Favorite blend Strength preference Cups per week Brewing temperature (°C) --- --- --- --- --- 1041 Green Mild 3 79.5 2208 Black Strong 9 96.0 0377 Herbal Medium 2 88.2 ... ... ... ... ... A helpful assistant clicks Average on every column. The spreadsheet obliges: the average customer ID is 1,208.7 and the average favorite blend is 2.4. Both answers are computed perfectly and mean nothing. Why? Not because of a rule, but because of something much simpler. Hold that thought.

secs.head: What can you do with two of them?
secs.body: Pick any two values from a column and ask what you can do with them. The answer sorts every column into four kinds. Kind The one thing you can do with two values Mira's column --- --- --- Nominal Say same or different Favorite blend (Green, Black, Herbal) Ordinal Also say which comes first (but not by how much) Strength preference (Mild < Medium < Strong) Discrete Also say how far apart : values you count , so whole numbers Cups per week (0, 1, 2, ...) Continuous Also say how far apart: values you measure , so any value in a range Brewing temperature Each row keeps everything the row above allowed. That also tells you which summaries are honest: - Same or different allows counting and percentages, and "the most common one". - Which comes first adds sorting, the middle value and rankings. - How far apart adds adding, subtracting and averaging, because a gap now means something. Averaging favorite blends needs "how far apart is Green from Oolong?", which nobody can answer. The spreadsheet did not know. You do. Labels in disguise. Customer ID 2208 is not "more" than 1041, and adding two IDs produces nothing. It is a nominal column written with digits, like postal codes, phone numbers and jersey numbers. The test is the same question: if "how far apart" is meaningless, it is a label, whatever it looks like. ☕ Try it before you scroll. Cups ordered per visit, a satisfaction rating of poor, fair or good, and a loyalty-card number: which question can you ask of each, same or different , which first , or how far apart ?

secs.head: Counting without losing the shape
secs.body: A frequency table counts how many times each value appears. It is the cheapest way to keep a crowd's outline: nothing is thrown away except the order in which people walked in. For categories it is the simplest table there is. Mira's 20 customers named a favorite blend: Blend Frequency f Percentage --- --- --- Black 5 25% Green 6 30% Herbal 4 20% Oolong 5 25% Total 20 100% The percentage is f / n × 100 . One check, every time: the frequencies add up to the sample size ( Σf = n ). If not, a customer went missing or was counted twice. Now a number column. Mira has her 20 tasters rate the new blend on a 0 to 120 quality scale. The scores, in order of arrival: Sort them and count each distinct value, and you have an ungrouped frequency table , one row per individual value: Score Frequency f Relative frequency f/n Percentage Cumulative frequency CF --- --- --- --- --- 52 1 0.05 5% 1 55 2 0.10 10% 3 58 3 0.15 15% 6 62 3 0.15 15% 9 71 2 0.10 10% 11 89 3 0.15 15% 14 93 2 0.10 10% 16 94 2 0.10 10% 18 95 1 0.05 5% 19 104 1 0.05 5% 20 Total 20 1.00 100% The extra columns are three questions about the same count: how many ( f ), what fraction ( f/n ), and how many this or lower ( CF , a running total). Read the row for 71: CF = 11 , so 11 of 20 tasters scored 71 or less, which is 55%. "What share sits at or below this value" will return as the percentile. The last CF must equal n . Now look at the shape, which is why we counted. The scores come in two clumps, 52 to 62 and 89 to 95, with nothing between 71 and 89. The average of all 20 is 75.2, right in the empty gap, describing nobody. The table shows that. A single number hides it. Stem and leaf is the same count with the raw values kept. Split each number into a stem (leading digits) and leaves (last digit): Turn your head 90 degrees and it is a bar chart made of the actual numbers (stem 5, leaf 2 is 52). With hundreds of values it becomes a wall. What if 500 readings are almost all different?

secs.head: Drawers for values: the grouped table
secs.body: Five hundred nearly distinct readings give an ungrouped table of 500 rows of f = 1 : the raw data in a table costume. The fix is a grouped frequency table . Think of drawers . Each drawer takes a stretch of values, and you count what ends up in each drawer. Using the 20 scores and 5 drawers of width 11: Class limits Frequency f Relative frequency CF --- --- --- --- 52 to 62 9 0.45 9 63 to 73 2 0.10 11 74 to 84 0 0.00 11 85 to 95 8 0.40 19 96 to 106 1 0.05 20 Total 20 1.00 The counts come straight from the ungrouped table: the first drawer holds 52 (1) + 55 (2) + 58 (3) + 62 (3) = 9, and the fourth holds 89 (3) + 93 (2) + 94 (2) + 95 (1) = 8. The empty drawer, 74 to 84, still shows the gap. The price. You can no longer tell whether the 9 scores in the first drawer were all 55 or spread from 52 to 62. Grouping trades detail for readability, and you cannot undo it. Draw stem and leaf first when n is small. Good drawers hold every value exactly once and have the same width , so counts compare fairly. The surprising part is the next one.

secs.head: Why the drawers must touch
secs.body: The first drawer says "52 to 62". Subtract: ten wide. Yet the width we used was eleven . Which is it? Here is the idea. A score of 62 on a quality scale is not truly "exactly 62". Quality, like temperature or time, is measured and then written rounded . A true 62.4 is written 62, and a true 62.6 is written 63. So the drawer holding "62" really holds everything from 61.5 up to 62.5. Every written value wears a half-unit halo . Stack the halos side by side and they touch with no gap: the first drawer really runs from 51.5 to 62.5, the next from 62.5 to 73.5, and so on. These cut-off points are the class boundaries . The drawer's true width is boundary to boundary: 62.5 − 51.5 = 11 . The limits (52 and 62) are only the smallest and largest values you can write in it. Class limits Class boundaries Width (upper − lower boundary) --- --- --- 52 to 62 51.5 to 62.5 11 63 to 73 62.5 to 73.5 11 74 to 84 73.5 to 84.5 11 85 to 95 84.5 to 95.5 11 96 to 106 95.5 to 106.5 11 The halo is half of one measuring unit : 0.5 for whole numbers, 0.05 for one decimal place, 0.005 for two. Boundary = limit ± half a unit. ☕ Try it before you scroll. Data recorded to one decimal place has a class running 12.4 to 18.4. What are its boundaries, and why is the width 6.1 and not 6.0?

secs.head: The recipe, short
secs.body: With the idea in hand, the recipe is five lines, each with its reason: 1. Range = largest − smallest. Here 104 − 52 = 52 . How much line must the drawers cover? 2. Number of drawers k : a handful. Too few hides the shape, too many reproduces the noise. A rule of thumb, Sturges' rule k ≈ 1 + 3.322 × log10(n) , gives 5.3 for n = 20 , so use 5. 3. Width h = Range / k = 52 / 5 = 10.4 , then round up to 11. Why up? Rounded down to 10, five drawers starting at 52 end at 101 and the score of 104 has nowhere to live. 4. Limits : start at the smallest value and add h for each next drawer (52 to 62, 63 to 73, and so on). 5. Count each drawer, and check that Σf = n . Takeaway: the kind of data tells you which questions are meaningful, a frequency table counts without losing the shape, and class boundaries are not a rule but the halo that lets drawers touch.

secs.head: Check yourself
secs.body: 1. Which question (same or different, which first, how far apart) fits each, and so what kind is it? (a) cups ordered per visit, (b) taste rating of poor, fair or good, (c) brewing temperature in °C, (d) blend name, (e) loyalty-card number. 2. In the ungrouped table above, how many tasters scored 89 or less , and what percentage is that? 3. A data set is recorded to one decimal place , with a minimum of 12.4 and a maximum of 48.9. You want 6 classes. Find h , write the class limits, and give the first class's boundaries. 4. A friend says, "The class 85 to 95 is ten wide, so the five classes should have width 10, not 11." What is the mistake? 5. A table of 40 customers shows frequencies of 12, 9, 11 and 7. What is wrong?

secs.head: Back to the story
secs.body: Mira deletes the two "Average" cells and rebuilds the sheet column by column, asking of each: what can I do with two of these? The customer ID is a label, so it gets nothing. The blend gets a category table. Cups per week and brewing temperature are the only two columns where an average now means something. When the helpful assistant offers to click "Average" again, she knows what to ask first. Challenge. An average of cups per week is now allowed, but the tasting scores' average, 75.2, described nobody. When can one number stand in for a column? The next cup is about that.

secs.head: Answers
secs.body: 1. (a) Discrete : counted, so how far apart works. (b) Ordinal : which first, but gaps are not measured. (c) Continuous . (d) Nominal : same or different only. (e) Nominal : the number is a label, however many digits it has. 2. The cumulative frequency at 89 is 14 , so 14 tasters, which is 14 / 20 = 70% . 3. Range = 48.9 − 12.4 = 36.5 , and h = 36.5 / 6 = 6.08... , so round up to one decimal place: h = 6.1 . The limits are 12.4 to 18.4, 18.5 to 24.5, 24.6 to 30.6, 30.7 to 36.7, 36.8 to 42.8 and 42.9 to 48.9. With one decimal place the halo is 0.05, so the first class's boundaries are 12.35 to 18.45 , a width of 6.1. (Limits 12.4 to 18.4 differ by only 6.0.) 4. Ten is the difference between the limits (95 − 85). The width is the distance between the boundaries (95.5 − 84.5 = 11), because each written value carries a half-unit halo and the drawers must touch. 5. The frequencies add up to 12 + 9 + 11 + 7 = 39 , not 40. A customer is missing, or one count is off by one.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, Histogram : a histogram divides the range of the data into equal-width bins (classes) and counts the observations in each. <https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/histogra.htm - Stevens, S. S. (1946), On the Theory of Scales of Measurement , Science 103(2684). Cited as the origin of the nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio scale levels; the paper was not retrieved here, so it is not quoted. - Sturges, H. A. (1926), The Choice of a Class Interval , Journal of the American Statistical Association 21(153). Cited as the origin of the class-count rule of thumb; not retrieved here, so it is not quoted. - Every number on this page was recomputed with Python 3.14.4.

label: Draw it first
title: Draw It Before You Describe It: Three Pictures of the Same Fifty Days
desc: Part 3 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It builds on the grouped tables from Mira's Notebook. By the

secs.head: Draw It Before You Describe It: Three Pictures of the Same Fifty Days
secs.body: Part 3 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It builds on the grouped tables from Mira's Notebook. By the end you will see that the histogram, the frequency polygon and the ogive are not three graphs to memorize: they are three questions you can ask of one table. The shop, the people and the counts are invented, and every number can be checked by hand.

secs.head: The idea in one minute
secs.body: A table of counts hides its shape. A picture shows it, and which picture you draw depends on the question: - "How much lives here?" Draw bars that touch, so that area means amount . That is the histogram. - "How do two crowds compare?" Draw the outline as a line, so two can be laid over each other. That is the frequency polygon. - "How many are at or below here?" Draw a running total, a staircase that can only go up. That is the ogive, and it sits on the upper edge of each class because a class is only counted once it is finished. The rest of the page is the reason behind those three sentences.

secs.head: Prologue: Ravi's blank stare
secs.body: Mira has counted the customers who came into Leaf & Kettle on each of the last 50 days, and grouped the counts into classes. She slides the table across the counter to her business partner Ravi, who is deciding how many baristas to schedule. Customers per day Days --- --- 100 to 104 2 105 to 109 8 110 to 114 18 115 to 119 13 120 to 124 7 125 to 129 1 130 to 134 1 Ravi reads the table. He reads it again. Then he looks up and says, "So... is that a lot?" The table is correct, and useless to him: it makes him see the shape himself. So Mira turns the napkin over and asks him the better question: "What do you actually want to know?"

secs.head: One table, three questions
secs.body: Because the counts are whole numbers, the class boundaries sit half a unit beyond the limits (as in the previous page): the first class runs from 99.5 to 104.5. Here is the one table every picture comes from. Class boundaries Frequency f Midpoint M Cumulative CF --- --- --- --- 99.5 to 104.5 2 102 2 104.5 to 109.5 8 107 10 109.5 to 114.5 18 112 28 114.5 to 119.5 13 117 41 119.5 to 124.5 7 122 48 124.5 to 129.5 1 127 49 129.5 to 134.5 1 132 50 The midpoint is (lower + upper) / 2 , so (99.5 + 104.5) / 2 = 102 . The cumulative column is the running total of f , and its last value must equal n = 50 . Three questions, one table. Which one is Ravi asking first? "Is that a lot?" is a question about amount .

secs.head: Question 1: how much lives here?
secs.body: ☕ Try it before you scroll. You draw one bar per class. Should the bars touch or have gaps between them? Hint: what would a gap between 104.5 and 105.5 claim about that stretch of customers? Think of the horizontal axis as a ruler. Every stretch of the ruler holds some number of days, and a bar is a way of saying "this stretch holds this much". Sideways, in text: Ravi's eyebrows go up: the days pile up in the 110s, with a thin tail of busy days toward 134. Three reasons, and the rest follows: - The bars touch because the ruler has no holes. A gap would claim a stretch of values that cannot occur. Favourite blends are different: tea types are separate things, not stretches of a ruler, so their bars have gaps. - The axis shows boundaries, not limits. Label the bars with limits (100 to 104, 105 to 109) and the reader sees a hole between 104 and 105 that is not there. - Area is the amount, and height is only a shortcut. When all classes are 5 wide, a taller bar means more days, so height seems to be the story. It is not. Suppose Mira merges the last three classes into one wide class from 119.5 to 134.5, holding 9 days. Drawn at height 9 it would tower over the 8-day class and look like a second peak, though those 9 days are spread over 15 units of the ruler. The honest height is frequency density , frequency divided by class width: 9 / 15 = 0.6 days per unit, against 8 / 5 = 1.6 for the neighbouring-sized class. Now area = height x width = count again, and the wide class looks as small as it is. This is why the histogram is the picture to draw first: part 6 shows the box plot is only a thin summary of it. Look first, then summarise. Ravi has one more worry: this summer against last summer.

secs.head: Question 2: how do two crowds compare?
secs.body: The second question is not about one crowd at all. Mira puts a dot above the midpoint of each class at the height of its frequency, and joins the dots. The dots are (102, 2), (107, 8), (112, 18), (117, 13), (122, 7), (127, 1), (132, 1). Close the shape by bringing the line down to zero at both ends, either with an empty class on each side (midpoints 97 and 137) or at the outer boundaries (99.5 and 134.5). Say which you used. Same information as the histogram, so why bother? Because lines overlay and bars do not. Two sets of bars on the same axes cover each other; two outlines show at a glance whether this summer's peak sits left, right or higher. Ravi's third question is of another kind altogether: "On how many days did we have 114 or fewer customers?"

secs.head: Question 3: how many are at or below here?
secs.body: With the histogram Ravi must add bars in his head. The ogive plots the running total, so each point answers "how many days up to here ?" That phrase explains the whole picture. - It only goes up. Counting days up to a value can never lose a day, so the curve starts at 0, never goes down, and ends at n = 50 . It is a staircase, with the steps smoothed into straight lines. Its steepest stretch is where the crowd is thickest. - It sits on the upper boundary. The count "up to 114.5" is only true once the whole 109.5 to 114.5 class has been counted, that is, at its top edge. Plot it at the midpoint or the lower edge and the curve claims days that have not happened yet. The first point is the lowest boundary with a count of zero. Boundary (x) 99.5 104.5 109.5 114.5 119.5 124.5 129.5 134.5 --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- Days up to x (y) 0 2 10 28 41 48 49 50 You can read it in two directions, and they answer two different families of question: - From x to y: "how many are at or below?" Whole numbers, so "114 or fewer" reaches exactly the boundary 114.5, and the curve reads 28 days , which is 28 / 50 = 56% . - From y to x: "what value splits the data?" Half of 50 is 25. At height 25 the curve lies on the straight stretch between (109.5, 10) and (114.5, 28), so Half the days had about 113.7 customers or fewer: the median , found by ruler. Other heights give percentiles (part 6). Caution: straight lines assume days are spread evenly inside each class, so the curve is exact at the boundaries and an estimate between them.

secs.head: The short recipe
secs.body: Write boundaries, f and the cumulative column (last value = n ). Then: histogram , touching bars on boundaries, height f (or f / width ); polygon , dots at (midpoint, f ), closed at both ends; ogive , points at (upper boundary, CF ) from (lowest boundary, 0).

secs.head: Ways these pictures lie
secs.body: Each trap is an idea broken. (Labelling bars with limits invents a hole, the same as gaps.) Trap Idea it breaks The fix --- --- --- Gaps between histogram bars The ruler has no holes Let bars touch, use boundaries Unequal widths, plain frequency as height Area is the amount Plot frequency density Ogive at midpoints or lower boundaries A count up to here needs the class finished Plot at upper boundaries

secs.head: Check yourself
secs.body: Use the table of 50 days above. 1. On how many days were there 119 customers or fewer, and what share is that? 2. Which two numbers make the first ogive point after (99.5, 0)? 3. You want to compare this summer's days with last summer's on one chart. Which picture, and why? 4. A bar chart of favourite blends has gaps, but a histogram of daily customers does not. Why? 5. Estimate the value below which the lowest 25% of days fall.

secs.head: Back to the story
secs.body: Ravi holds the napkin up to the light. "The tallest bar is the 110s," he says. "That's my normal day." "Eighteen of the fifty," says Mira. "And 114 or fewer on 28 days." He frowns. "How many were really busy, over 119?" Mira reads it off the staircase: 41 days at or below 119, so 9 days , a bit under one day in five. Ten minutes ago Ravi could not tell if the numbers were large. Now he asks his own questions: that is what a good picture is for. "Okay," he says. "Two baristas on ordinary days, a third on call. But what's the typical day, exactly? One number." Takeaway: do not memorize three graphs. Ask the question: how much, how do two compare, how many up to here. That is a harder question than it sounds, and it is the next cup: The Number on the Tin.

secs.head: Answers
secs.body: 1. The cumulative frequency at the boundary 119.5 is 41 , so 41 days, which is 41 / 50 = 82% . 2. The upper boundary 104.5 and its cumulative frequency 2 . 3. The frequency polygon . Outlines share one set of axes and the eye compares peaks and shifts. Two sets of bars would cover each other. 4. Blends are separate categories , not stretches of a ruler, so their bars stand apart. Daily customers lie on a continuous scale where classes share boundaries, so the bars touch. 5. 25% of 50 is 12.5. That height lies between (109.5, 10) and (114.5, 28), so x = 109.5 + (12.5 - 10) / 18 x 5 = 109.5 + 0.694 = about 110.2 . About a quarter of the days had roughly 110 customers or fewer.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Every number on this page (cumulative column, 41 and 9 days, 56% and 82%, the interpolations 113.7 and 110.2, the densities 0.6 and 1.6) was recomputed with Python 3.14.4. The merged-class example is an invented illustration. No external source was fetched for this page.

label: The number on the tin
title: The Number on the Tin: Mean, Median and Mode
desc: Part 4 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It continues from Draw It Before You Describe It, where Ravi

secs.head: The Number on the Tin: Mean, Median and Mode
secs.body: Part 4 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It continues from Draw It Before You Describe It, where Ravi asked for "one number" for a typical day. The scenario is invented, and every figure can be checked by hand.

secs.head: Prologue: the number on the tin
secs.body: Mira is about to print the labels for her new smoky blend. The tins will carry a line she has always wanted: "Typical taster score: ." She has the 20 tasting scores from earlier (on a 0 to 120 scale), and she knows how to find the average: add them up and divide. The sum is 1,504, and 1,504 divided by 20 is 75.2 . She sends "Typical taster score: 75" to the printer. Then she remembers the table she built a few days ago. Scores from 74 to 84 had a frequency of zero. Not one taster gave the blend anything close to 75. The "typical" score on every tin is a score nobody gave. The arithmetic was right. The question she asked was not the question she meant. ☕ Try it before you scroll. Before reading on: if someone asked you for the "typical" score of those 20, what would you actually say? Is it the same number you would give if the question were "which score did most people give?"

secs.head: The idea in one minute
secs.body: "Typical" is an ambiguous word. It hides three different questions, and each has an honest answer: Three questions, three answers. None of them is wrong. Each is wrong only when it answers a question you did not mean. So the skill is not memorizing three formulas. It is two habits: say which question you mean, and draw the picture first. The picture tells you whether a single "typical" even exists. For Mira's tin, it did not. The rest of the page gives each question a short recipe.

secs.head: The mean: where the seesaw balances
secs.body: Question: where would the data balance? Add up and divide by how many: Take eight tasting scores: 70, 65, 69, 85, 94, 62, 79, 100. The sum is 624, so x̄ = 624 / 8 = 78 . Picture each value as a weight on a seesaw. The mean is the pivot where it balances. The check is the deviations , x − 78 : they are −8, −13, −9, +7, +16, −16, +1, +22, and they add to zero . The pull from below equals the pull from above. That is what "balance point" means, and why one far-away value drags the mean so hard: a heavy weight on a long arm. The mean of a table. When the data arrive as a frequency table, each value simply counts f times, so the mean is a weighted average. When the table is grouped , the exact values inside a class are gone. So each class casts f votes for its midpoint M , a stand-in for the values we cannot see: Fifty visits to the shop, grouped by minutes inside: Class boundaries f Midpoint M f × M --- --- --- --- 9.5 to 12.5 4 11 44 12.5 to 15.5 12 14 168 15.5 to 18.5 20 17 340 18.5 to 21.5 14 20 280 Total 50 832 x̄ = 832 / 50 = 16.64 minutes. Because midpoints stand in for unknown values, this is an estimate .

secs.head: The median: the one in the middle of the line
secs.body: Question: if everyone lines up in order, who stands in the middle? Sort the data. Half sit on each side. - Odd: {3, 2, 6, 2, 7} sorted is 2, 2, 3, 6, 7. Position (5 + 1) / 2 = 3 , so the median is 3 . - Even: add an 8: 2, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8. Average the 3rd and 4th, (3 + 6) / 2 = 4.5 . With an even count the median need not be a data value. The eight scores sorted are 62, 65, 69, 70, 79, 85, 94, 100. The 4th and 5th are 70 and 79, so the median is (70 + 79) / 2 = 74.5 , near the mean of 78. Now the experiment that shows why the median exists. Change the 100 into a 1,000, as if one taster hit the wrong key: Original With the typo --- --- --- Mean 78 1,524 / 8 = 190.5 Median 74.5 74.5 (the 4th and 5th values are still 70 and 79) One wrong entry moved the mean by more than 110 points and the median by none. The median uses only the order of the values, not how far out the extremes are. That makes it resistant to outliers. The median of a grouped table. Here the raw values are gone, but you can still find the middle of the line, using one assumption: inside a class, the values are spread evenly. Then the median is the cumulative-frequency curve (the ogive from the previous page) read with a ruler. In symbols, with L the lower boundary of the class holding the middle position, cf the count before that class, f its count and h its width: Quality scores of 21 batches: Class boundaries f CF --- --- --- 50.5 to 55.5 2 2 55.5 to 60.5 7 9 60.5 to 65.5 8 17 65.5 to 70.5 4 21 The middle position is N/2 = 10.5 . The first class whose CF reaches it is 60.5 to 65.5, with cf = 9 , f = 8 , h = 5 : Why it works: nine values lie below the class and we need the 10.5th, so we need 1.5 more. If the 8 values are spread evenly, 1.5 of 8 is 18.75% of the way across the width of 5, which is 0.9375 above the boundary. For the 50 days of customers ( N/2 = 25 , class 109.5 to 114.5, cf = 10 , f = 18 ) it gives 109.5 + (15 / 18) × 5 ≈ 113.7 , the value you read off the ogive.

secs.head: The mode: the most popular
secs.body: Question: what did the most people say? The mode is the value that appears most often. It does three things the others cannot: - It works for any kind of data. Among 20 customers' favorite blends, Green was chosen by 6, more than any other. A mean of blend names does not exist. A mode does. - It may not exist. In the eight scores, every value appears once. - It may not be unique. In 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 7, 7, 8, 10, both 2 and 3 appear three times: bimodal . The 20 tasting scores have three values that tie at three: 58, 62 and 89. For a grouped table, use the modal class , the one with the highest frequency. For the 50 days it is 109.5 to 114.5, with 18 days.

secs.head: When the answers disagree
secs.body: Same data, three answers: Data Mean Median Mode --- --- --- --- 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 7, 7, 8, 10 4.64 3 2 and 3 50 days of customers (grouped) 114.2 113.7 modal class 109.5 to 114.5 The 20 tasting scores 75.2 71 58, 62 and 89 (The mean of the 50 days is 5,710 / 50 = 114.2 , from the midpoints on the previous page.) In the first two rows, mean median , and both have a tail on the right : the seesaw is dragged toward a long tail, while the median only counts positions. As a rule of thumb (not a law), mean median hints at a right tail, mean < median at a left tail. The third row is Mira's tin. The mean (75.2) and median (71) are close, and both mislead , for a different reason: there are two clumps . Nine tasters scored 62 or less, nine scored 89 or more, and two sit in between. No single answer rescues a data set with two centers. Only the picture shows it.

secs.head: What grouping costs you
secs.body: The grouped formulas are estimates. Mira can measure how good, because she has the raw 20 scores and a grouped version of the same data: Class boundaries f Midpoint M f × M CF --- --- --- --- --- 51.5 to 62.5 9 57 513 9 62.5 to 73.5 2 68 136 11 73.5 to 84.5 0 79 0 11 84.5 to 95.5 8 90 720 19 95.5 to 106.5 1 101 101 20 - Grouped mean: 1,470 / 20 = 73.5 , against the true 75.2. - Grouped median: N/2 = 10 falls in the second class, so 62.5 + ((10 − 9) / 2) × 11 = 68.0 , against the true 71. Both are off, because the real values neither sit at the midpoints nor spread evenly. That error is the price of having only the table. If you hold the raw data, use it.

secs.head: Choosing, and looking first
secs.body: Pick the question the data can answer and your reader cares about: Your data Best choice Reason --- --- --- Nominal (blend names) Mode No order and no arithmetic, so it is the only one that exists Ordinal (mild, medium, strong) Median (and mode) Order exists, distances do not Quantitative, roughly symmetric Mean Uses every value, the natural balance point Quantitative, skewed or with outliers Median It does not chase the extremes Two or more clumps None alone. Describe the clumps A single center hides the structure

secs.head: Check yourself
secs.body: 1. Find the mean and median of 4, 8, 6, 5, 3, 200. Which one answers "what is typical?" better, and why? 2. For 20 visits, a grouped table has boundaries 0.5 to 5.5 (frequency 3), 5.5 to 10.5 (9), 10.5 to 15.5 (6) and 15.5 to 20.5 (2). Estimate the mean and the median, and name the modal class. 3. Find the modes, the median and the mean of 5, 5, 7, 9, 9, 12. 4. Which measure of center works for the favorite-blend column, and why? 5. True or false: the mean computed from a grouped table is exact. 6. A café reports an average order of 12.40 but a median order of 8.10. What does the gap tell you?

secs.head: Back to the story
secs.body: Mira calls the printer before the labels go out. "Typical" was the wrong thing to ask for. The data were never one group with a typical member. They were two groups: nine tasters who scored the blend low, nine who scored it high, and two in between. So she changes the line. The new label says: "Divides opinion: about half of our tasters loved it, about half did not." Underneath, in small print, she adds the median, 71, for customers who like a number. Takeaway: "typical" is three questions in a trench coat. Ask which one you mean, and draw the picture before you trust any of them. Now a loose thread. Why these three questions, and not a fourth? Tala suspects they are not strangers: one question hides underneath all three, and once you see it, you will also see why Mira's scores, running from 52 to 104, deserve a second number beside the first. Next cup: How Far From the Middle?

secs.head: Answers
secs.body: 1. The sum is 226, so the mean is 226 / 6 ≈ 37.7 . Sorted: 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 200, so the median is (5 + 6) / 2 = 5.5 . The median answers it better: the mean is dominated by the 200, and five of the six values are below 9. 2. Midpoints are 3, 8, 13 and 18, so Σ f×M = 9 + 72 + 78 + 36 = 195 , and the mean ≈ 195 / 20 = 9.75 . For the median, N/2 = 10 ; cumulative frequencies are 3, 12, 18, 20, so the median class is 5.5 to 10.5 with cf = 3 , f = 9 , h = 5 : 5.5 + ((10 − 3) / 9) × 5 ≈ 9.39 . The modal class is 5.5 to 10.5 (frequency 9). 3. The values 5 and 9 each appear twice, so the modes are 5 and 9 . With n = 6 , the median is (7 + 9) / 2 = 8 . The sum is 47, so the mean is 47 / 6 ≈ 7.83 . 4. The mode . Blend names are nominal: no order, no arithmetic, so only "which appears most" is meaningful. 5. False. It is an estimate, because every value in a class is replaced by the class midpoint. 6. The mean is much higher than the median, which points to a tail on the right : a few very large orders pull the average up while most orders are small. The median describes the typical order better.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Every number on this page was recomputed with Python 3.14.4 ( statistics.mean , median , multimode , plus the grouped formulas written out by hand), including the typo experiment and both grouped tables. No external source was fetched for this rework.

label: How far from the middle
title: How Far From the Middle? One Question Behind Every Summary Number
desc: Part 5 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series, and the sequel to The Number on the Tin, where the "typical"

secs.head: How Far From the Middle? One Question Behind Every Summary Number
secs.body: Part 5 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series, and the sequel to The Number on the Tin, where the "typical" score was a score nobody gave. By the end you will know why there are three middles and a pile of spreads, and that they are one question asked with different rulers. Far less to memorize than it looked.

secs.head: Prologue: the cart on Kettle Street
secs.body: Mira rents a handcart for the weekend market. Seven regulars live along Kettle Street, and she writes down their block numbers: "Park it in the middle," says Tala. "Which middle?" says Ravi, who lives on block 9. "Mine is block 9. Funny, that." The cart can stand in exactly one place. So every answer to "where is the middle?" is secretly a rule for choosing one place . Last page gave you three rules and let you think they were rivals. They are not. ☕ Try it before you scroll. Houses on blocks 1, 2, 2, 3, 5, 9 and 20. You get one spot for the cart. Which block do you pick, and what rule did you just use? Hint: you used a rule whether you noticed or not.

secs.head: Three rules for one cart
secs.body: Every rule answers the same question: how much should a long walk hurt? One question, three answers. Each spot wins its own contest. Here is the street, scored all three ways: Cart at Name Total walk (blocks) Total of squared walks People at the door --- --- --- --- --- block 2 mode 30 384 2 block 3 median 29 335 1 block 6 mean 34 272 0 Each spot wins one column and loses the others. I also scanned every position from block 0 to block 20 in steps of 0.01: nothing beats block 3 on total walking, and nothing beats block 6 on total squared walking. So the three are not formulas to memorize. They are three attitudes toward distance: - Mode: distance does not matter, only "right here" does. - Median: distance matters in proportion. Ten blocks is ten times one block. - Mean: distance matters more than in proportion. Squaring makes one ten-block walk hurt as much as a hundred one-block walks. That last attitude is also why the mean is the one that chases tails. Block 20 is one person, but at the mean it owes 196 of the 272 in squared walking, 72% of the bill.

secs.head: Why the median counts heads and the mean balances
secs.body: You do not have to take the table on trust. Slide the cart one block to the right and ask who is happier. - For total walking: everyone on the left walks one block more, everyone on the right walks one block less. The total changes by (people on the left) − (people on the right) . So slide toward the side with more people, and stop when the two sides are equal. That is the median : half the heads on each side. (With an even number of people, any spot between the two middle houses ties.) - For squared walking: a far-away person's walk changes by much more when you slide. The total stops improving exactly when the pulls from the left and right cancel, which is when the deviations add up to zero. You met that last page as the seesaw. The balance point is the spot that minimizes squared walking. The seesaw was never a separate idea. It was this one. Which raises the next question. Once the cart is parked, someone still has to walk. How much?

secs.head: What is left over: spread
secs.body: Spread is the walking that remains after you pick the best spot. Each rule leaves its own kind of leftover, so each middle has a natural partner: Middle Leftover rule Name On Kettle Street --- --- --- --- Mean (block 6) Average squared walk Variance σ² 272 / 7 = 38.9 blocks² Mean The same, square-rooted Standard deviation σ 6.23 blocks Median (block 3) Average plain walk Mean absolute deviation 29 / 7 = 4.1 blocks Median Width of the middle half IQR (Q3 − Q1) 7 − 2 = 5 blocks none Farthest minus nearest Range 20 − 1 = 19 blocks Two notes: - Why the square root? Squaring turns blocks into blocks² , which nobody can picture. Taking the root brings it back to blocks. That is the whole reason standard deviation exists next to variance. - What is IQR? Q1 and Q3 are the values a quarter and three quarters of the data sit below, the edges of the middle half. The next page builds them properly. Here, take them as the edges of the crowd. The one-line memory: mean goes with standard deviation, median goes with IQR. Choose the pair, and you have chosen both.

secs.head: The one-house test
secs.body: How do you choose the pair? Ask the one-house question : if one value were wrong, how much would my number move? Mira's helper types house 20 as 200 . Watch the four numbers: Real data With the typo --- --- --- Mean 6 31.7 Standard deviation 6.23 68.75 Median 3 3 IQR 5 5 Squares let one house shout. The mean and standard deviation went wild, and the median and IQR did not even notice. So: Your data Use --- --- Roughly symmetric, every value matters, you care about totals Mean and standard deviation Skewed, or you cannot vouch for the extremes Median and IQR Two clumps Neither alone. Describe both clumps

secs.head: The n − 1 mystery
secs.body: Everything so far treated the seven houses as everyone , so we divided by 7. In real life you almost always see a sample , and textbooks tell you to divide by n − 1 instead. Nobody says why. Here is the reason, and you can verify it by hand. ☕ Try it before you scroll. A sample picks its own cart spot, its own mean. Is the sample's own squared walking, measured from that spot, bigger or smaller than the walking measured from the true mean? Hint: which spot did we just prove is the best for the sample? Smaller, always. The sample's mean is, by construction, the spot that suits that sample best. The true mean is farther from the sample on average. So squared walking measured from the sample's own mean comes out too small, and dividing by n inherits the shortfall. Take a tiny population you can enumerate: three houses at blocks 2, 4 and 9 . The true mean is 5, and the true variance is (9 + 1 + 16) / 3 = 8.67 . Now take every possible sample of two (nine equally likely draws, with replacement): Sample Sample mean Divide by n (= 2) Divide by n − 1 (= 1) --- --- --- --- 2, 2 2.0 0 0 2, 4 3.0 1 2 2, 9 5.5 12.25 24.5 4, 2 3.0 1 2 4, 4 4.0 0 0 4, 9 6.5 6.25 12.5 9, 2 5.5 12.25 24.5 9, 4 6.5 6.25 12.5 9, 9 9.0 0 0 Average 5.0 4.33 8.67 Dividing by n averages half the truth. Dividing by n − 1 lands on 8.67 exactly . With two points the shortfall is a factor of (n − 1) / n = 1/2 , and it fades as n grows, which is why nobody worries with big samples. One honest footnote: this fixes the variance on average. Its square root, the standard deviation, still comes out a little low on average (2.20 here, against a true 2.94), because taking a root bends the average. Standard practice accepts that. The rule: everyone in the room, divide by n . A sample from a bigger group, divide by n − 1 . Almost every real data set is the second kind.

secs.head: Check yourself
secs.body: 1. Houses at blocks 1, 3, 4 and 10. Where does the cart go for the least total walking ? Is the answer unique? 2. For the same houses, find the mean and the variance and standard deviation (treat them as everyone). 3. Why is variance measured in squared units, and what turns it back? 4. The twelve staff in Mira's shop, versus twelve customers picked from the loyalty cabinet. Which uses n , and which n − 1 ? 5. A sales column has one value mistyped by a factor of 100. Which pair of numbers survives?

secs.head: Back to the story
secs.body: Mira parks the cart on block 3, the median, the spot with the least total walking. Ravi, on block 9, still thinks it should be on block 9. Everyone's middle is their own doorstep, and he is not wrong about his. Then she goes back to the tin. The 20 tasting scores had a mean of 75.2, and their sample standard deviation is 17.67 . Only two of the twenty tasters sit within five points of the number on the tin. A spread that wide next to a center is the alarm that says the center is lying. Page 4 found the two clumps by looking at the table. Now a single number could have raised the alarm. Takeaway: every summary is a stand-in for a crowd, the middle is the best stand-in under one rule for how distance hurts, and the spread is how badly the stand-in still misses. Now the harder question. Tala scored 84 on the brewing exam and 61 on the cupping exam. Which is the better result? "Better than what?" Each exam has its own middle and its own leftover. Next cup: Where Do You Stand?

secs.head: Answers
secs.body: 1. Total walking is 10 at blocks 3, 3.5 and 4 (and anywhere between), so the answer is not unique . With an even number of people, any spot between the two middle houses ties. The usual choice is the midpoint, 3.5 , which is also the median. 2. The mean is (1 + 3 + 4 + 10) / 4 = 4.5 . The squared walks are 12.25, 2.25, 0.25 and 30.25, which total 45, so the variance is 45 / 4 = 11.25 and the standard deviation is 3.35 . Check: moving the cart to 3.5 raises the total to 49, to 4 raises it to 46, to 3 raises it to 54. None beats 45. 3. Because each walk is squared before averaging, so the result is in blocks², not blocks. The square root (the standard deviation) turns it back into blocks. 4. The twelve staff are everyone you care about, so use n . The twelve customers are a sample of a larger group, so use n − 1 . 5. Median and IQR. The typo is the farthest value, and only the squared pair (mean and SD) lets one far value dominate.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Python statistics module: pvariance , variance , pstdev , stdev (population divides by N , sample by N − 1 , "Bessel's correction"). Verified against Python 3.14.4. <https://docs.python.org/3/library/statistics.html - Every number on this page was recomputed with Python 3.14.4, including the scan of every cart position and the enumeration of all nine samples of two.

label: Where do you stand
title: Where Do You Stand? Percentiles, Z-Scores and the Box Plot
desc: Part 6 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It continues from How Far From the Middle?, where every summa

secs.head: Where Do You Stand? Percentiles, Z-Scores and the Box Plot
secs.body: Part 6 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It continues from How Far From the Middle?, where every summary was a stand-in for a crowd. By the end you will place any single value inside its crowd with two rulers, and see that the box plot is not a new graph to memorize but the staircase you already know, read at four marks. The scenario is invented, and every figure can be checked by hand.

secs.head: Prologue: 84 versus 61
secs.body: Tala has taken two apprentice exams this month and tapes both results to the till. - Brewing: she scored 84 . - Cupping: she scored 61 . "Brewing is my strong subject," she says. Mira looks at the till and asks the only question that matters: "Better than what?" It turns out the brewing exam was easy: the class averaged 70 , and scores typically landed about 7 away from that. The cupping exam was brutal: the class averaged 50 , with a typical distance of 4 . (Invented numbers, chosen to be easy to check.) Now which result is stronger? Before you do any arithmetic, notice what you just did: you went looking for the crowd .

secs.head: A score needs a crowd
secs.body: An 84 alone says nothing. It is a point on a number line with no landmarks. A position is a value plus its crowd , and there are two natural ways to say where a value sits in that crowd: Ruler The question it asks Name Uses --- --- --- --- Rank What share of the crowd is below me? Percentile Only the order of the data Distance How many "typical distances" am I from the middle? z-score The mean and the standard deviation These are the same two ideas from last page in a new costume: rank is the median's attitude (count heads), distance is the mean's attitude (measure steps in spread units).

secs.head: Ruler 1: rank, the percentile
secs.body: The percentile rank of a value is the share of the data below it. A common convention adds half of any ties, so a value is not penalized for sharing its place: Take the eight tasting scores sorted: 62, 65, 69, 70, 79, 85, 94, 100. For 85 : five values are below it, one equals it, so (5 + 0.5) / 8 = 68.75% . About the 69th percentile. Run it backwards and you get the percentile value : the 75th percentile is the value with 75% of the data below it. Three of these have their own names: Name Percentile What it marks --- --- --- Q1 , first quartile 25th A quarter of the data are below Q2 , the median 50th Half are below Q3 , third quartile 75th Three quarters are below The trap nobody mentions: different tools give different quartiles. For the numbers 1 to 9, Python's statistics.quantiles returns quartiles 2.5 and 7.5 by default ( method='exclusive' ) and 3 and 7 with method='inclusive' . Both are legitimate: they differ in how they interpolate between data points. R's documentation lists nine quantile types, with type 7 as the default, and cites Hyndman and Fan (1996), who recommended type 8. NumPy's documentation lists the same nine, numbered the same way, with its default linear being type 7. The advice: pick one method, write down which, and never compare quartiles across tools. On the pages here the quartiles use the inclusive method, which treats your data as the whole story. The story is the same under either. Only the decimals move.

secs.head: Ruler 2: distance, the z-score
secs.body: The z-score says how many standard deviations a value sits above (positive) or below (negative) the mean: Now Tala's question has an answer: Exam Her score Class mean Class SD z-score --- --- --- --- --- Brewing 84 70 7 (84 − 70) / 7 = 2.00 Cupping 61 50 4 (61 − 50) / 4 = 2.75 Cupping wins. Her 61 is 2.75 typical distances above a hard exam's middle, farther out than her 84 on an easy one. A z-score is a ruler that converts every crowd into the same units , which is why it lets you compare things that have different scales. It carries one condition from last page: the mean and SD must be a fair summary of the crowd. In a two-clump crowd like Mira's tasting scores, a z-score measures distance from a middle where nobody lives, and the number is technically correct and practically useless. ☕ Try it before you scroll. Mira's 20 tasting scores have quartiles 58, 71 and 93, and no value at all between 71 and 89. If you draw a box from Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median, will the picture show the two clumps? Hint: where does the box sit relative to the gap?

secs.head: Which ruler when
secs.body: Situation Ruler --- --- Comparing across different scales (two exams, two stalls) z-score Skewed data, outliers, or two clumps Percentile (it does not rely on a middle) "Top 10%", "bottom quarter", grading on rank Percentile You will go on to chance and the bell curve z-score : it is how the normal distribution is read, coming up

secs.head: Fewer graphs, not more
secs.body: The box plot sounds like a third or fourth graph to memorize. It is not. Look at where each picture comes from: Three graphs, one table. The box plot is the ogive with only its landmarks kept. You want to know Use --- --- The shape : where the bulk is, any tail, any clumps Histogram . Always draw this first How many are at or below a value Ogive How several groups compare at a glance Box plot , side by side The rule of thumb that saves you from drawing everything: histogram first, to look. Box plot second, to compare groups.

secs.head: The box plot, and the clump it cannot see
secs.body: A box plot is built from five landmarks: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum. The box runs from Q1 to Q3 (the middle half), the line inside marks the median, and the whiskers reach out to the farthest values that are not outliers. What counts as an outlier? NIST's handbook describes the usual rule: compute IQR = Q3 − Q1 and the fences Q1 − 1.5 × IQR and Q3 + 1.5 × IQR . The whiskers stop at the last data point inside the fences, and anything beyond a fence is drawn as its own dot. For Mira's 20 scores, Q1 = 58 , median 71 , Q3 = 93 , so IQR = 35 and the fences are 5.5 and 145.5. Nothing falls outside, so the whiskers run from 52 to 104: Now look at the histogram of the same 20 scores in classes five wide: The box plot shows one tidy box with the median sitting inside it. The histogram shows two clumps and a valley between them. The box plot is blind to the valley: the box simply swallows it. That is exactly why the rule above says to look at the histogram first. [!NOTE] A box plot answers "where is the middle half, and are there outliers?" It cannot answer "how many clumps?". That is not a flaw, it is a limit. Know which question you are asking before you pick the picture.

secs.head: Check yourself
secs.body: 1. In the eight scores (62, 65, 69, 70, 79, 85, 94, 100), what is the percentile rank of 70 ? 2. The mean of those eight is 78 and the sample SD is 13.94. What is the z-score of 100 ? 3. A test has mean 60 and SD 10. A student scores 55. What is the z-score, and what does it say? 4. Mira's 20 tasting scores form two clumps. Which ruler would you trust for a single taster's position, and why? 5. A data set has Q1 = 10 and Q3 = 18. Is a value of 31 an outlier by the 1.5 × IQR rule? What about 29?

secs.head: Back to the story
secs.body: Tala looks at her two exam results again. The 84 she was proud of was the easier exam . The 61 she was embarrassed by was 2.75 typical distances above a brutal crowd. She peels the brewing result off the till and moves the cupping one to the top. "So I am better at cupping." "Than most people on that exam," says Mira. "Which is the only kind of better there is." Every question so far has been about what already happened : where the data came from, what kind it is, what it looks like, its middle, its spread, one value's place in it. Then Ravi leans over the counter with a different kind of question: "How many people will walk in tomorrow?" That is not a question about data you have. It is a question about chance , and it needs a different language. Next cup: Counting the Ways. Takeaway: a value has no position without its crowd. Rank counts heads, distance counts spreads, and the box plot is the ogive with its landmarks kept.

secs.head: Answers
secs.body: 1. Three values are below 70 (62, 65, 69) and one equals it, so (3 + 0.5) / 8 × 100 = 43.75% . 2. (100 − 78) / 13.94 ≈ 1.58 . (With the population SD of 13.04 it would be 1.69: the divisor choice from last page again.) 3. (55 − 60) / 10 = −0.5 : half a typical distance below the middle. A little under average, nothing dramatic. 4. The percentile rank . The mean and SD describe a middle where nobody lives, so a z-score would measure distance from an empty spot. Rank only counts how many are below, and that stays meaningful. 5. IQR = 8 , so the fences are 10 − 12 = −2 and 18 + 12 = 30 . 31 is an outlier (beyond 30), 29 is not (inside the fence).

secs.head: References
secs.body: - NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, Box Plot : quartiles, the 1.5 × IQR fences and the outlier circles. <https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/boxplot.htm - Python statistics module: quantiles with method='exclusive' (default) and 'inclusive' . Verified against Python 3.14.4. <https://docs.python.org/3/library/statistics.html - NumPy percentile : nine selectable methods, default 'linear' . This page did not run NumPy (not installed in the test environment), so no NumPy output is shown. <https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.percentile.html - Hyndman, R. J. and Fan, Y. (1996), Sample Quantiles in Statistical Packages , The American Statistician 50(4). <https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.1996.10473566 . The origin of the nine-type numbering. The paper itself was not retrievable here, so it is cited through the R documentation below, which names it and states its recommendation. - R documentation, quantile (package stats): nine types, default type 7, Hyndman and Fan (1996) cited, type 8 recommended by them. <https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/quantile.html - Every other number on this page was recomputed with Python 3.14.4.

label: Counting the ways
