title: Counting the Ways: Probability as a Share of the List
desc: Part 7 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. Parts 1 to 6 described data you have ; from here on, chance.

secs.head: Counting the Ways: Probability as a Share of the List
secs.body: Part 7 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. Parts 1 to 6 described data you have ; from here on, chance. By the end you will see that most probability problems are counting problems in disguise, and that "or" adds and "and" multiplies because of what they do to a list. The scenario is invented, and every count was checked by listing the ways in Python.

secs.head: Prologue: the lucky roll
secs.body: Mira puts two dice and a sign by the till: "Roll a double, or a total of 8, and the biscuit is free." Ravi studies the sign like a man reading a contract. "A double is one in six. A total of 8 is five in thirty-six. So that's 6/36 plus 5/36, eleven in thirty-six. You'll go broke." "Roll," says Mira. Ravi rolls 4 and 4. A double, and a total of 8, in one throw. He cheers, then frowns: "Did that count twice?" It did not, and that frown is the whole page. (Invented promotion; the counts below are exact.)

secs.head: The list of ways
secs.body: Last pages gave you a crowd of what happened . Chance needs a crowd of what could happen , and you write it down before you do anything else. - The sample space is the list of all possible outcomes. - An event is any combination of outcomes: "a double", "total of 8". - If every outcome is equally likely, the probability of an event is its share of the list: OpenStax defines the sample space and event in exactly these words and gives this counting rule for equally likely outcomes. Two dice have 6 × 6 = 36 outcomes, and the picture is a grid, first die down the side, second across the top. Cells marked D are doubles, 8 are total-8, and X is both: The whole sample space. Probability is how many cells you shade, out of 36. Notice the link to part 2. A relative frequency is what happened divided by the number of throws; this is what could happen divided by the number of cells. They are twins: roll often enough and the first drifts toward the second. ☕ Try it before you scroll. Count the cells marked D or 8 on the grid. Is it 11?

secs.head: Or adds, unless the ways overlap
secs.body: Count the shaded cells: 6 doubles, 5 eights, and the cell X is in both groups. Ravi added the two lists and counted X twice. The honest count is 6 + 5 − 1 = 10 , so the chance is 10/36, about 28%. When two events cannot happen together (a roll cannot be both 3 and 5 in one die), the overlap is empty and "or" is plain addition. The subtraction only repairs the double counting. The failure is easy to repeat, so here is the sharper version. Chance of at least one six in two rolls? "One in six, twice, so 1/6 + 1/6 = 12/36." The grid says 11/36 , because (6, 6) is counted twice. Adding probabilities is adding lists, and you must not let one outcome sit on the list twice. Now to a faster way to get 11. Why count cells that contain a six when it is easier to count the ones that do not?

secs.head: At least one: count the none
secs.body: "At least one" hides a long list: a six on the first die, or the second, or both. The complement , no six at all, is one clean rectangle: 5 values for each die, 5 × 5 = 25 cells. The sample space is split in two with nothing left over: the cells where it happens and the cells where it does not. So whenever the question says "at least one", flip it: count the none, then subtract from the whole. Ravi, take note: this is how a shop works out the chance that at least one order in a busy morning goes wrong.

secs.head: And multiplies, when the dice do not talk
secs.body: "And" asks for the cells where both events hold. Take "first die is even" (3 rows of 6 = 18 cells) and "second die is 5 or 6" (6 rows of 2 columns = 12 cells). Where both hold, you get a block of 3 rows by 2 columns: 6 cells . That is independence , in plain words: knowing one tells you nothing about the other. Knowing the first die is even does not change the share of the second die that is 5 or 6; it is still 2 of 6. The grid shows it as a clean rectangle, and an area is a product. Now an event that does talk. Let A be "first die is a 6" (6 cells) and S "total is at least 10" (6 cells: 4+6, 5+5, 5+6, 6+4, 6+5, 6+6). Both hold in 3 cells, not 6/36 × 6/36 = 1 cell. If the first die is a 6, you are much closer to 10, so the events are not independent, and multiplying would have been wrong. The same idea kills the gambler's fallacy. After three sixes in a row, surely a six is "due"? Write down all 6⁴ = 1296 four-roll sequences. Exactly 6 start with three sixes, and in only 1 of those 6 is the fourth roll a six: 1/6 , same as always. The dice have no memory, so the list does not shrink.

secs.head: Counting without writing it all out
secs.body: Mira's second deal: "Pick two free samples from six blends." How many different picks are there? If order matters (first pick, second pick), you have 6 choices, then 5 left: 6 × 5 = 30 . If only the pair matters, each pair was counted twice (A then B, B then A), so 30 / 2 = 15 . Python has both as functions, and itertools lists them so you can see: Output, as printed by Python 3.14.4: Mira keeps two blends secret. Ravi picks a pair at random. Chance he gets both ? 1 pair in 15. Chance he gets at least one ? Count the none: pairs from the 4 other blends, math.comb(4, 2) = 6 , so 1 − 6/15 = 9/15 = 60% . (Listing all 15 pairs confirms 1, 9 and 6.) Only count this way when each pick is equally likely; if some outcomes are likelier than others, a share of the list is not a probability.

secs.head: Back to the story
secs.body: Mira writes the real odds on the sign: 10 in 36, a free biscuit about once in 3.6 rolls. Ravi's 11/36 was wrong by one cell, and it was wrong in the direction that sounds scarier than it is. "I added two lists with a shared name on them," he admits. "Everyone does. Now go sit down," says Mira. "You rolled a double and an eight, and you still owe me for the tea." Takeaway: probability is the share of equally likely ways. "Or" adds lists (minus the overlap), "and" multiplies when the events ignore each other, and "at least one" is easiest as 1 minus none. Challenge for next cup. A rare thing affects 1 person in 1000. A test catches it 99% of the time, and wrongly flags 1% of healthy people. Ravi tests positive. Grid or no grid, write the list of 100,000 people and count who is flagged. Is he 99% likely to have it? Find out in The Test That Was 99 Percent Accurate.

secs.head: Check yourself
secs.body: 1. Two dice: chance the total is 7? Count the cells. 2. Two dice: chance of at least one even number? Use the complement. 3. Why is P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) wrong for "double" and "total of 8"? What is the fixed version? 4. Flip a fair coin four times, getting heads each time. What is the chance the fifth flip is heads, and why? 5. How many ways to pick 3 blends from 6 when order does not matter? (Check with math.comb .) 6. "A is independent of B" in your own words. Give one pair from the dice that is, and one that is not.

secs.head: Answers
secs.body: 1. The total is 7 in 6 cells (1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1): 6/36 = 1/6 . 2. No even number means both dice odd: 3 × 3 = 9 cells. So 1 − 9/36 = 27/36 = 3/4 . 3. The cell (4, 4) is in both lists and gets counted twice. Fixed: 6/36 + 5/36 − 1/36 = 10/36 . 4. 1/2 . The tosses are independent, so the first four tell you nothing about the fifth. A streak does not make the next one "due". 5. math.comb(6, 3) = 20 (6 × 5 × 4 = 120 ordered picks, divided by the 6 orderings of each trio). 6. Independent means knowing one does not change the share of the other. "First die even" and "second die is 5 or 6" are independent (18/36 × 12/36 = 6/36). "First die is 6" and "total is at least 10" are not (3 cells, not 1).

secs.head: References
secs.body: - OpenStax, Introductory Statistics 2e , Ch. 3 "Probability Topics", section 3.1 Terminology: sample space, event, and probability as a count for equally likely outcomes (quoted from the page). The chapter covers the addition and multiplication rules, but the page fetched here did not define independence, so the definition above is this page's own plain-words version. <https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/3-1-terminology - Python itertools : product , permutations , combinations , and their lengths via math.perm and math.comb . <https://docs.python.org/3/library/itertools.html - Python math : comb(n, k) "without repetition and without order", perm(n, k) "without repetition and with order". Since 3.15 these are soft-deprecated aliases of math.integer versions; on 3.14.4 they work as shown. <https://docs.python.org/3/library/math.html - Every count on this page was recomputed by listing the outcomes with Python 3.14.4, including the 1296 four-roll sequences for the gambler's-fallacy count.

label: The 99% accurate test
title: The Test That Was 99% Accurate: Conditional Probability and Bayes' Rule
desc: Part 8 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It continues from Counting the Ways, where probability became

secs.head: The Test That Was 99% Accurate: Conditional Probability and Bayes' Rule
secs.body: Part 8 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It continues from Counting the Ways, where probability became "count the outcomes you want, over all the outcomes". By the end you will see conditional probability as one move, shrinking the crowd, and Bayes' rule as nothing more than that move seen from the other side. The scenario is invented, and every number can be checked by hand.

secs.head: Prologue: the alarm that rang
secs.body: A supplier sends Mira a rapid check for a rare problem: a contaminated tin in a delivery. The leaflet is proud: "99% accurate." Roughly one tin in a thousand is contaminated. (Invented numbers, as always.) Tala runs the check on a tin from the new delivery. Positive. She goes pale and reaches for the bin. "Wait," says Mira. "How sure are we that this tin is actually bad?" "Ninety-nine percent! It says so on the leaflet." Hold that number. By the end of the page you will know it is far from the truth, and you will be able to see why without any formula.

secs.head: Shrink the crowd, then count again
secs.body: Last page, probability was a count: wanted outcomes over all outcomes. Now someone hands you extra information: "the tin tested positive." What changes? The crowd. You throw away everyone who does not match the clue and count again inside what is left . That is all conditional probability is. P(A B) , read "the chance of A given B", means: restrict to the crowd where B happened, then ask what share of that crowd also has A. Without the clue With the clue --- --- Count among all tins Count among only the tins that tested positive Denominator: everyone Denominator: the people who match ☕ Try it before you scroll. One tin in a thousand is contaminated. The check catches 99% of the contaminated ones, and wrongly flags 1% of the clean ones. Out of 100,000 tins, about how many will test positive? Hint: there are two ways to be positive.

secs.head: Build the crowd: 100,000 tins
secs.body: Do not start with percentages. Start with people-sized things you can count : a crowd of 100,000 tins, split by what is true, then by what the test says. These are called natural frequencies . Read the leaves from the bottom up: the test is 99% right about each branch, and the branches are very unequal. Now apply the one move. Tala's tin tested positive, so shrink the crowd to the positives : 99 (really contaminated) plus 999 (false alarms) is 1,098 tins . Only 99 of them are contaminated. Not 99%. About 9% . Roughly nine alarms in ten are false. The check is not broken; the base rate is the issue. Contaminated tins are so rare that even a tiny false-alarm rate (1% of a huge clean crowd) produces ten times more false alarms than true catches. Ignoring that is called base-rate neglect , and doctors, juries and engineers all fall for it. Check it by machine too, with exact fractions so nothing hides in rounding: The naive answer, 99/100, answers a different question. Which one?

secs.head: Two questions that sound alike
secs.body: Question Crowd you count inside Answer --- --- --- P(positive \ contaminated) : if a tin is bad, does the test flag it? The 100 contaminated tins 99 / 100 = 99% P(contaminated \ positive) : if the test flags a tin, is it bad? The 1,098 flagged tins 99 / 1,098 = about 9% The leaflet reports the first. Tala needs the second. Same two events, different crowd , wildly different answer. The tree makes the mix-up impossible: the first question stays on the left branch, the second collects all the positives from both branches. So how do you get from the first answer to the second without drawing a tree? That is where the famous formula comes in.

secs.head: The formula, after the fact
secs.body: The tree gave 99 / (99 + 999) . Write each piece as a probability instead of a head count and you have Bayes' rule : Here A is "contaminated" and B is "positive". Fill it in: - P(B A) = 0.99 : the leaflet's number. - P(A) = 0.001 : the base rate. - P(B) : all the ways to be positive, 0.99 × 0.001 + 0.01 × 0.999 = 0.01098 . Same answer, as it must be: the numerator is the 99 true catches (as a share of 100,000), the denominator is all 1,098 positives. The formula is the tree with the people divided out. You never need to memorize it: rebuild the crowd, shrink it, count. The rule just tells you how to flip P(B A) into P(A B) : multiply by the base rate, divide by how common the clue is. [!NOTE] The tree-of-counts way of explaining Bayesian problems is the frequency format studied by Gigerenzer and Hoffrage (1995). Their paper is about how people reason with it; this page uses the idea, not any of their results.

secs.head: A second positive: beliefs move
secs.body: Ravi wanders in. "Just run it again." After the first positive, the right belief is not 0.1% (before) and not 99% (the leaflet): it is about 9% . That is now the new starting point. Run a second check on the same tin, assuming the two checks make independent mistakes (a big assumption, see below), and suppose it is positive again. Shrink the crowd again: from 1,098 flagged tins, 99 contaminated and 999 clean. - Of the 99 contaminated: about 98 flag again. - Of the 999 clean: about 10 flag again (rounded to whole tins). Positives now: 98 / (98 + 10) = 98/108 , about 90.7% . Exact fractions give 363/400 = 90.75% . That is updating : the old answer becomes the new base rate. One positive was weak evidence against a rare event; two independent ones are strong. Nothing about the test changed. Only the starting crowd did. [!WARNING] If the second check shares the first one's flaw (same dirty reagent, same bad batch), the mistakes are not independent, and repeating it teaches you much less. Count the crowd honestly: who really passed through each branch?

secs.head: Check yourself
secs.body: 1. In the tree, how many of the 100,000 tins test negative , and how many of those are contaminated? 2. Why is P(positive contaminated) not the same as P(contaminated positive) ? Which one is on the leaflet? 3. A school has 1,000 pupils; 10 are in the chess club; 6 of the chess club wear glasses and 90 of the other 990 wear glasses. What is the chance a pupil with glasses is in the chess club? 4. Suppose the same check, still 99% accurate, were used on a delivery where half the tins are contaminated. Without computing: would a positive be more or less trustworthy than 9%? 5. Why does the second positive move the belief so much further than the first?

secs.head: Back to the story
secs.body: Tala is still holding the tin over the bin. "So the leaflet was not lying," she says. "It told me how the test treats bad tins. I asked it about this tin." "And this tin sits in a crowd where almost everything is fine," says Mira. "Nine alarms in ten are false. We run it again, and we check the batch code while we wait." They run it again. Positive. Now the tin goes in the bin with a clear conscience, 90% sure rather than 99% fooled. Takeaway: conditional probability is "shrink the crowd to those who match the clue, then count again"; Bayes' rule is that count read the other way, and rare things make even good tests mostly wrong when positive. Ravi has been counting tins in his head. "That is a lot of 'about'. If I run the check on all 100,000 tins, how many alarms should I expect altogether?" That is a question about the average of a chance, and it needs its own tool. Next cup: What to Expect.

secs.head: Answers
secs.body: 1. 98,901 + 1 = 98,902 test negative, and 1 of them is contaminated (1/98,902, about 0.001%). A negative is very trustworthy here. 2. They count inside different crowds: the first inside the contaminated tins, the second inside the flagged tins. The leaflet reports P(positive contaminated) . 3. Glasses wearers: 6 in the club plus 90 outside = 96. 6 / 96 = 1/16 , about 6%. 4. More trustworthy. With 50,000 contaminated tins, 49,500 are caught and only 500 clean ones are flagged: 49,500 / 50,000 = 99% . The base rate did the work. 5. Because the first positive already moved the starting crowd from 100 contaminated out of 100,000 to 99 out of 1,098. The second check works inside that far richer crowd.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Gigerenzer, G. and Hoffrage, U. (1995), How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: Frequency formats , Psychological Review 102(4), 684-704. <https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.102.4.684 . Bibliographic details confirmed through Crossref's record for that DOI; the publisher's page would not load here, so the paper's text and findings are not quoted. - All counts, fractions and percentages on this page were recomputed with Python 3.14.4 using exact fractions.Fraction . The scenario and its rates (1 in 1,000, 99% and 1%) are invented for teaching.

label: What to expect
title: What to Expect: Random Variables and Expected Value
desc: Part 9 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series, after The Test That Was 99 Percent Accurate. By the end you w

secs.head: What to Expect: Random Variables and Expected Value
secs.body: Part 9 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series, after The Test That Was 99 Percent Accurate. By the end you will know that expected value is not a new idea : it is the seesaw of The Number on the Tin and the leftover walk of How Far From the Middle?, with probability in place of frequency.

secs.head: Prologue: the lucky tin
secs.body: Mira has an idea for the weekend market: the lucky tin . A customer pays 5 coins, pulls one card from a bag, and wins the prize printed on it. The bag is invented for this page, and every number can be checked by hand. Ten cards: "Is it a good deal for us?" asks Tala. "For them?" "On any one pull, who knows," says Mira. "Over a whole Saturday, I would like to know what to expect ." Ravi, first in line, says what everyone says: "Expect the most likely thing, a sticker." Hold that thought. It is going to be wrong, and the reason is the whole page. ☕ Try it before you scroll. If a customer pulled a card, put it back, and pulled again, 100 times, about how many coins of prizes would you hand out per pull? Just guess. Hint: you have done a "typical value of a table" before.

secs.head: A number for every way it could go
secs.body: A random variable is a number attached to each way things could turn out. That is the whole definition. Pulling a card is the chance; the prize printed on it is the random variable, call it X . The card is not a number, the prize is. Write down each possible X and how much probability it gets, and you have a probability table , the "who gets how much probability" list: Prize x 0 5 10 20 --- --- --- --- --- Probability p 5/10 3/10 1/10 1/10 The probabilities add to 1, because something must happen. This table looks exactly like the frequency table from Part 2, and that is not an accident. A frequency table is what a bag did produce. A probability table is what a bag would produce, in the model. Relative frequency in the data; probability in the model. Everything below uses that twin.

secs.head: The seesaw again
secs.body: Remember the mean as a balance point: put each value on a seesaw, weighted by how often it shows up, and the mean is where it balances. Here the weights are the probabilities instead: The twins: swap frequency for probability and the mean becomes the expected value. The expected value is each prize times its probability, added up. Use exact fractions so nothing hides in rounding: That is 0 0.5 + 5 0.3 + 10 0.1 + 20 0.1 = 4.5 coins. And here is the twin at work: put the same ten cards in a tray and take the plain mean of the ten prizes. Same number, because it is the same seesaw. With a pile of cards you take the mean; with a table of probabilities you weight. Nothing new to memorize. So the lucky tin hands out 4.5 coins per pull on average , and Mira charges 5. The customer is behind by half a coin per pull. But what is "4.5" to someone holding a single card?

secs.head: The surprise: nobody wins 4.5
secs.body: Look at the table. No card says 4.5. The expected value is not a possible prize , and that is fine, because it is not a prediction of one pull. Same story as the number on the tin: 75.2 was a score nobody gave, and it was still the balance point. Now fix Ravi's instinct. He said "expect the most likely thing". Compare: Question Answer --- --- Most likely prize (the mode ) 0, with probability 0.5 Expected value (the balance point ) 4.5 Chance that a pull pays exactly the expected value 0 The most likely outcome is 0 and the expected value is 4.5. They answer different questions: the mode asks "what one thing is likeliest?", the expected value asks "where does the pile of outcomes balance?". The 20-coin card is rare, but it sits far out on the seesaw and drags the balance point up. Expected does not mean likely. It means balanced. ☕ Try it before you scroll. Is the expected value ever a possible value? Hint: a fair six-sided die. What is its balance point? (Answer: 3.5, and no face says that.) How trustworthy is the 4.5, then? Only over many pulls, which we can test. But first, the other half of the twin.

secs.head: What is left over, again
secs.body: A balance point alone hides how wild the day will be. In Part 5 the leftover was the average squared walk from the mean. Same here, weighted by probability: the variance is the probability-weighted average of (x - 4.5)² , and a shortcut gives the same answer, E[X²] - (E[X])² . By exact fractions: The variance is 37.25 coins², the standard deviation about 6.1 coins . A typical pull misses the 4.5 by about 6 coins, which is more than the expected value itself: a lumpy game. The data twin pvariance agrees, since the ten cards are the whole bag, so we divide by n (Part 5's rule: everyone in the room).

secs.head: Expect, don't predict
secs.body: The honest reading of "expected value" is a long-run average : do it many times and the average drifts to it. Do it once and anything on the table can happen. Let a computer pull cards (simulated, random.seed(9) ): Ten pulls: 3.5, a full coin off. A thousand: 4.365. A hundred thousand: 4.485, nearly the exact 4.5. Notice the share of zeros hovers around 0.5 the whole time, while the average creeps toward 4.5 without ever being a prize. Why the long-run average settles down, and how fast, is the subject of Why Averages Behave.

secs.head: Shifting and adding
secs.body: Two rules save work, and you can check both by listing every outcome. Every customer pays 5, so the net result is X - 5 : Net expected value is -1/2 : shifting every value shifts the balance point by the same amount, and the variance stays 149/4, since a shifted walk is the same walk. Scaling by a multiplies the expected value by a and the variance by a² . Now two customers' pulls added, X + Y , listing all 16 combinations of cards: The expected total is 9 = 4.5 + 4.5 : expected values add, always. The variance also doubled to 149/2 here, because the two pulls are independent (the card is put back). That second part is a trap: variances add only when the pulls do not influence each other. Contrast 2X , one pull paid out twice, where the variance is 4 37.25 = 149 , twice as big as for two separate pulls. The rule: expected values always add; variances add only for independent pulls.

secs.head: Check yourself
secs.body: 1. A fair die: write the probability table and the expected value. Is it a possible roll? 2. The lucky tin charges 6 instead of 5. What is the customer's expected net, and what happens to the variance? 3. In 1,000 pulls, roughly how many coins of prizes does Mira hand out? Roughly how many pulls pay nothing? 4. Ravi says "expect a sticker." Which statement is true, and which is the thing he is confusing it with? 5. A pull is made twice and the prizes are added. What is the expected total, and why can the variance not simply be assumed to double?

secs.head: Back to the story
secs.body: Mira prints the sign: "Lucky tin: 5 coins, prizes worth 4.5 on average." Ravi pulls once and wins the big tin. "The deal is rigged in my favour!" One pull cannot show that. Over the whole Saturday, 4.5 is what the cards will average to, and the half coin lost per customer is Mira's pay for the lumpy ride. Takeaway: a random variable is a number for each way things could go, the expected value is the balance point of those numbers weighted by probability (the seesaw of Part 4), and the variance is the leftover walk (Part 5). It is what to expect on average, not what will happen on a single go. Now the challenge. Tala flips a coin 3 times and counts heads. The count is a random variable with a table of its own. What are its probabilities, and what is its expected value, with no cards in sight? Next cup: Coins and Calls

secs.head: Answers
secs.body: 1. Faces 1 to 6, each with probability 1/6. E = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 3.5 , and no face says 3.5. 2. The expected net becomes 4.5 - 6 = -1.5 . The variance is unchanged at 37.25, because shifting every value does not change the spread. 3. About 1000 4.5 = 4,500 coins , and about 500 pulls pay nothing (the simulation gave 512). 4. A sticker is the most likely single prize (probability 0.5). The expected value (4.5) is the balance point. They are different questions, and here they are far apart. 5. The expected total is 4.5 + 4.5 = 9 . Expected values always add. The variance doubles (to 149/2) only because the two pulls are independent; for dependent pulls, such as 2X , it does not.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Python fractions module: Fraction does rational arithmetic exactly. <https://docs.python.org/3/library/fractions.html - Python statistics module: fmean (with weights ), pvariance , pstdev . <https://docs.python.org/3/library/statistics.html - OpenStax, Introductory Statistics 2e , section 4.2 "Mean or Expected Value and Standard Deviation": the expected value as the long-term average, mu = sum of x P(x) . <https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/4-2-mean-or-expected-value-and-standard-deviation - Every number on this page was recomputed with Python 3.14.4 (exact fractions, and a seeded simulation, random.seed(9) ); the linearity claims were checked by enumeration for one table, not proved in general.

label: Coins and calls
title: Coins and Calls: Binomial and Poisson as Recipes
desc: Part 10 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It continues from What to Expect, where a long-run average (

secs.head: Coins and Calls: Binomial and Poisson as Recipes
secs.body: Part 10 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It continues from What to Expect, where a long-run average (E[X]) and a spread became two numbers you can compute from a table of chances. Here we build two such tables from a question. The scenario numbers are invented, and every figure was recomputed with Python.

secs.head: Prologue: ten customers, one smoky blend
secs.body: Mira has ordered a crate of her smoky blend, and she wants to know how many cups to brew ahead. "About three in ten customers pick it," she says. (Invented: 30%.) "Ten customers are in the queue. How many smoky orders?" Tala answers instantly: "Three." "Exactly three? How often?" Tala opens her mouth, shuts it, and reaches for a pencil. Three is the average . It is not the answer . The answer is a whole table of chances, and today we build it from scratch.

secs.head: A distribution is a recipe
secs.body: A distribution is a table that says how much probability each possible value gets. You met one in part 9. The trick of this page: you almost never write such a table by hand. You recognise the shape of the question and pick a recipe. Two questions, two recipes. The rest of the page is how each recipe is cooked and when it burns.

secs.head: Binomial: count the ways, weigh each way
secs.body: Start small: 4 customers, each smoky with probability 0.3, independently. Write every possible queue as a string of yes (smoky) and no. There are 2^4 = 16 strings. Each string with k yeses has the same probability, 0.3^k × 0.7^(4-k) , so group them by k (the counting from Counting the Ways): Smoky orders k Ways (strings) Chance of each way P(X = k) --- --- --- --- 0 1 0.7^4 0.2401 1 4 0.3 × 0.7^3 0.4116 2 6 0.3^2 × 0.7^2 0.2646 3 4 0.3^3 × 0.7 0.0756 4 1 0.3^4 0.0081 The whole recipe is one sentence: probability of k = (number of ways to place k yeses) × (probability of one such way). The ways column is a row of Pascal's triangle, 1, 4, 6, 4, 1. ☕ Try it before you scroll. For 10 customers, the table above grows to 11 rows. Before reading on: is "exactly 3 smoky" more likely than 50%, or much less? Hint: the rows must add to 1, and there are 11 of them.

secs.head: The shorthand, and what to expect
secs.body: For 10 customers there are 1024 strings, and the pencil gives up. A computer does not: it listed all 1024 and added up each string's probability (using exact fractions). Then it computed the shorthand comb(10, k) × 0.3^k × 0.7^(10-k) . Both tables were identical. The formula is only the counting, written short: k 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- Ways 1 10 45 120 210 252 210 120 45 P(X = k) 0.0282 0.1211 0.2335 0.2668 0.2001 0.1029 0.0368 0.0090 0.0014 ( k = 9 and 10 are 0.0001 and below.) So "exactly 3" happens only 26.7% of the time. Tala's "three" is the single most likely count, and it is still wrong nearly three times in four. Now part 9's two tools, applied to this table. Computing E[X] = sum of k × P(k) and the variance sum of (k − mean)^2 × P(k) exactly gives: Why np ? Each customer is worth 0.3 of a smoky order on average, and averages add over ten customers. Why p(1 − p) ? One customer's spread is biggest at p = 0.5 and shrinks to zero when the answer is nearly certain, and spreads of independent tries add. NIST's handbook states both results (mean np , standard deviation sqrt(np(1 − p)) ) and its one catch: p is fixed for all trials. The naive trap: "10 customers, 30% each, so the chance of at least one smoky is 10 × 0.3 = 300%." Adding chances that overlap overshoots. The honest route is the complement: 1 − 0.7^10 = 0.9718 . What did we assume? Two yes/no outcomes, the same p every time, and customers who do not influence one another. Remember that list. Next: what if there is no "n tries" to count?

secs.head: Poisson: many tiny chances
secs.body: Customers walk in at an average of 4 per 10 minutes (invented). How many in the next 10 minutes? There is no "n customers each saying yes". But we can build one: cut the 10 minutes into n equal slices so thin that at most one person fits in each, with chance 4/n per slice. Now it is a binomial with p = 4/n , and np = 4 stays fixed. Make the slices thinner and watch the table settle: k n = 10 n = 100 n = 1000 Poisson, rate 4 --- --- --- --- --- 0 0.0060 0.0169 0.0182 0.0183 1 0.0403 0.0703 0.0730 0.0733 2 0.1209 0.1450 0.1464 0.1465 3 0.2150 0.1973 0.1956 0.1954 4 0.2508 0.1994 0.1958 0.1954 5 0.2007 0.1595 0.1566 0.1563 6 0.1115 0.1052 0.1043 0.1042 The last column is the Poisson recipe, with rate λ (lambda, the average count per window): computed with math.exp . NIST gives this formula and its mean and variance. The "many tiny chances" link is shown here by the numbers (NIST's page does not discuss it), not proved. So Poisson is a binomial with the n thrown away: all you need is the average rate. Its signature is variance equals mean . A shop at rate 4 sees an empty 10 minutes e^(−4) = 1.8% of the time, and ten or more customers 0.8% of the time.

secs.head: When the recipe lies
secs.body: The Poisson recipe assumes a constant rate and independent arrivals . Ravi, who counts everything, has tallied arrivals in 12 ten-minute windows (invented): 8 quiet mid-morning windows, 1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 2, 1, 3 , and 4 lunchtime windows, 7, 8, 6, 9 . Variance twice the mean is the alarm. The rate was not constant, it was two rates (about 1.9 and 7.5) averaged into a number nobody lived at, like the two-clump scores in part 5. The fix is not a cleverer formula: use one Poisson per period. The binomial can break the same way through dependence. Suppose customers arrive as 5 couples who always order the same. The mean is still 3, but the variance jumps from 2.1 to 4.2, and "exactly 3 smoky" becomes impossible , because counts now come in twos. The recipe's formula would still print 26.7%. [!NOTE] The formula never checks its own assumptions. A distribution fits the world exactly as far as the story fits: independent, same p , same rate.

secs.head: Check yourself
secs.body: 1. Which recipe fits: (a) defective bulbs in a box of 12, (b) emails per hour, (c) heads in 8 flips? 2. For 4 customers at p = 0.3, why is the number of ways for k = 2 equal to 6? 3. What are the mean and variance for 20 customers at p = 0.1? 4. A counter's counts have mean 5 and variance 14. Does Poisson fit? 5. Why is "P(at least one) = n × p" wrong?

secs.head: Back to the story
secs.body: Mira brews three cups of smoky and hovers. Tala has the table now: "Five or more is 15%, so if we want to be safe 85% of the time, brew five." Ravi tallies the lunch rush and mutters that a single average hides two shops. "So that is two recipes for counting," says Tala. "Do the tables always look this lumpy?" Look back at the 10-customer row: it rises, peaks, falls. Make n huge and the lumps smooth into a curve that shows up everywhere. Next cup: The Bell Curve. Takeaway: a distribution is a recipe matched to a question. Binomial counts yeses in n independent tries (ways times chance of each way). Poisson counts events in a window (many tiny chances). Check the assumptions before you trust the table. Challenge: ten customers at p = 0.3 give a table that is lopsided. Using np and np(1 − p) , guess what happens to its shape when n is 1000.

secs.head: Answers
secs.body: 1. (a) Binomial (12 tries, defective or not), (b) Poisson (events in a window), (c) binomial (8 flips). 2. There are 6 places to put 2 yeses among 4 positions: comb(4, 2) = 4!/(2!2!) = 6 . 3. Mean 20 × 0.1 = 2 ; variance 20 × 0.1 × 0.9 = 1.8 . 4. No. Poisson needs variance close to the mean (5), and 14 is nearly three times that: look for mixed rates or clumped arrivals. 5. Chances overlap, and the sum can pass 1 (here 3.0). Use 1 − (1 − p)^n , which is 0.9718 for n = 10.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, Binomial Distribution (pmf, mean np , standard deviation sqrt(np(1 − p)) , p fixed across trials). <https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda366i.htm - NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook, Poisson Distribution (pmf, mean and variance λ ). <https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda366j.htm - Python math module: comb(n, k) , exp(x) . <https://docs.python.org/3/library/math.html - Every number on this page was recomputed with Python 3.14.4 ( math , fractions , brute-force enumeration of all 16 and 1024 strings). No simulation was used.

label: The bell curve
title: The Bell Curve: Probability as Area, and One Ruler for Every Bell
desc: Part 11 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It continues from Coins and Calls, where chance came as a ta

secs.head: The Bell Curve: Probability as Area, and One Ruler for Every Bell
secs.body: Part 11 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It continues from Coins and Calls, where chance came as a table of counts. By the end you will know where the bell comes from, why probability on a bell is an area and not a height, how one ruler (the z-score) makes every bell the same bell, and when to refuse to use it. The scenario is invented, and every figure was recomputed with Python.

secs.head: Prologue: the scale that is never exact
secs.body: Mira sells loose tea in bags marked 100 g . Tala weighs thirty of them on the shop scale and reports: "None weighs exactly 100. One is 100.3, one is 98.9, one is 101.4..." "Of course," says Mira. "What is the chance Ravi's bag weighs exactly 100.000 grams?" Tala thinks, then says something that sounds wrong and is right: "Zero." If the chance of any exact weight is zero, how can we ever talk about the chance of a weight at all?

secs.head: Where the bell comes from
secs.body: Start with something you already own: the table of coin-flip counts from last part. Flip a fair coin n times, count heads. Each flip is one small nudge, up or down, and the table shows how the nudges pile up (each is a share of the 2^n equally likely sequences): (Rows under 0.5% are left out. Exact counts, computed with Python.) Nobody drew a bell. The bell is what you get when many small independent nudges add up : the middle gets every mix of ups and downs, the ends need all the nudges to line up. Mira's bags are the same story, with tiny scoop errors pushing each bag a little up or down. What happens when the steps get so fine that no step is left?

secs.head: Probability is area
secs.body: With 30 flips there are 31 possible counts, and each has its own probability. A weight on a scale has infinitely many possible values between 99 and 101. Share 100% among infinitely many exact values and each gets nothing: P(weight = exactly 100.000...) = 0 . So we stop asking about points and ask about ranges . Draw the hill, and let the area under it be the probability. The whole area is 1; the area between 98 and 106 g is the chance a bag lands there. The height of the curve is not a probability, it is a density : how crowded the chances are near that spot. This is the histogram from part 3 taken to its end: a bar's area was the share of the data, and with infinitely thin bars the bars become a curve. A single line has no width, so it has no area. How do we measure the area under a hill?

secs.head: Two dials, one bell
secs.body: The curve with the nice formula is the normal distribution . It has exactly two dials: Dial What it does You already know it as --- --- --- Mean (μ) Slides the whole bell left or right The middle, part 4 Standard deviation (σ) Stretches or squeezes it (the total area stays 1) The spread, part 5 NIST's handbook calls these the location and scale parameters. Give me a mean and an SD and the whole bell is fixed. That is convenient, and a very strong claim about your data. But every pair of dials is a different hill, and areas need calculus. Do we need a table for each?

secs.head: The one ruler
secs.body: No. Remember the z-score from part 6: z = (x − mean) / SD converts any value into "how many typical distances from the middle". On a normal curve that conversion does something remarkable. Slide the bell to the middle (subtract the mean), then rescale so the SD is 1 (divide by it) and every normal bell becomes the same bell : the standard normal , mean 0, SD 1. Part 6's ruler finally earns its keep: one standardizing step, then one table for all bells. Python's statistics.NormalDist holds that one table. Its cdf(x) gives the area to the left of x , that is P(X <= x) . With the standard bell: That is the 68-95-99.7 rule , with its exact decimals: about 68.27% of a normal crowd lies within 1 SD of the mean, 95.45% within 2, 99.73% within 3. (The famous "95%" is really 1.96 SD, which gives 0.95 almost exactly; "2" is the friendly round version.) ☕ Try it before you scroll. Mira's bags are normal with mean 100 g and SD 4 g (invented). What share weigh under 106 g ? Hint: turn 106 into a z-score first. Here is Ravi's bag, on the ruler: A 106 g bag is z = 1.5, and 93.32% of bags weigh less. Between 98 and 106 g is the area from z = −0.5 to z = 1.5, so 0.9332 − 0.3085 = 0.6247, which matches the code. Over 108 g (z = 2) is the thin 2.28% tail. And the sliver around exactly 100 is 0.00002: tiny, and it only gets smaller. That answers the prologue. Same function, after one subtraction and one division. Remember that one fact. Now run the ruler backwards.

secs.head: From z back to a value
secs.body: Sometimes you know the share and want the value: "how heavy is a bag that beats 95% of bags?" That is a percentile , the rank ruler from part 6, and inv cdf is the inverse of cdf : The 95th percentile sits at z = 1.6449, so in grams it is 100 + 1.6449 × 4 = 106.58 . Two directions, one ruler: value → z → area ( cdf ), or area → z → value ( inv cdf ). So far the bell has behaved. What happens when the data disagree?

secs.head: When the data are not a bell
secs.body: Go back to Mira's 20 tasting scores, the two-clump crowd from earlier parts. Their mean is 75.2 and their SD 17.67. Treat them as normal and ask what the model predicts for how many scores lie within a given distance of the mean, then count: Read the three lines together. Within half an SD of the mean the bell expects nearly 8 scores and there are 2 : the mean sits in the valley where nobody lives. The 2 SD line, on its own, looks fine (19.1 versus 20), which is the trap: passing one check does not make a crowd normal. The shape failed where the middle is. A long tail breaks it too. Kettle Street's houses (1, 2, 2, 3, 5, 9, 20) have one huge value dragging the right side out, so a bell around their mean would give real probability to impossible negative values. Incomes and waiting times are lopsided the same way. So the habit from parts 3 and 6 comes first, before any NormalDist : draw the histogram. One hump, roughly symmetric, thin tails: a bell is a fair model. Two humps or a long tail: use percentiles and describe the shape.

secs.head: Check yourself
secs.body: 1. Why is the probability that a bag weighs exactly 100 g equal to zero, and why is that not a problem for asking about 98 to 106 g? 2. Bags have mean 100 g and SD 4 g. What are the z-scores of 92 g and 108 g, and what share of bags lies between them? 3. In a normal crowd, about what share lies more than 3 SD from the mean? 4. Tala scored 61 on a normal exam (mean 50, SD 4). What is her z-score and, in words, what does that say about her rank? 5. A histogram shows two clear humps. Can you use the 68-95-99.7 rule? Which ruler from part 6 do you use instead?

secs.head: Back to the story
secs.body: Ravi's bag turns out to weigh 106 g. "Is that suspiciously heavy?" he asks. Tala does not guess. She turns 106 into z = 1.5, says "93% of bags are lighter, 7% are heavier", and shrugs: "About one in fourteen. Unusual, not suspicious." Then Mira asks the question that is now sitting on the counter: "All that works if a bag's weight is bell-shaped. But Tala, if I weigh ten bags and average them, what do the averages look like?" Nobody knows yet. But it is the sort of question that decides whether anyone can trust a survey. Next cup: Why Averages Behave. Takeaway: a bell is many small nudges added up, probability on it is area, and the z-score is the one ruler that makes every bell the same bell, as long as the data really are one.

secs.head: Answers
secs.body: 1. A range between two numbers has width, so the area under the curve over it is not zero. A single point has no width, so its area is zero. We always ask about ranges. 2. (92 − 100) / 4 = −2 and (108 − 100) / 4 = +2 , so the share is the 2 SD figure, 95.45% ( 0.9772 − 0.0228 ). 3. 1 − 0.9973 = about 0.27% , split between both tails. 4. (61 − 50) / 4 = 2.75 . By the table, only a very small share (well under 1%) of that crowd scored higher: it is a top-of-the-class result. 5. No. The mean sits in a valley and the rule gets the shares wrong (the count test above). Use percentiles instead.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Python statistics.NormalDist : cdf , inv cdf and zscore , with mu and sigma as mean and standard deviation. Verified against Python 3.14.4. <https://docs.python.org/3/library/statistics.html - NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, Normal Distribution : the density with location and scale parameters, and the standard normal (mean 0, SD 1). The page does not state the 68-95-99.7 percentages, so those come from the run above. <https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda3661.htm - Every number and output on this page was recomputed with Python 3.14.4 (stdlib only).

label: Why averages behave
title: Why Averages Behave: The Sip You Could Take a Thousand Times
desc: Part 12 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It joins two halves: the sip from a stirred pot in Stir the

secs.head: Why Averages Behave: The Sip You Could Take a Thousand Times
secs.body: Part 12 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It joins two halves: the sip from a stirred pot in Stir the Pot First and the bell from The Bell Curve. By the end you will see an average as a random thing with its own shape and spread, and know exactly what makes it trustworthy and what cannot. Every number below was simulated with a fixed seed.

secs.head: Prologue: two sips, two answers
secs.body: Mira stirs the pot of tasting scores and takes a sip of two cups: the average is 57 . Tala stirs the same pot, sips two cups, and gets 99.5 . Same pot, same stirring, two honest averages, 42 points apart. "One of us is wrong," says Tala. "Neither," says Mira. "Each of us took a different sip . The surprise is not that we disagree. The surprise is how rarely a bigger sip would let us." Hold that thought: the average of a sample is not a fixed fact. It is whatever that sip happened to say.

secs.head: An average is a random thing
secs.body: The population here is the 20 tasting scores from earlier: two clumps, one around 58 and one around 93. Its mean is 75.20 and its standard deviation (dividing by N, since this is the whole pot) is 17.22 . Nobody scored near 75, so this is not a bell. Now do what no real shop can afford: take the sip over and over and write each average down. The collection of those averages has its own shape, centre and spread. It is called the sampling distribution of the mean: what the sip would say if you took the sip ten thousand times. You never see it in real life (you get one sip), but you can reason about it, and that reasoning is the whole of statistical inference. One pot, many sips, one pile of averages. The pile is what we study. ☕ Try it before you scroll. Sips of 30 cups instead of 2: will the pile of averages be wider, narrower, or the same width as the pile for 2? And will it still have two clumps? Hint: how likely is a 30-cup sip to be all low scores?

secs.head: Fact 1: the spread of averages shrinks
secs.body: Here is the experiment. Draw n scores from the pot (with replacement, so each draw is independent), average them, repeat 10,000 times. Python's random module, seeded so you can reproduce it: Output (simulated, Python 3.14.4): Two things to read off: - The centre does not move. The average of the averages sits at 75, the population mean, for every n. An average aimed at the right target stays aimed at it. - The spread falls like sigma over root n. The spread of the averages is called the standard error , and it tracks sigma / sqrt(n) closely: 17.22 for one cup, about 12 for two, 3.14 for thirty. That is the law of large numbers in its working form: bigger sips cluster tighter around the truth. The root is the catch. To halve the spread you need four times the sample, not twice. Going from 30 cups to 120 cups buys a second halving; going from 2 to 4 buys only a little. Precision gets expensive. In plain terms for n = 30: about 89% of the simulated averages landed within 5 points of 75.2, against only 41% for n = 2.

secs.head: Fact 2: the averages pile into a bell
secs.body: Spread is only half the shape. Print the pile of averages as a text histogram, one per 100 averages: The run printed three histograms; here are n = 2 and n = 30 (simulated): With n = 2 you still see the pot's two clumps, now smeared, with a new bump in the middle: one low cup plus one high cup averages to about 75. With n = 30 the two clumps are gone . One hump, centred near 75, falling away on both sides. A little lopsided, but a bell shape from a pot that has no bell in it. That is the central limit theorem : take the average of many independent draws, and the distribution of that average approaches a normal curve, whatever the shape of the crowd. NIST's handbook puts it this way: as the sample size becomes large, the sampling distribution of the mean becomes approximately normal regardless of the distribution of the original variable, is centred at the population mean, and has standard deviation approaching sigma over root N. Why a bell? One way to see it: averaging smooths. A single cup can be extreme. Thirty cups would need nearly all to be extreme in the same direction for the average to be, and the many ways of mixing highs and lows land in the middle. That is exactly the stacking-up-of-small-pushes picture from the bell curve page.

secs.head: What the theorem does not say
secs.body: These are the places people trip, so be exact: Tempting claim What is true --- --- "Large samples make the data bell-shaped." No. The 30 scores in your sample still show two clumps. Only the average over repeated samples is bell-shaped. "With n of at least 30, it is guaranteed normal." No. 30 is a rule of thumb , not a theorem. The theorem is a limit as n grows; how fast it arrives depends on how lopsided the crowd is. Heavily skewed crowds need more. "It works for any population." It needs a mean and standard deviation to exist (and independent draws). Some populations, such as the Cauchy distribution, have neither, so the theorem does not apply. "More data fixes everything." It shrinks random error only. See below. The condition comes from the statement in the MIT 18.05 reading (variables "having mean μ and standard deviation σ"). NIST's handbook lists the Cauchy distribution's mean and standard deviation as undefined, which is why it is the standard example of a crowd the theorem cannot tame.

secs.head: The failure path: a biased sip
secs.body: Remember the Saturday-morning poll: the first 30 people through the door were not a fair copy of the 4,000. Suppose Mira's sips only ever come from the high clump, the 11 scores of 70 or more (mean 89.27 ), because those are the cups people stay to finish. Repeat the experiment on that biased pool: (simulated.) The spread shrinks beautifully, 6.64 then 1.73 then 0.42, and the averages are confidently, tightly wrong : they converge on 89.3, not 75.2. A bigger biased sample is just a more precise answer to the wrong question. The law of large numbers promises convergence to the mean of what you are drawing from . Whether that is the pot you care about is decided before any arithmetic, by who gets sipped. Stirring the pot is not optional, and no n compensates for skipping it.

secs.head: Check yourself
secs.body: 1. A population has sigma = 20. What is the standard error of the average of n = 25? Of n = 100? 2. You want to cut the standard error to one third. By what factor must n grow? 3. The 30 scores in a sample show two clumps. Does the CLT say the sample should look like a bell? 4. A survey of 10,000 people is taken only from one city's train station. Does the large n help you estimate the whole country? 5. True or false: "n = 30 guarantees the sample mean is normal."

secs.head: Back to the story
secs.body: Mira and Tala line up their 2-cup averages: 57 and 99.5. "We were never going to agree," says Tala. "A two-cup sip is a wide pile." Mira takes a 30-cup sip, then Tala does, and their averages come out within a few points of each other, both near 75. "So how close is close enough?" asks Tala. "If I say the true average is 75, how wrong could I be?" Mira smiles. "Now you can answer that. You know the pile of averages is a bell, centred on the truth, with spread sigma over root n. Use the bell page's tricks on it." That is the next cup: How Sure Are You? Takeaway: an average is a random thing with its own distribution; its spread shrinks as sigma over root n, its shape tends to a bell whatever the crowd looks like, and none of that cures a biased sample. Challenge: you took one 30-cup sip and got an average of 78. You do not know the true mean. Using only the bell and the standard error, what range would you be willing to bet on?

secs.head: Answers
secs.body: 1. 20 / sqrt(25) = 4 and 20 / sqrt(100) = 2 . 2. Nine times: the standard error goes as 1/sqrt(n), so n must grow by 3 squared. 3. No. The theorem is about the distribution of averages across samples. A single sample still looks like its population. 4. No. It shrinks the random error about the station crowd, which is a different population. The estimate converges to the wrong value, tightly. 5. False. It is a rule of thumb. The theorem is a limit, and the speed depends on the shape of the population.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, section 1.3.6.6.1, Normal Distribution , "Theoretical Justification - Central Limit Theorem": the statements of approximate normality, the centre at the population mean and the sigma over root N standard deviation. <https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda3661.htm - MIT OpenCourseWare 18.05, Introduction to Probability and Statistics (Spring 2022), Class 6 reading on the central limit theorem and the law of large numbers, section 5.2: for independent, identically distributed variables with mean μ and standard deviation σ, the average is approximately N(μ, σ²/n) for large n, and the precise statement is that the cdf of the standardized average converges to the standard normal cdf. Read from the PDF's page images, since its text layer is not extractable. <https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/mit18 05 s22 class06-prep-b.pdf - OpenStax Introductory Statistics 2e , section 7.1, The Central Limit Theorem for Sample Means : sample means tend toward a normal distribution for any population shape, centred on the population mean with standard deviation σ/√n (the standard error); the text gives no minimum sample size, so "n ≥ 30" on this page is a rule of thumb, not something that source states. <https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/7-1-the-central-limit-theorem-for-sample-means-averages - NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook, section 1.3.6.6.3, Cauchy Distribution : the mean and standard deviation are listed as undefined. <https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda3663.htm - Python random module: seed and choices (draws with replacement); seeded output is reproducible on a given Python version but may change between versions. <https://docs.python.org/3/library/random.html - Every number on this page was simulated or recomputed with Python 3.14.4, standard library only, seed 12.

label: How sure are you
title: How Sure Are You? Confidence Intervals
desc: Part 13 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It continues from Why Averages Behave, where you learned how

secs.head: How Sure Are You? Confidence Intervals
secs.body: Part 13 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It continues from Why Averages Behave, where you learned how much a sample average wobbles (the standard error). By the end you will turn that wobble into an honest "give or take", know what the famous "95%" really claims, and know the one way a tight interval can still be wrong. The scenario is invented, and the simulation is labelled as simulated.

secs.head: Prologue: the number on the tin, again
secs.body: Mira wants a line on the new tin: "Customers love it: 78%." She asked 100 customers and 78 said yes. (Invented numbers.) Tala, who has been reading the previous part, frowns. "If you asked a different 100 people, would you get 78 again?" "Probably not. Maybe 74. Maybe 83." "Then what are we printing? A fact, or one draw out of the bag?" Mira has no answer. The honest label is a number with a size of doubt on it .

secs.head: One number or a net
secs.body: A sample average is one throw at an unseen target, the true value in the whole population. Last part measured how wide your throws scatter: the standard error , SD / sqrt(n) . A confidence interval just uses that scatter to turn one throw into a net : z is how many standard errors you stretch the net. For the usual 95% net, z = 1.96 (Python: NormalDist().inv cdf(0.975) : the middle 95% of a bell curve sits between -1.96 and +1.96 ). Mira's tin, checked by hand. A yes/no answer is an average of 1s and 0s, and its spread is sqrt(p × (1 − p)) , so: "Customers love it: 78%, give or take 8 points." That is a label Tala can defend. But what does the 95% promise? Almost everyone gets this wrong, including people who use the phrase daily.

secs.head: What the 95% is about
secs.body: Tempting reading: "there is a 95% chance the true value is in this interval." That is not what it says. The true value is not random. It is a fixed number, sitting still. What is random is the net , because each sample lands a different net. The 95% describes the method : pick samples over and over, build a net from each one, and about 95 of every 100 nets catch the truth. Any one net either caught it or did not, and you never learn which. The target never moves. The nets move. The 95% is a property of the net-making recipe. ☕ Try it before you scroll. Build 100 intervals with the 95% recipe, each from a fresh sample. How many do you expect to catch the truth: exactly 95, about 95, or at least 95? Hint: the samples are random. We can run it, because a simulation lets us do what real life never does: know the truth. Build a population of 10,000 tin ratings (1 to 5 stars, invented), keep its true mean, then send 100 pollsters, each asking 40 customers. (Python 3.14.4, seeded, simulated .) 93, not 95. About 95 means about 95, and 100 is a small count to judge a recipe by. It ran a little low because the recipe uses the sample's own SD in place of the unknown true one (more on that below). Seven careful pollsters printed a net with the truth outside. That is not an arithmetic mistake. It is what "95%" means. So can you shrink the net without taking more risk?

secs.head: More data, narrower net
secs.body: You buy it with data. The margin is z × SD / sqrt(n) , so it shrinks with the square root of the sample size. Same population, same method, average width of 200 intervals at each size ( simulated , from the second loop of the same script): Customers asked Net width (stars) Compared with the row above --- --- --- 25 0.887 100 0.441 4x the data, half the width 400 0.222 4x the data, half again 1600 0.111 4x the data, half again The price list: to halve your doubt, quadruple your sample. The first customers are bargains, the later ones are luxury.

secs.head: No formula: shake the bag
secs.body: The formula needs a bell-shaped average and an SD you trust. The bootstrap needs neither. Your sample is the best picture you have of the population, so treat it as the population: draw from it with replacement , as many as you originally had, compute the average, and repeat thousands of times. The middle 95% of those averages is your net. Continuing the script, one new sample of 40, both routes ( simulated ): The two nets agree closely (3.30 against 3.296 below, 4.075 against 4.104 above). They are two honest estimates of the same wobble, and neither is "the" answer.

secs.head: Small samples, and the trap of a tight wrong answer
secs.body: Small samples. The 1.96 is exact only if you knew the true SD. You do not: you estimate it from the same few values, and with a small sample that estimate is itself shaky. The fix is to use the t distribution , a bell curve with slightly fatter tails, whose critical value depends on the sample size (the "degrees of freedom", n − 1 ). The net gets wider to pay for the extra uncertainty. NIST's formula for the mean uses exactly this t-value, not z. I checked two values by numerically integrating the t density (stdlib only): for n = 10 the 95% multiplier is 2.262 , and for n = 40 it is 2.023 , against 1.96. By about n = 40 the difference is small, which also explains part of the "93, not 95" above. The trap. Everything so far assumes the sample is a fair draw. Now let Mira be lazy: she asks only people at the counter who already bought the tin twice, the fans. In the simulation, that means sampling only from the 4-star and 5-star customers ( simulated , same script): The true mean is 3.75. None of 100 nets caught it. Each one is also narrow, because the fans mostly agree with each other, so the standard error is small: a tight, confident, wrong answer. A confidence interval measures only the wobble from chance . It cannot see a flaw in who you asked : that was the lesson of Stir the Pot, and no formula repairs it. [!WARNING] Narrow does not mean right. Narrow means precise. A tight net around the wrong spot is the most dangerous number on the tin, because it looks careful.

secs.head: Check yourself
secs.body: 1. Out of 200 customers, 120 said they love the tin. Give the 95% interval for the share (use 1.96 ). 2. A pollster's 95% interval is 3.3 to 4.1. A colleague says "there is a 95% chance the true mean is between 3.3 and 4.1." What is the honest correction? 3. An interval has width 0.40 with 100 customers. About what width with 400? With 25? 4. In the bootstrap, why draw with replacement? 5. You ask only people leaving a five-star-review event. You ask 2000 of them. Is the interval trustworthy? Why or why not?

secs.head: Back to the story
secs.body: Mira prints a new label: "78% of 100 customers asked said they love it (about 70% to 86%)." It is less punchy and a lot more defensible. Then Ravi, who is never satisfied, pulls two tins off the shelf. "The new blend scored 3.9 from 40 people. The old one scored 3.75 from 40 people. So the new one is better, right?" Tala looks at the width of the nets. Each is about a third of a star wide. The gap between the blends is 0.15 stars. Takeaway: a confidence interval is estimate plus or minus a margin that measures chance wobble. The 95% is about the method , not the single interval, four times the data halves the width, and no interval can fix a biased sample. Challenge: is a gap of 0.15 stars real, or just two bags that happened to differ? Telling those apart is a decision, not a measurement, and it works like a trial. Next cup: The Courtroom for Numbers.

secs.head: Answers
secs.body: 1. p = 120 / 200 = 0.60 ; standard error = sqrt(0.6 × 0.4 / 200) = sqrt(0.0012) = 0.0346 ; margin = 1.96 × 0.0346 = 0.068 . Interval: 53.2% to 66.8% . 2. The true mean is a fixed number, so it either is in that interval or is not. The 95% describes the method : if you repeated the sampling, about 95 of 100 nets built this way would catch the truth. 3. Four times the data halves the width: about 0.20 with 400. A quarter of the data doubles it: about 0.80 with 25. 4. The sample stands in for the population, and a fresh draw from a population can repeat a value. Drawing as many values as you had keeps the wobble matched to your real sample size. 5. No. The 2000 are all fans, so the interval is tight and describes fans, not customers. Sample size shrinks chance wobble, never bias.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, Confidence Limits for the Mean : interval estimate, 90/95/99% levels, the t-value formula, the 95% level read over repeated samples, width shrinking with larger N. Fetched and confirmed. <https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda352.htm - Python statistics module: NormalDist.inv cdf , fmean , stdev . The docs do not discuss confidence intervals or the t distribution, so those parts of this page come from NIST and from the runs above. <https://docs.python.org/3/library/statistics.html - The t critical values (2.262 for 9 degrees of freedom, 2.023 for 39) were computed on this page's behalf by numerically integrating the t density with the standard library, not copied from a table. - Every simulated number is from Python 3.14.4 with the seeds shown. Every other number was recomputed by hand and with Python.

label: The courtroom for numbers
title: The Courtroom for Numbers: Could Plain Luck Do This?
desc: Part 14 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It continues from How Sure Are You?, where a confidence inte

secs.head: The Courtroom for Numbers: Could Plain Luck Do This?
secs.body: Part 14 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It continues from How Sure Are You?, where a confidence interval put honest error bars on one number. By the end you will see every hypothesis test as one question, "could plain luck have produced a difference this big?", answer it by shuffling and counting, and know the three ways the answer gets misread. The scenario is invented, and every figure was recomputed with Python 3.14.4 (standard library only).

secs.head: Prologue: the blend that won
secs.body: Mira has two house blends, A and B . Ten customers taste each blind and score it from 1 to 10 (invented scores): "A wins by 1.2 points," says Tala, reaching for the menu-board chalk. "Does it?" says Mira. "Put the same tea in both cups and I would still not get two identical averages. How big a gap does luck alone make?" ☕ Try it before you scroll. Write the 20 scores on cards, deal them at random into two piles of ten. How often would the A pile still beat the B pile by 1.2 or more?

secs.head: The presumption of innocence
secs.body: A hypothesis test works like a courtroom. Courtroom The test --- --- The defendant is presumed innocent The null hypothesis : the blends are the same, the gap is luck only The evidence The gap you actually saw: +1.2 "Could an innocent person look this guilty by coincidence?" "Could luck alone make a gap this big?" Convict only if coincidence is a poor explanation Reject the null only if luck is a poor explanation The whole method in four boxes. Everything else is bookkeeping. If the labels A and B mean nothing, any way of dealing the 20 scores into two piles was equally likely . That is a world you can build yourself, with cards.

secs.head: Shuffle the labels and count
secs.body: First a case small enough to do by hand. Three tasters per blend: A scored 8, 9, 7 and B scored 5, 6, 7. The gap is 8 − 6 = 2 . Under "luck only", the six scores 8 9 7 5 6 7 could have been dealt into two piles of three in 20 ways (that is 6 choose 3 , from Counting the Ways). Which deals give A a lead of 2 or more? The scores add to 42, so A's pile must add to 24 or more. Only two do: 8 9 7 (the real one) and the same pile with the other 7 swapped in. Two of twenty: 0.10 . Luck does that one time in ten. Now Mira's real data. Twenty scores into two piles of ten has 184,756 deals, too many for the chalkboard, so we shuffle many times and count : The simulated answer is 0.0143 : in about 1.4% of re-dealt piles, luck alone gave A a lead of 1.2 or more (we asked "A better by at least this much", a one-sided question). The first line matches the hand count; the second is a simulation, so another seed moves the last digits. The third line is for later. That number is the p-value : how often luck alone would produce a difference at least as extreme as the one you saw. The classical test is the same question with a shortcut. Instead of shuffling, the t-test divides the gap by its standard error (Why Averages Behave) and looks it up on a bell curve (The Bell Curve). It is faster and assumes more; when its assumptions hold, the answers agree closely.

secs.head: What the p-value is, and is not
secs.body: A p of 0.0143 says: if the blends were identical, we would see a gap this big about 1.4% of the time. Luck is a poor explanation. Three misreadings, all named in the American Statistical Association's 2016 statement: The tempting reading Why it is wrong --- --- "There is a 1.4% chance the blends are the same" The p-value assumes the null to compute itself . It is not the probability the null is true "A is much better" p says how surprising the gap is, not how big it is. The ASA: it "does not measure the size of an effect or the importance of a result" "p above 0.05 means no difference" It means luck is not a poor enough explanation yet. Absence of proof, not proof of absence Effect size versus significance. They come apart. With 50,000 tasters per blend and a true gap of 0.03 points, a simulation gave an observed gap of 0.0277 and p about 0.00001: wildly "significant", practically nothing. The link to part 13. A confidence interval is the same story in points instead of surprise. If the 95% interval for "A minus B" sits entirely above 0, "no difference" is not a comfortable value: the same message as a small p. The interval is the better report, since it also says how big .

secs.head: Two ways to be wrong
secs.body: A court can convict the innocent or free the guilty. So can a test. Luck only (truth) A real difference (truth) --- --- --- Test says "luck is a poor explanation" False alarm (Type I): convicted the innocent Right Test says "luck could explain it" Right Missed effect (Type II): freed the guilty The significance level, often 0.05, is the false-alarm rate you accept. NIST's handbook puts it as "A value of α = 0.05 implies that the null hypothesis is rejected 5 % of the time when it is in fact true". The handbook lists 0.1, 0.05 and 0.01 as common choices and calls the choice somewhat arbitrary. 0.05 is a convention, not a law : a different cost of being wrong would justify a different line. The missed effect is the one people forget. We simulated 400 experiments where B is truly a full standard deviation worse than A, with only 5 tasters per blend. The test caught the difference in 110 of 400, about 27.5% . Seven times in ten, a real, large effect was waved through. That is why "not significant" cannot mean "no effect". Only more data lowers both errors.

secs.head: Twenty tries
secs.body: Tala has an idea: "Let me also split by morning vs evening, by age, by day, by milk or none..." Twenty comparisons later, one has p below 0.05. She wants it on the board. Each comparison has a 5% chance of a false alarm when nothing is going on. The chance of no false alarm in twenty independent tries is 0.95^20 , so at least one is 1 − 0.95^20 = 0.6415 : about 64% . A "discovery" is more likely than not, even if everything is identical. Simulate it: 300 imaginary studies, each with 20 comparisons between two groups of ten drawn from the same distribution, each tested by shuffling: Each test is close to its promised 5%, yet 205 of 300 studies (68%, simulated) found a "significant" difference that was nothing but luck, against 64% calculated. The gap to 64% is the noise of only 300 studies. This is p-hacking : try enough things, report the one that "worked". The cure is the ASA's fourth principle: "Proper inference requires full reporting and transparency." Say how many things you tried.

secs.head: Back to the story
secs.body: Mira holds the chalk back. "Our one planned question had p = 0.0143, so A probably is better. The milk 'win' came from twenty tries, and twenty tries will always find something. Rerun it with fresh tasters before we believe it." Tala writes: "Preferred in a blind test of 10 per blend, +1.2 points." Not "proven". Takeaway: a test asks whether luck alone could do this. A small p-value says luck is a poor explanation. It does not say the effect is big, the null is false with some probability, or that an unsignificant result means nothing is there. Challenge. Ravi counts that on days it rains, more people order tea. Rain and sales move together, but does one cause the other? Next cup: Two Things Moving Together.

secs.head: Check yourself
secs.body: 1. In the three-per-blend example, why is the p-value 0.10 and not something small, even though A averaged 2 points more? 2. A study reports p = 0.03. Is there a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true? 3. Study X (20 people, p = 0.2) and study Y (20,000 people, p = 0.0001) find the same gap. Which effect is larger? 4. Compute the chance of at least one false alarm in 5 independent tests at the 0.05 level. 5. A test on 5 people per group is "not significant". Does that show the two groups do not differ?

secs.head: Answers
secs.body: 1. Only 20 deals exist, and two reach a lead of 2 (the real pile, and the one with the other 7 swapped in): 2 of 20 is 0.10. Small samples let luck make big gaps. 2. No. It is the chance of data this extreme given the null, not the chance of the null given the data (ASA principle 2). 3. You cannot tell: the gap is the same, and p reflects gap and sample size. 4. 1 − 0.95^5 = 1 − 0.7738 = 0.2262 , about 23%. 5. No. With 5 per group even a true 1-SD difference was caught only about 27.5% of the time (simulated). "Not significant" means "not shown".

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Wasserstein, R. L. and Lazar, N. A. (2016), The ASA's Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose , The American Statistician 70(2):129-133. <https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108 . The journal page returned HTTP 403, so the paper itself was not read. The six principles quoted above come from the ASA's own press release of the statement, which was retrieved: <https://www.amstat.org/asa/files/pdfs/p-valuestatement.pdf . - NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 7.1.3. What are statistical tests? (null and alternative hypotheses, the risk of the first and second kind) <https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/prc/section1/prc13.htm , and 7.1.3.1. Critical values and p values (the α = 0.05 sentence and the arbitrariness of the choice) <https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/prc/section1/prc131.htm . - Every number was recomputed with Python 3.14.4 ( python3 -I , standard library, fixed seeds). The 50,000-per-blend and 400-experiment simulations are described, but their code is not shown.

label: Two things moving together
title: Two Things Moving Together: Correlation and the Line
desc: Part 15 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It continues from The Courtroom for Numbers. By the end you

secs.head: Two Things Moving Together: Correlation and the Line
secs.body: Part 15 of 15. Part of the Probability & Statistics series. It continues from The Courtroom for Numbers. By the end you will measure how two columns move together, draw the line through them, and know exactly when to distrust both. There is nothing new to memorize: two ideas you already own are reused. The scenario is invented, and every figure can be checked by hand.

secs.head: Prologue: cold days, full cups
secs.body: Ravi has bought tea at Leaf & Kettle for months, and he has a theory. "The colder it is, the more you sell." Mira shrugs. "Feels true." "Feels," says Ravi, and asks for the till book. Tala copies eight days into two columns: the temperature at opening, and the cups sold that day. (Invented numbers, small enough to check with a pencil.) Day 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- Temperature (°C) 2 4 6 8 10 12 14 16 Cups sold 58 50 52 42 40 30 28 20 How do you put a number on "feels true"? And what would the number not tell you?

secs.head: Draw it first
secs.body: Part 3 said it: draw before you describe. For two columns, the picture is a scatter plot , one dot per day, temperature across and cups up. Here it is as text, each row a band of 10 cups: The dots slide down as you go right. No clumps, no strays, roughly a line. This is the picture to check the number against, and later you will see why you must. ☕ Try it before you scroll. A perfectly downhill line should score one extreme, a shapeless cloud the middle. What numbers? Hint: minus sign for "one rises as the other falls".

secs.head: Idea 1: do the z-scores rise and fall together?
secs.body: Temperature is in degrees, cups are in cups. Different units, different spreads. You already own the tool that makes them comparable: the z-score from Where Do You Stand?, distance from the middle in typical distances. Convert every day to two z-scores. Then ask one question: on a day when temperature is above its middle, is cups above or below its middle? Multiply the two z-scores of each day: - both above, or both below: product positive (they agree); - one above, one below: product negative (they disagree). The correlation coefficient r is the average of those products. That is the whole definition. It lands between -1 (perfect disagreement along a line) and +1 (perfect agreement), with about 0 for no straight-line pattern. Ravi's days (mean temperature 9, mean cups 40, SDs 4.58 and 12.33, the divide-by- n SD from part 5): Every product is zero or negative. Their average is -0.982 : nearly perfect disagreement. Python's statistics.correlation should say the same, and it does: Two honest notes: r says nothing about how steep the pattern is, only how tightly dots hug a straight line; and statistics.correlation (Python 3.10+) returns Pearson's r , while 3.12 added method='ranked' (Spearman, for any always-rising or always-falling pattern). So r = -0.98 . But Ravi wants to predict : how many cups tomorrow at 5 degrees?

secs.head: Idea 2: the line is least squared walking
secs.body: You have met this problem in disguise. In How Far From the Middle?, the mean was the spot that leaves the smallest total squared walk to the crowd. Now the crowd is eight dots and the thing we place is a line . The walk of each dot is the vertical gap between it and the line, called its residual (what is left over after the line has said its piece). The same rule applies: the line that leaves the smallest total squared residual wins. That is least squares , and it is the whole idea of regression. Read each number in plain units: Number Value Meaning --- --- --- Slope -2.643 Each extra degree goes with about 2.6 fewer cups Intercept 63.79 The line's height at 0 °C (a point on the line, not a promise) Residuals -0.5, -3.21, 4.07, ... The leftover per day: actual minus the line. They add up to 0, the seesaw again Squared miss 42.57 Left after the line, against 1216 if you guess the mean, 40, every day The line removed 96.5% of the total squared miss (1 - 42.57/1216), and that fraction equals r² (0.9823² = 0.965). The two ideas are one fact seen twice. They are tied by a formula too: slope = r × (SD of cups) / (SD of temperature) , which gives -0.9823 × 12.33 / 4.58 = -2.643. The candidates 64 - 2.5x and 67 - 3x both miss by exactly 64.0, worse than 42.57. At 5 degrees the line predicts 50.6 cups . Sensible, since 5 degrees is inside the temperatures Tala wrote down. At 40 degrees it predicts -41.9 cups . A shop does not sell negative tea. At 40 degrees a shop sells negative tea. Is r = -0.98 any safer?

secs.head: Where it lies: four traps
secs.body: Each trap below is a case where the numbers say one thing and the truth is another. 1. Prediction outside the data. The line was fitted on 2 to 16 degrees.
