label: Fake GPUs in Kubernetes
title: Fake GPUs in Kubernetes: Learn GPU Scheduling Without Owning a GPU
desc: Real GPUs are expensive, shared, and always booked by someone else. Fake GPUs are free, always available, and will never

secs.head: Fake GPUs in Kubernetes: Learn GPU Scheduling Without Owning a GPU
secs.body: Real GPUs are expensive, shared, and always booked by someone else. Fake GPUs are free, always available, and will never melt a rack. If what you want to learn is how Kubernetes schedules GPU workloads (who gets them, who waits, who sits Pending forever), you don't need hardware. You need one command and a slightly dishonest node. This page builds on the two-node lab. The trick it teaches is also the cleanest way to understand what a real GPU device plugin actually does. ---

secs.head: The one-sentence version
secs.body: Kubernetes doesn't know what a GPU is; it only knows named counters on nodes called extended resources, so you can add a counter called nvidia.com/gpu to a node by hand and the scheduler will treat it exactly like the real thing. That's not a hack around the system. It's the documented mechanism. The official docs say extended resources let cluster administrators advertise node-level resources that Kubernetes would otherwise not know about, and that they're opaque to Kubernetes: it knows only that a node has a certain number of them. ---

secs.head: How the real thing works (so the fake makes sense)
secs.body: On a real cluster, a device plugin runs on each GPU node. It discovers the hardware and advertises it, so the cluster exposes a schedulable resource such as nvidia.com/gpu or amd.com/gpu . Kubernetes has stable support for managing AMD and NVIDIA GPUs this way. Your pod then asks for GPUs in its container spec. The rules from the official GPU scheduling docs: - GPUs are only supposed to be specified in the limits section. - You can give a GPU limit with no request, because Kubernetes uses the limit as the request. - If you give both, they must be equal. - You cannot give a GPU request without a limit. By default, a GPU is handed out whole. Two pods don't quietly split one device. (Sharing exists, through NVIDIA's MIG partitioning and time-slicing, but you configure it deliberately. It is not the default.) So there are two halves: someone has to advertise the counter, and someone has to request it. The device plugin does the first on real hardware. In the lab, you do it with a patch. ---

secs.head: Step 1: advertise four GPUs that don't exist
secs.body: Unpacking the parts: Piece Why it's there --- --- --subresource=status Extended resources live in the node's status , so the patch has to target the status subresource, the same /status endpoint the official docs use /status/capacity/... What the node says it physically has /status/allocatable/... What's left over for pods to use. The scheduler places pods against this figure, so the lab sets it too nvidia.com~1gpu The resource name nvidia.com/gpu , with the slash escaped as ~1 , which is how JSON Patch spells a slash inside a path segment. Yes, really "4" Extended resources must be whole numbers. No half GPUs Resource names should carry a domain prefix you control or that matches the real convention. The kubernetes.io prefix is reserved, which is why the fake uses the same nvidia.com/gpu name the real device plugin would. Check that it took: You should see nvidia.com/gpu: 4 alongside CPU and memory. ---

secs.head: Step 2: request them
secs.body: Here's a pod that wants two GPUs. The container is a do-nothing pause image, because the GPU is imaginary and we only care about the accounting: It schedules and runs, and the node now has two GPUs spoken for. Now ask for more than exist: That pod can never fit: the only node with GPUs has four. It will sit in Pending , and kubectl describe pod gpu-waiting -n team-b will show a scheduling event explaining that no node has enough of the resource. That event is the single most useful thing to learn to read on a GPU cluster, and the rogues' gallery page goes deeper. ---

secs.head: What's real, and what isn't
secs.body: Real Fake --- --- The scheduler's arithmetic: capacity, allocatable, who requested what There is no device. nvidia-smi won't exist Pending pods that can't fit, and the events that say why No driver, no CUDA, no device plugin Quotas, namespaces and monitoring tools that read these fields No isolation between "GPU users", because there's nothing to isolate That second column is the point of the exercise and its limit. The fake teaches allocation (what the cluster has promised to whom), which is half the story. The other half is utilization (what the hardware is actually doing), and for that you need real GPUs and real telemetry. The next-but-one page is about exactly that gap. ---

secs.head: Cleaning up
secs.body: The patch is removable the same way the official docs show: a JSON Patch remove on the same path. Delete the fake pods first if you want a tidy cluster. And if the node object is ever deleted and re-created (for example, you destroy and re-join the worker), the counters go with it, so patch again. ---

secs.head: A warning about mixing fake and real
secs.body: Don't run this trick on a cluster that also has a real device plugin advertising the same resource name. The two would disagree about reality, and the scheduler would believe whichever spoke last. The lab is isolated on purpose. Tools that expect real GPUs, such as NVIDIA's Cluster Readiness Engine, launch real NCCL workloads and need actual hardware; a fake counter will pass the scheduler and then fail when a container tries to use a device that isn't there. ---

secs.head: The one-paragraph takeaway
secs.body: A GPU, to the Kubernetes scheduler, is a whole-number counter on a node that pods ask for under limits . A device plugin maintains that counter on real hardware, and a single kubectl patch can maintain it in a lab, which makes the scheduler's behaviour completely observable for free: pods that fit, pods that wait, and the events that explain which is which. Just remember what the fake can't do. It can promise a GPU, but it can't run anything on one. ---

secs.body: - Advertise Extended Resources for a Node: patching /status , JSON Patch ~1 escaping, integer amounts, opaque resources, removal - Schedule GPUs: device plugins, GPUs specified under limits , request and limit rules, node labels for mixed GPU types The lab fixtures ( gpu-train , gpu-waiting ) come from the author's own lab. The remark about sharing through MIG and time-slicing summarizes NVIDIA's documentation and isn't covered by the Kubernetes pages above.

label: Broken Pods, the Rogues' Gallery
title: Broken Pods: A Rogues' Gallery (and the One Command That Catches Them All)
desc: Healthy pods are boring. They run, they get no attention, and nobody writes a blog post about them. The interesting ones

secs.head: Broken Pods: A Rogues' Gallery (and the One Command That Catches Them All)
secs.body: Healthy pods are boring. They run, they get no attention, and nobody writes a blog post about them. The interesting ones are the delinquents: the pod that restarts every few minutes like a bad habit, the one that was killed for eating too much, the one that can't find its own image, and the one waiting for a GPU that doesn't exist. This page introduces four of them. They come from the two-node lab and the fake GPU trick, where you can create each one on purpose and learn to recognise it on sight. ---

secs.head: The one-sentence version
secs.body: Every broken pod leaves clues in the same three places: its status, its events, and its previous logs, and you should read them in that order before you touch anything. ---

secs.head: The detective's routine
secs.body: Whatever the symptom, start here: Read the events before you restart anything. Events are short-lived (the API server keeps them for one hour by default, as covered in Kubernetes in Five Nouns), and a restart can add noise on top of the evidence. One vocabulary point that trips people up: a pod has a phase ( Pending , Running , Succeeded , Failed ), and its containers have status reasons ( CrashLoopBackOff , ImagePullBackOff , OOMKilled ). CrashLoopBackOff is a container status reason, not a pod phase, which is why a pod can show it while the pod itself is technically still going. ---

secs.head: The gallery
secs.body: Rogue What it does What you'll see --- --- --- crashloop Starts, exits with an error, repeats forever CrashLoopBackOff , climbing restart count oom Uses more memory than its limit allows OOMKilled as the last termination reason badimage Points at an image that can't be pulled ErrImagePull , then ImagePullBackOff gpu-waiting Asks for more GPUs than any node has Stuck in Pending , with a scheduling event

secs.head: 1. The crash looper
secs.body: The container prints a line and exits with status 1. By default the pod's restart policy brings it back, so the kubelet restarts it, and it fails again. To keep a broken container from restarting in a frantic loop, the kubelet waits longer after each failure: the delay is exponential (10s, 20s, 40s, and so on) and capped at five minutes. If the container then runs for ten minutes without trouble, the kubelet resets the delay. That behaviour explains two things people find puzzling: - A pod in CrashLoopBackOff is not hung. It's between attempts , and the status shows while the kubelet waits out the delay. - Once the delay hits its cap, the pod only retries about once every five minutes, so a slow crash loop can look like an intermittent outage instead of a hard failure. How to investigate: --previous is the part beginners miss. The current container may have just started and have nothing to say; the interesting output belongs to the one that died.

secs.head: 2. The one that ate too much
secs.body: This one is created by giving a pod a deliberately tiny memory limit and a workload that allocates more than that. When a container exceeds its memory limit, the kernel kills it, and Kubernetes records the reason. Ask for it directly: If the restart policy brings it back, you'll see the same restart-and-back-off pattern as the crash looper, and the distinguishing clue is the lastState reason, which is why you ask for it by name. The usual fixes are raising the limit, or fixing the leak. Raising limits without understanding the leak just moves the cliff.

secs.head: 3. The one that can't find its image
secs.body: The .invalid top-level domain is reserved so that it can never resolve, which makes it a perfect stand-in for "this registry does not exist." The pod first reports ErrImagePull , and after failed attempts it settles into ImagePullBackOff , another back-off pattern, this time for pulling. In real life the causes are usually a typo in the image name or tag, a private registry without credentials, or a registry the node can't reach. kubectl describe pod shows the exact pull error in its events, which tells you which of those it is.

secs.head: 4. The one waiting for a GPU
secs.body: The lab's only GPU node advertises four GPUs, so no node can ever host this pod. It stays Pending , and the clue is in the events: A Pending pod isn't running, so it isn't consuming anything. It's a request that nobody can grant. That's different from the first three rogues, whose containers actually started and failed. The fix is on the cluster side (more capacity, a smaller request, or waiting for another job to finish), not in the container. ---

secs.head: A quick triage table
secs.body: Pod status Container started? First place to look --- --- --- Pending No (not scheduled yet) describe events: scheduling failures ErrImagePull / ImagePullBackOff No (image can't be fetched) describe events: the pull error CrashLoopBackOff Yes, and it exits logs --previous and the exit code Restarting with OOMKilled Yes, and it's killed lastState.terminated.reason , then memory limits Running but not ready Yes, but probes fail describe events, then readiness probe config ---

secs.head: Why this matters on HPC clusters
secs.body: On a batch system you're used to a job that fails once and stays failed. Kubernetes' default instinct is the opposite: keep trying. That's great for web servers and surprising for GPU jobs, where a crash-looping pod that holds GPUs between attempts is a quiet way to waste an expensive resource, and a Pending pod can hide a quota or capacity problem for hours. A good monitor treats these four states as first-class signals, which is exactly what the later pages on monitoring build on. ---

secs.head: The one-paragraph takeaway
secs.body: Broken pods are not mysterious; they're just chatty in three specific places. Read the status, read the events, read the previous logs, in that order, and you can usually name the culprit in under a minute: crash looping (look at --previous ), OOM killed (check lastState ), image pull failing (read the pull error), or Pending with a scheduling event (the cluster can't grant the request). Don't restart first. The evidence is fragile. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Kubernetes restart back-off behaviour (10s, 20s, 40s, capped at five minutes, reset after ten minutes without trouble): described in KEP-4603, Tune Crashloop Backoff in the Kubernetes enhancement proposals. The defaults can change in newer releases, so check the current Pod lifecycle documentation for your version. - Pods: controllers and restart behaviour - kube-apiserver reference: --event-ttl , default one hour - Schedule GPUs: GPUs requested under limits The four fixtures, the lab commands and the triage table are the author's own. The FailedScheduling event text and the exact status strings shown are typical kubectl output; yours may differ slightly by version, so check what your cluster prints.

label: GPU Allocation vs Utilization
title: Booked Is Not Busy: GPU Allocation vs Utilization
desc: Picture a restaurant with four tables. Four parties have reservations. Three of them haven't shown up, and one has order

secs.head: Booked Is Not Busy: GPU Allocation vs Utilization
secs.body: Picture a restaurant with four tables. Four parties have reservations. Three of them haven't shown up, and one has ordered a glass of water and is now reading a book. The dashboard at the door says 100% booked . The kitchen says it's the quietest night of the year . Both are telling the truth, and if you only look at one of them you'll make the wrong decision. That's the difference between GPU allocation and GPU utilization , and mixing them up is one of the most expensive misunderstandings on a shared cluster. ---

secs.head: The one-sentence version
secs.body: Allocation is how many GPUs the scheduler has promised to pods; utilization is how hard the hardware is actually working, and Kubernetes natively tracks only the first. ---

secs.head: Allocation: what the scheduler has promised
secs.body: A pod that wants GPUs asks for them under limits , as the fake GPU page covered. The scheduler counts those requests against what each node advertises as allocatable. By default, a GPU is handed out whole, so a pod that asks for four GPUs holds four GPUs from the moment it's placed until it finishes, whether or not it ever touches them. That makes allocation the right answer to the question every user asks first: "Why won't my job start?" Because somebody else is holding the GPUs, whether or not they're using them. A pod that requests four GPUs and then sleeps blocks four GPUs from everyone else. You can see allocation without installing anything: The second command lists every pod with the GPU count it asked for and the node it landed on. Add those up per node and compare with the node's allocatable figure, and you have the allocation picture. ---

secs.head: Utilization: what the hardware is doing
secs.body: Utilization asks a different question: "Is anyone actually using the GPUs they're holding?" Kubernetes has no idea. Its scheduler deals in whole-number counters; it never looks at what the silicon is doing. The answer comes from the device itself: utilization, memory use, power, temperature and error counters. On a single machine that's nvidia-smi . Across a cluster, the usual stack is NVIDIA's DCGM Exporter (per-GPU hardware metrics, run as a DaemonSet on the GPU nodes), kube-state-metrics (the state of Kubernetes objects), Prometheus to store the numbers, and Grafana to draw them. NVIDIA publishes guidance on assembling exactly that for GPU usage visibility across clusters. This is why the two views are complementary instead of redundant: Allocation Utilization --- --- --- Question "Who is holding the GPUs?" "Who is actually using them?" Source The scheduler and the Kubernetes API The hardware, via DCGM and friends Needs extra tooling? No, plain kubectl Yes, an exporter plus a metrics stack Good for Debugging a pending job, capacity planning Finding waste, justifying hardware, spotting a slow GPU Blind spot A held GPU may be idle A GPU can look idle to a metric but still be reserved ---

secs.head: Four situations, and which view answers them
secs.body: What's happening Allocation says Utilization says Reading --- --- --- --- Job won't start, cluster looks "full" 8/8 allocated Maybe 10% busy Hoarding. Someone holds GPUs they aren't using Job won't start, but GPUs are free in total 6/8 allocated Low Fragmentation. Free GPUs are spread across nodes, none with enough for a 4-GPU job Everything's allocated and busy 8/8 allocated ~95% Healthy, and a good reason to buy more Training is slow, nothing looks wrong Allocated as expected One GPU behind its peers Utilization (or an active test) is the only view that can see it The last row is the story from the Cluster Readiness Engine page: a quietly slow GPU doesn't show up in allocation, and passive telemetry may not flag it either. The point of putting all three views side by side is that each one catches what the others miss. ---

secs.head: Why GPUs make this worse than CPUs
secs.body: Two reasons. GPUs are coarse. CPU capacity is divided into small, fungible slices (millicores). A GPU, by default, is allocated as a whole unit. That's why fragmentation is a real thing: two nodes with two free GPUs each can't run a four-GPU job that needs them together on one node. Sharing a GPU is possible, through hardware partitioning (MIG) or time-slicing set up in NVIDIA's software, but it's an explicit configuration with trade-offs, not a free default. Distributed jobs need everyone at once. A 512-GPU training job isn't useful with 400 GPUs. Without gang scheduling, a half-placed job can hold GPUs while it waits for the rest, which is the single biggest waste on shared clusters: lots of allocation, zero useful work. The Cluster Readiness Engine page covers gang scheduling and why it exists. ---

secs.head: For Slurm people
secs.body: You already know both views, under different names. squeue and scontrol show node tell you what's allocated; nvidia-smi and your accounting data tell you what was used. A job that requested 8 GPUs and used 1 is a familiar sight. The Kubernetes version differs in one habit: because pods are meant to be disposable and the scheduler never looks at hardware activity, nothing in the default setup nudges anyone to release an idle allocation. Reclaiming them is a policy choice (quotas, queues, timeouts), not something Kubernetes does for you. ---

secs.head: What to do with this
secs.body: - Debugging a pending job: look at allocation first. It's free and answers "who's holding them?" in one command. - Judging efficiency: look at utilization over time, in Grafana, not a one-time snapshot. - Never present one as the other. "The cluster is 100% utilized" and "the cluster is 100% allocated" are different sentences, and a team that conflates them will either buy hardware it doesn't need or leave real waste untouched. - Label your dashboards. Say "allocated" or "utilized" on the chart itself. It prevents the argument before it starts. ---

secs.head: The one-paragraph takeaway
secs.body: Allocation is the reservation book; utilization is the kitchen. Kubernetes keeps the reservation book, so kubectl can tell you who is holding which GPUs and why your job is Pending . It does not watch the kitchen, so finding idle or underperforming GPUs needs DCGM-style telemetry and a metrics stack. Use allocation to unblock people today, utilization to fix waste over time, and an active test when neither explains why the job is slow. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Schedule GPUs: GPUs are specified under limits , and the request/limit rules - NVIDIA Technical Blog, Get Real-Time Visibility into GPU Usage Across Kubernetes Clusters: the DCGM Exporter, kube-state-metrics, Prometheus and Grafana stack. I listed this link as a related article from NVIDIA's cluster-readiness post and have not read its full text for this page, so check it for current setup details. - NVIDIA Technical Blog, Validate GPU Cluster Readiness Before AI Workloads Land: active vs passive validation and gang scheduling The restaurant analogy, the four-situations table and the Slurm comparison are the author's own framing, not official terminology. The statements about MIG and time-slicing summarize NVIDIA's documentation, not the Kubernetes pages above.

label: NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine
title: The Cluster That Passed Every Test Except the One That Mattered
desc: Every platform engineer has lived this morning. The dashboards are green, DCGM is smiling, the fabric reports no errors,

secs.head: The Cluster That Passed Every Test Except the One That Mattered
secs.body: Every platform engineer has lived this morning. The dashboards are green, DCGM is smiling, the fabric reports no errors, and every pod is Running . You announce the cluster ready, someone launches a 512-GPU training job, and the job proceeds to run like a laptop on 2% battery. Nothing is "broken." No alert fires. One GPU is a bit slow, one link only degrades when it's actually pushed, one route is quietly longer than intended. Yet a synchronous training job moves at the speed of its slowest rank, so a single shy GPU can hold hundreds of its colleagues hostage. This page is about the tool NVIDIA built for exactly that morning: NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine (NVCRE) . It's a good page to read after Kubernetes in Five Nouns, because it uses a Kubernetes pattern you'll meet everywhere: you declare what you want, and a controller does the work. ---

secs.head: The one-sentence version
secs.body: NVCRE is an open source Kubernetes controller that proves a GPU cluster is ready by running real distributed workloads on it, then tells you which nodes failed and why. The thesis is almost insultingly simple: the best way to find out whether a cluster can run a workload is to run the workload. On Slurm that's one srun away. On Kubernetes there's no built-in equivalent, because the test needs GPU and RDMA resource requests, NCCL settings matched to your fabric, a big enough shared-memory volume, and every pod starting together. NVCRE packages all that up. ---

secs.head: Why "all green" isn't "ready"
secs.body: Two kinds of tools watch a cluster, and they see different things. Passive (telemetry) Active (workload-driven) --- --- --- Question it answers "Is anything obviously broken?" "Will this cluster hold up under real load?" How it works Watches signals the cluster already emits Generates real load and measures the result Blind spot Problems that emit nothing It uses GPU time, so you can't run it all day Example here NVSentinel NVCRE A GPU running a few percent slow with no errors and no log lines is invisible to a passive watcher, because there's nothing to watch. It only shows up when something leans on the hardware. If this sounds familiar, it's the same lesson as the OSU benchmarks page: run different tests that exercise different layers, and let the layer that fails tell you where to dig. ---

secs.head: Readiness is a staircase, not a light switch
secs.body: A cluster doesn't flip from "not ready" to "ready." The article describes four stages: bring-up, burn-in, preproduction, production . Each one sets a higher bar, and a node that passes a smoke test is not automatically fit for a 512-GPU run. Most teams encode this staircase in runbooks, spreadsheets and shell scripts wrapped around hand-rolled NCCL tests. That's a second system to maintain next to everything else you're already running. NVCRE's pitch is to make the staircase a Kubernetes object instead. ---

secs.head: The architecture: three resources, one chain of custody
secs.body: Everything in NVCRE is a Custom Resource, so you can inspect it with kubectl and manage it with GitOps. There's no separate dashboard holding secrets. Resource What it is Your relationship with it --- --- --- Certification Which nodes to test and which categories to run You write this one Workflow One per category; applies defaults and overrides, sets iterations, creates the job It does the paperwork Job Runs the workload, watches node health, records measurements and failures It does the sweating Instructions flow down, and results flow back up the same chain. The job records which nodes failed and why, the workflow reports the category result, and the certification groups everything by category. That's how a report can say gpu-01 hit a hardware fault during the NCCL test while gpu-02 merely missed its bandwidth target. The blame is attributed by design, not guessed afterwards. A certification describes intent, not mechanism: Note the v1alpha1 . It's an early API version, so expect fields to change between releases and check the docs before copying anything into automation. You never say how to run an all-reduce. NVCRE detects the GPU architecture and cloud platform from the target nodes, then derives GPUs per node, the NCCL environment and platform-specific networking. The built-in catalog covers three domains: - Communication: five NCCL variants (all-reduce, all-gather, all-to-all, loopback, and loopback across NVSwitch) - Diagnostics: the DCGM level-4 diagnostic suite - Training: NeMo pretraining with Nemotron 5 at 8B and 56B parameters ---

secs.head: Pass or fail is an expression, not a vibe
secs.body: NVCRE ships with no default thresholds . You write the criteria yourself, in Common Expression Language (CEL), evaluated against measured metrics: Do not copy those numbers. NVIDIA's own article calls them illustrative values for GB200 NVL72-class systems. Your threshold comes from the same place as in the OSU page: a known-good baseline for your hardware, or what your application actually needs. The design point worth remembering is that "the job finished" and "the job hit its target" are different facts. A training run that completes at 60% of expected goodput technically succeeded and told you the cluster isn't ready. NVCRE records the second case as a ValidationFailed condition, separate from whether the run itself succeeded, and treats it as a failure. ---

secs.head: Scale decides what you're measuring
secs.body: The same test at a different scale answers a different question. An NCCL test inside one NVLink domain measures NVLink. The same test across three racks measures the scale-out fabric. So NVCRE makes scale explicit with testScale : Mode What it does --- --- Intra-node Tests each node on its own Intra-rack Groups nodes by topology domain (via the nvidia.com/gpu.clique label) Full-scale Puts every node in one big group Diagnose Adaptive fault isolation, described next ---

secs.head: The detective: adaptive fault isolation
secs.body: Here is the nightmare it solves. A 64-node all-reduce returns low bandwidth. Every node in the group is equally suspect, and the old answer was days of engineers bisecting racks by hand while the GPUs sat idle. With testScale: diagnose , NVCRE does the bisecting itself. It splits a failing group, reruns the halves, and keeps going until it hits a floor size ( minGroupSize ). Groups that still fail at the floor become suspects. A maxConcurrent setting caps how many jobs run at once, so the detective doesn't saturate the very fabric it's measuring. The output is a short list of suspect nodes with a reason each, instead of a shrug aimed at an entire rack. A failing report looks like this: ---

secs.head: WorkloadRun : the plumbing, available separately
secs.body: Underneath certification sits WorkloadRun , which solves a more mundane problem. Running any multi-node GPU workload on Kubernetes needs the same pile of setup every time: platform detection, framework wiring, GPU and network requests, and cleanup when a run dies halfway. You give it an image, a framework and a node count. The framework is exactly one of: - torch for distributed training through torchrun - mpi for NCCL tests and other MPI workloads - exec for an arbitrary command NVCRE then generates the matching Kubeflow TrainingRuntime , injects the shared-memory volume, sets the NCCL and platform environment variables, and enables NVLink scale-up networking where the hardware supports it.

secs.head: The gang scheduling aside
secs.body: This is the most transferable idea on the page. Without a gang scheduler, Kubernetes places pods independently. On a busy cluster that can deadlock: some pods land, grab their GPUs, and wait forever at the framework's rendezvous for peers that can't be scheduled. Everyone is holding a seat and nobody can start the meeting. Setting spec.gangScheduler opts the workload's pods into a gang-aware scheduler such as KAI Scheduler, which holds all pods until the whole gang can be placed at once. It's all-or-nothing placement, the Kubernetes answer to a habit Slurm users take for granted. Because WorkloadRun is a plain CRD, other tools can call it without adopting the rest of NVCRE. ---

secs.head: Three questions, three layers
secs.body: NVIDIA frames a production cluster as needing three separate answers, one per layer of its DSX OS stack: Question Layer Style --- --- --- Is it configured correctly? AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) Version-locked, validated recipes for drivers, operators and kernels; detects drift Is it ready to run real work? NVCRE Active: generates load, finds failures that emit no telemetry Is it healthy right now? NVSentinel Passive: watches DCGM metrics, Xid errors, logs and cloud maintenance events NVSentinel costs no GPU time, so it can run forever in production. NVCRE costs GPU time, so you run it before workloads land. They don't compete. One covers what emits signals, the other covers what stays quiet. NVCRE also deliberately does not act on what it finds . It doesn't cordon, taint or patch node conditions, which avoids conflicting actions and half-cleaned-up state. The NVSentinel NVCRE Certification Monitor can turn a failed certification into a health event, and your NVSentinel policies can then quarantine, drain or trigger remediation. A later passing certification can clear the signal and release the taint. Find and fix stay in separate lanes. ---

secs.head: Getting started
secs.body: Prerequisites on the target cluster: - Kubernetes 1.29 or later, kubectl and Helm 3.x - NVIDIA GPU Operator - NVIDIA DRA Driver for GPUs, if you're on GB200 or GB300 NVL72 (those catalog entries create ComputeDomain resources) - The standalone DCGM service, for the DCGM level-4 category - A gang-aware scheduler such as KAI Scheduler, optional but recommended on busy shared clusters Then the whole loop is four commands: nvcrectl setup init installs the CRDs, the controller, Kubeflow Trainer and the default log profiles. As with any installer you pipe into bash , read it first on anything that matters. ---

secs.head: What it doesn't tell you (yet)
secs.body: - It's alpha-versioned ( v1alpha1 ). Treat field names as subject to change. - No default thresholds. It will not tell you whether 932 GB/s is good for your fabric. You decide that. - Not in the lab series yet. The two-node k3s lab in this series has no real GPUs, so nothing here was run by the author. The page summarizes NVIDIA's documentation and article. ---

secs.head: The one-paragraph takeaway
secs.body: A cluster can pass every health check it owns and still fail the only test that counts, because the failures that hurt (a slightly slow GPU, a link that sulks under load) emit nothing until real work pushes on them. NVCRE's answer is almost rude in its simplicity: run the real workload before production does, measure it against thresholds you choose, and bisect automatically when the numbers are bad. Pair it with a passive watcher like NVSentinel, and readiness stops being an assumption and becomes something you can prove before the first customer job lands. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - NVIDIA Technical Blog, Validate GPU Cluster Readiness Before AI Workloads Land (Sept 23, 2026; Dhvani Chheda and Kai Wombacher). The architecture, catalog, testScale modes, adaptive isolation, WorkloadRun , prerequisites and install commands on this page come from this article. - NVCRE on GitHub and its documentation, where the current API is defined - NVSentinel overview The comparison tables and the framing around the OSU page are the author's own.

label: Isolating GPU Workloads
title: Isolating GPU Workloads: Taints, Labels and the Device Plugin
desc: Page 7 of the Kubernetes series. Page 3 faked GPUs with a hand-patched counter. This page is the real thing: how a devic

secs.head: Isolating GPU Workloads: Taints, Labels and the Device Plugin
secs.body: Page 7 of the Kubernetes series. Page 3 faked GPUs with a hand-patched counter. This page is the real thing: how a device plugin advertises GPUs, how to keep web services off your GPU nodes and GPU jobs on them, and why a 64-GPU training job needs a kind of scheduling Kubernetes was never built for. By the end you'll be able to design GPU isolation on a shared cluster and explain where Kubernetes still differs from Slurm.

secs.head: The logging agent that ate a GPU node
secs.body: A company runs one Kubernetes cluster for everything: the website, internal tools, and a pool of 8-GPU H100 nodes for model training. Monday morning, a 32-GPU training job sits Pending . Four GPU nodes exist. Every one has 8 free GPUs. So why won't it schedule? Because the scheduler doesn't only count GPUs. It also counts CPU and memory. Over the weekend, a dozen web pods, a log shipper and a batch report job drifted onto the GPU nodes, because those nodes had the most free CPU and RAM in the cluster. Each GPU node now has its GPUs free and its memory full. The training pods don't fit anywhere. Nobody did anything wrong. Kubernetes did exactly what it was built to do: pack services onto whatever capacity is free. It just had no idea those nodes were special. This page is about telling it. ---

secs.head: Concept 1: the device plugin is a translator
secs.body: Kubernetes doesn't know what a GPU is. As page 3 showed, it only knows extended resources : named counters on nodes, like nvidia.com/gpu: 8 . A device plugin is the translator between real hardware and those counters. NVIDIA's runs as a DaemonSet, one pod on every GPU node, and does three things: 1. Discovers the GPUs on its node. 2. Advertises them to the kubelet, which publishes nvidia.com/gpu in the node's capacity. 3. Hands them out : when a pod that asked for GPUs lands on the node, the plugin tells the kubelet which specific devices to expose to that container. Pods ask for GPUs in limits , as page 3 covered: In production, the plugin rarely comes alone. NVIDIA's GPU Operator installs the whole stack as Kubernetes components: the driver, the container toolkit, the device plugin, GPU Feature Discovery (which labels nodes with facts like the GPU model), and the DCGM exporter for metrics. One install, every GPU node configured the same way. What a GPU request does not do: it says nothing about which kind of node or who else may land there. A pod asking for 8 GPUs can only go where 8 are free. But a pod asking for zero GPUs can go anywhere, GPU nodes included. That's the logging agent's loophole. ---

secs.head: Concept 2: labels attract, taints repel
secs.body: Kubernetes has two opposite tools for placement, and the official docs put the contrast neatly: node affinity attracts pods to nodes; taints let a node repel pods. Tool Lives on Effect Analogy ------ ---------- -------- --------- Label + nodeSelector / node affinity Label on node, selector on pod "This pod should go only to nodes like these" A pod's destination address Taint Node "Keep every pod away unless it tolerates me" A "staff only" sign on a door Toleration Pod "I'm allowed past that sign" A staff badge A taint has a key, a value and an effect : Effect Meaning -------- --------- NoSchedule New pods without a matching toleration won't be placed here PreferNoSchedule The scheduler tries to avoid placing them here NoExecute Also evicts already-running pods that don't tolerate it The docs list GPU nodes as a textbook case: in a cluster where a small subset of nodes have special hardware, taint those nodes so pods that don't need the hardware stay off, leaving room for pods that do. Now the web pods and the log shipper bounce off the GPU nodes. Monday's problem is solved. There's even a built-in shortcut. The docs recommend representing special hardware as an extended resource, tainting those nodes with the extended resource's name, and enabling the ExtendedResourceToleration admission controller. Then any pod that requests nvidia.com/gpu automatically gets the matching toleration. GPU users don't have to remember anything. [!TIP] Some system DaemonSets, like the device plugin itself, the GPU Operator's components and node monitoring agents, must run on GPU nodes. Give those pods the toleration deliberately; the taint will block them too. ---

secs.head: The trap: a toleration is a permission, not a destination
secs.body: Here's where most GPU isolation designs go wrong. The docs say it in one line: tolerations allow, but do not require , pods to schedule onto nodes with matching taints. A toleration is a staff badge. It lets you into the staff area. It doesn't make you go there. So picture a data-preprocessing pod: CPU-heavy, no GPUs, but it belongs to the ML team, so someone gave it the GPU toleration "so it can run next to the training job." The scheduler is now free to put it on a GPU node or any ordinary node. Worse, if it lands on a GPU node, it's eating CPU and memory that training pods need, recreating Monday's problem from the inside. The docs' recipe for dedicated nodes uses both tools together: 1. Taint the GPU nodes, so outsiders stay off. 2. Label the same nodes (for example node-pool=gpu-training ). 3. Give the pods that belong there a toleration and a node affinity or nodeSelector for that label, so they go there and only there. You want Taint on node Toleration on pod Affinity on pod ---------- :---: :---: :---: Keep outsiders off GPU nodes Yes - - Let GPU pods onto GPU nodes Yes Yes - Keep a team's pods only on their nodes Yes Yes Yes The rule of thumb: taints guard the door; labels give directions. You almost always need both. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Three pods on a cluster where GPU nodes are tainted nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule and labeled node-pool=gpu . Where can each one land? 1. A web server with no tolerations and no selectors. 2. A training pod requesting 8 GPUs, with the toleration (added automatically by ExtendedResourceToleration ). 3. A CPU-only preprocessing pod with the toleration but no node selector. Answers: (1) only non-GPU nodes: the taint repels it; (2) only GPU nodes, but because it asked for GPUs, not because of the toleration; (3) anywhere , GPU nodes included, which is probably not what anyone intended. Add nodeSelector: {node-pool: gpu} if it should be there, or remove the toleration if it shouldn't. ---

secs.head: Concept 3: training jobs need all-or-nothing
secs.body: Isolation gets the right pods onto the right nodes. Distributed training needs one more thing: all of its pods at once. A 32-GPU job is four pods of 8 GPUs, and it can't take a single training step until all four are running. The traditional kube-scheduler placed pods one at a time . Two jobs that each need four pods, on a cluster with room for four, could each grab two pods and wait forever for the rest, both holding GPUs and neither running. That's a scheduling deadlock, and it's why the batch world invented gang scheduling : place all of a group's pods, or none. For years, the answer on Kubernetes was an add-on: Kueue (job queueing and admission) or Volcano (a batch scheduler), among others. That's changing. Kubernetes 1.35 added a Workload API with an initial alpha implementation of gang scheduling; the Kubernetes project's 1.36 post describes a redesigned Workload and PodGroup API ( scheduling.k8s.io/v1alpha2 ) and a dedicated PodGroup scheduling cycle in kube-scheduler. Release coverage of 1.37 reports these APIs moving to beta. [!IMPORTANT] These APIs changed incompatibly between alpha versions: per the 1.36 announcement, v1alpha2 completely replaced v1alpha1 . Check your cluster's version and feature gates before relying on native gang scheduling, and keep Kueue or Volcano until it's stable for you. This is the clearest place where Kubernetes's roots show. It grew up placing long-running services that each work alone. Batch schedulers like Slurm grew up placing jobs that need many nodes at the same moment. ---

secs.head: Slurm and Kubernetes, side by side
secs.body: Concern Slurm Kubernetes --------- ------- ------------ Design center Batch jobs that start, run, finish Long-running services, kept at a desired state GPU discovery GRES, configured in gres.conf or autodetected via NVML Device plugin advertising nvidia.com/gpu Keeping workloads apart Partitions, features, accounts and QOS Taints, tolerations, labels, affinity, namespaces All-or-nothing multi-node start Built in: a job gets all its nodes or waits Add-ons (Kueue, Volcano); native gang scheduling arriving in recent releases Tenant quotas and fairness Associations, Grp/Max limits, fairshare (see the Slurm page) ResourceQuota per namespace; Kueue adds queues, quotas and borrowing Mixed GPU types Typed GRES, constraints, heterogeneous jobs (see the series) Node labels such as GPU Feature Discovery's GPU model label, plus affinity Neither is "better." A common pattern at large AI organizations is both: Slurm for big training runs, Kubernetes for inference services and tooling, sometimes on the same hardware pool. Takeaway: the device plugin turns GPUs into counters, taints keep outsiders off GPU nodes, labels and affinity send the right pods there, and distributed training still needs all-or-nothing scheduling that Kubernetes is only now building in. Isolation decides where pods may go. To follow one training job through every component, from kubectl apply to its first all-reduce, continue to page 8, the job execution journey.

label: The Job Execution Journey
title: The Job Execution Journey: From kubectl apply to the First All-Reduce
desc: Page 8 of the Kubernetes series. A distributed training job passes through about a dozen components before its first gra

secs.head: The Job Execution Journey: From kubectl apply to the First All-Reduce
secs.body: Page 8 of the Kubernetes series. A distributed training job passes through about a dozen components before its first gradient crosses the network. This page follows one 8-GPU job through all of them, in the order they actually run, and fact-checks a popular description of that journey along the way. By the end you'll know which component to blame when a job is stuck, and you'll be able to narrate the whole path in an interview without the three mistakes most descriptions make.

secs.head: Where is my job?
secs.body: A researcher runs kubectl apply -f training-job.yaml for an 8-GPU run: two nodes, four GPUs each. The command returns instantly: trainjob.trainer.kubeflow.org/llama-ft created . Then nothing. No pods. kubectl get pods shows an empty list for ten minutes. She messages the platform team: "Kubernetes lost my job." It didn't. Her job is sitting, on purpose, at stop 2 of a six-stop journey, exactly where the cluster was designed to park it. The platform engineer who knows the stops finds it in thirty seconds. The one who doesn't starts restarting things. Let's learn the stops. ---

secs.head: The popular version, fact-checked
secs.body: A widely shared description of this journey has five steps. It's a good skeleton with three real errors, and they matter because they send you to the wrong component when something breaks. Step in the popular version Verdict What's actually true ---------------------------- --------- ---------------------- 1. API server authenticates, validates the custom resource, stores it in etcd Mostly right It also authorizes the request and runs admission control , which can change or reject it, before validation and storage 2. The PyTorch Operator watches for PyTorchJob s and creates a launcher pod, worker pods and headless Services Outdated, and out of order Kubeflow Trainer v2's TrainJob replaces framework-specific CRDs like PyTorchJob . "Launcher" is an MPI concept; PyTorchJob used master and worker. And with Kueue, the operator creates no pods until the job is admitted 3. Kueue intercepts unscheduled pods, gang-schedules them and binds them to nodes Wrong about what Kueue is Kueue is a job queueing and admission controller. It holds whole jobs suspended until quota allows, then lets them start; kube-scheduler places and binds the pods 4. The kubelet asks the device plugin over gRPC; the plugin finds free GPU PCIe addresses and has the runtime mount drivers and CUDA libraries Partly right The kubelet's device manager tracks and assigns device IDs; the plugin's Allocate tells the kubelet how to expose them; the NVIDIA Container Toolkit injects the driver libraries. The CUDA toolkit libraries come from the container image 5. The runtime pulls images and boots containers; Multus adds RDMA interfaces via SR-IOV; NCCL uses them Right, but the order is reversed The pod's network, including Multus's extra interfaces, is set up when the pod sandbox is created, before the training containers start Now the stops, in the order they really happen. ---

secs.head: Stop 1: the API server's four gates
secs.body: Every request to Kubernetes goes through kube-apiserver , and the official docs describe it as a series of gates: 1. Authentication : who are you? Client certificate, token, or an identity provider. Fail: HTTP 401. 2. Authorization : are you allowed to create this, in this namespace? Usually RBAC. Fail: HTTP 403. 3. Admission control : modules that can modify or reject the object. The docs stress the difference: if any admission controller rejects, the request is rejected immediately, and admission controllers can also set defaults. 4. Validation and storage : the object is checked against its schema (for a custom resource, the schema its CRD defines) and written to etcd . Gate 3 is the one people forget, and it's where our job's fate gets decided. Kueue installs an admission webhook. When the TrainJob arrives in a namespace that uses a Kueue queue, the webhook marks the job suspended before it's even stored. That's why the researcher's pods never appeared. ---

secs.head: Stop 2: Kueue says "not yet"
secs.body: Kueue's own README describes it precisely: a job-level manager that decides when a job should be admitted to start (as in, pods can be created) and when it should stop . The original Kueue announcement on the Kubernetes blog explains the design choice: rather than replacing kube-scheduler, Kueue uses the job's suspend field to say "start" or "wait," and delegates the actual pod-to-node scheduling to kube-scheduler . So Kueue never touches a pod. It works one level up: 1. The suspended job joins a queue . 2. When it reaches the head of its ClusterQueue, Kueue checks whether all of the job's resource requests fit the available quota . By default it never admits part of a job. 3. If they fit, Kueue un-suspends the job, optionally adding node selectors for the right kind of nodes. That's Kueue's main defense for all-or-nothing behavior, and its docs are honest about the limits. Quota alone is blind to node layout : eight GPUs of quota doesn't guarantee two nodes with four free GPUs each. Two more mechanisms close the gap: Mechanism What it adds ----------- ------------- Topology Aware Scheduling (TAS) Kueue only admits the job if all its pods fit into the requested topology domains, checking real placement before committing waitForPodsReady A timeout-based safety net: if an admitted job's pods aren't all running in time, Kueue suspends it again and requeues it Our researcher's job is here: queued behind two other teams' jobs, waiting for quota. Nothing is lost. It's in line. [!NOTE] Kueue isn't the only option. Volcano is a separate batch scheduler that does place pods itself, and recent Kubernetes releases have been adding native gang scheduling to kube-scheduler (page 7). Know which one your cluster runs before you debug. ---

secs.head: Stop 3: the operator builds the job
secs.body: Once admitted, the training operator turns one high-level object into the pieces a distributed job needs. The current Kubeflow project, Kubeflow Trainer v2 , replaces the old per-framework CRDs ( PyTorchJob , TFJob , MPIJob ) with a single TrainJob , which points at a reusable training runtime such as torch-distributed . Under the hood, Trainer v2 translates each TrainJob into a JobSet , a Kubernetes API for running a group of Jobs as one unit, which creates: - the pods for each training node, - a headless Service , so pods can find each other by stable DNS names, which is how torchrun 's nodes locate their rendezvous point, - and the environment torchrun needs (node count, ranks, master address), filled in by the runtime. If your cluster still runs the older Training Operator v1, a PyTorchJob produces a master pod and worker pods with Services. The "launcher" pod in the popular description belongs to MPIJob , where a launcher starts mpirun across workers. ---

secs.head: Stop 4: kube-scheduler picks nodes
secs.body: Now there are pods, and each one is unscheduled . kube-scheduler takes them one by one (or as a group, with native gang scheduling) through two phases: - Filter : drop nodes that can't run the pod. Not enough free nvidia.com/gpu ? Out. A taint the pod doesn't tolerate? Out. Doesn't match the node selector Kueue added? Out. - Score : rank the survivors and pick the best. Then it binds the pod: it records the chosen node name on the pod object through the API server. That's all "scheduling" means in Kubernetes. Nothing has started running yet. This is also where page 7's taints, tolerations and affinity do their work, here in kube-scheduler, not in Kueue. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Three stuck jobs. At which stop is each one waiting? 1. The TrainJob exists, but kubectl get pods shows nothing for that job. 2. The pods exist, all Pending , with an event saying 0/12 nodes are available: insufficient nvidia.com/gpu . 3. The pods are assigned to nodes, but stuck in ContainerCreating . Answers: (1) stop 2 : Kueue hasn't admitted it, so check the workload's status and the queue; (2) stop 4 : kube-scheduler can't find room, often because Kueue's quota said yes but no node has enough free GPUs, exactly the gap TAS closes; (3) stop 5 or 6 : on the node, so check device allocation, image pulls and network attachment. ---

secs.head: Stop 5: the kubelet and the device plugin
secs.body: On each chosen node, the kubelet notices a pod bound to it and starts making it real. For the GPUs, three components cooperate, and the popular description blurs them together. The kubelet's device manager does the bookkeeping. The NVIDIA device plugin, running as a DaemonSet, registered with the kubelet over gRPC on a Unix socket under /var/lib/kubelet/device-plugins/ and has been streaming its list of healthy GPUs ever since ( ListAndWatch ). The kubelet only reports the count to the API server; it keeps the device IDs itself and decides which ones this pod gets. A plugin can suggest a preferred set ( GetPreferredAllocation ), useful for picking GPUs that share an NVLink or PCIe switch. The device plugin says how to expose them. The official docs say Allocate is called during container creation so the plugin can run device-specific steps and instruct the kubelet how to make the devices available: environment variables, device nodes, mounts, or, since the kubelet gained support for it (GA in Kubernetes 1.31), fully qualified CDI device names. The NVIDIA Container Toolkit does the injection. When the container runtime creates the container, NVIDIA's toolkit, either as a runtime hook or through a CDI specification generated with nvidia-ctk cdi generate , injects the selected GPUs' device nodes and the host's driver libraries into the container. What's not injected: the CUDA toolkit . NVIDIA's toolkit docs note that you don't need the CUDA toolkit on the host at all, only the driver. CUDA libraries like cuBLAS and NCCL come from the container image. That's why one node can run containers built for different CUDA versions, as long as the host driver is new enough for all of them. [!TIP] There's a newer path. Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) , GA since Kubernetes 1.34, lets a workload describe the devices it needs and leaves it to the scheduler to allocate actual devices. Device plugins still dominate GPU clusters today, but DRA is where Kubernetes device management is heading. ---

secs.head: Stop 6: network first, then containers
secs.body: Before any of your containers start, the kubelet asks the container runtime (containerd or CRI-O) to create the pod's sandbox , and that's when networking is set up, by calling the cluster's CNI plugins. Only then are images pulled and the training containers created. The default pod network is an overlay , fine for web traffic and far too slow for all-reduces. So GPU clusters add a second network: - Multus is a meta-plugin : it doesn't implement networking itself, it calls other CNI plugins, so a pod can have its normal interface plus extra ones described by NetworkAttachmentDefinition resources. - The SR-IOV device plugin advertises a NIC's virtual functions (slices of one physical card that look like separate PCIe devices) as schedulable resources, and the SR-IOV CNI plugs one into the pod. Alternatively, an RDMA shared device plugin exposes RDMA devices to pods without slicing. - NVIDIA's Network Operator installs these pieces, along with the networking driver and the peer-memory support that GPUDirect RDMA needs. Then the containers start, torchrun finds its peers through the headless Service, and NCCL's first all-reduce goes over the RDMA interface, ideally GPU memory to network card to GPU memory, with no CPU in the way (RDMA and GPUDirect). The first gradient has crossed the network. Six stops, about a dozen components. ---

secs.head: The whole journey on one page
secs.body: Stop Component Decides Common mix-up ------ ----------- --------- --------------- 1 kube-apiserver (+ etcd) Whether the request is allowed and well-formed Forgetting authorization and admission 2 Kueue When the whole job may start Thinking it schedules or binds pods 3 Training operator / JobSet What pods and Services exist PyTorchJob "launcher" pods 4 kube-scheduler Where each pod runs Crediting Kueue with placement 5 kubelet, device plugin, NVIDIA Container Toolkit Which GPUs, and how they appear in the container Thinking CUDA libraries come from the host 6 Container runtime, CNI, Multus The pod's networks, then its containers Network set up after containers start ---

secs.head: When it gets stuck: which stop to check
secs.body: Symptom Stop First command --------- ------ --------------- kubectl apply fails with 401 or 403 1 Check your kubeconfig credentials and RBAC ( kubectl auth can-i create trainjobs ) apply rejected with a webhook error 1 Read the message: an admission webhook (often Kueue or a policy engine) refused it Job exists, no pods 2 kubectl get workloads -n <ns and the ClusterQueue's status Pods Pending , insufficient nvidia.com/gpu 4 kubectl describe pod : quota admitted it but no node fits; consider TAS Pods Pending , untolerated taint 4 Tolerations and selectors (page 7) ContainerCreating for a long time 5-6 kubectl describe pod events: image pull, device allocation, or network attachment errors Containers run, NCCL is slow or falls back to TCP 6 Check the pod has its RDMA interface and NCCL sees it (NCCL benchmark guide) Admitted job requeued after a timeout 2 waitForPodsReady fired: some pods never became ready Takeaway: the API server admits the request, Kueue decides when the whole job may start, the operator decides what pods exist, kube-scheduler decides where they run, the kubelet and device plugin decide which GPUs they get, and the network is plumbed before the containers start, so when a job is stuck, find the stop before you touch anything. Back to the series README.

secs.body: - Kubernetes: Controlling Access to the Kubernetes API (authentication, authorization, admission, storage) - Kubernetes blog: Introducing Kueue (suspend, delegation to kube-scheduler) - Kueue: All-or-nothing scheduling (quota admission, TAS, waitForPodsReady) - Kueue repository README - Kubeflow Trainer: Migrating to Trainer v2 (TrainJob replaces PyTorchJob) - Kubeflow blog: Introducing Kubeflow Trainer V2 - Kubernetes: Device Plugins (registration, ListAndWatch, Allocate, CDI) - NVIDIA Container Toolkit: Architecture Overview - Kubernetes blog: Kubernetes v1.34, DRA has graduated to GA - NVIDIA developer blog: NVIDIA Network Operator (Multus, SR-IOV, RDMA shared device plugin) - Red Hat: Demystifying Multus

label: Draining a GPU node
title: Draining a GPU Node With a Three-Day Run on It
desc: Page 9 of the Kubernetes series. One word means two opposite things in Slurm and Kubernetes, and a three-day training ru

secs.head: Draining a GPU Node With a Three-Day Run on It
secs.body: Page 9 of the Kubernetes series. One word means two opposite things in Slurm and Kubernetes, and a three-day training run pays for the difference. By the end you'll know which command is the polite one, what the termination clock does to your checkpoint, and how to set up a run that survives maintenance night. Written against Kubernetes 1.31 and later. The story is invented; nothing here was run on a live cluster . Claims trace to the docs in the references, and the commands and YAML follow the patterns those docs show. The Python sketch is mine, not the docs'.

secs.head: Two tickets, one word
secs.body: Tuesday, two tickets land in the platform team's queue. Ticket 1 (from a Slurm cluster): "I drained gpu-09 for a firmware update. My job on it is still running. Is drain broken?" Ticket 2 (from the new Kubernetes cluster): "I drained gpu-17 for a firmware update. My three-day training run is gone, and so is the checkpoint I was counting on." Sana, who ran Slurm for six years and joined the Kubernetes team last month, reads both. Ticket 1 is a customer who expected drain to evict. Ticket 2 is Sana, three hours ago, who expected it not to. Same word. Opposite behavior. To see why, think of the node as a hotel.

secs.head: The hotel with two signs
secs.body: In Slurm, drain hangs a No Vacancy sign: guests already inside stay until they check out, and nobody new gets a room. In Kubernetes, there are two signs, and they have different names: You want Slurm Kubernetes --- --- --- No new guests, current guests stay State=DRAIN kubectl cordon No new guests, and current guests leave cancel the jobs kubectl drain Reopen the hotel State=RESUME kubectl uncordon The kubectl drain reference says it plainly: the node is marked unschedulable "to prevent new pods from arriving", and then drain evicts what is there. Cordon is the first half of drain. Slurm's drain is Kubernetes's cordon. What kubectl drain adds is the night manager knocking on every door. One caveat from the drain task page: pods that tolerate the node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable taint can still land on a cordoned node, so No Vacancy has exceptions. ☕ Try it before you scroll. Sana wants the run to finish on its own, with gpu-17 empty by Friday. Which command does she run tonight? (Hint: which sign did she actually want?) kubectl cordon gpu-17 , then wait. But some night she will need the room back, and the manager will have to knock. What exactly does he do?

secs.head: What the night manager does
secs.body: Per the kubectl drain reference, the manager evicts every guest through the Eviction API, which respects PodDisruptionBudgets. He never touches the staff (DaemonSet pods) and refuses to start unless you say --ignore-daemonsets , which on a GPU node is always, because the device plugin is a DaemonSet. He refuses guests with emptyDir luggage unless you pass --delete-emptydir-data . And he waits : "You should not operate on the machine until the command completes." Two flags will matter in a minute: - --grace-period defaults to -1 , meaning "use the pod's own value". Any number you type overrides what the job's author chose. - --timeout defaults to 0 , which means wait forever. So the manager knocks. How long does the guest get to pack?

secs.head: The packing clock
secs.body: The knock (SIGTERM) comes with a deadline. The lock change (SIGKILL) comes after it. The default clock, terminationGracePeriodSeconds , is 30 seconds . Fine for a web server. Absurd for a trainer that needs minutes to write a checkpoint. The preStop hook and your shutdown run on the same clock. The pod lifecycle docs say a slow hook means you "must modify terminationGracePeriodSeconds ", and the kubelet grants only one 2-second extension. The docs never say "one shared budget" in a sentence; it follows from the flow, so budget as if it were. Exit codes tell the story afterward. By the usual 128 + signal convention, 137 is SIGKILL (the lock change) and 143 is a SIGTERM nobody caught. If that sounds like Slurm's KillWait , it is: ask politely, wait a fixed time, kill. So how does a run still die even when the manager is polite?

secs.head: Five ways the guest leaves without the suitcase
secs.body: 1. Nobody answers the door. The knock goes to PID 1, and PID 1 is special. Per pid namespaces(7) , init receives a signal from inside its namespace or from an ancestor only if it installed a handler for it. A trainer with no SIGTERM handler never hears the eviction. Only SIGKILL is forced through. The usual accomplice is command: ["sh", "-c", "python train.py"] : the shell is PID 1 and Python never hears the knock. Use the exec form ( ["python", "train.py"] ) or exec python train.py . A sketch of the trainer side (my own illustration, not from the Kubernetes docs, and not run): 2. Ten minutes to pack, thirty seconds on the clock. A checkpoint that takes minutes against a 30-second clock ends in SIGKILL mid-write: a half-file that looks like a checkpoint. Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds to your measured worst case plus margin. The sneaky version hides in a runbook: a copied drain --grace-period=30 quietly throws away the number the author chose. 3. The suitcase stayed in the room. The --delete-emptydir-data error is a warning, not an obstacle, and adding the flag to silence it is the temptation. Anything on emptyDir or the container's own filesystem dies with the pod. Checkpoints belong on a PersistentVolumeClaim, and the trainer must look there at startup. 4. The hotel bans the guest after a few evictions. A Job gives up after backoffLimit failed pods (default 6), and by default an evicted pod is a failed pod. Enough maintenance nights and the run is declared failed for reasons that have nothing to do with its code. The fix is the pod failure policy , stable since 1.31 (the rule is in the Job spec below). Disruptions such as preemption, API-initiated eviction (that is drain ), taint-based eviction, node-pressure eviction and graceful node shutdown get a DisruptionTarget condition, and an Ignore rule keeps them out of the backoffLimit count. Exceeding the container's own limits does not get it, "because the disruptions were probably caused by the Pod and would reoccur on retry". It requires restartPolicy: Never . 5. One guest is the whole party. For a single-pod run, one eviction is one failure. For a distributed run, evicting one pod usually takes the whole job down, because collectives stall when a rank disappears. Whether your framework aborts, hangs or restarts elastically is something to find out before the window, not during it. (Isolating GPU Workloads covers why such jobs are scheduled all-or-nothing.) Which leaves one more question: can someone say "this guest does not leave tonight"?

secs.head: The guest who refuses to leave
secs.body: A PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) limits how many pods of a set may be down at once through voluntary disruptions, and a drain is one. If an eviction would break the budget, the Eviction API answers 429 Too Many Requests and drain keeps retrying. With the default infinite --timeout , the night manager stands at the door until morning. Two things from the docs change the plan for a training Job: - For a restartable batch Job, the docs' advice is not to create a PDB. The Job controller replaces the pod anyway, which is why the pod failure policy exists. - A PDB on pods not owned by a Deployment, ReplicaSet, StatefulSet, ReplicationController or a custom resource with a scale subresource is restricted. Only an integer minAvailable works: no maxUnavailable , no percentage. A copied maxUnavailable: 0 recipe will not do what you expect. If you want a hard brake anyway, an integer minAvailable equal to the pod count does it. Then set a --timeout , so a stuck drain names the pod in the way. Know that --disable-eviction skips the PDB check entirely ("use with caution"): it turns a protected run into a dead one. And decide who may override the brake before the night you need it, because automated node upgrades drain nodes too.

secs.head: A maintenance night that keeps the checkpoint
secs.body: What the docs back: --field-selector spec.nodeName=... is a supported Pod selector; kubectl wait --for=condition=<name and --timeout are in the reference, though its examples use Pods, so the Complete condition on a Job comes from the Job's own status; drain --dry-run=server is in the drain reference. Step 4 leaves out --grace-period and --delete-emptydir-data on purpose: if drain asks for the second, find out why a pod has local data. The 30m is an example; pick it to cover your longest checkpoint. And a Job that makes the whole story survivable. The podFailurePolicy rule and restartPolicy: Never are the pattern from the Job docs; the rest is a typical GPU trainer, not run: --resume-latest is a flag of the example trainer, not of Kubernetes. It makes the replacement pod resume instead of start over: the Job controller creates the new pod, and nothing makes it continue where the old one stopped. Slurm's --requeue has the same trap: a requeue is a re-run, not a resume.

secs.head: Back to the two tickets
secs.body: Ticket 1 gets a one-line answer: Slurm's drain is a cordon, and nothing is broken. Ticket 2 takes longer. Sana's kubectl drain did exactly what its reference says: cordon, evict, SIGTERM, 30 seconds, SIGKILL. Her trainer had no handler, her checkpoint sat on the wrong volume, and the clock was the default, so she hit four of the five doors. One Slurm habit survives the move, though: Slurm can warn a job minutes before its end with --signal=B:USR1@300 , and as far as I could find Kubernetes has no equivalent, so the pod hears about an eviction only when the clock has already started. Checkpoint regularly , and treat the SIGTERM checkpoint as the last chance, not the only one. (A pod stuck in Terminating is a cousin of Kill task failed; for the Slurm-side order of operations see rolling reboot order.) Takeaway: in Kubernetes the gentle command is cordon , and drain is the one that evicts. Give a long run a handler, a PVC, a measured grace period and a pod failure policy before maintenance night. Challenge: your 64-GPU job spans eight nodes and one must be patched. Cordon or drain, and what do the other seven ranks do when one leaves? Find out on a test run. Related: Broken Pods, the Rogues' Gallery shows what 137 and 143 look like in the wild, and the next page, The Pod Killed With Memory to Spare, is a SIGKILL that no drain asked for.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - kubectl drain (Kubernetes reference): cordon, eviction, flags and defaults. - Safely drain a node (Kubernetes task): PDB behaviour and the unschedulable taint caveat. - API-initiated eviction: the 200, 429 and 500 answers and the termination steps. - Pod lifecycle: termination of Pods: grace period, preStop, SIGTERM, SIGKILL. - Disruptions: pod disruption conditions: the DisruptionTarget reasons. - Job: pod failure policy and backoff limit: Ignore , restartPolicy: Never , stable since 1.31. - Specifying a PodDisruptionBudget: arbitrary workloads and the integer minAvailable restriction. - kubectl wait and Field selectors: --timeout default, spec.nodeName . - pid namespaces(7): signals to the init process of a PID namespace.

label: OOMKilled with memory to spare
title: The Pod Killed With Memory to Spare
desc: Page 10 of the Kubernetes series. A training pod dies with OOMKilled while every dashboard says the node has gigabytes f

secs.head: The Pod Killed With Memory to Spare
secs.body: Page 10 of the Kubernetes series. A training pod dies with OOMKilled while every dashboard says the node has gigabytes free. By the end you'll know which of three different killers struck, why the number you were watching could not show it, and how a harmless-looking /dev/shm fix spends your memory budget. Written against Kubernetes 1.31 and later and cgroup v2. The story is invented; nothing here was run on a live cluster . Claims trace to the docs in the references, and the places I could not confirm a fact are marked on the page.

secs.head: The dashboard that said everything was fine
secs.body: At 02:14 a training pod restarts. Karim, the engineer on call in this story, looks at the dashboards the next morning and finds nothing wrong: - The node has tens of gigabytes of memory free. - The pod's memory graph peaks around 11Gi, under its 16Gi limit. - kubectl top pod shows a modest number, because the pod has just restarted. And yet: Picture the node as a warehouse, half empty. Each container rents a storage unit with a fixed size. Karim is staring at the warehouse floor plan. The unit that overflowed is not on it. Three different things can clear out a unit, and they look alike at 02:14. Which one came for Karim?

secs.head: Three killers, three crime scenes
secs.body: Container OOM Node OOM Kubelet eviction --- --- --- --- Who The kernel, at the container's cgroup limit The kernel, when the whole node runs out before the kubelet reacts The kubelet, when node memory.available crosses a threshold Picture The lock-cutter clears one unit that is over its size A fire marshal clears whoever scores worst in a full warehouse The manager empties whole units when the warehouse nears full You see OOMKilled , exit code 137 Kernel log lines, possibly several pods hit Pod phase Failed , status Evicted Next The kubelet may restart the container per its restartPolicy Same as the first The pod is not restarted in place: it is Failed , and its controller makes a new one Needs a short node? No Yes Yes The Kubernetes docs back the first column: memory limits are applied by the kubelet and container runtime and "ultimately enforced by the kernel" through cgroups, and kubectl describe pod shows Reason: OOMKilled with exit code 137 for a container that went over its limit. Exit code 137 is 128 + 9, a SIGKILL: no chance to catch it, no chance to write a checkpoint. (Draining a GPU Node covers the polite way to die. This is the other way.) ☕ Try it before you scroll. The node has 200Gi free and the pod's limit is 16Gi. Can the pod be OOMKilled? (Hint: whose size matters to a storage unit?) Yes, and that is Karim's column. So what exactly is the unit's size, and who reads it?

secs.head: The storage unit has its own size
secs.body: Field Read by Effect --- --- --- requests.memory The scheduler, and the kubelet when it ranks pods Decides where the pod fits. The kubelet reserves at least the request for the container limits.memory The kernel, through the container's cgroup The size of the unit CPU and memory differ here. A container near its CPU limit is throttled . A container over its memory limit may be killed , because there is nothing to slow down. The docs add an honest nuance: memory limits are enforced reactively . Terminations "only happen when the kernel detects memory pressure", so a container can run over its limit for a while and not be killed yet. The kernel doc for memory.max says the same from the other side: the OOM killer runs "if a cgroup's memory usage reaches this limit and can't be reduced". Two words in that sentence matter: reaches , and can't be reduced . What can be reduced?

secs.head: Which memory number?
secs.body: Inside the unit, some things can be thrown out and some cannot. Packing peanuts (inactive file cache) go first. Furniture (anonymous memory) stays. Number Source What it counts --- --- --- container memory usage bytes cAdvisor "all memory regardless of when it was accessed" container memory working set bytes cAdvisor The working set container memory rss cAdvisor RSS memory.stat : anon , file , shmem Kernel cgroup v2 doc Anonymous mappings; filesystem cache including tmpfs and shared memory ; the swap-backed part of that cache The node-pressure page gives the rule the kubelet itself uses: memory.available is node capacity minus the node's working set, read from cgroupfs rather than free -m , and the kubelet excludes inactive file because it assumes that memory is reclaimable under pressure. Read the memory.stat row twice. The kernel counts tmpfs and shared memory inside file , the same bucket as cache, yet that memory has nowhere to go when pressure comes. That is the shared column of free one level down (see free vs available). So where does Karim's unit hide such memory?

secs.head: The freezer you plugged in
secs.body: Karim's job uses data-loader worker processes that hand batches to the main process through shared memory, which in a container lives in /dev/shm , a tmpfs. Multiprocessing data loaders typically work this way; I could not retrieve the PyTorch page to cite it, so treat that as general knowledge, not a checked claim. Two facts then collide: 1. /dev/shm is small by default in a container. It is commonly reported as 64MB. The Docker CLI reference I checked says only "Size of /dev/shm", with no default, so check df -h /dev/shm on your runtime. Workers that outgrow it fail, which sends people looking for a fix. 2. The usual fix spends your limit. Mount an emptyDir with medium: Memory at /dev/shm . The docs say the kubelet "tracks tmpfs emptyDir volumes as container memory use, rather than as local ephemeral storage". Without a sizeLimit , the volume "may consume up to that pod's memory limit". The docs warn about the part that bites: files on a memory-backed volume are managed by the application, and "Neither Kubernetes nor the OS may automatically delete files from a volume, so memory used by those files can not be reclaimed when the system or the pod are under memory pressure." You plugged a freezer into your storage unit, and it counts as furniture. A spec that makes the budget explicit (the emptyDir fields follow the docs; the numbers are invented): Budget the 24Gi like a floor plan: up to 8Gi for the freezer, the main process's anonymous memory, and headroom for kernel memory and active cache. If those leave no room, the pod is a candidate for another 02:14. But what if the warehouse itself fills up? Who goes first?

secs.head: Who gets cleared out first
secs.body: Two different rules apply, and the docs keep them apart. The kubelet's eviction ranks pods by whether usage exceeds requests, then by Pod Priority, then by how far over they are. The docs state that the kubelet "does not use the pod's QoS class to determine the eviction order", though QoS lets you estimate the likely order. The default hard threshold is memory.available<100Mi on Linux. For hard thresholds the kubelet does not respect PodDisruptionBudgets or terminationGracePeriodSeconds , so this is not the polite death of the draining page. The kernel's OOM killer acts if the node runs out before the kubelet reclaims. The kubelet sets oom score adj per container from the QoS class: QoS class Rule oom score adj --- --- --- Guaranteed Every container has CPU and memory requests equal to limits -997 Burstable Not Guaranteed, but some request or limit set min(max(2, 1000 − 1000 × memoryRequestBytes / machineMemoryCapacityBytes), 999) BestEffort No requests or limits 1000 The kernel scores each container by the share of node memory it uses, adds oom score adj , and kills the highest. In the docs' words, containers in low-QoS pods that use a lot of memory relative to their requests are killed first. One more detail explains the second killer: the kubelet polls cAdvisor on an interval, and "if memory usage increases within that window rapidly, the kubelet may not observe MemoryPressure fast enough, and the OOM killer will still be invoked". The docs suggest kernelMemcgNotification for immediate notification, or kubeReserved and systemReserved as a workaround. Karim's pod was Guaranteed, so a node-level kill was unlikely. That leaves the lock-cutter. But if the kill is so loud, why did no graph see it?

secs.head: The photo every thirty seconds
secs.body: The graph is a sample . A monitoring system takes a photo of the unit every so often. A burst that fills the unit, triggers the kill and ends the container between two photos is in none of them, and the restarted container looks calm. kubectl top only shows the present. The kernel keeps its own books. Where to look: Source What it tells you --- --- kubectl describe pod , Last State That a kill happened, and when kube pod container status last terminated reason{reason="OOMKilled"} A kube-state-metrics gauge you can alert on (documented as EXPERIMENTAL) memory.events oom kill : processes in the cgroup killed by any kind of OOM killer; max : times usage was about to exceed the limit; oom : times allocation was about to fail memory.peak The highest usage recorded since the cgroup was created or the counter was reset: no photo needed memory.stat The split into anon , file , shmem and the rest The cgroup files exist only while the container does, so read them in a container that is still alive and heading for trouble.

secs.head: Debugging runbook
secs.body: Commands follow the docs above; the cgroup path assumes cgroup v2 as seen from inside the container, so check it on your nodes. Reading step 4: if anon plus shmem sits near memory.max , the unit is full of things that cannot leave. If memory.events shows oom kill above zero, the kernel has already acted, whatever the dashboard says. Fixes, roughly in order: 1. Find what actually grew. Anonymous, shared and kernel memory have different cures. 2. Bound the freezer. Set sizeLimit on the memory emptyDir and cap worker count and prefetch depth. 3. Size the limit from the working-set peak , not the average, and leave headroom. The docs' advice, if the app behaves as expected, is a higher limit and possibly a higher request. 4.
