Make the run survive a kill. Checkpoint regularly to a PersistentVolumeClaim: SIGKILL gives no warning to write one at the last moment.

secs.head: The Slurm and Linux mirror
secs.body: This page Elsewhere in the repo --- --- The container's memory limit Slurm's ConstrainRAMSpace , with the same kernel OOM killer behind it (cgroups page) Kernel kills one container, the kubelet may restart it With Slurm, OOMKillStep makes the whole step die instead (same page) Working set vs usage "Available" vs "free" at container scale (free vs available) /dev/shm and memory emptyDir in the limit The shared column in free A scrape hiding a spike MaxRSS , polled every 30 s by default Kubelet eviction at memory.available No Slurm equivalent: the kernel decides

secs.head: Back to Karim
secs.body: At 02:14 the unit, not the warehouse, was full. The worker processes had been filling a memory-backed /dev/shm with prefetched batches, the volume had no sizeLimit , and the freezer counted against the 16Gi limit alongside the main process's tensors. The kernel cut the lock. The 11Gi on the graph was a photo taken before the break-in. Takeaway: the node having memory to spare is irrelevant to a container at its own limit; watch the working set against the container's limit, bound anything memory-backed, and trust memory.events over a dashboard. Challenge: a pod shows Evicted instead of OOMKilled . Which killer was it, who decided, and did its terminationGracePeriodSeconds apply? If you can answer all three, the Rogues' Gallery is easier the second time.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Resource management for pods and containers: limit enforcement, OOMKilled , memory-backed emptyDir . - Node-pressure eviction: memory.available , thresholds, eviction order, oom score adj , known issues. - Pod Quality of Service classes: Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort. - Assign memory resources to containers: exceeding a limit and restart. - Control Group v2 (kernel docs): memory.max , memory.peak , memory.events , memory.stat . - cAdvisor Prometheus metrics and kube-state-metrics pod metrics: metric names and descriptions. - docker container run: --shm-size (no default stated).

label: k3s vs kubeadm
title: k3s vs kubeadm: Furnished Flat or Empty Unit?
desc: Part 11 of the Kubernetes series. Two colleagues, two confident answers, one cluster to stand up. By the end you'll know

secs.head: k3s vs kubeadm: Furnished Flat or Empty Unit?
secs.body: Part 11 of the Kubernetes series. Two colleagues, two confident answers, one cluster to stand up. By the end you'll know what each tool actually installs, what each leaves for you, and which one to pick for a lab, an edge box and a GPU cluster. - The Friday request - Same landlord, different keys - What you get on day one - The part nobody asks about: day two - High availability, honestly - Picking one - Back to Priya - References ---

secs.head: The Friday request
secs.body: Priya runs the batch cluster at a small research site. On Monday she is told to "stand up Kubernetes" for the new GPU nodes. She built a lab on her laptop with k3s (part 2), and it took twenty minutes. On Tuesday two colleagues review her plan. Dmitri says: "k3s is a toy. Production means kubeadm." Aiko says: "kubeadm is a month of yak shaving. k3s is the same Kubernetes in one binary." Both sound sure. Both can't be right. Priya does what any sensible engineer does and opens a spreadsheet, and the spreadsheet is wrong in the first row, because the first row is "which one is real Kubernetes?" Both are. Start there. ---

secs.head: Same landlord, different keys
secs.body: The series has used one picture since part 1: Kubernetes is the landlord with opinions. A distribution is how the building gets delivered to you. - k3s is a furnished flat. Bed, kettle and a lease come with the keys. You can move in tonight and replace the sofa later. - kubeadm is an empty unit with a very good checklist. The walls are sound and the plumbing is certified, but you choose and install the furniture, and you bring your own movers for the heavy parts. The landlord is the same in both. The docs for each say so in their own words: Tool What its docs claim --- --- k3s "a fully compliant Kubernetes distribution", shipped as a single binary of less than 100 MB kubeadm creates a cluster that "conforms to best practices" and can pass the Kubernetes Conformance tests kubectl , your manifests, your Deployments and your nvidia.com/gpu requests behave the same on both. What differs is who assembles the building and who maintains it afterwards. [!NOTE] Neither is a toy and neither is "the production one". The question is how much assembly you want to own, and that is a cost question, not a quality one. So what exactly arrives with the keys? ---

secs.head: What you get on day one
secs.body: ☕ Try it before you scroll. On a bare Ubuntu host you run kubeadm init and it succeeds. Is the node ready to run your first pod? Hint: look at what the output asks you to do next. The answer is no, and the tool tells you so. After kubeadm init finishes, its output says: "You should now deploy a Pod network to the cluster." The Kubernetes docs add a caution: you must deploy a CNI-based Pod network add-on so pods can talk to each other, and CoreDNS will not start before a network is installed. Before that, you also had to install a container runtime and kubeadm on every host yourself. k3s makes those choices for you and ships them together: Piece k3s kubeadm --- --- --- Container runtime containerd, bundled You install one first Pod network (CNI) Flannel, bundled You pick and apply one Cluster DNS CoreDNS, packaged Added with the cluster, but idle until a CNI exists Ingress Traefik, packaged Not included LoadBalancer for Services ServiceLB, embedded Not included Datastore SQLite by default for one server etcd Install curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io \ sh - Packages on every host, then kubeadm init and kubeadm join The k3s extras are optional. You switch a packaged component off with --disable=traefik (comma-separate several, or repeat the flag), and k3s removes it from the cluster. An empty traefik.yaml.skip file does the same before the first start, but creating it afterwards removes nothing. Both paths end at a Ready node. One has more steps you choose, the other has more steps already chosen. Priya notices something else in that table. Every empty cell on the kubeadm side is a decision, and every decision is a future conversation with a security team. That can be a feature. For an HPC site with strict network rules, picking your own CNI might be the entire point. But the first day is the easy day. What about the day you have to upgrade? ---

secs.head: The part nobody asks about: day two
secs.body: Installing is a story you tell once. Upgrading is a story you tell every quarter. k3s kubeadm --- --- --- Upgrade order Servers first, one at a time, then agents First control-plane node, other control-plane nodes, then workers How Re-run the install script with INSTALL K3S VERSION pinned, repeating your original config, or use the system-upgrade-controller Upgrade the kubeadm package, run kubeadm upgrade , then upgrade kubelet and kubectl on each node Draining Your choice Required before a minor-version kubelet upgrade Skipping minor versions Don't Unsupported Two lessons hide in that table. 1. Neither lets you skip a minor version. If you stood the cluster up and left it for a year, you'll upgrade in steps, in both worlds. 2. kubeadm makes you drain a node for a minor kubelet upgrade. On a GPU node with a long run on it, that is exactly part 9's problem. The upgrade calendar needs to know when the training windows are. The k3s docs don't make draining a rule for upgrades, but upgrading a node under a long run is still your call to plan around. [!WARNING] With the k3s install script, re-run it with the same configuration you used originally. The docs warn that settings you leave out are lost. Next question: what if one control-plane box dying must not take the cluster with it? ---

secs.head: High availability, honestly
secs.body: Both tools can run several control planes. The shapes differ. k3s kubeadm --- --- --- Default One server, embedded SQLite One control-plane node HA with built-in storage Three or more servers with embedded etcd Stacked etcd: three or more control-plane nodes, etcd on the same machines HA with separate storage Two or more servers with an external SQL database or etcd External etcd: three or more control-plane nodes plus three or more etcd machines In front of the API Agents use a local load balancer to reach servers You provide a load balancer whose address matches ControlPlaneEndpoint The k3s docs describe this honestly: SQLite is for a single server, and embedded etcd needs three servers. Moving from the first to the second is a project, not a flag, so decide before the cluster has users. kubeadm is more explicit and more work. You build the load balancer, health-check TCP port 6443 on each control-plane node, and keep its address in step with kubeadm's configuration. In return you decide every part of the topology. ---

secs.head: Picking one
secs.body: A rule of thumb, not a law: the more of the stack your site already has opinions about, the closer you are to kubeadm. My recommendation, with the trade-off named: - Lab, CI, edge, a three-node proof of concept: k3s. You'll learn Kubernetes instead of installers, which is why part 2 uses it. - A GPU cluster with a site CNI, a security review and a platform team: kubeadm. The extra assembly buys you a stack you chose rather than one you inherited. - Everything in between: start with k3s, and keep the manifests plain. Your Deployments don't care which distribution runs them, so moving later costs you the cluster rebuild and not an application rewrite. [!IMPORTANT] Nothing on this page was run on a test cluster. Every statement comes from the k3s and Kubernetes documentation read on 8 November 2026. Check the version-specific pages (upgrades especially, which are written against a specific minor release) before you plan a real change. ---

secs.head: Back to Priya
secs.body: She writes one line in the spreadsheet's first row: "Both are conformant Kubernetes." Then she answers Dmitri and Aiko in the same email. For the lab, k3s stays. For the GPU cluster, her site's network team wants its own CNI and a written upgrade policy, so it's kubeadm, with one rule borrowed from the k3s world: keep the manifests plain. Dmitri was right about the cluster and wrong about the lab. Aiko was right about the lab and wrong about the cluster. Nobody got a trophy. Takeaway: k3s and kubeadm deliver the same Kubernetes, so choose by how much of the stack you want to own, and plan the upgrade day before the install day. Challenge: your GPU cluster uses kubeadm and a three-day training run sits on a node that needs a minor kubelet upgrade. Using part 9, what do you do first, and what does the run need to survive it? ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - K3s documentation: what K3s is, the single binary, and the bundled components. - K3s architecture: server and agent roles, SQLite and embedded etcd datastores. - K3s requirements: minimum hardware and ports. - K3s packaged components: AddOns, --disable and .skip files. - K3s manual upgrades: the install script, upgrade order and minor-version rule. - Creating a cluster with kubeadm: kubeadm init , the Pod network add-on and join tokens. - Installing kubeadm: requirements and swap. - Upgrading kubeadm clusters: upgrade order, draining and skipped minor versions. - Creating Highly Available clusters with kubeadm: stacked and external etcd, and the load balancer.

label: Your kubeconfig is a house key
title: Your kubeconfig Is a House Key
desc: Part 12 of the Kubernetes series. A file called config sits in your home directory and opens the whole cluster. By the e

secs.head: Your kubeconfig Is a House Key
secs.body: Part 12 of the Kubernetes series. A file called config sits in your home directory and opens the whole cluster. By the end you'll know what's inside it, how kubectl picks which one to use, and how to hand out a smaller key. - The ticket - What's on the key ring - Which key does kubectl pick? - The key you can't take back - Where the master key comes from - Cutting a smaller key - Back to the ticket - References ---

secs.head: The ticket
secs.body: A contractor, Mateo, is stuck. His pods won't schedule and he's blocked. To help, a well-meaning teammate attaches her ~/.kube/config to the ticket: "just use mine, it works." It does work. It also lets Mateo delete the production namespace, read every Secret, and run a pod on any node. The ticket system keeps attachments forever, and so does everyone with search access to it. The file looked like boring config. It was the master key. Why is that file so powerful? ---

secs.head: What's on the key ring
secs.body: A kubeconfig is a small YAML file that "organizes information about clusters, users, namespaces, and authentication mechanisms." Back to the series' landlord picture: it's your key ring, with three kinds of entries. Entry In the picture What's inside --- --- --- clusters Which building The API server address and the CA certificate used to trust it users Which key A client certificate and private key, a token, or a credential plugin contexts A key for a building, plus a room A triple: cluster, user and namespace The docs give the example: a dev-frontend context says "use the credentials of the developer user to access the frontend namespace of the development cluster." A context is only a label that ties three things together. The user entry holds the part that opens the door. Certificate and key can be a file path or the data inline: add the -data suffix, for example client-key-data . The inline form is what makes one file copyable, and one file leakable. [!CAUTION] The Kubernetes docs say storing passwords in client config is risky and suggest a credential plugin that keeps them elsewhere. ☕ Try it before you scroll. You have a config for the lab and one for production. You run kubectl delete namespace test . Which cluster loses it? Hint: it isn't the one you were thinking about. ---

secs.head: Which key does kubectl pick?
secs.body: The answer is the current context , and kubectl decides it in this order: 1. If you pass --kubeconfig , it uses only that file and does not merge. 2. Otherwise it reads the KUBECONFIG environment variable, a colon-separated list on Linux and Mac, and merges the files. 3. If that variable isn't set, it uses $HOME/.kube/config . Merging has simple rules: the first file to set a value wins, and a later file never overrides it. Within the result, the --context flag beats current-context . The commands you'll use daily: I haven't run these here; the use-context behaviour is from the docs. My recommendation: never leave production as your current context. Prefer --context for one-off commands on a cluster that matters, so a command run from muscle memory goes to the lab, not production. There's one more trap in the same docs. A kubeconfig can make kubectl run code and read files, so "only use kubeconfig files from trusted sources". Treat a file someone sends you like a shell script: read it before you use it. So a copied key works, and you can't easily make it stop. Why not? ---

secs.head: The key you can't take back
secs.body: Kubernetes has no user objects. The authentication docs say "Kubernetes does not have objects which represent normal user accounts," so a user is whatever name a valid credential carries. For a client certificate, the username comes from the certificate's common name, and groups come from its organization fields. The docs' example: /CN=alovelace/O=app1/O=app2 is the user alovelace in groups app1 and app2 . Now the sentence that should change your habits. The docs for Kubernetes 1.37 say: "Kubernetes 1.37 does not support certificate revocation . Any certificate that is issued remains valid until it expires." So a leaked certificate-based kubeconfig can't be cancelled. You wait for expiry, or you rotate the CA, which is a very bad afternoon. That's why the lifetime of a key matters more than anyone tells you when you create it. If the key leaks... What actually helps --- --- A certificate with a long life Nothing quick. It stays valid until it expires A certificate with a short life It dies on its own, soon A permission set that's narrow The thief can do little, even while the key works Which is why the next question is where yours came from. ---

secs.head: Where the master key comes from
secs.body: Every cluster has to hand someone the first, all-powerful key. The tools you met in part 11 do it differently. Admin kubeconfig Notes from the docs --- --- --- k3s /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml Copy it to ~/.kube/config on your machine and change server to your K3s server's address. K3s refreshes the certificates in it each time it starts, so an old copy can expire kubeadm /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf kubeadm init tells you to copy it to $HOME/.kube/config . Client certificates kubeadm generates expire after 1 year by default kubeadm also writes a super-admin.conf , and the docs for an external CA say to delete or move it to a safe place. If you read that and thought "nobody has said that to me before", you're not alone. [!WARNING] Copying the admin file to a laptop turns the laptop into a cluster-admin. Do it on purpose, for your own machine, and then stop handing the file around. Treat chmod 600 and an encrypted disk as the minimum. The way out is not hiding the master key better. It's cutting smaller ones. ---

secs.head: Cutting a smaller key
secs.body: For a person who needs temporary access, the Kubernetes certificate API can issue a client certificate with a lifetime you choose. A CertificateSigningRequest carries a required signerName , and since Kubernetes v1.22 an optional expirationSeconds , whose minimum is 600 (ten minutes). Someone with approval rights must approve the request, with kubectl certificate approve . The flow, in order: 1. The person generates a private key and a CSR with the name and groups they need. 2. You submit it as a CertificateSigningRequest with a short expirationSeconds . 3. An approver approves it. 4. You hand back the signed certificate, never the private key. 5. They add it to their own kubeconfig with kubectl config set-credentials and set-context . [!IMPORTANT] I did not run this flow, and the CSR page I fetched was cut off before the user-certificate example. Use the "Kubernetes signers" section of that page for the exact manifest, and test it on the k3s lab before relying on it. Two things the new key can't do by itself: it doesn't say what its owner is allowed to do. A freshly issued certificate for mateo proves who he is and nothing more. What he may do is a separate question, answered by roles and bindings. That is the next page. ---

secs.head: Back to the ticket
secs.body: The teammate deletes the attachment, which doesn't recall it. Her certificate remains valid until it expires, because Kubernetes can't revoke it, and she's told that rotating it means asking for a new one. Mateo gets a certificate of his own with a short life, and a narrow role that fits his namespace. The cost of the shortcut was a week of cleanup. The cost of the right way was fifteen minutes and an approval. Takeaway: a kubeconfig is a key, not a setting; Kubernetes can't revoke a certificate, so give each person their own short-lived key instead of sharing yours. Challenge: your certificate for mateo is signed and valid for an hour. Before RBAC grants it anything, what can he do on the cluster? The next page, on RBAC and the limited viewer, answers that. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Organizing cluster access using kubeconfig files: contents, KUBECONFIG , merge rules, the trusted-source warning. - Configure access to multiple clusters: set-cluster , set-credentials , set-context , use-context , inline -data fields. - Authenticating: no user objects, certificate username and groups, no revocation. - Certificates and Certificate Signing Requests: signerName , expirationSeconds , approval. - Creating a cluster with kubeadm: copying admin.conf to $HOME/.kube/config . - Certificate management with kubeadm: the one-year client certificate default. - PKI certificates and requirements: where kubeadm keeps user account certificates. - K3s cluster access: /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml , copying it off the server, certificate refresh on start.

label: RBAC and the limited viewer
title: RBAC: The Error Message Writes the Rule for You
desc: Part 13 of the Kubernetes series. Mateo has his certificate and gets a wall of "Forbidden". By the end you'll read that

secs.head: RBAC: The Error Message Writes the Rule for You
secs.body: Part 13 of the Kubernetes series. Mateo has his certificate and gets a wall of "Forbidden". By the end you'll read that error as a ready-made recipe, build a read-only user in four commands, and see why RBAC refuses to let anyone hand out keys they don't hold. - Forbidden, again - The error is a sentence - Four objects, one grammar - Build the limited viewer - Ask before you break things - Bind groups, not people - Three traps that are actually guardrails - Revoking at the binding - Back to Mateo - References ---

secs.head: Forbidden, again
secs.body: Mateo from part 12 has a certificate of his own, valid for an hour. He runs his first command: The teammate who cut his key sighs. "RBAC is a headache. Just bind him to cluster-admin and move on." Don't. That message isn't a wall. It's the exact rule you need, written out in plain words, and most people never read it. ---

secs.head: The error is a sentence
secs.body: Read it again, slowly: User "mateo" cannot list resource "pods" in API group "" in the namespace "dev". The authorization docs say every request carries the same attributes: the user, its groups, a verb, a resource, an API group and a namespace. The server compares that sentence with the rules it holds. Access is denied by default, and if no rule says yes, the answer is HTTP 403. So the error maps onto a rule field by field: The error says The rule field is --- --- User "mateo" the subject in a binding list verbs resource "pods" resources API group "" apiGroups (an empty string is the core group) namespace "dev" where the Role and its binding live That table is most of RBAC. Everything else is the plumbing that turns the sentence into a yes. ---

secs.head: Four objects, one grammar
secs.body: RBAC has four kinds of object, and permissions are purely additive: there are no "deny" rules. That is why it's simpler than it looks. You only ever write the sentences you want to allow. Object Role in the grammar Scope --- --- --- Role A list of allowed sentences: verbs on resources One namespace ClusterRole The same list, or rules for cluster-wide things like nodes No namespace RoleBinding "These subjects get that list", here One namespace ClusterRoleBinding "These subjects get that list", everywhere Whole cluster A subject is a user, a group or a ServiceAccount. A RoleBinding can point at a Role in its own namespace or at a ClusterRole, which grants it only inside the binding's namespace. That second trick is how one reusable ClusterRole serves many namespaces. The binding is the glue and the namespace. The role is only a list. ☕ Try it before you scroll. Mateo has a RoleBinding in dev to the built-in view ClusterRole. He runs kubectl get pods -n prod . Does it work? Hint: where does a RoleBinding grant its role? No. A RoleBinding grants only in its own namespace, even when it points at a ClusterRole. The proof is in Bind groups, not people. ---

secs.head: Build the limited viewer
secs.body: [!NOTE] Everything in this section was run on a throwaway single-node k3s VM (k3s v1.37.2+k3s1 on Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 5.15), then destroyed. Outputs are real, trimmed only where marked. Mateo's certificate says /CN=mateo/O=viewers , so he arrives as user mateo in group viewers . First, the state before any rule exists: He's authenticated and can do nothing. Now the limited viewer, as an admin, in two commands: Then Mateo tries things. Real results: Command Result --- --- get pods -n dev works get pods -n prod Forbidden: ... cannot list resource "pods" ... in the namespace "prod" get secrets -n dev Forbidden: ... cannot list resource "secrets" ... delete pod web -n dev Forbidden: ... cannot delete resource "pods" ... get nodes Forbidden: ... cannot list resource "nodes" ... at the cluster scope Same user, same cluster, and every neighbour is closed. Log access needed its own entry, pods/log , because a subresource is a separate resource in the rule. [!WARNING] The first thing that failed in this test wasn't RBAC. Creating a pod right after kubectl create namespace dev returned error looking up service account dev/default: serviceaccount "default" not found , because the namespace's default ServiceAccount is created a moment later. So no pod existed in dev , and logs and exec were not exercised end to end. kubectl auth can-i get pods/log answered yes ; treat the rest as untested. ---

secs.head: Ask before you break things
secs.body: The most useful RBAC command isn't one that changes anything. kubectl auth can-i asks the server a yes/no question, and as an admin you can ask it as someone else with --as . Add --list to see everything he can do in a namespace. After the binding, Mateo's list gained exactly two rows, pods and pods/log , each [get list watch] . Even before any binding it wasn't empty: every user gets selfsubjectreviews , selfsubjectaccessreviews , selfsubjectrulesreviews and a few read-only discovery URLs like /healthz and /version . That's how whoami works for someone who can't see anything else. Build the habit: write the rule, then ask the server whether it does what you meant. It takes seconds and replaces a Slack message that starts with "it still says forbidden". ---

secs.head: Bind groups, not people
secs.body: Binding mateo by name works, but now every new colleague is another binding. The certificate's O=viewers already put him in a group, so bind that instead, to the built-in view ClusterRole: Results: get pods -n dev works, get pods -n prod stays Forbidden , and get secrets -n dev stays Forbidden too. That last one is by design. The docs say view does not allow reading Secrets, because a Secret can hold a ServiceAccount token that would give API access as that account. In the test, can-i list secrets --as mateo --as-group viewers answered no . The built-in roles are worth knowing by name: ClusterRole In one line (from the docs) --- --- view Read most things in a namespace; no Secrets, no Roles or RoleBindings edit Read and write most things; can read Secrets and run pods as any ServiceAccount there, so it can act as them admin Everything in a namespace, including Roles and RoleBindings cluster-admin Anything, anywhere. Bound to the system:masters group My recommendation: start from view , bind a group, and add a small Role beside it only for what's missing. ---

secs.head: Three traps that are actually guardrails
secs.body: Each of these looks like RBAC being annoying. Each is RBAC protecting you. All three were run. 1. You can't edit what a binding points at. Trying to swap the role on viewers-view for admin : Delete the binding and create a new one. The docs explain why: someone allowed to change a binding's subjects can't quietly change what it grants. 2. You can't hand out keys you don't hold. Mateo was given the right to create Roles and RoleBindings in dev , but no right to read Secrets. He tries to write himself a Secret-reading role: A role for pods, which he already can read, was created fine. Binding himself to admin was refused too, with a list of every permission he lacked. (That list was long, so I've cut it.) The docs call this privilege escalation prevention, and it's enforced by the API itself. It's why delegating "can manage access in this namespace" is much safer than it sounds. 3. A ServiceAccount starts with nothing. The docs list this as the best practice: a role for a specific ServiceAccount, in a specific namespace. Pods you deploy inherit whatever you give that account, so a monitoring tool should never share the default one. [!IMPORTANT] Not tested here: wildcards, resourceNames , kubectl auth reconcile . The docs warn that a wildcard in resources or verbs also grants any resource or verb added later. Prefer explicit lists. ---

secs.head: Revoking at the binding
secs.body: Part 12's uncomfortable fact was that Kubernetes can't revoke a certificate. RBAC gives you the way around it. The test: remove Mateo's bindings, and even delete his CSR object. The key still turns in the lock. It opens nothing. Authentication proves who he is, and RBAC decides what that's worth. So the real "off switch" for a person is the binding, and the real safety net is a short lifetime on the certificate. ---

secs.head: Back to Mateo
secs.body: Mateo's first Forbidden message told us the rule to write. We wrote it in two commands, tested it with can-i before he tried, and checked that the neighbours stayed locked. Later we closed it by deleting the binding, and his certificate became a keyring ornament. Nobody had to bind cluster-admin . The headache was reading the error as a complaint instead of a spec. Takeaway: a Forbidden message is a rule written in advance, namely subject, verb, resource, group and namespace, so read it, write exactly that, and check with kubectl auth can-i --as before anyone else does. Challenge: a monitoring tool needs to list pods, nodes and events across the whole cluster, read-only, and nothing else. Which of the four objects do you need, which resources and verbs go in it, and why must it use its own ServiceAccount? The next page, on polite API server monitoring, builds it. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Using RBAC Authorization: the four objects, additive permissions, roleRef immutability, subresources, user-facing roles, escalation prevention, ServiceAccount permissions, wildcard caution. - Authorization: request attributes, default deny, HTTP 403, and kubectl auth can-i with --as . - Authenticating: certificate username and groups, and kubectl auth whoami . - Certificates and Certificate Signing Requests: how Mateo's certificate was issued.

label: Polite API server monitoring
title: Polite API Server Monitoring: Leave Your Number, Don't Knock Every Second
desc: Part 14 of the Kubernetes series. A wallboard that "just refreshes every second" is a stack of requests on the cluster's

secs.head: Polite API Server Monitoring: Leave Your Number, Don't Knock Every Second
secs.body: Part 14 of the Kubernetes series. A wallboard that "just refreshes every second" is a stack of requests on the cluster's front desk. By the end you'll know what a poll costs, how a watch costs almost nothing, which queue your tool stands in, and the five habits that make a monitor polite. - The wallboard - Knocking vs leaving your number - What one list costs - The pattern: list once, then watch - Which queue are you in? - A key that only reads - The right tool for the question - Five habits - Back to the wallboard - References ---

secs.head: The wallboard
secs.body: Someone on the platform team writes a GPU wallboard. It runs kubectl get pods -A in a loop, once a second, and shows the result on a screen. It's lovely. The team likes it so much that a dozen engineers run their own copy on their laptops. Nothing breaks. The cluster just gets a little slower for everyone, and nobody connects it to a small shell loop. The control plane has a front desk, and a dozen people have started knocking on it every second to ask the same question: "anything new?" You can ask the desk to call you instead. First, how bad is the knocking? ---

secs.head: Knocking vs leaving your number
secs.body: [!NOTE] Everything with numbers on this page was run on a throwaway single-node k3s VM (k3s v1.37.2+k3s1, Ubuntu 22.04) with 80 small pods, 86 pods in total with k3s's own, and then destroyed. The counts come from the API server's own apiserver request total metric. Same 20 seconds, three ways: What ran LIST pods requests WATCH pods requests --- --- --- Nothing (an idle control) +0 +0 kubectl get pods -A once a second, 20 times +20 +0 One kubectl get pods -A -w , while two scale changes happened +1 +1 Twenty polls made twenty full lists. The watcher made one list and one long-lived watch request, and the changes arrived as they happened. Its output was 115 lines: the 86 pods of the first list, then 29 change events. A watcher pays the cost of a list once and then hears only what changed. ☕ Try it before you scroll. One poller at one request per second: how many list requests does it make in an hour, and how many does a dozen laptops make? Hint: 60 times 60. That's 3,600 lists an hour for one poller, and 43,200 for twelve. Each of those returns the whole collection. How big is that? ---

secs.head: What one list costs
secs.body: The same 86 pods, fetched different ways through the API, with the byte counts measured: How the list was asked Bytes returned --- --- Full objects (plain JSON) 899,207 Server-side Table (what kubectl get uses) 469,407 Metadata only ( PartialObjectMetadataList ) 420,143 Full objects, first 10 only ( limit=10 ) 159,731 Full objects, a label selector that matches nothing 111 Four lessons are hiding here. 1. A full list is heavy. About 0.9 MB for a small lab. The docs warn that retrieving all pods across all namespaces can be a very large response, 10-20 MB, on large clusters. 2. Asking for less really helps. The Table format is roughly half the size of full objects, and a selector can shrink a response to almost nothing. 3. Metadata alone is not small. 420 KB for 86 pods, close to the Table. Don't expect "just names and labels" to be tiny. 4. Pages work. limit=10 returned 10 items, a continue token, and remainingItemCount: 76 . Per the docs, you fetch the next page with that token, and the collection stays a consistent snapshot across pages. Using the Table size and the poller from above, one poller moves roughly 1.7 GB an hour from the API server. This is arithmetic on the measured numbers, not a separate measurement. Bytes aren't the only price. The docs on API Priority and Fairness say a list the server expects to be large occupies more than one "seat" in its queue, in proportion to the estimated number of objects. So a heavy list also makes everyone else wait longer. ---

secs.head: The pattern: list once, then watch
secs.body: Every Kubernetes object has a resourceVersion , and a list response carries one for the whole collection. The pattern from the docs: 1. List and remember the resourceVersion . 2. Watch from that version. The server streams changes, with no missed events. 3. If the watch drops, watch again from the last version you saw . 4. If the server answers 410 Gone , your version is too old: clear your cache, list again, watch again . The docs say a cluster using etcd 3 keeps the last 5 minutes of changes by default, and a continue token for a chunked list expires after about 5 minutes too. For the stale case, I asked for a watch from resourceVersion=1 : That's the 410 in the flesh. Your client must handle it, and the client libraries already do: the Go client's Reflector implements list-then-watch for you. Watch bookmarks ( allowWatchBookmarks=true ) help a short history window by sending small events that carry only a newer resourceVersion . I did not test bookmarks. [!TIP] Don't write this loop by hand. Use a client library's informer or reflector, or a tool built on one. Write your own, and the 410 case is the one you'll forget. ---

secs.head: Which queue are you in?
secs.body: The API server doesn't treat all callers alike. API Priority and Fairness sorts every request into a priority level with its own concurrency, and fair-queues within it. Here is the table from the lab cluster, trimmed to the rows that matter: FlowSchema Priority level For --- --- --- system-nodes system Kubelets kube-controller-manager , kube-scheduler workload-high Built-in controllers kube-system-service-accounts workload-high ServiceAccounts in kube-system service-accounts workload-low Every other ServiceAccount global-default global-default Everything else, such as a person's kubectl A monitoring tool running in a pod with its own ServiceAccount lands in workload-low , where the docs say requests from "any other service account" go. In the test, the API server's counter confirmed it: apiserver flowcontrol dispatched requests total{flow schema="service-accounts",priority level="workload-low"} was 118. That has two implications. A polite monitor doesn't lean on the high-priority lanes, and an impolite one is competing in a lane meant for ordinary workloads. When the queue overflows, the server answers HTTP 429. The counter for that, apiserver flowcontrol rejected requests total , had no series at all on the quiet lab, which means nothing was ever rejected. On your real cluster, it's the first number to chart. The stable metrics worth a dashboard: Metric What it tells you --- --- apiserver request total Requests by verb, resource and response code apiserver request duration seconds How long they take apiserver current inflight requests Load, per request kind apiserver flowcontrol rejected requests total Requests turned away (beta) ---

secs.head: A key that only reads
secs.body: This is part 13 put to work. The lab's monitor got its own ServiceAccount, a read-only ClusterRole and a binding, all with the commands from the docs: What it could and couldn't do, as run: Command as the monitor Result --- --- get pods -A works (86 pods) get nodes works get secrets -A Forbidden: ... cannot list resource "secrets" ... at the cluster scope delete pod -n load -l app=web --dry-run=server 80 Forbidden lines, one per pod. Even a dry run is refused get --raw /metrics Forbidden: ... cannot get path "/metrics" That last row is a small trap. The API server's own metrics aren't a resource, so they need a separate nonResourceURLs rule. If your monitor scrapes /metrics , give it that one explicitly and nothing more. ---

secs.head: The right tool for the question
secs.body: Not every number should come from asking the API server. Question Right source Note --- --- --- Is the pod pending, crash-looping, out of GPUs? The object state: a watch, or kube-state-metrics kube-state-metrics describes itself as listening to the API server and keeping a snapshot of cluster state in memory How much CPU and memory is it using right now? metrics-server, for autoscaling and kubectl top Its README says it's meant only for autoscaling and not an accurate source of usage, and tells monitoring to scrape the kubelet's /metrics/resource Is the API server itself healthy? Its /metrics endpoint The table above In the lab, kubectl top nodes as admin showed 969m CPU and 1903Mi memory, and the raw Metrics API showed "window":"10.058s" : an average over a short window, not a timeline. [!NOTE] The monitor identity failed kubectl top nodes with "Metrics API not available". I did not investigate why, so don't read it as a rule. ---

secs.head: Five habits
secs.body: 1. Watch, don't poll. One list, then a watch from its resourceVersion , with a client library handling 410. 2. Ask for less. Label and field selectors, namespaces, and limit with continue . A selector that matches nothing cost 111 bytes in the test. 3. Own your lane. A dedicated ServiceAccount and a read-only ClusterRole with explicit resources and verbs. No wildcards. 4. Back off when told. On 429, wait and retry; on 410, relist. Never answer a rejection by asking faster. 5. One collector, many viewers. A dozen wallboards should read from one cached collector, not a dozen API watchers. This is my recommendation, not a doc rule, and it's the biggest saving of the five. ---

secs.head: Back to the wallboard
secs.body: The platform team replaces the shell loop with a single small collector. It lists once, watches, and serves the screens from its own cache. A dozen laptops stop knocking, and the front desk gets quiet. Where the API server used to see 43,200 lists an hour, it now sees one list and one watch. The wallboard looks exactly the same. That's the best kind of fix. Takeaway: a poll asks the API server the whole question again every time, so list once, watch from the resourceVersion , filter on the server, and run it all as a read-only ServiceAccount. Challenge: on a cluster of a few thousand nodes with many teams' controllers, everything on this page gets bigger, and some of it gets different. Which of the five habits stops being optional first? The next page, Kubernetes at HPC scale, takes that on. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Kubernetes API concepts: efficient detection of changes, resourceVersion , 410 Gone, watch bookmarks, chunked lists. - API Priority and Fairness: priority levels, seats for large lists, HTTP 429 and the rejected-requests metric. - Kubernetes metrics reference: apiserver request total , apiserver request duration seconds , apiserver current inflight requests . - Resource metrics pipeline: the Metrics API and metrics-server's purpose. - metrics-server README: its intended use and the advice about monitoring. - kube-state-metrics README: what it exposes and how it differs from metrics-server. - RBAC and the limited viewer: the read-only key this page builds on.

label: Kubernetes at HPC scale
title: Kubernetes at HPC Scale: The Front Desk Meets a 100,000-Task Array
desc: Part 15 of the Kubernetes series. A Slurm habit that costs nothing on Slurm can bury a Kubernetes cluster. By the end yo

secs.head: Kubernetes at HPC Scale: The Front Desk Meets a 100,000-Task Array
secs.body: Part 15 of the Kubernetes series. A Slurm habit that costs nothing on Slurm can bury a Kubernetes cluster. By the end you'll know the limits the project publishes, where the pressure lands first, and how to turn a job array into one object that the cluster can carry. - The array - What the project promises - Where the pressure lands - Your array, as one Job - What gang scheduling changes at this size - Back to the array - References ---

secs.head: The array
secs.body: Noor has run Slurm for years. A researcher asks her to move a parameter sweep to the new Kubernetes cluster. On Slurm it was one line, sbatch --array=0-99999 , and the scheduler barely noticed. Noor does the obvious translation. A small script loops from 0 to 99,999 and runs kubectl create job for each task. It starts well. Then the commands slow down, the dashboards from part 14 crawl, and an hour later the finished pods are still sitting there, because nobody told the cluster to clean up. Nothing is broken. Noor sent 100,000 separate letters to the front desk, and each one was filed forever. So how big is the building, really? ---

secs.head: What the project promises
secs.body: The series' landlord has had a front desk since part 1: the API server, with etcd as the filing cabinet behind it. Every object, whether a Job, a pod or an Event, is a file in that cabinet. The Kubernetes docs for v1.37 say the project "supports clusters with up to 5,000 nodes", and that it is designed for configurations that meet all of these criteria at once: Limit Value --- --- Pods per node No more than 110 Nodes No more than 5,000 Pods in total No more than 150,000 Containers in total No more than 300,000 Two things to notice. These are design targets for the whole cluster, not per-feature promises. And the pod limit is a count of objects , not of running work: a finished pod you didn't delete is still a file in the cabinet. ☕ Try it before you scroll. Noor's 100,000 tasks are all done and nothing was cleaned up. Is she under the 150,000-pod figure? Hint: what else lives in the cluster already? She's under it on paper, and she has used two thirds of the budget for one sweep. Every other team now shares what's left. The next question is which part complains first. ---

secs.head: Where the pressure lands
secs.body: Everything goes through the API server. Load that grows with the number of objects or nodes lands on the same four places. The Kubernetes docs name these ones. For each, I add what it means for an HPC site. Part What the docs say What it means for you --- --- --- Control plane A large cluster "needs a control plane with sufficient compute and other resources." Typically one or two instances per failure zone, "scaling those instances vertically first". The page gives no sizing numbers Size it before the cluster is busy, and watch it, politely, with the page 14 habits etcd You can store Event objects in a separate dedicated etcd instance. etcd's default request limit is 1.5 MiB, its default storage limit is 2 GiB, and 8 GiB is "a suggested maximum size for normal environments" Events are noisy when thousands of pods start and fail. Keeping them out of the main cabinet is a project, so plan it early Scheduler See below See below Add-ons Their default limits "are typically based on data collected from experience running each addon on small or medium Kubernetes clusters", and on large clusters they "may continuously get killed because they keep hitting the memory limit" This is part 10 for the platform itself. Raise limits as you grow, and give CoreDNS and metrics-server a system PriorityClass Cloud quotas Request increases ahead of time, and bring up new nodes in batches with a pause between them Matters if you burst onto rented nodes The scheduler is the interesting one. By default it doesn't score every node. If you don't set percentageOfNodesToScore , Kubernetes computes it with a linear formula that "yields 50% for a 100-node cluster and yields 10% for a 5000-node cluster", with a lower bound of 5%. There is also a hardcoded minimum of 100 nodes. So on a 5,000-node cluster, it stops searching once it has found enough feasible nodes, which is about 500 by the docs' 10%. The docs warn: don't set it below 10% "unless the scheduler's throughput is critical for your application and the score of nodes is not important." That sentence is the HPC catch. On a web cluster, any decent node is a good node. On a GPU cluster, node choice can mean the right NVLink domain or the wrong one. My recommendation: leave the default alone, and when placement quality matters, ask for it explicitly with the topology tools from part 7, not by hoping the scheduler looked at enough nodes. I haven't measured scheduler behaviour here. [!NOTE] Nothing on this page was run on a test cluster. A two-VM lab can't show the effect of 5,000 nodes, and I won't present numbers I didn't measure. Every figure comes from the documentation read on 8 November 2026 (Kubernetes v1.37 pages). So the cabinet and the desk have limits. How does Noor send the work without paying for 100,000 files? ---

secs.head: Your array, as one Job
secs.body: The Kubernetes Job docs describe the trade-off in one sentence: "One Job per work item creates some overhead for the user and for the system to manage large numbers of Job objects. A single Job for all work items is better for large numbers of items." The Slurm array has a Kubernetes sibling: the Indexed Job , stable since v1.24. Its pods get a completion index from 0 to completions - 1 , exposed to the container as the JOB COMPLETION INDEX environment variable. It plays the role of the array task index in a Slurm script. Slurm array Indexed Job --- --- --array=0-99999 completions: 100000 , completionMode: Indexed --array=0-99999%50 parallelism: 50 The task index in the script JOB COMPLETION INDEX A failed task is requeued by hand, or by the site's policy backoffLimitPerIndex and maxFailedIndexes Old jobs age out of the accounting database ttlSecondsAfterFinished The % in Slurm's --array=0-15%4 "specifies a maximum number of simultaneously running tasks", which is what parallelism does here. Here is Noor's sweep as one object. It is built from the field examples in the Job docs. I haven't applied it to a cluster. Three lines matter most. - parallelism: 50 . parallelism is the number of pods the Job runs at once, so the Job doesn't need 100,000 pods to exist together. That's the difference between one big Job and a loop of small ones. - backoffLimitPerIndex . With it, "a failing index does not interrupt execution of other indexes." Failed ones land in .status.failedIndexes , and maxFailedIndexes stops a broken sweep before it burns the whole allocation. One catch from the docs: if any index fails, the Job ends up marked Failed, "even if some, potentially nearly all, of the indexes were processed successfully." - ttlSecondsAfterFinished . This is the habit Noor skipped. The docs recommend it because Jobs you create directly have a default deletion policy of orphanDependents , which leaves their pods around after the Job is deleted. Set the TTL, and the TTL controller deletes the Job together with its pods. [!WARNING] restartPolicy: Never is also required if you add a podFailurePolicy , which lets you stop retrying on an exit code that means "this will never work" ( FailJob ) and ignore failures caused by a node drain ( Ignore on the DisruptionTarget condition). The drain part ties back to part 9. [!TIP] Many tiny tasks are better as fewer, longer ones. The Job docs say "having each Pod process multiple work items is better for large numbers of items." If a task takes seconds, make each index a chunk of tasks. I haven't measured it, but a pod is a heavier object than a Slurm task, so fewer, longer ones are the safer default. An array is many independent tasks. What about the other HPC shape, one job that needs a hundred GPUs at the same moment? ---

secs.head: What gang scheduling changes at this size
secs.body: Page 7 explained why a big training job needs all-or-nothing placement, and page 8 showed Kueue holding the job back until quota fits. This is what the current docs add: Fact from the docs Version What it means --- --- --- The gang policy places a group of pods "on an 'all-or-nothing' basis", and if the group can't fit, none are bound Beta since v1.37, behind the GenericWorkload feature gate, disabled by default Native gang scheduling exists, but you have to turn it on The Job controller can create the Workload and PodGroup for a Job from .spec.scheduling Alpha since v1.36, behind WorkloadWithJob , disabled by default Not something to build a production plan on yet CompositePodGroup groups child groups, for example for gangs of gangs Alpha since v1.37, disabled by default Interesting for multi-slice jobs, and still experimental One more sentence is worth reading twice. The scheduler never admits fewer than minCount pods at first, but "the actual runtime count of scheduled Pods can drop below this threshold if running Pods are later deleted or evicted." A gang is guaranteed at the start, not for life. For a three-day run, checkpoints still matter more than any scheduler feature. And Kueue's own page says it "works alongside kube-scheduler, cluster-autoscaler and your job controllers instead of replacing them". Which means that at scale you run both, and you need to know which one is saying no. ---

secs.head: Back to the array
secs.body: Noor deletes the loop and writes one Indexed Job. It runs 50 pods at a time, retries each failed index once, stops itself if 500 indexes fail, and cleans up an hour after it ends. The cabinet holds 50 pods at a time instead of 100,000. The other teams don't notice anything. On Slurm that would have been a one-liner. On Kubernetes it's twenty lines, and the twenty lines are the price of a general-purpose building. Takeaway: the cluster's limits are counts of objects, so send an array as one Indexed Job with a parallelism cap and a TTL, and leave the scheduler's defaults alone until you've measured a reason. Challenge: index 417 of Noor's Job failed twice and shows up in .status.failedIndexes . In one command, how do you find that pod's log, and which three commands would you run first if the pod is already gone? The kubectl troubleshooting cheat sheet answers it. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Considerations for large clusters: the 110, 5,000, 150,000 and 300,000 figures, control plane sizing advice, separate etcd for Events, add-on limits. - Scheduler performance tuning: percentageOfNodesToScore , the 50% to 10% formula, the 5% floor, the 100-node minimum. - etcd limits: the request size and storage limits. - Jobs: Indexed completion mode, backoffLimitPerIndex , maxFailedIndexes , pod failure policy, ttlSecondsAfterFinished , job patterns, and the alpha Job-level gang scheduling. - Gang scheduling: the gang policy, feature gates, stages, and the minCount caveat. - Kueue: what it decides and how it works alongside kube-scheduler. - sbatch: --array ranges and the % limit. - Polite API server monitoring and Isolating GPU workloads: the pages this one builds on.

label: kubectl troubleshooting
title: kubectl Troubleshooting Cheat Sheet: Five Questions, in Order
desc: A companion to the Kubernetes series. It's 6 PM, a pod is wrong, and you remember half of a command. This page is the sh

secs.head: kubectl Troubleshooting Cheat Sheet: Five Questions, in Order
secs.body: A companion to the Kubernetes series. It's 6 PM, a pod is wrong, and you remember half of a command. This page is the shelf: five questions, asked in the same order every time, with the command for each. - The ritual - 1. Where is it? - 2. What does it say? - 3. What did the cluster say? - 4. Why did it die? - 5. How do I look inside? - The Job that lost index 417 - References ---

secs.head: The ritual
secs.body: Think of a nurse doing rounds. She doesn't start with surgery. She checks the same five things, in the same order, on every patient, and most of the time the answer is on the second one. Do the same with a pod. Where is it, what does it say, what did the cluster say about it, why did it die, and only then, how do I look inside. The order matters because each step is cheaper than the next, and the first three fix most tickets. Part 4 is the long version of this ritual with the gallery of failures. This page is the short one. [!NOTE] The commands come from the Kubernetes reference pages. I also ran them on 8 November 2026 against deliberately broken pods and a failing Indexed Job, on a throwaway single-node k3s v1.37.2+k3s1 (Ubuntu 22.04.3, kernel 5.15.0-91), destroyed afterwards. Where the real output differed from what I expected, the page says so. Not tested: a multi-node cluster, other Kubernetes versions, and kubectl debug in a real terminal (my run had no TTY, so it fell back to streaming logs). Replace POD , NS and JOB with your own names. ---

secs.head: 1. Where is it?
secs.body: -o wide adds the node name. A pod that is Pending has no node yet, and a pod on the wrong node tells you to look at taints and selectors (part 7). The docs give the first split: a pod stuck in Pending "can not be scheduled onto a node", usually because of insufficient resources. A pod stuck in Waiting was scheduled but "can't run on that machine", most often because the image can't be pulled. ---

secs.head: 2. What does it say?
secs.body: The one people forget is -p . A pod in CrashLoopBackOff keeps restarting, so the container you ask for may be a new one with nothing in it yet. The docs describe --previous as printing "the logs for the previous instance of the container in a pod if it exists." What the test showed: - On a pod that exits with code 3, plain kubectl logs crasher printed starting and fatal-detail-here , because it was between restarts and the last instance had just died. kubectl logs -p crasher printed unable to retrieve container logs for containerd://... instead. So if -p fails, try plain logs as well, and the other way round. - kubectl logs -p on a pod that never restarted failed with previous terminated container "c" in pod "fine" not found . That's the correct answer: there is no previous instance. - With a label selector, one bad pod makes the whole command exit 1, although the other pods' logs still print. In the test, kubectl logs -l app=demo --all-containers printed the healthy pod and then container "c" in pod "badimage" is waiting to start: image can't be pulled . Two limits from the docs: with a selector, --tail defaults to 10 lines, and --max-log-requests defaults to 5 pods followed at once. ---

secs.head: 3. What did the cluster say?
secs.body: describe prints "a detailed description of the selected resources, including related resources such as events". Read the Events section at the bottom first: the scheduler writes its reason there. In the test, a pod asking for 64 CPUs got 0/1 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient cpu. preemption: 0/1 nodes are available: 1 Preemption is not helpful for scheduling. A GPU request fails the same way, with Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu . The bad-image pod showed ErrImagePull first and ImagePullBackOff a few seconds later, with the registry's not found message in between. [!TIP] For several pods or a prefix match, describe doesn't show events unless you ask: --show-events defaults to true only for a single object. Name the pod. ---

secs.head: 4. Why did it die?
secs.body: Logs show what the program said. The pod status shows what Kubernetes saw: the exit code and the reason. Look for lastState.terminated : it carries exitCode , reason and message . In the test, a container that tried to hold about 100 MB under a 20Mi limit showed OOMKilled exit 137 . That means the memory limit, and part 10 explains why it can happen with RAM to spare. Your program can leave a note too. The docs say Kubernetes reads a termination message from /dev/termination-log by default. If the file is empty and the container failed, setting terminationMessagePolicy: FallbackToLogsOnError uses the last chunk of the log instead, limited to 2048 bytes or 80 lines. You can't change terminationMessagePath after the pod has started. In the test, a container that wrote fatal-detail-here to stderr and exited with 3 got that line back in lastState.terminated.message with FallbackToLogsOnError , and the same field was empty for a pod that had never started. [!NOTE] lastState holds the previous run. For a pod with restartPolicy: Never , such as a Job's pod, there is no restart, so look under state.terminated instead. What you see Where to look --- --- Pending describe , Events: the scheduler's reason ImagePullBackOff describe : the image name, the registry, the pull secret Error , then CrashLoopBackOff logs and logs -p , then lastState.terminated OOMKilled lastState.terminated.reason , then the memory limit Completed but wrong logs : the exit code was 0, so look at the program ---

secs.head: 5. How do I look inside?
secs.body: Only now. If the pod is up and its image has no shell, kubectl debug adds one: The docs describe the first form as adding "an ephemeral container to an already running pod, for example to add debugging utilities without restarting the pod." For a node, "the host's filesystem will be mounted at /host". My recommendation: prefer --copy-to on anything that matters. A debug session in the real pod can disturb the very problem you came to see, and a copy can be thrown away. What the test showed: all three forms worked. The ephemeral container appeared in spec.ephemeralContainers and, with --target , could see the original container's process ( sh -c echo all good; sleep 3600 as PID 1). The --copy-to copy ran as a second pod, fine-debug , with 2/2 containers, and the node form listed the host's / . A copy is a real pod: delete it when you're done, and look at kubectl get pods afterwards for a leftover node-debugger pod. I didn't check what happens to that one. [!WARNING] kubectl debug node/... runs in the node's host namespaces. Treat it like root on that machine, and check who is allowed to do it (part 13). ---

secs.head: The Job that lost index 417
secs.body: Page 15 ended on a challenge: index 417 of an Indexed Job failed twice. Here is the same ritual, applied to a small version of it: a 6-index Job where index 4 always exits 1, with backoffLimitPerIndex: 1 and ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 60 . What the test showed: - failedIndexes printed 4 , and completedIndexes printed 0-3,5 . The Job's status was Failed with 5/6 completions, as the docs say it would be. - Index 4 had two pods , sweep-4-b9ljl and sweep-4-4clfz , both in Error . With restartPolicy: Never a retry is a new pod, not a restart, so the selector returns every attempt and logs printed both. - kubectl logs -p failed here: previous terminated container "task" in pod "sweep-4-4clfz" not found . Use plain logs . - kubectl logs job/JOB is not the way to find the failure. It printed Found 7 pods, using pod/sweep-0-29gs6 : the first pod, which was a healthy one. - The pods carry both batch.kubernetes.io/job-name=sweep and the older job-name=sweep , so you can scope the selector to one Job. If the pods are already gone, what is left depends on what deleted them: After I deleted the two pods by hand, all three still worked. The Job's events showed a SuccessfulCreate line per pod and FailedIndexes , and the conditions showed reason: FailedIndexes . After ttlSecondsAfterFinished fired, kubectl get job sweep and describe job sweep returned jobs.batch "sweep" not found , and kubectl get pods showed nothing for it. The TTL controller had deleted the Job together with its pods, as the docs say. Only kubectl events --for job/sweep still printed lines, and they only say that pods were created and that indexes failed. That was about 90 seconds in. I didn't measure how long events stay. They say nothing about why index 4 failed: the log lines index-4-broke and task 4 were gone with the pods. So the TTL decides how long you can debug. My recommendation: ship logs off the cluster, or set the TTL long enough for the humans, before you rely on ttlSecondsAfterFinished . That is advice, not a Kubernetes rule. Takeaway: ask the same five questions in the same order, read the Events section before anything else, and remember that a Job's TTL deletes the evidence along with the pods. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Debug Pods: describe , Pending and Waiting pods. - kubectl logs: --previous , selectors, --tail , --since , --max-log-requests . - kubectl events: --for , --types , --watch . - kubectl describe: events and --show-events . - kubectl get: -o wide , selectors, output formats. - Determine the reason for Pod failure: lastState.terminated , termination messages, FallbackToLogsOnError . - kubectl debug: ephemeral containers, --copy-to , node debugging. - Jobs: failedIndexes , the completion index label, ttlSecondsAfterFinished .

label: **Ansible**
title: Ansible, for People Who Manage More Nodes Than They Can SSH Into
desc: A story-first series for cluster admins who are comfortable with a root shell and tired of for n in $(seq ...) loops. Ea

secs.head: Ansible, for People Who Manage More Nodes Than They Can SSH Into
secs.body: A story-first series for cluster admins who are comfortable with a root shell and tired of for n in $(seq ...) loops. Each page starts with something that went wrong, fixes it with Ansible, and goes back to the story at the end. The pages build one project, cluster-ansible , that manages a small Slurm cluster. Written against ansible-core 2.22.0 (released November 2026) on Python 3.13, with ansible-lint 26.11.0. ---

secs.head: Contents
secs.body: File Description --- --- 1. The Laptop That Ran Ansible 2.16 A pinned install per project, which Python the controller and the nodes need, ansible.cfg , SSH host keys, and the first-run errors 2. Four Nodes Said "Too Many Open Files" Inventory groups and ranges, group vars , targeting patterns, ad-hoc commands, and checking a change in a fresh login 3. The Playbook That Restarted slurmd Every Night changed vs ok , why shell lies, handlers, --check --diff , and the handler that never ran 4. The GPU Node That Thought It Had 1000 MB Roles, OS-specific variables, variable precedence, hostvars in templates, and a check that every node got the same config 5. The Reboot That Killed a Week of Jobs Rolling maintenance: drain through Slurm, a canary, stop on first failure, a dry run that really is dry, and rollback 6. The Munge Key in Git ansible-vault , rotating a leaked key, the 2.22 secret masking and where it stops, no log , and a commit guard 7. Cheatsheet Every step from the series in order, as copy-paste commands, with a quick-reference table ---

secs.head: How the pages were tested
secs.body: - Lab: six Ubuntu 24.04 nodes ( head01 , cn001 – cn004 , gpu001 ) running systemd, Slurm 23.11.4 and munge 0.5.15, in containers on a throwaway sandbox (Linux 6.18). The controller ran ansible-core 2.22.0 on Python 3.13. - Not run: Rocky/RHEL steps. No Rocky image could be fetched in the sandbox, so those parts come from Red Hat and Fedora documentation and are marked on each page. - Lab artefacts are called out where the container setup differed from real hardware: resource-limit caps, the boot-time check for reboots, and a Slurm scheduling quirk. - Failure paths too: every check on these pages was also run against a broken input to prove it fails. Several of our own checks didn't fail at first; the pages show how we found out.

secs.head: Related pages
secs.body: - Node Health Check: what to run on a node before you hand it back to Slurm (part 5). - VictoriaMetrics series: another stack you could deploy with the roles pattern from part 4.

label: 1. Installing Ansible
title: The Laptop That Ran Ansible 2.16: An Install You Can Trust
desc: Part 1 of the Ansible series. By the end you'll have a pinned Ansible in a project folder, a config file it actually rea

secs.head: The Laptop That Ran Ansible 2.16: An Install You Can Trust
secs.body: Part 1 of the Ansible series. By the end you'll have a pinned Ansible in a project folder, a config file it actually reads, every node's SSH host key checked, and a ping that answers pong from the whole cluster. - Two laptops, one playbook - Which Ansible, which Python - Step 1: a pinned install per project - Step 2: an ansible.cfg it will actually read - Step 3: a first inventory - Step 4: first contact and host keys - When a node is reinstalled - When a node's Python is too old - Which Python did it pick? - Your editor - Back to the two laptops - References ---

secs.head: Two laptops, one playbook
secs.body: Two admins share one Git repo of playbooks. Sara installed Ansible with apt two years ago. Omar ran pip install ansible-core last week. Same repo, same command, different results. Sara's run works everywhere, including the old Rocky 8 nodes nobody wants to touch. Omar's fails on exactly those nodes: Omar concludes his laptop is broken. It isn't. Sara is running an ansible-core that went out of support in July 2025, and Omar is running one that no longer talks to the Python those nodes ship with. Neither of them chose a version. Their package managers did. This page fixes that: one pinned version per project, chosen on purpose, the same on every laptop. [!NOTE] Lab: ansible-core 2.22.0 on Python 3.13 (control machine), six Ubuntu 24.04 nodes with Python 3.12. Rocky/RHEL steps weren't run (no Rocky image in the sandbox); they come from Red Hat's documentation and are marked. ---

secs.head: Which Ansible, which Python
secs.body: Ansible runs on your machine, the control node , and copies small Python programs, modules , to each managed node (target), where they run with that node's Python. So two Pythons matter, and each ansible-core release supports a range of both. From the official support matrix: ansible-core Status (Nov 2026) Control node Python Target Python --- --- --- --- 2.22 Current, GA Nov 2026 3.13 – 3.15 3.9 – 3.15 2.21 Critical fixes until Nov 2026, security until May 2027 3.12 – 3.14 3.9 – 3.14 2.20 Security phase ended 2 Nov 2026; end of life May 2027 3.12 – 3.14 3.9 – 3.14 2.18, 2.19 2.18 end of life May 2026; 2.19 end of life Nov 2026 3.11 – 3.13 3.8 – 3.13 2.16 End of life since July 2025 3.10 – 3.12 2.7, 3.6 – 3.12 What that means on real machines: What you do What you get Why --- --- --- apt install ansible-core on Ubuntu 24.04 2.16.3 That's the version in Ubuntu's archive pip install ansible-core on Python 3.12 (Ubuntu 24.04's) 2.21.6 pip quietly picks the newest release that supports your Python pip install ansible-core==2.22.0 on Python 3.12 An error 2.22.0 requires Python 3.13 pip install ansible (the big package with collections) 14.6.0, which pins core 2.21.6 The community package trails ansible-core We ran all four in the lab. The third one says so plainly: And on the target side, the trap from the story: Rocky/RHEL 8's built-in Python is 3.6 ( platform-python , used by dnf itself). Every ansible-core since 2.17 refuses it. We come back to that below. Rule of thumb: pin ansible-core per project, and pick the version from your oldest node's Python, not from your laptop. ---

secs.head: Step 1: a pinned install per project
secs.body: We use uv , a Python package manager that can also download the Python version a project needs. That matters here: ansible-core 2.22 needs Python 3.13, and Ubuntu 24.04 ships 3.12. Install uv with any method from its docs; in the lab we used pip install uv . 1. Make the project and write down the versions: 2. Create the environment with its own Python, and install exactly those versions: 3. Check it: Commit requirements.txt ; add .venv/ to .gitignore . Anyone who clones the repo runs the same two uv commands and gets the same Ansible. [!TIP] Always source .venv/bin/activate first. Without it, ansible-lint printed WARNING: PATH altered to include .../.venv/bin ... This is usually a sign of broken local setup in our lab. If you'd rather use Mamba, as an earlier version of this page did, the same idea applies: one environment per project, with the version pinned ( mamba install ansible-core=2.22.0 ). We didn't test that route this time, and conda-forge has to carry the version you pin. ---

secs.head: Step 2: an ansible.cfg it will actually read
secs.body: Put the settings in the project, next to the playbooks: Setting Why --- --- inventory So you never need -i and never run against the wrong list remote user The account Ansible logs in as on every node interpreter python = auto silent Finds each node's Python without a warning per host forks = 20 How many nodes it works on at once. The default is 5 pipelining = True Fewer SSH round trips per task; noticeably faster on many nodes Ansible uses the first config file it finds, in this order: the file named by ANSIBLE CONFIG , ./ansible.cfg in the current directory, ~/.ansible.cfg , then /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg . That's why you run Ansible from the project folder. Here's the trap. If the current directory is world-writable , Ansible ignores the ansible.cfg in it, because anyone could have planted it. We ran chmod o+w . in the project: No config, so no inventory, so a playbook against all runs against nothing and finishes. Shared project folders on NFS are where this bites. Check with ansible --version : the config file = line must show your file. ---

secs.head: Step 3: a first inventory
secs.body: Part 2 explains inventories properly. For now, this file says which machines exist and how they're grouped: Save it as inventory/hosts.yml . The node names must resolve (DNS or /etc/hosts ), and the admin user needs your SSH key and passwordless sudo on every node. ---

secs.head: Step 4: first contact and host keys
secs.body: On a fresh setup, every node failed: Ansible uses OpenSSH, and OpenSSH won't talk to a machine whose host key it hasn't seen. Interactive ssh would ask you; Ansible can't. The tempting fix is host key checking = False . Don't: that's the exact check that tells you someone is impersonating a node. Collect the keys once, and compare them with what the nodes report about themselves: On the node itself (through the BMC console, or your provisioning logs), ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh host ed25519 key.pub must print the same fingerprint. In the lab, cn001 printed SHA256:80kw4rx6...gAM , a match. Then trust them: Success is a pong from every node and exit code 0. When any node is unreachable, Ansible carries on with the others and exits 4 . Scripts should check for that. [!NOTE] The -o (one line per host) option still works in 2.22 but prints a deprecation warning: it goes away in 2.23. Don't build scripts on it. ---

secs.head: When a node is reinstalled
secs.body: You reinstall cn004. It comes back with new host keys, and the next run says: We reproduced this by rebuilding cn004 in the lab. Everything else kept working; cn004 was UNREACHABLE! and the run exited 4. The fix is the same as first contact, for one node: remove the old key, scan, compare, trust. Do it only when you know the node was reinstalled. If you didn't reinstall it, that warning is the one that matters. ---

secs.head: When a node's Python is too old
secs.body: Back to Omar's error. In the lab we pointed one node at a Python 3.8 to reproduce it: Older ansible-core versions failed differently on old Pythons; an earlier version of this page shows SyntaxError: future feature annotations is not defined from a CentOS 7 node with Python 2.7. Same cause: a target Python older than the release supports. The fix is a newer Python on the node, not an older Ansible. For Rocky/RHEL 8, Red Hat's documentation says: - platform-python (3.6) is for system tools and isn't meant for you to use. Don't remove it; dnf needs it. - Newer Pythons are packages: python3.11 (RHEL 8.8 and later) and python3.12 (8.10 and later). So on those nodes, install one and tell Ansible to use it, in that group's variables ( inventory/group vars/el8.yml , for a group called el8 ): We couldn't run this on Rocky 8 in the lab. Check the path with ls /usr/bin/python3 on one node first. CentOS 7 reached end of life in June 2024; the earlier advice to compile Python from source there is a workaround for a system you should be replacing. ---

secs.head: Which Python did it pick?
secs.body: A small playbook to see which interpreter Ansible uses on each node. It's the fixed version of a snippet from an earlier version of this page, which had two bugs: wrong indentation, and a fact that isn't always there. discovered interpreter python only exists when Ansible had to discover the interpreter. If you set ansible python interpreter yourself, as for the el8 group above, it doesn't exist, and the plain version of this task fails: With default(ansible python interpreter) , it printed /usr/bin/python3.12 for discovered nodes and /usr/bin/python3 for the one we'd set by hand. It passes ansible-lint on the production profile. ---

secs.head: Your editor
secs.body: If you use VS Code with the Ansible extension, point it at the project's environment so it lints with the same versions you pinned. In the extension's settings, set the Ansible path to .venv/bin/ansible , the Python interpreter to .venv/bin/python , and the lint path to .venv/bin/ansible-lint . We didn't test the extension itself in the lab. ---

secs.head: Back to the two laptops
secs.body: Sara and Omar delete their system Ansibles. Both clone the repo, run the two uv commands, and get ansible-core 2.22.0 on Python 3.13, the version written in requirements.txt . Their runs now behave identically, because they are identical. The Rocky 8 nodes still say "requires Python 3.9". Now that's the right answer, not a laptop problem: they get python3.12 from AppStream and one line in group vars/el8.yml . The next admin who joins doesn't inherit Sara's out-of-support version or Omar's surprise. And when it's time for 2.23, upgrading is a one-line change in a reviewed commit, not something a package manager decided on a Tuesday. Takeaway: pin ansible-core per project from your oldest node's Python, keep ansible.cfg in the project folder, and check host keys instead of switching checking off. Next: Part 2, Four Nodes Said "Too Many Open Files", makes the inventory do real work. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Releases and maintenance: the ansible-core support matrix with control and target Python versions and end-of-life dates. - ansible-core 2.22 changelog: dropping Python 3.12 on the controller. - ansible-core source, module utils/basic.py : the target Python minimum ( PY MIN = (3, 9) ) and its error message. - ansible-core source, config/manager.py : config file search order and the world-writable directory check. - Installing Ansible: ansible vs ansible-core and installation with pip. - Interpreter discovery: how Ansible picks the target Python and the auto silent setting. - ansible-core on PyPI and ansible on PyPI: Requires-Python and versions. - Ubuntu noble: ansible-core: the 2.16.3 package in Ubuntu 24.04. - Red Hat: Installing and using dynamic programming languages (RHEL 8): platform-python , python3.11 , python3.12 . - uv documentation: installing uv, Python versions and virtual environments. - ssh-keyscan(1) and ssh-keygen(1): collecting and fingerprinting host keys.

label: 2. Inventory and ad-hoc
title: Four Nodes Said "Too Many Open Files": Inventories and Ad-Hoc Commands
desc: Part 2 of the Ansible series. Part 1 got a pinned Ansible talking to every node. By the end of this page you'll describe

secs.head: Four Nodes Said "Too Many Open Files": Inventories and Ad-Hoc Commands
secs.body: Part 2 of the Ansible series. Part 1 got a pinned Ansible talking to every node. By the end of this page you'll describe the cluster in an inventory, change one setting on exactly the right nodes, catch the one that missed it, and prove the change in a fresh login. - The loop that skipped a node - An inventory is a map with groups - Variables live next to the groups - Aim before you fire - The change, as one command - The trap: checking through a reused connection - A check you can rerun - Catching up the node that was down - What ad-hoc commands are not for - Back to the loop - References ---

secs.head: The loop that skipped a node
secs.body: A user's data-loading job dies with OSError: [Errno 24] Too many open files . The fix is well known: raise the open-files limit on the compute nodes. Someone does it the quick way: It scrolls past, mostly fine. Three weeks later the same error comes back, but only for jobs that land on four particular nodes. Those nodes were down for repair that afternoon. The loop printed ssh: connect to host ... No route to host four times among four hundred lines, and nobody read them. Two other nodes now have the line twice, from when someone reran the loop "to be safe". This page does the same change so that a missed node can't hide. [!NOTE] Lab: ansible-core 2.22.0 , Ubuntu 24.04 nodes with the usual default soft limit of 1024 open files. The lab container capped the hard limit at 20000, so we used values below that. The per-limit numbers here are examples, not recommendations. ---

secs.head: An inventory is a map with groups
secs.body: An inventory lists your machines and puts them in groups . You'll use the groups everywhere: to choose where a task runs, and to attach settings. This is the lab's inventory/hosts.yml : Three things to notice: - cn[001:004] is a range : cn001 to cn004. A real cluster writes cn[001:400] and gets 400 hosts. - nodes has no hosts of its own. Its children are other groups, so nodes means "every machine that runs jobs". - Groups describe roles, not hardware racks. Add rack07 if you need it; a host can be in many groups. See what Ansible understood: [!WARNING] Ranges don't guess your padding. cn[1:4] expands to cn1 cn2 cn3 cn4 , not cn001 .
