We checked: ansible -i unpadded.yml all --list-hosts printed cn1 cn2 cn3 cn4 . If your names have leading zeros, so does the range. ---

secs.head: Variables live next to the groups
secs.body: Values that differ between groups go in inventory/group vars/<group .yml . Ansible loads them automatically for every host in that group. gpu001 is in both nodes and gpu . The more specific group wins: a child group overrides its parent. Check before you rely on it: Rule of thumb: if you're about to type a number into a command, it probably belongs in group vars . ---

secs.head: Aim before you fire
secs.body: A pattern picks hosts. Before any change, ask Ansible who it would touch with --list-hosts : Pattern Means In the lab --- --- --- nodes The group cn001–cn004, gpu001 nodes:!cn003 The group, minus a host cn001, cn002, cn004, gpu001 compute:gpu Either group cn001–cn004, gpu001 nodes:&gpu In both groups gpu001 cn001,cn002 A list cn001, cn002 Now the trap. Mistype a group name in an ad-hoc command and Ansible warns, does nothing, and exits 0 : A wrapper script would call that a success. The same typo in a playbook's --limit is treated properly: --limit cn0003 failed with no hosts to target and exit 1. When you script ad-hoc commands, check the host list first. ---

secs.head: The change, as one command
secs.body: An ad-hoc command runs one module on a set of hosts from the command line. No playbook file. Here's the whole change: Piece Meaning --- --- nodes The pattern: where -b Become root with sudo on the node -m ansible.builtin.copy The module: write a file with exactly this content {{ nofile limit }} Filled in per host from group vars : 8192 on compute, 16384 on gpu001 Two differences from the for loop already. copy sets the file's content instead of appending to it, so running it twice gives the same file, not two lines. And Ansible reports every host. In the lab we ran it with cn003 switched off: Exit code 4. cn003 can't hide among the others. ---

secs.head: The trap: checking through a reused connection
secs.body: You want to see the new limit, so you ask the nodes straight away: Every node said 1024 , the old value. At the same moment, a plain new SSH login to cn001 already showed the new one. We waited 65 seconds and asked through Ansible again: now every node showed its new value too. Here's why. The limit is applied by PAM when you log in , and Ansible doesn't log in for every command. By default it keeps each SSH connection open for 60 seconds ( ControlPersist=60s in its default ssh args ) and reuses it. Within that minute you're asking an old session. So the change worked; the check was lying. This one cost us a confused ten minutes in the lab, and it'll do the same to anyone verifying limits, group memberships or anything else that's set at login. ---

secs.head: A check you can rerun
secs.body: Turn the check into a small playbook that resets the connection, so it always reads a fresh login, and that compares the result with the inventory instead of with your eyes. Save it as playbooks/check-nofile.yml : changed when: false tells Ansible that reading a value changes nothing, so it doesn't report a change. Part 3 is about why that matters. With cn003 back up but still missing the change, the check named it and exited 2: Before we lowered the GPU value under the lab's cap, the same check also caught gpu001 holding a value the inventory didn't expect. It fails when it should. It passes ansible-lint on the production profile. ---

secs.head: Catching up the node that was down
secs.body: Run the same change on just the node that missed it: cn003 CHANGED . Then the important test: run it on all nodes again. Every host answered SUCCESS , not CHANGED . Nothing to do, so nothing done. And the check: [!IMPORTANT] A login limit doesn't reach processes that are already running, and Slurm jobs don't log in through PAM on the node. By default Slurm copies the limits from where the job was submitted ( PropagateResourceLimits in slurm.conf ), and slurmd's own limit caps what a job can have. So set the limit on the login nodes too, and restart slurmd after raising its limit. See the Slurm documentation in the references; we didn't test the Slurm side in this lab. ---

secs.head: What ad-hoc commands are not for
secs.body: Ad-hoc is for questions and one-off fixes: "what's the kernel version everywhere?", "restart this daemon on these three nodes". It's not for changes you want to keep. Nobody can review a command in your shell history, and nobody will rerun it on the node you add next month. Once a change matters, it goes into a playbook in Git. That's part 3. ---

secs.head: Back to the loop
secs.body: Same request, same 400 nodes, this inventory. The change is one command with the value in group vars , so GPU nodes get theirs without a second loop. Four nodes are down; the output says UNREACHABLE! four times, the run exits 4, and that's impossible to scroll past in a script. Nobody reruns anything "to be safe", because rerunning changes nothing. When the four nodes come back, check-nofile.yml names them. One --limit run catches them up, and the check passes on all 400. Three weeks later there's no mystery error, because the check would have failed first. It's a five-second job to put it in the node health checks. Takeaway: describe the cluster once in an inventory, keep values in group vars , aim with --list-hosts , and verify with a check that logs in fresh and compares against the inventory. Next: Part 3, The Playbook That Restarted slurmd Every Night, turns one-off commands into playbooks you can trust to rerun. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - How to build your inventory: YAML inventories, ranges, child groups, group vars and how group variables merge. - Patterns: targeting hosts and groups: : , ! , & and --limit . - Introduction to ad hoc commands: running modules from the command line, -b . - ansible.builtin.copy, ansible.builtin.assert, ansible.builtin.meta: the modules used here, including reset connection . - ansible.builtin.ssh connection: the default ssh args with ControlPersist=60s . - limits.conf(5) and pam limits(8): when login limits apply. - slurm.conf: PropagateResourceLimits: how Slurm passes limits from the submit host to jobs.

label: 3. Idempotence and handlers
title: The Playbook That Restarted slurmd Every Night: Idempotence and Handlers
desc: Part 3 of the Ansible series. Part 2 made one-off changes with ad-hoc commands. This page writes a playbook that deploys

secs.head: The Playbook That Restarted slurmd Every Night: Idempotence and Handlers
secs.body: Part 3 of the Ansible series. Part 2 made one-off changes with ad-hoc commands. This page writes a playbook that deploys slurm.conf to the whole cluster, restarts daemons only when the file really changed, previews changes before making them, and survives a failure halfway through. - Changed, every night - Idempotent: say what, not how - The version that started it all - A template and two handlers - Preview with --check --diff - The handler that never ran - Started, then restarted - The finished playbook - Back to the nightly run - References ---

secs.head: Changed, every night
secs.body: A cron job runs the Slurm playbook every night "to keep things in line". Every morning the summary says the same thing: changed=2 on every node. Everyone learns to ignore it. Then someone edits slurm.conf by hand on one node to test something and forgets to undo it. The nightly run fixes the file, which is good. But the report says changed=2 on that node, the same as on every other node, every other night. Nobody notices that this time it meant something. Meanwhile every node's slurmd has been restarted every night for a year, and once a month that restart lands during a burst of job launches. A run that always says "changed" tells you nothing. This page makes "changed" mean something again. [!NOTE] Lab: ansible-core 2.22.0 , Slurm 23.11.4 from Ubuntu 24.04's packages, with systemd running on every node. Two Slurm settings in the template below ( SlurmUser=slurm , MpiDefault=none ) were added after the lab's first run failed without them; they match Ubuntu's packaging. ---

secs.head: Idempotent: say what, not how
secs.body: A task is idempotent when running it twice leaves the system the same as running it once, and the second run reports ok instead of changed . Ansible's modules are built for this: you describe the end state ("this file has this content", "this service is running"), and the module checks before it acts. Every task ends in one of these states: State Means What you should feel --- --- --- ok Already right, nothing done Nothing. That's the goal changed It was wrong, now it's right Look: something drifted, or you shipped a change skipped A condition said "not here" Nothing failed Couldn't make it right Act Rule of thumb: a clean second run should be all ok . If it isn't, the playbook is lying to you. ---

secs.head: The version that started it all
secs.body: This is the playbook from the story, in miniature: shell and command just run what you give them. Ansible can't know whether that changed anything, so it always says changed . We ran it twice: Two runs, two restarts, identical reports. And in check mode (next section) both tasks are simply skipped : you can't preview anything. ansible-lint flags all of it: shell and command aren't banned. Use them for things no module does, and tell Ansible when they change something ( changed when: ), as part 2's check did with changed when: false . ---

secs.head: A template and two handlers
secs.body: Two ideas fix this. A template is a file with placeholders, filled in per host from variables. The ansible.builtin.template module renders it, compares the result with the file on the node, and writes only if they differ. Save as playbooks/templates/slurm.conf.j2 : The node list comes from the inventory: add a host to compute , and it appears in every node's slurm.conf on the next run. The values go in inventory/group vars/all.yml : (The lab's containers have one CPU and plenty of memory. Use your hardware's real numbers; slurmd -C on a node prints them.) A handler is a task that runs only when another task notifies it, and only if that task reported changed . Handlers run once, at the end of the play, however many tasks notified them. So "restart slurmd" becomes a handler, notified by the template task. Same file, no change, no restart. The full playbook is further down. First, what it does. On the second run, every host reported changed=0 and no handler ran. That's the whole point: When we really changed something (adding SlurmUser=slurm to the template), only then did the handlers run: ---

secs.head: Preview with --check --diff
secs.body: Check mode ( --check ) runs the playbook without changing anything: modules that support it report what they would do. Diff mode ( --diff ) shows the line-level change for files. Together, they're the dry run you show a colleague before the real one. We changed slurm node memory mb from 950 to 1000 and asked: You see the exact line, and that slurmd would restart. The file's checksum was the same before and after: nothing was written. [!TIP] On Ubuntu, check mode for package tasks needs python3-apt on the node. A minimal image without it failed with python3-apt must be installed to use check mode . Normal runs install it automatically; check mode can't, because that would be a change. ---

secs.head: The handler that never ran
secs.body: Here's the trap that bites good playbooks. Handlers run at the end of the play. If a host fails anywhere after the notifying task, that host's handlers don't run. We reproduced it: changed a value, and added a task after the template that fails on cn002, standing in for a full /var , a typo, anything. cn002 got the new slurm.conf ( changed=1 ), but its slurmd kept running with the old one. We compared slurmd's start time with the file's modification time: Then we removed the failure and ran again. cn002 said changed=0 , because the file was already correct. No change, no notification, no restart, ever. cn002 stayed stale until someone restarted it by hand. The fix is one line at the play level: With it, Ansible runs the notified handlers for a host even when that host failed. Same failure on cn002, this time: The run still fails, as it should, but no daemon is left running on a config that's no longer on disk. ( --force-handlers on the command line does the same for one run.) ---

secs.head: Started, then restarted
secs.body: One more subtle one, found in the controller's log on the very first deploy. The playbook had two tasks in this order: "make sure slurmctld is started", then (at the end of the play) the "restart slurmctld" handler. On a fresh node that means: Started, then immediately restarted, because the config was new. Harmless here, wasteful on a real controller, and confusing when you read the log. meta: flush handlers runs any pending handlers right there , instead of at the end. Put it between the template and the "started" tasks: a changed config restarts (or first-starts) the daemon, and the "started" task finds it already running. We reinstalled cn004 and counted daemon starts in its log on the first deploy: Order slurmd starts on first deploy --- --- started task, then handler at end of play 2 template, flush handlers , then started task 1 ---

secs.head: The finished playbook
secs.body: Save as playbooks/slurm-config.yml : On the lab cluster: sinfo showed all five nodes idle , a batch job ran on the node we asked for, the second run was all changed=0 , and ansible-lint passed on the production profile. [!NOTE] This template writes the same CPUs and RealMemory for every node. That's fine while every node is the same. Part 4 gives the GPU node its own value and finds the bug hiding in that loop. ---

secs.head: Back to the nightly run
secs.body: The cron job runs the new playbook. Most mornings the summary is changed=0 everywhere and no daemon restarted overnight. The burst-of-launches incident stops, because nothing restarts unless something changed. Then comes the morning someone hand-edited slurm.conf on one node. The summary shows changed=2 on exactly one host. It stands out like a red light on a quiet panel. The template put the file back, the handler restarted that one slurmd, and --diff in the log shows exactly which line drifted. If anything had failed halfway, force handlers would still have restarted the daemon, so no node is left running a config that isn't on its disk. Takeaway: describe end states with modules, restart through handlers, preview with --check --diff , and set force handlers so a failure can't leave a daemon on a stale config. Next: Part 4, The GPU Node That Thought It Had 1000 MB, turns this playbook into a reusable role. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Intro to playbooks: desired state and idempotency. - Handlers: running operations on change: notification, meta: flush handlers , and handlers after failures. - Error handling in playbooks: force handlers , changed when . - Validating tasks: check mode and diff mode: --check , --diff and module support. - ansible.builtin.template, ansible.builtin.systemd service, ansible.builtin.command: the modules used. - ansible-lint rules: no-changed-when , command-instead-of-module . - slurm.conf(5): SlurmUser , MpiDefault , ReturnToService , node and partition definitions. - slurmd(8): slurmd -C prints a node's real hardware for slurm.conf .

label: 4. Roles and variables
title: The GPU Node That Thought It Had 1000 MB: Roles and Variables
desc: Part 4 of the Ansible series. Part 3 built a playbook that deploys slurm.conf safely. This page turns it into a role tha

secs.head: The GPU Node That Thought It Had 1000 MB: Roles and Variables
secs.body: Part 4 of the Ansible series. Part 3 built a playbook that deploys slurm.conf safely. This page turns it into a role that works on Ubuntu and Rocky, takes per-group values from the inventory, and proves every node ended up with the same file. - Big jobs that never start - What a role is - The OS-family maze, done right - defaults or vars? The precedence trap - Whose value is it? - Prove every node got the same file - The finished role - Back to the big jobs - References ---

secs.head: Big jobs that never start
secs.body: A new GPU node arrives with far more memory than the compute nodes. The admin does it by the book from part 2: one line in group vars/gpu.yml with the bigger memory size, run the Slurm playbook, all green. A week later, users complain that jobs asking for lots of memory sit in the queue forever. The scheduler is sure the GPU node is a small one. slurm.conf on gpu001 says the big number. slurm.conf on the controller says the small one. And the controller's log has been saying it for a week: Nothing failed, and every task was green. The template did exactly what it was told. This page is about telling it the right thing. [!NOTE] Lab: ansible-core 2.22.0 , Ubuntu 24.04 nodes, Slurm 23.11.4. The memory numbers are lab-sized (1000 and 4000 MB). The Rocky/RHEL variables file wasn't run; there was no Rocky image in the sandbox. ---

secs.head: What a role is
secs.body: A role is a folder with a fixed layout that bundles tasks, handlers, templates and variables, so a playbook can say "this host gets Slurm" in one line. Ansible finds each piece by its folder name: Folder Holds Loaded --- --- --- tasks/main.yml The steps Always handlers/main.yml Restarts and reloads When notified templates/ .j2 files for the template module By name, no path needed defaults/main.yml Settings a site may change Always, lowest precedence vars/ Facts about the OS or the software, not choices vars/main.yml always, high precedence; other files when you load them meta/main.yml Author, supported platforms, dependencies By tools and Galaxy With part 1's roles path = roles in ansible.cfg , the role lives in roles/slurm/ , and the playbook shrinks to this ( playbooks/slurm.yml ): ---

secs.head: The OS-family maze, done right
secs.body: Ubuntu and Rocky package Slurm under different names. An earlier version of the Ansible page tried to pick OS-specific task files by building a path from a fact, and hit this. We reproduced it on 2.22: import tasks is static : Ansible reads it when it loads the playbook, before it has talked to any host, so no facts exist yet. include tasks is dynamic : it's resolved when the task runs, after facts are gathered. Switching to include tasks fixed it, and the relative path worked as is. The earlier advice to make the path absolute isn't needed on 2.22. But usually you don't need different tasks , only different names . Same steps, different package names. So keep one set of tasks and load the OS-specific values: first found takes the first file that exists: Ubuntu-24.yml if you ever need one for a specific release, otherwise Debian.yml (Ubuntu's OS family) or RedHat.yml (Rocky's). roles/slurm/vars/Debian.yml : roles/slurm/vars/RedHat.yml , with the EPEL package names: And the failure path. We hid Debian.yml to stand in for an OS the role doesn't support. The run stopped at the first task, before touching anything, with exit 2: That's what you want from an unsupported OS: a clear stop, not a half-configured node. ---

secs.head: defaults or vars? The precedence trap
secs.body: Ansible has more than twenty places a variable can come from, and an order that decides which wins. You need two facts from that list: Where Beats inventory group vars ? --- --- Role defaults/main.yml No. It's the lowest of all Inventory group vars and host vars n/a Role vars/main.yml , and include vars files Yes So a value in the role's vars/ silently beats your inventory. We tested it: the inventory says slurm cluster name: acot . We put slurm cluster name: cluster in roles/slurm/vars/main.yml and dry-ran: The inventory lost, with no warning. Moved to defaults/main.yml , the inventory won again and the dry run showed no change. Rule of thumb: defaults/ is for choices, vars/ is for facts. Cluster name, memory sizes, the controller's name: choices, so defaults/ . Package names on Ubuntu: facts, so vars/Debian.yml . roles/slurm/defaults/main.yml : ---

secs.head: Whose value is it?
secs.body: Now the bug from the story. Part 3's template had this loop: A template is rendered once per host, with that host's variables. Inside the loop, slurm node memory mb isn't the memory of node ; it's the memory of the host the file is being written for. We gave the GPU group its own size: and looked at two nodes' copies of the file: Every node wrote every line with its own number. The controller (not a GPU node) believes gpu001 is small, so big jobs never go there. Slurm noticed the mismatch and logged the error from the story. The fix: inside a loop over other hosts, read their variables through hostvars[node] : Why the default(...) ? hostvars holds inventory variables and facts, not role defaults. When we removed slurm node cpus from the inventory to rely on the role's default, the plain hostvars[node]['slurm node cpus'] failed: The default() falls back to the role default when the inventory doesn't set one. After the fix, every copy agreed: NodeName=gpu001 CPUs=1 RealMemory=4000 on both cn001 and gpu001. A side effect worth knowing: because hostvars doesn't see role variables at all, the precedence trap above can't reach values read this way. It still reaches every plain {{ variable }} , like ClusterName . ---

secs.head: Prove every node got the same file
secs.body: slurm.conf must be identical everywhere. Slurm warns when it isn't, but only in a log. So make the role check it and fail the run instead. These two tasks go at the end of tasks/main.yml : Each host records its file's checksum; one host ( run once ) collects all of them and asserts there's exactly one distinct value. We proved it fails when it should: with the buggy template and the GPU override, the run stopped with exit 2 at this task. With the fixed template it passed, exit 0. [!TIP] Run the role with --limit and this check compares only the hosts in that run. It catches a bad template, not an old file on a host you left out. ---

secs.head: The finished role
secs.body: roles/slurm/tasks/main.yml , between the include vars task at the top and the two check tasks at the bottom (both shown above): handlers/main.yml holds part 3's two handlers unchanged, and templates/slurm.conf.j2 is part 3's template with two edits: the header says (role slurm) , and the NodeName line is the hostvars version above. PartitionName uses {{ slurm partition }} instead of a fixed batch . On the lab cluster, the role's first dry run against part 3's deployment showed one difference: the header comment. The real run, the rerun with changed=0 on all six hosts, and ansible-lint on the production profile all passed. ---

secs.head: Back to the big jobs
secs.body: Run the story again with the finished role. The GPU node's size goes into group vars/gpu.yml exactly as before. This time the controller renders gpu001's line from gpu001's own variables. Every copy of slurm.conf says the GPU node is the big one, the checksum check passes on every host, and big jobs land on the GPU node the moment it's idle. Had the template still been wrong, the run would have stopped red at "Fail unless every host has the same slurm.conf" the first day, instead of a week of green runs and a log nobody read. And when the Rocky nodes join, they need one tested vars/RedHat.yml , not a second playbook. Takeaway: in a role, put choices in defaults/ and facts in vars/ , read other hosts' values through hostvars[node] with a default, and make the role prove every node got the same config. Next: Part 5, The Reboot That Killed a Week of Jobs, changes nodes that are busy running jobs. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Roles: role layout, defaults vs vars , roles path , meta/main.yml . - Re-using Ansible artifacts: import tasks (static) vs include tasks (dynamic). - Using variables: variable precedence: the full precedence list. - Special variables: hostvars , groups , ansible play hosts . - ansible.builtin.first found lookup and ansible.builtin.include vars: loading OS-specific variables. - ansible.builtin.stat, ansible.builtin.assert, ansible.builtin.package: modules used. - Fedora/EPEL: slurm-slurmctld and slurm-slurmd: package names for Rocky/RHEL. - Ubuntu noble: slurmctld: Ubuntu's package names. - slurm.conf(5): every node and the controller must share the same file.

label: 5. Rolling maintenance
title: The Reboot That Killed a Week of Jobs: Rolling Maintenance with Slurm
desc: Part 5 of the Ansible series. Part 4 built a role that configures Slurm. This page changes nodes that are busy running j

secs.head: The Reboot That Killed a Week of Jobs: Rolling Maintenance with Slurm
secs.body: Part 5 of the Ansible series. Part 4 built a role that configures Slurm. This page changes nodes that are busy running jobs: drain each node, wait for its jobs to finish, do the work, prove it came back healthy, return it to service. One canary first, and a full stop at the first failure. - All at once, at 14:00 - The mental model: drain, change, prove, resume - The playbook - What each piece buys you - Step 1: dry run - The dry run that hung - Step 2: canary, then the rest - When the canary comes back broken - Rollback - How we caught our own weak health check - Back to 14:00 - References ---

secs.head: All at once, at 14:00
secs.body: A driver update has to go out, and it needs a reboot. The playbook is ready and tested on a spare node. At 14:00 someone runs it against compute . Without serial , Ansible runs each task on every host before moving to the next (5 hosts in parallel by default, 20 with part 1's forks ), with no idea that a node has jobs on it. Batch after batch, nodes reboot under running jobs. Some jobs had been running for six days. Worse, the new driver has a problem on one hardware revision. Those nodes come back without their GPUs, and Slurm hands them new jobs immediately. Those fail too. Every piece worked as written. Nobody wrote "wait for the jobs" or "stop if it goes wrong". [!NOTE] Lab: ansible-core 2.22.0 , Slurm 23.11.4 on five Ubuntu 24.04 nodes in containers. Two lab differences, both disclosed where they matter: reboots needed one extra setting because containers share the host's boot ID, and the lab's Slurm (no accounting database) logged "invalid account" for new jobs; the backfill scheduler still started them within its 30-second cycle. ---

secs.head: The mental model: drain, change, prove, resume
secs.body: Four ideas, each a few lines of YAML: Idea Slurm or Ansible feature Meaning --- --- --- Drain scontrol update state=drain No new jobs land on the node; running jobs finish normally Batches serial: Work on a few nodes at a time; the rest keep running jobs Canary serial: [1, ...] The first batch is a single node. If it goes wrong, one node is affected Stop on failure max fail percentage: 0 Any failure in a batch stops the whole run before the next batch The Slurm commands run on the controller, not on the node being changed. That's delegate to : "run this task on another host, on behalf of this one". Rule of thumb: a node is out of service from the moment you drain it until you've proven it healthy, not until the reboot finishes. ---

secs.head: The playbook
secs.body: Save as playbooks/rolling-maintenance.yml : The actual change lives in its own file, playbooks/tasks/maintenance.yml , so this playbook never changes. In the lab it just records what was done: [!NOTE] In the lab, the playbook ran with one extra play setting: module defaults giving ansible.builtin.reboot a boot time command of stat -c %Z /proc/1 . Containers share the host's boot ID, so the default check never saw a new boot and timed out after the container had restarted fine. Real nodes don't need it; the default is right for them. ---

secs.head: What each piece buys you
secs.body: Line Without it --- --- serial: [1, "25%"] Every node at once (well, 20 at a time) order: sorted The canary is whichever host the inventory lists first. Sorting keeps it stable when someone reorders the inventory max fail percentage: 0 By default the run stops only when every host in a batch fails. A canary batch of one stops either way, but in a batch of 100, 99 failures wouldn't. The percentage must be exceeded , so 0 means "any failure stops the run" Drain, then wait for drained draining means jobs are still running. Only drained means the node is empty drain wait retries default 360 × 10 s One hour per node. Raise it for long jobs, or use -e drain wait retries=... Reason with a ticket number sinfo -R tells everyone why the node is out, and who to ask Health checks before resume A broken node goes back into service and eats jobs Batch sizes from percentages are rounded down, with a minimum of one host ( pct to int in ansible-core's source). On our five nodes, 25% is one node per batch; on 400 nodes it's 100. Pick a percentage that leaves enough of the cluster running. Don't trust --list-hosts to tell you who the canary will be. In the lab it listed the hosts in a different order every time ( gpu001 first, once), while real runs always started with cn001. It shows which hosts, not in what order. ---

secs.head: Step 1: dry run
secs.body: You see the change the maintenance would make, and that a reboot would happen. Nothing actually happened: in the lab, the node wasn't drained, wasn't rebooted (PID 1's start time was the same before and after), and the file still had the old ticket. ---

secs.head: The dry run that hung
secs.body: The first version of this playbook didn't have the when: not ansible check mode lines, and its dry run never finished. We killed it after five minutes. With the retries turned down to two, it showed what was going on: In check mode, command doesn't run: the task returns "Command would have run if not in check mode" and an empty output. An empty output never equals drained , so until retried, 360 times, ten seconds apart. The drain was skipped too, so even a real sinfo couldn't have said drained . Wait loops only mean something in a real run, so they're skipped in check mode. Same for the "remember when slurmd registered" task, which only feeds a wait loop. ---

secs.head: Step 2: canary, then the rest
secs.body: Before the real run in the lab, we put a 45-second job on cn001 and another on cn002: The controller's log tells the story better than Ansible's output: cn001 was drained at 14:00:49 with its job still running. Ansible waited (five retries in its log) until the job finished on its own at 14:01:30 with exit 0. Then it did the change, rebooted, proved the node was back, and resumed it at 14:01:46. cn002's job had finished by the time its turn came. The run ended with exit 0, failed=0 on every node, the change on all five, and sinfo showing all five idle. ---

secs.head: When the canary comes back broken
secs.body: The story's second problem: a node that comes back wrong. We stood in for the bad driver by masking slurmd on cn001, so it wouldn't start after the reboot, and ran the playbook again: Exit 2. The run stopped after the canary. Look at what that left behind: Node State --- --- cn001 Drained, with the ticket as the reason. No jobs will land on it cn002, cn003, cn004, gpu001 Untouched: no drain, no change, no reboot, still running jobs That's the point of a canary: the failure cost one node, and that node is parked safely. ---

secs.head: Rollback
secs.body: There's no magic undo for a driver. Rollback means two things: fix or revert the node, and return it to service only once it's healthy. In the lab: 1. Fix the canary (here, unmask and start slurmd; in real life, roll back the package or the change in maintenance.yml ): 2. Return it to service, by hand, deliberately: sinfo showed cn001 idle . 3. Then either stop there (the change is bad), or continue with the nodes that haven't had it yet: That finished with exit 0 on the remaining four, all five idle, and the change recorded on every node. [!CAUTION] Rerunning without --limit drains and reboots every node again, including the ones that are done. This playbook is an operation, not a desired state: it isn't idempotent, by design. ---

secs.head: How we caught our own weak health check
secs.body: Our first version had a different last check: "wait until sinfo says the node is drained " (drained and responding). It passed. But right after resume, sinfo showed cn002 as idle ; the asterisk means "not responding". The controller's log explained it: The container rebooted in seconds, faster than the controller noticed it had gone. So drained was the controller's old opinion, and our check proved nothing. On real hardware the reboot takes minutes, but the same race exists: the controller only marks a node not responding after missed contacts. The fix is the version above. Record SlurmdStartTime before the reboot, and wait until it has changed, meaning slurmd has started and registered since the reboot. On the next real run, cn003's slurmd started at 14:22:15 and the check saw the new time. To prove it fails when it should, we ran the record-and-wait pair on cn004 without a reboot: SlurmdStartTime never changed, and it failed after its retries, exit 2. A one-second idle right after resume still showed up once in the lab. It cleared on its own at the controller's next contact. [!TIP] For a real health check before resume, run Node Health Check on the node as one more task. Checking that GPUs, mounts and InfiniBand came back is exactly what it's for. ---

secs.head: Back to 14:00
secs.body: Run the story again with this playbook. At 14:00 the canary drains. It has a six-day job on it, so the playbook waits, and the job finishes on its own that evening. The node reboots onto the new driver, and it's one of the bad hardware revisions: no GPUs. slurmd doesn't come up healthy, the assertion fails, the run stops. One node is drained with CHG-1042 as the reason; the rest of the cluster never noticed. Next morning the admin reads sinfo -R , rolls the driver back on that one node, resumes it, and excludes that hardware revision from the change with a --limit . Then the rest goes through, one batch at a time, each node empty before it reboots. Nobody's six-day job was killed, and no job ever landed on a node without its GPUs. Takeaway: for busy nodes, drain through Slurm, canary first, stop on the first failure, prove the node re-registered before resuming, and make sure your dry run is really dry. Next: Part 6, The Munge Key in Git, handles the secrets these playbooks need. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Controlling playbook execution: strategies and more: serial with lists and percentages, order , rolling updates. - Error handling in playbooks: max fail percentage (must be exceeded, not equaled), any errors fatal . - Controlling where tasks run: delegation: delegate to . - Retrying a task until a condition is met: until , retries , delay . - Validating tasks: check mode and diff mode: ansible check mode and how modules behave in check mode. - ansible.builtin.reboot: reboot timeout , boot time command . - scontrol(1): update state=drain resume , show node , SlurmdStartTime . - sinfo(1): node states ( draining , drained , for not responding) and -R . - Node Health Check: health checks to run before returning a node to service.

label: 6. Secrets and vault
title: The Munge Key in Git: Secrets, Vault and Rotation
desc: Part 6 of the Ansible series. Part 5 changed busy nodes safely. This last page handles the secrets those playbooks need:

secs.head: The Munge Key in Git: Secrets, Vault and Rotation
secs.body: Part 6 of the Ansible series. Part 5 changed busy nodes safely. This last page handles the secrets those playbooks need: encrypt them in the repo, replace one that leaked, roll the new one out without breaking the cluster, and keep secrets out of logs. - The Munge Key in Git: Secrets, Vault and Rotation - Found in a fork - Why this key matters - Vault in five minutes - Encrypting isn't enough: history - Rotating without splitting the cluster - What ansible-core 2.22 hides, and what it doesn't - When the password is missing or wrong - A guard that stops the next one - Back to the fork - References ---

secs.head: Found in a fork
secs.body: Two years ago someone added the munge role to the playbook repo. The key went in where every other file goes: roles/munge/files/munge.key , in plain bytes. Since then the repo has been cloned by four admins, a contractor, and a CI runner, and mirrored to a second Git server "for backup". Today a security review finds it. Somebody says "let's just encrypt it with vault", runs one command, commits, and calls it done. It isn't done. Every clone, every mirror, and every old commit still has the original key. This page does the whole job. [!NOTE] Lab: ansible-core 2.22.0 (and 2.21.6 for one comparison), munge 0.5.15 , Slurm 23.11.4 on six Ubuntu 24.04 nodes. The passwords on this page are fakes made for the lab. ---

secs.head: Why this key matters
secs.body: munge is how Slurm daemons and commands prove who they are to each other. Every host has the same key; a credential made with it says "this is uid 1000 on head01", and anyone with the key is believed. With the cluster's munge key you can mint credentials that the cluster accepts. The mungekey man page puts it simply: every munged in a security realm must use the same key, created on one host and copied securely to the others. So a leaked munge key means two jobs: stop storing secrets in plain text, and replace the key that leaked. ---

secs.head: Vault in five minutes
secs.body: ansible-vault encrypts files (or single values) with a password, using AES-256. Ansible decrypts them in memory when a playbook needs them, so the repo only ever holds ciphertext. 1. Keep the vault password outside the repo, readable only by you: Share it with the other admins the way you share any admin password (a password manager), never through the repo. 2. Tell Ansible where it is, in ansible.cfg under [defaults] : 3. Put secret variables in their own fully encrypted file. Here, the password the Slurm accounting daemon would use, for the head group. A group vars entry can be a folder instead of a file, so plain and secret variables sit side by side: Day to day you use ansible-vault view and ansible-vault edit on that file, and never decrypt it to disk. [!TIP] You can also encrypt single values inside a plain YAML file ( ansible-vault encrypt string ). It works, but then a file named vault.yml is half plain text, and a simple "is this file encrypted?" check can't tell. We use whole-file encryption so the guard at the end stays simple. Our guard flagged the inline style the first time we ran it. ---

secs.head: Encrypting isn't enough: history
secs.body: Back to the key. Encrypting the file in place hides the current version. Git keeps every old one. In the lab we committed a plain key, then later replaced it with an encrypted file, then asked Git for the old commit: Byte for byte, the leaked key. Rewriting history doesn't fix it either: the clones and the mirror still have it. So the only real fix is a new key , made fresh, never committed in plain text: That's 1024 random bytes, 8192 bits, the top of the 256–8192-bit range mungekey(8) accepts. mungekey itself can create the key too, but it writes to the munge directory on the host you run it on; for a repo, dd is simpler. The copy module decrypts a vault-encrypted src file automatically when it deploys it. The role ( roles/munge/tasks/main.yml ) doesn't mention vault at all: and roles/munge/handlers/main.yml : ---

secs.head: Rotating without splitting the cluster
secs.body: Here's the trap. Every host must have the same key at the same time. Part 5 taught you to change nodes a few at a time; do that here and you split the cluster in two. We showed it in the lab by deploying the new key to cn001 only. A credential made on head01 (old key) was rejected by cn001 and accepted by cn002: A minute later the controller had marked cn001 as not responding ( idle in sinfo ), and logged Zero Bytes were transmitted or received talking to it. So the playbook ( playbooks/munge.yml ) targets every host in one go, with no serial : Every host that didn't have the new key yet reported changed=2 (the file and the restart); cn001, which already had it, reported changed=0 . Then: Check Result in the lab --- --- A credential from head01, decoded on cn001, cn004, gpu001 Success (0) on all three cn001 in sinfo Back to idle on its own, about 75 seconds later (the controller's next check) A batch job sent to cn001 Started JobId=6 in batch on cn001 , exit status 0 Run the playbook again changed=0 on all six hosts Restarting munged was enough. We didn't restart slurmd or slurmctld; the Slurm daemons ask munged for every credential. [!CAUTION] We rotated with no jobs running. While hosts disagree about the key (between the first and last host's restart), any Slurm traffic between them fails, including job launches. Do it in a quiet window, or drain the partition first and resume it afterwards. Never with serial . ---

secs.head: What ansible-core 2.22 hides, and what it doesn't
secs.body: The classic second leak: you run with --diff or -v to see what changed, and the secret is right there in the output, in your terminal and in your CI logs. ansible-core 2.22 changed this. Its changelog: Ansible now automatically redacts known secret values from its output, including the plaintext of vault-encrypted values and every value in a vault-encrypted variables file, replacing them with $REDACTED$ . Masking only affects output; tasks still get the real value. We tested where it holds and where it stops, with the same vault and the same play on 2.22.0 and 2.21.6: What's printed ansible-core 2.21.6 ansible-core 2.22.0 --- --- --- The secret itself ( debug ) Tr0ub4dor&3-not-real $REDACTED$ The secret inside command output ( grep StoragePass on the deployed file) StoragePass=Tr0ub4dor&3-not-real StoragePass=$REDACTED$ --diff of a file containing the secret +StoragePass=Tr0ub4dor&3-not-real +StoragePass=$REDACTED$ A value derived from the secret ( \ b64encode ) VHIwdWI0ZG9yJjMtbm90LXJlYWw= VHIwdWI0ZG9yJjMtbm90LXJlYWw= That last row is the gap: masking matches the exact secret strings it knows about. Transform the secret (encode it, hash it, build a connection string from parts), and the result isn't recognized. Decode that base64 and you have the password. The deployed file itself still has the real password, of course; masking is about output only. So for any task that handles a secret in a way you're not sure masking catches, and for anyone still on 2.21 or older, keep the old defence: With no log: true , the task's output was hidden completely on 2.22. Add diff: false to template or copy tasks that write secrets, so --diff doesn't show their content on older versions. Rule of thumb: masking is a seatbelt, not a reason to drive faster. Keep no log on tasks that touch secrets. ---

secs.head: When the password is missing or wrong
secs.body: Both failures are clear and stop the run before anything changes. We ran the munge playbook with a config that had no vault password file : And with only a wrong password: Both exited 2. One thing that surprised us while testing: passing --vault-password-file with a wrong password as well as the right one in ansible.cfg worked fine. Ansible tries every password it has, so to test "wrong password", remove the right one. ---

secs.head: A guard that stops the next one
secs.body: The leak happened because nothing stopped a plain key from being committed. This script fails if any file that should be secret isn't vault-encrypted. Save as tools/check-secrets.sh : Run against the repo before the fix, it caught both problems and exited 1: (The second was the inline encrypt string style from the tip above.) After the fix: secrets check: ok , exit 0. Make Git run it before every commit: We tested it by adding a plain test.key : git commit printed NOT ENCRYPTED: roles/munge/files/test.key , exited 1, and no commit was made. A Git hook lives in each clone and isn't shared, so also run the script in CI, where nobody can skip it. ---

secs.head: Back to the fork
secs.body: The security review finds the key, and this time the team does the whole job. They generate a new key and encrypt it before it's ever committed. The playbook rolls it to every host in one go during a quiet hour, credentials verify everywhere, and the one node that briefly showed idle comes back by itself. The old key, still sitting in every clone and in the mirror, now opens nothing. The slurmdbd password moves into an encrypted vault.yml . The pipeline that prints --diff shows $REDACTED$ on 2.22, and the tasks that transform secrets carry no log . And the next person who drops a plain key into roles/ gets a red NOT ENCRYPTED from their own commit and from CI, before it ever reaches a fork. Takeaway: encrypt secrets with vault before the first commit, rotate anything that was ever committed in plain text, roll shared keys to every host at once, and keep no log even though 2.22 masks most secrets. Next: Part 7, the cheatsheet, has every step from the series as copy-paste commands. Back to: the Ansible series index. From here, the Node Health Check pages are a natural thing to deploy and run with these roles. ---

secs.body: - Protecting sensitive data with Ansible vault: encrypting files and variables, password files, view and edit . - Ansible vault: managing passwords: vault password file and multiple vault passwords. - ansible-core 2.22 changelog: secret masking, what is registered as a secret, and $REDACTED$ . - Logging Ansible output: no log and what reaches logs. - ansible.builtin.copy: decrypt (default true) for vault-encrypted src files. - mungekey(8) (Ubuntu 24.04): every munged in a realm uses the same key, key size range. - Slurm: Authentication plugins: how Slurm uses munge. - githooks(5): the pre-commit hook.

desc: Part 7 of Ansible The series as one list of commands, in the order you'd build the cluster-ansible project. Each step li

secs.head: Ansible Cheatsheet: Every Step from the Series
secs.body: Part 7 of Ansible The series as one list of commands, in the order you'd build the cluster-ansible project. Each step links to the page that explains it, shows its output, and shows how it fails. - Ansible Cheatsheet: Every Step from the Series - Before you start - 1. A pinned install - 2. ansible.cfg - 3. Inventory and host keys - 4. Variables and patterns - 5. Ad-hoc change, and a check that logs in fresh - 6. An idempotent playbook with handlers - 7. The slurm role - 8. Rolling maintenance - 9. Secrets with vault - Quick reference - References ---

secs.head: Before you start
secs.body: [!NOTE] Every command here appears on one of the series pages, where it was run with ansible-core 2.22.0 on Python 3.13 against six Ubuntu 24.04 nodes ( head01 , cn001 – cn004 , gpu001 ) running Slurm 23.11.4. Rocky/RHEL lines weren't run and are marked. This sheet collects the commands; it wasn't re-run from top to bottom as one script. The nodes need: names that resolve, an admin user with your SSH key, passwordless sudo , and Python 3.9 or newer. ---

secs.head: 1. A pinned install
secs.body: Part 1, step 1. ansible-core 2.22 needs Python 3.13 on the controller; uv downloads it. Expected: ansible [core 2.22.0] and config file = .../cluster-ansible/ansible.cfg (after step 2). Always source .venv/bin/activate first. ---

secs.head: 2. ansible.cfg
secs.body: Part 1, step 2. In the project folder: ( vault password file comes from step 9; leave it out until then.) Ansible ignores ansible.cfg in a world-writable directory and then runs against nothing. ansible --version must show your file on the config file = line. ---

secs.head: 3. Inventory and host keys
secs.body: Part 1, steps 3 and 4. inventory/hosts.yml : Trust host keys after comparing fingerprints, never with host key checking = False : Expected: pong from every node, exit=0 . Any unreachable node: exit 4 . After you know a node was reinstalled: A node with Python older than 3.9 fails with Ansible requires Python 3.9 or newer on the target . Fix the node, not Ansible. On Rocky/RHEL 8 (not run): dnf install -y python3.12 , then ansible python interpreter: /usr/bin/python3.12 in that group's group vars . ---

secs.head: 4. Variables and patterns
secs.body: Part 2. Pattern Means --- --- nodes The group nodes:!cn003 The group minus a host compute:gpu Either group nodes:&gpu In both cn001,cn002 A list A typo in an ad-hoc pattern warns and exits 0 ( No hosts matched ). In ansible-playbook --limit it exits 1. Check the host list in scripts. ---

secs.head: 5. Ad-hoc change, and a check that logs in fresh
secs.body: Part 2. Checking login limits through Ansible right away shows the old value: it reuses each SSH connection for 60 s. playbooks/check-nofile.yml resets the connection first: Expected: changed=0 failed=0 on every node, exit=0 . A node that missed the change fails with has 1024, expected 8192 . Rerun the copy on just that node; on all nodes again it should say SUCCESS , not CHANGED . ---

secs.head: 6. An idempotent playbook with handlers
secs.body: Part 3. The template, the variables and the full playbooks/slurm-config.yml are on that page. The parts that matter: Piece Why --- --- ansible.builtin.template instead of shell Writes only when the content differs, so changed means changed Handlers notified by the template Restart only when the config changed force handlers: true on the play A host that fails later still gets its restart; otherwise it runs the old config forever meta: flush handlers before the "started" tasks A new config restarts (or first-starts) the daemon once, not start-then-restart changed when: false on read-only commands Reading isn't a change Check mode for package tasks on Ubuntu needs python3-apt on the node. ---

secs.head: 7. The slurm role
secs.body: Part 4. Rules from that page: - defaults/ for choices, vars/ for facts. A value in vars/ silently beats your inventory. - Load per-OS facts with include vars + first found ( <distribution -<major .yml , then <os family .yml ). An unsupported OS stops at the first task. - Facts don't exist at import tasks time; use include tasks for paths built from facts. - In a template loop over other hosts, read their values: hostvars[node]['slurm node memory mb'] default(slurm node memory mb) . hostvars doesn't include role defaults, hence the default() . - End the role with a run once assert that every host's slurm.conf has the same checksum. playbooks/slurm.yml : ---

secs.head: 8. Rolling maintenance
secs.body: Part 5. The full playbooks/rolling-maintenance.yml is on that page: drain through Slurm, wait for drained , run tasks/maintenance.yml , reboot, check slurmd is active and has re-registered since the reboot ( SlurmdStartTime changed), then resume. Play setting Why --- --- serial: [1, "25%"] One canary, then a quarter at a time order: sorted A stable canary max fail percentage: 0 Any failure stops the run when: not ansible check mode on wait loops Otherwise the dry run retries forever If the canary fails, it stays drained with the ticket as the reason, and nothing else is touched. Roll back: This playbook isn't idempotent by design: rerunning it without --limit reboots every node again. ---

secs.head: 9. Secrets with vault
secs.body: Part 6. - A leaked secret stays in Git history: encrypting it now doesn't help. Make a new one. - Rotate the munge key on all hosts in one run. Half-rotated, hosts reject each other's credentials ( unmunge: Error: Invalid credential ). - 2.22 masks known secret values as $REDACTED$ in output, but not values derived from them ( b64encode ). Keep no log: true on tasks that handle secrets. The commit guard tools/check-secrets.sh is printed on that page. Install it as a hook, and run it in CI too: Expected: secrets check: ok . A plain .key or vault.yml prints NOT ENCRYPTED: <file and blocks the commit. ---

secs.head: Quick reference
secs.body: Task Command --- --- Who would a pattern hit? ansible '<pattern ' --list-hosts A host's merged variables ansible-inventory --host <host Ping everything ansible all -m ansible.builtin.ping Run as root add -b Dry run with diffs ansible-playbook <play --check --diff Limit a run --limit 'nodes:!cn003' Override a variable -e name=value Run handlers even on failure (one run) --force-handlers Lint ansible-lint Exit codes 0 ok, 2 a task failed, 4 a host unreachable Takeaway: pin the version per project, check ansible.cfg is the one in use, trust host keys deliberately, keep numbers in group vars , write tasks that say what not how, restart only through handlers with force handlers , roll through the cluster with a canary, and never commit a secret in plain text. Series index: Ansible. The same Slurm lab is built step by step in the Slurm lab cheatsheet. ---

desc: A short series on VictoriaMetrics, the Prometheus-compatible metrics database, written for people who run clusters and a

secs.head: VictoriaMetrics, for People Whose Prometheus Keeps Running Out of Room
secs.body: A short series on VictoriaMetrics, the Prometheus-compatible metrics database, written for people who run clusters and are comfortable with a root shell. Start at page 1 and work down. Every command was run on a throwaway lab, and each page says what the docs say, what the lab showed, and what we recommend, separately. Written against VictoriaMetrics v1.156.0 (released 2026-11-09), with Prometheus 3.16.0 and node exporter 1.12.1 for comparison. ---

secs.head: Contents
secs.body: File Description --- --- 1. The Prometheus That Ate the Head Node What VictoriaMetrics is, its components, single-node vs cluster, what's free and what isn't, and what it's not for 2. A Single Node You Can Trust Verified install, systemd unit, scrape config, safe reloads, and the delete endpoint that is open by default 3. vmagent and the Network Blip Buffering through an outage, the URL edit that silently deletes the buffer, and how to size the queue 4. Retention, Full Disks and Backups What retention really deletes and when, read-only mode that /health won't report, and backups proven by a restore 5. MetricsQL Surprises and Alerts You Can Test Why increase() disagrees with Prometheus, rules with unit tests that fail when they should, and alerting from outside 6. Cheatsheet Every step from the series in order, as copy-paste commands, with a quick-reference table ---

secs.head: How the pages were tested
secs.body: - Where: a throwaway Ubuntu 24.04.5 sandbox (Linux 6.18, systemd 255), destroyed afterwards. It was a container, not a VM, so systemd wasn't running: unit files were linted with systemd-analyze verify but never started. Each page marks what wasn't run. - Binaries: official release tarballs, checked against the published SHA-256 sums before use. - Failure paths too: every check on these pages was also run against a broken input to prove it fails. Two of our own tests passed when they shouldn't have, and page 5 shows how we caught it.

secs.body: - GPU Allocation vs Utilization: what the numbers you store actually mean. - Predicting GPU node failures: a use for the metrics once you keep them long enough.

label: 1. Why VictoriaMetrics
title: The Prometheus That Ate the Head Node: Why VictoriaMetrics
desc: Part 1 of the VictoriaMetrics series. No commands yet, just the mental model. By the end you'll know what VictoriaMetric

secs.head: The Prometheus That Ate the Head Node: Why VictoriaMetrics
secs.body: Part 1 of the VictoriaMetrics series. No commands yet, just the mental model. By the end you'll know what VictoriaMetrics is, which of its pieces you need, whether one box will do, and what it won't do for you. - The 02:40 page - One binary that stores, scrapes and answers - The cast - One box or a cluster? - What's free and what isn't - What it's not for - Back to the head node - References ---

secs.head: The 02:40 page
secs.body: Friday afternoon, someone turns on extra GPU metrics across the training partition. More labels per GPU, more series per node. Nobody thinks of it as a monitoring change. It's "just an exporter flag". At 02:40 the Prometheus on the head node gets OOM-killed. systemd restarts it, it replays its write-ahead log, it eats the RAM again, it dies again. By morning there's a seven-hour hole in every dashboard, and the one night you needed GPU temperatures is the one night you don't have them. The fix people reach for first is "give it more RAM". The fix that lasts is to ask a different question: does the thing collecting the metrics also have to be the thing storing them for months? That question is where VictoriaMetrics comes in. [!NOTE] The story is a composite, not a measured incident. Every number further down this page comes from the VictoriaMetrics documentation, and the docs' own performance numbers are labelled as the vendor's claims. ---

secs.head: One binary that stores, scrapes and answers
secs.body: VictoriaMetrics is a time series database that speaks Prometheus. It accepts the same scrape config, answers the same query API on port 8428 , and Grafana talks to it as if it were Prometheus. Its query language, MetricsQL , is built to be backwards-compatible with PromQL, adds extra functions, and has a few deliberate differences (part 5 shows them on real data). The single-node version is one executable with no external dependencies. All configuration is command-line flags, and all data lives in one directory set by -storageDataPath . Two flags matter on day one: Flag Default What it does --- --- --- -storageDataPath victoria-metrics-data in the current directory Where every byte of data goes -retentionPeriod 1M (31 days); minimum 1d How long data is kept before deletion Here's the mental model. Prometheus is one process that does four jobs: discover targets, scrape them, store the samples, evaluate rules. VictoriaMetrics lets you split those jobs across small programs, so one job running out of room doesn't take the others with it. Collect at the edge, store in one place, alert from rules. Each arrow is a job Prometheus does inside one process. You don't have to split anything on day one. The single node can scrape targets itself with the same prometheus.yml . The split is there for when you need it. ---

secs.head: The cast
secs.body: Every component ships in the official release tarballs. You'll meet most of them in this series. Component What it does When you need it --- --- --- victoria-metrics (single-node) Stores samples, answers queries, can scrape targets itself Always. This is the database vmagent Scrapes and accepts pushed metrics, relabels them, buffers to disk when storage is down When collection and storage live on different hosts, or the link between them isn't perfect (part 3) vmalert Evaluates Prometheus-style alerting and recording rules against VictoriaMetrics When you want alerts. It sends them to Alertmanager; it doesn't route them itself (part 5) vmalert-tool Unit-tests alert rules against fake series Before every rule change (part 5) vmbackup / vmrestore Backs up from instant snapshots to S3, GCS, Azure or a local path; restores them From the first day you'd be sad to lose the data (part 4) vmauth Auth proxy and load balancer in front of the other components When anything outside a trusted network needs access vmctl Migrates data in from Prometheus, Thanos, InfluxDB, OpenTSDB and others Moving history from an existing system vminsert / vmselect / vmstorage The cluster version: ingestion, querying and storage as separate scalable services When one machine truly isn't enough (next section) Rule of thumb: one job per program, and only the programs you need. For most clusters that's the single node, vmagent, vmalert and vmbackup. ---

secs.head: One box or a cluster?
secs.body: The docs are blunt about this: try single-node first, and move to the cluster version only when you hit its limits. Single-node avoids shipping data between processes over the network, so for moderate workloads it's the most efficient option. How big is "moderate"? The capacity planning section lists a single node working in production, according to VictoriaMetrics' own case studies, at 1.5+ million samples per second ingested and 50+ million active time series. Treat those as the vendor's numbers, not a promise for your hardware, but they're far above what most HPC sites push. Question Single-node Cluster --- --- --- Moving parts One process Three services, each with replicas Scales Vertically: bigger box Horizontally: more boxes High availability Two identical nodes, vmagent writing to both Built into the design Multitenancy Not built in; emulated with a tenant label enforced by vmauth or Grafana Native tenants Upgrade path Data format differs from the cluster's; moving needs re-ingestion n/a The trade-off nobody mentions until it's too late is the last row. Single-node and cluster store data differently on disk, so you can't copy a single node's data into vmstorage . The docs say you can query both side by side while old data ages out, or re-ingest it. Recommendation: start with one single node, sized with the capacity planning method in part 4. Add a second identical node fed by vmagent when "metrics down" becomes an incident instead of an inconvenience. Reach for the cluster when one machine's RAM or disk can't hold your active series and retention, or when you need tenants. "It sounds more serious" isn't a reason. ---

secs.head: What's free and what isn't
secs.body: VictoriaMetrics is Apache 2.0 licensed, and the community edition is the full database. Some features are Enterprise-only. These are the ones admins ask about most: Feature Community Enterprise Community workaround --- --- --- --- Single-node, cluster, vmagent, vmalert, vmbackup, vmrestore, vmauth Yes Yes n/a One retention for all data Yes Yes n/a Different retention per series ( -retentionFilter ) No Yes Run one instance per retention, put vmauth in front Downsampling old data ( -downsampling.period ) No Yes Keep less raw data, or record aggregates with vmalert Scheduled backups with rotation (vmbackupmanager) No Yes vmbackup from a cron job or systemd timer (part 4) Long-term support release lines No Yes Track the latest release [!NOTE] As of v1.156.0, the old -license flags are deprecated and treated as -eula . Only matters if you run Enterprise binaries. ---

secs.head: What it's not for
secs.body: Knowing what a tool won't do saves you from bolting it onto the wrong problem. - Logs. VictoriaMetrics stores numbers over time, not text lines. The same company makes VictoriaLogs for that. - Traces. Same story: a separate product, VictoriaTraces. - Routing and silencing alerts. vmalert decides that an alert fires. Who gets paged, grouping and silences still belong to Alertmanager. - Per-event records. "Which job ran on cn042 at 14:03" is a Slurm accounting question. Metrics tell you that cn042's GPU 3 was at 98% utilisation, not who put it there. - Being reachable from the internet. The docs say all components must sit in a protected network, with vmauth or vmgateway in front of anything untrusted. Part 2 shows why that's not paranoia. ---

secs.head: Back to the head node
secs.body: The fix for the 02:40 page isn't a bigger Prometheus. Each thing that went wrong that night has its own fix, and each part of this series builds one: What went wrong at 02:40 What fixes it Where --- --- --- Storing months of data shared a process and a box with collecting it A dedicated single node, sized from a day-long test, with 50% RAM spare Part 2, part 4 While storage was down, nothing wrote the samples down A vmagent per rack that queues on disk and catches up afterwards Part 3 Nobody knew until morning Alerts on the database's own health, evaluated from outside it, with tests that catch a broken rule Part 5 A bad night could have been a lost disk Hourly backups, and a restore you've actually run Part 4 Run that Friday again with all four in place. The new GPU metrics push the series count up, and the storage box has headroom for it. If it hadn't, an alert would say so at 02:41, vmagent would hold the samples while someone fixed it, and the morning dashboards would have temperatures in them. Takeaway: VictoriaMetrics is a Prometheus-compatible store you can split into collect, store and alert; start with one single node and only add moving parts when a real limit asks for them. Next: Part 2, A Single Node You Can Trust, installs one and locks it down. ---

secs.body: - VictoriaMetrics single-node docs: prominent features, components, default flags and port, capacity planning, scalability and cluster version, retention filters, downsampling, security recommendations. - VictoriaMetrics Enterprise: the list of Enterprise-only features. - LTS releases: long-term support lines are Enterprise-only. - Cluster version docs: vminsert, vmselect, vmstorage and multitenancy. - vmalert docs: relies on Alertmanager via -notifier.url . - MetricsQL: compatibility with PromQL and the intentional differences. - VictoriaMetrics changelog 2026: v1.156.0 release notes, including the -license deprecation. - VictoriaMetrics LICENSE: Apache License 2.0.

label: 2. A single node you can trust
title: A Single Node You Can Trust: Installing VictoriaMetrics Properly
desc: Part 2 of the VictoriaMetrics series. Part 1 explained what VictoriaMetrics is. By the end of this page you'll have a si

secs.head: A Single Node You Can Trust: Installing VictoriaMetrics Properly
secs.body: Part 2 of the VictoriaMetrics series. Part 1 explained what VictoriaMetrics is. By the end of this page you'll have a single node running under systemd, scraping targets, reloading config without surprises, and refusing to delete data for strangers. - A Single Node You Can Trust: Installing VictoriaMetrics Properly - The intern and the empty dashboard - Before you start - Step 1: download and verify - Step 2: a user and two directories - Step 3: what to scrape - Step 4: two admin keys - Step 5: the systemd unit - Step 6: start it and check it - Two things that look broken but aren't - Changing config without a surprise - Why the admin keys matter - Back to the intern - References ---

secs.head: The intern and the empty dashboard
secs.body: An intern is cleaning up "test metrics" from Grafana. They find a VictoriaMetrics URL, read that /api/v1/admin/tsdb/delete series deletes series, and send it a match for everything starting with node . It works on the first try. No password, no prompt. Every node metric for the whole retention period is gone. Nothing about that is a bug. It's the default. This page installs VictoriaMetrics the way you'd want it on a shared network: verified binary, its own user, a bound address, and keys on the endpoints that can destroy or copy data. ---

secs.head: Before you start
secs.body: [!NOTE] Written against VictoriaMetrics v1.156.0 . Every step was run on a throwaway Ubuntu 24.04.5 sandbox (Linux 6.18, systemd 255) with node exporter 1.12.1 as a target. systemd wasn't running there, so the unit in step 5 was linted with systemd-analyze verify and its exact command line was run by hand as the service user, but systemctl start itself wasn't run. You need: a Linux x86-64 host, root, and outbound HTTPS to GitHub. The examples use 10.0.0.5 as the host's internal address. Replace it with yours. ---

secs.head: Step 1: download and verify
secs.body: Pin the version, download the tarball and its checksum file, and check one against the other before you run anything. Success looks like this, with exit code 0: We also appended one line of junk to the tarball to prove the check bites. It printed FAILED and exited 1: Then install the binary and confirm the version: [!TIP] The binary is called victoria-metrics-prod , not victoria-metrics . Keep the name; the docs and every example online use it. ---

secs.head: Step 2: a user and two directories
secs.body: The database should own its data and nothing else. Success: ls -ld /var/lib/victoriametrics shows drwxr-x--- victoriametrics victoriametrics . Put /var/lib/victoriametrics on its own filesystem if you can. When the disk fills, you want the database to stop, not the whole host. Part 4 covers what "stop" means here, and it isn't what you'd guess. ---

secs.head: Step 3: what to scrape
secs.body: Single-node VictoriaMetrics reads a normal Prometheus scrape configs file. Start with node exporter and the database itself: Check the file before the database ever sees it: A good file prints nothing and exits 0. A broken one (we dropped a colon) exits 255 with the line number: Keep this command. You'll use it before every reload. ---

secs.head: Step 4: two admin keys
secs.body: Several endpoints can delete or copy your data, and each can be protected by a key. Make two: one for deleting series, one for snapshots. They're separate on purpose. The backup tool in part 4 needs the snapshot key, and it prints that key in its logs, so a leaked backup log mustn't be able to delete anything. Success: ls -l /etc/victoriametrics/ shows both files as -rw-r----- root victoriametrics . The trailing newline that openssl writes is fine; the keys still matched in testing. We also checked they don't cross: the delete key got 401 on /snapshot/list , and the snapshot key got 401 on the delete endpoint. ---

secs.head: Step 5: the systemd unit
secs.body: What each choice buys you: Line Why --- --- -retentionPeriod=90d The default is 31 days. Say what you mean, and read part 4 before you pick -httpListenAddr=10.0.0.5:8428 Without it, the database binds :8428 , every interface. Bind to the internal one -deleteAuthKey , -snapshotAuthKey Closes the delete and snapshot endpoints to anyone without the right key ExecReload=... -HUP A HUP re-reads the scrape file. Flags still need a restart LimitNOFILE=1048576 Raising the open-files limit is the one OS tweak the docs' tuning section recommends Now lint it. Here's a trap we hit: systemd-analyze verify (systemd 255) exits 0 even when it finds a bad value . With Restart=on-falure it printed a warning and still returned 0: So check its output, not its exit code: Success: LINT OK . On the typo'd copy, the same check printed LINT FAIL and returned non-zero. ---

secs.head: Step 6: start it and check it
secs.body: Success: OK exit=0 . Then look at the targets: And ask a real question: vmui , the built-in query UI, lives at http://10.0.0.5:8428/vmui/ if you'd rather click. ---

secs.head: Two things that look broken but aren't
secs.body: Both showed up in the lab within the first minute, and both make people restart things that are fine. A new target shows down before its first scrape. Right after start, /api/v1/targets showed node down with an empty lastError . Twenty seconds later it was up . Scrapes are spread out over the interval, so the first one can take up to one scrape interval . An empty lastError means "not tried yet". A real failure always carries a message. A query returns nothing for the newest data. Our first up query came back empty even though the targets had just been scraped: That's -search.latencyOffset , which defaults to 30 seconds: points younger than that are hidden from queries so you don't see half-written data. The same query with latency offset=1s returned both series. Leave the default alone; it's there for a reason. Just know it exists when you test with curl straight after a start. ---

secs.head: Changing config without a surprise
secs.body: Here's the trap. When you HUP with a broken scrape file, VictoriaMetrics logs an error and keeps running the old config : The process stays up, targets stay the same, and nobody notices your new target was never added. So reload in three steps: check, reload, confirm. 1. Check the file with the dry run from step 3. Stop if the exit code isn't 0. 2. Reload: systemctl reload victoriametrics . 3. Confirm the reload took: In the lab this metric went to 0 after the bad HUP and back to 1 after a good one. Part 5 turns it into an alert. [!NOTE] systemctl reload wasn't run in the lab (no systemd). We sent kill -HUP directly, which is what the unit's ExecReload does. ---

secs.head: Why the admin keys matter
secs.body: Back to the intern. Without -deleteAuthKey , we imported a scratch series and deleted it with one unauthenticated request. HTTP 204, series gone: With the key set, the same request was refused, and so was a wrong key: Only ?authKey=<the key got 204. /snapshot/create behaved the same way with -snapshotAuthKey . The keys protect a handful of dangerous endpoints, and the server itself is careful with them: its startup log prints -snapshotAuthKey="secret" , not the value. They don't protect queries or ingestion. The docs list more endpoint keys ( -reloadAuthKey , -configAuthKey , -flagsAuthKey , -pprofAuthKey and others) and say plainly that every component belongs in a private network, with vmauth in front of anything that untrusted clients can reach. Rule of thumb: bind to the inside, key the dangerous doors, proxy everything else. ---

secs.head: Back to the intern
secs.body: Same intern, same cleanup idea, same Friday. This time the database was installed with this page: What the intern tries What happens now Which step stopped it --- --- --- Sends delete series for node . with no key 401 Expected to receive non-empty authKey when -deleteAuthKey is set Step 4 and step 5 Goes looking for the key /etc/victoriametrics/delete.key is -rw-r----- , readable by root and the victoriametrics group only Step 4 Tries the snapshot key from a backup log 401 : it can take snapshots, not delete Step 4 Connects from a network that shouldn't reach it Nothing listens there: the database is bound to 10.0.0.5 , and anything wider goes through vmauth Step 5 Someone with root deletes the series anyway The hourly backup from part 4 restores them Part 4 The cleanup can still happen. The intern asks, someone holding the delete key runs it, on purpose, with a match they've read twice. Deleting history should take a decision, not just a curl . And when the same intern adds a new target with a typo in the YAML, the dry run catches it before the reload, and the reload metric catches it if they skip the dry run. Takeaway: a verified binary, its own user, a bound address, admin keys and a check-reload-confirm habit turn a "just run it" database into one you can leave on a shared network. Next: Part 3, vmagent and the Network Blip, moves scraping to the edge and keeps data through an outage. ---
