secs.body: - VictoriaMetrics single-node docs: how to start, scraping with -promscrape.config , how to apply new config, security recommendations and protected endpoints, deleting series, snapshots. - Common command-line flags: -promscrape.config.dryRun , -search.latencyOffset (default 30s), -deleteAuthKey , -snapshotAuthKey , -httpListenAddr . - VictoriaMetrics v1.156.0 release: tarballs and checksum files. - vmui: the built-in query UI. - vmauth: the auth proxy recommended in front of VictoriaMetrics. - systemd-analyze(1): the verify command. - node exporter: the example target.

label: 3. vmagent and the network blip
title: vmagent and the Network Blip: Keeping Metrics Through an Outage
desc: Part 3 of the VictoriaMetrics series. Part 2 gave you a single node that scrapes its own targets. This page moves scrapi

secs.head: vmagent and the Network Blip: Keeping Metrics Through an Outage
secs.body: Part 3 of the VictoriaMetrics series. Part 2 gave you a single node that scrapes its own targets. This page moves scraping to a vmagent and proves, on a lab, that it keeps every sample through a storage outage, and the one edit that throws them away. - The switch upgrade - Collect at the edge, store in the middle - Run it - The outage test - The trap: tidy up a URL, lose the buffer - The fix: pin the queue path - How big should the buffer be? - What vmagent is not for - Back to the switch upgrade - References ---

secs.head: The switch upgrade
secs.body: The network team upgrades the core switch on Sunday morning. Forty minutes of maintenance, announced weeks ago. The compute nodes keep running jobs. The monitoring server, in another rack, can't be reached. On Monday someone asks why a training run slowed down on Sunday. The dashboard has a forty-minute hole exactly where the answer should be. The exporters were fine the whole time. Nobody was writing down what they said. You want something next to the exporters that writes it down and hands it over when the network comes back. That's vmagent . ---

secs.head: Collect at the edge, store in the middle
secs.body: vmagent scrapes targets (same scrape configs as Prometheus) and sends the samples to one or more -remoteWrite.url destinations. When a destination can't take data, vmagent writes it to a persistent queue on local disk and keeps retrying. When the destination comes back, it sends the backlog. Four facts from the docs shape everything below: Fact Consequence --- --- The queue lives under -remoteWrite.tmpDataPath (default vmagent-remotewrite-data ) It's local disk on the vmagent host. Put it somewhere with room Its size per URL is capped by -remoteWrite.maxDiskUsagePerURL , default 0 = unlimited A long outage can fill that disk unless you set a cap When the cap is reached, vmagent drops the oldest data to make room You lose the start of an outage, never the end The backlog is sent oldest-first (FIFO) After a long outage, fresh data shows up late until the backlog drains Where to run it: one vmagent per rack, per site, or on the login nodes. Anywhere that stays reachable from the exporters when the link to storage doesn't. ---

secs.head: Run it
secs.body: [!NOTE] Everything with numbers below was run with vmagent and VictoriaMetrics v1.156.0 on a throwaway Ubuntu 24.04.5 sandbox, scraping a real node exporter 1.12.1 every 5 seconds. The 5-second interval is only there to make a one-minute outage produce enough samples to count. The vmagent binary is in the vmutils tarball from the same release, verified the same way as in part 2. A minimal run: Hold that -remoteWrite.queuePath line. The rest of the page is about why it's there. ---

secs.head: The outage test
secs.body: We ran vmagent against a central VictoriaMetrics, waited 20 seconds, killed the central database, waited a minute, and looked at vmagent's own metrics: About 150 KB waiting, and the log said what it was doing: ( 1:secret-url is vmagent hiding the URL in its own metrics and logs. That's on purpose.) Then we started the central database again and counted samples in the outage window. The outage lasted 64 seconds; at one sample every 5 seconds that's about 13: Thirteen. No gap. Pending bytes went back to 0 . That's the behaviour you're paying for. ---

secs.head: The trap: tidy up a URL, lose the buffer
secs.body: Same setup, second outage. This time, while the central database is down and 108 KB are queued, someone "tidies" the config: http://127.0.0.1:8429/... becomes http://localhost:8429/... . Same server. They restart vmagent. Here's what it logged on start: At info level, not warn . When the database came back, the outage window had 1 sample where 10 were expected. Why: by default the queue directory's name is built from the URL's position in the flag list plus a hash of the URL itself. Change the host spelling, reorder two -remoteWrite.url flags, or add one in front, and the name changes. On the next start, the old directory has no matching URL, so vmagent calls it dangling and deletes it. The docs describe this exactly; it's easy to miss until it costs you a weekend's data. [!CAUTION] Never edit, reorder or insert -remoteWrite.url flags on a vmagent that has a backlog, unless each URL has a pinned -remoteWrite.queuePath . Check first: vmagent remotewrite pending data bytes should be 0 . Query parameters and fragments are left out of the hash, so ?extra label=... edits don't trigger this. Host, port and path changes do. ---

secs.head: The fix: pin the queue path
secs.body: v1.156.0 added -remoteWrite.queuePath : one per -remoteWrite.url , in the same order, naming the queue directory yourself. We repeated the whole trap with it set: No dangling queue, and the outage window had 10 of about 10 samples once the database returned. Rules for the flag, from the docs: - Every -remoteWrite.queuePath must be a directory used by one URL only. vmagent deletes the contents of a directory that doesn't hold a valid queue, so never point it at something else. - vmagent doesn't remember which URL a directory belonged to. Point a directory at a different URL and its backlog goes to the new destination. - Directories you stop using aren't cleaned up. Remove them yourself. - Upgrading an existing vmagent? Pass the current auto-named directory as the path ( -remoteWrite.queuePath=<tmpDataPath /persistent-queue/1 9CE28D37044E5A42 ) and the backlog carries over. On versions before v1.156.0 the flag doesn't exist. The only protection there is -remoteWrite.keepDanglingQueues , which keeps orphaned directories on disk instead of deleting them, but doesn't send their contents anywhere. Recommendation: on v1.156.0 and later, always set -remoteWrite.queuePath . On older versions, set -remoteWrite.keepDanglingQueues and drain the queue before you touch a URL. ---

secs.head: How big should the buffer be?
secs.body: Pick how long an outage you want to survive, then measure what vmagent actually sends. The docs give the query: That's the gigabytes needed to hold 6 hours. Use your own number of hours. Then set -remoteWrite.maxDiskUsagePerURL to that, rounded up to a multiple of 500 MB because the queue is stored in roughly 500 MB chunks. The docs' floor is 500 MiB per URL. Choice What happens in a long outage --- --- No cap (the default) Nothing is dropped until the disk fills. Then whatever else lives on that disk suffers too A cap The oldest data is dropped once the cap is reached. You keep the most recent hours -remoteWrite.disableOnDiskQueue Nothing is buffered. Scraped samples are dropped while storage can't keep up Rule of thumb: cap it, and size the cap to your longest planned maintenance plus a margin. Put the queue on its own filesystem if you can. [!TIP] After a long outage, fresh samples wait behind the backlog. If dashboards need "now" more than they need order, -remoteWrite.inmemoryQueues (since v1.146.0) adds workers that send recent data while the backlog drains. The catch: samples can arrive out of order, so don't use it with storage that rejects that. We didn't test this flag. Then watch it. Part 5 adds an alert on vmagent remotewrite pending data bytes that doesn't fire for every short blip. ---

secs.head: What vmagent is not for
secs.body: - Long-term storage. The queue is a waiting room, not a database. You can't query it. - High availability by itself. One vmagent is one point of failure for its targets. The docs' HA pattern is two identically configured vmagents writing to deduplicating storage, which is a bigger topic than this page. - Fixing a storage server that's too small. If the central database can't keep up all the time, the queue just grows until it hits the cap. Fix the server. ---

secs.head: Back to the switch upgrade
secs.body: Run that Sunday again, with a vmagent in each rack and this page's flags. The core switch goes down. The exporters keep answering their rack's vmagent, which keeps scraping and writes everything to its queue on local disk. Halfway through, a colleague notices the remote-write URL still says the old hostname, "fixes" it and restarts vmagent. The queue path is pinned, so the backlog stays put, just as the lab's 139 KB did. The switch comes back, vmagent sends the backlog oldest first, and the newest minutes show up a little late. On Monday the dashboard has no hole. Whoever asks about the slow training run gets an answer. Our lab outages lasted about a minute. Forty minutes is a sizing question, not something we ran, so do these three checks before the maintenance window instead of after: Before the window How --- --- The queue cap covers the outage plus a margin Run the vmagent remotewrite bytes sent total query from above with your window instead of 6h , and compare with -remoteWrite.maxDiskUsagePerURL Every URL has its own pinned queue One -remoteWrite.queuePath per -remoteWrite.url Nobody is mid-backlog when config changes vmagent remotewrite pending data bytes is 0 before anyone restarts vmagent If the queue still isn't draining 15 minutes after the switch is back, the VMAgentQueueBacklog alert in part 5 tells you, instead of a Monday question. Takeaway: vmagent turns a storage outage into a delay instead of a gap, as long as you cap its queue and pin each queue's path so a URL edit can't delete it. Next: Part 4, Retention, Full Disks and Backups, looks after the data once it arrives. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - vmagent docs: features, on-disk persistence, manual persistence paths ( -remoteWrite.queuePath ), processing order and -remoteWrite.inmemoryQueues , disabling on-disk persistence, calculating disk space for the queue. - vmagent command-line flags: -remoteWrite.tmpDataPath , -remoteWrite.maxDiskUsagePerURL , -remoteWrite.keepDanglingQueues , -remoteWrite.disableOnDiskQueue . - VictoriaMetrics changelog 2026: v1.156.0 adds -remoteWrite.queuePath . - High availability for writes: replicating through vmagent, with deduplication on the storage side. - Part 2, A Single Node You Can Trust: verifying release tarballs.

label: 4. Retention, disks and backups
title: Retention, Full Disks and Backups: Looking After the Data Once It Lands
desc: Part 4 of the VictoriaMetrics series. Part 3 got every sample to the database. This page keeps them there: how much disk

secs.head: Retention, Full Disks and Backups: Looking After the Data Once It Lands
secs.body: Part 4 of the VictoriaMetrics series. Part 3 got every sample to the database. This page keeps them there: how much disk you really need, what happens when it runs out, and a backup you've actually restored. - Healthy, according to the health check - What retention really deletes, and when - Sizing the disk from a real test - When the disk fills up - Backups: snapshot, copy, restore - An hourly job you can leave running - Proving the backup - Changing retention safely - Back to the weekend - References ---

secs.head: Healthy, according to the health check
secs.body: The metrics disk fills up on a Saturday. Your uptime checker polls /health every minute, gets OK , and stays green all weekend. On Monday the dashboards end at Saturday 03:00. The database was up the whole time. It just wasn't storing anything. We reproduced that exact situation in the lab. It's the most important thing on this page, and it's in When the disk fills up. First, how the disk gets used. [!NOTE] Lab: VictoriaMetrics v1.156.0 on a throwaway Ubuntu 24.04.5 sandbox, scraping node exporter 1.12.1. The backup job ran as the victoriametrics user against the layout from part 2, with 127.0.0.1 in place of 10.0.0.5 . systemd wasn't running, so the timer was linted but not started. ---

secs.head: What retention really deletes, and when
secs.body: -retentionPeriod takes a number and a unit: h , d , w , M (months) or y . With no unit it means months. The default is 1M , which is 31 days, and the minimum is 1d . [!WARNING] Lowercase m is minutes, and for retention it's refused outright. -retentionPeriod=3m exited 2 in the lab: "duration in months must be set with capital M suffix, lower case m means minutes and not allowed". Good: one character can't quietly turn three months into three minutes. Data is stored in monthly partitions (folders like 2026 11 ) made of parts . That shapes deletion: - A whole partition outside retention is deleted on the first day of the next month . - A part outside retention is deleted eventually , during a background merge, and only once the part is entirely outside retention. So the docs' rule is that disk usage peaks at retention plus one month . With -retentionPeriod=1 , January's data is deleted on March 1st. Plan the disk for the peak, not for the setting. -retentionPeriod Plan disk for about --- --- 31d (the default) 2 months of data 90d 4 months of data 1y 13 months of data ---

secs.head: Sizing the disk from a real test
secs.body: The docs' method: run a test instance on the real workload for a day , measure the data directory, and multiply. Ten gigabytes after one day means at least 1 TB for 100 days. Why a full day and not ten minutes? Our lab shows the trap. After a short run, here's what the database reported about itself: That's 1.35 bytes per sample for the data, and an index bigger than the data itself. After forcing the background merge that normally happens over time ( /internal/force merge ), the same 39,990 samples took 27,127 bytes: 0.68 bytes per sample. Halved, just from merging. A short test over-counts the data, because it hasn't been merged yet, and over-weights the index, because every series is new. A day-long test catches both, plus your daily churn. Then leave room on top of the peak. The docs recommend: Resource Keep free Why --- --- --- Disk at -storageDataPath At least 20% Merges need room. Without it, parts pile up and queries slow down RAM 50% Less chance of OOM; going past it causes cache evictions and slowdowns CPU 50% Headroom for spikes Rule of thumb: disk = (one test day) × (retention days + 31) ÷ 0.8. ---

secs.head: When the disk fills up
secs.body: When free space at -storageDataPath drops below -storage.minFreeDiskSpaceBytes (default 100 MB in v1.156.0), the database switches to read-only mode : queries still work, new data is refused. We forced it without filling a disk, by setting the threshold to 100 TB on a disk with 30 GB free: Writes were refused with HTTP 503, and the mode clears by itself once space is freed (tested further down): And here's the trap: /health says OK while every write is being rejected. It tells you the process is up, not that it's storing anything. The signal is a metric: Now the second trap. We turned on self-scraping ( -selfScrapeInterval=5s ) on the read-only instance and waited 45 seconds. Querying vm storage is read only on that same instance returned nothing . Of course: it's read-only, so it can't store its own metrics either. A database that monitors only itself goes blind in exactly the failure you care about. [!IMPORTANT] Scrape every VictoriaMetrics from somewhere else , a second small instance or a vmagent writing to one, and alert on vm storage is read only == 1 there. In the lab, vmalert on a separate monitoring instance fired VMStorageReadOnly for the read-only one within two minutes. Part 5 has the rule and its tests. Data sent through a buffer survives read-only mode. We pointed a vmagent at a read-only instance. In the first run, after 30 seconds it had twenty 503 s, 46 KB queued and nothing dropped. In a second, timed run of 63 seconds, it delivered every sample for the read-only window once the threshold was lifted: 12 of 12. Targets scraped by the read-only node itself have no buffer, so those samples are simply lost. One more reason for the vmagent in part 3. ---

secs.head: Backups: snapshot, copy, restore
secs.body: A snapshot is an instant, read-only view of the data directory, made with hard links, so it's free to create. vmbackup asks the database for a snapshot, copies it to the destination ( s3:// , gs:// , azblob:// or fs:// ), and deletes the snapshot. If the destination already holds a backup, only the changed files are uploaded. vmrestore copies a backup back into a stopped database's data directory. Every failure path we tried was refused cleanly: What we tried What happened --- --- Backup without the snapshot key 401 from /snapshot/create , exit 255 Backup into the data directory itself Refused: -dst ... can not point to the directory with VictoriaMetrics data , exit 255 Restore while the database was running on that directory Panic: cannot acquire lock on file ".../flock.lock" , exit 2, nothing touched Restore into a fresh directory, then start on it 645 series, same as the source Second backup to the same destination Incremental: 97 bytes uploaded Two traps worth knowing before you automate it: The key ends up in the log. You can keep the key out of ps with %{ENV VAR} in the flag value: VictoriaMetrics expands it itself, and in the lab a running process's command line showed the literal %{K} , not the key. But vmbackup then logs the expanded URL, key included. Both on success: and on failure. That's why part 2 uses a separate snapshot key that can't delete anything. An interrupted backup leaves a snapshot behind. We throttled a backup with -maxBytesPerSecond=2000 and killed it after 3 seconds. vm snapshots went from 0 to 1, and stayed at 1 after a successful rerun. Old snapshots hold on to parts that merges would otherwise free, so they slowly eat disk. Since v1.122.0 , -snapshotsMaxAge defaults to 3d , and in the lab a 60-second setting deleted the orphan on schedule. On older versions the default is to keep snapshots forever, so set it yourself, longer than your slowest backup. ---

secs.head: An hourly job you can leave running
secs.body: This follows the docs' "smart backups" pattern: an hourly incremental into latest/ , and once a day a server-side copy of latest/ into a dated folder. The docs say the two shouldn't overlap, so one script does both, in order. set -e means the daily copy only happens after a successful hourly run. 1. Install vmbackup and vmrestore from the vmutils tarball (verify it like in part 2), and make the backup folder: 2. The script: The pruning loop uses if , not [[ ]] && [ ] && rm , on purpose: with set -e , a && chain that's false on the last folder makes the whole script exit non-zero after a perfectly good backup. 3. Run it once by hand and check: In the lab we also ran it with DAILY HOUR set to the current hour. It made the dated copy, deleted a planted 20200101 folder, and kept a 3-day-old one and a folder called notes . With a wrong key, and with the database stopped, it exited 255. 4. The timer: Success: systemctl list-timers vm-backup.timer shows the next run at five past the hour. Both units passed the output-based lint from part 2, but weren't started in the lab. [!CAUTION] fs:// on a local disk protects you from mistakes, not from losing the machine. Point DST at an NFS mount on another host, or switch to s3:// with -credsFilePath , before you call this a backup. vmbackup is the same tool either way. ---

secs.head: Proving the backup
secs.body: A backup you haven't restored is a rumour. Once a month, restore the latest dated backup somewhere harmless and compare it to the live database: In the lab, the restored copy and the live database both answered 645 . Remember the restore target must not be in use: vmrestore makes the folder match the backup exactly, deleting anything extra, like rsync --delete . That's what the lock file protects you from. ---

secs.head: Changing retention safely
secs.body: Raising -retentionPeriod is safe. Lowering it deletes data, eventually, with no undo. Treat it like any risky change: 1. Dry run: work out what goes. Everything older than the new retention, at the next merge or month boundary. 2. Backup: run vm-backup by hand and confirm exit=0 . 3. Canary: if you run two identical nodes behind vmagent (part 3), change one first and watch vm data size bytes for a day. 4. Enforce: change the other. 5. Rollback: there's no un-deleting. Rollback means vmrestore from step 2 into a stopped node. ---

secs.head: Back to the weekend
secs.body: The same Saturday, with this page in place. The disk was sized for retention plus a month, with 20% to spare, so on its own it doesn't fill. Say it fills anyway, because someone parked a core dump on the same filesystem. At 03:00 the database switches to read-only. /health still says OK , but the monitoring instance is scraping it from outside, sees vm storage is read only 1 , and VMStorageReadOnly pages after a minute. In the lab it fired in under two. Nothing sent through vmagent is lost while that page waits for a human: the queue absorbs the 503 s, just as it delivered 12 of 12 samples in the lab. The on-call admin deletes the core dump. That's it. No restart. The database re-checks free space about once a second and switches itself back. We tested that on a real full disk: a 300 MB tmpfs with a 150 MB threshold. Writing a 200 MB file turned writes from 204 into 503 ; deleting it turned them back into 204 within seconds, and the log said so both ways: vmagent drains its queue, and Monday's dashboards have Saturday in them. If it had been worse and the disk had died, the hourly backup caps the loss at the hour since the last run, and you already know the restore works because you tested it last month. Takeaway: plan disk for retention plus a month, alert on vm storage is read only from outside the database, and keep a backup job whose restore you've actually tested. Next: Part 5, MetricsQL Surprises and Alerts You Can Test, writes the alerts this page keeps promising. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - VictoriaMetrics single-node docs: retention, storage (partitions, parts, merges, 20% free disk), capacity planning, snapshots and snapshot troubleshooting, environment variables and %{ENV VAR} , self-scraping. - Common command-line flags: -retentionPeriod , -storage.minFreeDiskSpaceBytes (default 100000000), -snapshotsMaxAge , -selfScrapeInterval . - vmbackup: storage types, incremental and smart backups, server-side copy, how it works, troubleshooting. - vmrestore: the database must be stopped; restore syncs like rsync --delete . - VictoriaMetrics changelog 2025: v1.122.0 changed the -snapshotsMaxAge default to 3d . - systemd.timer(5): OnCalendar and Persistent .

label: 5. MetricsQL and tested alerts
title: MetricsQL Surprises and Alerts You Can Test
desc: Part 5 of the VictoriaMetrics series. Part 4 kept the data safe. This page is about asking it questions: where MetricsQL

secs.head: MetricsQL Surprises and Alerts You Can Test
secs.body: Part 5 of the VictoriaMetrics series. Part 4 kept the data safe. This page is about asking it questions: where MetricsQL and PromQL disagree on the same data, and how to write alert rules with tests that would actually catch a broken rule. - MetricsQL Surprises and Alerts You Can Test - The bug report that wasn't - Same data, two answers - Why they disagree - Prometheus 3.16 closed the gap, and VictoriaMetrics can't read it - Other differences you'll notice - Three rules that watch the watchers - Tests that can fail - How our own tests lied to us - Run vmalert - Back to the bug report - References ---

secs.head: The bug report that wasn't
secs.body: You're halfway through a migration. Prometheus and VictoriaMetrics both scrape the Slurm exporter, and someone puts the same panel on both: "jobs finished in the last 5 minutes". Prometheus says 15.79. VictoriaMetrics says 15. The ticket says "VictoriaMetrics is losing data". It isn't. Fifteen is the right answer, and 15.79 is a deliberate estimate. Here's the proof. ---

secs.head: Same data, two answers
secs.body: [!NOTE] Lab: Prometheus 3.16.0 and VictoriaMetrics v1.156.0 on a throwaway Ubuntu 24.04.5 sandbox. Our first try scraped one counter with both databases at once. Even the raw value disagreed (5 vs 4), because the two scrapers hit the target at different moments. That compares scrape timing, not query languages. So we loaded identical samples into both: a counter jobs finished total , sampled every 15 seconds for 30 minutes, going up by exactly 1 every 20 seconds. Prometheus got it through promtool tsdb create-blocks-from openmetrics , VictoriaMetrics through /api/v1/import/prometheus . Then we asked both the same questions at the same timestamp, 15 minutes in: Query Truth Prometheus 3.16.0 VictoriaMetrics v1.156.0 --- --- --- --- jobs finished total 45 45 45 increase(jobs finished total[1m]) 3 4 3 increase(jobs finished total[2m]) 6 6.857142857142857 6 increase(jobs finished total[5m]) 15 15.789473684210526 15 rate(jobs finished total[5m]) 0.05 0.05263157894736842 0.05 "Truth" is the counter's value at the query time minus its value one window earlier. VictoriaMetrics matched it every time. Prometheus was off by up to a third. ---

secs.head: Why they disagree
secs.body: A window like [5m] rarely starts and ends exactly on a sample. Each database fills the gaps at the edges differently. Prometheus uses only the samples inside the window, then extrapolates the slope out to the window's edges. That's why it returns fractions for a counter that only ever moves in whole steps. MetricsQL also uses the last sample before the window as the starting point, and doesn't extrapolate. So increase() over a whole-number counter returns a whole number: the actual difference. Neither is a bug; they answer slightly different questions. But for counters you'll read as "how many", like jobs, restarts or ECC errors, the MetricsQL answer is the one a human expects. Rule of thumb: when two dashboards disagree during a migration, compare raw samples first, functions second. Most "data loss" turns out to be scrape timing or extrapolation. ---

secs.head: Prometheus 3.16 closed the gap, and VictoriaMetrics can't read it
secs.body: Before writing "Prometheus can't do this", we checked. Prometheus 3.7.0 added two experimental range selector modifiers behind the promql-extended-range-selectors flag, and 3.16.0 made them stable and always on. Starting 3.16.0 with the old flag just logs that it's a no-op. On the same data: Query Prometheus 3.16.0 --- --- increase(jobs finished total[5m] anchored) 15 increase(jobs finished total[1m] anchored) 3 increase(jobs finished total[5m] smoothed) 15 anchored uses the sample in effect at the window's start and the last sample at its end, without extrapolation. That's the same idea as MetricsQL. Now the trap. Send that to VictoriaMetrics v1.156.0: HTTP 400. A Grafana dashboard written against Prometheus 3.16 with anchored will break when you point it at VictoriaMetrics, and plain increase() will quietly change its numbers in the other direction. Recommendation: while you run both, keep shared dashboards to plain increase() / rate() and accept that the numbers differ slightly. Once you've moved, write queries for the database you actually run. ---

secs.head: Other differences you'll notice
secs.body: From the MetricsQL docs, the ones that show up on real dashboards. We ran the first three on the same lab data; the last row is from the docs only. What Prometheus 3.16.0 VictoriaMetrics v1.156.0 --- --- --- (-1)^0.5 NaN Empty result: NaN is dropped round(jobs finished total) , min over time(jobs finished total[1m]) Result has no name Keeps name ="jobs finished total" rate(jobs finished total) , no window parse error: expected type range vector 0.05 ; window picked from step and the scrape interval rate() when Grafana's step is smaller than the scrape interval Can return empty, per the MetricsQL docs Returns values, per the docs (not tested) Grafana doesn't draw NaN either, so the first row usually looks identical on screen. The last row is handy, but a query using it won't run on Prometheus. ---

secs.head: Three rules that watch the watchers
secs.body: Parts 2 to 4 each found a failure the database won't announce. Here they are as alert rules, in a file vmalert reads: Rule Comes from Why this for --- --- --- VMStorageReadOnly Part 4: /health says OK while writes fail Every minute is lost data for unbuffered targets. Page fast VMScrapeConfigReloadFailed Part 2: a bad HUP keeps the old config silently Gives a human time to fix their own typo before it pages VMAgentQueueBacklog Part 3: the queue grows during any outage Short blips drain on their own. Fifteen minutes means it's not a blip Pick the 100 MB threshold from your own queue cap in part 3, not ours. [!IMPORTANT] These rules must run against a VictoriaMetrics that isn't the one being watched. Part 4 showed a read-only instance can't store its own vm storage is read only . ---

secs.head: Tests that can fail
secs.body: vmalert-tool runs alert rules against fake series and checks what fires and when. The test file uses the Prometheus rule-test format, except that promql expr test is called metricsql expr test . Save this as rules test.yml next to rules.yml : The values shorthand reads as one sample per interval : '0 0 1 1 1 1' with a 30s interval means 0 at 0s and 30s, then 1 from 60s on. A green test only proves something if a broken rule turns it red. So break the rules on purpose and make sure each break is caught. This script does that, and it's what we'd put in CI: Each mutant is a copy of the rules with one realistic mistake. If a mutant passes the tests, the tests have a blind spot. The SKIP check exists because a mutant that no longer matches anything (after someone edits a rule) would otherwise "pass" forever without testing anything. ---

secs.head: How our own tests lied to us
secs.body: Writing those tests, we got three wrong. Each looked fine until a mutant ran. 1. A failure for the wrong reason. Our first broken copy lived in a subfolder, and vmalert-tool said FAILED . Great, except the message was found no rule group in [broken/broken/rules.yml] . Paths in rule files are resolved relative to the test file , not your shell. The rules never loaded. Always read why a test failed. 2. Checking at the wrong moment. The backlog test first checked at 5m. A broken rule with for: 1m passed, because by 5m the backlog was gone and nothing would fire under either rule. Moving the check to 3m, mid-backlog, caught it. 3. Same mistake, different rule. The reload test checked only at 7m, after vm2 had recovered. A for: 1m rule passed again. Adding a 3m check, while both were failing, fixed it. The pattern in all three: a test written to pass will pass. Write the "should not fire" check at the moment a broken rule would fire. [!NOTE] vmalert-tool evaluates every group at the file's evaluation interval (default 1m ) and ignores each group's own interval . That's why the test file sets evaluation interval: 30s to match the group. Leave them different and you're testing different timing than production runs. ---

secs.head: Run vmalert
secs.body: Check the rules file the same way as the scrape file in part 2. A broken file exits 255; a good one exits 0: Then run it against the monitoring instance, the one that scrapes your main database from outside: -datasource.url is where rules are evaluated, -remoteWrite.url is where alert state is written back (as the ALERTS series), and -notifier.url is your Alertmanager. In the lab we replaced -notifier.url with -notifier.blackhole (no Alertmanager there), pointed a monitoring instance at a deliberately read-only one, and waited: The ALERTS{alertname="VMStorageReadOnly", alertstate="firing"} series showed up in the monitoring instance too. Delivery through Alertmanager wasn't tested. ---

secs.head: Back to the bug report
secs.body: The ticket gets closed with three lines: the raw samples are identical in both databases (45 and 45), Prometheus extrapolates increase() to the edges of the window, and 15 is the real number of jobs. If the team wants Prometheus to agree, increase(...[5m] anchored) does that on 3.16, as long as that panel never has to run on VictoriaMetrics. The bigger change is what doesn't become a ticket any more. Each story in this series now ends in an alert, and each alert has a test that has caught a broken copy of it: The story What used to happen What happens now --- --- --- Part 2: a typo in the scrape file The old config ran silently and the new target never appeared VMScrapeConfigReloadFailed after 5 minutes Part 3: storage unreachable Nobody knew until someone looked at a dashboard VMAgentQueueBacklog once the queue has been over 100 MB for 15 minutes Part 4: disk full, /health green A weekend of missing data VMStorageReadOnly after 1 minute, from a separate instance The next time two dashboards disagree, compare samples before functions. The next time something breaks, it should page you, and you'll already have proof the page works. Takeaway: compare raw samples before blaming a database, and trust an alert rule only after its tests have caught a deliberately broken copy of it. Next: Part 6, the cheatsheet, has every step from the series as copy-paste commands. Series index: VictoriaMetrics. Natural next steps are Grafana on top, and the cluster version once one node isn't enough. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - MetricsQL: intentional differences from PromQL, including rate / increase behaviour, NaN handling and kept metric names. - vmalert-tool: unit tests, the test file format, metricsql expr test , and the evaluation interval limitation. - vmalert: -datasource.url , -remoteWrite.url , -notifier.url , -notifier.blackhole , -dryRun . - Prometheus rule unit testing: the test format vmalert-tool is compatible with. - Prometheus changelog: 3.7.0 adds experimental anchored and smoothed ; 3.16.0 makes them stable and always on. - Prometheus feature flags (3.14): what anchored and smoothed do. - promtool tsdb: backfilling from OpenMetrics, used to load identical data. - VictoriaMetrics single-node docs, import: the import endpoint used for the same data.

label: 6. Cheatsheet
title: VictoriaMetrics Cheatsheet: Every Step from the Series
desc: Part 6 of VictoriaMetrics The series as one list of commands, in the order you'd run them on a new host. Each step links

secs.head: VictoriaMetrics Cheatsheet: Every Step from the Series
secs.body: Part 6 of VictoriaMetrics The series as one list of commands, in the order you'd run them on a new host. Each step links to the page that explains it, shows its output, and shows how it fails. - VictoriaMetrics Cheatsheet: Every Step from the Series - Before you start - 1. Download and verify - 2. User, directories, keys - 3. Scrape config - 4. The service - 5. Reload safely - 6. vmagent at the edge - 7. Retention and disk - 8. Backups - 9. Prove the backup - 10. Alerts with tests - 11. Run vmalert - Quick reference - References ---

secs.head: Before you start
secs.body: [!NOTE] Every command here appears on one of the series pages, where it was run on a throwaway Ubuntu 24.04.5 sandbox with VictoriaMetrics v1.156.0 . That sandbox had no running systemd: the unit files were linted but systemctl start wasn't run, as each page says. This sheet collects the commands; it wasn't re-run from top to bottom as one script. Replace 10.0.0.5 (the database) and 10.0.0.6 (a separate monitoring instance) with your addresses. ---

secs.head: 1. Download and verify
secs.body: Part 2, step 1. Expected: ...tar.gz: OK for each tarball (a tampered one prints FAILED and exits 1), then victoria-metrics-...-tags-v1.156.0-... . ---

secs.head: 2. User, directories, keys
secs.body: Part 2, steps 2 and 4. Two keys on purpose: vmbackup logs the snapshot key, so it must not be able to delete anything. Put /var/lib/victoriametrics on its own filesystem if you can. ---

secs.head: 3. Scrape config
secs.body: Part 2, step 3. Expected: no output, exit=0 . A broken file exits 255 with the line number. ---

secs.head: 4. The service
secs.body: Part 2, steps 5 and 6. Expected: LINT OK , OK exit=0 , then every job up . A target can show down with an empty lastError for up to one scrape interval after start; that means "not tried yet". The newest 30 s of data are hidden from queries by -search.latencyOffset , so a query straight after start can come back empty. ---

secs.head: 5. Reload safely
secs.body: Part 2. A HUP with a broken file keeps the old config and only logs an error. So: check, reload, confirm. Expected: vm promscrape config last reload successful 1 . Flags need a restart, not a reload. ---

secs.head: 6. vmagent at the edge
secs.body: Part 3. Buffers on disk while the database is unreachable. - Always set -remoteWrite.queuePath (v1.156.0+), one per -remoteWrite.url , in the same order. Without it, editing or reordering a URL makes vmagent delete its queue as "dangling" on the next start. Before v1.156.0, use -remoteWrite.keepDanglingQueues and drain the queue before touching a URL. - Each queue path is used by one URL only; vmagent deletes the contents of a directory that isn't a valid queue. - Size the cap from what you actually send, here for 6 hours: - Check the backlog before any URL change: vmagent remotewrite pending data bytes should be 0 . ---

secs.head: 7. Retention and disk
secs.body: Part 4. Fact Value --- --- Default -retentionPeriod 1M = 31 days. Units h d w M y ; bare number = months; lowercase m is refused Disk peaks at Retention plus one month (monthly partitions are deleted on the 1st) Size the disk Run one real day, then disk = day × (retention days + 31) ÷ 0.8 Disk full Read-only below -storage.minFreeDiskSpaceBytes (default 100 MB). /health still says OK . Watch vm storage is read only Monitor it from Another instance. A read-only database can't store its own metrics Lowering retention deletes data with no undo: back up first, change one node, watch vm data size bytes , then the rest. ---

secs.head: 8. Backups
secs.body: Part 4. Hourly incremental into latest/ , daily server-side copy into a dated folder, 14 days kept. Expected: vm-backup: ok , exit=0 , and the next run at five past the hour. fs:// on a local disk isn't a backup of the machine: point DST at another host, or use s3:// with -credsFilePath . Since v1.122.0, -snapshotsMaxAge (default 3d ) removes snapshots an interrupted backup left behind; on older versions set it yourself. ---

secs.head: 9. Prove the backup
secs.body: Part 4. Monthly. vmrestore makes the target match the backup exactly, so never point it at a live data directory (it refuses while the lock is held). Expected: the same count as the same query on the live database. ---

secs.head: 10. Alerts with tests
secs.body: Part 5. Save the rules as /etc/vmalert/rules.yml : The test file rules test.yml and the mutation script check-rules.sh are printed in full in Tests that can fail. Run both: Expected: SUCCESS , then PASS real rules and one PASS mutant caught per mutant, exit=0 . Three things that made our own tests lie: - rule files paths are relative to the test file , not your shell. - Put each "should not fire" check at the moment a broken rule would fire. - vmalert-tool ignores a group's interval and uses the file's evaluation interval : set them equal. ---

secs.head: 11. Run vmalert
secs.body: Part 5. On the monitoring instance, not the one being watched. Expected: exit=0 from the dry run. Firing alerts also appear as ALERTS{alertstate="firing"} series in the monitoring instance. ---

secs.head: Quick reference
secs.body: Task Command or setting --- --- Health (process only, not writes) curl http://10.0.0.5:8428/health Is it actually storing? vm storage is read only == 0 Did the last reload work? vm promscrape config last reload successful == 1 vmagent backlog vmagent remotewrite pending data bytes Data on disk vm data size bytes Query UI http://10.0.0.5:8428/vmui/ Delete series (needs the delete key) curl -X POST 'http://10.0.0.5:8428/api/v1/admin/tsdb/delete series?authKey=...' --data-urlencode 'match[]=...' Expose to untrusted clients Only through vmauth , never directly increase() disagrees with Prometheus Expected: VictoriaMetrics doesn't extrapolate. See part 5 Takeaway: verify the binary, run it as its own user on an internal address with admin keys, reload by check-reload-confirm, buffer with a pinned vmagent queue, size the disk for retention plus a month, back up hourly and restore monthly, and alert from a second instance with rules whose tests can fail. Series index: VictoriaMetrics. To scrape Slurm into it, see Slurm Metrics Without an Exporter. ---

label: **Digital Image Processing**
title: Digital Image Processing - Overview
desc: A nine-part series for people returning to digital image processing (DIP) who want the why behind the formulas before go

secs.head: Digital Image Processing - Overview
secs.body: A nine-part series for people returning to digital image processing (DIP) who want the why behind the formulas before going back to the textbook. By the end you'll read s = c·r^γ , F(u,v) and H(u,v)G(u,v) without flinching, and know which one to reach for when a real image misbehaves.

secs.head: Welcome to Pixel Town
secs.body: Picture a town laid out as a perfect grid. Every citizen stands on one square and holds up a card with a single number: how bright they are. That's an image. Everything in this series is about what you can do to that town. Learn what a citizen is, then move the whole town to a new map without losing anyone ( pages 1, 2 ). Change what the cards say ( page 3 ). Let neighbours vote on each other's numbers ( pages 4, 5 ). Stop looking at who stands where and listen to the town as a choir instead ( pages 6, 7 ). Work out what the town looked like before someone sneezed on the camera ( page 8 ). Look at the town at several zoom levels at once ( page 9 ). Same town, nine points of view. The math is only the language we use to describe them. ---

secs.head: The route
secs.body: Page The question it answers --- ------ ------------------------- 1 Images are just matrices Why does my 16-bit image look black, and what is a pixel anyway? 2 Geometric transforms and interpolation Why does a rotated scan come out jagged? 3 Intensity transforms and histograms How do you rescue an image that's too dark, with one formula? 4 Spatial filtering What is a kernel, and why is blurring "a vote"? 5 Edges and sharpening Why does sharpening make noise louder? Interlude Meet Fourier Who was Fourier, and why is heat a blur filter? 6 The Fourier transform for images What does an image sound like? 7 Frequency filtering and aliasing Why do striped shirts shimmer on video? 8 Noise and restoration Why does "un-blurring" a photo explode into static? 9 Wavelets and multiresolution processing Where in the picture is the scratch, and at what scale? Each page ends with the question the next one answers. Read them in order the first time; later, jump straight to the formula you need. ---

secs.head: Who this is for
secs.body: You took a DIP course (or half of one), the formulas are fuzzy, and the textbook looks heavier than you remember. You don't need a signal-processing background. You do need to be comfortable with sums, a little matrix notation, and the idea of a function. The route follows the topic order of the course's main reference, R. C. Gonzalez and R. E. Woods, Digital Image Processing , 4th ed. (Pearson, 2018): fundamentals and geometry, intensity and spatial filtering, the frequency domain, restoration, then wavelets. Each page cites the chapter to open next. This is a starter , not a replacement. It trades completeness for intuition so that the reference book becomes readable again. ---

secs.head: Conventions used in the series
secs.body: Item Convention ------ ------------ Image f(x, y) is the input, g(x, y) the output Origin Top-left corner; x runs along the column, y runs down the row Gray levels L = 2^k levels, from 0 (black) to L−1 (white), unless a page says normalized [0, 1] Sources Gonzalez and Woods, Digital Image Processing , 4th ed.; library behaviour from the OpenCV and NumPy docs Code Short snippets are not executed by the author; worked numbers are computed by hand and checkable with a calculator [!NOTE] Textbooks and libraries disagree on small conventions (which axis is first, where a 1/N factor goes). Each page names the convention it uses and where libraries differ.

secs.body: File Description ------ ------------- images-are-just-matrices Sampling, quantization, bit depth, coordinates and neighbours geometric-transforms-and-interpolation Affine transforms, inverse mapping, bilinear and bicubic interpolation intensity-transforms-and-histograms Negative, log, gamma and histogram equalization spatial-filtering Kernels, correlation vs convolution, padding, separability edges-and-sharpening Gradient, Sobel, Laplacian and unsharp masking meet-fourier The story of Joseph Fourier and why heat flow is a blur filter fourier-transform-for-images The 2D DFT, magnitude vs phase, the convolution theorem frequency-filtering-and-aliasing Low-pass, high-pass and notch filters; sampling and aliasing noise-and-restoration Noise models, inverse and Wiener filtering, PSNR wavelets-and-multiresolution-processing Pyramids, the Haar transform, subbands, wavelet denoising
