secs.head: Generative AI - LLM VSCode
secs.body: How to get code suggestions, code generation and code review from a language model without leaving VS Code, using the LLM-VSCode extension and StarCoder. Large language models (LLMs) have the potential to revolutionize programming, making it more efficient, accessible, and creative.

secs.head: Motivation
secs.body: LLMs can help programmers in a variety of ways, including: - Code suggestion: LLMs can suggest code completions, snippets, and even entire functions based on the context of the programmer's work. This can save programmers a lot of time and effort, and help them to write better code. - Code generation: LLMs can be used to generate code from natural language descriptions. This can be useful for prototyping new ideas, or for automating repetitive tasks. - Code review: LLMs can be used to review code for potential errors, security vulnerabilities, and stylistic problems. This can help programmers to write more reliable and maintainable code. LLM-VSCode is a popular extension for the VSCode code editor that integrates LLMs with the IDE. This allows programmers to get code suggestions, generate code, and review code directly from within VSCode. Here are some examples of how LLM models can be used to help programming: - A programmer is working on a new feature for a web application. They can use an LLM to generate a basic skeleton of the code, and then fill in the details themselves. - A programmer is debugging a complex piece of code. They can use an LLM to review the code for potential errors, and to get suggestions for how to fix the errors. - A programmer is learning a new programming language. They can use an LLM to get help with the syntax and semantics of the language. LLM models are still under development, but they have the potential to make a major impact on the field of programming. As LLMs become more powerful and accurate, they will be able to help programmers in even more ways. Here are some additional thoughts on the power of LLM models to help programming: - LLMs can help to democratize programming by making it more accessible to people who do not have a formal background in computer science. - LLMs can help to increase the productivity of programmers by automating repetitive tasks and helping them to write code more efficiently. - LLMs can help to improve the quality of code by helping programmers to find errors and security vulnerabilities. - LLMs can help to foster creativity and innovation in programming by making it easier for programmers to try new ideas and experiment with different solutions. Overall, LLM models have the potential to make programming more efficient, accessible, creative, and reliable.

secs.head: Llm-VsCode
secs.body: LLM-VSCode is a Visual Studio Code extension that provides a suite of tools and features for developing, testing, and deploying machine learning models. It is designed to simplify the machine learning development workflow and provide a consistent experience across different programming languages and frameworks. The acronym "LLM" stands for "Language Learning Machine," which reflects the extension's focus on natural language processing and machine learning tasks. Here are some of the key features and capabilities of LLM-VSCode: Key Feature Details -- -- Multi-language support LLM-VSCode supports a wide range of programming languages, including Python, R, Julia, MATLAB, and JavaScript. It also provides syntax highlighting, autocompletion, and debugging tools for each language. Machine learning libraries The extension integrates popular machine learning libraries like TensorFlow, PyTorch, Scikit-Learn, and Keras, allowing developers to build, train, and deploy machine learning models directly within VSCode. Data exploration and visualization LLM-VSCode includes several data exploration and visualization tools, enabling developers to analyze and visualize their datasets, create data visualizations, and generate reports. Testing and debugging The extension provides tools for testing and debugging machine learning models, including unit testing, integration testing, and debugging tools for TensorBoard and other visualization tools. Deployment LLM-VSCode allows developers to deploy their machine learning models to various platforms, including cloud services like AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure, as well as local environments. Collaboration The extension supports collaboration features like version control, continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD), and GitHub integration, making it easier for teams to work together on machine learning projects. Education LLM-VSCode offers educational resources, including tutorials, courses, and documentation, to help users learn about machine learning and develop their skills. Overall, LLM-VSCode aims to streamline the machine learning development workflow, providing a single, integrated environment for building, testing, and deploying machine learning models. Its multi-language support, integration with popular machine learning libraries, and collaboration features make it a valuable tool for both individual developers and teams working on machine learning projects.

Code snippets The extension includes a range of code snippets that can be used to quickly create common components of a Transformers project, such as data loaders, model architectures, and training loops. Model debugging Starcoder includes tools for debugging and visualizing the behavior of Transformers models during training and inference. label: Encoder-Decoder
title: Generative AI - Machine Translator
desc: In the journey of NLP, short for Natural Langauge Processing, starting with basic architecture of an encoder-decoder mod

secs.head: Generative AI - Machine Translator
secs.body: In the journey of NLP, short for Natural Langauge Processing, starting with basic architecture of an encoder-decoder model, that we will apply a neural network in.

secs.head: What is Machine Translator?
secs.body: Machine translation is the task of automatically converting source text in one language to text in another language. Given a sequence of text in a source language, there is no one single best translation of that text to another language. This is because of the natural ambiguity and flexibility of human language. This makes the challenge of automatic machine translation difficult, perhaps one of the most difficult in artificial intelligence.</br — “Machine Learning Mastery” by Jason Brownlee, Ph.D. [1]

secs.head: What is Neural Machine Translator?
secs.body: Initially machine translation (MT) problems were faced using statistical approaches, based mainly on Bayes probabilities. But when neural networks became more powerful and popular, researchers began to explore the capabilities of this technology and new solutions were found. It is called neural machine translation (NMT). From the above, we can deduce that NMT is a problem where we process an input sequence to produce an output sequence — that is, a sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) problem. The encoder-decoder architecture for recurrent neural networks is the standard method.

secs.head: Encoder-Decoder A Basic Approach
secs.body: Image source: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks The seq2seq model consists of two sub-networks, the encoder and the decoder. The encoder, on the left hand, receives sequences from the source language as inputs and produces, as a result, a compact representation of the input sequence, trying to summarize or condense all of its information. Then that output becomes an input or initial state to the decoder, which can also receive another external input. At each time step, the decoder generates an element of its output sequence based on the input received and its current state, as well as updating its own state for the next time step. - This illustrate the 4 arrows (two inputs: input received & its current state, two outputs: output sequence & updating its own state for next step) from a decoder unit.

secs.head: Input & Output Shape
secs.body: The input and output sequences are of fixed size, but they don’t have to match the length of the input sequence may differ from that of the output sequence.

secs.head: Critical Point: Input Vector
secs.body: The critical point of this model is how to get the encoder to provide the most complete and meaningful representation of its input sequence in a single output element to the decoder because this vector or state is the only information the decoder will receive from the input to generate the corresponding output. The longer the input, the harder it’ll be to compress into a single vector.

title: LLM Inference Performance - Overview
desc: A six-part series on the most expensive misunderstanding in AI infrastructure: buying compute when you're short of bandw

secs.head: LLM Inference Performance - Overview
secs.body: A six-part series on the most expensive misunderstanding in AI infrastructure: buying compute when you're short of bandwidth. By the end you'll be able to predict a model's speed on any GPU with a pencil, explain why vLLM, quantization, tensor parallelism and 2:4 sparsity work instead of just naming them, and decode the asterisk on every GPU datasheet.

secs.head: The upgrade that didn't upgrade
secs.body: A team runs their chatbot on A100s. Leadership approves the upgrade to H100s. The slide says it all: dense BF16 compute goes from 312 to 989 TFLOPS. Three times faster. Migration weekend. New hardware, same model. Monday morning, someone runs the benchmark. Prompt processing: close to 3× faster. Great. The answers streaming back to users: about 1.6× faster . Not great. Nothing is broken. No bug, no misconfiguration. The datasheet told them exactly what would happen. They just read the wrong line. The answer was two rows down, next to "GPU memory bandwidth": 2,039 GB/s on the A100, 3.35 TB/s on the H100. 1.6×. This series explains why the second number decided their week, and why it decides most of LLM serving. ---

secs.head: The route
secs.body: Page The question it answers --- ------ ------------------------- 1 Compute-bound vs memory-bandwidth-bound Why does a 3× faster chip sometimes give you 1.6×? 2 LLM inference on the roofline Why does the answer start fast but stream slowly? 3 Sizing a 70B model with a pencil Can you predict a model's speed in an interview, live, on a whiteboard? 4 Optimizations, mapped to the roofline Which of the five "fixes" proposed in the meeting will actually work? 5 2:4 sparsity: half the weights, not half the time What is the "with sparsity" asterisk on the datasheet, and what does it really buy? 6 Sparsity vs quantization Who pays for pruning, what does accuracy lose, and which lever comes first? Each page ends with the question the next one answers. Page 3 is the one to rehearse: doing the arithmetic live is what wins the room. ---

secs.head: Who this is for
secs.body: Infrastructure and platform engineers who run GPUs for AI and keep getting asked "why is it slow?" and "what should we buy?". You don't need to write CUDA. You need to be happy multiplying big numbers and dividing them by other big numbers. And if you're preparing for the interview question "How would you serve a 70B model?" , this series is the long version of a great answer. ---

secs.body: All hardware figures from NVIDIA datasheets; the model from the Llama 2 paper and its published configuration. Real systems land below. Ceilings are still the right tool. They tell you which resource you've run out of, and they catch vendor claims that break physics.

label: 1. Compute vs memory bound
title: Compute-Bound vs Memory-Bandwidth-Bound
desc: Part 1 of the LLM Inference Performance series. A GPU has two speed limits, and your workload always hits one of them fi

secs.head: Compute-Bound vs Memory-Bandwidth-Bound
secs.body: Part 1 of the LLM Inference Performance series. A GPU has two speed limits, and your workload always hits one of them first. By the end of this page you'll know which one, using only a datasheet and one division, and you'll never again be surprised by an "upgrade" that didn't upgrade.

secs.head: The pizza place that hired the wrong person
secs.body: A pizza place is losing customers. Orders take too long. The owner watches the kitchen for an evening and sees a chef who's clearly a genius: hands moving faster than you can follow, dough stretched in seconds. So he hires a second genius chef. Nothing improves. Not one minute. Then he notices the walk-in fridge is at the far end of the building, and there's one teenager fetching every ingredient, one tray at a time. Both chefs spend most of the night standing still, arms crossed, waiting for mozzarella. The kitchen was never short of chef. It was short of fetching . Now swap the menu. Instead of pizza, the place sells hand-folded dumplings: one bag of ingredients becomes two hundred dumplings of fiddly work. Suddenly the teenager is sitting idle and the chefs are drowning. That kitchen needs another chef. Same kitchen. Same staff. Different recipe, different bottleneck. A GPU is that kitchen: Kitchen GPU --------- ----- Chefs Tensor cores, the math units Walk-in fridge HBM, the memory stacked beside the chip The teenager's speed Memory bandwidth, in bytes per second The recipe Your workload The team in the overview bought a kitchen with 3× faster chefs and a 1.6× faster teenager. Whether that was a good buy depends entirely on the recipe. So how do you read a recipe? ---

secs.head: One number about the recipe
secs.body: Count two things: how much math the work needs, and how many bytes it has to fetch from memory. Divide. $$\text{arithmetic intensity} = \frac{\text{FLOPs performed}}{\text{bytes moved to or from memory}}$$ A FLOP is one floating-point operation: one multiply, or one add. So intensity is math per byte fetched . - Low intensity is the pizza: grab an ingredient, do a little with it, grab the next. Every byte gets used once and thrown away. - High intensity is the dumplings: fetch once, then work on it for ages. Every byte gets reused many times while it sits in fast on-chip memory. Here's the nice part: intensity belongs to the work , not to the GPU. You can compute it on paper before you've bought anything. But a recipe's number means nothing until you know what the kitchen can handle. Where's the line between "too much chopping" and "too much fetching"? ---

secs.head: One number about the kitchen
secs.body: Divide the chefs' top speed by the teenager's top speed: $$\text{ridge point} = \frac{\text{peak FLOP/s}}{\text{peak memory bandwidth (bytes/s)}}$$ That's the ridge point : how much math you must do per byte just to keep the chefs busy. Below it, chefs wait. Above it, the fetcher waits. GPU Dense BF16 compute HBM bandwidth Ridge point ----- ------------------- --------------- ------------- A100 80GB SXM 312 TFLOPS 2,039 GB/s ~153 FLOP/byte H100 SXM 989 TFLOPS 3.35 TB/s ~295 FLOP/byte The rule: Your work's intensity You are A faster chip helps? More bandwidth helps? ----------------------- --------- --------------------- ---------------------- Below the ridge Memory-bandwidth-bound No Yes Above the ridge Compute-bound Yes No Now look at the table again. A100 to H100: compute up about 3.2× , bandwidth up about 1.6× . The ridge point doubled . That's the plot of the overview story in one line. NVIDIA hired a much faster chef and a somewhat faster teenager. Work that kept an A100 balanced leaves an H100's tensor cores waiting. Every new GPU generation makes it harder to be compute-bound. Remember that; it'll come back in every page of this series. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Grab a pen. Two jobs. For each, guess: pizza or dumplings? 1. Add two long lists of numbers , element by element ( c = a + b ), in 32-bit floats. 2. Multiply two big square matrices , 4096 × 4096, in 16-bit floats. Got your guesses? Scroll on. ---

secs.head: The roofline: the whole idea in one picture
secs.body: Before the answers, the picture that makes them obvious. Put intensity on the x-axis and achievable speed (FLOP/s) on the y-axis, both on log scales. The GPU's limits draw a roof: - On the left, a slanted roof : speed = intensity × bandwidth. You're waiting on the teenager. Want to go faster? Fetch less, or fetch faster. - On the right, a flat roof : speed = peak compute. You're waiting on the chefs. Want to go faster? Faster or more chefs. - They meet at the ridge point. This is the roofline model (Williams, Waterman and Patterson, 2009), and its superpower is ruling things out. If your work sits on the slanted part, every optimization that adds math speed is guaranteed to do nothing. You can kill a bad proposal in one sentence. Now, the answers. ---

secs.head: Two workloads, opposite fates
secs.body: Job 1: adding two lists. Per element: read 4 bytes, read 4 bytes, write 4 bytes. One addition. $$\frac{1 \text{ FLOP}}{12 \text{ bytes}} \approx 0.08 \text{ FLOP/byte}$$ That's thousands of times below the H100's ridge. Pure pizza. The tensor cores might as well not exist; this runs at exactly the speed of memory. Job 2: multiplying big matrices. About 2N³ FLOPs. At best, three N×N matrices of 2 bytes each cross the memory boundary: $$\frac{2N^3}{6N^2} = \frac{N}{3} \approx 1{,}365 \text{ FLOP/byte for } N = 4096$$ Way past the ridge. Pure dumplings. Each number fetched gets used thousands of times. This is the job tensor cores were invented for. Same GPU, idle for one job and maxed out for the other. The only difference: how many times each byte gets reused. Hold onto that phrase. In part 2 you'll find out that generating text with an LLM looks a lot more like Job 1 than Job 2, which is why the team in the overview got 1.6× and not 3×. ---

secs.head: Plot twist: there are four walls, not two
secs.body: "Compute-bound or memory-bound" is the headline. In real debugging, you'll meet four walls: Wall What's short What you see Usual fix ------ ------------- -------------- ----------- Compute Math units Tensor cores busy Lower-precision math, more GPUs Memory bandwidth Bytes per second Memory busy, tensor cores idle Fetch fewer bytes: batching, quantization, fusion Memory capacity Bytes that fit Out-of-memory, or a capped batch size Shard across GPUs, quantize, waste less Overhead / latency Time between work Nothing is busy Fuse kernels, bigger batches, fewer sync points The trap: people say "memory-bound" for both the second and third walls. They're different problems. A 70B model that won't fit on one GPU is a capacity problem. Once it fits, its speed is a bandwidth problem. Tensor parallelism happens to fix both at once, which is exactly why they get blurred. Separate them out loud in an interview and you'll sound like someone who's actually been paged about it. ---

secs.head: The asterisk that doubles your mistake
secs.body: One last trap, hiding in plain sight. The H100 datasheet lists BF16 Tensor Core performance as 1,979 TFLOPS . Look closer: there's an asterisk. That number is with sparsity , a special 2:4 pattern where half the weights are zero. Ordinary models aren't like that. The dense number is half: 989 TFLOPS . The A100 sheet does the same (624 with sparsity, 312 dense). Use the headline number and your ridge point doubles. Every workload suddenly looks twice as bandwidth-bound as it really is, and your capacity plan is built on sand. Here's what that misdiagnosis looks like. A team profiles a kernel at 400 FLOP/byte on an H100. Ridge point computed from Ridge Verdict for 400 FLOP/byte What the team does next --------------------------- ------- --------------------------- ------------------------- Dense BF16, 989 TFLOPS ÷ 3.35 TB/s ~295 Compute-bound (correct) Looks for faster math: FP8, better tensor-core use Sparse BF16, 1,979 TFLOPS ÷ 3.35 TB/s ~590 "Bandwidth-bound" (wrong) Spends a sprint cutting memory traffic, and nothing gets faster Everything between the real ridge and the inflated one gets misfiled. The team optimizes the wrong axis, exactly the mistake the roofline exists to prevent. The sparse number only becomes the right one once a model really is pruned to 2:4, which part 5 covers. Also remember the datasheet bandwidth is a peak. Real kernels get a fraction of it, so real ceilings sit a bit lower than the ones you'll compute in this series.

secs.head: What the roofline is not
secs.body: - Not a prediction. It's a ceiling. Real code lives under the roof, sometimes far under. - Not the whole memory story. The simple version only counts trips to HBM. Clever kernels keep data on-chip and change the math; part 4 shows how. - Not multi-GPU. Talking between GPUs is a third roof. We'll hit it in part 3. Takeaway: divide the work's FLOPs by its bytes; if that's below the GPU's ridge point (about 295 for an H100), you're short of fetching, not chefs, and no amount of TFLOPS will save you. So where does an LLM sit on this roof? Here's a hint that should bother you: it's fast at reading your prompt and slow at writing the answer. Same model, same GPU. Why? That's part 2.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU datasheet - NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU datasheet - Williams, Waterman, Patterson, "Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures", Communications of the ACM, 2009 - NVIDIA Nsight Compute: Profiling Guide (roofline charts)

label: 2. LLM inference on the roofline
title: LLM Inference on the Roofline
desc: Part 2 of the LLM Inference Performance series. An LLM is two completely different workloads pretending to be one. By th

secs.head: LLM Inference on the Roofline
secs.body: Part 2 of the LLM Inference Performance series. An LLM is two completely different workloads pretending to be one. By the end of this page you'll know which half is pizza and which is dumplings, why batching is the closest thing to free money in AI infrastructure, and the one piece of memory that batching can never fix.

secs.head: Two tickets in the support queue
secs.body: Monday, two tickets land in the platform team's queue. Ticket 1: "I pasted a 40-page contract into the assistant. It took a noticeable pause before it started answering." Ticket 2: "I asked a one-line question. It started instantly, but the answer dribbles out word by word." A junior engineer reads both and writes: "Model is slow, need more GPUs." Closes both. They're wrong twice. These are two different bottlenecks, on opposite sides of the roofline from part 1. More GPUs of the same kind might help one and do nothing for the other. To see why, watch what the model actually does with each request. It does two jobs: 1. Prefill : read the whole prompt at once, and produce the first token of the answer. 2. Decode : write the rest of the answer one token at a time , each token depending on everything before it. Same weights, same GPU. Opposite personalities. ---

secs.head: The librarian who reads the whole library for one word
secs.body: Start with decode, because it's the strange one. Imagine a librarian who answers questions one word at a time. To produce each word, she has to walk past every shelf in the library and glance at every book. Then she writes one word. Then she walks the whole library again for the next word. That's decode. The "library" is the model's weights: billions of numbers. To produce one token, every one of them is read from HBM and used in one multiply and one add. For a model with P parameters stored in 16 bits (2 bytes): $$\text{intensity} \approx \frac{2P \text{ FLOPs}}{2P \text{ bytes}} = 1 \text{ FLOP/byte}$$ One. The H100's ridge point is about 295. Generating text for one user sits roughly 300× below the line where the tensor cores would be busy. It's the vector addition from part 1 wearing a trench coat. Which gives the single most useful formula in LLM serving: $$\text{max tokens/s (one user)} \approx \frac{\text{memory bandwidth}}{\text{model size in bytes}}$$ Look at what's missing: TFLOPS. Double the compute, keep the bandwidth, and one user's answer streams no faster at all . Now reread the overview's story. Answers streamed 1.6× faster after the upgrade. That's the bandwidth ratio. It had to be. That's Ticket 2: the dribble. So why was Ticket 1, the giant prompt, a different problem? ---

secs.head: Reading the prompt: the dumpling phase
secs.body: Prefill is the librarian on her best day. She walks past every shelf once and, on that single walk, handles all T words of your prompt together. Each weight fetched gets used T times: $$\text{intensity} \approx \frac{2P \times T}{2P} = T \text{ FLOP/byte}$$ A 2,000-token prompt: about 2,000 FLOP/byte. Way past the ridge. Prefill is compute-bound. It finally uses the tensor cores the way they were built to be used. So Ticket 1, the pause before a 40-page contract, is a compute problem, and Ticket 2 is a bandwidth problem. "LLM inference is memory-bound" is only half true. Decode is. Prefill isn't. Being able to say that crisply is one of the clearest signals of seniority in an inference interview. Fine. Decode wastes the tensor cores. Can we give them something to do while the librarian walks? ---

secs.head: Batching: the bus instead of the taxi
secs.body: Decode's problem is that every walk through the library serves one person. So stop doing that. Run the next step for B users at once . The librarian walks past every shelf one time and writes the next word for all B answers on the way. Weights are read once and used B times: $$\text{intensity of the weight reads} \approx B \text{ FLOP/byte}$$ It's a bus instead of a taxi. The road (bandwidth) is the same. The trip takes about as long. But it carries 64 people instead of one. That's why batching is the closest thing to free money in serving: total throughput rises almost linearly with batch size while each user's streaming speed barely moves. One catch with old-style batching: the bus waits until its slowest passenger arrives before leaving again. Short answers finish, their seats sit empty, and the bus keeps driving half-full. Continuous batching (also called in-flight or iteration-level batching) fixes that: at every single decode step, finished passengers get off and new ones get on. vLLM and other modern engines work this way. So here's the obvious question. If batch B gives intensity B, and the ridge is 295... just batch 300 users and become compute-bound? ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Before reading on, think about it for ten seconds. Batching shares the weights across users. Is there anything the model reads at every step that can't be shared between users? Hint: the model has to remember each conversation. ---

secs.head: The KV cache: the luggage that doesn't share
secs.body: When the model writes word 500 of your answer, attention needs to look back at words 1 through 499. Recomputing all of that at every step would be absurd, so the model stores two vectors for every past token in every layer: a key and a value . That store is the KV cache . Here's the catch. Your KV cache is yours. The bus can share the road (the weights), but every passenger brings their own luggage, and the luggage has to be carried at every stop. Each decode step reads every user's entire KV cache, and each byte of it serves exactly one user. The size per token is set by the model's shape: $$\text{KV bytes per token} = 2 \times \text{layers} \times \text{KV heads} \times \text{head dim} \times \text{bytes per value}$$ This luggage causes two separate problems. Problem 1: the bus fills up. Every passenger's luggage takes memory, and it grows with every word they generate. Once memory is full, nobody else gets on. The KV cache, not the GPU's speed, often decides the maximum batch size. Wasting that memory is expensive, which is the problem PagedAttention solves in part 4. Problem 2: luggage never gets cheaper to carry. Since each cached byte serves one user, attention's intensity is fixed by the model's shape, not by the batch. If the model has H q query heads sharing H kv key/value heads: $$\text{attention intensity} \approx \frac{H q}{H {kv}} \text{ FLOP/byte}$$ Attention design Query heads per KV head Attention intensity ------------------ ------------------------ --------------------- Classic multi-head attention 1 ~1 FLOP/byte Grouped-query attention, Llama 2 70B (64 query, 8 KV) 8 ~8 FLOP/byte Single digits. At any batch size. At any context length. And the longer the conversations, the more of each step's bytes are luggage, so the whole step slides further from the ridge, not closer. That's why model designers care about grouped-query attention : fewer KV heads means smaller luggage (more passengers fit) and more work per byte of luggage carried. Llama 2 adopted it for the 70B model for exactly this kind of inference scalability. So: can you batch your way to compute-bound? With long conversations, no. You'll see the exact numbers in part 3. ---

secs.head: The whole story on one roof
secs.body: Work Intensity (16-bit) On the H100 roofline ------ ------------------- ---------------------- Decode, 1 user ~1 FLOP/byte Far left: waiting on memory Attention over the KV cache (GQA ×8) ~8 FLOP/byte Left, at any batch size Decode, 64 users, weight reads ~64 FLOP/byte Left, much better The H100 ridge point ~295 FLOP/byte The corner Prefill, 2,000-token prompt ~2,000 FLOP/byte Right: waiting on math Everything left of the ridge is fixed with bytes : fetch fewer, share more, or get more bandwidth. Everything right of it is fixed with math . ---

secs.head: What users actually feel
secs.body: Back to the two tickets. Serving engines report two latency numbers, and each one belongs to one phase: Metric Means Phase Bound by -------- ------- ------- ---------- TTFT , time to first token The pause before the answer starts Prefill Compute TPOT , time per output token How fast the answer streams Decode Memory bandwidth Ticket 1 is a TTFT complaint. Ticket 2 is a TPOT complaint. Different physics, different fixes. This also explains three things that otherwise look like bugs: - A huge prompt delays the start, but the answer then streams at normal speed. - Adding users to a server barely slows anyone's streaming, until KV-cache memory fills up and new users start queuing. - When someone pastes a giant document, everyone else's stream stutters for a moment: that compute-heavy prefill elbows its way in between their decode steps. Hold that thought; part 4 has a fix. Takeaway: reading the prompt reuses every weight thousands of times and is compute-bound; writing the answer walks the whole library for each word and is bandwidth-bound; batching shares the walk, but every user's KV-cache luggage still has to be carried. You now have every formula you need. So here's the challenge: an interviewer hands you a marker and says "Llama 2 70B, eight H100s. How fast can it go?" Can you answer in five minutes, from memory? That's part 3.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Touvron et al., "Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models", arXiv:2307.09288 (grouped-query attention for 70B) - Kwon et al., "Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention", SOSP 2023, arXiv:2309.06180 - NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU datasheet - Williams, Waterman, Patterson, "Roofline", CACM 2009

label: 3. Sizing a 70B model
title: Sizing a 70B Model with a Pencil
desc: Part 3 of the LLM Inference Performance series. This page is a whiteboard session. One real model, one real server, seve

secs.head: Sizing a 70B Model with a Pencil
secs.body: Part 3 of the LLM Inference Performance series. This page is a whiteboard session. One real model, one real server, seven questions an interviewer could ask, and the arithmetic to answer each one live. By the end you'll be able to size any model on any GPU in about five minutes, and you'll have caught the batching myth red-handed.

secs.head: The marker is in your hand
secs.body: Interview room. Whiteboard. The interviewer leans back. "We want to serve Llama 2 70B on one server with eight H100s. Talk me through it. How fast can it go?" Most candidates start listing tools: vLLM, quantization, tensor parallelism. The interviewer nods politely. They've heard it forty times. You pick up the marker and write the inputs instead. Input Value ------- ------- Model Llama 2 70B: 80 layers, hidden size 8192, 64 query heads, 8 KV heads , head dim 128 (8192 ÷ 64), context up to 4,096 tokens Precision 16-bit: 2 bytes per weight and per cached value One H100 SXM 80 GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s , 989 TFLOPS dense BF16 Eight of them 640 GB, 26.8 TB/s, ~7.9 PFLOPS "Everything I compute is a ceiling: 100% of datasheet numbers, no overheads. Real systems land below. But ceilings tell us which resource we'll run out of first." The interviewer sits up a little. Let's go. ---

secs.head: Question 1: "Does it fit?"
secs.body: $$70 \times 10^9 \times 2 \text{ bytes} \approx 140 \text{ GB}$$ One H100 holds 80 GB. It doesn't fit. That's a capacity problem, and it's the first reason for tensor parallelism : slice every weight matrix across the GPUs. Eight GPUs, about 17.5 GB of weights each. Now say the subtle bit out loud: "Two GPUs would hold the weights. We're using eight for bandwidth and for room to store conversations." That sentence sets up everything that follows. ---

secs.head: Question 2: "How much does each conversation cost?"
secs.body: Every token in every conversation leaves luggage in the KV cache (part 2): $$2 \times 80 \text{ layers} \times 8 \text{ KV heads} \times 128 \times 2 \text{ bytes} = 327{,}680 \text{ bytes} \approx 0.33 \text{ MB per token}$$ A full 4,096-token conversation: $$4{,}096 \times 0.33 \text{ MB} \approx 1.34 \text{ GB}$$ Now the flourish that makes interviewers smile. "This is cheap because Llama 2 70B uses grouped-query attention. With classic multi-head attention, all 64 heads would store their own keys and values: 8× more, about 2.6 MB per token, 10.7 GB per conversation. Seven long chats would weigh more than the model." ---

secs.head: Question 3: "How many users can we hold?"
secs.body: Keep some memory back for activations and runtime buffers. Engines expose this as a setting; assume 10% headroom. GB --- --- Eight GPUs 640 Usable at 90% 576 Minus the weights −140 Left for KV cache ~436 $$\frac{436}{1.34} \approx 325 \text{ full-length conversations}$$ That's if every conversation runs to the full 4,096 tokens. Most are shorter, so more fit... but only if you don't reserve the full 4,096 for every request up front. Older systems did exactly that and wasted most of the space on tokens nobody ever generated. File that away; it's the villain PagedAttention defeats in part 4. ---

secs.head: Question 4: "How fast for one user?"
secs.body: One user means decode at batch 1: every weight read once per token. $$\frac{140 \text{ GB}}{26.8 \text{ TB/s}} \approx 5.2 \text{ ms per token} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{at most } \sim 190 \text{ tokens/s}$$ Now compute how long the math takes for that token: 2 × 70×10⁹ ≈ 1.4×10¹¹ FLOPs, at 7.9 PFLOPS, about 0.02 ms . Write both numbers side by side on the board. 5.2 ms of fetching, 0.02 ms of thinking. The tensor cores spend 99.7% of the time waiting. That's part 2's "300× below the ridge," made physical. One more line for depth: "If the model somehow fit on one H100, the ceiling would be 140 GB ÷ 3.35 TB/s, about 24 tokens per second. Eight GPUs give 8× the single-user speed because they add bandwidth, not because they add compute." [!NOTE] Real numbers land below 190. Tensor parallelism also has to talk : in the standard Megatron-LM design, each layer needs two all-reduce operations across the GPUs. That's 160 small messages per token for 80 layers, over NVLink. At batch 1 those messages are tiny, so their cost is latency, not bandwidth. It's a third roof the simple model doesn't draw. ---

secs.head: Question 5: "And with 64 users?"
secs.body: Sixty-four conversations, each with a full 4,096-token history, each getting its next token in the same step. Bytes read per step GB --------------------- ----- Weights, read once and shared by all 64 140 KV caches, 64 × 1.34 GB, not shared ~86 Total ~226 $$\frac{226 \text{ GB}}{26.8 \text{ TB/s}} \approx 8.4 \text{ ms per step}$$ And each step now produces 64 tokens. Put it in a table, because this table is the punchline of the whole page: 1 user 64 users --- --- --- Time per step 5.2 ms 8.4 ms Tokens per step 1 64 Server throughput ceiling ~190 tokens/s ~7,600 tokens/s Each user's speed ceiling ~190 tokens/s ~120 tokens/s Throughput up about 40× . Each user slowed by about a third. That's the bus from part 2, in numbers. Quick compute check: 64 × 1.4×10¹¹ ≈ 9×10¹² FLOPs, about 1.1 ms. Still seven times less than the fetching. "Even at batch 64, we're bandwidth-bound by about 7×." ---

secs.head: Question 6: "So just batch more until it's compute-bound?"
secs.body: The interviewer is testing you now. The tempting answer: weight intensity ≈ batch size, ridge ≈ 295, so batch 295 and you're compute-bound. ☕ Try it before you scroll. You've got every number you need. Does it work? ... Here's the board at batch 295, full 4,096-token contexts: Value --- --- Bytes per step 140 GB of weights + 295 × 1.34 GB of KV ≈ 535 GB FLOPs per step weights: 295 × 1.4×10¹¹ ≈ 4.1×10¹³; attention: about 0.3×10¹³ more Intensity 4.4×10¹³ ÷ 5.35×10¹¹ ≈ 83 FLOP/byte Eighty-three. Not 295. Not even close. The luggage won. By batch 295, the KV caches weigh almost three times as much as the model, and they run at about 8 FLOP/byte no matter what. Every passenger you add brings more luggage than useful work. And from Question 3, only about 325 such conversations fit in memory anyway. Say it plainly: "With long contexts, decode is bandwidth-bound at every batch size that fits in memory. Short contexts get closer to the ridge, because then the weights are most of the bytes. So context length isn't a detail; it's a capacity-planning input." That's the moment the interviewer stops checking their phone. ---

secs.head: Question 7: "What about the prompt?"
secs.body: Flip to prefill. A 2,000-token prompt: Value --- --- FLOPs 2 × 70×10⁹ × 2,000 ≈ 2.8×10¹⁴ Time for the math at 7.9 PFLOPS ≈ 35 ms Time to read the weights once ≈ 5.2 ms Now the math is the slow part, by about 7×. Compute-bound , just as part 2 predicted. Roughly 35 ms is the ceiling on time to first token for this prompt, and more bandwidth wouldn't move it. More compute would. Same model, same server, opposite bottleneck. Two tickets, two physics. ---

secs.head: Bonus round: FP8
secs.body: "What if we quantize to 8-bit?" H100 tensor cores support FP8. The bytes halve: 16-bit FP8 weights --- --- --- Weight memory 140 GB 70 GB One-user ceiling ~190 tokens/s ~380 tokens/s Room for KV cache (of 576 GB usable) ~436 GB ~506 GB The bandwidth didn't change. The model just needs half the bytes per token. Quantize the KV cache to 8 bits as well and the luggage halves too: more users fit and every step reads less. The careful closing line: "Those are ceilings. Whether quality holds at 8 bits is something we'd measure on our own evals. The roofline can't tell us that." ---

secs.head: The five-line cheat sheet
secs.body: That whole session, for any model on any GPU: Question Formula ---------- --------- Does it fit? parameters × bytes per weight Cost per token of context 2 × layers × KV heads × head dim × bytes per value How many users? (usable memory − weights) ÷ (KV per token × context length) How fast per step? (weights + users × KV per user) ÷ total bandwidth Which wall? FLOPs ÷ bytes, compared with peak FLOPS ÷ bandwidth Takeaway: for Llama 2 70B on 8×H100, the weights take 140 GB, each long conversation 1.34 GB more, one user tops out near 190 tokens/s, and even 64 users stay about 7× bandwidth-bound, so plan capacity in bytes, not FLOPs. Then the interviewer smiles and asks the follow-up: "Great. So, my team proposed five optimizations last week. Which ones would actually help?" That's part 4.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Touvron et al., "Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models", arXiv:2307.09288 - Llama 2 70B configuration (published config.json , mirrored) - NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU datasheet - Shoeybi et al., "Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism", arXiv:1909.08053 - Kwon et al., "Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention", arXiv:2309.06180

label: 4. Optimizations on the roofline
title: Optimizations, Mapped to the Roofline
desc: Part 4 of the LLM Inference Performance series. Every LLM serving optimization pulls one of five levers. Once you can na

secs.head: Optimizations, Mapped to the Roofline
secs.body: Part 4 of the LLM Inference Performance series. Every LLM serving optimization pulls one of five levers. Once you can name the lever, you can predict whether an idea will work before anyone spends a dollar on it. By the end of this page you'll judge five real proposals, meet three clever tricks nobody proposed, catch a dashboard lying to you, and give the 70B interview answer with reasons.

secs.head: The meeting
secs.body: Friday, 4 PM. The 70B chatbot from part 3 is popular, and users say it's slow. Five people, five proposals: 1. The manager: "Next-gen GPUs have way more TFLOPS. Let's upgrade." 2. The ML engineer: "Switch our serving to vLLM." 3. The researcher: "Quantize the model to FP8." 4. The infrastructure lead: "Spread tensor parallelism across two servers, 16 GPUs instead of 8." 5. The intern, quietly: "Could we stop the long prompts from slowing everyone down?" Everyone looks at you. You have a datasheet and a pencil. ☕ Try it before you scroll. Using parts 1 to 3, sort the five: likely to help, likely not to, or "it depends". Then compare with the verdicts below. ---

secs.head: The five levers
secs.body: Decode speed is roughly bytes per step ÷ bandwidth , and batch size is capped by memory. That leaves exactly five things an optimization can do: Lever What it does on the roofline Helps ------- ------------------------------ ------- Reuse each byte more Moves the work right, toward the ridge Throughput Fetch fewer bytes Same work, less time on the slanted roof Latency and throughput Add bandwidth Raises the slanted roof Latency and throughput Fit more in memory Lets the batch grow, which then reuses bytes more Throughput Separate the phases Stops compute-bound prefill from colliding with bandwidth-bound decode Predictable latency Faster math isn't on the list for decode. Keep that in mind for proposal 1. ---

secs.head: Proposal 1: "More TFLOPS" — doesn't help the complaint
secs.body: Users complain about slow streaming. Streaming is decode. Decode is bandwidth-bound: in part 3 the math for a token took 0.02 ms and the fetching 5.2 ms. Making 0.02 ms faster changes nothing anyone can feel. It's the overview story all over again: compute up 3.2×, streaming up 1.6×, because bandwidth went up 1.6×. When comparing GPUs for decode, read the bandwidth row, not the TFLOPS row. More TFLOPS would shorten the pause before long answers start (prefill), so it's not useless, just aimed at the wrong ticket.

secs.head: Proposal 2: "vLLM" — helps, by fitting more people on the bus
secs.body: vLLM brings two things. Continuous batching. At every decode step, finished requests leave and new ones join, so the batch stays full (part 2). Lever: reuse each byte more . PagedAttention. Remember the villain from part 3: systems that reserved KV memory for the maximum possible conversation length, up front, for every request. Kwon et al. found that KV-cache memory was being badly wasted through fragmentation and reservation, which capped batch sizes. PagedAttention stores the KV cache in small fixed-size blocks that don't need to sit next to each other, the way an operating system pages virtual memory. Their paper reports near-zero KV-cache waste and 2-4× higher throughput than earlier systems at the same latency. Lever: fit more in memory . Blocks can even be shared, for example a system prompt that every request starts with. Notice what PagedAttention doesn't do: it doesn't make any single fetch faster. It lets more users fit, so each weight fetch serves more of them. Verdict: helps throughput a lot. Each user's speed stays about the same.

secs.head: Proposal 3: "Quantize to FP8" — helps everyone, with a quality check
secs.body: Half the bytes per weight, half the fetching. Part 3's numbers: the one-user ceiling goes from about 190 to about 380 tokens/s, and 70 GB of memory frees up for KV cache. Quantize the KV cache too and you shrink the luggage that batching can never share. Lever: fetch fewer bytes . One of the few optimizations that speeds up a single user, not just the crowd. The catch is quality. Lower precision can hurt answers, and only your own evaluations can tell you by how much. Very low-bit formats (4-bit methods such as AWQ or GPTQ) also make the kernels unpack the weights, spending some of that idle compute. Verdict: helps, if the evals agree.

secs.head: Proposal 4: "16 GPUs across two servers" — probably hurts
secs.body: Tensor parallelism inside one server pulls two levers at once: capacity and bandwidth . Eight GPUs gave 8× the single-user ceiling in part 3. But it has a cost: in the Megatron-LM design, every layer ends with two all-reduce operations, so the GPUs exchange data 160 times per token for an 80-layer model. Inside a server that happens over NVLink. Across two servers it goes over the network, which is much slower, and you pay it 160 times per token. The extra bandwidth from 8 more GPUs can easily be eaten by the waiting. That's why tensor parallelism usually stops at the edge of one NVLink-connected server. To serve more users, run a second copy of the model on the second server and split traffic between them. Verdict: replicate, don't stretch.

secs.head: Proposal 5: the intern's — helps, and it's the cleverest one
secs.body: The intern noticed the stutter from part 2: when someone pastes a giant document, its compute-bound prefill barges in between everyone else's bandwidth-bound decode steps, and every stream hiccups. Two kinds of fix: - Split prefill into chunks and interleave them with decode steps, so no single giant prompt blocks everyone. - Separate the phases entirely. Systems such as Splitwise (Patel et al.) and DistServe (Zhong et al.) run prefill and decode on separate GPU pools and send the KV cache from one to the other. Each pool is sized for its own side of the roofline: compute for prefill, bandwidth and memory for decode. Lever: separate the phases . Cost: moving KV caches between pools, and a smarter scheduler. Verdict: helps latency predictability, especially with long prompts. Give the intern a raise.

secs.head: The scorecard
secs.body: Proposal Lever Verdict ---------- ------- --------- 1. More TFLOPS None for decode Doesn't fix streaming; helps prefill 2. vLLM Reuse + capacity Big throughput win 3. FP8 Fewer bytes Faster for everyone, check quality 4. TP across servers Bandwidth, but network-bound Replicate instead 5. Tame long prompts Separation Smoother latency ---

secs.head: Grouped-query attention: luggage diet (chosen at training time)
secs.body: Sharing each key/value head across several query heads shrinks the KV cache and raises attention's intensity by the group size. Llama 2 70B shares 8 KV heads among 64 query heads: an 8× lighter cache than classic attention (part 3, question 2). You can't add it to a model after training, but you should check for it when choosing which model to serve.

secs.head: FlashAttention and kernel fusion: stop leaving the kitchen
secs.body: Naive attention writes big intermediate tables out to HBM and reads them straight back. That's the teenager carrying a half-made pizza to the fridge and back between every step. FlashAttention (Dao et al.) is IO-aware : it computes attention in tiles that stay in fast on-chip memory, cutting trips to HBM. Kernel fusion does the same for chains of small operations. Lever: fetch fewer bytes . Biggest wins on long sequences and prefill.

secs.head: Speculative decoding: let the chefs guess ahead
secs.body: Decode leaves the tensor cores idle. Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al.) puts them to work: a small, fast draft model guesses the next few tokens, and the big model checks all of them in one pass. Checking several tokens at once looks like a tiny prefill, so one walk through the library can produce several words. When the guesses are right, you get several tokens for one weight fetch, and the output matches what the big model would have produced alone. Lever: reuse each byte more , for a single user , which batching can't do. Cost: the draft model's own work, and wasted checks when guesses miss. Shines when the draft guesses well and the server isn't already packed with users. ---

secs.head: The dashboard that says 100%
secs.body: Monday. You've shipped vLLM and FP8. Someone posts a screenshot: GPU utilization: 100% . "We're maxed out. Time to buy more GPUs?" Not so fast. The standard "GPU utilization" number (from nvidia-smi , and DCGM FI DEV GPU UTIL in dcgm-exporter) comes from NVML, which defines it as the percent of time during which one or more kernels was executing . It tells you the GPU was busy , not how much of it was working. A decode kernel waiting on memory shows 100% while the tensor cores twiddle their thumbs. Two other metrics in dcgm-exporter's default counters tell you which side of the roofline you're on: Metric Defined as -------- ----------- DCGM FI PROF PIPE TENSOR ACTIVE Ratio of cycles the tensor (HMMA) pipe is active DCGM FI PROF DRAM ACTIVE Ratio of cycles the device memory interface is active sending or receiving data Read them as a pair: Tensor active Memory active Diagnosis Reach for --------------- --------------- ----------- ----------- Low High Bandwidth-bound: typical decode Fewer bytes, more reuse High Lower Compute-bound: typical prefill Faster math Low Low Overhead-bound: tiny batches, launch gaps, waiting on communication Bigger batches, fusion, fewer sync points High High Balanced, near the ridge You're in good shape For deeper digging: Nsight Compute draws each kernel on an actual roofline chart, Nsight Systems shows the timeline gaps, and your serving engine reports time to first token, time per output token and KV-cache usage. KV cache near full with requests queuing means you've hit the capacity wall. [!TIP] Compare real tokens/s with your part 3 ceiling. Hitting 50-70% of a bandwidth ceiling means the system is healthy and the next win needs a new lever. Hitting 10% means something outside the roofline (scheduling, communication, CPU) is eating your time. ---

secs.head: Myths, busted
secs.body: Myth Reality ------ --------- "More TFLOPS, faster generation." Generation follows bandwidth . The math for a token took 0.02 ms of a 5.2 ms step. "Quantization increases memory bandwidth." Bandwidth is fixed by the hardware. Quantization cuts the bytes you need. "LLM inference is memory-bound." Decode is. Prefill is compute-bound. "Tensor parallelism is only to make the model fit." It also multiplies bandwidth, so it speeds up one user even when the model already fits. "Batch enough and decode becomes compute-bound." Not at long contexts: KV luggage grows faster than useful work (part 3). "100% utilization means maxed out." It means a kernel was running . Check tensor and memory activity. ---

secs.head: The interview answer
secs.body: "How would you serve a 70B model with high throughput and low latency?" "Start with the physics. In 16-bit the weights are about 140 GB, so they don't fit on one 80 GB GPU. And generation is memory-bandwidth-bound: each token reads every weight and does about one FLOP per byte, while an H100 needs about 300 to keep its tensor cores busy. So I plan in bytes, not TFLOPS. I'd use tensor parallelism inside one 8-GPU NVLink server. That fits the model and multiplies bandwidth, for a single-user ceiling around 190 tokens per second. For throughput, an engine with continuous batching and PagedAttention, like vLLM, so each weight read serves many users and KV memory isn't wasted. At 64 users with 4K contexts that's a ceiling around 7,600 tokens per second. Then FP8 for weights and KV cache, which halves the bytes, after checking quality on our evals. To scale further I'd replicate across servers rather than stretch tensor parallelism over the network. I'd track time to first token and time per output token separately, because prefill is compute-bound and decode is bandwidth-bound. If long prompts hurt streaming, I'd chunk prefill or split it onto its own GPUs. And I'd verify on DCGM: high memory activity with low tensor activity confirms we're on the bandwidth side, so I know which optimizations can still help." Takeaway: every serving optimization reuses bytes, fetches fewer bytes, adds bandwidth, frees memory or separates the phases, so name the lever before you spend the money, and check tensor activity against memory activity before you believe a utilization dashboard. You walked in wondering why a 3× faster chip gave 1.6×. You can now predict it with a pencil. But one number on the datasheet is still unexplained: the H100's headline 1,979 TFLOPS, the one with the asterisk. What is "with sparsity," and can your models ever use it? That's part 5.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Kwon et al., "Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention", SOSP 2023, arXiv:2309.06180 - Dao et al., "FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness", arXiv:2205.14135 - Leviathan, Kalman, Matias, "Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding", arXiv:2211.17192 - Patel et al., "Splitwise: Efficient Generative LLM Inference Using Phase Splitting", arXiv:2311.18677 - Zhong et al., "DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-optimized Large Language Model Serving", arXiv:2401.09670 - Shoeybi et al., "Megatron-LM", arXiv:1909.08053 - Touvron et al., "Llama 2", arXiv:2307.09288 - dcgm-exporter etc/default-counters.csv (profiling metric definitions) - NVML API reference: nvmlUtilization t - NVIDIA Nsight Compute Profiling Guide - NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU datasheet

label: 5. 2:4 structured sparsity
title: 2:4 Sparsity: Half the Weights, Not Half the Time
desc: Part 5 of the LLM Inference Performance series. Remember the asterisk from part 1? The H100's headline 1,979 TFLOPS is "

secs.head: 2:4 Sparsity: Half the Weights, Not Half the Time
secs.body: Part 5 of the LLM Inference Performance series. Remember the asterisk from part 1? The H100's headline 1,979 TFLOPS is "with sparsity." This page is about that asterisk: what 2:4 structured sparsity is, what the hardware actually does with it, and what it buys you on the roofline. By the end you'll be able to fact-check every common claim about it, including a few that sound right and aren't.

secs.head: The slide with the big number
secs.body: A procurement meeting. The vendor's slide shows the H100 at 3,958 TFLOPS of FP8. Someone does quick math: "Our current model runs at 989-ish BF16. So this is four times faster?" The room nods. Nobody reads the footnote. The footnote says with sparsity . Six weeks later, the deployed model, dense as the day it was trained, runs at the speed the dense numbers predict. Not one TFLOP of the "sparsity" half ever showed up. It couldn't. The model had no sparsity to use. That's not a scam. It's a real hardware feature with a real price tag, paid by the research team, not the infrastructure team. Let's see what it is. ---

secs.head: The pattern: two of every four
secs.body: Take any weight matrix. Walk along each row in groups of four neighboring values. 2:4 structured sparsity requires that in every group, at least two values are zero . Exactly half the weights are gone. But which half is constrained: you can't zero out a whole row and keep another row dense. Every group of four keeps two. Why such a fussy rule? Because it's a compromise between two extremes: Kind of sparsity Accuracy after pruning Hardware speedup ------------------ ---------------------- ------------------ Unstructured (zero any weights you like) Best: the pruner has full freedom Hard: irregular zeros are difficult for hardware to skip efficiently Coarse structured (remove whole rows, channels, heads) Worst: big chunks vanish Easy: the matrix just gets smaller 2:4 fine-grained structured In between Built into the Tensor Cores NVIDIA's paper introducing it (Mishra et al., 2021) makes the same trade explicit: networks pruned with unstructured sparsity tend to keep more accuracy, but rarely use the hardware well. 2:4 is regular enough for silicon and fine-grained enough that accuracy can usually be recovered. ---

secs.head: What the hardware actually does
secs.body: Three steps, and it's worth knowing which ones happen where. 1. Prune (research side, before deployment). Someone zeroes two of every four weights and, usually, fine-tunes the model to win back accuracy. Part 6 covers this. 2. Compress (software, ahead of time). The pruned matrix is packed into a compressed format: only the non-zero values, plus a small metadata index per value saying which of the four slots it came from. With four possible positions, each index needs 2 bits. Libraries do this before inference: NVIDIA's cuSPARSELt library exposes pruning and compression functions, and inference stacks like TensorRT do it when building the engine. The Tensor Cores don't compress anything on the fly; they consume the already-compressed format. 3. Multiply (Sparse Tensor Cores). Introduced with the Ampere architecture (A100), Sparse Tensor Cores use the metadata to pick out only the matching values from the other matrix and skip the zeros entirely. The paper's wording: they double math throughput for matrix multiplies when the first argument is a compressed 2:4 sparse matrix . Note that last condition. One operand is sparse: the weights . The activations flowing through the model, and the KV cache, stay dense. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ A 2:4-compressed matrix stores half the values. Does it take half the memory? Think about what else has to be stored. Then scroll. ---

secs.head: The metadata tax: 44%, not 50%
secs.body: Half the values are gone, but every surviving value carries a 2-bit position tag. Count the bits for one group of four weights: Format Dense group of 4 2:4 compressed group Compressed size Saving -------- ------------------ --------------------- ----------------- -------- 16-bit (FP16/BF16) 4 × 16 = 64 bits 2 × 16 + 2 × 2 = 36 bits 56% ~44% 8-bit (FP8/INT8) 4 × 8 = 32 bits 2 × 8 + 2 × 2 = 20 bits 62.5% ~38% These match the storage savings NVIDIA's paper reports: about 44% for 16-bit and 38% for 8-bit operands. Notice the trend: the smaller each value, the bigger the metadata's share. At 8 bits, the tags are a fifth of the compressed storage. That matters when you combine sparsity with quantization in part 6. So "2:4 halves memory and bandwidth" is close but wrong. It cuts weight bytes by a bit less than half, and only for the weight matrices that were actually pruned. ---

secs.head: Sparsity on the roofline: two different gifts
secs.body: Here's where the roofline earns its keep. 2:4 sparsity gives you two separate things , and each one helps a different phase: Gift Size Helps Because ------ ------ ------- --------- Double peak math for sparse matrix multiplies Up to 2× Prefill Prefill is compute-bound (part 2): the flat roof matters Fewer weight bytes to fetch ~44% less at 16-bit Decode Decode is bandwidth-bound: the slanted roof matters This is the single most important point on the page. The headline feature, doubled TFLOPS, does almost nothing for decode. Generating tokens was already leaving the tensor cores ~99% idle in part 3. Doubling the speed of idle hardware changes nothing. What decode feels is the smaller weights: fewer bytes per token, the same lever as quantization. So when someone says "sparsity lets us finally reach peak TFLOPS," ask: for which phase? For prefill, maybe. For streaming tokens, the TFLOPS were never the bottleneck. And even for prefill, 2× only applies to the matrix multiplies. Attention over the KV cache, normalization, activations and communication don't get faster. The PyTorch tutorial that prunes BERT to 2:4 reports an end-to-end inference speedup of 1.3× , not 2×. That's Amdahl's law in action: speed up part of the work, and the rest sets the ceiling. ---

secs.head: The 70B model, pruned
secs.body: Back to Llama 2 70B on 8×H100 from part 3. Suppose every weight matrix were pruned to 2:4 (in practice some layers are often left dense, so treat these as best cases). Same method: weight bytes ÷ 26.8 TB/s. Format Weight memory One-user decode ceiling Room for KV cache (of 576 GB usable) -------- --------------- ------------------------ -------------------------------------- BF16 dense 140 GB ~190 tokens/s ~436 GB BF16, 2:4 sparse ~79 GB ~340 tokens/s ~497 GB FP8 dense 70 GB ~380 tokens/s ~506 GB FP8, 2:4 sparse ~44 GB ~610 tokens/s ~532 GB Two surprises in that table: - FP8 dense beats BF16 sparse for decode. Halving every value's width saves more bytes than deleting half the values and tagging the rest. And FP8 doesn't require changing the model's structure. - They stack. FP8 plus 2:4 gets weights down to under a third of BF16 dense. On the datasheet, that's also where the 3,958 TFLOPS lives: FP8 and sparse. For prefill, sparse matrix multiplies at up to double speed would bring the 2,000-token prompt's matmul time from about 35 ms toward about 18 ms, as a ceiling, with the non-matmul work unchanged. [!NOTE] These are ceilings from datasheet bandwidth, as everywhere in this series. Whether a serving engine has fast 2:4 kernels for your precision and batch sizes, especially the small batches of decode, is something to benchmark, not assume. ---

secs.head: Fact-checking the usual pitch
secs.body: Here's a typical summary of 2:4 sparsity, checked line by line: Claim Verdict ------- --------- "Two out of every four adjacent weights must be zero." Correct. At least two of every group of four. "The Tensor Cores compress the matrix." Not quite. Compression is a software step done ahead of time (cuSPARSELt, TensorRT). Tensor Cores consume the compressed format. "Stores non-zeros plus a 2-bit index for each." Correct. "The silicon skips the math for the zeros, doubling TFLOPS." Correct for the matmul itself (sparse first operand). End-to-end speedups are smaller: 1.3× in PyTorch's BERT example. "It halves the bandwidth needed to fetch weights." Close. About 44% at 16-bit, 38% at 8-bit, because of metadata. "It doubles inference speed." Wrong. Decode is bandwidth-bound and gains from the byte savings, not the TFLOPS. Prefill gains up to 2× on matmuls only. "You can't run a dense model and get the boost." Correct , and the most important line. "It frees VRAM for larger batches." Correct. About 44% of weight memory at 16-bit. The KV cache isn't affected. Takeaway: 2:4 sparsity gives two gifts, double matmul math (which helps compute-bound prefill) and ~44% fewer weight bytes (which helps bandwidth-bound decode), and neither shows up until someone prunes the model. That "until someone prunes the model" is doing a lot of work. What does pruning cost, how much accuracy goes with it, and is it a better deal than quantization? That's part 6.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Mishra et al., "Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks", arXiv:2104.08378 (NVIDIA) - NVIDIA cuSPARSE and cuSPARSELt (2:4 structured sparsity, pruning and compression APIs) - PyTorch tutorial: Accelerating BERT with semi-structured (2:4) sparsity - NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU datasheet (sparsity figures) - NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU datasheet

label: 6. Sparsity vs quantization
title: Sparsity vs Quantization: Who Pays, and Who Wins
desc: Part 6 of the LLM Inference Performance series, the last one. Part 5 showed what 2:4 sparsity does once a model is prune

secs.head: Sparsity vs Quantization: Who Pays, and Who Wins
secs.body: Part 6 of the LLM Inference Performance series, the last one. Part 5 showed what 2:4 sparsity does once a model is pruned. This page is about getting there: what pruning costs, what it does to accuracy, and how it stacks up against the cheaper-looking alternative, quantization. By the end you'll know which lever to pull first, and how to split the work between the research team and the infrastructure team.

secs.head: "Can't you just turn it on?"
secs.body: The infrastructure lead has just read part 5. She walks over to the research team, excited. "The H100s have 2× sparse math. We're leaving half the chip on the table. Can you just turn on sparsity?" The research lead puts down her coffee. "Sure. Which half of the model would you like me to delete?" That's the conversation in one line. 2:4 sparsity isn't a switch on the GPU. It's a change to the model : half of every weight matrix becomes zero. Somebody has to choose which half, make sure the model still works afterwards, and prove it. That somebody is rarely the person who wanted the speedup. ---

secs.head: The original recipe: prune, then retrain
secs.body: NVIDIA's paper describes a simple workflow: take a trained dense model, zero out the two smallest-magnitude weights in each group of four, then retrain with the same settings as the original training. The authors report that it eliminated accuracy loss across many standard networks in vision, translation and language. PyTorch's 2:4 tutorial summarizes the same finding: prune once, retrain, and accuracy ends up nearly identical. For a vision model or a BERT, that retraining is affordable. For a 70B LLM, "repeat the original training" can mean a large slice of the original compute budget. That's the catch.

secs.head: The LLM shortcut: one-shot pruning
secs.body: Researchers built methods that prune large language models without retraining : - SparseGPT (Frantar and Alistarh, ICML 2023) prunes layer by layer, adjusting the remaining weights so each layer's outputs stay close to the original. It was the first accurate one-shot method for 10-100+ billion parameter models, and it supports the 2:4 and 4:8 patterns. The authors ran it on 175B-parameter models in under 4.5 hours. - Wanda (Sun et al., 2023) is even simpler: it scores each weight by its size times the size of the activations flowing into it, and prunes the lowest scores, again with no retraining. One-shot pruning turns a training project into a post-processing step. But "no retraining" also means "no chance to win back what was lost." Which raises the real question. ---

secs.head: What it does to accuracy
secs.body: SparseGPT's results on OPT-175B, one of the largest open models at the time, make the trade visible. Accuracy on the ARC-Challenge benchmark: Model ARC-Challenge accuracy ------- ------------------------ Dense 43.94 50% sparse, unstructured (SparseGPT) 41.30 50% sparse, 2:4 (SparseGPT) 38.99 50% sparse, naive magnitude pruning 25.60 Three lessons in four rows: - Pruning method matters enormously. Naive magnitude pruning at 50% wrecked the model. A careful method kept most of the accuracy. - The 2:4 rule costs extra. Same 50% of weights removed, but forcing the hardware-friendly pattern lost more than letting the pruner choose freely. That's the price of a pattern the silicon can read. - Size helps. The SparseGPT paper's broader finding is that larger models are more compressible: they lose less accuracy at a given sparsity. The authors also showed that sparsity stacks with quantization: 50% sparsity combined with 4-bit weights gave a negligible increase in perplexity on OPT-175B. [!WARNING] Benchmarks like these are averages over public test sets. Your model, your tasks and your users can lose more, or less. Every pruned model needs to pass the same evaluation gate as any other model change before it serves traffic. ---

secs.head: Two diets for the same model
secs.body: Sparsity and quantization both put the model on a diet. Different diets: - Quantization keeps every weight, but stores each with fewer bits. Like keeping every page of a book but printing it in smaller type. - 2:4 sparsity keeps half the weights at full width, and adds a tag saying where each one sat. Like tearing out half the words on every line, and adding a tiny marker so you know where the gaps were. Here's how they compare against a 16-bit dense baseline, on an H100: Lever Weight bytes saved Peak matmul math Changes model structure? Typical preparation ------- ------------------- ------------------ -------------------------- --------------------- FP8 (weights and activations) 50% 2× (989 → 1,979 TFLOPS dense) No Post-training calibration, sometimes fine-tuning 4-bit weights (GPTQ, AWQ) About 75%, minus scale factors No gain: weights are unpacked for 16-bit math No One-shot post-training, calibration data 2:4 sparsity, 16-bit ~44% 2× for sparse matmuls Yes : half the weights are zero Pruning, ideally plus fine-tuning FP8 + 2:4 ~69% 4× (up to 3,958 TFLOPS) Yes Both of the above (GPTQ and AWQ are both one-shot weight-only quantization methods for LLMs, from Frantar et al. 2022 and Lin et al. 2023.) Now map that onto the roofline from part 1: - Decode (bandwidth-bound) wants fewer bytes . 4-bit weights win, FP8 next, 2:4 at 16-bit last. - Prefill (compute-bound) wants more math . FP8 and 2:4 both double it; together they quadruple the peak. 4-bit weight-only doesn't help here. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Three workloads. Which lever would you reach for first? 1. A chatbot where users complain the answers stream slowly. 2. A batch job that scores millions of long documents with a model, producing one short label each. 3. A team that's already on FP8 and has a research budget for fine-tuning. Answers: (1) quantization, ideally 4-bit weights or FP8: decode wants bytes; (2) FP8, then consider 2:4: it's almost all prefill, which wants math, and both levers double it; (3) 2:4 on top of FP8: they stack, and the team can afford the pruning and fine-tuning to protect accuracy. ---

secs.head: Quantize first, sparsify second
secs.body: The recommendation, with the reasoning behind it: Quantize first. Add 2:4 sparsity when quantization is done and the workload or the budget justifies the model surgery. Why quantization first: - More bytes saved for decode. FP8 saves 50% of weight bytes and 4-bit about 75%, against 2:4's 44%. Decode is usually what users feel. - No structural change. Every weight stays. Quality risk is easier to reason about and usually easier to recover. - Cheaper to prepare. Post-training quantization is typically a calibration pass, not a pruning-plus-retraining project. When 2:4 earns its place: - Prefill-heavy workloads : long prompts, retrieval-augmented generation with big contexts, batch scoring, embedding generation. That's where doubled math shows up. - Stacking : once you're on FP8, 2:4 is the next ~38% of bytes and the next 2× of math, the only path to the datasheet's 3,958. - Large models : they tolerate pruning better, per SparseGPT's findings. - A research team with budget to prune carefully and fine-tune. The trade-off, stated plainly: 2:4 is the only lever that raises the compute ceiling without a lower-precision number format, but it's also the only one that changes what the model is . That's a research decision with infrastructure benefits, not the other way round. ---

secs.head: Who owns what
secs.body: Task Research team Infrastructure team ------ --------------- -------------------- Choose the pruning method (retrain, SparseGPT, Wanda) Owns Advises on budget Decide which layers stay dense Owns Reports which layers dominate runtime Fine-tune to recover accuracy Owns Provides the compute Evaluation gate before serving Co-owns Co-owns: blocks deploys that fail it Hardware support (Ampere or later; 2:4 needs Sparse Tensor Cores, compute capability 8.0+) Informed Owns Engine support: does your serving stack have fast 2:4 kernels for your precision and batch sizes? Informed Owns Benchmark prefill and decode separately , dense vs sparse Informed Owns Keep the dense model as a fallback Agrees Owns the rollout and rollback The infrastructure lead from the opening story should leave the conversation with this split, not with "please turn it on." ---

secs.head: The interview answer
secs.body: "How does 2:4 structured sparsity help with serving large models, and how does it compare with quantization?" "2:4 sparsity means at least two of every four adjacent weights are zero. The model is compressed ahead of time to the non-zero values plus a 2-bit position index each, and Ampere and Hopper Sparse Tensor Cores skip the zeros, doubling peak matmul throughput. On the roofline it gives two different things. Doubled math helps prefill, which is compute-bound. Decode is bandwidth-bound, so it only feels the byte savings, and because of the metadata that's about 44% at 16-bit, not 50%. End-to-end gains are smaller than 2× because attention and other non-matmul work don't speed up. The real cost is on the research side: someone has to prune the model and recover accuracy, either by retraining or with one-shot methods like SparseGPT. The 2:4 pattern loses more accuracy than unstructured pruning, though large models tolerate it better. So I'd quantize first: FP8 or 4-bit weights save more bytes for decode without changing the model's structure. Then I'd add 2:4 on top for prefill-heavy workloads or to stack with FP8, which is the only way to reach the H100's 3,958 TFLOPS sparse FP8 figure, gated on our evals and benchmarked separately for prefill and decode." Takeaway: quantization shrinks every weight and 2:4 sparsity deletes half of them; for decode, fewer bytes wins, so quantize first and add sparsity when prefill speed or stacking justifies the pruning and the accuracy work. That's the series. You started with a 3× faster chip that gave 1.6×, and you're finishing with the asterisk on its datasheet explained. Back to the overview.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Mishra et al., "Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks", arXiv:2104.08378 (NVIDIA) - Frantar and Alistarh, "SparseGPT: Massive Language Models Can Be Accurately Pruned in One-Shot", ICML 2023 - Sun et al., "A Simple and Effective Pruning Approach for Large Language Models" (Wanda), arXiv:2306.11695 - Frantar et al., "GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers", arXiv:2210.17323 - Lin et al., "AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration", arXiv:2306.00978 - PyTorch tutorial: Accelerating BERT with semi-structured (2:4) sparsity - NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU datasheet

title: Packages - Conda
desc: The package and environment manager program bundled with Anaconda that installs and updates conda packages and their dep

secs.head: 1.1- What is Conda?
secs.body: The package and environment manager program bundled with Anaconda that installs and updates conda packages and their dependencies. Conda also lets you easily switch between conda environments on your local computer. Fetched from the documentation on Glossary .

secs.head: 1.2- What is a conda environment ?
secs.body: A folder or directory that contains a specific collection of conda packages and their dependencies, so they can be maintained and run separately without interference from each other. Fetched from the documentation on Glossary .

secs.head: 1.3- Base Environment
secs.body: It is the 'base' environment of conda, where everything gets start. We usually do not install a lot of complicated packages in this environment. The most important thing we do in the base environment, is that we create other environments for different projects based on the task required, so we can install all required necessary packages and libraries.

secs.head: 1.4- Create a New Environment
secs.body: The very simplest way to create an environment is through: That's great, we have created our "cupoftea env" environment. Note : Try to give your env a proper name, that describe what is used for, even this name is package related name, or project specific name.
