label: Slurm accounting & multi-tenancy
title: Slurm Multi-Tenancy: Who Stores the Rules, Who Enforces Them
desc: Part of the schedulers directory. The intro sketched Slurm's three daemons. This page zooms in on the part that makes a

secs.head: Slurm Multi-Tenancy: Who Stores the Rules, Who Enforces Them
secs.body: Part of the schedulers directory. The intro sketched Slurm's three daemons. This page zooms in on the part that makes a shared cluster fair: accounts, limits and usage history. By the end you'll know which daemon stores the rules, which one enforces them, what sacctmgr actually is, and the one missing line in slurm.conf that makes every limit you set do nothing.

secs.head: The limit that wasn't
secs.body: A university buys a GPU cluster. Three labs share it. The vision lab is promised at most 16 GPUs at a time. The admin opens a terminal and runs: sacctmgr says the change was made. The admin closes the ticket. Two weeks later, the NLP lab's PI sends an angry email with a screenshot: the vision lab is running on 40 GPUs. The limit is right there in the database. sacctmgr show assoc displays it proudly. And Slurm is ignoring it completely. Nothing is broken. Slurm's resource-limits docs say that to enforce scheduling policy you set AccountingStorageEnforce in slurm.conf , and its limits option is the one that enforces association limits. Leave it unset, the default, and the limits sit in the database doing nothing. The admin stored the rule. Nobody told the enforcer to read it. That gap, between where rules are stored and where they're enforced , is the whole story of this page. ---

secs.head: Four programs, four jobs
secs.body: Program Kind Runs on Its job --------- ------ --------- --------- slurmctld Daemon (the controller) Head node, plus an optional backup Holds the live state of nodes, partitions and jobs; makes every scheduling decision; enforces limits when enforcement is turned on slurmd Daemon (the node agent) Every compute node Launches job steps, contains them with cgroups, reports back slurmdbd Daemon (the database front end) A database host, often the head node or a dedicated server Stores accounts, users, limits, QOS definitions and job history in MySQL/MariaDB; serves them to controllers and commands sacctmgr Command-line client Anywhere with Slurm clients installed Edits the accounting database through slurmdbd Plus the quiet fifth member: MUNGE , the authentication service. Slurm's resource-limits docs note that slurmdbd authenticates its traffic through a Slurm authentication plugin such as MUNGE, so a controller or command can't just claim to be someone else. A useful way to picture it: slurmdbd is the filing cabinet , slurmctld is the bouncer at the door , and sacctmgr is the pen you write rules with. Writing a rule into the cabinet doesn't make the bouncer check it. How the rules travel, per SchedMD's own architecture slides: slurmdbd sits between users and the database so nobody needs direct database access, and it pushes updates out to slurmctld on each cluster. The controller keeps its own working copy, which is why scheduling doesn't stop for a database round trip on every job. ---

secs.head: Correcting a common summary
secs.body: You'll often see multi-tenancy summarized like this: "accounting, resource limits and historical data are managed entirely by slurmdbd, while sacctmgr is merely a client." Half right: Claim Verdict ------- --------- " sacctmgr is a command-line client of slurmdbd ." Correct. It reads and writes accounting data through the daemon. " slurmdbd stores accounts, limits and history." Correct. It's the system of record, backed by a database. "Limits are managed entirely by slurmdbd ." Wrong where it matters. slurmdbd stores them; slurmctld enforces them, and only if AccountingStorageEnforce says so. "Without slurmdbd , no accounting." Mostly true for multi-tenant setups: Slurm's docs strongly recommend slurmdbd as the front end to the database for security and performance. The precise version: slurmdbd remembers, slurmctld decides. ---

secs.head: Associations: the unit of fairness
secs.body: Every rule hangs off an association . The resource-limits docs define it as a 4-tuple: cluster, account, user and (optionally) partition . Accounting and scheduling policy are both configured per association. Accounts nest, which is how organizations map onto the cluster: A user can belong to several accounts and choose one per job with --account . Each (cluster, account, user) combination is a separate association with its own limits and its own usage history. A typical setup, using sacctmgr : These are standard sacctmgr operations from SchedMD's documentation; they weren't run on a live cluster for this page. ---

secs.head: Limits: Grp versus Max
secs.body: Slurm tracks resources as TRES (trackable resources): CPUs, memory, nodes, GPUs as gres/gpu , and more. Limits come in two families, and mixing them up is the most common policy bug: Family Meaning Example Use it for -------- --------- --------- ------------ Grp A ceiling on the whole association and everything under it , added up across all its running jobs GrpTRES=gres/gpu=16 on vision : the lab's jobs together can't hold more than 16 GPUs Lab or team quotas Max A ceiling on each single job (or each user, depending on the limit) MaxTRESPerJob=gres/gpu=8 : no single job above 8 GPUs Stopping one job from swallowing the cluster Grp limits are budgets for a group. Max limits are size caps for individuals. A lab quota written as a Max limit lets the lab run as many 16-GPU jobs as it likes. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ The vision account has GrpTRES=gres/gpu=16 . Alice submits two 8-GPU jobs; both run. Bob submits a 4-GPU job. AccountingStorageEnforce=limits is set. What happens to Bob's job? It pends . The account's running jobs already hold 16 GPUs, its group ceiling. Bob's job waits until one of Alice's finishes, even if half the cluster is idle. That's the point of a group limit, and also its cost: quotas can leave GPUs idle. That trade-off is why many sites pair hard limits with fairshare, below. ---

secs.head: QOS and fairshare: the other two dials
secs.body: Limits say how much . Two more mechanisms say who goes first . QOS (Quality of Service) is a named policy a job runs under: priority boost, preemption rules, its own limits. A site might have normal , high for deadline work, and scavenger for preemptible jobs that soak up idle GPUs. With qos in AccountingStorageEnforce , every job must use a valid QOS, given explicitly or by default. Fairshare adjusts priority by recent usage. An association that has consumed more than its share recently drops in priority; one that's been quiet rises. It's how a cluster stays fair without hard caps: heavy users aren't blocked, they just wait behind lighter ones. It needs usage history, which is exactly what the accounting database keeps. Dial Answers Blocks jobs? ------ --------- -------------- Grp/Max limits "How much may you hold?" Yes, hard QOS "Under which policy does this job run?" Can, through its own limits Fairshare "Who goes next?" No, it reorders A preemption rule is just a field on a QOS. The preemptor lists the QOS it may evict, and the victim says how it is evicted: It only takes effect once PreemptType=preempt/qos is set in slurm.conf . The Guest List walks through the whole setup with a drill, and Autopsy of a Job shows how to read the result in sacct . The opinionated default for a shared GPU cluster: fairshare for everyday fairness, Grp limits only for promises you've actually made (like "the vision lab gets 16 GPUs"), and a preemptible QOS so idle GPUs don't stay idle. ---

secs.head: Turning it on safely
secs.body: AccountingStorageEnforce takes a comma-separated list. From the slurm.conf man page and resource-limits docs: Option Effect -------- -------- associations Jobs only run if the user and account exist in the database limits Enforces association limits; implies associations qos Jobs must use a valid QOS; implies associations safe Only starts jobs that can finish within their limits; implies limits and associations wckeys Requires a valid workload characterization key [!WARNING] Turning on associations blocks every user who isn't in the accounting database. On an existing cluster, load every user and account with sacctmgr first , then enable enforcement. The slurm.conf man page also notes that changing AccountingStorageEnforce needs a slurmctld restart, not just scontrol reconfigure ; check the man page for your version. A safe rollout: 1. Populate. Create accounts and users with sacctmgr . Check with sacctmgr show assoc format=account,user,grptres . 2. Enable associations in a maintenance window. Watch for jobs rejected for invalid accounts; fix the gaps. 3. Add limits (and qos if you use it). Verify a test account actually pends at its limit. 4. Keep the rollback ready: remove the option and restart slurmctld . ---

secs.head: When slurmdbd goes down
secs.body: The filing cabinet being locked shouldn't stop the bouncer. SchedMD's slides on the database daemon say slurmctld caches data if slurmdbd isn't responding , so the cluster keeps scheduling with the limits it already knows, and job records wait until the database comes back. What you lose while it's down: changes . sacctmgr edits can't land, new users can't be added, and reports from sacct or sreport won't show the newest jobs. Treat slurmdbd as important but not critical-path, and monitor it so "a few minutes down" doesn't quietly become "a week of cached records." Takeaway: slurmdbd remembers, slurmctld decides, and sacctmgr is just the pen, so a limit only exists once AccountingStorageEnforce tells the controller to read it. For what happens when tenants ask for different hardware in one job, see mixing GPU types in Slurm. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Slurm: Accounting and Resource Limits - Slurm: Resource Limits (associations, enforcement options) - Slurm slurm.conf man page, AccountingStorageEnforce - SchedMD, "Slurm Database Daemon" (Slurm User Group 2012 slides)

label: Backfill tuning
title: Backfill Tuning: The Planner That Can Only See One Day Ahead
desc: Part of the schedulers directory. The intro explains what backfill is. This page is about the knobs, the failure modes,

secs.head: Backfill Tuning: The Planner That Can Only See One Day Ahead
secs.body: Part of the schedulers directory. The intro explains what backfill is. This page is about the knobs, the failure modes, and the one counter screen ( sdiag ) that tells you whether either matters. Defaults and option descriptions come from SchedMD's Scheduling Configuration Guide for Slurm 26.05 and the sdiag man page. Tuning advice and logs come from SchedMD support tickets and the slurm-users list. Nothing here was run on a live cluster, the invented scenario is just that, and the sdiag sample uses made-up numbers.

secs.head: The planner with a one-day calendar
secs.body: An invented but common story. A cluster allows jobs of up to 7 days. A user submits a 64-node job with a 6-day time limit. It is the highest-priority job in the queue, and it waits. And waits. Meanwhile hundreds of small jobs start, run and finish around it. The big job's reason is Priority or Resources , and squeue --start shows nothing useful. Nothing is broken. The backfill scheduler plans resources into the future so that small jobs cannot steal what a big job is waiting for. But it only plans as far ahead as bf window , and bf window defaults to 1440 minutes, one day . A job that needs a slot that only opens beyond that horizon never gets protected, so the small jobs keep filling the gaps in front of it. SchedMD states the rule in one sentence, in both the guide and the slurm.conf man page: a bf window at least as long as the highest allowed time limit is generally advisable to prevent job starvation. One support ticket shows it in real life: a site with a 1-day window suspected exactly this when its larger MPI jobs would not schedule, and the SchedMD engineer's reply was to set bf window to the maximum time limit allowed on the cluster, 7 days, and raise bf resolution to 10 minutes: The rest of this page is why that works, what it costs, and how to know whether your cluster needs it.

secs.head: Two schedulers, several clocks
secs.body: Slurm has two scheduling mechanisms, and people often mix them up when they read tuning advice. Mechanism When it runs How far it looks Key knobs (default) --- --- --- --- Event-triggered At job submission, job completion and config changes A quick attempt at the top of the queue default queue depth (100 jobs) Main loop Every sched interval All jobs, limited by partition job depth sched interval (60 s), partition job depth (0, no limit) Backfill Every bf interval Pending jobs in priority order, planned into the future bf interval (30 s), bf window (1440 min), bf resolution (60 s), bf max job test (100) The first two follow a strict rule. Jobs are evaluated in priority order, and once any job in a partition is left pending, no other jobs in that partition are scheduled , so lower-priority jobs cannot take the resources of the waiting one. Without backfill, that rule alone gives you head-of-line blocking and, in SchedMD's words, significantly lower utilization. Backfill is the clever part. It lets lower-priority jobs start now if doing so does not delay the expected start of any higher-priority job. That promise depends on two things: how far ahead it can see, and how well it can guess when running jobs will end.

secs.head: How backfill actually thinks
secs.body: From the guide, in order: 1. It considers every running job and works out when each will end. 2. It walks the pending jobs in priority order and works out when and where each could start, taking preemption, gang scheduling, GRES and memory into account. 3. If a job can start now without hurting the expected start of any higher-priority job, it starts. 4. Otherwise, the resources it will need are reserved for its expected execution time , and its expected start time is recorded. The nodes involved show up in a Planned state. Three consequences deserve their own lines: - "Any higher priority job" is stricter than it sounds. Backfill does not protect only the job at the head of the queue. It builds a plan for as many pending jobs as it manages to test, which is why bf max job test matters so much (see below). - Backfill reserves whole nodes , even for jobs that do not need whole nodes. The guide says this is for performance. On a cluster full of small jobs, reservations can look much bigger than the jobs behind them. - A job submitted to several partitions appears once per partition in the list backfill walks, and may reserve resources in each, though it only starts in the reservation with the earliest start. That multiplies its cost in the backfill's work queue. The option bf one resv per job limits it to one reservation per job, at the price of no longer guaranteeing the earliest-partition start.

secs.head: The window and the resolution
secs.body: bf window is how many minutes into the future backfill plans. bf resolution is the granularity in seconds of that plan. The guide's tuning advice ties them together: if you raise the window, raise the resolution too, to limit the amount of data backfill has to manage. The arithmetic shows why. Here is a back-of-envelope count of time slots in the plan, which is my own illustration of the trade-off and not a figure from the docs: bf window bf resolution Slots in the plan --- --- --- 1,440 min (default, 1 day) 60 s (default) 1,440 10,080 min (7 days) 60 s 10,080 10,080 min (7 days) 600 s 1,008 Going from a 1-day to a 7-day window at the default resolution makes the plan seven times larger, which means more work in every cycle and, per the man page, "more overhead and less responsiveness". Coarsening the resolution to 10 minutes gives you the week of vision for roughly the cost of the original day. The price is imprecision: start times are planned on a coarser grid. The docs say larger resolutions suit sites where time limits are imprecise anyway, or where a small delay in starting jobs is an acceptable trade for higher utilization. Practical rules: - Set the window from your longest MaxTime across all partitions, converted to minutes. A 7-day MaxTime is 10,080. - The window has hard limits. The man page gives a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 43,200 minutes (30 days). - Unlimited time limits break the plan. On the list, a user whose jobs had no --time and no partition limit was told that if the resulting runtime is more than 28 days, the scheduler does not reserve slots for those jobs. A job that cannot fit inside the window cannot be planned. - Re-check the window when MaxTime changes. Raising a partition's limit to 14 days without touching bf window quietly recreates the starvation problem. [!NOTE] The precise mechanism by which a job beyond the window loses its protection is not spelled out in the guide. What the docs and the ticket establish is the rule (window at least as long as the longest time limit) and the symptom (large jobs not starting). The explanation above is the standard reading of those two facts.

secs.head: Backfill is only as honest as your time limits
secs.body: Backfill plans from the time limits of running jobs, not from how long they will really run. The guide says it plainly: because the expected start time of pending jobs depends on the expected completion time of running jobs, reasonably accurate time limits are important for backfill to work well, and backfill is difficult without reasonable time limit estimates. Think of it as a reservation system at a restaurant where every party books a table "until closing". The host cannot promise anyone a table. A few lines in slurm.conf give you some control over that: Setting What it does --- --- DefaultTime (per partition) The time limit given to jobs that do not specify one MaxTime (per partition) The ceiling on time limits OverTimeLimit Grace beyond the limit before a job is killed (system-wide) If DefaultTime is not set, a job without --time inherits the partition MaxTime , so a cluster with a 7-day maximum and no default quietly turns every careless submission into a 7-day reservation. On the list, a site new to Slurm asked whether a job-submit plugin that requires --time is the way out. That is a reasonable policy lever, and a short DefaultTime is a gentler one. Measure the gap. A rough script that compares what users asked for with what they used, per user. It is a sketch and untested, so run it on a small date range first: A ratio near 1.0 means honest limits. A ratio of 0.1 means that user is booking ten times the table they use. Reports like this are better used for a friendly conversation than for punishment, since users have good reasons to pad (a job killed at the limit loses all its work), and the preemption page covers making jobs safe to shorten.

secs.head: Why squeue --start drifts
secs.body: squeue --start shows the expected start time that backfill assigned. It is a forecast , and like any forecast it changes when its inputs change. Reasons for drift, with the evidence for each: Cause Direction Source --- --- --- A running job finishes earlier than its time limit Start moves earlier The guide: expected start depends on expected completion of running jobs A higher-priority job arrives and is planned ahead of yours Start moves later Follows from backfill planning in priority order Fairshare usage decays or accumulates, reordering the queue Either Follows from priority-ordered planning Nodes drain, reservations appear Later Resources the plan counted on are gone The job is not in the plan at all this cycle Shows N/A or "now" See below The cycle is cut short by bf max time or bf max job test before reaching the job Stale or missing See Depth and the time budget The "not in the plan" row has a well-documented oddity. In a SchedMD ticket from a large site, a pending job's START TIME flipped between N/A and a time one second from now, every ten seconds, while nodes sat idle. The controller log said "StartTime set but no backfill reservation created". The engineer's suspicion was bf min age reserve , set to 6 hours at that site: jobs younger than that get no backfill reservation, so their start time is placeholder noise. They suggested trying the default of 0 and finding the smallest value that fit. The case was closed as timed out without a confirmed root cause, and the reporter observed jobs starting before the age threshold, so treat that one as a lead rather than a rule. A cheap check when a start time looks odd: LastSchedEval says when a scheduler last evaluated the job, and Scheduler=Backfill: (as it appeared in the ticket) says who. A LastSchedEval that is minutes old on a busy cluster suggests backfill is not reaching that job. [!TIP] Treat squeue --start as a hint, never a promise. Users who plan around it will be disappointed in both directions.

secs.head: Depth and the time budget
secs.body: The window decides how far ahead backfill looks. These settings decide how many jobs it looks at and how long it is allowed to think . Setting Default Plain English --- --- --- bf max job test 100 Jobs considered per cycle. Past this depth, jobs are not tested at all bf max time = bf interval (30 s) Wall-clock limit for one cycle, sleeping included bf interval 30 s Pause between cycles bf continue off Keep going after the periodic lock release bf yield interval 2,000,000 µs How often backfill gives the locks back bf yield sleep 500,000 µs How long it stays out bf max job user 0 (no limit) Jobs per user that may start per cycle bf max job part 0 (no limit) Jobs per partition that may start per cycle bf max job start 0 (no limit) Jobs that may start per cycle The default bf max job test of 100 is worth pausing on. On a cluster with thousands of pending jobs, the backfill scheduler by default never reaches the 101st job in priority order, so lower-priority work deep in the queue is invisible to it. A SchedMD engineer's suggestion on one ticket was bf max job test=500 , alongside bf window=480 matching an 8-hour maximum limit and bf resolution=300 . A very large site in another ticket runs bf max job test=25000 with several per-user and per-partition caps. Both are examples of what some sites do, not recommendations. Why bf continue matters. Backfill is a long-running operation holding locks that job submissions need, so it releases the locks every bf yield interval (2 seconds by default) for bf yield sleep . The guide describes bf continue as continuing backfill "after periodically releasing locks", and says doing so ignores newly submitted jobs. Without it, a lock release can cut a long cycle short, so on a deep queue backfill may never get far down the list. The trade the guide names: more jobs considered, but newly submitted jobs may be scheduled later. Why per-user limits matter. A single user who submits thousands of separate jobs (for example with a shell loop around sbatch ) can fill the depth budget with their own jobs. bf max job user and bf max job part cap how much of each cycle one user or partition can consume. Job arrays behave differently, and the next section covers both.

secs.head: What bf max job user does
secs.body: The slurm.conf man page describes bf max job user as the maximum number of jobs per user that backfill will attempt to start , counted across all partitions. Its stated purpose is to stop a user from flooding the backfill queue with jobs that cannot start and that keep other users' jobs from starting. The man page compares it to the MAXIJOB limit in Maui, says it applies only to sched/backfill , and advises setting bf max job test to a value much higher than bf max job user . Take bf max job user=50 and a user with 100 separate pending jobs: Question Answer --- --- How many of that user's jobs does one backfill cycle attempt? At most 50, in priority order. The other 50 are skipped for that cycle Are the other 50 rejected? No. They stay pending and move into the top 50 on later cycles as earlier ones start or finish Is this a cap on queue size or running jobs? No. Those are association limits such as MaxSubmitJobs and MaxJobs Do the skipped jobs get a backfill reservation? Not in that cycle, so they are unprotected and their squeue --start may show N/A Does it save backfill much work? Less than you might expect. A SchedMD reply on ticket 2762 says skipped jobs are still briefly looked at and still count against bf max job test and bf max job part Do blocked jobs count? Yes. On the same ticket, each job tested counts toward the limit, even when a QOS or TRES limit then stops it. Fifty stuck jobs at the head of a user's queue can shadow runnable jobs behind them Does it stop the main scheduler from starting those jobs? No. The limit applies only to the backfill scheduler

secs.head: Reading the 12345 [1-1000] lines
secs.body: If you have not met job arrays, the squeue output looks odd at first. An array is many similar jobs submitted as one: Each task gets an index in SLURM ARRAY TASK ID and shares SLURM ARRAY JOB ID . In output file names, %A is the array job ID and %a the task index. The largest index is MaxArraySize - 1 , and the default MaxArraySize is 1001, so indices run 0 to 1000 on a default configuration. The official guide says squeue reports all the pending tasks of one record on one line , with the task IDs written as a range. A sketch of what you see (job IDs and names invented, layout from the guide): You see It means --- --- 12345 [8-1000] with PD One line standing for all pending tasks, 8 to 1000 12345 7 with R Task 7 has started and now has a record of its own 12345 [20,23-24] A pending set that is not contiguous (this form appears in a real ticket) 12345 [1-1000%50] The same, with a limit of 50 running at once (my recollection of the notation, so check it on your version) Useful commands:

secs.head: How arrays meet the scheduler
secs.body: - Records are created progressively. The guide says job records for the tasks are created as the array runs, not all up front. A pending array normally costs one record, and sdiag counts it as one job until tasks start, are requeued or are individually modified. - The main scheduler walks an array one task at a time. Once a task of an array is left pending, no other tasks of that array are considered, which is why arrays tend to start in a steady trickle. - Backfill reservations for arrays have their own knob. bf max job array resv limits how many tasks of one array get resources reserved. I have not confirmed its default, and the sites in the tickets I read set it to values like 2 and 20. - MaxJobCount still counts every task. The man page says each task of an array counts as one job even though it has no separate record until modified or started. A few large arrays can reach the limit, which is why site admins pair arrays with MaxSubmitJobs and MaxJobs .

secs.head: So what about 1000 tasks and bf max job user=50?
secs.body: I could not find a source that says exactly how bf max job user counts the tasks of a pending array, so this part is inference. Because a pending array is normally one record, it most likely uses one of the 50 slots, and running tasks are not "attempts to start". If so, the limit rarely bites an array. It bites the user who submits 1000 separate jobs in a loop, which creates 1000 records. That is the practical argument for steering users toward arrays with a %N throttle. A quick way to settle it on your own cluster:

secs.head: Reading sdiag
secs.body: sdiag is the stethoscope. It reports what slurmctld has been doing since the counters were last reset, which by default happens at midnight UTC. ( sdiag -r resets them by hand, as root.) The backfill block is the part this page cares about. Below is an illustrative layout using field names from the man page, with invented numbers: How to read it. These are heuristics built from the field definitions, not official thresholds: What you see What it suggests --- --- Depth Mean (try sched) equals bf max job test Backfill is hitting its depth cap every cycle Last queue length much bigger than depth Most of the queue is never tested. The man page counts a job once per partition it requested Max cycle close to bf max time in µs (30 s is 30,000,000) Cycles are being cut off by the time budget Mean cycle close to or above bf interval Backfill is barely finishing before the next one is due Mean table size growing after you raise bf window The plan is bigger, so each cycle costs more. The man page says larger counts increase backfill time Total backfilled jobs small next to Jobs started Backfill is contributing little, which may be fine on a quiet cluster Two details from the man page that stop misreadings: - "Last cycle" and "Max cycle" count execution time only , with the sleeping time during lock releases removed. A cycle that took 30 seconds on the clock may show less. - "Depth" and "Depth (try sched)" are different. The first counts every job examined, even ones that cannot start because of dependencies or limits. The second counts only jobs that had a chance to start. The second is the one that makes backfill heavy. The same output also reports main-scheduler cycles and RPC counts per user, which is where you look when someone's watch squeue loop is the actual problem.

secs.head: A tuning recipe: one knob at a time
secs.body: Backfill parameters interact, so change one thing, wait a representative period, and look at sdiag again. 1. Baseline. Save sdiag output and the current line: 2. Fix the window first. It is the one with a rule. Set bf window to your longest MaxTime in minutes, and raise bf resolution with it: Keep the existing options in the line. Replacing the whole value drops anything not repeated. 3. Check depth. If Depth Mean (try sched) sits at bf max job test and the queue is longer, raise it in steps (for example 100, then 300, then 500) and watch Mean cycle and Max cycle . 4. Give it room to think. If cycles are cut off, look at bf max time , and consider bf continue . If submissions feel slow, shorten the yield interval, as the docs suggest for high-throughput sites. 5. Stop one user eating the depth. Add bf max job user and, if needed, bf max job part . 6. Re-measure. After at least a day, compare against the baseline. Remember the counters reset at midnight UTC. Apply changes and confirm them: One ticket from 2019 told the user to restart slurmctld and then reconfigure; a recent site guide says scontrol reconfigure is enough for SlurmctldParameters . Check what your version does on a test controller before touching production.

secs.head: When you need to watch it think
secs.body: If a job refuses to start and the numbers do not explain why, turn on backfill logging for a short time, then switch it off: The ticket above also asked for debug3 and the Priority and Accrue flags for the same short window, and for the log level to go back to normal right after. Lines worth knowing from that ticket: Log line Meaning --- --- dump job test: Test JobId=... Backfill is evaluating that job this cycle ... has a prio reserve of ... The bf min prio reserve threshold is in play for that job StartTime set but no backfill reservation created The job got a start time without a reservation (see the drift section) start job: Started JobId=... Backfill started the job These logs are large. Capture a ten-minute window, filter by the job ID, and put the log level back.

secs.head: Cheat sheet
secs.body: Backfill is a planner with two inputs it cannot fix itself: a horizon, and the truthfulness of the people booking the tables. The horizon is one line of configuration. The truthfulness is a long-term project.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Slurm: Scheduling Configuration Guide - Slurm: sdiag man page, and the Debian 13 copy with the full field list - SchedMD ticket 7207: backfill for HPC cluster (1-day window, set to 7 days) - SchedMD ticket 6688: tuning suggestions for bf and max rpc cnt - SchedMD ticket 14608: start time constantly pushed, bf min age reserve - SchedMD ticket 2762: what bf max job user limits - slurm-users: bf max job user and bf max job user part man page text (2020) - Slurm: Job Array Support (squeue display, task records, MaxArraySize) - SchedMD SUG 2014: scheduling tutorial slides (array scheduling rule) - UL HPC: job arrays and MaxArraySize - Niflheim: Slurm configuration (MaxJobCount and job arrays) - slurm-users: large memory jobs stuck pending, bf window and --time (2025) - Niflheim: Slurm job scheduler configuration

label: Job forensics with sacct
title: Autopsy of a Job: Reading sacct Like a Coroner
desc: Part of the schedulers directory. The outputs below were produced on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4, accounting

secs.head: Autopsy of a Job: Reading sacct Like a Coroner
secs.body: Part of the schedulers directory. The outputs below were produced on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4, accounting on, both slurmd daemons on one Ubuntu 24.04 machine), with jobs created to die in each way. Job numbers and users are invented. sacct needs the accounting database, so on a cluster without slurmdbd it has nothing to read.

secs.head: The job that vanished
secs.body: A student writes to the admin: "my job disappeared". It is not in squeue . The output file is half written. There is no error message anywhere. The student is not sure it ever finished, never mind how it ended. The admin could grep logs on three machines. Or run one command, because Slurm keeps a record of every job's life and death, and the coroner's tool for reading it is sacct . It answers four questions: did the job finish, was it killed, who did it, and was it even the job's fault? ---

secs.head: First, find the body
secs.body: Each job has a main line, and below it a line per step : .batch is your script, .0 , .1 are the srun steps. The main line is the verdict. The step lines are the evidence. Four options do most of the work: Option What it does --- --- -j <ids Pick the jobs -X Show only the main line per job, with no step lines -o JobID,State,ExitCode,... Choose the columns -P Plain pipe-separated output, with nothing truncated, which is what you want for pasting By default sacct looks at jobs from today. For an older job, give a start date with -S 2026-11-01 . Without it, an older job simply does not appear, which is a good way to convince yourself a job never existed. ---

secs.head: Reading the verdict
secs.body: The State says how the job ended. ExitCode is two numbers, exit code : signal . The first is what the script returned. The second is the signal that stopped it, if any. Job What the test did Verdict How to read it --- --- --- --- 44 sleep 2 COMPLETED 0:0 The ordinary, happy ending 45 exit 3 FAILED 3:0 The script itself returned 3. The bug is in the script 46 kill -9 $$ FAILED 0:9 Exit code 0, signal 9 : something killed it with SIGKILL . The out-of-memory killer and an admin's kill -9 look the same here 47 scancel by a user CANCELLED by 30033 A person, and 30033 is their user ID. Not the job's fault The signal half is the coroner's best friend. 0:9 is SIGKILL and 0:15 is SIGTERM . Notice job 47's step line in the earlier table: .batch shows 0:15 , because scancel sends SIGTERM first, and the job line shows 0:0 because nothing failed. Different lines of the same record tell different parts of the story. (In the narrow default table the state is cut to CANCELLED+ . The + means "there is more": widen it with -o State%20 , or use -P , and the "by 30033" appears.) ---

secs.head: Dying of old age
secs.body: A job that runs into its time limit is killed by Slurm, and the record says so: TIMEOUT is unambiguous. The Elapsed is longer than the Timelimit here, by 26 seconds, because Slurm checks limits on a periodic tick and then waits KillWait for the job to exit after SIGTERM . The signals cheat sheet has the timings. In that test the job ignored SIGTERM on purpose, which is why the signal in ExitCode is 9 . ---

secs.head: The job that was evicted
secs.body: Under QOS preemption, the verdict is PREEMPTED . What happens next depends on whether the job could be requeued, and sacct shows both endings. A victim that could not be requeued is simply gone: A victim that was requeued has two lives. A plain sacct shows only the latest one. Add -D ( --duplicates ) to see every run: Job 55 appears twice: first run PREEMPTED , second run RUNNING . Without -D , a requeued job showed only its latest run in the test (checked on a similar job, where the plain line read CANCELLED and -D revealed the earlier PREEMPTED ). While the job is still alive, scontrol show job 55 grep Restarts gives the count ( Restarts=1 ). So "my job restarted from the beginning and I lost a day" is answered by -D : yes, it was evicted at that time by that QOS. That is a question for the preemption page, not for the filesystem. ---

secs.head: The fields worth knowing
secs.body: sacct --helpformat lists the columns. A few that earn their place: Column Tells you --- --- Submit , Eligible , Start , End , Elapsed The timeline: how long it waited, how long it ran Timelimit and Elapsed Whether it died of old age, and how close it came QOS , Partition , Account Under which policy and charge it ran NodeList Where it ran, which matters when a node turns out to be sick Reason Why a job that was not running was waiting Reservation Which reservation it used, if any SubmitLine , WorkDir , Comment What was typed, and from where ReqTRES , AllocTRES What was asked for, and what was given MaxRSS Peak memory of the steps. Empty unless the cluster gathers it ( JobAcctGatherType ); the cgroups page explains why those numbers are samples ( Restart is not a column. The test cluster refused it. Use -D and scontrol show job .) ---

secs.head: The neighbors on the shelf
secs.body: Tool For Remember --- --- --- scontrol show job <id Details of a job that is queued, running, or finished only moments ago Slurm forgets finished jobs from memory after a while. After that, only sacct remembers sacct The record of any job, after the fact Needs slurmdbd ; defaults to today sstat -j <id A running job's live usage Needs a usage-gathering plugin sreport Totals per account or user over time A summary, not one job seff <id A one-line efficiency summary A contributed script, not part of every install: it was not on the test cluster ---

secs.head: Four questions for the coroner
secs.body: When a job is missing, ask in this order: 1. Was it a person? CANCELLED by <uid . Not a bug, maybe a misunderstanding. 2. Was it the clock? TIMEOUT , and Elapsed at the Timelimit . Ask for more time or save checkpoints. 3. Was it the code? FAILED with a non-zero exit code, or a signal in the second number. Read the script's own output. 4. Was it the cluster? PREEMPTED , and also other states you will meet such as NODE FAIL and OUT OF MEMORY , which this page did not reproduce. Then it is not the job's fault, and the admin should look at the node or the QOS. ---

secs.head: Version notes
secs.body: Outputs are from 23.11.4. Later versions add the job's output, error and input paths to accounting (24.05), ReqReservation and step TimeLimit columns (25.05), and in 26.05 sluid and step submit line in --json and --yaml , with a 26.05.4 fix for corrupted earlier requeue records. The notes for the development 26.11 say the name, not the UID, of whoever cancelled a job is recorded, so the CANCELLED by 30033 form above may change. Version changes 23.11 to 26.05 has the list. ---

secs.head: Back to the vanished job
secs.body: Replay the student's email. The admin runs sacct -X -D -j <id -o JobID,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,Timelimit,NodeList -P , and reads one line: TIMEOUT , Elapsed equal to the Timelimit , on the third node of the rack. Nothing disappeared. The job was allowed twelve hours, used twelve hours, and was ended on time. The reply takes one minute: "your job hit its time limit; it needed longer, or it needed to save progress". No logs on three machines, no theory about the filesystem. The record had been in the database all along. Takeaway: sacct keeps the cause of death for every job, so read State and the two-part ExitCode (exit code : signal), add -D to see every life of a requeued job, and ask four questions: a person, the clock, the code, or the cluster. Next: the opposite problem, a job that has not started yet, is covered by Why Is My Job Still Pending?. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Slurm: sacct (job states, --duplicates , format fields) - Slurm: sstat - Slurm: sreport - Slurm: scontrol ( show job )

label: The job script tale
title: The Tale of a Slurm Job Script: Submission Is a Commitment, Not a Promise
desc: Part of the schedulers directory. The story below is the original tale. The sections after it check its claims against t

secs.head: The Tale of a Slurm Job Script: Submission Is a Commitment, Not a Promise
secs.body: Part of the schedulers directory. The story below is the original tale. The sections after it check its claims against the Slurm man pages, SchedMD support tickets and the slurm-users list, and add what the story leaves out. The commands were not run on a live cluster for this page, so try them with a short test job first. The sources date from 2019 to 2023, and the accounting flags in the last sections need Slurm 21.08 or newer.

secs.head: The tale
secs.body: You fixed the bug in job.sh at 18:02. Job 2 was still pending, so you assumed it would pick up the fix. At 03:00 it started, ran the old script, and burned the night on the bug you'd already fixed. Here's why. When you run sbatch job.sh , Slurm doesn't keep a live link to your file. Instead, at the moment of submission, it reads the script, copies its contents into the job record (spooled internally, typically under StateSaveLocation ), and hands it a JobID. From that instant on, the job is frozen in time — it carries its own private copy of the script. So here's what's happening in your case: - Job 1 (running) — using the snapshot taken when you submitted it. Editing job.sh now does nothing to it. It's already off living its own life. - Job 2 (pending) — same story. Even though it hasn't started yet, Slurm already took its snapshot at submission time, not at start time. It's sitting in the queue holding onto the old version of the script, waiting for resources — not waiting to "check" the file again. When does your edit matter? Only for the next sbatch job.sh you run. Any submission after your edit will pick up the new snapshot. That's it. [!NOTE] The core of the tale checks out. The sections below make the picture more exact in four places: where the copy lives, what "frozen" covers, which options exist besides cancelling, and what the versioning advice can and cannot do.

secs.head: Where the snapshot actually lives
secs.body: "Typically under StateSaveLocation " is right, and it can be made precise. Three sources agree: - The layout. A SchedMD commit message describes a hash. subdirectory based on the last digit of the job ID, added so file systems with limited files per directory can cope with many jobs. A support ticket then shows the path in full, <StateSaveLocation /hash.6/job.25596/script , and a log from another ticket shows the same pattern with hash.4/job.33767454/script . - There are two files, not one. Tools that archive jobs read both script and environment from that job directory, and the ticket about a controller that would not start mentions the script file and the environment file both being empty. - The controller does the keeping, not your file system. A slurm-users reply explains the flow: sbatch submits the script over the network to slurmctld , which stores it in StateSaveLocation and sends it to slurmd at dispatch time. The node then stores it under its own SlurmdSpoolDir . So the controller host never needs to see your home directory. Two consequences worth knowing: - A damaged state directory can be fatal for a job. In a SchedMD ticket, a zero-length script file made slurmctld log that it could not find the batch script and stop with "Check file system serving StateSaveLocation as that directory may be missing or corrupted". That is why the upgrade page backs this directory up before anything else. - Arrays share one copy. A SchedMD talk on cluster field notes points out that array jobs cost far less than many individual jobs, because only one job script and environment file is kept for the whole array. On the node side, the spool directory page explains why a full disk there drains the node: slurmd cannot write the script it is about to run.

secs.head: Frozen in time? Only the script and its environment
secs.body: "Frozen in time" is accurate for the script text. It is too strong for everything the script touches. Slurm freezes a small set of things and leaves the rest of your world alive: What Frozen at submit? Notes --- --- --- The script text Yes The script file above Your SBATCH options Yes Resolved into the job record Your environment variables Yes The environment file. This includes loaded modules, because they live in variables Your working directory Yes The job starts where you ran sbatch , unless --chdir says otherwise train.py , helper scripts, configs, data No Read at run time, from whatever is on disk then The sbatch man page is explicit about the last row: other than the batch script itself, Slurm does no movement of user files. A cluster guide from VSC spells out the environment row: by default sbatch copies the environment it sees, so every module loaded when you submitted is loaded in the job. Now go back to your two jobs, and suppose job.sh contains python train.py : You edit Job 1 (running) Job 2 (pending) --- --- --- job.sh Unchanged Unchanged train.py , before the job reaches it Sees the new code Sees the new code Your shell's loaded modules Unchanged Unchanged That is the trap behind "the old script with the new code". A pending job that holds the old --lr 1.0 and runs a freshly fixed train.py is a combination nobody tested. Even a running job can pick up a change, if the script later runs source config.sh or the Python process imports a module it has not loaded yet.

secs.head: How sbatch reads the script
secs.body: Three rules from the man page explain surprises at submission time: - Directives stop at the first command. After the first non-comment, non-whitespace line, sbatch processes no more SBATCH lines. A directive below a command is ignored as an ordinary comment. - Directives are literal text. They are read by Slurm, not the shell, so SBATCH --output=$HOME/out.txt does not expand $HOME . Filename patterns such as %j are Slurm's own and do work. - Precedence. The man page says SBATCH environment variables override options in the script, and command-line options override those variables. A leftover SBATCH PARTITION in a .bashrc can quietly outvote the script. If a job came out with the wrong limit or partition, check scontrol show job <id first, then env grep ^SBATCH .

secs.head: Peeking at the frozen copy
secs.body: You can ask Slurm for the exact script it holds: From a SchedMD ticket: the file defaults to slurm-<job id .sh , - writes to stdout, and only an admin, an operator or the job's owner can retrieve it. It works while the controller still holds the job. A finished job's record is purged after MinJobAge seconds, which the sbatch man page mentions when it explains dependencies on finished jobs. Admins have a second route, the same ticket notes: copy <StateSaveLocation /hash.N/job.<id /script directly.

secs.head: Changing your mind without starting over
secs.body: Cancel and resubmit is the only way to change the script . For some other changes, though, it is not the only option, and it costs you your place in the queue (the job's age restarts, which is my inference from how the age factor works rather than a documented statement). You want to change While pending? How --- --- --- Time limit, partition, QOS, account, dependency, name Often scontrol update JobId=<id ... . The sbatch man page notes, for instance, that the account can be changed after submission. Which fields a regular user may change is site policy Pause a job without losing it Yes scontrol hold <id , then scontrol release <id The script text No Cancel, edit, resubmit The captured environment No Resubmit from the right environment Two related cases: - Requeue. A requeued job returns to pending and runs again. Since the controller holds the script, I would expect the original text to run even if you have edited the file since, but I found no source that says so. Test it with a short job. The preemption page covers writing scripts that survive requeue. - Dependent jobs. If job2 was submitted with --dependency=afterok:<job1 , it carries its own snapshot taken when it was submitted. Fixing job.sh and resubmitting job 1 does not update job 2.

secs.head: Best practice
secs.body: If you want to change what's running or queued: Cancel and resubmit: scancel then sbatch job.sh — cleanest option. Version your scripts: job v1.sh , job v2.sh , or better, tag by commit hash / date, so squeue output and your script history stay traceable to what actually ran. Never edit-in-place while jobs are pending if you're debugging — you'll convince yourself the fix "should" apply and burn time confused when it doesn't. Slurm treats submission as a commitment, not a promise to check back later.

secs.head: Making runs traceable
secs.body: The versioning advice is right, with one catch: squeue shows the job name , not the script file. A file called job v2.sh does not show up anywhere unless you carry the version into something Slurm records. Where Shows the version? --- --- squeue , sacct job name Yes, if you pass it: sbatch --job-name=train-a1b2c3d job.sh --comment Yes, but sacct only keeps it if AccountingStoreFlags includes job comment (the configuration tool lists job comment among the flags) scontrol show job → Command= Only the path of the script, not its content. After an edit, it points at a file that no longer matches what ran, which is the complaint in a 2021 slurm-users thread A pattern that pins both the script and the code to a commit: And a self-documenting habit, adapted from the same slurm-users thread, which describes capturing the original script with each run. Put this at the top of the script body so every run keeps its own record (the filenames are my own):

secs.head: The afterlife of a script
secs.body: After the job ends and the controller purges its record, can you still get the script back? - By default, no. A 2021 slurm-users reply says the accounting database stores neither the job's Command nor the script. - Since 21.08, optionally yes. The release notes add AccountingStoreFlags=job script to store the batch script and job env to store the environment variables. With the flags on: The man page says -B prints NONE when the job had no script. SchedMD's SC21 slides show the idea with a wrapped sleep job whose generated !/bin/sh script comes back through sacct --batch-script . Two cautions that are my own, not from the docs. [!WARNING] Don't switch on job env cluster-wide first. Scripts and environments can hold secrets, so think about who can read the accounting database before enabling job env . And storing them grows the database, which makes dumps and schema conversions slower. Safe path: enable job script alone first, check database size after a week of normal load, then decide on job env . Rollback is removing the flag from AccountingStoreFlags and reconfiguring. Rows already stored probably stay in the database (my inference, untested).

secs.head: Cheat sheet
secs.body: Takeaway: Submission freezes the letter and its envelope (script, options, environment). Everything the letter points to is still out in the world. Next: slurmstepd: The Small Daemon That Actually Runs Your Job

label: slurmstepd
title: slurmstepd: The Small Daemon That Actually Runs Your Job
desc: Part of the schedulers directory. The intro draws slurmctld and slurmd and then waves at "the job". This page is about t

secs.head: slurmstepd: The Small Daemon That Actually Runs Your Job
secs.body: Part of the schedulers directory. The intro draws slurmctld and slurmd and then waves at "the job". This page is about the process that sits between slurmd and your code. Facts come from SchedMD's Job Launch Design Guide, support tickets, slurmd man pages and the Slurm source as I read it. Nothing was run on a live cluster for this page, and some details (such as socket handling) are from source files of different versions, so they are marked where it matters.

secs.head: The middle manager nobody draws
secs.body: Every architecture diagram of Slurm has the same three boxes: the controller, the compute-node daemon and the job. It is a clean picture, and it skips the part where the work happens. A better org chart looks like this: Role Process What it does --- --- --- Executive slurmctld Decides who gets what and when. Deliberately kept out of task launch to protect itself from load Receptionist slurmd Accepts requests, validates credentials, and forks a stepd for each step Middle manager slurmstepd Runs one step, start to finish, on one node Staff Your tasks The reason anyone showed up The Job Launch Design Guide says it in one dry sentence: each slurmstepd program executes a single job step. That sentence has consequences, and the rest of this page unpacks them.

secs.head: One stepd per step per node
secs.body: Per the guide, slurmd tests that the job was not cancelled since the credential was issued, then spawns a slurmstepd to manage the step. Every step type works this way: Step Runs where What it runs --- --- --- extern Every node of the job, if PrologFlags=contain is set Nothing of yours. It exists to hold processes started outside Slurm, like ssh sessions adopted by pam slurm adopt batch The first node of an sbatch job Your batch script interactive The node with your shell, for salloc with LaunchParameters=use interactive step The shell or command normal Every node of each srun inside the job, shown in sacct as jobid.stepid The command given to srun A normal step has one stepd per node in that step, and each stepd can run several tasks. An invented but typical case: a two-node sbatch job that calls srun twice. On the first node you can expect an extern stepd, a batch stepd and one stepd for each of the two srun steps. On the second node you can expect the extern stepd and the two step stepds. That makes four stepds on the first node and three on the second, seven small processes for one job, none of them yours. That count matters when you hear a story about a node with a job count of 40 and a process list that looks like a small town.

secs.head: What it does before your code runs
secs.body: The guide lists the stepd's functions in order. Between the fork and your first instruction, it: 1. Performs MPI setup, using the appropriate plugin 2. Calls the switch plugin to do any network configuration 3. Creates a container for the step using a proctrack plugin 4. Changes user ID to that of the user 5. Configures I/O for the tasks, either with files or with a socket connection back to srun 6. Sets up environment variables, including many task-specific ones 7. Forks and execs the tasks And in between, it runs several SPANK plugin hooks at various points. Three observations that explain things people find odd: - The stepd is why your job runs as you. slurmd runs as root. The step changes to your UID in step 4, before any task starts. A root-owned slurmd never runs your code directly. - The stepd owns the container. Process tracking (and, with the cgroup plugins, the resource limits described on the cgroups page) is set up here, which is how "kill the job" later reaches every process. - Output does not travel through slurmd . The stepd sets up the I/O path itself, either writing to files or connecting back to srun .

secs.head: Why restarting slurmd does not kill jobs
secs.body: An old SchedMD ticket answers a question every new admin eventually asks: can I restart the daemons while jobs run? The reply is worth quoting in spirit. The controller keeps its state in the StateSaveLocation directory and the job information in the SlurmdSpoolDir , so as long as those directories exist, the information needed to restore state is there. And each job is administered by its stepd, which is forked from slurmd and responsible for monitoring the job and collecting its resource data. The stepd is unaffected by a slurmd restart , so restarting slurmd does not affect the job. The reply adds a caveat in the same breath: lose the stepd and you lose the job. It also says that in practice this almost never happens, because the stepd is small and stable. The ticket dates from 2014, so treat the folklore with some age in mind, but the design has not changed in shape. This is why the upgrade page can say that running jobs survive a slurmd upgrade, and why the same page warns that a job started before the upgrade keeps running with the old stepd.

secs.head: The socket in the spool directory
secs.body: How does a freshly restarted slurmd find a stepd it did not start? Through the filesystem. In the source I read, each stepd creates a Unix domain socket in SlurmdSpoolDir with a name built from the node name, job ID and step ID: Other tools use the same naming to talk to a running step. The stepd API describes scanning a directory for sockets whose names begin with the node name as the way to find running step daemons, and the request types on that socket include signalling tasks, asking for state and info, attaching, and listing PIDs in the container. The older source I read creates the socket world-accessible and enforces who may do what inside the request handler, which checks for root or SlurmUser on privileged requests. Two details from the source that matter in practice: - A stale socket is cleaned up with some patience. If a connection to a socket is refused (nothing is listening), the client treats it as stray, and in the version I read it removes the socket if it is at least ten minutes old. - A step cannot be created twice. If a socket with the same name already exists, the stepd logs that the socket already exists and fails to start the step. The practical rule that follows is a simple one, and the spool directory page builds on it: do not clean up SlurmdSpoolDir by hand while jobs are running. The directory is where slurmd and its stepds find each other. That rule is my inference from the design rather than a sentence in the docs, so check with ls and a test node before you improvise.

secs.head: Who actually kills the job
secs.body: A subtle point from the Job Launch Design Guide. When a job is cancelled or hits its limit, the termination sequence is described as work done by slurmd : 1. Send SIGCONT and SIGTERM to user tasks 2. Wait KillWait seconds if tasks remain 3. Send SIGKILL 4. Wait for all tasks to complete 5. Run the Epilog 6. Send an epilog complete RPC to slurmctld The stepd is the one holding the container that makes step 3 reach every process, and it is the one that reports when tasks exit. When step 4 never finishes, you get the drained node described in Kill Task Failed. One log line from a support ticket on that failure reads "STEPD TERMINATED ON <node ... DUE TO JOB NOT ENDING WITH SIGNALS", which is the stepd's side of the same story.

secs.head: The stepd has a memory footprint too
secs.body: The stepd is small, but on a busy node there are a lot of them, and some jobs make theirs grow. Slurm's documentation makes a few separate points: - Reserving memory for the daemons. MemSpecLimit reserves memory for system use. The slurm.conf description says that, with task/cgroup and ConstrainRAMSpace=yes , the compute node daemons ( slurmd plus slurmstepd ) are allocated that limit, and the OOM killer is disabled for the daemons' memory cgroup. - A version caveat. The cgroups guide says that under cgroup v1 the reserved resources are also used by slurmstepd , while under cgroup v2 slurmstepd is not constrained by resource specialization. Its example is an MPI job whose PMI setup makes slurmstepd use a lot of memory. If those two statements seem to disagree on your version, trust a test over my summary. - Pinning it in memory. slurmd -M locks slurmd into memory, and the man page suggests setting LaunchParameters=slurmstepd memlock in slurm.conf along with it. That helps on nodes that get marked DOWN during heavy swap activity. - Limits are inherited. The stepds, and so your tasks, run under the limits of the slurmd systemd service ( LimitNOFILE , LimitMEMLOCK , LimitSTACK , LimitCORE ), not the ones in /etc/security/limits.conf . Check them with cat /proc/$(pgrep -u 0 slurmd)/limits . A note from Niflheim's documentation adds a multiplication that is easy to forget: LimitNOFILE applies per job step, so a node running N jobs needs the kernel's fs.file-max to allow N times that value.

secs.head: The step manager: stepd with a promotion
secs.body: Newer Slurm releases changed who creates steps. Traditionally srun asks slurmctld for a step, and the controller does the work. SchedMD's SLUG 2024 slides describe a step manager (stepmgr) design that reduces RPC congestion and locking on the controller: one stepd of the job (the batch, extern or interactive one) is designated as the step manager, the job allocation tells clients which slurmd hosts it, and srun sends its step-create request there instead. The slides also say that scontrol show steps without a job ID lists the steps managed by the controller, including the extern, batch and interactive ones. I have only read the slides, not the release notes, so check your version's release notes for how it is enabled and which commands behave differently.

secs.head: Field guide: find it, count it, read it
secs.body: Find stepds on a node. Their process titles carry the step ID in brackets, such as [12345.batch] , [12345.extern] and [12345.0] : To see the independence for yourself on a test node, note a stepd's PID and parent PID, restart slurmd , and look again. The stepd keeps running with its PID unchanged. That is a test, not a documented guarantee, so try it before you rely on it. Count steps per job. See the job's processes. scontrol listpids <jobid on the node lists the PIDs Slurm tracks for the job. If your process is running on the node and missing from that list, it escaped containment. Look at the sockets. Read the logs. Step messages land in the node's slurmd log, prefixed with the step in brackets, as in [91099.batch] error: ... . SlurmdDebug=debug2 gives more detail on the node while you test. Typical lines from support tickets include "Abandoning IO 60 secs after job shutdown initiated" and "done with job".

secs.head: Cheat sheet
secs.body: The middle manager is small, quiet, and holds the keys. Most of what is strange about Slurm on a compute node becomes less strange once you ask which stepd it belongs to.

secs.body: - Slurm: Job Launch Design Guide - SchedMD ticket 689: advice for running in production (restarting daemons and stepds) - SchedMD ticket 11103: unkillable step log lines - SchedMD ticket 22425: STEPD TERMINATED ... DUE TO JOB NOT ENDING WITH SIGNALS - Slurm: slurmd man page (-M, slurmstepd memlock ) - Slurm: Control Group in Slurm - Slurm source: stepd api.c (socket naming and stale-socket cleanup) - SchedMD SLUG 2024: Step Management slides - Niflheim: Slurm configuration (slurmd systemd limits)

label: Slurm cgroups in practice
title: Slurm cgroups in Practice: What Gets Constrained, and Where the Numbers Lie
desc: Part of the schedulers directory. The intro says slurmd "enforces resource containment" with task/cgroup . This page ope

secs.head: Slurm cgroups in Practice: What Gets Constrained, and Where the Numbers Lie
secs.body: Part of the schedulers directory. The intro says slurmd "enforces resource containment" with task/cgroup . This page opens that sentence up: what exactly is fenced, what is not, and how to check which one you have. Commands and option names come from SchedMD's documentation for Slurm 26.05. They were not run on a live cluster for this page, so try them on a test node first.

secs.head: The eight-GPU job that could see eight GPUs
secs.body: Picture a node with eight GPUs. A user submits a job with --gres=gpu:2 . Slurm allocates two, sets CUDA VISIBLE DEVICES to match, and the training script behaves. Then someone runs nvidia-smi inside the job and sees all eight. A more curious user unsets CUDA VISIBLE DEVICES , and PyTorch happily opens a GPU that belongs to someone else's job. Nothing is misconfigured here, at least not by the usual definition. CUDA VISIBLE DEVICES is a request that the CUDA runtime politely honors. NVML tools such as nvidia-smi ignore it. What actually stops a process from touching a device file is the kernel, and the kernel only gets involved if Slurm asks it to. The setting that asks is ConstrainDevices , and its documented default is no . That is the whole theme of this page. Slurm's containment is a set of independent opt-in switches, and the shipped default for each one is off. A cluster can run task/cgroup for years and still leak GPUs, cores or memory, because the plugin being loaded and the constraint being applied are two different things.

secs.head: One switchboard, two files
secs.body: Two files cooperate. slurm.conf loads the plugins. cgroup.conf (same directory) decides what they enforce. Setting File What it does Default --- --- --- --- ProctrackType=proctrack/cgroup slurm.conf Tracks every process in a step, so a cancel reaches all of them n/a TaskPlugin=task/cgroup,task/affinity slurm.conf Loads the plugin that applies the Constrain switches below n/a PrologFlags=Contain slurm.conf Creates the "extern" step that pam slurm adopt needs off ConstrainCores cgroup.conf Limits a job to its allocated cores (cpuset) no ConstrainDevices cgroup.conf Limits access to GRES devices, meaning GPUs no ConstrainRAMSpace cgroup.conf Sets soft and hard RAM limits from the allocation no ConstrainSwapSpace cgroup.conf Limits swap on top of RAM no SignalChildrenProcesses cgroup.conf Sends signals to all children, not just the parent process of a step no Two small prerequisites trip people up: - Memory constraints do nothing unless slurm.conf selects a memory-aware consumable resource mode (a CR Memory value in SelectTypeParameters ). - SchedMD's example config pairs task/cgroup with task/affinity . The ConstrainCores entry notes that an old hwloc bug can make task/affinity necessary for cpuset binding to work properly. SchedMD's own example cgroup.conf turns on cores, devices, RAM and swap together. If your file is shorter than that, it is worth asking which of the four you decided to leave out and why. [!NOTE] The same example config says nodes should either set MemSpecLimit or declare RealMemory below the physical total, so the OS and daemons always have memory the jobs cannot take. Compare your node definitions with the output of slurmd -C .

secs.head: cgroup v1 or v2: check before you debug
secs.body: CgroupPlugin defaults to autodetect , so Slurm picks whichever the node has, and mixed v1/v2 fleets are supported. The v1 plugin is marked deprecated with no new features coming, so any cluster still on v1 has a migration waiting for it. A quick way to see which one a node runs: Differences that matter in practice: - Devices are enforced with eBPF on v2. The device controller of cgroup v2 is eBPF-based, which is why Slurm's v2 documentation tells you to read up on eBPF before debugging odd GPU-access behavior. - Job paths changed in 26.05. On v2 the job directories used to be named by job ID, as in /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/slurmstepd.scope/job 123/ . In 26.05 they are named with an opaque ID unless you set CgroupJobIdPaths=yes . If you run exporters or scripts that find a job's cgroup by number, this is the first thing to check after an upgrade. - Resource specialization behaves differently. With v1, the cores and memory you reserve for the system are also used by slurmstepd . With v2, slurmstepd is not constrained by that reservation. SchedMD's example is an MPI job whose PMI setup makes slurmstepd grow. - Debian and Ubuntu historically ship without the memory and swap controllers enabled. The cgroup.conf man page still lists cgroup enable=memory swapaccount=1 on the kernel command line for those systems, so check your distro before assuming ConstrainRAMSpace is doing anything. Moving a node from v1 to v2 is a boot-parameter change (the docs list systemd.unified cgroup hierarchy=1 systemd.legacy systemd cgroup controller=0 cgroup no v1=all ), but plan it like a maintenance task: it touches every job on the node.

secs.head: Memory: two killers, pick one
secs.body: Slurm has two separate mechanisms that can kill a job for using too much memory, and they behave very differently. ConstrainRAMSpace (cgroup) OverMemoryKill ( JobAcctGatherParams ) --- --- --- Who kills The kernel OOM killer Slurm, after polling usage What dies One or more processes in the step The whole step When As soon as the cgroup limit is hit At the next sample Step afterwards Marked OOM, but may keep running Killed or cancelled Per the man page, with cgroup enforcement the step is flagged as OOM but keeps running, and other processes in it may carry on. For a single-process job that is invisible. For a multi-rank job it can mean one rank dies while the rest sit waiting for it. Whether that shows up as a hang or a clean failure depends on your launcher, so check what your own stack does before the first big run. There is a middle option for exactly this problem. TaskPluginParam=OOMKillStep in slurm.conf makes Slurm kill the whole step, on all nodes, when an OOM event hits any task in it. It does not apply to the extern step, and a user can override it. It requires the task/cgroup plugin, cgroup v2 and a kernel newer than 4.19. I found it in the Niflheim site documentation, which cites SchedMD ticket 25478, so read the current slurm.conf page for the exact wording before enabling it. SchedMD's release notes and support replies treat the two mechanisms as incompatible: since 18.08 the default is to enforce memory with neither, and the advice is not to combine cgroup enforcement with OverMemoryKill . Pick one deliberately. Three details from the man page that save an afternoon: - Soft and hard limits. ConstrainRAMSpace sets the soft limit at the allocation and the hard limit at the allocation times AllowedRAMSpace (default 100%). Setting it above 100 can cause system-wide OOM events, because jobs may then take more than the node has. - AllowedSwapSpace=0 does not forbid swapping. It limits RAM plus swap to the RAM limit. How eagerly the kernel swaps is a separate knob, and MemorySwappiness applies only to v1. - There is a throughput cost. The docs warn that ConstrainRAMSpace can noticeably reduce per-node job throughput, so high-throughput sites have a real trade-off to weigh. When an OOM kill does happen, the kernel logs it. dmesg or the journal on the node will say so, and sacct should report the state as OUT OF MEMORY .

secs.head: Where the numbers lie
secs.body: After a job dies of memory, the natural next step is sacct -o JobID,State,ReqMem,MaxRSS . Sometimes MaxRSS is far below ReqMem , and the job still says OUT OF MEMORY . Believe the state, not the number. MaxRSS is a sample . The task-level gather plugin polls on a timer, and the default JobAcctGatherFrequency is 30 seconds. A process that allocates fast, spikes and dies between two polls leaves no trace in the accounting data. SchedMD staff say exactly this when users ask why a fast-growing task is under-reported. More ways the number can mislead: - The plugin decides what "RSS" means. jobacct gather/linux reads RSS from /proc , with UsePSS and NoShare options that change the calculation. Two clusters with different settings can report different MaxRSS for the same job. - jobacct gather/cgroup on v2 has no virtual memory. The sstat man page notes that combination reports 0 for the virtual-memory fields, because of what the kernel exposes. - Sampling can be switched off. With the task interval set to 0 (as in JobAcctGatherFrequency=task=0 ), data is collected only when the job ends. - Gathering costs something. SchedMD's large-cluster guidance calls jobacct gather/none the best choice for throughput and, if you need job accounting, says to tune the sampling interval. If you want a number you can trust, read it from the kernel while the job is alive. On cgroup v2 each job's cgroup has memory.events (look for oom kill ) and, on newer kernels, memory.peak . The cgroup is removed when the job ends, so this is a live-debugging tool, not a post-mortem one:

secs.head: systemd and the scope nobody sees
secs.body: On cgroup v2, Slurm cannot just build a directory tree and walk away, because systemd owns the hierarchy and will tidy up anything it did not create. Slurm's answer is a dedicated scope, slurmstepd.scope , delegated to Slurm. Step processes live there rather than under the slurmd service, so restarting slurmd does not take running jobs with it. A small slurmstepd infinity process sits in the scope to keep it alive. Knobs worth knowing: - CgroupSlice moves the scope out of the default system.slice . - SystemdTimeout is how long Slurm waits for the scope at slurmd start. It defaults to 1000 ms, which can be too short on a busy or virtualized node. - IgnoreSystemd exists for development. The docs call it dangerous on a systemd machine, because systemd may modify the cgroups under running jobs. - EnableControllers is for old kernels and old systemd (RHEL8 is the documented example) where not every controller is enabled down the tree. This is also where pam slurm adopt plugs in. The cgroup.conf example says sites should configure it so users cannot escape the cgroups through ssh , and the cgroup v2 guide has its own section on running it there.

secs.head: Verify it in ten minutes
secs.body: On a test node, with a test account: Read the results like this: Result Meaning --- --- nvidia-smi -L lists every GPU on the node ConstrainDevices is off, or the GPU device files are not known to Slurm nproc shows more cores than requested ConstrainCores is off, or affinity binding is not working The Python line prints survived Memory is not being constrained (check ConstrainRAMSpace , CR Memory and the memory controller) MaxRSS is tiny but the state says OOM Sampling missed the spike; the state is the truth [!TIP] Run test 2 before and after switching on ConstrainDevices . Seeing eight GPUs shrink to one is the clearest way to explain this page to a colleague.

secs.head: The mental model to keep
secs.body: Loading task/cgroup is not the same as constraining anything, and sacct is a sampled summary, not a flight recorder.
