secs.body: - Slurm: cgroup.conf man page - Slurm: Control Group in Slurm - Slurm: Control Group v2 plugin - slurm-users: accounting sampling and fast-growing tasks - slurm-users: memory enforcement mechanisms and OverMemoryKill - SchedMD ticket 10538: how MaxRSS is calculated per plugin - sstat man page: jobacct gather/cgroup on v2 and virtual memory

label: GPU affinity and the socket lie
title: Your GPU Has Core Affinity. Slurm Has Socket Affinity. They Are Not Speaking.
desc: Part of the schedulers directory , and the missing neighbor of the mixed-GPU series: that series is about which GPUs a j

secs.head: Your GPU Has Core Affinity. Slurm Has Socket Affinity. They Are Not Speaking.
secs.body: Part of the schedulers directory , and the missing neighbor of the mixed-GPU series: that series is about which GPUs a job gets, this page is about where they sit. Everything below comes from SchedMD's GRES documentation for Slurm 26.05 and the gres.conf man page. None of it was run on a live cluster for this page.

secs.head: The comforting misconception
secs.body: An admin writes this in gres.conf : It reads like a promise: GPU 0 gets cores 0 to 15, GPU 1 gets cores 16 to 31, and Slurm will keep jobs on matching pairs. It is a lovely picture of NUMA-aware scheduling. SchedMD's GRES documentation has a polite name for what happens next. It calls it a common misconception .

secs.head: What the docs actually say
secs.body: The GRES guide puts it plainly: Slurm handles GRES affinity on a socket basis internally. The Cores field in gres.conf creates the impression that core-level affinity is respected during scheduling, "which it does not and never has". The gres.conf man page says the same thing from the other side: Slurm can track resources at the CPU or thread level, but the scheduling algorithms that co-allocate GRES with CPUs operate at socket level. The practical trouble shows up with job steps . Jobs are placed by socket, steps look at cores, and the two views can disagree. To stop admins from writing affinity that Slurm cannot honor, Slurm now checks that any Cores value lines up with socket boundaries, and it complains if it does not: That message turns up on modern CPUs with many cache domains. The GPU driver reports an affinity based on the real hardware topology, Slurm believes the node has two big sockets, and the two descriptions do not nest. What --gres-flags changes, per the man page: Flag on the job Effect --- --- (none) The cores listed for a GPU are preferred , not required --gres-flags=enforce-binding Only the listed cores may be allocated with that GPU. Better performance, possibly longer queue time --gres-flags=disable-binding Any core may be used. Faster scheduling, possibly worse application performance. Needed if a job wants more CPUs than are bound to a GPU So the setting is real, but it operates inside Slurm's socket-shaped view of the node, not on the physical layout you drew on the whiteboard.

secs.head: Making Slurm's sockets match the hardware
secs.body: The documented fix is to change what Slurm believes a "socket" is, so that it matches the GPU affinity boundaries. Two topology parameters do this: l3cache as socket and numa node as socket . Test first, change second: If one of the options lines the socket count and cores per socket up with the GPU affinity you see in nvidia-smi topo -m , make it permanent. Per node is the recommended form when only some nodes need it: Then let AutoDetect=nvml in gres.conf pick up the affinity. The socket count may now differ from the number of physical sockets on the board. That is expected and not a bug. The manual alternative is to turn AutoDetect off for that node and write Cores= yourself, still aligned to socket boundaries or it gets rejected: [!WARNING] Cores in gres.conf uses Slurm's logical core index, not the physical one. A mismatch between the two is a quiet way to build a topology that validates and is still wrong.

secs.head: One GPU, four names
secs.body: The GRES guide spends a surprising number of lines on numbering, and for good reason. The same physical GPU can be known by four different numbers. Where How it is numbered --- --- nvidia-smi (NVML) By PCI bus ID, lowest to highest CUDA Not necessarily the same, unless CUDA DEVICE ORDER=PCI BUS ID is set /dev/nvidiaN By Linux minor number. The mapping to NVML numbers is, in the docs' words, nondeterministic and system dependent, and can change between boots after hardware or OS changes Inside a job with device cgroups Renumbered from 0, whatever the physical device was That last row has a consequence that trips up site scripts. If a job is allocated /dev/nvidia1 and devices are constrained by cgroup (see the cgroups page), the job sees CUDA VISIBLE DEVICES=0 . The Prolog and Epilog, which run outside any cgroup, see CUDA VISIBLE DEVICES=1 . An epilog that cleans up "the GPU the job used" by reading its own environment has to translate between the two. Two housekeeping rules from the docs: list File= entries in increasing numeric order, and do an after-boot check that each device file still belongs to the GPU you think it does. The docs describe the assignment as "fairly stable", which is a phrase worth remembering at 3 a.m.

secs.head: AutoDetect: nvml, nvidia, and what each can see
secs.body: Setting Needs the NVML library? Detects MIG and NVLink? --- --- --- AutoDetect=nvml Yes Yes AutoDetect=nvidia (added in 24.11) No No Other values exist for AMD ( rsmi ), Intel ( oneapi ) and nrt . With AutoDetect on, you still need the Gres= line in slurm.conf so slurmctld knows how many to expect. And counts are enforced: a node that finds fewer resources than configured is drained, and a node whose detected GPUs are not all covered by the config is drained too. Type matching has a charming quirk. It must equal, or be a substring of, the name the hardware reports with spaces turned into underscores. So geforce rtx 2060 can be written as geforce , rtx , 2060 or the whole thing. Two commands show you what Slurm sees: If gres.conf specifies Type and File that match a real GPU, any Cores or Links you added become a sanity check against the detected values. A GPU that disagrees with its configuration is omitted from the node with an error. That is useful, because it turns a silent hardware change into a loud one.

secs.head: The library that will not let go
secs.body: Here is an interaction that few people see until it bites. With AutoDetect=nvml or rsmi , slurmstepd loads the management library and holds it open to account for GPU use in any step that asked for a GPU. slurmd does the same if AcctGatherEnergyType=acct gather energy/gpu is set. The docs state the consequence directly: while a process holds the library open, no other process can configure the GPU. That matters if your Prolog tries to change GPU settings (persistence mode, clocks and similar). The documented escape hatches: - Do not set AcctGatherEnergyType=acct gather energy/gpu if a Prolog needs to configure GPUs. - If jobs share GPUs on the node, you may also need JobAcctGatherParams=DisableGPUAcct . The library is also held when a job requests --gpu-freq . On the plus side, with AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu and AutoDetect=nvml , Slurm gathers gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil per step, and sacct shows them in the TRESUsageIn fields. For once the accounting has a view of GPU utilization , not just allocation. MIG devices are the exception, because NVML does not provide utilization metrics for them.

secs.head: Sharing a GPU: MIG, MPS, shards
secs.body: Three ways to put more than one job on a GPU, with very different guarantees. Mechanism What it gives you The catch, per the docs --- --- --- MIG Hardware-isolated GPU instances (up to seven on an A100), each treated as a GPU with cgroup isolation and task binding Partitions must already exist, because Slurm does not do dynamic MIG partitioning. No gpumem / gpuutil accounting for MIG MPS Several jobs sharing a GPU, each given a percentage A request must fit on one GPU. A job cannot request both gpu and mps . Only one user can have an active MPS server on a system, so different users are time-sliced , not truly concurrent Shards A generic way to let several jobs share a GPU Does not fence the processes on the GPU. Works best with homogeneous workloads A few notes that save debugging time: - A MIG Type must be a substring of the "MIG Profile" string in the slurmd log at debug2 level, for example nvidia a100 3g.20gb . - MPS needs a Prolog to start and stop the MPS servers. A sample ships in etc/prolog.example in the Slurm distribution. - Count for MPS is translated to a percentage, so it is normally a multiple of 100. - The same GPU can be allocated as gpu or as mps / shard , never both at once. - Shards and MPS both require the select/cons tres plugin.

secs.head: Steps want all your GPUs by default
secs.body: A job allocation is one thing and a job step is another. By default a step is given all the GRES the job requested, except those implicitly requested by an exclusive job. SchedMD's explanation is that granting less by default would force steps that need no GPU to say so explicitly. The consequence shows up when you launch parallel steps inside one allocation. The docs' own example is a batch script that starts several srun steps in the background, each asking for its own count: Leave the --gres off and each step claims everything. Also note the typing rule: a job requested as gpu:2 cannot start a step requesting gpu:tesla:2 , and the reverse holds too. Typed and untyped requests must be consistent within a job.

secs.head: A debugging routine for a bad GPU node
secs.body: Remember step 5 gives numbers from inside the job's own view, which may not match what an epilog or monitoring agent sees. Symptom First suspect --- --- doesn't match socket boundaries error at start Autodetected GPU affinity does not nest in Slurm's socket layout Node drained with fewer GRES than configured A GPU fell off the bus, or Gres= in slurm.conf says more than the node has Prolog cannot change GPU settings A process (often slurmstepd or slurmd ) holds the management library open Two parallel srun steps fight over the same GPUs Steps default to all the job's GRES Scripts disagree about which GPU is "1" Four numbering schemes; check CUDA DEVICE ORDER and cgroup renumbering

secs.body: - Slurm: Generic Resource (GRES) Scheduling - Slurm: gres.conf man page - Slurm: Prolog and Epilog Guide - NVIDIA: MIG User Guide - NVIDIA: MPS documentation

secs.head: Dying Politely: Preemption, Requeue and Signals
secs.body: A high-priority job arrives and a running job has to make room. Whether it dies cleanly, loses a day of training, or restarts by itself depends on settings most clusters never test. This series goes from the theory to a working setup to a signal reference. Read parts 1 to 3 in order. Part 4 is the reference you come back to. ---

secs.head: Contents
secs.body: File Description --- --- 1. Dying Politely Preemption modes, GraceTime , signals your training job ignores, and a requeue-safe wrapper 2. The Guest List Setting up QOS preemption with requeue, step by step, with a drill that proves it works 3. job submit.lua Routing jobs to the right QOS, requiring time limits, and how the plugin fails 4. Who Gets Told What Every signal Slurm sends, whether the batch shell or the srun steps hear it, and how late it arrives ---

secs.head: Related pages
secs.body: - Multi-tenancy: who stores the rules: QOS, associations and fairshare, the prerequisite for part 2. - Autopsy of a job: sacct : reading how a preempted or requeued job ended. - Inside a Slurm job: the daemon and cgroups that deliver the signals. - What changed between Slurm 23.11 and 26.05: version differences for preemption, Lua and signals.

label: Preemption, requeue and signals
title: Dying Politely: Preemption, Requeue and the Signals Your Training Job Ignores
desc: Part of the schedulers directory. Preemption behavior comes from SchedMD's Preemption guide for Slurm 26.05. Signal deta

secs.head: Dying Politely: Preemption, Requeue and the Signals Your Training Job Ignores
secs.body: Part of the schedulers directory. Preemption behavior comes from SchedMD's Preemption guide for Slurm 26.05. Signal details come from site documentation and the sbatch options as described there. Where a paragraph says Tested , the behavior was measured on a two-node test cluster running Slurm 23.11.4, so it can differ from the 26.05 guide and from your version. The wrapper script is still a sketch and was not run as a whole, so test it with a short job before trusting a week-long run to it. The signals cheat sheet holds the measured timelines.

secs.head: The week-long run that wasn't
secs.body: A researcher submits a training job to a low-priority partition on Friday. It runs happily until Sunday, when someone from a better-funded group submits a job that needs those nodes. Slurm requeues the researcher's job. The training script, which saves a checkpoint every six hours, restarts from the beginning of the script. The latest checkpoint is five hours old, and the script never looks for it. Nobody did anything wrong in the dramatic sense. Everybody just assumed that "requeue" meant "resume". It means "start the script again". What happens next is up to your script.

secs.head: Four ways to be evicted
secs.body: PreemptMode decides what happens to a job that gets pushed off its resources. The Preemption guide lists the modes: Mode What happens to the victim Fine print --- --- --- CANCEL Cancelled Simple and final REQUEUE Requeued, or cancelled if it cannot be The job needs --requeue , or the cluster-wide JobRequeue=1 . Without either, it is cancelled SUSPEND Paused in memory, resumed later by the gang scheduler Always needs the GANG option. Memory stays occupied OFF Nothing, preemption is disabled The default PreemptType decides who may preempt whom: preempt/partition prio compares partition PriorityTier values, and preempt/qos uses rules stored in the accounting database. PreemptMode can then be set per partition or per QOS, so one cluster can requeue one queue and suspend another. Tested: a victim with JobRequeue=0 and no --requeue ended as PREEMPTED and vanished from the queue; the same eviction with the job requeueable left a second run waiting. Two more details from the same tests: PreemptType=preempt/none is the off switch, but it must be paired with PreemptMode=OFF , because preempt/none with PreemptMode=REQUEUE is refused and the controller will not start. And PreemptMode accepted a WITHIN modifier (shown as WITHIN,REQUEUE ), though what it does was not tested. The commands to set all of this up are in the QOS preemption setup page. [!WARNING] Suspend and GPUs make an awkward couple. The GRES guide says that when a job is suspended, its generic resources do not become available to other jobs . A suspended job keeps its GPUs allocated, so suspending is a poor way to free GPUs for a preemptor. Requeue or cancel is the way to actually release them.

secs.head: GraceTime: the polite notice (and its twist)
secs.body: GraceTime (per partition or QOS) gives a victim some time to react. Defaults and semantics, per the guide: - The default is 0 , meaning no delay. - When a job is selected for preemption, its end time becomes now plus GraceTime , or stays as it was if that is already sooner. A job whose time limit would expire first gets only what is left of it. - The job is immediately sent SIGCONT and SIGTERM . - When the new end time arrives, it gets the sequence again: SIGCONT , SIGTERM , then SIGKILL . Read that again: the job receives SIGTERM twice . Once when preemption starts, and once when the grace period ends. A handler that checkpoints and then exits will be fine. A handler that does something irreversible on every SIGTERM will do it twice, so make yours idempotent. [!WARNING] Tested: "the job" here means the job's srun steps. With GraceTime=30 , a step started with srun got SIGTERM and SIGCONT about a second after the preemptor was submitted. The batch shell heard nothing at that moment, and was told only when the grace period ended. A command in your script that is not behind srun is a child of the batch shell, so it misses the early warning too. Section A requeue-safe wrapper runs the trainer exactly that way, so read its note before relying on SIGTERM . A few more things worth knowing: - The end of the window is noticed late. On the test cluster a 30-second grace period was noticed at about 33, 41 and 55 seconds, and a 60-second one at 64 and 83. A job that ignores SIGTERM then gets KillWait (30 seconds there) before SIGKILL , and only after that does the preemptor start. Budget the checkpoint accordingly. - A job that exits early still counts as preempted. If the job leaves before GraceTime runs out, Slurm handles it according to PreemptMode , regardless of why it exited. It cannot tell a clean checkpoint exit from an unrelated crash that happened to land in the window. - GraceTime is not used with SUSPEND . There is a separate suspend grace time for that.

secs.head: --signal: the other notice
secs.body: GraceTime is set by the admin and only matters when a job is preempted. --signal is set by the user and fires when the job is within N seconds of its end time . Because preemption moves the end time to "now plus GraceTime ", you might expect it to fire at preemption too, if GraceTime is shorter than the lead time you asked for. One university guide describes it that way. Tested: it does not, unless the admin asks for it. With GraceTime=60 and --signal=B:USR1@300 , the batch shell received no USR1 at preemption and heard only the final SIGTERM . With PreemptParameters=send user signal set in slurm.conf , the same job received USR1 about a second after the preemptor was submitted. That parameter is what turns --signal into a real preemption warning, and it is an admin setting. Format: Part Meaning --- --- B: Send only to the batch shell (the script itself). Without it, the signal goes to the job steps instead, not to the batch script USR1 The signal. A user-defined one is a good choice, because srun passes it through @300 Send it 300 seconds before the limit. With no number, the default is 60 The important footnote: because of how Slurm handles events, the signal can arrive up to 60 seconds earlier than requested. Treat the lead time as a minimum, not an appointment. Tested: on a 2-minute job, --signal=B:USR1@90 arrived at 68 seconds, 52 seconds before the end instead of 90, and the time limit itself was enforced about 26 seconds late. The controller works on a periodic tick, so the lead time is approximate in both directions, and the safe plan is a checkpoint that fits the smaller window. How this fits with the other clock, KillWait : on a cancel or a time limit, the sequence is SIGTERM , then a KillWait pause (30 seconds on the sites I read), then SIGKILL . If your checkpoint takes longer than that, --signal is how you buy more time. Site documentation puts it well: a checkpoint plus final sync has to fit inside whichever window you actually have.

secs.head: Why your trap never fires
secs.body: Here is the bug that eats weekends. You write: and the trap does not run until train.py finishes. That is how bash works: a trap handler runs after the current foreground command completes. If the foreground command is the thing that runs for hours, the signal sits waiting while SIGKILL approaches. The cure is to run the long command in the background and wait for it. wait is interruptible by trapped signals, so the handler can run at once. This is also the structure that university cluster guides use in their checkpoint wrappers. The trainer must cooperate too. A signal handler in Python should set a flag, not write a 20 GB checkpoint from inside the handler. The training loop checks the flag at a safe step boundary, saves, and exits.

secs.head: A requeue-safe wrapper
secs.body: A sketch that combines everything above. It asks the trainer to checkpoint on USR1 , waits for it, then requeues the job itself. What each piece is for: Piece Why --- --- --requeue Without it, a REQUEUE preemption becomes a cancel --open-mode=append Slurm's default is truncate , so a requeued run erases the log of the earlier run & plus wait Lets the trap run immediately SLURM RESTART COUNT Slurm sets it whenever a job restarts, and it is unset on the first run. Use it to cap restarts and to tell a fresh start from a resume --resume-latest The part that makes a requeue a resume. Slurm will not do this for you [!NOTE] The wrapper handles USR1 . A preemption with GraceTime delivers SIGTERM to the job instead, and you may want a second trap for it that calls the same function. Remember the double SIGTERM described earlier. [!WARNING] Tested: this wrapper does not receive the early SIGTERM . It starts the trainer with python train.py & , which is a child of the batch shell and not a step, and the early GraceTime signal went only to srun steps. Two ways to close the gap: start the trainer with srun python train.py & so it hears the early SIGTERM itself, or have the admin set PreemptParameters=send user signal so the USR1 from --signal reaches the batch shell at preemption. In both cases the final SIGTERM at the end of the grace period still arrives, so keep the trap for it. The signals cheat sheet lays out the choice.

secs.head: Requeue without the infinite loop
secs.body: Self-requeueing scripts have an old failure mode: a job that crashes in ten seconds requeues itself, crashes again, and keeps going until an administrator notices. Site documentation recommends two guards, which the wrapper above only partly implements: - Cap the restarts with SLURM RESTART COUNT , as shown. - Require a minimum runtime before a requeue is allowed. If the job has been alive for less than, say, a minute, it died of something that a restart will not fix, so do not requeue. SLURM JOB START TIME is available for the second check. Also note that a requeued job goes back to pending and may show a short begin-time hold before it starts again; one site's guide describes that as Slurm avoiding thrash.

secs.head: Preemption fine print
secs.body: For the administrators, a handful of details from the guide that are easy to miss: - Backfill reserves whole nodes. If a job preempts during a backfill pass, the whole nodes of the preempted jobs are reserved for the preemptor, even when it asked for less. One preemptor can therefore evict more than it needed to. - PreemptExemptTime sets a minimum runtime before a job may be preempted, honored for REQUEUE and CANCEL . - Exclusivity blocks preemption. --exclusive=user and --exclusive=mcs stop a job from preempting or being preempted by other users' jobs. The guide suggests using a job-submit plugin to disable those options if you rely on preemption. Tested: a Lua submit script can do exactly that, by turning --exclusive=user ( job desc.shared == 2 ) into plain --exclusive . Plain --exclusive did not block preemption in the tests. - Heterogeneous jobs are preempted only if all components are eligible, and one component's mode ( SUSPEND beats REQUEUE beats CANCEL ) sets the mode for all. - Licenses are not freed by suspend. Reclaiming them needs REQUEUE or CANCEL plus PreemptParameters=reclaim licenses . - Plugin changes need a restart. Changing PriorityTier or OverSubscribe only needs scontrol reconfig ; changing preemption plugin settings needs a full restart of the daemons.

secs.head: Setting it up
secs.body: Everything above assumes preemption is switched on, and it is off by default. The short version for QOS-based requeue (the full walkthrough, with a drill that proves it works, is on its own page): Preempt= goes on the preemptor and PreemptMode , GraceTime and PreemptExemptTime go on the victim. Changing PreemptType needs a slurmctld restart. If you want jobs to land in low or high <account without users typing the full name, a Lua submit script does the routing.

secs.head: Version notes
secs.body: The signal measurements on this page were taken on 23.11.4. Between 23.11 and 26.05 the changelogs record these preemption changes: - 24.05: a job signalled during GraceTime is assumed to have been preempted, for PreemptMode=CANCEL and REQUEUE . - 25.05: a new PRIORITY preemption option, and deleting a QOS removes it from other QOSes' preempt lists. - 26.05: PreemptExemptTime also applies to suspend,gang under preempt/partition prio . No changelog entry mentions the GraceTime signal targets or send user signal , so rerun the probe on your version. The full list is on Version changes 23.11 to 26.05.

secs.head: Cheat sheet
secs.body: Preemption is not a failure of the cluster. It is a contract, and the job's side of it is a script that can be killed at any moment and still make progress.

secs.head: Back to the week-long run
secs.body: Replay the Friday submission with this page open. The researcher's job runs under a preemptible QOS, and the admin has switched on send user signal . Her wrapper starts the trainer with srun , so it hears SIGTERM itself, and --signal=B:USR1@300 warns the batch shell as well. Both handlers do the same small thing: set a flag, save at the next step boundary, exit. On Sunday the better-funded group's job arrives. A second later the trainer is told to wrap up, and within a minute it has written a checkpoint and left. Slurm, seeing the job exit inside the grace period, treats it as preempted and puts it back in the queue (the changelog says that rule was added in 24.05 for CANCEL and REQUEUE , and a clean exit inside the window was not tested on 23.11). When a node frees up, the script runs again, finds the checkpoint, and carries on. The latest checkpoint is a minute old, not five hours. Nobody was dramatic. "Requeue" still meant "start the script again", but this time the script knew where it had stopped. Takeaway: requeue means "start the script again", so the job must catch its warning (steps hear GraceTime 's SIGTERM , the batch shell hears --signal=B: only with send user signal ), save at a safe boundary, and find its own checkpoint on restart. Next: The Guest List shows how to switch preemption on and prove it works with a drill.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Slurm: Preemption - Slurm: Generic Resource (GRES) Scheduling (suspended jobs keep their GRES) - Slurm: sbatch ( --signal , --requeue , --open-mode ) - CoreWeave SUNK: handling Slurm signals - CoreWeave SUNK: checkpoint and restart - LRZ: handling jobs running into TIMEOUT - University of Chicago DSI: batch jobs and the checkpoint contract

label: QOS preemption setup
title: The Guest List: Setting Up QOS Preemption Without Starting a War
desc: Part of the schedulers directory. The preemption page explains what preemption is . This page is the other half: the com

secs.head: The Guest List: Setting Up QOS Preemption Without Starting a War
secs.body: Part of the schedulers directory. The preemption page explains what preemption is . This page is the other half: the commands that switch it on. Everything here was run on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4, accounting on, both slurmd daemons on one Ubuntu 24.04 machine) and then adapted to read well. The names are invented. Your site's defaults, and your Slurm version, may differ, so run the drill in step 4 before you trust it.

secs.head: The Thursday before the deadline
secs.body: It is Thursday evening. The bio lab has a paper due Monday, and Priya needs eight GPUs for a final run. All the GPUs are busy. Most of them are held by a hyperparameter sweep that a student in another time zone started three days ago, and that, honestly, could stop and restart tomorrow without anyone noticing. The admin has three options. Message the student and wait for a reply that arrives Saturday. Cancel the sweep and lose the student's trust forever. Or have set things up beforehand, so the scheduler can ask the sweep to step aside, politely, and put it back in line afterwards. The third option takes four small steps. None of them is hard, but each has one sentence of fine print, and the fine print is the whole page. ---

secs.head: Three dials, one cluster
secs.body: Preemption by QOS is not one setting. It is three settings living in three places, and they have to agree: Dial Lives in Says --- --- --- Preemption on, and how slurm.conf "Use QOS rules; victims are requeued" The tiers themselves The accounting database ( sacctmgr ) " low exists; high bio may evict low " Who may use which tier Associations ( sacctmgr ) "Users in account bio may submit to high bio " A fourth, optional piece decides which tier a job lands in when the user doesn't say. That is either a default QOS on the association or the Lua submit script. Neither is preemption itself: they only put a label on the job. ---

secs.head: Step 1: switch preemption on
secs.body: Preemption is off by default ( PreemptMode=OFF ). In slurm.conf : PreemptType picks the rulebook. It takes one value, so QOS rules and partition-priority rules are alternatives, not layers. PreemptMode is the cluster-wide fate of a victim, and each QOS can override it. Check what the controller actually loaded: [!WARNING] Changing PreemptType needs a restart of slurmctld ; scontrol reconfigure is not enough. A restart does not touch running jobs, but submissions fail for a few seconds while the daemon is down, so pick a quiet moment. AccountingStorageEnforce needs qos in it, or Slurm does not hold users to the QOS they are allowed. That is the same switch described in the accounting page. ---

secs.head: Step 2: define the two tiers
secs.body: One victim tier, and one high tier per account that is allowed to evict: cluster in the PreemptMode column means "use the cluster-wide mode from slurm.conf ". Only low overrides it. The settings sit on opposite sides, and mixing them up is the commonest mistake: Setting Goes on Meaning --- --- --- Preempt=low the preemptor ( high bio ) "I may evict these QOSs" PreemptMode , GraceTime , PreemptExemptTime the victim ( low ) "this is what happens to me, and when" Priority helps order the queue, but under preempt/qos it is the Preempt= list that decides who may evict whom. A high- Priority QOS with no Preempt= evicts nobody. PreemptExemptTime is a minimum runtime before a job may be evicted. It is a good idea in production (nobody wants a job evicted a minute after it starts) and a trap in a drill, where it makes nothing happen for half an hour. Set it to 00:00:00 while testing. ---

secs.head: Step 3: let people use the tiers
secs.body: A QOS nobody may submit to is a very tidy decoration. Add both tiers to each account, with += so existing QOSs are kept: Now the question from the beginning: which tier does a job get when the user types nothing? Two answers, and both work: Way How Good for --- --- --- Default QOS on the association sacctmgr modify user alice set DefaultQOS=low Plain defaults, nothing to maintain Submit script job submit.lua Rewriting what the user typed, e.g. --qos=high into high <account In the test cluster, a job submitted with no --qos by a user whose DefaultQOS was low came out as low , with the submit script doing nothing. If "everyone types --qos=high bio themselves" is acceptable, you can stop here and skip Lua entirely. ---

secs.head: Partition priority instead?
secs.body: The same idea works with PreemptType=preempt/partition prio : a job in a partition with a higher PriorityTier may evict jobs in a lower-tier partition that share its nodes. Choose by how your cluster is already organized: Choose When --- --- preempt/qos Policy follows groups, projects or users; you want several tiers in one partition preempt/partition prio The cluster is already split into queues such as high and low , over the same nodes You cannot mix them. Pick one, and remember that changing it is a controller restart. ---

secs.head: Step 4: prove it with a drill
secs.body: Do this on a quiet node, as a normal user in a real account. Give low drill-sized settings first, PreemptExemptTime=00:00:00 and a short GraceTime , and put the real values back afterwards: Then two jobs on one node, --exclusive so they cannot share it: Read the output like a detective. Job 55 appears twice because -D shows every run of a requeued job: first run PREEMPTED , second run RUNNING again. Restarts=1 is the proof of a requeue, as opposed to a cancel. And the preemptor ran, which is the point. After the high job finishes, the victim starts again on its own. A script that does not look for its own checkpoint will start from the top, which is why the preemption page spends so long on resuming. [!NOTE] The drill's victim used sleep , which dies on the first SIGTERM , so the preemptor started as soon as the victim was told. A real training job that ignores SIGTERM gets KillWait (30 seconds here) on top of the grace time before SIGKILL . The signals cheat sheet has the measured timings. ---

secs.head: Five ways this goes quietly wrong
secs.body: Symptom Cause What to check --- --- --- The victim is gone , not requeued. sacct shows PREEMPTED and no second run It was not requeueable: JobRequeue=0 and no --requeue scontrol show job <id shows Requeue=0 . Set JobRequeue=1 , or make the submit script set it Nothing is ever evicted Preempt= is missing on the high QOS, or on the wrong side sacctmgr show qos format=Name,Preempt Nothing is evicted for the first half hour PreemptExemptTime is longer than the job has run The exempt time on the victim QOS Invalid qos specification on submit The user's association does not include that QOS sacctmgr show assoc user=<name format=Account,QOS%30 A high job still waits behind a low one The low job asked for --exclusive=user or --exclusive=mcs , which block cross-user preemption Plain --exclusive was fine in the test; see the preemption page Two more are worth a sentence each. Jobs that were already running or pending before you switched this on keep their old QOS and are not preemptible until they finish, and that is a feature. And PreemptMode=SUSPEND keeps a suspended job's GPUs allocated, so for GPU clusters requeue is the mode that actually frees anything. ---

secs.head: Rolling it out, and back
secs.body: The safe order is the order of the steps, because each one is invisible until the next: 1. Create the QOSs and grant them to accounts (steps 2 and 3). Nothing changes yet. 2. Set the slurm.conf lines (step 1). If PreemptType changed, restart slurmctld in a quiet moment. 3. Run the drill (step 4) on one node. 4. Only then tell users the low tier exists. To roll back, set both PreemptType=preempt/none and PreemptMode=OFF , and restart slurmctld . Together is the point: in the test, preempt/none with PreemptMode=REQUEUE was refused with "PreemptType and PreemptMode values incompatible", and the controller would not start. With both set, it started and a high-QOS job simply waited ( Resources ) instead of evicting anything. The QOSs can stay in the database. Unused QOSs cost nothing. ---

secs.head: Version notes
secs.body: The drill output on this page came from Slurm 23.11.4. Since then: 24.05 treats a job that was signalled during GraceTime as preempted for CANCEL and REQUEUE ; 25.05 adds a PRIORITY option and removes a deleted QOS from other QOSes' preempt lists; 26.05 applies PreemptExemptTime to suspend,gang under preempt/partition prio . Rerun the drill after any upgrade. Version changes 23.11 to 26.05 has the list. ---

secs.head: Back to the Thursday
secs.body: Replay the evening with this page applied. Priya submits with --qos=high , which becomes high bio on the way in. The scheduler looks at the nodes, finds the sweep running under low , sends it a polite signal and, once the grace time is up, puts it back in the queue. The sweep's own script, which saves a checkpoint every hour, picks up where it left off the moment a node is free. The student wakes up in the morning to a log with one extra line and a job that is still running. Nobody sent a message. Nobody cancelled anything. Priya's run finished on Friday afternoon. Takeaway: preemption by QOS is three settings that must agree ( slurm.conf , the QOS rules, and who may use them), Preempt= goes on the preemptor and GraceTime on the victim, and only a drill with Restarts=1 proves it works. Next: The Receptionist Who Rewrites Your Badge shows how a submit script routes jobs into these tiers automatically. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Slurm: Preemption - Slurm: Quality of Service (QOS) - Slurm: sacctmgr - Slurm: slurm.conf ( PreemptType , PreemptMode , JobRequeue , KillWait )

label: Job submit plugin (Lua)
title: The Receptionist Who Rewrites Your Badge: job submit.lua
desc: Part of the schedulers directory. Everything here was run on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4, accounting on, both

secs.head: The Receptionist Who Rewrites Your Badge: job submit.lua
secs.body: Part of the schedulers directory. Everything here was run on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4, accounting on, both slurmd daemons on one Ubuntu 24.04 machine), including the failures. Names and stories are invented. Field names and return codes can differ between Slurm versions, so print what your version gives you (the probe in What the script can see) before you build on it.

secs.head: The seven-day job nobody meant
secs.body: On Monday morning the admin opens the queue and finds forty pending jobs, each one claiming a time limit of seven days. Nobody asked for seven days. The partition's MaxTime is seven days, and a job that does not say --time quietly inherits it. To the scheduler, every one of those jobs is a boulder. The backfill page explains the consequence: backfill plans from time limits, so a queue full of week-long boulders leaves no gaps for the short jobs that could have run in minutes. The admin could send an email that says "please always set --time ". Nobody reads that email. What the cluster needs is a doorman who checks the badge on the way in. Slurm has one. It is called the job submit plugin, and the version most people end up using is written in Lua. ---

secs.head: What the plugin is
secs.body: The job submit/lua plugin runs a script of yours inside slurmctld , every time a job is submitted or modified . The script receives the job as a table, job desc , and may change it, accept it, or refuse it, all before the scheduler has seen the job. Two functions make a script. Slurm calls them by name: Function Called when Typical use --- --- --- slurm job submit(job desc, part list, submit uid) A job is submitted Defaults, routing, rejecting slurm job modify(job desc, job rec, part list, modify uid) A job is changed with scontrol update Applying the same rules, so nobody bypasses them This is the receptionist from the title. She sees every visitor, can write a different name on the badge, and can turn people away at the door. She does not decide who gets a seat (that is the scheduler), and she knows nothing about preemption. She only decides what the badge says. ---

secs.head: Turning it on
secs.body: Two things, in this order: 1. Put job submit.lua in the same directory as the slurm.conf the controller runs with. That is /etc/slurm on many sites and somewhere else on others. On the test cluster the controller was started with SLURM CONF=/opt/.../slurm.conf and the script sat next to that file, with no copy in /etc/slurm . It loaded. 2. Then add JobSubmitPlugins=lua to slurm.conf and run scontrol reconfigure . [!WARNING] The order matters. With JobSubmitPlugins=lua set and the file missing, slurmctld refuses to start: the log says it is unable to stat .../job submit.lua , and users see "Unable to contact slurm controller". Put the file there first, and check it with luac -p job submit.lua if you have luac . Confirm it loaded: ---

secs.head: What the script can see
secs.body: The job desc table holds what the user asked for. A field the user did not set is nil , or a "not set" number. To see what your version gives you, put a probe in the script and submit a few jobs: What the log showed for a plain sbatch --hold by a user whose default account is physics : Field Value seen What it means --- --- --- job desc.account nil The user did not pass -A . Not "the user has no account" job desc.default account physics The user's default account. nil for a user with no account at all job desc.qos nil No --qos typed job desc.time limit 4294967294 ( slurm.NO VAL ) No --time typed job desc.shared 65534 Unset. 0 for --exclusive , 1 for --oversubscribe , 2 for --exclusive=user So "which account will this be charged to" is two lookups, account first and default account as the fallback. Forgetting the fallback makes the script reject every user who relies on a default account. ---

secs.head: What the script can say back
secs.body: The return value decides the fate of the job: Return Effect --- --- slurm.SUCCESS Accept (with whatever edits the script made) slurm.ERROR Refuse with the generic "Unspecified error" slurm.ESLURM INVALID TIME LIMIT , slurm.ESLURM INVALID QOS , slurm.ESLURM INVALID ACCOUNT , slurm.ESLURM ACCESS DENIED , ... Refuse with the standard Slurm message for that error And two logging calls, which go to different places: Call Goes to --- --- slurm.log info(fmt, ...) slurmctld.log , with a lua: prefix. For the admin slurm.log user(text) The user's terminal, as sbatch: error: <text . For the human at the door Together, a refusal that explains itself looks like this: The first line is log user ; the second is the standard text for the error code the script returned. Without log user the user would get only the second line and write to you. ---

secs.head: Recipe 1: default the QOS and route "high"
secs.body: The most common job for the receptionist, and the reason this page exists next to the QOS preemption setup. A job with no QOS goes to low . A job that asks for plain high is renamed to the account's own tier, high <account . Users type one simple word. Behind it, every account has its own QOS, which means its own limits. I know of no plain-configuration way to map one typed name to a different QOS per account, which is why this is a script's job. [!NOTE] If you only need the default , no script is required: sacctmgr modify user alice set DefaultQOS=low made a job with no --qos come out as low in the test. Lua is for rewriting what the user typed. ---

secs.head: Recipe 2: demand a time limit
secs.body: The cure for the opening story. A missing --time shows up as slurm.NO VAL : The error text is the one shown earlier. If you would rather not be strict, the alternative is a DefaultTime on the partition, which is gentler but is also a guess about what each user meant. ---

secs.head: Recipe 3: make the victims requeueable
secs.body: A job evicted under PreemptMode=REQUEUE is only requeued if it is requeueable. With JobRequeue=0 on the cluster and no --requeue from the user, the test victim ended as PREEMPTED and was gone from the queue. When the script set job desc.requeue = 1 , scontrol show job showed Requeue=1 and the same eviction ended with a second run waiting in the queue: If your cluster has JobRequeue=1 (a common default), this recipe changes nothing and you can leave it out. ---

secs.head: Recipe 4: defuse user-exclusive jobs
secs.body: The preemption page notes that --exclusive=user and --exclusive=mcs stop a job from preempting or being preempted by other users' jobs, and suggests a submit plugin to disable them where you rely on preemption. In job desc.shared , --exclusive=user is 2 and plain --exclusive is 0 : Checking with scontrol show job : a held --exclusive=user job showed OverSubscribe=USER with a do-nothing script and OverSubscribe=NO with this rule. [!CAUTION] This silently changes what a user asked for. It is the right call only if your cluster depends on cross-user preemption, and the log user line should say so, or you will receive a very confused email. ---

secs.head: The whole script
secs.body: All four rules together, as run on the test cluster. Every branch was checked against a real controller: no --time is refused, no QOS becomes low , --qos=high becomes high physics (also through the default account), --exclusive=user becomes --exclusive , a user with no account asking for high gets the message, scontrol update QOS=high is routed the same way, and any other QOS passes through. ---

secs.head: Breaking it on purpose
secs.body: A script runs inside the controller, so a mistake in it is a mistake in the most important daemon you have. These are the failures the test cluster produced: What you do What happens --- --- Edit the script while slurmctld runs The next submission picks it up and logs job submit.lua loaded again. No reconfigure needed Save a script with a syntax error , controller running The log says error: job submit/lua: ... using previous script . The controller keeps running on the last good version Restart slurmctld with a broken script fatal: failed to initialize job submit plugin . The controller does not start, users see "Unable to contact slurm controller" scontrol reconfigure with a broken script slurm reconfigure error: Unspecified error and the same fatal line in the log. In the test the controller stayed up and kept accepting jobs, but I did not check which script it was running JobSubmitPlugins=lua and no file slurmctld refuses to start (see Turning it on) The pattern is that a running controller forgives a bad edit, and a starting controller does not. That gives the rules: - Edit in place, never restart the controller to "apply" a change. - Run luac -p before saving, and keep the previous version next to it. - Test with a throwaway account and a held job ( sbatch --hold ) before you announce anything. - One small footnote: an edit saved in the same second as the previous load was not picked up on my first try. A pause of a couple of seconds fixed it, which matters only if you test by script. ---

secs.head: Things the script is not
secs.body: - It is not free. It runs on every submission, in the controller. Keep it short, with no file reads, no network calls and no waiting. - It does not see jobs already in the queue. Existing jobs keep what they had until someone modifies them, and then slurm job modify applies. - It is not one call per job for heterogeneous jobs. Slurm's documentation notes that it runs separately for each component; see where hetjobs shine. - It does not do preemption. It labels jobs. The QOS setup decides what the labels mean. ---

secs.head: Version notes
secs.body: The script on this page was tested on Slurm 23.11.4. Later versions add: curr dependency (24.05.2); assoc qos and slurm.get qos priority() (24.11); a crash fix when reading assoc qos for an association that does not exist (25.05.3); and, in 26.05, a stack trace in the log on runtime errors plus core spec and thread spec in job desc . 26.05 also replaces ExclusiveUser and ExclusiveTopo in partition definitions with Exclusive=[NO NODE USER TOPO] , which is worth knowing for Recipe 4. None of these were tested here. Version changes 23.11 to 26.05 has the details. ---

secs.head: Back to the seven-day job
secs.body: Replay Monday. A researcher submits without --time . In under a second she gets a line in her terminal: Please set --time, jobs without one are not accepted . She adds --time=4:00:00 , submits again, and the job lands in the queue as a four-hour job, small enough for backfill to slot into a gap. By the following Monday there are no boulders. Nobody was shamed in an email. The doorman just checks the badge, and the badge now says how long you intend to stay. Takeaway: the Lua submit script is a receptionist inside slurmctld : it can read, rewrite or refuse every job at the door, a running controller forgives a broken edit but a restarting one does not, so put the file in place first and check its syntax before you save. Next: Who Gets Told What covers every signal Slurm sends to a job, and who actually receives it. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Slurm: Job Submit Plugins - Slurm: slurm.conf ( JobSubmitPlugins , JobRequeue , DefaultTime ) - Slurm: Quality of Service (QOS)

label: Signals cheat sheet
title: Who Gets Told What: Every Signal Slurm Sends, and Who Actually Hears It
desc: Part of the schedulers directory. The timings below were measured on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4, KillWait=30

secs.head: Who Gets Told What: Every Signal Slurm Sends, and Who Actually Hears It
secs.body: Part of the schedulers directory. The timings below were measured on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4, KillWait=30 , accounting on, both slurmd daemons on one Ubuntu 24.04 machine), with a probe script that logged every signal it received and ignored SIGTERM on purpose, so the kill deadline could be seen. Each number is one run, so read them as a shape and not as a specification. Another Slurm version may behave differently, and the preemption page quotes the newer 26.05 guide. Run the probe in Measure it yourself on your own cluster.

secs.head: The message that went to the wrong address
secs.body: Ana has done everything the preemption page asked. Her batch script traps SIGTERM , runs the trainer in the background, and waits. Her admin has set a two-minute GraceTime on the cluster. On Saturday night her job is preempted, and she reads the log on Sunday expecting a calm "caught signal, checkpoint saved". The log says nothing at all until the very last second, when everything dies at once. The checkpoint is a day old. The signal was sent. It simply went to a different address. A Slurm job has two kinds of listeners, and the early warning was addressed to the one Ana was not. ---

secs.head: Two kinds of listeners
secs.body: Listener What it is Example --- --- --- The batch shell The bash process running your sbatch script The wrapper with the trap The steps Anything launched with srun inside the job srun python train.py The difference is easy to miss, because a command in your script that is not behind srun is not a step at all. It is a child of the batch shell: Almost every signal in this page is addressed to one listener or the other. That is the whole mystery. ---

secs.head: Who sends what, and to whom
secs.body: Event Signal Batch shell srun steps --- --- --- --- Preemption begins, GraceTime 0 SIGCONT + SIGTERM No (measured) Yes, about 1 s later Preemption begins, GraceTime = 0 SIGCONT + SIGTERM Yes Yes End of grace, time limit, or scancel of the job SIGCONT + SIGTERM , then after KillWait , SIGKILL Yes Yes --signal=B:USR1@N near the time limit USR1 Yes No --signal=USR1@N (no B: ) near the time limit USR1 No Yes Preemption begins with PreemptParameters=send user signal and a --signal The --signal signal, at once Yes if B: Yes if no B: scancel -s USR1 <job USR1 No Yes scancel -s USR1 --batch <job USR1 Yes No Measured on the test cluster: the preemption rows, the kill sequence, --signal=B: (both near the time limit and with send user signal ) and the two scancel rows. Not measured: the --signal row without B: and the step half of the send user signal row, which follow the sbatch documentation, where a signal without B: goes to the job steps rather than the batch script. scancel --full is described in its man page as signalling the batch script and its children. In one test, a SIGCONT sent with it was reported only by the batch shell, so test it before relying on it. ---

secs.head: The timelines
secs.body: Each timeline starts when the preempting job is submitted ( t = 0 ). The victim's probe logged the signals, and ignored SIGTERM , so it had to be killed. GraceTime = 0. There is no grace period, but a job that ignores SIGTERM still gets KillWait before SIGKILL : GraceTime = 30, trainer under srun . The step is warned at the start, everybody is told at the end: GraceTime = 30, trainer in the batch shell only. No early warning exists for it: GraceTime = 60 with --signal=B:USR1@300 , without and with PreemptParameters=send user signal : Without send user signal , the USR1 never fired at preemption, even though the grace period (60 s) was shorter than the 300 s lead time asked for. The idea that --signal might fire at preemption anyway, because preemption moves the job's end time closer, did not hold in this version. ---

secs.head: Everything arrives late (and sometimes early)
secs.body: Slurm checks time limits and grace windows on a periodic tick in the controller, not on a stopwatch: What Asked for Observed --- --- --- End of a 30 s grace window 30 s noticed at 41 s and at 55 s (two runs); at about 33 s in an earlier run End of a 60 s grace window 60 s noticed at 64 s and at 83 s (two runs) --signal=B:USR1@90 on a 120 s job 90 s before the end arrived at 68 s: 52 s before the end The 120 s time limit itself 120 s TERM at 146 s; sacct showed TIMEOUT and Elapsed 00:02:26 SIGKILL after SIGTERM KillWait = 30 s the preemptor started 30 s after the second SIGTERM Two lessons. The lead time in --signal is a target, not a promise: the sbatch documentation says the signal can come up to 60 seconds early, and in this test it came about 38 seconds late. And the grace window is GraceTime plus a few to 25 extra seconds on this cluster, so size your checkpoint with room on both sides. A job that exits quickly on the first SIGTERM makes all of this moot: the preemptor starts as soon as the victim is gone. ---

secs.head: Which design to choose
secs.body: Where does the trainer run? Early warning you get What to do --- --- --- srun python train.py (a step) SIGTERM + SIGCONT about 1 s after preemption begins, if GraceTime 0 Let the trainer handle SIGTERM : set a flag, checkpoint at a safe boundary, exit python train.py & in the batch script None from GraceTime Set PreemptParameters=send user signal and SBATCH --signal=B:USR1@N , and trap USR1 in the script. Otherwise you hear only at the end of the window Anywhere Always the final SIGTERM Trap TERM too. It arrives more than once for steps, so make the handler idempotent Whichever you pick, do not write the checkpoint inside the signal handler. Set a flag, return, and let the training loop save at a step boundary. ---

secs.head: Measure it yourself
secs.body: Because versions differ, thirty minutes with a probe beats a week of guessing. A job script that logs every signal with a timestamp: Submit it as the victim ( --exclusive , requeueable, on a node you can spare), land a preemptor on the same node, and subtract the preemptor's submit time from each logged time. For the step case, put the same traps in a second script and start it with srun script.sh & followed by wait . Repeat with GraceTime at 0 and at 30, with and without --signal and send user signal . The same probe tells you what your version does. ---

secs.head: Cheat sheet
secs.body: Signals are letters with an address on them. Half of the debugging is checking whether the address was the shell or the step. ---

secs.head: Version notes
secs.body: Every timing above is from 23.11.4. The changelogs add: a default UnkillableStepTimeout of 60 s (24.05); SIGKILL through the cgroup.kill interface (25.05); and in 26.05 "KillWait will be honored when the task does not end with the TERM signal", srun --ignore-signals , and no delay in cancelling a job while slurmstepd is launching a task. The KillWait line concerns exactly the case measured here, so rerun the probe first. Version changes 23.11 to 26.05 has the list. ---

secs.head: Back to Ana's Saturday night
secs.body: With this page in hand, Ana changes one line: the wrapper starts the trainer with srun , so the trainer is a step and receives the early SIGTERM itself. Her admin also sets PreemptParameters=send user signal , and she adds --signal=B:USR1@120 , so the batch shell is warned too. Both handlers do the same thing: set a flag, checkpoint at the next step boundary, exit. Next Saturday the job is preempted again. This time the log has a calm line about a caught signal, a checkpoint that is two minutes old, and a requeue. The message had not been lost on the way to her; it had just been addressed to a step. Takeaway: a job has two listeners, the batch shell and the srun steps; the early GraceTime warning goes to the steps, the --signal=B: warning goes to the shell (and only at preemption with send user signal ), and every timing is a tick, so budget for lateness. Next: back to Dying Politely for the checkpoint-and-requeue wrapper that these signals feed. ---

secs.body: - Slurm: Preemption ( GraceTime , signals at preemption) - Slurm: sbatch ( --signal , B: ) - Slurm: scancel ( --signal , --batch , --full ) - Slurm: slurm.conf ( KillWait , PreemptParameters )
