label: Reservations and maintenance
title: Calling Dibs on Nodes: Reservations, Maintenance Windows and the Job That Fit
desc: Part of the schedulers directory. Every command and output here was run on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4, accou

secs.head: Calling Dibs on Nodes: Reservations, Maintenance Windows and the Job That Fit
secs.body: Part of the schedulers directory. Every command and output here was run on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4, accounting on, both slurmd daemons on one Ubuntu 24.04 machine). The names, dates and the story are invented. Reservation flags have many options, so this page covers the maintenance and "hold it for me" cases and points to the man page for the rest.

secs.head: Firmware Saturday
secs.body: The vendor has released a firmware update for the compute nodes, and the admin has booked Saturday at six in the morning for it. On Wednesday, the admin has a problem: the nodes are full of jobs that were never told about Saturday, and some of them have a time limit of three days. There are the usual three answers. Drain the nodes now, and the cluster sits half empty for days, which makes everyone who wanted those nodes loudly unhappy. Send an email, which will be read by exactly the people who did not need it. Or kill whatever is running at five fifty-nine on Saturday and take the angry messages on Monday. There is a fourth answer, and it makes the cluster tidy itself. Tell the scheduler on Wednesday that the nodes are already taken from Saturday six o'clock. From that moment the scheduler plans around the window, and only starts jobs that will be finished before it opens. ---

secs.head: Three ways to clear a node
secs.body: Way What it does The catch --- --- --- Drain the nodes ( scontrol update State=DRAIN ) No new jobs, now. Running ones finish The nodes sit idle from the moment the last job ends, however long before the maintenance that is Reserve the nodes ahead of time Jobs that fit before the window start as normal. Longer ones wait Needs honest time limits. Jobs without --time never fit Reboot on demand ( scontrol reboot ASAP ) Drains, reboots and returns each node for you Fine for a reboot; the reboot order page covers when it is not enough A reservation is the only one of the three that uses the idle time before the window. The scheduler knows when the window opens, so it keeps filling the nodes with jobs that will end in time. This is the same trick backfill plays with a reserved start for a big job: the short jobs slip into the gap. ---

secs.head: Creating the reservation
secs.body: On the test cluster, a one-hour maintenance window on node2 that opens in ten minutes: Field Meaning --- --- StartTime When the window opens. A timestamp, or now+10minutes Duration Length of the window in minutes ( 60 came back as 01:00:00 ) Nodes Which nodes. NodeCnt= or PartitionName= are alternatives Users , Accounts Who may use the reserved nodes during the window. A maintenance window usually lists only root, or the admins Flags=MAINT Marks it as maintenance. It shows up in scontrol show reservation and in the node's state while the window is open Flags=IGNORE JOBS Create the reservation even though jobs are running on the nodes right now. It does not kill them Look at what you made: State=INACTIVE means the window has not opened yet. The reservation is a promise, and the scheduler already plans around it. ---

secs.head: The job that fits, and the job that does not
secs.body: Two jobs asked for node2 while the window was ten minutes away. One wanted five minutes; the other wanted thirty: The five-minute job started at once, because it would be finished long before the window opens. The thirty-minute job waits, because it would still be running when the window opened. Neither was refused. The scheduler just did the arithmetic. That arithmetic uses the time limit , not how long the job really takes. A job with no --time inherits the partition's MaxTime , which is usually days, and it can never fit a window. This is the reason the Lua submit script insists on --time , and why the backfill page keeps asking whether the limits are honest. [!NOTE] The reason text does not say "maintenance". The pending reason in the test was ReqNodeNotAvail, May be reserved for other job , both before the window opened and while it was open. It is the same generic message you see for any reservation. When a user asks why their job waits, look at the reservation, not the reason: sinfo -T and scontrol show reservation give the real answer. The pending reasons page covers the codes. ---

secs.head: When the window opens
secs.body: At the start time the reservation becomes ACTIVE , and the node's own state shows it: If jobs were still running on the node when the window opened, the state reads MIXED+MAINTENANCE+RESERVED instead. The test confirmed that a running job is not killed when the window opens . It kept running on node2 and the reservation simply blocked every new job. A new one-minute job submitted during the window waited with the same ReqNodeNotAvail reason. That detail matters for planning. The reservation protects the window from new work. It does nothing about work that overlaps the start, so the quality of your maintenance window depends on the time limits of the jobs that were already running when you booked it. Check them ( squeue -w node2 -o "%i %u %L" ) and decide, for each, whether it will end in time or needs a conversation. When the work is done, release the nodes. Either let the reservation expire at its end time, or delete it early: The nodes went back to idle straight away. The order for a real maintenance (reserve, wait, reboot, resume, delete) fits with the reboot order page. ---

secs.head: Reservations for people, not just for maintenance
secs.body: The same command holds nodes for a person, which is useful for a demo, a class, or a deadline run. On the test cluster, a reservation for one user on node1 , starting now: The user then asks for it explicitly: Both jobs below were submitted by the reservation's user, and the difference was just --reservation : The node was held for the demo even against its own user, until the job said which reservation it was using. Other users are kept off it too, since that is what the Users list is for (a second user was not tested). ---

secs.head: Things that go wrong
secs.body: Symptom Cause Check --- --- --- The window opens and the node is still full Jobs that were already running overlap it. IGNORE JOBS lets you create the reservation, not kill them squeue -w <node -o "%i %u %L" before the window Nothing ever starts on the reserved nodes, even for the right user The job did not name the reservation --reservation=<name , and the user must be in Users or Accounts The short jobs do not slip in before the window They have no --time , so they inherit the partition MaxTime A required --time , from the submit script A user cannot tell why their job waits The reason text does not mention the reservation sinfo -T The reservation is gone after a controller problem Reservations are saved in the controller's state directory Back up StateSaveLocation , as the spool directory page notes ---

secs.head: Version notes
secs.body: Tested on 23.11.4. Later versions add the USER DELETE flag (24.05), FORCE START for recurring reservations and a ReqReservation field in sacct (25.05), AllowQOS and AllowPartition access controls (25.11), and in 26.05 "Do not allocate maintenance nodes to new reservations". Version changes 23.11 to 26.05 has the list. ---

secs.head: Back to Firmware Saturday
secs.body: Replay Wednesday with the reservation. The admin creates maint for Saturday at six, then looks at what is running on the nodes and finds two jobs with limits that run into the weekend. Two short emails go to two people instead of an announcement to everyone. From Wednesday to Saturday the scheduler does the rest. Short jobs keep arriving and keep running, because they fit before the window. Long jobs wait in the queue instead of arriving at six o'clock on Saturday morning and being killed. At five fifty-nine the nodes are nearly empty, with no drain and no idle days beforehand. Takeaway: a reservation tells the scheduler about the window in advance, so jobs that fit run first and jobs that do not wait, it blocks only new work, so check the running jobs' time limits before it opens, and when a user asks why their job waits, look at sinfo -T , not at the reason text. Next: Autopsy of a Job shows how to read what happened to a job after it has gone. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Slurm: Advanced Resource Reservation Guide - Slurm: scontrol ( create reservation , update , delete , reboot ) - Slurm: sinfo ( -T )

label: Rebooting a Slurm Cluster
title: Rebooting a Slurm Cluster Without Losing Your Job (Or Anyone Else's)
desc: Part of the schedulers/ series. Sourced and expanded from a classic r/HPC thread that every cluster admin eventually red

secs.head: Rebooting a Slurm Cluster Without Losing Your Job (Or Anyone Else's)
secs.body: Part of the schedulers/ series. Sourced and expanded from a classic r/HPC thread that every cluster admin eventually rediscovers the hard way. The full-outage sequence is for when the control plane needs rebooting too; if only compute nodes do, Slurm can do it for you without an outage.

secs.head: The question every new admin eventually asks
secs.body: "What's the actual order for restarting the nodes? At what point do I drain the compute nodes? Should slurmdbd , slurmd , and slurmctld stay auto-enabled across a reboot? Do I just shutdown -r now a node, or stop the daemons first with scontrol shutdown ? And where does a maintenance reservation fit into all of this?" This is a rite of passage — everyone runs into it the first time they need to patch a Slurm cluster without a) losing queued jobs, b) corrupting the accounting database, or c) getting paged at 2 AM because a node came back up in a weird state and started eating jobs it shouldn't have. Below is the order that actually works, assuming you are not upgrading Slurm itself — just patching/rebooting the underlying OS. ---

secs.head: Before you touch anything: five things to have ready
secs.body: Skipping this section is how a 2-hour maintenance window turns into a 14-hour incident. - [ ] Estimate the work and the time it'll take. Vague estimates turn into angry Slack threads from users mid-maintenance. - [ ] Prepare a small test job. A tiny xhpl instance is perfect — cheap to run, and immediately tells you if compute nodes are actually healthy post-reboot. - [ ] Create a hidden Slurm partition reserved for you (root only). You want somewhere to test job submission before opening the floodgates back to real users. - [ ] Have a node-health-check mechanism ready — NHC (Node Health Check) or equivalent, so bad nodes get flagged automatically instead of silently eating jobs. - [ ] Confirm you have root credentials and OOB/BMC/IPMI console access to every server. Losing thousands of core-hours because a node hung at GRUB and you couldn't remember how to reach its console is a genuinely common, genuinely avoidable failure mode. [!TIP] If you have a test/lab system, dry-run the entire upgrade path there before day D. There is no substitute for having already seen the failure once. ---

secs.head: Phase 0 — Scheduling
secs.body: 1. Estimate when currently running jobs will finish , and schedule your maintenance start time safely after that. Pick your weekday carefully: [!WARNING] Avoid Thursdays and Fridays. Users can't submit new jobs during the blackout, the system sits under-utilized over the weekend, and if something breaks Friday night, nobody's around to help you fix it. 2. Create a reservation with the MAINT flag , starting at your chosen time — with a safe overlap buffer built in, because maintenance windows always run long. 3. Wait for day D, time T. If you have a test/lab system, use the waiting period to dry-run the upgrade path there.

secs.head: Phase 1 — Locking down access
secs.body: 4. Place /etc/nologin on the front-end/login nodes to block non-root users from doing anything unexpected while you work. (Make sure your own root login still works before you do this.) 5. Confirm State=DOWN is set on partitions in slurm.conf — this is your safety net against a badly-restarted slurmd /node grabbing and executing jobs before you're ready.

secs.head: Phase 2 — Control plane first
secs.body: 6. Stop and disable slurmctld , then slurmdbd — controller before database daemon, in that order. 7. Take a consistent backup of the Slurm SQL database. This is your one clean window to do it — everything is quiesced, nothing is writing to it mid-backup. Future-you will be extremely grateful you didn't skip this step. 8. Stop and disable MariaDB/MySQL. 9. Reboot the Slurm and DB servers and perform whatever underlying OS maintenance you actually came here to do. 10. Bring services back up in order: DB → slurmdbd → slurmctld . Check the logs carefully — confirm services started cleanly and that partitions are genuinely showing DOWN (not silently back up and accepting work).

secs.head: Phase 3 — Front-end nodes
secs.body: 11. Reboot the front-end/login servers now that the control plane is confirmed healthy. Re-apply /etc/nologin here too — it gets wiped during the boot process, so it won't persist automatically. 12. Verify InfiniBand, filesystem mounts, and Slurm client connectivity on the front-ends. Kernel version changes are a classic way to break third-party kernel modules (IB drivers especially) — don't assume "it booted" means "it works." Once confirmed healthy, remove /etc/nologin and let users back onto the front-ends. Partitions are still DOWN , so they can queue jobs — nothing will actually execute yet.

secs.head: Phase 4 — Compute nodes
secs.body: 13. Reboot the compute nodes. If they're already empty (which they should be, per your Phase 0 scheduling), there's no real need to fuss with drain state first. 14. Clear the "unexpectedly rebooted" flag by setting node state to idle , and let your node health check mechanism (NHC or equivalent) do its job of flagging anything unhealthy.

secs.head: Phase 5 — Controlled reopening
secs.body: 15. Flip your hidden root-only partition to UP and submit your test job (that small xhpl instance from your prep checklist) there first. 16. If the test job runs clean — open the real partitions. State=UP , and you're done. ---

secs.head: The order, visualized
secs.body: ★ = the one irreversible step in the whole sequence — get your DB backup before touching MariaDB/MySQL, not after. ---

secs.head: Why this order and not another
secs.body: The sequence isn't arbitrary — it follows a simple dependency chain: Bring anything up out of order — say, compute nodes before the controller is confirmed healthy — and you risk exactly the failure mode this whole checklist exists to prevent: a node rejoining the pool in a bad state and silently swallowing jobs before you've verified anything. ---

secs.head: When only the compute nodes need a reboot
secs.body: Most reboots aren't whole-cluster events. A kernel or driver update on the compute nodes doesn't need the controller, the database or the login nodes to go anywhere. For that, Slurm has a rolling reboot built in: Piece What it does --- --- reboot Runs RebootProgram from slurm.conf on each node when it's idle. Nothing happens without RebootProgram set ASAP Drains each node right away, so no new jobs land there; running jobs finish normally first nextstate=RESUME Clears the drain and the reason once the node has rebooted and slurmd registered again. nextstate=DOWN leaves it down for you to check. With ASAP and no nextstate , newer man pages (26.11) say it defaults to UNDRAIN ; the 23.11 page doesn't say, so set it explicitly reason= What sinfo -R shows while it's out. Put the ticket there We ran it on two lab nodes (Slurm 23.11.4, RebootProgram=/usr/sbin/reboot ): cn001 was idle, cn002 had a 40-second job. cn001 went straight to reboot ( ^ = reboot issued). cn002 drained ( @ = reboot pending) and waited; its job finished COMPLETED 0:0 , and only then did the node reboot. No job was killed, and nobody ran a loop. The last step didn't complete in our lab, and the reason is worth knowing. Both containers did reboot, but stayed in reboot^ until we resumed them by hand. The controller only accepts a reboot once the node reports a boot time later than the reboot request ( waiting for node boot() in node mgr.c ), and containers report their host's boot time, so it never moves. On real hardware the boot time changes and the node returns on its own. The same check is what catches a node that didn't reboot: after ResumeTimeout it's marked DOWN instead of quietly resuming. When to use which: Situation Use --- --- Compute nodes only: kernel, driver, firmware scontrol reboot ASAP nextstate=RESUME , maybe a few racks at a time You need a canary and a health check before resume A rolling playbook, like Rolling maintenance in the Ansible series Controller, database or login nodes too The full sequence on this page nextstate=RESUME puts the node back as soon as slurmd registers, but not blindly: the man page says slurmd runs HealthCheckProgram once after the reboot, before it registers. If that's NHC, a node that comes back without its mounts or GPUs is drained instead of resumed. ---

secs.head: The honest caveat
secs.body: This exact sequence scales down cleanly to a handful of nodes and a weekend maintenance window. On genuinely large systems, expect the process to stretch, and expect pressure from whoever's paying the bills — every hour of downtime on a large cluster can cost thousands of euros , and that pressure is real regardless of how careful you're being. Two things help more than anything else at that scale: a longer prep list than you think you need, and enough colleagues in the loop that the to-do list isn't resting on one person's memory at 3 AM. Takeaway: for a whole-cluster outage, go database → slurmdbd → slurmctld → front-ends → compute with partitions held DOWN ; for compute-only reboots, let scontrol reboot ASAP nextstate=RESUME drain and return each node for you. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - scontrol(1): reboot: ASAP , nextstate , reason . - slurm.conf(5): RebootProgram, ResumeTimeout, ReturnToService. - sinfo(1): node state codes: @ reboot pending, ^ reboot issued. - Slurm reservations: the MAINT flag. - Slurm source, node mgr.c : waiting for node boot() , the boot-time check. - r/HPC: Slurm reboot order: the thread this page grew from.

label: Upgrading Slurm
title: Upgrading Slurm: The Order, the Window, and the Parts That Bite
desc: Part of the schedulers directory. The reboot-order page covers patching the OS underneath Slurm and says plainly that it

secs.head: Upgrading Slurm: The Order, the Window, and the Parts That Bite
secs.body: Part of the schedulers directory. The reboot-order page covers patching the OS underneath Slurm and says plainly that it assumes you are not upgrading Slurm itself. This is the other half. Everything here comes from SchedMD's Upgrade Guide and is not tested on a live cluster; read the guide for your exact target version before a real maintenance window. For what changed in the versions between 23.11 and 26.05, see Version changes.

secs.head: The upgrade that fails on startup
secs.body: Imagine a cluster that has run happily on Slurm 22.05 for years. Someone decides to jump straight to 25.05 over a long weekend, installs the new packages everywhere and starts the daemons. The daemons refuse. SchedMD's guide is blunt about this: upgrades from incompatible versions fail immediately on startup. It adds a harsher sentence for the careless case. The compatibility requirements apply to running jobs too, so going outside the window kills them and loses their accounting. That is the good outcome, the one where the software stops you. The rest of this page is about the ways to get hurt even inside the rules.

secs.head: The compatibility window
secs.body: Slurm releases twice a year now. The version number is the release month: 25.05 is May 2025 and 25.11 is November 2025. Releases moved to this six-month cycle with 24.05, and each one gets roughly 18 months of support. How far back an upgrade may reach has changed, and plenty of older write-ups still carry the old rule: - Up to 24.05: you could upgrade from the previous two major releases. - From 24.11 on: you can upgrade from the previous three , to keep a similar support duration with the faster cycle. The guide's table of compatible prior versions: Release Can be upgraded from --- --- 23.02 22.05, 21.08 23.11 23.02, 22.05 24.05 23.11, 23.02 24.11 24.05, 23.11, 23.02 25.05 24.11, 24.05, 23.11 25.11 25.05, 24.11, 24.05 The copy of the guide I read stops at 25.11. The rest of this repo cites the 26.05 docs, so check the live table for your target before planning. When your starting point is outside the window, you go in steps, and each step must land on a version compatible with where you are. A worked example using the table above, from 22.05 to 25.05: Two hops, with a real validation between them. SchedMD recommends exactly this: upgrade everything to the intermediate version, verify it works, then continue. Skipping the verification defeats the purpose, since each hop is only supported if it starts from a healthy cluster.

secs.head: The order, and why it is the order
secs.body: The rule underneath it: slurmdbd must be at the same or a higher major release than slurmctld , and close enough to be within the window. That forces the database daemon to go first. If you run a backup slurmdbd host, upgrade it at the same time as the primary. Everything below the database follows the same dependency logic as the reboot order: the thing others talk to goes first, the things that talk to it follow.

secs.head: Backups: three things, not one
secs.body: The reboot page backs up the SQL database, and that is the right instinct for a reboot. An upgrade needs more, because the daemons rewrite their own state files on first start. SchedMD's minimum: What How to find it Why --- --- --- StateSaveLocation scontrol show config \ grep StateSaveLocation Controller state: jobs, nodes, reservations The Slurm config directory Usually /etc/slurm/ Every .conf file, including gres.conf and cgroup.conf The accounting database mysqldump --databases slurm acct db backup.sql Associations, limits, QOS, job history A note on the dump. The guide prefers taking it after slurmdbd is shut down, when nothing is writing. You can use --single-transaction to dump a live database, but the guide lists the catches: it can slow the database, the restore only has the state from when the dump began, and the dump may be incorrect or fail if certain operations overlap, such as upgrading the database, adding or removing a cluster, or archiving and purging accounting data. [!TIP] If you are about to upgrade, purge accounting records you no longer need first. SchedMD notes that a large database means a longer dump and a long, unresponsive schema update, so trimming it before the window can shorten the outage noticeably.

secs.head: Stage 1: slurmdbd, the slow one
secs.body: slurmdbd is the stage most likely to turn a short window into a long one. On a big accounting database, the upgraded daemon can be unresponsive for tens of minutes while it converts the schema. The guide's procedure, condensed: 1. Stop slurmdbd gracefully ( sacctmgr shutdown or systemctl stop slurmdbd ) and wait until it is fully down . Stopping too early risks losing data that was not yet saved. 2. Back up the database. 3. Check that innodb buffer pool size in my.cnf is larger than the default (the accounting page in the Slurm docs has the recommendation). 4. Upgrade the packages on the slurmdbd host only . 5. Start it, and here is the part that surprises people: the first start after an upgrade should be run by hand as the Slurm user , not through systemd. The reason is a timeout. If you start the daemon with systemd and the conversion outlasts the unit's start timeout, systemd kills the daemon halfway through a database update, which can cause data loss. After the foreground run completes, exit and start it normally. 6. Start the backup slurmdbd if you have one. 7. Check that sacct and sacctmgr return data. What the rest of the cluster does meanwhile. Scheduling continues. slurmctld queues accounting messages in its DBD Agent queue. While slurmdbd is down, sacct , sacctmgr and any slurmrestd paths containing slurmdb fail. Watch slurmctld memory and the agent queue size in sdiag , because the guide says the queue must not exceed the configured MaxDBDMsgs , and a long outage puts accounting records at risk. This is the same cache-while-down behavior described in the multi-tenancy page, now with a deadline attached. [!NOTE] If you are also moving the accounting database to MariaDB 10.2.1 or later from an older MariaDB or from MySQL, the guide says to be on slurmdbd 22.05.7 or newer first, because those versions handle the changed MariaDB defaults.

secs.head: Stage 2: slurmctld, with the timeouts raised
secs.body: The controller goes down briefly. Job submissions are refused, queued jobs are not scheduled, and information about completing jobs waits. All of it resumes when the new controller starts. SchedMD prefers upgrading slurmctld , slurmd and the client commands together, because the effects of downtime on controller and node daemons are largely the same, so doing them together minimizes the total duration. Rolling upgrades are possible if the controller goes first. The step that people skip is the first one: 1. Raise SlurmdTimeout and SlurmctldTimeout , then run scontrol reconfig . Make the new values long enough to cover your whole upgrade method. If the timeout is reached while daemons are down, nodes may be marked DOWN and their jobs killed. 2. Stop slurmctld (all of them, if you run more than one). 3. Optionally stop slurmd on the compute nodes too. 4. Back up StateSaveLocation . 5. Upgrade the packages. 6. Start slurmd again if you stopped it, then start slurmctld . 7. Check node communication and that a job can start and finish. 8. Put the timeouts back and run scontrol reconfig again. Step 8 is the one that gets forgotten. A cluster left with a very long SlurmdTimeout will take far longer than intended to notice a node that has genuinely died.

secs.head: Stage 3: slurmd, and the old stepds
secs.body: Running jobs survive a slurmd upgrade as long as SlurmdTimeout is not reached. While a node's slurmd is down, new jobs do not start on it, and finishing jobs wait to report back until it returns. SchedMD recommends upgrading all nodes with the controller, but a rolling upgrade in groups is allowed, and the guidance is to keep the time spent running mixed versions short. The point most guides skip is easy to state: a job started before a node was upgraded keeps running with the old slurmstepd . The upgrade guide says to wait for all jobs that were already running to finish before you consider the upgrade complete, because starting another upgrade, or relying on a new feature, while old stepds are still alive may cause problems. On a cluster with multi-day training jobs, that means "upgraded" is a state that arrives gradually. The practical consequences: - Do not schedule the next hop of a multi-step upgrade until the old jobs have drained. - Do not announce a new feature to users the moment the daemons restart. - This is one more reason to use the MAINT reservation approach from the reboot page: an empty cluster has no old stepds.

secs.head: Stage 4: everything that links against Slurm
secs.body: Client commands and login nodes need no special handling except where the release notes say so. Upgrade them after the core daemons. JSON and YAML output. If you or your tools use --json or --yaml with Slurm commands, or run slurmrestd , the output format is produced by versioned data parser plugins, and the default is the newest one, which may not match the previous format. Old plugins are removed on a schedule (the guide lists each release and the one that drops it). Pin the version in anything that parses the output: slurmrestd clients show the plugin in the URL path, for example /slurm/v0.0.40/jobs , and that path keeps working until the plugin is removed. Regenerate and retest any generated OpenAPI clients before the upgrade. Locally built plugins and applications. libslurm.so gets a new version number with every major release, so anything linked against it must be recompiled, and locally written plugins usually need code changes as well. A quick check: MPI stacks are mostly spared, because OpenMPI and MVAPICH2 link against Slurm's PMI-1 and PMI-2 libraries, which are meant to stay fixed. The documented exception is MPICH built with Slurm support and the Hydra process manager, which uses the Slurm API and needs a rebuild.

secs.head: Packaging traps
secs.body: Three that have nothing to do with Slurm itself: - EPEL. A Slurm package exists in EPEL that SchedMD does not provide or support, and a routine system update can pull it in and change your version outside a maintenance window. The guide recommends adding exclude=slurm to the [epel] section of the repo file. - Daemons sharing a host. Slurm daemons on one machine may have to be upgraded together because of their dependencies on the common slurm package. Start them in the usual order afterwards. SchedMD says outright that this layout is not recommended for production and advises one core daemon per system. - Distribution packages. Some distro packaging couples slurmdbd and slurmctld so tightly that you cannot upgrade them one at a time the way the guide describes. If that is your situation, plan around it before the window opens, not during it. For sites that build their own Slurm, the guide describes "seamless upgrades": install each version into its own directory and point a symlink in PATH at the active one. That lets you stage the new version ahead of the window and switch back with one command, and it avoids library conflicts from mixing versions in one directory.

secs.head: There is no undo
secs.body: Reverting an upgrade is not supported once any Slurm daemon has been started. On first start the daemons rewrite their state files and databases into the new format. An older daemon will not recognize them, which can mean lost or corrupted state and accounting, and the old daemon will likely refuse to start. The only way back is restoring from backups: StateSaveLocation and the accounting database, plus the config directory. That brings back the old state and also erases everything that happened after the backup was taken, including jobs submitted and finished in between. Two softer notes from the guide: - Minor releases (the .4 in 23.11.4) follow the same procedure, but it is faster and more forgiving of mixed versions and in-place downgrades. Keep current backups anyway. - Pre-release versions (release candidates, the master branch) can crash, change behavior and lose state. Run them on test machines, not production.

secs.head: Pre-flight checklist
secs.body: - [ ] Read RELEASE NOTES for the target and every release in between; look for removed or changed options. - [ ] Prepare and test config changes on a test system first. - [ ] Confirm the hop is inside the compatibility window, or plan the intermediate step. - [ ] Check --json / --yaml users and slurmrestd clients; pin data parser versions. - [ ] Plan for recompiling libslurm -linked software and any custom plugins. - [ ] Purge old accounting records if the database is large. - [ ] Back up StateSaveLocation , the config directory and the database. - [ ] Verify innodb buffer pool size is above the default. - [ ] Raise SlurmdTimeout and SlurmctldTimeout and plan to restore them. - [ ] Tell users the expected downtime; avoid scheduling it outside vendor support hours. - [ ] Have a hidden test partition and a small test job ready, as in the reboot checklist. - [ ] Upgrade in order: slurmdbd (hand-started first run), slurmctld , slurmd , clients, plugins. - [ ] Do not call it finished until pre-upgrade jobs have drained.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Slurm: Upgrade Guide - Slurm: Accounting and Resource Limits (the innodb buffer pool size recommendation) - slurm-users: upgrading slurmdbd and daemon packaging, March 2025

label: Version changes 23.11 to 26.05
title: The Changelog Nobody Reads: What Moved Between Slurm 23.11 and 26.05
desc: Part of the schedulers directory. This page was assembled from SchedMD's changelogs and release notes, read through a we

secs.head: The Changelog Nobody Reads: What Moved Between Slurm 23.11 and 26.05
secs.body: Part of the schedulers directory. This page was assembled from SchedMD's changelogs and release notes, read through a web fetch and summarized, so it quotes short lines and names the version each one belongs to. Nothing here was run: the tested pages in this directory ran on Slurm 23.11.4, and the sources and coverage section says exactly what was and was not read. For a real upgrade, read the official notes for every version you cross.

secs.head: The config that survived three upgrades
secs.body: A site has a slurm.conf that was written in 2023. It has been copied to every new cluster since, with the care people give to a recipe from a grandmother: nobody remembers why each line is there, and nobody dares remove one. This autumn the admin plans to move from 23.11 to 26.05, because the old version stopped getting fixes, and checks the plan by reading the one page everybody reads: the install guide. Nobody reads the changelog. It is long, written by developers, and mostly about things that do not apply to you. The few lines that do apply are scattered across five releases: a default that changed, an option that was renamed, a path that now has a different name. Each is harmless to know in advance and annoying to discover on a Monday. This page is those lines, collected by topic. ---

secs.head: Sources and coverage
secs.body: Version What was read Limits --- --- --- 24.05 The changelog Read in full for the topics below 24.11 Release notes Not the full changelog 25.05 The changelog Read in full for the topics below 25.11 Release notes Not the changelog, so bug fixes are missing 26.05 The changelog Read in full for the topics below 26.11 Release notes from the development branch Not a stable release for the purposes of this page. Check whether it has been released before relying on it A topic with no entry for a version means nothing turned up in what was read, not that nothing changed. ---

secs.head: The security timeline
secs.body: Security fixes did not wait for 26.05. They arrived as point releases on the branches that were supported at the time: Fix Where it appears What it was --- --- --- CVE-2024-42511 24.05.2, with matching releases on 23.11 and 23.02 Access control around network and IMEX channel resources in the HPE Slingshot and NVIDIA IMEX switch plugins CVE-2024-48936 24.05.4 A stepmgr flaw that could let an attacker execute processes CVE-2025-43904 24.05.8, 24.11.5, 23.11.11, 25.05.0 A coordinator could add a user with elevated privileges Eight CVEs, including CVE-2026-65107 to 65109, 65138 to 65140, 65165 and 65168 26.05.4, 25.11.8, 25.05.9 sbcast credential checks, a slurmstepd stack overflow, OCI cleanup deleting files outside its directory, a malformed-RPC heap over-read, unsafe cluster names reaching accounting queries, and an operator editing Administrator accounts Two things follow. First, 23.11 did receive security releases, up to at least 23.11.11 for the privilege issue above. A cluster still on 23.11.4, like the test cluster behind these pages, is missing even those. Second, the 2026 batch was released for 26.05, 25.11 and 25.05. The announcement does not say whether 23.11 or 24.x are affected. It lists those three branches as fixed, so an older branch is not going to receive them, whether or not it is affected. Whichever version you run, take the latest point release of a supported branch. ---

secs.head: Preemption
secs.body: Version Change --- --- 24.05 "For PreemptMode=CANCEL and PreemptMode=REQUEUE assume that job signalled for GraceTime was preempted." A job that is signalled during GraceTime and then leaves is recorded as preempted 24.05.4 A fix for QOS preemptability being lost after clearing a preempt list with preempt='' 25.05 A new PRIORITY preemption option so that a preemptor can preempt only when its priority is higher than the victim's. Deleting a QOS now removes it from the other QOSes' preempt lists 25.05.1, 25.05.5 preempt/partition prio no longer lets a partition's PreemptMode default to PRIORITY . A fatal error when min exempt priority was not the last PreemptParameters option was fixed 26.05 PreemptExemptTime now also applies to PreemptMode=suspend,gang under preempt/partition prio . Partitions can be created or updated dynamically with PreemptMode=Priority . A segfault with QOS SUSPEND on an OverSubscribe=YES partition was fixed in 26.05.3 What this means for the preemption pages: the 24.05 line affects how a victim that exits cleanly during GraceTime shows up in sacct . On 23.11 that was not tested here. The GraceTime signal behavior itself (the early SIGTERM reaching steps and not the batch shell) was measured on 23.11.4 only, and none of the changelogs read mention it, so it needs a rerun on the version you use. ---

secs.head: job submit/lua
secs.body: Version Change --- --- 24.05.2 curr dependency is exposed in job submit.lua and jobcomp.lua 24.11 job desc gains assoc qos , and there is a slurm.get qos priority() function. burst buffer/lua loses slurm.job info to string() 25.05.3 A controller crash was fixed when a script read job desc.assoc qos for an association that does not exist 26.05 A Lua stack trace is logged on runtime errors in slurm job submit() and slurm job modify() . core spec and thread spec are exposed in job desc 26.05 In partition definitions Exclusive=[NO\ NODE\ USER\ TOPO] replaces ExclusiveUser and ExclusiveTopo The Lua page says a broken script is hard to debug. From 26.05 a runtime error leaves a stack trace in the log, which makes the failure-mode table there easier to use. That idea was not tested. ---

secs.head: Signals and killing jobs

After a task returns a non-zero code, SIGCONT , SIGTERM and SIGKILL go to the remaining tasks. Job cancellation is no longer delayed while slurmstepd is launching a task (26.05.2) The signals cheat sheet measured the KillWait and SIGKILL timing on 23.11.4 with a task that ignored SIGTERM . The 26.05 KillWait line is exactly about that case, so those timings are the first thing to rerun with the probe. The kill-task-failed page is also affected by the UnkillableStepTimeout default. ---

EnableExtraControllers is added to cgroup.conf 25.11 slurmd can be launched in a cgroup slice other than system.slice 26.05 cgroup v2 paths are built from the SLUID instead of the numeric job ID. 26.05.2 adds an option to use the job ID again, and the default stays SLUID The cgroups page already covers the 26.05 path change. secs.head: Back to the config that survived three upgrades
secs.body: Replay the plan with this page open. The admin reads the changelog entries for each hop, and ends up with a short list instead of a surprise. The cgroup v1 deprecation goes on the calendar. The UnkillableStepTimeout default is noted, because the old value would be changed under them. The tested pages' claims get a Friday afternoon rerun on a test controller, with the probe from the signals page, and the three that differ are written down. None of it is dramatic. The upgrade happens on a Saturday, the config line nobody remembered is still there and still harmless, and Monday is dull in the way upgrades should be. Takeaway: security fixes came as point releases on supported branches, so the goal is the latest point release of a supported version, not a particular major one, and the changes worth knowing are small and scattered (GraceTime and KillWait handling, Exclusive= , cgroup v1 deprecation, SLUID paths), so read each hop's notes before you cross it. Next: the upgrade order page covers which daemons to upgrade first on each hop. ---

label: Slurm SSH Access
title: The SSH Backdoor Every Slurm Cluster Has (Until You Close It)
desc: Part of the schedulers/ series. By the end you'll have SSH on compute nodes limited to users with a job there, their ses

secs.head: The SSH Backdoor Every Slurm Cluster Has (Until You Close It)
secs.body: Part of the schedulers/ series. By the end you'll have SSH on compute nodes limited to users with a job there, their sessions inside the job's limits, and your admins still able to log in. Tested with Slurm 23.11.4 and libpam-slurm-adopt on Ubuntu 24.04 nodes (cgroup v1), against the pam slurm adopt documentation for Slurm 26.11.

secs.head: The problem nobody notices until it bites
secs.body: Here's a scenario that plays out on unprotected clusters constantly: A user submits a job through sbatch . Slurm dutifully allocates a slice of a compute node, wraps it in a cgroup, and enforces the CPU/memory limits that job asked for. So far, so good — the scheduler is doing its job. Then the same user, out of habit or curiosity, does this: And... it just works. No job context, no cgroup, no resource accounting. That SSH session lands on the node completely outside Slurm's supervision. From there, a user (or a stray leftover process) can: - 🔓 Consume resources that aren't counted under any job's cgroup - 🔓 Escape the job's CPU/memory limits entirely - 🔓 Keep running long after the job that "owned" the node has ended None of this requires malicious intent — it's usually just someone debugging or checking on a running job the easy way. But the effect is the same: your scheduler's accounting is now a polite fiction.

secs.head: Enter pam slurm adopt
secs.body: This is a PAM (Pluggable Authentication Module) module that ships with Slurm, and its job is refreshingly narrow: Every login or process on a compute node must belong to a Slurm job — no exceptions. [!NOTE] Official reference: Slurm documentation — pam slurm adopt

secs.head: How it actually decides who gets in
secs.body: When a user tries to SSH into a compute node, here's the decision Slurm makes on their behalf: The practical upshot: - ✅ Only users with a currently running job on that specific node can log in. - ✅ Whatever they do once they're in — spawn processes, run a quick htop , debug something — stays inside the job's resource allocation. No more phantom, unaccounted-for work. ---

secs.head: Installing it
secs.body: Nothing exotic here — follow Slurm's own installation guide. It typically ships alongside your Slurm build/package, so if you're already building Slurm from source with the standard contribs enabled, you likely already have the module available. ---

secs.head: Configuring it — three places, three changes
secs.body: Per the official documentation, the module itself needs three configuration surfaces. Skip any one of them and it either won't function or won't have anything to "adopt" into. Steps 4 and 5 are the ones people skip: without them, it looks like it works.

secs.head: 1. Slurm side
secs.body: - [ ] Enable the task/cgroup plugin in slurm.conf . This is a hard prerequisite — pam slurm adopt has nothing to adopt sessions into without cgroup containment already active. Walk through the Slurm cgroups guide if you haven't set this up yet. - [ ] Set PrologFlags=contain in slurm.conf . This is the flag that actually creates the "extern" step — the container that SSH-launched processes get folded into. [!WARNING] Jobs launched without PrologFlags=contain don't get an extern step at all — which means pam slurm adopt has no valid target to adopt an SSH session into for those jobs, regardless of how correctly everything else is configured. [!TIP] UsePAM in slurm.conf is a completely different setting and has nothing to do with pam slurm adopt . Don't confuse the two while troubleshooting — chasing UsePAM when the real issue is PrologFlags is a common dead end.

secs.head: 2. SSH side
secs.body: - [ ] In /etc/ssh/sshd config , confirm: This is typically the default already — but confirm it explicitly rather than assuming, especially on hardened or custom-imaged nodes.

secs.head: 3. PAM side
secs.body: - [ ] In your /etc/pam.d config (typically the sshd service file), add: [!NOTE] You can use either required or sufficient as the PAM control flag, depending on how strict you want the enforcement stacked against other account rules already in that file. Also check that nothing earlier in the account stack short-circuits it. The docs call out account sufficient pam localuser.so in some distributions' included files: it succeeds for every local user before pam slurm adopt is ever asked.

secs.head: 4. Turn off pam systemd
secs.body: This is the trap that makes everything above look fine while doing nothing. We tested it on a node with only steps 1–3 done. Alice had a job on the node with a 500 MB memory limit, so her SSH login was allowed. Then we looked at where her shell landed: Systemd's user session, not the job. pam systemd , which runs later in the session phase on most distributions, moved the process into its own user.slice after pam slurm adopt had adopted it. Admitted, but unconfined. The docs say it plainly: pam systemd conflicts with pam slurm adopt and must be disabled in every file included by sshd ( common-session on Debian and Ubuntu, password-auth and system-auth on RHEL). On Ubuntu: Same login, same job, afterwards: Inside the job's extern step, under its 500 MB limit ( memory.limit in bytes read 524288000 ). The price: no systemd user session on compute nodes. /run/user/$UID isn't created and XDG RUNTIME DIR is unset (we saw unset in that same login). Software that needs a user D-Bus won't work there. The docs offer a partial workaround, a TaskProlog that points XDG RUNTIME DIR at a per-user directory in /dev/shm .

secs.head: 5. Keep the admins in, and fail closed
secs.body: pam slurm adopt lets root in always. Everyone else needs a job, and that includes your admins. With only the line from step 3, our Ansible account was locked out of the node the same way as a user with no job: That's every playbook in the Ansible series failing with UNREACHABLE! on that node. The docs' fix is to stack pam access in front of it, for an admin group: and in /etc/pam.d/sshd , replacing the line from step 3: pam access as sufficient lets the admin group straight through; for everyone else it fails, and the decision falls to pam slurm adopt . The two action ... failure=deny options matter just as much. By default, if adoption itself fails, or the module hits an error, the login is allowed : the default is chosen so you don't lock yourself out while testing. In production that means a plugin problem quietly lets users in unconfined. The docs recommend setting both to deny once it works. (We didn't simulate a module failure in the lab; this is from the documentation.) [!CAUTION] Test from a second session that's already open as root before you log out. A PAM mistake on sshd locks out everyone but root, and only if root SSH login is allowed. ---

secs.head: Proving it on a node
secs.body: With all five steps on one node, we ran the whole matrix: Who Situation Result --- --- --- admin (in hpcadmins ) No job Logged in alice Job running on the node Logged in, inside job 2/step extern alice Same job, just cancelled Denied bob Never had a job Denied Ansible ( admin ) ansible cn001 -m ping SUCCESS Roll it out like any risky change: one node first, this matrix, then the rest, with a root session open the whole time. ---

secs.head: The mental model to keep
secs.body: One module, PrologFlags=contain , pam systemd out of the way, and a door for admins: the gap between "what Slurm thinks is running" and "what's actually running" closes. Skip the pam systemd step and you get the worst of both: users believe they're contained, and they aren't. Takeaway: pam slurm adopt only confines SSH sessions if pam systemd is off and adoption failures are set to deny; check where a real login lands with /proc/self/cgroup before you trust it. ---

secs.body: - pam slurm adopt: installation, PrologFlags=contain , the pam systemd conflict and XDG workaround, pam access stacking for admins, and the action options. - slurm.conf: PrologFlags: Contain and the extern step. - Slurm cgroups guide: task/cgroup and proctrack/cgroup . - pam access(8) and access.conf(5): the admin group rule. - pam systemd(8): what it does to a login session.

label: Kill task failed
title: Kill Task Failed: A Murder Mystery With No Body (and One Drained Node)
desc: Part of the schedulers directory. Option names and the kill sequence come from the Slurm documentation and from support

secs.head: Kill Task Failed: A Murder Mystery With No Body (and One Drained Node)
secs.body: Part of the schedulers directory. Option names and the kill sequence come from the Slurm documentation and from support tickets and mailing-list threads where SchedMD staff and site admins describe the behavior. Nothing here was run on a live cluster for this page. Scenarios are invented for illustration.

secs.head: The call comes in at 3 a.m.
secs.body: You run sinfo -R and find a node that has been quietly drained overnight: The job is gone. The queue moved on. slurmctld has nothing to say, because from its point of view nothing went wrong in the controller. The node has simply declared that it can no longer be trusted, and Slurm took it at its word. Where did the job go? That is the mystery. The honest answer is that it may not have gone anywhere. One of its processes might still be on that node, alive, deaf and dangerous.

secs.head: How a job is supposed to die
secs.body: Cancelling a job, hitting a time limit, or being preempted all end in the same sequence. SchedMD staff describe it in a support ticket, and the pieces line up like this: Two timers, two different questions: Timer Question it answers Seen in practice --- --- --- KillWait How long do we wait between the polite request and SIGKILL ? 30 seconds on the clusters in the threads I read UnkillableStepTimeout After SIGKILL , how long before we decide a process is unkillable? 60 seconds in older threads; one site on 25.05 shows 300 Defaults have moved between versions and many sites change them, so ask your own cluster: The slurmstepd log line you are looking for says the step was terminated "due to job not ending with signals". That is the node reporting, in a slightly Victorian tone, that it sent the signals and nothing happened.

secs.head: Suspect 1: the process that cannot hear you
secs.body: SIGKILL cannot be caught, blocked or ignored. It can, however, be postponed . A process in uninterruptible sleep (state D in ps ) is waiting for the kernel to finish something, usually I/O, and the kernel will not deliver a fatal signal until that wait ends. The usual accomplice is a network or parallel filesystem having a bad night. Admins in the mailing-list threads blame laggy storage again and again, and one thread adds a useful detail: the I/O may complete after Slurm drained the node, leaving a perfectly clean machine wearing a drain flag. One support ticket even includes the kernel's own confession in the node log, a line saying a task had been blocked for more than 362 seconds. That kind of message in dmesg or the journal is your best evidence that the suspect was stuck in a system call. A few things this implies: - It is rarely the job's fault. A user cancelling a healthy job on a sick filesystem is enough. - Mass cancels amplify it. One thread describes a workflow tool that stops a run by cancelling many jobs at once, and nodes drain in batches, presumably because they all hit the same stalled mount at the same moment. - Not every case is storage. One admin in the threads reports the same drain on a site with no Lustre at all. Treat "storage" as the leading suspect, not the only one. [!NOTE] Slurm's own reasoning, as one list reply puts it, is a heuristic: if a process could not be killed, something is wrong with the node, so keep new jobs away until a human looks.

secs.head: Suspect 2: the epilog with a temper
secs.body: There is a second way to get a drained node after a job ends, and it looks similar from the outside. Slurm's Prolog and Epilog guide says that if the Epilog exits with a non-zero code, the node is set to DRAIN . A site epilog that checks for leftover GPU processes, full scratch space or stale mounts will drain a node the moment its check fails, which is its job. So when you see a drained node after a job, check which story it is: Clue Likely cause --- --- Reason says "Kill task failed" A step process survived SIGKILL for UnkillableStepTimeout seconds slurmd log shows the epilog finishing with an error Your epilog returned non-zero dmesg shows hung-task warnings The kernel was already unhappy before Slurm noticed The epilog also runs outside the job's cgroup, which matters if your check looks at device numbers. The cgroups page and the GPU affinity page explain how the same GPU can have different numbers inside and outside.

secs.head: Why raising the timeout is mostly a delay
secs.body: The obvious fix is to raise UnkillableStepTimeout . SchedMD's own troubleshooting guide suggests it for nodes stuck in COMPLETING, so it is a legitimate tool. But admins report the limits of it: - One admin who tried it says it mostly prolonged the time before the failure. - A site with the timeout at 180 seconds still reports drains several times a day. - Another thread has a user cancelling a job at 120 seconds and still getting a drained node. The reasoning is simple. If the storage is down for ten minutes, a three-minute timeout drains the node and a nine-minute timeout does too, just later. A longer timeout helps only when the stall is shorter than the new value. Also, the drained node does not undrain itself. A list reply is explicit that even when the job finally terminates, the node is not resumed. Somebody has to do that.

secs.head: The detective kit
secs.body: UnkillableStepProgram runs a script of your choosing when a step is unkillable. Admins in the threads recommend it as a debugging tool, and it is the best thing you can do for your future self, because it captures the scene while the body is still warm. A sketch of what such a script might gather. This is a suggestion, not a Slurm-provided script, so test it before relying on it: Set it in slurm.conf : Two more habits from the threads: check core-file locations around the timestamp in the reason, and keep a cron job that emails you the Reason of every newly drained node, so the 3 a.m. discovery becomes a 9 a.m. one.

secs.head: Releasing the node
secs.body: First make sure the culprit is really gone. If it is, return the node to service: If processes are still stuck, resuming just feeds the next job to the same problem. At that point the options are fixing the filesystem path, rebooting the node (see the reboot order page), or both.

secs.head: Case closed: the short version
secs.body: The culprit is nearly always not the job, not Slurm, but a kernel call waiting on something that is not answering.

label: SlurmdSpoolDir is full
title: SlurmdSpoolDir Is Full: The Drain That Is Not About the Spool Directory
desc: Part of the schedulers directory. The reason string, the recovery steps and the contents of the directory come from site

secs.head: SlurmdSpoolDir Is Full: The Drain That Is Not About the Spool Directory
secs.body: Part of the schedulers directory. The reason string, the recovery steps and the contents of the directory come from site documentation, mailing-list threads, a vendor support article and the slurmd man page. Nothing was run on a live cluster for this page, and the invented scenario is just that.

secs.head: The drain with the wrong name
secs.body: Picture a GPU node that has been training for six days. Nothing in the job fails. Then sinfo -R shows a node drained with this reason: The reaction is natural: go look at /var/spool/slurmd . It holds a few megabytes. Everyone's spool directory holds a few megabytes. The name of the error is a little misleading, and the rest of this page is about why. The behavior itself is old. A commit from the early days of the project, by Moe Jette, carries a one-line message: "Slurmd will drain a compute node when the SlurmdSpoolDir is full." A vendor guide for GPU clouds describes it as a safety measure: when the filesystem holding the spool directory runs out of space, slurmd can no longer write its own state, so it drains the node.

secs.head: The directory is innocent, the filesystem is not
secs.body: A user on the slurm-users list reported the error on a few nodes of a 242-node run, even though the spool directory had roughly 38 GB of free space and nothing was intentionally written there. Three replies explain the pattern: - "It is the partition that is full, not the directory itself." The cause could be log files in /var/log just as easily as anything in /var/spool , because /var or /var/spool may sit on a partition shared with other things. - "This is basically always somebody filling up /tmp ," when /tmp resides on the same filesystem as the spool directory. The reply is blunt, and it matches the vendor guide's own example: a node running long training jobs accumulates over a hundred gigabytes of temporary files in /tmp over several days and fills its root disk entirely. - One site's troubleshooting notes list the symptom from the user's side: no slurm- .out files appear, or jobs fail, when /tmp , /var/tmp or /var/spool fills, and they point out that /var/spool and /var/tmp typically share the same underlying storage, so filling one affects the other. So the diagnosis is rarely "something wrote a lot into the spool directory". It is "something wrote a lot onto the same disk, and slurmd was the first thing polite enough to notice".

secs.head: What slurmd actually keeps in there
secs.body: The administrator documentation is thin on this, and the person who started the 2023 thread said so. The answers from the list and from site documentation add up to this inventory: Item What it is Where I saw it --- --- --- jobNNNNN/slurm script The batch script of each job on this node. One reply on the list describes finding "job scripts and various cached data" and typically a few megabytes in total A permissions-error thread quoting .../job00136/slurm script ; the 2023 thread cred state (and .old , .new ) Credential state that slurmd rewrites; a cred state.new write is the file in the failure message below A permissions thread listing the directory; a site troubleshooting page hwloc topo whole.xml A cached topology file The same permissions thread conf-cache/ Configuration files fetched by slurmd in configless mode, with /run/slurm/conf pointing at it Niflheim site documentation <nodename <jobid .<stepid Unix sockets for running steps, described on the slurmstepd page Slurm source A core file, if slurmd crashes The man page says a core file goes to SlurmdSpoolDir , or /var/tmp/ as a last resort, unless slurmd runs with -D slurmd man page Batch scripts are bounded: max script size in SchedulerParameters defaults to 4 MB. To fill a disk with scripts you would need an extraordinary number of jobs, which is why the list's first reaction was "can your job scripts contain large amounts of data?" and its second was "is the spool directory on shared storage?". That second question matters. The Slurm configuration tool says the directory for slurmd state must be unique on each compute server, on local disk . A spool directory on shared storage is a different problem with a different smell. Site documentation adds one more rule: the directory is not created by the RPM packages. You create it and set the owner yourself. The failure itself, when it happens, looks like this in the logs (this exact message was posted by a site that hit it):

secs.head: The evidence that leaves the scene
secs.body: The 2023 thread contains a detail that every admin who has chased a full disk will recognize. When the author finally looked, df -h showed about 38 GB free. Large files that existed during the failure had been removed by the time anyone checked. The disk had been full, and then it was not, and the node was still drained. There are two common ways for the evidence to disappear: - A job ended and its temporary files were cleaned up (or the user deleted them) after slurmd had already drained the node. - A process holds a deleted file open . Space is not returned while the file is still open, so df shows the disk full while du finds nothing to explain it. The vendor guide's answer is lsof +L1 , which lists open files that have been unlinked. Either way, look for the explanation in the logs from the time of the event as well as in the current state of the disk. The reason timestamp from scontrol show node tells you where to start.

secs.head: A triage runbook
secs.body: Notes on reading the results: Finding What it suggests --- --- /tmp is huge and on the root filesystem Jobs writing scratch data to the default temp location /var/log is huge Logs not rotated, or debug logging left on df is full, du finds little A deleted-but-open file, so check lsof +L1 df -h fine, df -i full Inode exhaustion from millions of small files A core file in the spool directory A slurmd crash. Check the logs before restarting anything [!WARNING] Be careful with rm inside SlurmdSpoolDir itself. It holds the batch scripts and step sockets of jobs that may still be running, and an older SchedMD ticket describes the directory as part of how job state is restored. Clean up the temporary files that filled the disk, not the spool directory's own contents, unless you have drained the node and confirmed nothing is running on it. That advice is my reading of the design, so verify it on a test node.

secs.head: Bringing the node back
secs.body: Once there is real free space, tell Slurm the node may take jobs again: The drain does not clear itself when the disk recovers, so this step is manual. A good sign afterward is a job that starts and finishes cleanly, which proves slurmd can write its state again. If the node drains again within the hour, something is still filling the disk, and the cleanup treated a symptom.

secs.head: Prevention: give temp files somewhere else to live
secs.body: The documentation point that explains the whole story is in Niflheim's notes: jobs store temporary files in /tmp , /scratch and /dev/shm , and no cleanup is done after the job exits . Add a large, shared, default temp directory and a long-running job, and the full disk becomes a matter of time. Options, from most to least integrated: Approach How it works Notes --- --- --- Namespace/tmpfs plugin Gives each job private /tmp , /var/tmp and /dev/shm mounts backed by a base path, removed when the job ends Needs PrologFlags=Contain and a job container.conf . Renamed in 25.11 from job container/tmpfs to namespace/tmpfs , configured with NamespaceType= instead of JobContainerType= auto tmpdir (SPANK plugin) Creates and cleans a per-job temp directory Third-party. A new Slurm major version needs a rebuild on a test node spank-private-tmp Private temp dirs Does not clean up, so you must add cleanup Cron cleanup Removes old files from scratch Crude, but it works. The site example removes files older than seven days under /scratch A configuration sketch from the Niflheim documentation: The Shared=true option, from Slurm 23.02, is the one they flag as important when home directories are automounted, because older versions had trouble with NFS automounts under the tmpfs plugin. One suggestion of my own, not from the documentation: choose a BasePath on a filesystem other than the one holding SlurmdSpoolDir and the OS logs, so that a runaway job fills its own scratch space rather than the disk slurmd depends on. Other habits that pay off: - Separate filesystems. Put /tmp , /scratch and /var/log on different filesystems from the spool directory and the root disk, or at least apply quotas. - Know your TmpFS . TmpDisk for a node is defined as the size of its TmpFS filesystem (default /tmp ), and jobs can request space with --tmp . Set TmpFS=/scratch if that is where jobs really write. - Alert early. A node health check that looks at free space on local filesystems (Niflheim's NHC notes show DF FLAGS set to list only local filesystems) turns a surprise drain into a warning, and it can run on a schedule through HealthCheckProgram . - Rotate logs and keep debug off. The slurmd log is on the same disk, and SlurmdDebug=debug2 is not a long-term setting.

secs.head: Two spool directories, two different jobs
secs.body: It is common to mix up the two directories that Slurm needs. They live on different machines and fail in different ways. Setting Lives on Holds Remember --- --- --- --- SlurmdSpoolDir Every compute node, local disk Per-node job scripts, credential state, config cache, step sockets Fills up with the node's disk. Full means the node drains StateSaveLocation The controller (and shared for HA) The controller's state: jobs, nodes, reservations Back it up before upgrades, as in the upgrade page An old SchedMD reply sums up the division in one line: the controller keeps its state in StateSaveLocation and the job information in SlurmdSpoolDir , so with both directories intact you have what you need to restore state after a restart.

secs.head: Cheat sheet
secs.body: A node that drains itself over disk space is not being dramatic. It is the one daemon on the box that refuses to run jobs it cannot keep track of.

label: **Smoke Tests**
title: Slurm Smoke Tests: Does It Still Work?
desc: A cluster can pass every glance and still be broken: sinfo shows a tidy table while the accounting daemon is down, a rul

secs.head: Slurm Smoke Tests: Does It Still Work?
secs.body: A cluster can pass every glance and still be broken: sinfo shows a tidy table while the accounting daemon is down, a rule refuses every monitoring job, or a node reports idle with half its cores. A smoke test is the short list of things that must all work, run every time something changes. Each page opens with a failure, then builds the check that would have caught it. Every script was run on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4), against failures injected on purpose. SchedMD does not define a "smoke test", so the series synthesises what its admin, troubleshooting and upgrade guides say to verify, and adds what the tests turned up. The pages stand alone. Read part 1 first if you are new to this; the rest each name what they build on. ---

secs.head: Contents
secs.body: File Description --- --- 1. The Cluster That Worked Perfectly and Remembered Nothing A six-check, two-minute smoke test (MUNGE, controller, nodes, srun , sbatch , sacct ) as one script with three outcomes, tested against four failures 2. Measure Twice, Reconfigure Once What a bad slurm.conf does, and the dry runs that catch it: a snapshot diff, sbatch --test-only , a canary partition 3. The Morning After the Upgrade A backup you have restored, versions on every node, a snapshot comparison, and why you cannot undo an upgrade 4. Does the Rulebook Still Work? A two-stage policy test: routing and refusals with no resources, then a real preemption drill 5. Back From the Repair Shop Why idle proves little, a hardware-versus-config check, and a reservation fence for a probe job 6. When Smoke Becomes a Fire Drill SchedMD's test suite and ReFrame, and the baseline rule ---

secs.head: Which check, when
secs.body: What just happened Run --- --- Any change at all Part 1: the control-plane script, as an ordinary user Editing slurm.conf Part 2: snapshot before and after, --test-only , canary partition An upgrade Part 3: proven backup first, then versions, part 1, snapshot diff A change to QOS, limits, the submit script or preemption Part 4: stage 1 always, stage 2 for preemption changes A node returning from repair or reboot Part 5: hardware comparison, then a probe job inside a fence A big change on a test cluster Part 6: a regression suite, compared with a baseline ---

secs.head: What the tests turned up
secs.body: The surprises are the reason the checks look the way they do: - A dead slurmd is invisible to sinfo for a while, so only launching a task on every node finds it quickly. - With slurmdbd stopped, jobs run perfectly and nothing is recorded. - A drained node and a full cluster give srun the same "busy" message, and a dead node can look like a full cluster to sbatch , so a smoke test needs a third outcome: inconclusive. - A typo in slurm.conf is caught by scontrol before the controller sees it, but a partition naming a missing node survives a reconfigure and stops the next restart from working. - A submit rule that requires --time broke the first draft of the smoke test, and, most probably, 18 failures in SchedMD's suite. - With config overrides , a node with half its configured CPUs shows idle . Without it, Slurm marks the node inval . - A drained node cannot run a job even inside a reservation, so a probe needs the reservation first and the resume second. ---

secs.head: What was not tested
secs.body: No GPU commands were run (the test cluster has none). No upgrade between versions was performed. SchedMD's unit and expect suites were not run. NHC was not installed. Each page says so where it matters. ---

secs.head: Related pages
secs.body: - Why is my job still pending?: the reason codes behind a smoke test's WAIT . - Autopsy of a job: sacct : reading what the accounting check recorded. - Dying Politely: preemption and signals: the policy that part 4 tests. - Cluster operations: upgrade order, reboots and reservations around parts 3 and 5. - When a GPU falls off the bus: the health-check program that part 5 points to.

label: Control-plane smoke test
title: The Cluster That Worked Perfectly and Remembered Nothing: a Two-Minute Slurm Smoke Test
desc: Part 1 of Slurm Smoke Tests. Every command, script and output here was run on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4, ac

secs.head: The Cluster That Worked Perfectly and Remembered Nothing: a Two-Minute Slurm Smoke Test
secs.body: Part 1 of Slurm Smoke Tests. Every command, script and output here was run on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4, accounting on, both slurmd daemons on one Ubuntu 24.04 machine), including the failures, which were injected on purpose. The node names, users and the story are invented. SchedMD does not define a "smoke test", so the checks below are a synthesis of what its admin, troubleshooting and upgrade guides tell you to verify, in one script.

secs.head: The cluster that remembered nothing
secs.body: On Friday at five to five, Tarek restarts the Slurm controller after a small change. He runs sinfo , sees a tidy table with every node idle , and goes home. On Monday the finance office asks why the weekend's usage report is empty. Researchers say their jobs ran fine. They did: for three days the cluster ran every job it was given and recorded none of them, because the accounting daemon had not come back with the controller. Nothing was broken in the way anybody was looking. sinfo was right. squeue was right. The only thing wrong was the part that nobody checks until someone needs the numbers. A smoke test is the habit that would have caught it in two minutes on Friday. It is a short list of things that must all work for the cluster to be useful, run every time something changes. Its name comes from electronics: plug the board in, and if smoke comes out, stop. ---

secs.head: What a smoke test is, and is not
secs.body: A smoke test answers one question: is it basically working? It does not measure performance, it does not test every option, and it does not replace a regression suite (that is part 6). It earns its place by being cheap enough to run every time and by covering every layer a job passes through. Layer What it proves The check --- --- --- Authentication This host can make and read a MUNGE credential munge -n \ unmunge Controller slurmctld answers scontrol ping Nodes No node is down, drained or silent sinfo states Launching A task really starts on every node srun across all nodes Batch path A script is accepted, scheduled, run, and writes output sbatch and a wait Accounting The database recorded what ran sacct for that job Each layer can fail while the one above it looks fine. Tarek's morning is the last row failing alone. ---

secs.head: The script
secs.body: It runs as an ordinary user, not as root, because that is how real jobs arrive: through the same submit rules and the same associations. It uses the commands the Slurm guides mention, scontrol ping and srun across nodes, plus sbatch and sacct , which the upgrade guide names as the way to validate "communication with nodes and a job's ability to successfully start and finish". The script is slurm-smoke.sh , a plain file you can read on this site, open on GitHub or fetch with its raw link. On the healthy test cluster it finished in one second: A few choices in the script matter: - $SLURMD NODENAME , not hostname . It is the name Slurm uses for the node. On the test cluster both nodes live on one machine, so hostname printed the same name twice and the check failed on a healthy cluster. It is also immune to fully qualified names that differ from the node name. - --immediate . A smoke test must not sit in the queue behind real work. With --immediate , srun gives up with a clear message instead of waiting. - Cleanup. The script cancels its own jobs on exit. The first version used sbatch --wait under timeout , and a timed-out run left a job pending in the queue. ---

secs.head: Break it on purpose
secs.body: A check you have never seen fail is a check you do not know works. Four failures were injected, one at a time, on the test cluster. The script ran as an ordinary user with a 15-second limit per step. Injected failure What the script printed Which check caught it --- --- --- slurmd on node2 killed FAIL srun rc=233: srun: error: Task launch for StepId=92.0 failed on node node2: Communication connection failure srun only. The nodes check passed , because the controller had not noticed yet slurmdbd stopped PASS sbatch job 101 ran and wrote its output , then FAIL sacct job 101 in the database: 'nothing' sacct only. Jobs kept running; srun alone worked too slurmctld stopped FAIL ping Slurmctld(primary) at vm is DOWN , FAIL nodes sinfo: slurm load partitions: Unable to contact slurm controller (connect failure) , FAIL sbatch submit refused: ... Three checks at once node2 drained FAIL nodes node2 drained; nodes . The batch job still passed, because it needed only one node Two lessons come straight from the table. A dead slurmd is invisible to sinfo until the controller's own timeout notices it ( SlurmdTimeout ), so launching a task on every node is the only check that finds it quickly. And a stopped slurmdbd is Tarek's Friday: everything works except the record. Only the last row of the script sees it. ---

secs.head: When the cluster is just busy
secs.body: The first version of the script treated every pending job as a failure, and a smoke test that cries wolf gets switched off. With both nodes occupied by a large job, the final script reports: That is exit status 2, a third outcome next to pass and fail, and it means "I could not tell". It deserves its own colour on a dashboard. Two cautions from the tests: - A dead node can look busy. After a killed slurmd , the batch job sat pending with the reason Resources , the same text a full cluster shows. The FAIL from srun outranked it, but a WAIT on its own is not proof of health. - A drained node reads as busy to srun . In the drained run, srun reported "Requested nodes are busy", while the nodes check printed the real cause. Read the whole report, not one line. Run on a quiet partition, or give the smoke test its own lane (a canary partition, which part 2 builds), and WAIT becomes rare. ---

secs.head: Things that make a healthy cluster fail
secs.body: Real causes of false failures, all seen during these tests: Symptom Cause Fix --- --- --- sbatch: error: Please set --time, jobs without one are not accepted A submit script requires a time limit, and the test job had none Give the test job -t . The script's SMOKE TIME does this Job FAILED with ExitCode 0:53 , log says Slurmd could not connect IO The submission directory was not writable by the user, so the output file could not be created Run from a writable directory, or give -o a path that is writable. The script uses a temporary directory A WAIT or odd result right after a restart Probably nodes still settling after the daemons came back: a run two seconds after a restart reported Requested nodes are busy , and a run six seconds after did not. The cause was not isolated Wait several seconds after a restart before the check sacct empty for a job that finished The database daemon is down, or accounting is not enabled on this cluster That is exactly what check 6 is for. On a cluster without accounting, leave it out ---

secs.head: Where to run it
secs.body: - After every change: a restart, a reconfigure, an upgrade, a node coming back. Part 2 and part 3 cover the two big cases. - On a schedule: every few minutes from a login node, as a canary, with the result sent to your monitoring. The script's exit status is the signal. Watch the cost: each run submits a real job, so a one-minute check on a large cluster is a job per minute. - Not as root. Root bypasses the rules a user meets, which is where many failures live. ---

secs.head: Version notes
secs.body: Everything above ran on Slurm 23.11.4. sacctmgr ping appeared in 24.11 and queries the status of slurmdbd directly, so on newer clusters it makes a cheaper accounting check than a full job. Whether it replaces the sacct round trip is a judgment: it proves the daemon answers, while the sacct check proves a job was recorded. The version-changes page lists what else moved. ---

secs.head: Back to the cluster that remembered nothing
secs.body: Replay Friday at five to five. Tarek restarts the controller and runs the script. Munge, ping and the nodes pass. The srun and sbatch lines pass. Then the last line: It takes two minutes, and he has not left his desk. He starts slurmdbd , reruns the script, reads ALL PASS , and goes home. On Monday the report has three days of usage in it, not zero. Nothing about this required cleverness. It required one more command than sinfo , run by someone who knew that "the table looks fine" and "the cluster works" are different statements. Takeaway: a smoke test checks every layer a job passes through (MUNGE, controller, nodes, launching, batch, accounting), runs as an ordinary user after every change, and has three outcomes (pass, fail, inconclusive-because-busy), because each layer can fail while the one above it looks fine. Next: Measure Twice, Reconfigure Once is what to do before you change slurm.conf , so the smoke test above has nothing to find. ---
