secs.body: - Slurm: Quick Start Administrator Guide ( -D -v , srun -N1 /bin/hostname , scontrol ping ) - Slurm: Troubleshooting Guide ( scontrol ping , scontrol show node , scontrol show slurmd ) - Slurm: Upgrade Guide (step 8, "Test key functionality") - Slurm: srun ( --immediate ) - Slurm: sacct

label: After a config change
title: Measure Twice, Reconfigure Once: Smoke-Testing a slurm.conf Change
desc: Part 2 of Slurm Smoke Tests. Everything here was run on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4, accounting on, both slur

secs.head: Measure Twice, Reconfigure Once: Smoke-Testing a slurm.conf Change
secs.body: Part 2 of Slurm Smoke Tests. Everything here was run on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4, accounting on, both slurmd daemons on one Ubuntu 24.04 machine), including the mistakes, which were made on purpose. Names and the story are invented. The control-plane smoke test is the check this page runs at the end, so read it first.

secs.head: The partition for nodes that were not there yet
secs.body: Layla is adding eight nodes next week. To save time, she writes the partition for them today, in slurm.conf , naming nodes that exist on the purchase order but not yet in the rack, and runs scontrol reconfigure . It prints an error. The cluster, she checks, is still fine: jobs are running, squeue answers. She decides the error is about the new nodes, which is true, and leaves it for next week. Three weeks later the controller is restarted for an unrelated reason. It does not come back. Nothing in Layla's story is careless in a way that feels careless at the time. The error looked non-fatal because it was. The running controller really did keep working. The problem was that the file on disk had become a time bomb, and a restart is the thing that reads the file. ---

secs.head: What Slurm does with a bad file
secs.body: Four mistakes were made in slurm.conf on the test cluster, one at a time, each followed by scontrol reconfigure . The original file was restored after each. Mistake What scontrol reconfigure did --- --- An unknown key, SchedulerTypo=yes scontrol: error: parse next key: Parsing error at unrecognized key: SchedulerTypo , then fatal: Unable to process configuration file , exit status 1 A bad number, MaxJobCount=banana error: MaxJobCount value (banana) is not a valid number , then the same fatal , exit status 1 A bad value, State=SIDEWAYS on a partition error: Bad value "SIDEWAYS" for State , then the same fatal , exit status 1 A partition naming a missing node, Nodes=node9 slurm reconfigure error: Unspecified error , exit status 1 Look at who said what. The first three were caught by scontrol itself , which parses the file on your machine before it sends anything. The running controller never saw them. A side effect: while the file is broken, every scontrol command fails the same way, including scontrol ping . The fourth got past the client, because the file was valid syntax. The error came back from the controller as the unhelpful "Unspecified error", and the real reason was only in the controller log: After that failed reconfigure, scontrol ping still said UP and jobs kept running: the old process stayed in charge. Then the same file was left in place and the controller was restarted: The same mistake that a reconfigure survives, a restart does not. A failed reconfigure is a warning with a delay on it. ---

secs.head: Rung 1: look at the diff
secs.body: Before touching anything, write down what is running and compare it with what will be. scontrol show config is the obvious tool, but on its own it is not enough. In the test it did not show a newly added partition at all, only the global settings, and its only differences after a reconfigure were two timestamps. A useful snapshot needs the partitions, nodes, reservations and accounting rules too: The script is slurm-snapshot.sh , a plain file you can read on this site, open on GitHub or fetch with its raw link. A change was made on the test cluster: a hidden canary partition added to slurm.conf , and a new QOS called trial added with a 45-second GraceTime . The diff: The same diff also flagged the node2 line as changed. The cause, once the full line was read, was that Partitions= now listed canary as well. The tool did its job: it showed an effect nobody asked for in the change, which is exactly why you diff. Keep the snapshots. When something misbehaves on Thursday, "what changed since Monday" is a diff . ---

secs.head: Rung 2: ask Slurm without running anything
secs.body: sbatch --test-only validates a job and says when and where it would start, without queueing it. It is the cheapest end-to-end check that the rules still accept what users send. On the test cluster, with a valid job, it ran the whole submit path and left the queue empty: The same flag, for jobs that should be refused, produced a different message for each cause: Test job Response --- --- No --time , with a submit script that requires it sbatch: error: Please set --time, jobs without one are not accepted -N5 on a two-node cluster allocation failure: Requested node configuration is not available A partition that does not exist sbatch: error: invalid partition specified: nosuch A user with no account allocation failure: Invalid account or account/partition combination specified That makes it the right dry run for a policy change: a submit rule, a limit, a partition option. Run a handful of jobs that should work and a handful that should fail, and compare the answers with what you intended. The checks that cannot be done with it are the ones that need a real node: it does not start anything, so it proves the rules, not the machine. There is no equivalent for the file itself on this version. The slurmctld -h output of 23.11 lists no option to check a configuration and exit. Do not assume newer versions are the same without reading their help. ---

secs.head: Rung 3: a canary lane
secs.body: Give the change a small place to land first. The test cluster got a partition made of one node, hidden from the normal partition list: Users do not see a hidden partition in sinfo , but they can still submit to it by name, and so can your smoke test: A canary partition has a second use: it is the place for the scheduled smoke test from part 1, so its jobs never queue behind real work and never turn into WAIT . For a change that needs to be tried on real nodes (a new QOS, a new limit), put the change on the canary partition first, with a small group of users, and widen it only after a day of green results. ---

secs.head: Rung 4: reconfigure, then check
secs.body: By now the file has been diffed, the rules dry-run and the partition tried. The reconfigure itself was uneventful in the test. A job that was running ( sleep 300 , job 105) was still RUNNING on node1 after it. The only change in scontrol show config was BOOT TIME , which moved to the reconfigure time, one of the two lines the snapshot script drops. After it, repeat the same three steps in the same order: 1. The smoke test, as a normal user. 2. slurm-snapshot.sh /tmp/after and a diff -ru against the one taken before. 3. A look at the controller log for new error: lines. The failed reconfigure above produced a fatal: that never reached the terminal. Some settings need a daemon restart and not a reconfigure. The slurm.conf man page marks them, and this page did not test which ones. ---

secs.head: Version notes
secs.body: Tests were on 23.11.4. From 26.05, a runtime error in a Lua submit script writes a stack trace to the log, which helps with a failing policy change. Version changes 23.11 to 26.05 has the entry. Whether newer versions give a clearer reason than "Unspecified error" for a partition that names a missing node was not checked. ---

secs.head: Back to the partition for nodes that were not there yet
secs.body: Replay Layla's afternoon with the ladder. She snapshots the cluster, adds the partition for the future nodes, and runs scontrol reconfigure . The error is the same. This time the rule she follows is that an error on a reconfigure is a failure, not a message. She removes the partition, reconfigures cleanly, runs the smoke test, and reads the diff. It shows nothing changed. Next week, when the eight nodes are in the rack and defined, the partition goes in with them, on the canary lane first. Three weeks later the controller restarts for an unrelated reason and comes back in the time it takes to read the log. Takeaway: syntax mistakes are stopped by scontrol before the controller sees them, but a semantic mistake can survive a reconfigure and kill the next restart, so treat any reconfigure error as a failure, snapshot before and after, dry-run policy with sbatch --test-only , try new rules on a hidden canary partition, and finish with the smoke test. Next: The Morning After the Upgrade applies the same discipline to the one change you cannot undo. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Slurm: slurm.conf (which parameters need a restart) - Slurm: scontrol ( reconfigure , show config , show partition ) - Slurm: sbatch ( --test-only ) - Slurm: Upgrade Guide ("Always prepare and test configuration changes in a test environment before upgrading in production")

label: After an upgrade
title: The Morning After the Upgrade: Smoke Tests for the Change You Cannot Undo
desc: Part 3 of Slurm Smoke Tests. The commands and outputs below were run on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4, accounti

secs.head: The Morning After the Upgrade: Smoke Tests for the Change You Cannot Undo
secs.body: Part 3 of Slurm Smoke Tests. The commands and outputs below were run on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4, accounting on, both slurmd daemons on one Ubuntu 24.04 machine). No Slurm upgrade was performed : there was only one version installed. What was tested is everything that surrounds one, namely the backup, the version reports, the snapshot and the restarts. The upgrade procedure itself is quoted from the Slurm upgrade guide. The names and the story are invented. The order in which to upgrade the daemons is on the upgrade order page.

secs.head: The undo button that isn't
secs.body: Samira starts the upgrade at ten on Saturday night. The plan is the usual one: stop the accounting daemon, upgrade it, start it and let it convert its database, then the controller, then the nodes. By half past eleven the daemons are all running and she runs her smoke test. Everything passes except the last line. Jobs run, and the database has recorded none of them. Now she has a decision with a clock on it. She can fix forward, reading logs at midnight with an unknown number of causes. Or she can go back. The Slurm upgrade guide has a blunt sentence about going back: "Reverting an upgrade (or downgrading) is not supported once any of the Slurm daemons have been started." The only way back is the backup, and the backup, the guide adds, loses "anything that happened after the backups were created." Samira has a nightly database dump. She has never tried to restore it. At half past eleven on a Saturday, that is a poor time to find out whether it works. ---

secs.head: What the guide says to test
secs.body: The upgrade guide lists nine steps, and one of them is a smoke test with a different name: Step The guide's wording Where it is covered --- --- --- 1 Prepare cluster for the upgrade (release notes, configuration changes, downtime) Version changes 2 Create backups Rung 1 below 3 Upgrade slurmdbd , then validate accounting Rung 3 4 to 7 Upgrade slurmctld , slurmd , login nodes, customised plugins Upgrade order 8 Test key functionality The control-plane smoke test, plus Rung 3 9 Archive backup data, once the upgrade is confirmed After a few good days, not the same night Two sentences from the guide frame everything: "Always prepare and test configuration changes in a test environment before upgrading in production", and "Sites are encouraged to actively run pre-release versions on test machines before each major release." A smoke test on production tells you whether tonight went well. A smoke test on a test cluster tells you whether tonight is a good idea. ---

secs.head: Rung 1: a backup you have restored
secs.body: A backup that has never been restored is a hope. The check is small: dump the accounting database, restore the dump into a scratch database, and compare the row counts of the tables that matter. This script does it and cleans up after itself: The script is slurm-db-backup-check.sh , a plain file you can read on this site, open on GitHub or fetch with its raw link. On the test cluster: The tables are named after the cluster, here smoke , which is why the script looks them up instead of hard-coding them. Two limits are worth saying out loud. This ran while slurmdbd was up, using a transaction-consistent dump, which is fine for a rehearsal. The guide's own procedure takes the real dump with slurmdbd stopped, and the script's header says so. And matching row counts show the dump is complete, not that every row is right. It catches the failures that matter, an empty, truncated or unreadable dump, which are the ones nobody finds until they need it. A second backup comes with the first: the controller's state directory ( StateSaveLocation ), which holds the queue and reservations. The spool directory page covers where that lives. ---

secs.head: Rung 2: take the snapshot
secs.body: Save what the cluster looks like before, so the morning after has something to compare with. The slurm-snapshot.sh script from part 2 records the running configuration, partitions, nodes, reservations, QOS and associations as plain text: After the upgrade, run it again into another directory and diff -ru the two. Expect differences: the version on every node, and probably a few new default parameters in config.txt . What should not differ is the list of partitions, the QOS and association rules, and the reservations. If one does, it is either a consequence the release notes warned about or something to investigate before the users find it. ---

secs.head: Rung 3: after the daemons are back
secs.body: Each of these takes seconds: Check Command What it should show --- --- --- Version of every daemon slurmctld -V , slurmdbd -V , slurmd -V , sinfo -V The target version. On the test cluster all four read slurm-wlm 23.11.4 Version of every node, as the controller sees it scontrol show node -o \ grep -o 'NodeName=[^ ] \ Version=[^ ] ' \ paste - - One line per node with the same version The control plane slurm-smoke.sh , as an ordinary user ALL PASS Accounting answers sacctmgr ping (24.11 and newer), and sacct for an old job The old job is still readable, and the last smoke job is recorded The state matches before diff -ru of the two snapshots Only the expected differences Custom plugins and SPANK Submit a job that uses each one They load. The 24.11 release notes say all SPANK plugins must be recompiled when upgrading from an earlier version The per-node line on the test cluster: A node that was missed shows its old version here, which is the cheapest way to find the one slurmd that did not restart. A version mismatch is the first thing the troubleshooting guide suggests ruling out, with sinfo -V or rpm -qa grep slurm . sacctmgr ping does not exist on 23.11. On the test cluster it answered invalid keyword: ping . It was added in 24.11, so the script from part 1 still uses sacct , which works on every version. ---

secs.head: Do jobs survive the restart?
secs.body: The upgrade guide has you stop and start every daemon, with users' jobs running through it. Whether they survive is something to know before the real night. On the test cluster, a 300-second job was started on node1 . Then slurmdbd , slurmctld and the slurmd on node1 were all stopped, and everything restarted: The job was still running, and a smoke test straight after passed. That is one job, with default settings and a process tracker that does not use cgroups, so it is evidence, not a guarantee. A rehearsal on a test cluster with your real configuration, long-running jobs and a node restart is worth more than this table. ---

secs.head: Version notes
secs.body: Nothing on this page was run across two versions, so there are no measured differences. From the release notes read for the version changes page: 24.11 can be upgraded directly from 23.02, 23.11 or 24.05, and the notes say to update slurmdbd first; 25.11 from 25.05, 24.11 or 24.05. The upgrade path for 26.05 was not checked. A jump from 23.11 to 26.05 is therefore several upgrades, and each one deserves its own backup and its own run of this page. ---

secs.head: Back to the undo button that isn't
secs.body: Replay Saturday with a rehearsed Friday. On Friday afternoon Samira ran the backup check and saw BACKUP RESTORES , with the same row counts on both sides. She saved a snapshot. She stopped slurmdbd , took the real dump, and started. At half past eleven the smoke test fails on the last line, as before. This time the decision takes five minutes and not an hour. She has a dump she knows can be restored, a snapshot to compare against, and a clear question: is this a quick fix? She reads the accounting daemon's log, finds the cause, fixes it, and reruns the script. ALL PASS . She did not need the restore, and she knew exactly what it would have cost. Takeaway: a Slurm upgrade cannot be rolled back once a daemon has started, so the real smoke test happens before it (a backup you have restored, a saved snapshot, a rehearsal on a test cluster) and after it (versions on every node, the control-plane smoke test, accounting, and a diff of the snapshots). Next: Does the Rulebook Still Work? tests the layer an upgrade is most likely to change quietly: QOS, submit rules and preemption. ---

secs.body: - Slurm: Upgrade Guide (the nine steps, "Test key functionality", no downgrade) - Slurm: Troubleshooting Guide ( sinfo -V , version compatibility) - Slurm: Quick Start Administrator Guide - Slurm 24.11 release notes, mirror ( sacctmgr ping , upgrade paths, SPANK recompile)

label: Policy and preemption
title: Does the Rulebook Still Work? Smoke-Testing QOS, Submit Rules and Preemption
desc: Part 4 of Slurm Smoke Tests. The script and every output below were run on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4, accou

secs.head: Does the Rulebook Still Work? Smoke-Testing QOS, Submit Rules and Preemption
secs.body: Part 4 of Slurm Smoke Tests. The script and every output below were run on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4, accounting on, QOS preemption with requeue, a job submit.lua that routes and refuses jobs, both slurmd daemons on one Ubuntu 24.04 machine). The accounts, users and the story are invented. The policy under test is the one built in The Guest List and The Receptionist Who Rewrites Your Badge. Read the control-plane smoke test first.

secs.head: The monitor that was refused
secs.body: On Wednesday, Omar adds a rule to the submit script: every job must say how long it will run. It is a good rule. The backfill scheduler works better with honest time limits, and the nodes stop filling with week-long jobs nobody meant. For two days nothing seems different. Then a researcher asks why the cluster's "is it up?" page has shown green since Wednesday morning. The page is fed by a cron job that submits a one-minute test job every five minutes. Since Wednesday, every one of those submissions has been refused with "Please set --time". The cron script printed the error into a mail spool nobody reads, and the last good result stayed on the page. The monitor was the first casualty of the new rule, and nothing noticed, because the monitor was the thing that was supposed to notice. A smoke test for policy has two jobs: check that the rules do what they should, and be a user who is subject to them. ---

secs.head: Why policy needs its own test
secs.body: QOS tiers, account limits, a Lua submit script and preemption settings are all rules, and rules change quietly. Someone edits a QOS on Tuesday. A Lua file is replaced on Wednesday. An upgrade changes a default. None of that touches the control plane, so the six-check smoke test stays green while the policy is wrong. The test has two stages. The first uses no resources at all: held jobs and a dry run. The second stages a real eviction, because "the rule says high beats low" and "a high job really evicted a low one and the low one came back" are different statements. ---

secs.head: The script
secs.body: It runs as an ordinary user who belongs to the test account and may use the low QOS and the high QOS for that account. It picks an idle node on its own, cancels everything it submitted on exit, and exits non-zero on any failure. The script is slurm-policy-smoke.sh , a plain file you can read on this site, open on GitHub or fetch with its raw link. Its result on the test cluster: The whole run took three minutes and twenty-six seconds, nearly all of it in stage 2. The log tells the story in three lines: the low job started, was cancelled "due to preemption" about 50 seconds after the high job arrived ( GraceTime was 30 seconds, plus the controller's own tick), and started again with restart=1 . The same job had been put back in the queue. ---

secs.head: What each check proves
secs.body: Check If it fails, then --- --- no --qos becomes low The submit script is not loaded, is broken, or the default routing changed. Users are now landing in the wrong tier --qos=high becomes high <account Routing for the preemptor broke. High jobs will be refused, or will run without preempting anything a job without --time is refused The time-limit rule is off. (The test passes when the job is refused ) high job got the node The preemptor never started: PreemptType , PreemptMode or the QOS Preempt= list is wrong low job was requeued The victim was cancelled, not requeued: the QOS victim mode, JobRequeue or --requeue is wrong low job restarted The requeued job never came back: it is stuck pending, or held Two more things the script cannot see. It does not look at the signals the victim received, because that depends on whether the job is a batch shell or an srun step, and the timings are the subject of the signals cheat sheet. And it does not test that a real job's checkpoint is valid: it can prove a job was evicted and restarted, not that it resumed correctly. That needs a drill with your own workload. ---

secs.head: Things the drill showed
secs.body: - The victim restarted late. The preempted job was put back in the queue at once, but it did not start again until 08:13:08, about two and a half minutes after it was cancelled, long after the high job's 15 seconds were done. The cause was not investigated, and the script's WAIT of 150 seconds was only just enough. If you test with a tight limit, a correct policy can look like a failure. - A test job without --time is refused. That is Omar's story, and it happened on the test cluster: the first version of the part 1 script failed with Please set --time, jobs without one are not accepted until it was given -t . An earlier version of this drill, read against the same rule, would be refused the same way (it was not rerun). The version above passes -t everywhere. - Where the eviction lands. The script pins both jobs to one idle node with --exclusive , so the high job should only evict the low job the script itself started a moment earlier. It would still be better to run it on a canary partition (see part 2), where a real user's low job can never be the victim. - A user with no account was not tested here. The routing check should also be run by hand for a user with no default account: asking for --qos=high should produce a clear refusal. ---

secs.head: When to run it
secs.body: Run stage 1 whenever anything near the rules changes: a QOS edit, a new Lua file, a reconfigure, an upgrade. It costs nothing. Run stage 2 after any change to PreemptType , PreemptMode , QOS preemption lists or the submit script's routing, and after an upgrade. It evicts a real job, so do not put stage 2 on a schedule against production nodes. ---

secs.head: Version notes
secs.body: Run on 23.11.4. For the preemption settings this page exercises, the changelogs read for the version changes page record: 24.05 treats a job signalled during GraceTime as preempted under CANCEL and REQUEUE ; 25.05 adds a PRIORITY preemption option; 26.05 applies PreemptExemptTime to suspend,gang under preempt/partition prio . None of those were tried. Run the drill after an upgrade before trusting any of them. ---

secs.head: Back to the monitor that was refused
secs.body: Replay Wednesday with the drill. Omar edits the submit script, and before he leaves he runs stage 1: The third line passes, which is what he wanted. Then the cron monitor, which is itself a user, runs the control-plane test and the script prints FAIL sbatch submit refused: Please set --time , in red, on the status page. Omar changes the monitor to pass -t 2 and the page goes green within five minutes. The researcher never asks why the page has been green since Wednesday. Takeaway: policy is code that changes quietly, so test it as a user in two stages (routing and refusals with no resources, then a real eviction and requeue), make your own monitoring subject to the same rules, and run the drill after any change to QOS, preemption settings, the submit script or the version. Next: Back From the Repair Shop moves from the rules to the hardware: how to tell that a node is really fit to go back into service. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Slurm: Preemption - Slurm: Quality of Service (QOS) - Slurm: job submit plugin - Slurm: sbatch ( --test-only , --requeue , --hold )

label: Node readiness
title: Back From the Repair Shop: Is This Node Fit to Return to Service?
desc: Part 5 of Slurm Smoke Tests. The commands and outputs below were run on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4, accounti

secs.head: Back From the Repair Shop: Is This Node Fit to Return to Service?
secs.body: Part 5 of Slurm Smoke Tests. The commands and outputs below were run on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4, accounting on, both slurmd daemons on one Ubuntu 24.04 machine, which has 2 CPUs and about 8 GB of memory). The test cluster has no GPUs , so nothing here was run against one, and the GPU section says so. The names and the story are invented. For the health-check program that drains a node by itself, read When a GPU Falls Off the Bus, which this page does not repeat.

secs.head: Node 17 is idle
secs.body: Node 17 spends a week at the repair shop and comes back with a new motherboard. The technician resets the BIOS to defaults on the way, which turns off half the cores. Nobody remarks on this, because nobody looked. The admin plugs it in. The cluster's slurm.conf was copied from a cloud template and sets config overrides , a setting that makes the controller believe the file and not the hardware. slurmd starts, registers with the controller, and sinfo prints idle . The admin is relieved and resumes the node. For the next two days a handful of jobs that asked for 64 CPUs on node 17 run half as fast as their siblings, and one time out. The users blame the filesystem. The admin blames the users. The node is exactly as broken as it was on arrival, and Slurm has been calling it idle the whole time. The word idle means that slurmd is running and has registered. It says nothing about whether the machine behind it is the machine the configuration describes. ---

secs.head: What idle does and does not prove
secs.body: What you see What it proves What it does not --- --- --- idle in sinfo slurmd is up and the controller heard from it That the CPUs, memory or devices are what slurm.conf says A passing job on the node One task ran That the node is healthy ; the job may have been tiny scontrol show node numbers What the controller was told What the node has , if config overrides is on The third row is the sneaky one, and it is worth seeing happen. ---

secs.head: What Slurm does by default
secs.body: On the test cluster, slurm.conf says each node has CPUs=4 . The machine really has 2. With the site's usual setting, SlurmdParameters=config overrides , the controller believes the file and the nodes show idle . Then that line was removed, the daemons restarted, and the same file with the same nodes gave: By default, Slurm compares what slurmd finds with what the file claims, and refuses to let a node with fewer resources than promised take jobs. That is exactly the protection node 17 would have had. config overrides ("use the configuration file, ignore the hardware") is a legitimate setting, common in containers, test clusters and some cloud setups, and it turns the protection off. With it on, you do the comparison yourself. After the file was fixed to say CPUs=2 and the daemons were restarted, the nodes came back as idle and the comparison below passed. ---

secs.head: Compare the hardware with the promise
secs.body: slurmd -C prints what the daemon detects on the machine it runs on, in the format of a NodeName= line. The controller's view is in scontrol show node . This script, run on the node itself, compares the two and checks the state: The script is node-fit.sh , a plain file you can read on this site, open on GitHub or fetch with its raw link. With config overrides on and the file saying CPUs=4 , on a machine with two: sinfo said idle for this node at the same moment. The PASS on state is the whole problem in one line. With the file corrected: Memory is checked in one direction only: configured must not exceed what the node has. A node configured for less than it has is wasteful but safe, and sites often leave headroom for the operating system on purpose. The script covers CPUs and memory. Sockets, cores, threads, GPUs and other generic resources need their own lines, in the same shape. ---

secs.head: Run a probe before the users do
secs.body: Even a correct configuration does not prove a returning node can run a job: it may have a dead network card or an unmounted filesystem. The safest way to find out is to run a probe job on the node before anyone else can. The obvious plan fails: A drained node accepts no new jobs, not even those inside a reservation. So the order matters: fence the node first, then let it out . A reservation that only you can use goes up while the node is still drained, and only then is the node resumed: The node was idle, and yet an ordinary user's job asking for it waited: A job in the reservation ran: sacct recorded it as COMPLETED . The last step is to release the fence, and the waiting job started on the node as soon as it went: The Duration=10 is a safety net: if you forget the last step, the fence expires on its own after ten minutes. Make the probe job honest. A one-line hostname proves the node accepts jobs; a real probe should exercise what the node is for: write a file to the shared filesystem, load the software stack, run a short GPU kernel, a network ping to another node. The reservations page explains what else a reservation does, including that it never kills jobs already running. ---

secs.head: Let a health check do the routine part
secs.body: A probe is for the moment a node comes back. For everything after that, Slurm can run a program on every node on a timer and drain the ones that fail. The setting is HealthCheckProgram together with HealthCheckInterval , and the GPU health-check page builds and tests one, including a bug where it overwrote the administrator's drain reason. A ready-made option is LBNL's Node Health Check (NHC). Its documentation shows it wired in with two lines: It is configured in /etc/nhc/nhc.conf with one check per line, for example check fs mount rw / , check hw cpuinfo 2 8 8 and check hw physmem 1k 1TB , which cover much of what node-fit.sh does by hand. NHC was not installed on the test cluster, so none of this was run. The slurm.conf it needs must match across the whole cluster, as its documentation notes. ---

secs.head: And the GPUs?
secs.body: The test cluster has none, so this part is a plan and not a result. A node-fit check for a GPU node should compare the number of GPUs the machine reports ( nvidia-smi -L ) with the number configured for the node (the Gres line in scontrol show node ), and the probe job should run something on each GPU, not only list them. A GPU that has "fallen off the bus" still has an entry in the configuration. The GPU health-check page has a tested version of the idea for a missing device. ---

secs.head: Version notes
secs.body: Run on 23.11.4. The GPU health-check page notes that a per-GPU drain, draining one GPU instead of the whole node, comes in 26.11. The hardware comparison and the reservation fence were not run on any other version. Whether the default inval behaviour is the same on newer releases was not checked. ---

secs.head: Back to node 17
secs.body: Replay the afternoon with the checks. The admin plugs node 17 in and runs node-fit.sh on it before resuming anything: (Node 17's numbers are invented. The shape is the output above. The state line fails because the node is still drained, which is expected before it is resumed. The cpus line is the one that matters.) The failure takes seconds to find and a trip into the BIOS to fix. Then the fence goes up, the node is resumed, a probe job runs from the reservation and writes to the shared filesystem, and the fence comes down. Two days later nobody has any theories about the filesystem. Takeaway: idle only means the daemon registered, so before a node returns to service compare what slurmd -C finds with what the controller was told (especially with config overrides , which hides the difference), then fence the node with a reservation and run a real probe job before users can. Next: When Smoke Becomes a Fire Drill covers the heavier tools, SchedMD's own test suite and ReFrame, and where to stop. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Slurm: slurm.conf ( SlurmdParameters=config overrides , HealthCheckProgram ) - Slurm: slurmd ( -C ) - Slurm: Advanced Resource Reservation Guide - LBNL Node Health Check user guide

label: Regression suites
title: When Smoke Becomes a Fire Drill: SchedMD's Test Suite, ReFrame and the Baseline Rule
desc: Part 6 of Slurm Smoke Tests. The runs below were done on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4 from the Ubuntu package,

secs.head: When Smoke Becomes a Fire Drill: SchedMD's Test Suite, ReFrame and the Baseline Rule
secs.body: Part 6 of Slurm Smoke Tests. The runs below were done on a two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4 from the Ubuntu package, accounting on, a Lua submit script that requires --time , both slurmd daemons on one Ubuntu 24.04 machine with 2 CPUs). Both tools were run as an ordinary user. Each run is one run, on a deliberately small and unusual machine, so the pass and fail counts describe this cluster, not Slurm. The names and the story are invented. Do not run either suite against a production cluster without reading its documentation first. SchedMD's own README says its automatic-configuration mode "is not supported for use with local installations".

secs.head: The night before
secs.body: Priya has an upgrade on Saturday. On Friday evening she remembers that SchedMD ships a test suite, runs it against the cluster, and goes to get dinner. When she comes back the summary says 32 failures and 7 errors. She does what anyone would do. She opens a ticket with her manager, drafts a message asking to postpone the upgrade, and starts reading the first failure. It says Please set --time, jobs without one are not accepted . That is not a Slurm problem. That is her own submit rule, from a Wednesday two months ago, refusing a test that did not know it existed. A test suite is a very loud instrument. It only helps if you know what it sounded like before you changed anything. ---

secs.head: Smoke test or regression suite
secs.body: Smoke test Regression suite --- --- --- Question Is it basically working? Did anything that used to work stop working? Size 6 to 10 checks Hundreds of tests Time Seconds to minutes Minutes to hours Runs After every change Before and after the big ones: an upgrade, a new plugin Where Production, as a user A test cluster, or production only with a lot of care Failures mean Something important is down Something differs . Often your own policy Examples The control-plane script SchedMD's suite, ReFrame ---

secs.head: SchedMD's own suite
secs.body: The Slurm source tree has a testsuite directory. Its README describes three suites run through one command, run-tests : a unit suite, an expect suite of shell-style tests grouped by area, and a python suite run under pytest. The python suite has two modes: - Local-config mode is for an existing installation. It aims to avoid changing "your Slurm configuration, accounting database configuration and system environment", and tests that need a different configuration are skipped. - Auto-config mode reconfigures Slurm for each test, and is "intended to be used primarily within automated systems" such as containers. Local-config is the only sensible mode for a real cluster, and the testsuite README notes that several tests say to use a throwaway database. Only the python suite was run here.

secs.head: How it was run
secs.body: The source of the version in use was cloned (the tag for 23.11.4, so the tests match the daemons), given a four-line config, and run as an ordinary user: Two things were not in the README's steps. The wrapper starts pytest-3 , which this machine did not have, so a symlink named pytest-3 pointing at pytest had to be put on the PATH . And the tests need the pexpect Python package. The README has you copy testsuite.conf.sample , which the build generates. The source was not built here, so the four keys were written by hand. The README also says that if the test user is the SlurmUser , you should name an unprivileged user in SlurmTestUser . Running as a normal user avoided that.

secs.head: A first try
secs.body: Three tests, chosen at random, ran in 0.11 seconds:

secs.head: The whole python suite, twice
secs.body: The python suite has 127 test files. The full run, as an ordinary user, with the site's Lua rule switched off and then on: Run Passed Failed Errors Skipped Time --- --- --- --- --- --- Lua submit script off 54 9 5 361 2 min 42 s Lua submit script on (requires --time ) 37 25 7 360 1 min 6 s The huge skip count is the local-config mode doing what the README says: most tests need a configuration this cluster does not have, so they are skipped, not failed. The second run's log has 46 lines containing Please set --time . The first has none. The failing tests were saved to a file for each run, sorted, and compared: The result: 14 failures in the baseline, 32 with the policy on, 18 present only with the policy on, and none present only in the baseline . Those 18 included test 116 22.py::test chdir , test 116 41.py::test job name and test 122 1.py::test submit and cancel . Only some of the messages were read, and the one for test 122 1 quoted sbatch --wrap "sleep 60" being refused for lacking a time limit. The 46 mentions of the rule in the log make it the likely cause of the rest, but each was not checked. The suite did not find 18 broken things. It most probably found one rule, many times. The 14 that remained with the policy off were not investigated. Their names suggest causes specific to this setup: four test version tests, a failing sgather --usage , and tests that need more CPUs than a 2-CPU machine has. That is a guess from the test names, not a finding. It is the point of a baseline: those 14 are noise on this cluster, and they stay noise until something changes. ---

secs.head: ReFrame
secs.body: ReFrame is a framework for writing regression tests for HPC systems. A test is a Python class that says what to run and what a correct answer looks like; ReFrame generates the job script, submits it to the scheduler, waits, and checks the output. Its documentation says it does not assume a run succeeded: the test carries its own validation. Installed into a virtualenv with pip install reframe-hpc (version 4.11.0 here), it needs two files. A settings file tells it how to reach Slurm: And a test file holds the checks. One passes on purpose and one fails on purpose: Behind the scenes it wrote this job script and submitted it with sbatch : Note the --time line: ReFrame set it from time limit , which is why it worked on a cluster that refuses jobs without one. Note also what sacct said about the failing test's job: COMPLETED . The job ran perfectly. The answer was wrong, and only the framework that knew what the right answer was could tell. A smoke test that only looks at job states would have passed it. Two practical points come from the ReFrame documentation and were not tested on a second setup. Its stage and output directories must live on storage shared with the compute nodes, so pass --prefix pointing there. And its Slurm backend gets job state from sacct , so it needs accounting enabled; with accounting off, its squeue -based backend is the alternative. ---

secs.head: Which tool for which question
secs.body: Question Tool --- --- "Did my change break the basics?" The control-plane smoke test, every time "Do my rules still do what I mean?" The policy smoke test "Did the upgrade change behaviour I did not know I relied on?" SchedMD's suite, on a test cluster, before and after, with a baseline "Does my site's software, filesystem and network still work for my users?" ReFrame (or similar) tests written for your own workloads, so they can also check performance SchedMD's suite tests Slurm. It knows nothing about your filesystem, your container runtime or your GPU drivers. ReFrame tests what you teach it. Neither replaces the smoke test, and the smoke test replaces neither. ---

secs.head: Version notes
secs.body: The suite was run on 23.11.4 only, with that version's tests. Newer source trees have more tests, and the layout of testsuite may change, so read the README of the version you run. The unit and expect suites were not run at all. One thing worth knowing: the suite found the Lua policy in one run, and the changelog lists 26.05 as logging a stack trace for runtime errors in a submit script, which makes a policy failure inside a test easier to read. ---

secs.head: Back to the night before
secs.body: Replay Friday with the baseline rule. Last month, on a quiet evening, Priya ran the suite once and saved the list of failures: 14 of them, all things she could explain or at least recognise. She wrote the file into the cluster's runbook with the date and the Slurm version. On Friday she runs it again, as the first step of the upgrade rehearsal on the test cluster, and compares. comm -13 prints 18 names, and she reads the first one: Please set --time . She switches the time-limit rule off on the test cluster for the run, reruns, and the 18 disappear. The Saturday upgrade goes ahead. After it, she runs the suite one more time and compares with the same file. Nothing is new. Takeaway: a regression suite finds differences , not faults, so run it on a test cluster, save the list of failures as a baseline before the change, and compare after (new failures are your findings, old ones are noise), and use ReFrame when the question is whether your own site's workloads still work, because it can check the answer and not only the job state. Next: back to the series overview, which has a one-page checklist that ties the six together. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - SchedMD Slurm testsuite README ( run-tests , the unit, expect and python suites, testsuite.conf ) - SchedMD Slurm python testsuite README (local-config and auto-config modes) - ReFrame tutorial (tests as Python classes, the slurm scheduler backend) - Slurm: Upgrade Guide ("Test key functionality")

label: **Mixing GPU Types in Slurm**
title: Mixing GPU Types in Slurm - Overview
desc: A three-part series on a question that sounds simple: can one Slurm job get H100s and A100s at the same time? Short answ

secs.head: Mixing GPU Types in Slurm - Overview
secs.body: A three-part series on a question that sounds simple: can one Slurm job get H100s and A100s at the same time? Short answer: yes, in four different ways. Long answer: the scheduler part works fine; what usually breaks is the job you put on top of it. By the end you'll know which way to use, which to avoid, and how to explain the difference.

secs.head: The myth, the correction, and the real answer
secs.body: There are three stages most people go through with this question. Stage 1, the myth: "Slurm can't give one job two kinds of GPU. A job gets one kind of node." Stage 2, the correction: "Oh, it can. There's a thing called heterogeneous jobs. But it doesn't really work." Stage 3, the real answer: Slurm has supported heterogeneous jobs since version 17.11, and there are three other ways to end up with mixed GPUs besides. The scheduling works as documented. What "doesn't work" is something else: putting one tightly synchronized training run across GPUs of different speeds, and paying the scheduling costs that co-scheduling brings. Those are real, but they're about the workload and the queue , not a broken feature. The difference matters. "Slurm can't" ends the conversation. "Slurm can, here's when it's worth it" is what a senior engineer says. ---

secs.head: The route
secs.body: Page The question it answers --- ------ ------------------------- 1 Four ways to ask for mixed GPUs What exactly can Slurm do, and which innocent-looking option mixes GPUs by accident? 2 Why mixed training disappoints Why does a 16-GPU job with 8 H100s run like 16 A100s, and what does co-scheduling cost in the queue? 3 Where heterogeneous jobs shine Which workloads actually benefit, how should admins set up the cluster, and what's the interview answer? ---

secs.head: Who this is for
secs.body: HPC and AI platform engineers running Slurm on clusters that grew over time: a rack of A100s from two years ago, a row of H100s from last quarter, maybe something newer on order. Also anyone preparing for a scheduler question in an AI-infrastructure interview. ---

secs.head: What this series is based on
secs.body: Source Used for -------- ---------- Slurm documentation (version 26.05): Heterogeneous Job Support , Generic Resource (GRES) Scheduling , the sbatch man page Every Slurm behavior and limitation described NVIDIA A100 and H100 datasheets Every GPU speed comparison [!IMPORTANT] The Slurm commands in this series are taken from SchedMD's documentation and weren't run on a live cluster while writing. Try them on a test partition first. Behavior can differ between Slurm versions; the pages note the version a feature arrived in where it matters.

label: 1. Four ways to mix GPUs
title: Four Ways to Ask Slurm for Mixed GPUs
desc: Part 1 of the Mixing GPU Types in Slurm series. Slurm doesn't have one way to give a job different GPUs. It has four, an

secs.head: Four Ways to Ask Slurm for Mixed GPUs
secs.body: Part 1 of the Mixing GPU Types in Slurm series. Slurm doesn't have one way to give a job different GPUs. It has four, and they behave very differently. By the end of this page you'll know what each one allocates, which one to reach for, and why a single in a constraint has quietly mixed GPU types on more clusters than any heterogeneous job ever has.

secs.head: The job that started fast and ran slow
secs.body: A researcher needs 16 GPUs for a training run. The H100 partition has a two-day queue. The A100 nodes are busy too. So she gets clever and writes: "Either kind is fine," she thinks. The job starts in twenty minutes. She goes for lunch feeling smart. When she comes back, the loss curve is crawling. squeue shows the job is running on two H100 nodes and two A100 nodes. Slurm did exactly what she asked: give me nodes that have H100s or A100s. It never promised they'd all be the same. She didn't submit a "heterogeneous job." She doesn't know the term. She mixed GPU types with one character. That's the first lesson of this series: mixed allocations happen by accident far more often than on purpose. To see why, start with how Slurm tells GPUs apart at all. ---

secs.head: First, how Slurm knows a GPU's type
secs.body: Slurm describes GPUs as GRES (generic resources). An admin can give each GPU a type , either in gres.conf or by letting Slurm detect it through NVML. With autodetection, Slurm matches the type you configure against the GPU's reported name, and any substring works: the GRES docs show a GPU detected as geforce rtx 2060 that can be typed as geforce , rtx or 2060 . Admins can also tag nodes with features , free-form labels like h100 or a100 that jobs match with --constraint . So there are two separate labeling systems: Label Lives on Requested with Answers ------- ---------- ---------------- --------- GRES type Each GPU --gres=gpu:h100:4 , --gpus=h100:8 "Which GPUs inside the node?" Feature Each node --constraint=h100 "Which nodes?" Every way of mixing GPUs uses one or both. Here they are, from the most common to the most deliberate. ---

secs.head: Way 1: typed GRES, one kind per request
secs.body: The everyday request names a type and a count: The GRES docs define the form as name[:type:count] for --gres and [type]:count for the --gpu options. One detail matters a lot here: --gres is per node. It asks for the same thing on every node in the job. That gives one legitimate way to get two types: a node that physically contains both. The GRES docs' own example configures nodes with Gres=gpu:tesla:2,gpu:kepler:2 , two kinds of GPU in one chassis. On nodes like that, a job can ask for some of each. Data-center GPU servers are rarely built that way, so for A100-plus-H100 this is mostly a curiosity. Another rule from the same docs: typed and untyped requests must be consistent within a job. If the allocation asked for --gres=gpu:2 , a step can't then ask for --gres=gpu:tesla:2 , and vice versa. So a single, uniform per-node request can't say "H100s on these nodes, A100s on those." For that you need different nodes to be treated differently, which is where constraints come in. ---

secs.head: Way 2: constraints, and the trap in the bar
secs.body: --constraint filters nodes by feature. The sbatch man page lists several operators, and the difference between two of them is the whole story of the researcher's lost afternoon. Operator Example Means ---------- --------- ------- AND --constraint="intel&gpu" Every node has both features OR --constraint="h100\ a100" Every node has at least one of them. Different nodes can have different ones Matching OR --constraint="[h100\ a100]" All nodes have the same one, but either is fine Multiple counts --constraint="[h100 2&a100 2]" Exactly 2 nodes with h100 and 2 with a100 Read the second and third rows twice. They differ by a pair of square brackets. - Plain OR is an accidental mixer . In a multi-node job it can hand you a blend. That's what happened to the researcher. - Matching OR is what she meant: "give me whichever kind starts first, but don't mix." The man page's own example is [rack1 rack2 rack3 rack4] : all nodes on one rack, any rack. - Multiple counts is a deliberate mixer . You say exactly how many nodes of each feature you want. Combined with an untyped GPU request like --gres=gpu:4 , every node gets 4 GPUs, of whatever kind that node has. A SchedMD engineer, discussing the feature-parsing code, described square-bracket counts as "essentially the same as a heterogeneous job." That's a good way to think of it: a lightweight version, where every node still gets the same per-node request. [!WARNING] Audit your users' constraints. On any cluster with more than one GPU generation, search job scripts for --constraint with a bare and no brackets. Every multi-node job using it can land on mixed hardware, and the user probably doesn't know. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Three requests. For each, could the job end up with both H100 and A100 nodes? 1. --nodes=4 --gres=gpu:4 --constraint="[h100 a100]" 2. --nodes=4 --gres=gpu:h100:4 3. --nodes=4 --gres=gpu:4 --constraint="h100 a100" Answers: (1) no, matching OR keeps all nodes the same; (2) no, every node must have 4 H100s; (3) yes, plain OR allows a mix. If you got all three, you already understand constraints better than most job scripts on most clusters. Now for the feature that was actually built for mixing. ---

secs.head: Way 3: heterogeneous jobs, the real thing
secs.body: A heterogeneous job is a job made of several components , each with its own full set of options. Slurm's docs say each component has "virtually all job options available including partition, account and QOS." You separate components with : on the command line, or with SBATCH hetjob lines in a script: Here's what you get, all from the heterogeneous-jobs documentation: - Separate job IDs, one family. Each component gets its own job id ; they share a het job id equal to the first component's ID. squeue shows them as 123+0 , 123+1 . - Started together. Components are scheduled at the same time or not at all. - The script runs once, on the first node of component 0. - srun launches on component 0 by default. --het-group chooses others. - Per-component environment. Variables get a HET GROUP <n suffix, like SLURM JOB NODELIST HET GROUP 1 . - One MPI world, if you want it. srun prog0 : prog1 puts both components in a single MPI COMM WORLD with non-overlapping ranks. Separate srun calls give separate worlds. The docs add two warnings about that last point, in capitals: running one application across components doesn't work with all MPI implementations or Slurm MPI plugins , and mpirun "would require substantial modification" to support it, with no such work known to SchedMD. Admins can switch cross-component steps off entirely with SchedulerParameters=disable hetjob steps . So heterogeneous jobs really do allocate H100s and A100s to one job, cleanly, with each part sized independently. "Can't" is wrong. But notice the shape of the example: the H100s and A100s run different programs . Keep that in mind; it's the key to part 3. ---

secs.head: Way 4: heterogeneous steps, mixing inside one allocation
secs.body: Since Slurm 20.11 , you can also do the reverse: get one ordinary allocation, then launch a single step with different layouts on different nodes, using the same : syntax with srun . The docs' example takes two exclusive nodes with 10 GPUs and gives one step 4 tasks with 4 GPUs on one node and 1 task with 6 GPUs on the other. Two limits from the docs: the step components must run on unique nodes , and you can't request heterogeneous steps from within a heterogeneous job . Useful when the allocation is uniform but the work isn't, for example one process that wants a whole node's GPUs and several that want one each. ---

secs.head: The four ways side by side
secs.body: Way Syntax Mixes types? On purpose? Best for ----- -------- ------------- ------------- ---------- Typed GRES --gres=gpu:h100:4 Only on nodes that contain both Yes Asking for one specific kind Constraint, plain OR -C "h100\ a100" Yes, possibly Usually not Single-node jobs only Constraint, matching OR -C "[h100\ a100]" No Yes "Either kind, whichever starts first" Constraint, counts -C "[h100 2&a100 2]" Yes, exact node counts Yes Simple splits with the same per-node request Heterogeneous job ... : ... / SBATCH hetjob Yes, fully independent parts Yes Different programs on different hardware Heterogeneous step srun ... : ... in one allocation Layout only (same allocation) Yes Uneven work inside a uniform allocation Takeaway: Slurm can absolutely give one job H100s and A100s, deliberately with heterogeneous jobs or constraint counts, and accidentally with a bare , so learn the brackets and audit for the bar. So it works. Then why does everyone who tries to train across H100s and A100s come back disappointed? That's part 2. ---

label: 2. Why mixed training disappoints
title: Why Mixed-GPU Training Disappoints
desc: Part 2 of the Mixing GPU Types in Slurm series. Part 1 showed that Slurm can allocate H100s and A100s to one job. This p

secs.head: Why Mixed-GPU Training Disappoints
secs.body: Part 2 of the Mixing GPU Types in Slurm series. Part 1 showed that Slurm can allocate H100s and A100s to one job. This page is about what happens next. By the end you'll be able to explain, with datasheet numbers, why a mixed training run is slower than it looks, and list the scheduling costs heterogeneous jobs carry even when the workload is perfect.

secs.head: Doing it properly this time
secs.body: After the accidental mix in part 1, our researcher reads the docs. She learns about heterogeneous jobs and does it properly: component 0 is two nodes of 4 H100s, component 1 is two nodes of 4 A100s. One srun across both groups, one distributed training run over 16 GPUs. It schedules. It launches. It trains. And it runs at almost exactly the speed it would have on 16 A100s. Her eight H100s, the most expensive hardware in the building, spend most of every training step doing nothing. Nothing is broken. Slurm delivered precisely the allocation she asked for. The problem is the shape of the workload, and it has a name. ---

secs.head: The rowing boat rule
secs.body: Picture a rowing boat with eight rowers. Four are Olympic athletes. Four are enthusiastic amateurs. The boat moves as one: every stroke starts together, and the next stroke can't start until everyone has finished this one. How fast does the boat go? The athletes finish each stroke early, then sit with oars raised, waiting. The boat moves at the amateurs' pace . The athletes add almost nothing. Standard data-parallel training is that boat. Every GPU processes its share of the batch, then all GPUs exchange gradients (an all-reduce , on NVIDIA GPUs usually performed by the NCCL library) before anyone can take the next step. That exchange is a meeting point: nobody leaves until everybody arrives. So the rule is: A synchronous job runs at the speed of its slowest participant. Every faster GPU in the job finishes early and waits at the all-reduce. The waiting doesn't show up as an error. It shows up as a GPU that's "allocated" and "busy" on your dashboards while doing no useful work. ---

secs.head: The numbers: how much the fast GPUs wait
secs.body: Here's how far apart the two generations are, from NVIDIA's datasheets (80 GB SXM versions): A100 H100 H100 ÷ A100 --- --- --- --- Dense BF16 Tensor Core 312 TFLOPS 989 TFLOPS ~3.2× HBM bandwidth 2,039 GB/s 3.35 TB/s ~1.6× NVLink per GPU 600 GB/s 900 GB/s 1.5× Memory 80 GB 80 GB 1× Take the simplest case: each GPU gets the same share of the batch, and the step is limited by math, as large training steps usually are. An H100 finishes its share in about 1/3.2 of the time an A100 takes. Then it waits. $$\text{H100 idle fraction} \approx 1 - \frac{312}{989} \approx 68\%$$ Roughly two-thirds of every H100's time is spent waiting for the A100s. Throughput is set by 16 GPUs moving at A100 pace: you've built a 16-A100 job that happens to cost H100 hours. If the step is limited by memory bandwidth instead, the gap is smaller (about 1.6×) and the H100s wait about 40% of the time. Either way, the fast GPUs pay for the slow ones. [!NOTE] These are ceiling-based ratios from datasheets, not measurements. Real training steps mix math, memory and communication, so the exact waiting share will differ. The direction never does: in a synchronous job, the faster GPUs always wait. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ A team has 8 H100s free and 8 A100s free. Option A: one 16-GPU mixed job. Option B: run on the 8 H100s alone. For a compute-bound training run with perfect scaling, which finishes sooner? Work it out in "A100-equivalents." Option A: 16 GPUs at A100 pace = 16 A100-equivalents. Option B: 8 H100s at about 3.2× each = about 25 A100-equivalents. The 8 H100s alone beat all 16 GPUs together , on these ceiling numbers. Adding the A100s didn't just fail to help; it made the job slower. And it tied up eight A100s that another team could have used for their own job. That's the counterintuitive heart of this page: adding slower GPUs to a synchronous job can reduce its speed. ---

secs.head: The features the A100s switch off
secs.body: Speed isn't the only mismatch. The two generations don't support the same things. FP8. The H100 datasheet lists FP8 Tensor Core performance (1,979 TFLOPS dense). The A100 datasheet has no FP8 row at all; its lowest floating-point Tensor Core formats are BF16 and FP16. Training recipes that use FP8 on Hopper can't use it on Ampere. A single run spanning both has to drop to a format both support, giving up the H100's biggest speed lever. Interconnect inside the node. A100 systems use NVLink at 600 GB/s per GPU, H100 systems 900 GB/s. Collective operations that span both kinds of node run at the pace of the slower links, plus whatever network connects the two groups. Memory size, if the models differ. Both GPUs in the table have 80 GB, so that pairing is fine. Mix an 80 GB H100 with a 40 GB A100 and the smaller memory caps the per-GPU batch for everyone, or crashes the ranks that run out first. Software paths. Kernels, libraries and container images are often built and tuned per architecture. A mixed job needs one software stack that runs correctly, and ideally fast, on both. That's more testing for every upgrade, forever. ---

secs.head: Can you rebalance the work?
secs.body: The obvious fix: give the H100s more of the batch, about 3× as many samples per step, so everyone finishes together. It's possible. It's also your problem to build and maintain: - The data loading has to hand out uneven shares and keep them balanced as speeds drift. - Gradients from uneven shares must be weighted correctly, or the training math changes. - The right ratio depends on the model, sequence length and precision, so it has to be measured, not guessed. - Memory limits still apply: a larger share on the H100s must still fit in 80 GB. Teams that try this usually discover that the engineering time costs more than the A100s were worth to the job. Rebalancing is a research project, not a scheduler setting. ---

secs.head: The queue tax: what co-scheduling costs
secs.body: Even with a perfect workload, heterogeneous jobs pay a price in the queue. Every item below is from Slurm's heterogeneous-jobs documentation. All components start together, or none do. Each component might be able to start at a different time on its own. A heterogeneous job waits until every component can start at once. The more components, and the busier each partition, the longer that wait. Only the backfill scheduler can start them. The docs say the more frequently executed main scheduling logic works first-in, first-out and can't schedule all components together, so heterogeneous jobs are left entirely to the backfill scheduler. Their pending reason isn't even set until a backfill pass has looked at them. Backfill makes simplifying assumptions. It typically needs to be able to place each component on a different node to begin the allocation, even if components could actually share a node. You can starve yourself. With overlapping partitions, an early component can grab nodes that a later component needed. The docs give an example: partition p1 has 10 nodes and p2 uses 5 of the same nodes. Ask for 5 nodes in each, and the scheduler may hand some p2 nodes to the first component, leaving a job that can never start. Limits count every component. Each component counts as a "job" for resource limits. The docs' example: a user limited to 2 running jobs submits a 3-component heterogeneous job, which "will have an adverse effect upon scheduling other jobs." Some features don't come along. From the limitations list: Not available Detail --------------- -------- Job arrays Arrays of heterogeneous jobs aren't supported Licenses on later components License requests only on the first component Gang scheduling Not supported Moving between federated clusters The whole job runs on the submitting cluster Magnetic reservations Won't attract a heterogeneous job unless it names the reservation Cancelling one pending component Only the whole job can be cancelled while pending Requeue, suspend, resume per component Leader only, applies to all None of this means the feature is broken. It means co-scheduling is a hard problem, and Slurm makes you pay for it in queue time and flexibility. ---

secs.head: So is it "not functional"?
secs.body: Here's the honest scorecard: Claim Verdict ------- --------- "Slurm can't allocate H100s and A100s to one job." False. Heterogeneous jobs, constraint counts, and even a stray \ all do it "The heterogeneous-jobs feature doesn't work." False. It schedules and launches as documented, with documented limits "One synchronous training run across H100s and A100s is a bad deal." True, usually. It runs at A100 pace and loses H100-only features "Heterogeneous jobs cost extra queue time and flexibility." True. Co-scheduling, backfill only, no arrays, limits per component So the precise way to say it: Slurm's mixed allocation is functional; tightly coupled training on mixed GPUs usually isn't worth it. The feature works. The rowing boat doesn't. Takeaway: in a synchronous job every GPU waits for the slowest one, so 8 H100s plus 8 A100s train like 16 A100s, often slower than the 8 H100s alone, and co-scheduling adds a queue tax on top. So if mixing H100s and A100s in one training run is usually a bad idea, why did SchedMD build heterogeneous jobs at all? Because the boat was never the point. Part 3 shows the workloads where different hardware for different parts is exactly right. ---

secs.body: - Slurm: Heterogeneous Job Support (limitations, scheduling, system administrator information) - NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU datasheet - NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU datasheet

label: 3. Where hetjobs shine
title: Where Heterogeneous Jobs Shine
desc: Part 3 of the Mixing GPU Types in Slurm series, the last one. Part 2 showed why one synchronous training run across H100

secs.head: Where Heterogeneous Jobs Shine
secs.body: Part 3 of the Mixing GPU Types in Slurm series, the last one. Part 2 showed why one synchronous training run across H100s and A100s is usually a bad deal. This page is the other half: the jobs where different hardware for different parts is exactly the right design. By the end you'll have the rule that separates the two, a setup guide for admins, and an answer that turns "Slurm can't do that" into a strong interview moment.

secs.head: The restaurant, not the rowing boat
secs.body: A rowing boat needs identical rowers because everyone does the same job at the same moment. A restaurant is different. It has a head chef, line cooks, a dishwasher and waiters. Nobody expects the dishwasher to be as fast at cooking as the head chef. They do different jobs , connected by queues: orders go in, plates come out. If the dishwasher is slower, a stack of plates builds up, but the kitchen keeps cooking. That's what heterogeneous jobs were designed for. Look at the example in Slurm's own documentation: one node with lots of memory running a program called server , and 32 other nodes running a program called client . Different programs, different hardware, each sized for its role. Nobody in that example is rowing in sync. ---

secs.head: The rule: mix across roles, not within a role
secs.body: Part 2's problem was that every GPU did the same job , in lockstep . Take either of those away and mixing makes sense. Mix hardware across roles, not within a role. Question If yes If no ---------- -------- ------- Do the GPU types run different programs or roles? Mixing can fit Same role on different speeds: the rowing boat Are the parts connected by queues or occasional messages, rather than a per-step barrier? Each part runs at its own pace Everyone waits for the slowest Does each part have needs that suit one kind of hardware? Put each part where it fits best No reason to mix Three yeses is a heterogeneous job. Here are the patterns that pass. ---

secs.head: Pattern 1: trainer and rollout workers
secs.body: Reinforcement learning on language models often has two roles: - A trainer that updates the model's weights: big matrix math, compute-heavy, benefits from the fastest GPUs. - Rollout workers that run the current model to generate samples: mostly inference, and as the LLM inference series explains, text generation is limited by memory bandwidth far more than by compute. The roles are connected by a queue of samples going one way and occasional weight updates going the other. They don't meet at every step. That's a natural heterogeneous job: component 0 on H100s for the trainer, component 1 on A100s for the workers. Each runs at its own pace. The A100s do useful work instead of slowing anyone down. Two srun calls, two separate worlds, one allocation that starts and ends together. The trainer can find its workers through the per-component variables such as SLURM JOB NODELIST HET GROUP 1 . ---

secs.head: Pattern 2: server and clients
secs.body: The documentation's own pattern, generalized: one component is a coordinator, a parameter store, a database or an inference endpoint; the other is a fleet of workers that talk to it. The coordinator might want a big-memory node; the workers want GPUs. Or the coordinator wants one H100 node and the workers are happy on older GPUs. Slurm gives each its own size, partition, account and QOS, and guarantees they start together, so workers never come up before the thing they connect to. ---

secs.head: Pattern 3: "either kind, never both"
secs.body: Sometimes the honest need isn't mixing at all. It's flexibility: "I can run on H100s or A100s; give me whichever is free first." That's matching OR from part 1: All four nodes are the same kind, so the rowing boat stays matched. The job just starts sooner. For most researchers who think they want "mixed GPUs," this is the request they actually need. Make sure the job adapts to whichever kind it gets: for example, enable FP8 only when it lands on H100s. ---

secs.head: Pattern 4: uneven layouts in one allocation
secs.body: When the allocation is uniform but the work inside it isn't, a heterogeneous step (Slurm 20.11 and later) lets one srun give different nodes different layouts. The docs' example splits a 10-GPU, 2-node allocation into one node with 4 tasks on 4 GPUs and another with 1 task on 6 GPUs. No co-scheduling of separate jobs, so none of the queue tax from part 2. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Four requests from users. Heterogeneous job, matching OR, or "please don't"? 1. "I want to fine-tune on 8 H100s plus the 4 idle A100s to go faster." 2. "My evaluation harness runs a judge model next to my training job, and I want them to start together." 3. "I don't care which GPUs, I just want to start today." 4. "My simulation runs on CPU nodes and streams data to a GPU model." Answers: (1) please don't: same role in lockstep, the rowing boat; (2) heterogeneous job: different roles, loosely connected; (3) matching OR; (4) heterogeneous job: CPU and GPU components, connected by a stream. ---

secs.head: For admins: setting up a multi-generation cluster
secs.body: The configuration below uses standard slurm.conf and gres.conf parameters described in Slurm's GRES documentation and man pages. Adapt names to your site and try it on a test partition first.

secs.head: Label GPUs and nodes the same way
secs.body: Give every node both a GRES type (for --gres / --gpus ) and a feature (for --constraint ), using the same short names so users only learn one vocabulary: With AutoDetect=nvml in gres.conf , Slurm reads the GPUs from the driver, and the type in slurm.conf only needs to be a substring of the detected name. Check what a node reports with slurmd -C before choosing names.

secs.head: Decide how partitions map to generations
secs.body: Layout Upside Downside -------- -------- ---------- One partition per generation Simple; plain OR can't mix across partitions by accident Users must pick; idle capacity in one isn't visible from the other One shared GPU partition, features to choose Flexible; matching OR lets jobs take whichever is free A bare \ can mix generations in multi-node jobs If you choose the shared partition, guard it.

secs.head: Guard against the accidental mix
secs.body: Slurm's docs note the job submit plugin runs independently for each component of a heterogeneous job, and it sees every regular job too. That's the place to enforce site policy, for example: flag or reject multi-node GPU jobs whose constraint uses a bare without brackets, with a message pointing users to matching OR.

secs.head: Tune the controls heterogeneous jobs care about
secs.body: Setting What it does, per the docs --------- --------------------------- SchedulerParameters=disable hetjob steps Disables steps that span more than one component cluster-wide (useful if your MPI stack can't handle them) SchedulerParameters=whole hetjob Makes cancel, hold and release on any component apply to the whole job Per-user running-job limits Remember every component counts as a job; a low limit can block multi-component jobs

secs.head: Teach users the three lines
secs.body: Most mixing problems are vocabulary problems. Put this in your user docs: You want Write ---------- ------- A specific kind --gres=gpu:h100:4 Either kind, all the same --constraint="[h100\ a100]" Different hardware for different programs A heterogeneous job ( SBATCH hetjob ) ---

secs.head: The decision table
secs.body: Your situation Use Why ---------------- ----- ----- One training run, same role on every GPU One GPU type Synchronous jobs run at the slowest GPU's pace Flexible about the type, but not mixing Matching OR [h100\ a100] Faster start, matched hardware Different programs that start together and talk loosely Heterogeneous job Each part sized for its role Uniform allocation, uneven work inside Heterogeneous step No co-scheduling cost Need job arrays, gang scheduling or migration between federated clusters Not a heterogeneous job Unsupported for heterogeneous jobs Fixed node split, same per-node request Constraint counts [h100 2&a100 2] Lightweight, but you're mixing: be sure the workload tolerates it ---

secs.head: The interview answer
secs.body: "Can Slurm allocate different GPU types, say H100s and A100s, to one job?" "Yes. Since 17.11 it supports heterogeneous jobs: several components, each with its own resources, partition and QOS, scheduled together. You can also get a fixed split with constraint counts, or mix by accident with a plain OR constraint, which is why I'd use matching OR, the bracketed form, when users just want either type. The real question is whether you should. For one synchronous training run, no: every step waits at the all-reduce for the slowest GPU, so eight H100s plus eight A100s train at A100 pace, and on datasheet numbers the eight H100s alone would be faster. You also lose H100-only features like FP8. Heterogeneous jobs also pay a queue cost: all components must start together, only the backfill scheduler places them, and they don't support job arrays. Where they shine is different roles on different hardware: a trainer on H100s with rollout or inference workers on A100s, or a server with a fleet of clients. The rule I use is: mix hardware across roles, not within a role." Takeaway: heterogeneous jobs are for restaurants, not rowing boats, so give different roles different hardware, give one synchronous role one kind of GPU, and give flexible users matching OR. That's the series. You started with "Slurm can't" and "it doesn't really work." You're leaving with "it works, here's exactly when to use it." Back to the overview. ---

title: Why Is My Job Still Pending?
desc: The question every cluster admin answers ten times a week, and every user asks the moment their job doesn't start. This

secs.head: Why Is My Job Still Pending?
secs.body: The question every cluster admin answers ten times a week, and every user asks the moment their job doesn't start. This series answers it properly, for both sides of the ticket: what the reason column means, how Slurm decides who goes first, and which limits make a job wait forever without telling anyone. Tested on Slurm 23.11.4 (Ubuntu 24.04 packages) with slurmdbd and MariaDB, and checked against the Slurm 26.11 documentation for anything that changed since. ---

secs.head: Contents
secs.body: File Description --- --- 1. Reading the Reason Column What each common pending reason means, which ones fix themselves, which never will, and a small triage script 2. Who Goes First The multifactor priority formula, fairshare, age and QOS weights, reading sprio and sshare , and the all-zero default 3. Limits That Wait Forever QOS and account limits in practice, the second QOS that bypasses your cap, partition QOS, and DenyOnLimit ---

secs.head: How the pages were tested
secs.body: - Lab: a controller ( head01 ) running slurmctld, slurmdbd and MariaDB 10.11, four CPU nodes ( cn001 – cn004 , 2 CPUs each) and one GPU node ( gpu001 ) with four GPUs, all Ubuntu 24.04 containers. - The GPUs were fake: four device files, enough for Slurm to schedule and count them, not to run CUDA. Every GPU result on these pages is about scheduling, which is all these pages claim. - Every reason on these pages was produced on purpose and its output copied from the terminal. The triage script was run against each reason, and had a bug that the pages show.
