Read it first if sacctmgr is new to you. - Backfill tuning: why squeue --start estimates drift, and how the backfill scheduler finds gaps. - Lab build cheatsheet: every step used to build this lab, as copy-paste commands. - Slurm for AI Clusters: the next series, on the same lab.

label: 1. Reading the reason column
title: Reading the Reason Column: Why Is My Slurm Job Pending?
desc: Part 1 of Why Is My Job Still Pending? By the end you'll read any pending job's reason in one look, know whether it will

secs.head: Reading the Reason Column: Why Is My Slurm Job Pending?
secs.body: Part 1 of Why Is My Job Still Pending? By the end you'll read any pending job's reason in one look, know whether it will ever start, and have a script that tells users what to try before they open a ticket. - Two days in the queue - Where the reason lives - Only one job says Resources - The common reasons, produced on purpose - Rejected before it ever queues - What users can fix themselves - A triage script, and the bug we found in it - Back to the two days - References ---

secs.head: Two days in the queue
secs.body: A PhD student submits a training job on Monday morning and checks on Wednesday. Still PD . They've watched other people's jobs start and finish around theirs. They open a ticket: "the scheduler is broken, my job isn't starting". The admin runs one command and sees PartitionTimeLimit . The student asked for three days on a partition whose limit is two. The job was never going to start, and Slurm said so from the first second, in a column nobody read. Most pending jobs are fine; they're just waiting. A few will wait forever. The reason column tells you which, if you know how to read it. [!NOTE] Lab: Slurm 23.11.4 with slurmdbd, four CPU nodes in partition cpu (2 CPUs each, 2-day MaxTime ) and one node in partition gpu . Every reason below was produced on purpose and copied from the terminal. Reason names come from squeue(1) , section JOB REASON CODES. ---

secs.head: Where the reason lives
secs.body: Slurm records one reason for every pending job: its best single explanation of why that job isn't running right now . Three ways to see it: The default squeue output puts the reason in the last column, in brackets, as NODELIST(REASON) . Easy to miss when you're looking for a node list. ---

secs.head: Only one job says Resources
secs.body: We filled the cpu partition, then submitted more jobs. This is the most misread line on any cluster: Reason Means --- --- Resources This job is first in line for the partition. It's waiting for nodes to free up Priority One or more jobs with higher priority are ahead of it in the same partition Only the top job in a partition shows Resources . Everyone behind it shows Priority , even when they'd fit the moment something frees up. So Priority doesn't mean "your priority is low"; it means "you're not first". (Alice submitted before bob and carol, and still sits behind both. That's fairshare, and it's part 2.) Smaller jobs behind the queue can still start early, through the backfill scheduler, if they fit in a gap without delaying the top job. See backfill tuning. ---

secs.head: The common reasons, produced on purpose
secs.body: Here's every reason we produced, with the command that caused it, whether it fixes itself, and who can fix it: Reason How we caused it Starts by itself? Fix --- --- --- --- Resources Partition full Yes Wait. squeue --start gives an estimate Priority Behind other jobs Yes Wait. Part 2 explains the order Dependency --dependency=afterok:12 , job 12 still pending Yes, when 12 succeeds Wait DependencyNeverSatisfied afterok on a job that exited 3 Never scancel it and resubmit BeginTime --begin=now+2hours Yes, at that time Nothing, or scontrol update jobid=<id starttime=now JobHeldUser sbatch -H Never scontrol release <id ReqNodeNotAvail, Unavail -w cn004 while cn004 was drained Only when the node returns Drop the -w , or ask why it's drained: sinfo -R PartitionTimeLimit -t 3-00:00:00 on a 2-day partition Never Lower the time limit QOSMaxGRESPerUser More GPUs than the QOS allows per user Depends; see part 3 Wait for your other jobs, or ask less AssocGrpGRES The account's GPU limit was reached When the account's other jobs end Wait, or talk to your group The three marked Never are the ones that generate tickets. Nothing about the cluster will change their fate. PartitionTimeLimit is the sneakiest: by default Slurm accepts the job and lets it wait. ( EnforcePartLimits in slurm.conf makes it reject such jobs at submission instead.) JobHeldUser showed priority 0 in our lab. A held job isn't considered at all. ---

secs.head: Rejected before it ever queues
secs.body: Some mistakes never get as far as a reason. sbatch refuses them and prints why. From the same lab: What we asked What sbatch said --- --- --mem=64G on nodes with 3 GB configured Memory specification can not be satisfied / Requested node configuration is not available -A chem by a user who isn't in that account Invalid account or account/partition combination specified --dependency=afternotok:999999 (no such job) Job dependency problem These are the good failures: immediate, specific, and impossible to miss. ---

secs.head: What users can fix themselves
secs.body: Several fixes don't need an admin. A user can update their own pending job, as long as the change makes it smaller or later : Both ran as the job's owner in the lab, exit 0, and both jobs moved to Priority . Asking for more is refused: Only an operator or admin can raise a limit. That's on purpose: otherwise a user could submit a short job to get backfilled, then extend it. ---

secs.head: A triage script, and the bug we found in it
secs.body: Most of the tickets above have the same answer, so put the answer next to the question. This script takes a job ID, reads the reason, and prints what to try. Save it as /usr/local/bin/whypending on login nodes: We ran it against every reason above. A few of the answers: An unknown job ID prints Slurm's own Invalid job id specified and exits 1. The bug: the first version counted only jobs with higher priority as "ahead". Two jobs from the same user had the same priority (2000), and the second one was told: True, and useless: it was second in line. Slurm breaks priority ties by submission order, so the count now includes equal-priority jobs with a lower job ID. Retested: the first job said First in line , the second 1 pending job(s) in cpu are ahead of it . [!TIP] The script uses only squeue , so any user can run it on their own jobs. It doesn't need accounting access. ---

secs.head: Back to the two days
secs.body: Run Monday again with this page on the wiki. The student submits, sees PD , runs whypending , and reads: "Time limit is above the partition's MaxTime. Lower it." One scontrol update later, the job is Priority , then Resources , and it's running before lunch. No ticket, two days saved. And when the reason is Priority , the script says how many jobs are ahead and points at sprio . That's the right question for part 2: not "is the scheduler broken" but "why are those jobs ahead of mine". Takeaway: Resources means first in line and Priority means not first; check for the three reasons that never clear ( DependencyNeverSatisfied , held jobs, PartitionTimeLimit ) before waiting any longer. Next: Part 2, Who Goes First, opens up the priority number. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - squeue(1): output format codes ( %r , %Q ), --start , and the JOB REASON CODES section. - Slurm: Resource Limits: the limit-related reasons and how they're enforced. - scontrol(1): update jobid=... timelimit= , release , and what users may change. - sbatch(1): --dependency , --begin , -H , -w . - slurm.conf(5): EnforcePartLimits: rejecting jobs that exceed partition limits at submission. - Backfill tuning: how jobs behind the queue can still start early.

label: 2. Who goes first
title: Who Goes First: Slurm's Priority Number, Taken Apart
desc: Part 2 of Why Is My Job Still Pending? Part 1 showed that Priority means "not first in line". This page opens up the num

secs.head: Who Goes First: Slurm's Priority Number, Taken Apart
secs.body: Part 2 of Why Is My Job Still Pending? Part 1 showed that Priority means "not first in line". This page opens up the number that decides the line, so you can explain any order to a user and set the weights on purpose. - "She submitted after me" - The formula - The default that does nothing - Reading sprio - Fairshare: why alice got 0.2 - Age: the slow climb - QOS: the express lane - Choosing weights - Back to the complaint - References ---

secs.head: "She submitted after me"
secs.body: Alice submits a job at 09:00. Bob submits at 09:01, carol at 09:05. Carol's job starts first, then bob's. Alice's is still waiting at lunch. She sends the obvious email: "Slurm is supposed to be first come, first served. She submitted after me." It isn't, and on a shared cluster you don't want it to be. Alice had been running jobs all week; carol hadn't run anything. A queue that ignored that would let whoever submits most often take the whole machine. This page shows exactly how Slurm decided, with the numbers from our lab. [!NOTE] Lab: Slurm 23.11.4 with slurmdbd. Two accounts, physics (users alice, bob, admin) and chem (user carol). Alice had used about a minute of CPU time before the test; nobody else had used anything. Weights: fairshare 10000, QOS 5000, age 1000. PriorityCalcPeriod=1 (minutes) so priorities updated quickly; the default is 5. ---

secs.head: The formula
secs.body: With PriorityType=priority/multifactor , each pending job's priority is a weighted sum. From the docs: Every factor is a number between 0.0 and 1.0. Every weight is an integer you choose in slurm.conf . So the weights decide what matters, and how much: Factor 1.0 means Weight in our lab --- --- --- Age The job has waited PriorityMaxAge or longer 1000 Fairshare This user is the most under-served 10000 QOS The job's QOS has the highest QOS priority 5000 Job size, partition, association, TRES Various 0 (off) Rule of thumb: the weights are the policy. A factor with weight 0 doesn't exist. ---

secs.head: The default that does nothing
secs.body: priority/multifactor is the default PriorityType . And every PriorityWeight setting defaults to 0 . Put those together, and a cluster nobody tuned computes this for every job: We set all weights to 0 on the lab and looked: Every job has priority 1. Ties go by submission order, so this is plain first come, first served: alice's job 39 was first in line ( Resources ). Carol's job 43 was submitted with an "urgent" QOS that should put it first; with a QOS weight of 0, it was last of the five. So if your users say the queue is FIFO, check scontrol show config grep PriorityWeight before anything else. Fairshare limits you set in sacctmgr do nothing for the order unless PriorityWeightFairshare is above 0. ---

secs.head: Reading sprio
secs.body: sprio shows each pending job's priority split into its factors, already multiplied by their weights. With the lab's weights: Read across: carol's job 42 has fairshare 1.0 × 10000. Job 43 has the same fairshare plus the QOS bonus. Alice's job gets 0.2 × 10000 = 2000. That's the whole answer to her email: carol's jobs outrank hers by 8000 and 13000 before anyone has waited a minute. sprio -j <id -l adds every column, including the ones at weight 0. ---

secs.head: Fairshare: why alice got 0.2
secs.body: Fairshare compares how much each user and account has used with how much they're entitled to (their shares in sacctmgr ), and favours the under-served. Since 19.05 Slurm uses the Fair Tree algorithm by default. It ranks every user, and gives each a fairshare factor of their rank divided by the number of user associations. sshare shows the inputs: There are five user associations, so ranks become fifths: Step Result --- --- chem and physics have equal shares. chem used nothing, physics used everything chem ranks above physics . Carol gets the top rank: 1.0 Inside physics , admin and bob used nothing; alice used all of it admin and bob tie at rank 3 of 5: 0.6 . Alice is last: 0.2 Two things follow. Bob's fairshare is pulled down by his account's usage, not his own: he'd used nothing, yet ranks below carol, because his account-mates used the cluster. And to see why one user outranks another, the docs' advice is to find their first common ancestor account in sshare , and compare there. Usage doesn't count forever. It decays with a half-life of PriorityDecayHalfLife , 7 days by default, so last week's heavy user is this week's normal one. ---

secs.head: Age: the slow climb
secs.body: Age rises linearly from 0 to 1.0 over PriorityMaxAge (default 7 days), so a job that has waited long enough eventually beats newer work. We set PriorityMaxAge to 10 minutes to see it move, and waited five: Half of 10 minutes, about half of the 1000 weight. With the defaults, a job gains its full age weight only after a week of waiting. The trade-off is in the ratio. Here the age weight (1000) is a tenth of fairshare (10000): even a week-old job from a heavy user would never pass a fresh job from an idle one. That might be what you want. If not, raise the age weight until a long wait can win. ---

secs.head: QOS: the express lane
secs.body: The QOS factor is the job's QOS priority divided by the highest QOS priority on the cluster. We created one QOS with a priority: urgent is the only QOS with a priority, so its factor is 1.0, and carol's job got the full 5000 on top (job 43 above). A QOS with Priority=50 would get half. This is the right tool for "deadline this week" requests: a QOS that only some users may use, often with a limit on how many jobs can use it at once (part 3), instead of an admin raising one job's priority by hand. ---

secs.head: Choosing weights
secs.body: There's no correct set, but there is a sensible way to choose. The size of each weight is what matters relative to the others: If you want Then --- --- Fair use between groups to dominate Fairshare weight largest, by a clear margin No job to wait forever Age weight big enough that a full PriorityMaxAge beats a fairshare gap Urgent work to jump the line QOS weight above any realistic fairshare difference, and the QOS restricted Big jobs not to starve behind small ones Some job size weight, or a reservation Weights are integers, so use large ones (like 10000) to leave room for fine distinctions. After any change, run sprio -l on a busy queue and check the order looks like your policy. Then tell your users what the policy is. "Fairshare first, then age" in the user guide prevents half of the emails like alice's. ---

secs.head: Back to the complaint
secs.body: Alice's email gets a two-line reply with numbers in it: "Your job's priority is 2000 and carol's is 10000. This week you've used most of physics' share and chem hasn't used any, so the scheduler is putting chem first. Your usage halves every 7 days." That's the queue working as designed, explained in a way she can check herself with sprio and sshare . If the design itself is wrong (say, alice has a deadline), that's a policy decision, made with a QOS, not by a quiet scontrol update on one job. And if a cluster's users are right that it's FIFO, the fix is a few lines in slurm.conf , because every weight started at zero. Takeaway: priority is a weighted sum of factors, every weight defaults to 0, and sprio plus sshare explain any order; under Fair Tree, a user's fairshare is their rank among all users. Next: Part 3, Limits That Wait Forever, covers the jobs that wait no matter what their priority is. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Multifactor Priority Plugin: the formula, each factor, sprio . - Fair Tree Fairshare Algorithm: ranking, the rank / user assoc count factor, ties, and the common-ancestor rule. - slurm.conf(5): PriorityType (default multifactor), PriorityWeight (default 0), PriorityMaxAge and PriorityDecayHalfLife (default 7 days), PriorityCalcPeriod (default 5 minutes). - sprio(1) and sshare(1): reading priorities and fairshare. - Slurm QOS: QOS priority and the QOS factor.

label: 3. Limits that wait forever
title: Limits That Wait Forever: QOS and Account Limits in Practice
desc: Part 3 of Why Is My Job Still Pending? Part 2 decided the order of the queue. Limits decide whether a job may start at a

secs.head: Limits That Wait Forever: QOS and Account Limits in Practice
secs.body: Part 3 of Why Is My Job Still Pending? Part 2 decided the order of the queue. Limits decide whether a job may start at all, whatever its priority. By the end you'll set a per-user GPU cap that actually holds, reject jobs that could never run, and read how close anyone is to a limit. - The cap that didn't hold - Two places a limit can live - The lab's limits - A limit that clears by itself - A job that can never run - The second QOS - Closing it with a partition QOS - Who is using what, right now - Rolling out a new limit - Back to the cap - References ---

secs.head: The cap that didn't hold
secs.body: The GPU partition keeps filling up with one group's jobs. The admins agree on a rule: at most two GPUs per user at a time. One sacctmgr command puts the cap on the GPU QOS, and the announcement goes out. Two things happen in the next week. A new user submits a 4-GPU job, which shows QOSMaxGRESPerUser and sits in the queue for six days before anyone notices it can never start. And the same heavy user from before is somehow running three GPUs. Nobody broke anything. Both are exactly how the limit was written. [!NOTE] Lab: Slurm 23.11.4 , slurmdbd, AccountingStorageEnforce=associations,limits,qos,safe . One GPU node with four GPUs (fake device files, enough for scheduling). If limits seem to do nothing on your cluster at all, check AccountingStorageEnforce first: Slurm multi-tenancy covers that trap. ---

secs.head: Two places a limit can live
secs.body: Where Set with Applies to Reason names start with --- --- --- --- An association (an account, or a user in an account) sacctmgr modify account/user ... set ... Every job charged to that account or user Assoc A QOS sacctmgr modify qos ... set ... Only jobs running under that QOS QOS And each limit is one of two kinds: Kind Example Means --- --- --- Grp... GrpTRES=gres/gpu=3 Shared total for everyone under it Max... MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu=2 Per user (or per job), each on their own The second row of the first table is the one that bites: a QOS limit only applies to jobs in that QOS. ---

secs.head: The lab's limits
secs.body: So: each user may hold two GPUs under gpu-normal , and the physics account (alice, bob, admin) may hold three in total. Every user can also still use the default normal QOS. That's the usual setup, and it's the source of the hole below. ---

secs.head: A limit that clears by itself
secs.body: Alice runs a 2-GPU job, then asks for one more GPU: That's the cap doing its job. When job 22 ends, job 23 starts. This kind of QOS... or Assoc... reason clears by itself: the job is fine on its own, it just has to wait for the user's (or account's) other jobs. ---

secs.head: A job that can never run
secs.body: Carol asks for four GPUs at once, under a QOS that allows two per user: Same reason as alice's job, but a completely different situation: even with the whole cluster empty, this job breaks the limit by itself. It will wait forever, and by default Slurm accepts it and lets it. The QOS flag DenyOnLimit makes Slurm reject such jobs at submission instead: Carol's same submission, after: Immediate and specific. DenyOnLimit judges each job on its own : a job that only goes over the limit because of the user's other running jobs is still accepted and waits, as alice's did above. The QOS documentation spells this out. So it removes the waiting-forever case without turning every busy moment into an error. ---

secs.head: The second QOS
secs.body: Now the hole. With alice's two GPUs running, bob submitted a 1-GPU job without asking for any QOS, so it ran under normal : Job 26 ran . The per-user cap lives on gpu-normal , and job 26 isn't in gpu-normal . The only thing that stopped bob from taking even more was the account limit: physics was now at 3 GPUs, so his next job waited on AssocGrpGRES . A user in an account without a GrpTRES limit could have filled the node through normal . This is the week-one surprise from the story: the heavy user's third GPU came in through a different QOS. ---

secs.head: Closing it with a partition QOS
secs.body: A QOS can be attached to a partition . Then its limits apply to every job in that partition, whatever QOS the job asked for. In slurm.conf : After scontrol reconfigure (we redeployed and restarted), scontrol show partition gpu showed QoS=gpu-normal . Then bob ran a 2-GPU job and tried to sneak one more in under normal : Both jobs are under normal , and the cap held anyway: the partition QOS counted them. The docs say the partition QOS overrides the job's QOS. The exception is a job QOS with the OverPartQOS flag, which reverses the order. Give that flag only to a QOS you'd let skip the partition's rules. Rule of thumb: a limit on a resource belongs on the partition that has the resource. A QOS that users choose is for priority and special cases, not for the main cap. ---

secs.head: Who is using what, right now
secs.body: sacctmgr shows limits. To see a limit next to current usage, ask the controller: Trimmed, with alice running two GPUs: Each value reads limit(in use) : gres/gpu=2(2) means a limit of 2 with 2 in use, so alice's next GPU job waits. N means no limit. The GrpTRES line is the physics account: 2 of its 3 GPUs in use. This is the command to run when a user asks "which limit is holding me?". ---

secs.head: Rolling out a new limit
secs.body: A new limit changes what runs tomorrow, so treat it as a change, not a command: 1. Dry run: count who would be over it today. scontrol show assoc mgr with the new values in mind, or squeue -o "%u %b" -t R for current GPU use per user. 2. Announce the limit and the date, with the whypending script from part 1 so users can see why they're waiting. 3. Enforce on the partition QOS, with DenyOnLimit . Running jobs aren't killed when a limit is added; with the safe enforcement option, the docs say a running job isn't killed even if limits change under it. 4. Rollback is one sacctmgr modify ... set MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu=-1 ( -1 clears a limit), and takes effect for the next scheduling pass. ---

secs.head: Back to the cap
secs.body: Same rule, written properly this time. The 2-GPU cap goes on a QOS attached to the GPU partition, with DenyOnLimit . The new user's 4-GPU job is rejected the moment they submit it, with a message that names the limit, so they resubmit as two 2-GPU jobs or ask for an exception. The heavy user's third GPU waits on QOSMaxGRESPerUser whichever QOS they pick. And when someone asks why they're waiting, scontrol show assoc mgr shows the limit and the usage side by side. Nothing in the queue can wait forever any more. Every pending job is either first in line, behind someone with a better claim, or waiting for its own user's jobs to finish. Takeaway: a QOS limit only binds jobs in that QOS, so put caps on a partition QOS; add DenyOnLimit so jobs that could never run are rejected, and read live usage with scontrol show assoc mgr . Series index: Why Is My Job Still Pending?. For the scheduler that fits small jobs into gaps around all of this, see backfill tuning. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Slurm QOS: QOS limits, partition QOS, OverPartQOS , DenyOnLimit . - Slurm: Resource Limits: association limits, Grp vs Max , AccountingStorageEnforce options including safe . - sacctmgr(1): setting and clearing limits ( -1 ). - scontrol(1): show assoc mgr: live limits and usage. - squeue(1): JOB REASON CODES: QOSMaxGRESPerUser , AssocGrpGRES and the rest. - Slurm multi-tenancy: associations, enforcement, and the limit that silently does nothing.

label: **Slurm for AI Clusters**
title: Slurm for AI Clusters
desc: A GPU cluster is a Slurm cluster with expensive opinions. A training job wants its nodes close together on the network,

secs.head: Slurm for AI Clusters
secs.body: A GPU cluster is a Slurm cluster with expensive opinions. A training job wants its nodes close together on the network, every rank started with the right environment, the same container on every node, GPUs that are actually there, and someone watching the numbers. Slurm can do all of that, but very little of it is on by default. Each page opens with a failure we reproduced in a lab, then fixes it. ---

secs.head: Contents
secs.body: File Description --- --- 1. Keep the Job on One Switch topology/tree and topology/block , --switches , the 25.05 topology.yaml , and what each does to a 2-node job 2. Launching Distributed Training The batch script runs on one node; srun with rank variables vs torchrun , and the double-launch trap 3. Containers with Pyxis and Enroot --container-image on srun , read-only images, mounts, named containers, and the node that silently ran outside the container 4. GPU Health Checks Draining a node when a GPU disappears, without overwriting the admin's reason, and the 26.11 per-GPU drain 5. Metrics into VictoriaMetrics The 25.11+ OpenMetrics endpoints, the idle CPUs nobody could use, units that change in 26.11, and a tested alert 6. Lab Build Cheatsheet Every step used to build the lab for both Slurm series, in order, as copy-paste commands ---

secs.head: How the pages were tested
secs.body: - Main lab: Slurm 23.11.4 from the Ubuntu 24.04 packages, with slurmdbd and MariaDB 10.11. A controller ( head01 ), four CPU nodes ( cn001 – cn004 , 2 CPUs each) and one GPU node ( gpu001 ), all systemd containers on one Docker network. - Newer Slurm: 26.05.6 built from source on three more containers ( s26a – s26c ), for topology.yaml and the OpenMetrics endpoints, which 23.11 doesn't have. Slurm 26.11 was at rc1 when this was written; its features are documented from the 26.11 source tree's man pages and release notes, not tested. - No real GPUs. gpu001 has four fake device files, enough for Slurm to schedule, count and health-check them, not to run CUDA. Distributed training was tested with PyTorch 2.15.0 on CPUs with the Gloo backend; the launch mechanics are the same for NCCL on GPUs, the performance is not. - Containers: Enroot built from the v4.2.1 tag and Pyxis v0.24.0 , from source. The lab could not reach a container registry, so images were squashfs files built locally. - Metrics: VictoriaMetrics v1.156.0 , from the VictoriaMetrics series.

label: 1. Keep the job on one switch
title: Keep the Job on One Switch: Topology-Aware Placement in Slurm
desc: Part 1 of Slurm for AI Clusters A multi-node training job is only as fast as the slowest link between its nodes. By the

secs.head: Keep the Job on One Switch: Topology-Aware Placement in Slurm
secs.body: Part 1 of Slurm for AI Clusters A multi-node training job is only as fast as the slowest link between its nodes. By the end you'll know where Slurm puts a job when it knows nothing about your network, how to tell it, and the difference between "prefer one switch" and "never leave the block". - The Tuesday slowdown - Where Slurm puts a job by default - topology/tree: prefer one switch - --switches: wait for one switch - topology/block: never straddle - Two topologies in one cluster (25.05+) - Which one to use - Back to Tuesday - References ---

secs.head: The Tuesday slowdown
secs.body: A team runs the same 2-node fine-tuning job every night. Most nights it takes four hours. Some nights it takes five and a half, with the same code, the same data and the same GPU model. Nobody can find a pattern, until someone lists the node pairs: the slow nights are the ones where the two nodes sit under different leaf switches, and every gradient all-reduce crosses the spine. Slurm picked those nodes. It had no idea the switches existed, because nobody told it. [!NOTE] Lab: Slurm 23.11.4 , four CPU nodes cn001 – cn004 with 2 CPUs each, plus gpu001 . The "network" is invented: we declare cn[001-002] under one leaf and cn[003-004] under another. Containers share one real network, so these tests show placement , not speed. Slurm 26.05.6 on s26a – s26c for topology.yaml . ---

secs.head: Where Slurm puts a job by default
secs.body: With no topology plugin, the scheduler treats nodes as a flat list. We filled cn001 with a 2-CPU job, then asked for two nodes: cn002 and cn003 : the first two free nodes in order. On our invented network, that's one node under each leaf. Exactly the slow nights. ---

secs.head: topology/tree: prefer one switch
secs.body: topology/tree reads a switch hierarchy from topology.conf and tries to fit each job under the lowest common switch. In slurm.conf : And /etc/slurm/topology.conf , on the controller and every node: After restarting slurmctld and the slurmd s, Slurm shows what it understood: Same test, same busy cn001 : Both nodes under leaf2 . That's the whole fix for the Tuesday slowdown, as long as one leaf has room. When no single leaf has room, tree still starts the job, spread across leaves. The docs say a job that can't fit under one leaf "will be spread across as many leaf switches as possible". It prefers one switch, it doesn't insist. [!WARNING] Nodes on switches with no common parent never share a job (unless TopologyParam=TopoOptional ). Forget the spine line and no job can ever span leaf1 and leaf2 . That's sometimes useful, usually a typo. And the docs note that node Weight overrides topology-based selection. ---

secs.head: --switches: wait for one switch
secs.body: A user who'd rather wait than straddle can say so: --switches=count@max-time : at most one leaf switch, and wait up to one minute for that. We made one node busy under each leaf ( cn001 and cn003 ), so the only free pair, cn002 and cn004 , straddled: It waited, then gave up and took the straddling pair, 98 seconds after submission (69 seconds in an earlier run). The wait is checked on scheduling passes, so it runs over the limit by however long the next pass takes. Without a time, the wait is capped by the cluster-wide max switch wait in SchedulerParameters (default 300 seconds, per slurm.conf(5) ). ---

secs.head: topology/block: never straddle
secs.body: topology/block is the stricter model, built for systems like NVLink racks where a job either fits inside a block of nodes or performs badly. topology.conf : With cn001 busy, the 2-node job went to cn[003-004] , like tree . The difference shows when no block has room. One busy node per block, then a 2-node and a 3-node job: Two free nodes sat idle for 90 seconds, and the job waited rather than straddle. When cn003 freed up, it started inside nvl2 . That's the trade: perfect placement, paid for in idle nodes and queue time. Two things bit us while setting it up: What we did What happened --- --- Added BlockName=nvl3 Nodes=gpu001 : a block of 1 next to blocks of 2 slurmctld exited: fatal: Block configuration (nvl3) children count no equal bblock node cnt . Every block at a level must be the same size Left gpu001 out of every block warning: blocks lack access to 1 nodes: gpu001 in the controller log. Jobs in the gpu partition still ran on gpu001 The first one takes the controller down, so test a new topology.conf on a lab controller before production. The docs list more limits of block : -w/--nodelist can conflict with block placement and leave the job unallocated, and node-count ranges ( -N 2-8 ) make the scheduler evaluate every value. --segment=<size , which builds a block job's allocation out of segments of that many nodes, isn't in 23.11 ( sbatch: unrecognized option '--segment=2' ). The 26.11 docs describe it for block and add a per-partition default, DefSegmentSize . ---

secs.head: Two topologies in one cluster (25.05+)
secs.body: One cluster often has both: a switch tree for most nodes, and NVLink blocks for a few racks. Before 25.05 you had to pick one plugin. Since 25.05, topology.yaml defines several topologies and each partition chooses one with Topology= . On the 26.05 lab: scontrol show topology lists the default tree; scontrol show topology nvl names the other: A -p nvl -N2 job ran on s26a,s26b . Same nodes, two placement policies, chosen by partition. Our 26.05 slurm.conf had no TopologyPlugin line at all. The file sits next to slurm.conf , and the docs say that when topology.yaml exists, topology.conf is ignored. ---

secs.head: Which one to use
secs.body: Your network Use Users get --- --- --- Fat tree, small oversubscription tree Best effort, no extra waiting Tree with heavy oversubscription at the spine tree , and teach --switches=1@<time for big jobs A choice: wait, or run slower NVLink domains, or racks where crossing hurts a lot block Fast placement or no placement Both (25.05+) topology.yaml , one topology per partition The right policy per partition Generate the switch list from the fabric rather than by hand. The Slurm docs point at community tools such as slurmibtopology for InfiniBand. ---

secs.head: Back to Tuesday
secs.body: With topology/tree and a topology.conf that matches the real switches, the nightly job lands under one leaf whenever one leaf has room, which on that cluster is almost every night. For the few nights it doesn't, the team added --switches=1@01:00:00 to the job: wait up to an hour for one switch, then run anyway. A one-hour wait beats a ninety-minute slowdown. The slow nights didn't come from the GPUs. Slurm didn't know where the cables went. Takeaway: without a topology plugin Slurm picks nodes in list order; topology/tree prefers one switch, --switches makes a job wait for one, topology/block refuses to straddle at all, and since 25.05 each partition can pick its own. Next: Part 2, Launching Distributed Training, gets every rank started on the nodes this page picked. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Slurm: Topology Guide: tree , block , BlockSizes , block limitations, topology.yaml , --segment , configuration generators. - topology.conf(5) and topology.yaml(5): file formats. - sbatch(1): --switches: count@max-time . - slurm.conf(5): SchedulerParameters: max switch wait ; TopologyParam=TopoOptional . - Slurm 26.11 release notes: DefSegmentSize .

label: 2. Launching distributed training
title: Launching Distributed Training on Slurm: srun, torchrun, and the Rank Contract
desc: Part 2 of Slurm for AI Clusters Part 1 got the job good nodes. This page gets a process started on each of them with the

secs.head: Launching Distributed Training on Slurm: srun, torchrun, and the Rank Contract
secs.body: Part 2 of Slurm for AI Clusters Part 1 got the job good nodes. This page gets a process started on each of them with the right rank. By the end you'll have two working launch scripts, and you'll recognise the three ways they usually break. - Sixteen GPUs, eight busy - The batch script runs on one node - What PyTorch needs from Slurm - Way 1: srun starts every rank - Way 2: srun starts torchrun, torchrun starts the ranks - Three ways it breaks - On real GPUs - Back to the eight idle GPUs - References ---

secs.head: Sixteen GPUs, eight busy
secs.body: A researcher moves a training script from one 8-GPU node to two. The job asks for -N 2 --gpus-per-node=8 , Slurm allocates both nodes, the job runs, and it's exactly as fast as before. Monitoring shows the second node's GPUs at 0% for the whole run. Nobody gets an error. The job finishes, and they paid for two nodes and used one. The batch script was: [!NOTE] Lab: Slurm 23.11.4 , CPU nodes cn001 – cn004 (2 CPUs each), PyTorch 2.15.0 from PyPI in a venv at /opt/torchenv on every node, the Gloo backend on CPUs. No GPUs: the launch mechanics are what's tested here, and they don't depend on the device. Every output below is from the lab. ---

secs.head: The batch script runs on one node
secs.body: A Slurm allocation is a set of nodes. The batch script itself is a single shell process, and it runs on the first node of the allocation. To run anything on the other nodes, you start a job step with srun . Two nodes, one test: hostname alone ran once, on cn001 . srun hostname ran once per task, on both nodes. The researcher's python train.py is the first line: one process, one node, sixteen GPUs allocated. So every multi-node training job needs srun somewhere. The only question is what srun starts. ---

secs.head: What PyTorch needs from Slurm
secs.body: torch.distributed.init process group() with the default env:// method reads four environment variables. Slurm sets its own versions of them for each task: PyTorch reads Means Slurm sets --- --- --- RANK This process's global number, 0..N-1 SLURM PROCID WORLD SIZE Total number of processes SLURM NTASKS LOCAL RANK Number on this node, picks the GPU SLURM LOCALID MASTER ADDR , MASTER PORT Where rank 0 listens Nothing. You choose: usually the first node, scontrol show hostnames "$SLURM JOB NODELIST" \ head -n 1 The test program: every rank adds its rank + 1, so with 4 ranks every rank must print sum=10 . ---

secs.head: Way 1: srun starts every rank
secs.body: One Slurm task per process. Slurm starts them all; a one-line wrapper renames Slurm's variables to PyTorch's: The single quotes matter: the variables must expand inside each task, not once in the batch script. On GPUs, --ntasks-per-node equals the GPUs per node, and each rank uses GPU LOCAL RANK . The output also had a few lines like this, which are harmless in a container without IPv6: Good for: Slurm accounts for every rank as a task, scancel and time limits hit every process directly, and sacct shows one step with N tasks. ---

secs.head: Way 2: srun starts torchrun, torchrun starts the ranks
secs.body: One Slurm task per node . Each runs torchrun , which starts the per-node processes itself and sets RANK , LOCAL RANK and WORLD SIZE for them: Same answer, 6 seconds of wall time. torchrun also printed a warning that it set OMP NUM THREADS=1 for each process; set it yourself if your data loading needs more threads. Note --cpus-per-task=2 : the one Slurm task must own all the CPUs (and on GPU nodes, all the GPUs) its child processes will use. Good for: scripts already written for torchrun , and torchrun 's elastic features (restarting workers on failure, --max-restarts ). Way 1: srun per rank Way 2: srun + torchrun --- --- --- Slurm tasks One per process One per node Who sets RANK Your wrapper, from SLURM PROCID torchrun --ntasks-per-node = processes per node 1 Rendezvous MASTER ADDR:MASTER PORT --rdzv-endpoint (c10d) ---

secs.head: Three ways it breaks
secs.body: Mistake What we saw --- --- No srun at all Runs once, on the first node (the story above). No error srun python without setting RANK ValueError: Error initializing torch.distributed using env:// rendezvous: environment variable RANK expected, but not set , every task exits 1, job FAILED torchrun with --ntasks-per-node=2 (copied from Way 1) Four torchrun agents for a 2-node rendezvous. Two formed the group and the 4 ranks printed sum=10 ; the other two crashed with RendezvousConnectionError: The connection to the C10d store has failed . Job state FAILED The third one is the nasty one: the training ran, then the job reported failure, with a long traceback that never says "you started torchrun twice per node". In our run the two winning agents happened to be on different nodes. If both had been on the same node, all four ranks would have run there, on that node's GPUs only. Rule of thumb: count the processes. nodes × ntasks-per-node × nproc-per-node must equal the world size you meant. ---

secs.head: On real GPUs
secs.body: The same two scripts, with these changes. These are from the PyTorch and Slurm docs, not tested in this lab: - Backend nccl instead of gloo , and torch.cuda.set device(int(os.environ["LOCAL RANK"])) before creating the process group. - Ask for GPUs per node: --gpus-per-node=8 . With Way 1, --ntasks-per-node=8 ; with Way 2, --ntasks-per-node=1 and --nproc-per-node=8 . - NCCL picks a network interface on its own and can pick the wrong one on multi-homed nodes. NCCL DEBUG=INFO prints which interface and transport it chose; NCCL SOCKET IFNAME forces one. - If you use containers, part 3 shows an Enroot hook that sets RANK , WORLD SIZE , MASTER ADDR and friends for you, tested in the lab. ---

secs.head: Back to the eight idle GPUs
secs.body: The researcher's script becomes Way 2, because train.py was already written for torchrun : The first log line now says world size=16 , both nodes' GPUs show load, and the epoch time drops. The fix was one srun , because the batch script only ever ran on the first node. Takeaway: the batch script runs on the first node only; start ranks with srun , either one task per rank with RANK=$SLURM PROCID , or one task per node running torchrun , and make sure nodes × tasks × processes equals the world size. Next: Part 3, Containers with Pyxis and Enroot, runs the same ranks inside a container. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - sbatch(1): the batch script runs on the first allocated node; SLURM output environment variables. - srun(1): SLURM PROCID , SLURM LOCALID , SLURM NTASKS . - PyTorch: torchrun (Elastic Launch): --nnodes , --nproc-per-node , c10d rendezvous, the environment it sets. - PyTorch: torch.distributed: init process group , env:// initialization, backends. - NCCL environment variables: NCCL DEBUG , NCCL SOCKET IFNAME . - The job script tale: what Slurm does with the batch script.

label: 3. Containers with Pyxis and Enroot
title: Containers on Slurm with Pyxis and Enroot
desc: Part 3 of Slurm for AI Clusters Part 2 started the ranks. Now they run inside a container image, so every node has the s

secs.head: Containers on Slurm with Pyxis and Enroot
secs.body: Part 3 of Slurm for AI Clusters Part 2 started the ranks. Now they run inside a container image, so every node has the same CUDA, the same PyTorch, the same everything. By the end you'll run a multi-node step in a container with one srun flag, and you'll know the settings that make it work for every user, not just the admin who tested it. - Two ranks from a different universe - What Pyxis and Enroot are - Installing, and the dependencies nobody lists - The first container step - It works as admin, fails as a user - Read-only by default, and mounts - Named containers outlive the job - The PyTorch hook - Images from a registry - Back to the two odd ranks - References ---

secs.head: Two ranks from a different universe
secs.body: A 4-node job in a container crashes with a mismatch nobody can explain: ranks 0–5 report one PyTorch version, ranks 6 and 7 another. Same srun , same --container-image . The two odd ranks were on a node added to the cluster last week, and their "container" was the node's own operating system. The new node was built without the Pyxis plugin, and srun didn't complain. We reproduced it. cn003 has no Pyxis; the image's /etc/os-release says acot lab image 1.0 : Exit 0, and it ran on the host. srun on the login node knew the --container-image option because Pyxis was loaded there . The node that ran the task had never heard of it. [!NOTE] Lab: Slurm 23.11.4 . Enroot built from the v4.2.1 tag (it reports 4.2.0 ), Pyxis v0.24.0 , both from source. head01 , cn001 and cn002 have them; cn003 doesn't, on purpose. The lab can't reach a container registry, so the images are small squashfs files we built (busybox plus an os-release ). Pulling from a registry is docs-only below. ---

secs.head: What Pyxis and Enroot are
secs.body: Piece What it is Runs where --- --- --- Enroot NVIDIA's tool that turns a container image into an unprivileged sandbox: a root filesystem plus user namespaces, no daemon Every compute node Pyxis A Slurm SPANK plugin that adds --container- options to srun and calls Enroot for each job step Every node that runs srun , and every compute node SPANK plugins are listed in plugstack.conf and loaded by srun , salloc , sbatch and slurmstepd . That's the trap from the story: the option is parsed where you type it, and acted on (or not) where the task runs. ---

secs.head: Installing, and the dependencies nobody lists
secs.body: Both build from their GitHub repositories. Enroot needs its git submodules, one of which (musl) is fetched from git.musl-libc.org ; Pyxis needs the Slurm headers ( libslurm-dev on Ubuntu, matching your Slurm version). The full commands are in the lab cheatsheet. Enroot is mostly shell scripts, and it fails at run time, not install time, when a tool is missing. Each of these produced an error inside a Slurm job in our lab: Missing When it showed up Error in the job output --- --- --- curl Importing from a registry [ERROR] Command not found: curl column ( bsdextrautils on Ubuntu) Any named container [ERROR] Command not found: column / couldn't get list of existing container filesystems unsquashfs ( squashfs-tools ) Creating a container from a .sqsh file (installed before testing) enroot check lists what the kernel and host need. Run it on one node of each hardware type before rolling out. One more from our own build: we built with the default sysconfdir , then installed with sysconfdir=/etc . The enroot script kept looking in /usr/local/etc/enroot , so none of the hooks in /etc/enroot/hooks.d ran. If the hooks seem to do nothing, check: Then on every node, /etc/slurm/plugstack.conf : and restart slurmd . required means a node that can't load the plugin fails the step, instead of running it without. ---

secs.head: The first container step
secs.body: A path to a squashfs file is the simplest image source: no registry, no import, the same file on every node. In production it lives on a shared filesystem; in the lab we copied it to each node. Slurm's per-task variables reach the container unchanged: ( SLURM PROCID , SLURM LOCALID , hostname, image name, from srun -n4 ... sh -c 'echo $SLURM PROCID $SLURM LOCALID ...' .) So both launch styles from part 2 work unchanged inside a container. ---

secs.head: It works as admin, fails as a user
secs.body: The first multi-node test as user alice worked on cn001 and failed on cn002 : Enroot's defaults put its runtime, cache and data under the XDG directories, like ${XDG RUNTIME DIR}/enroot . /run/user/2001 only exists while alice has a login session on that node. She'd logged into cn001 earlier; she'd never logged into cn002 . Batch jobs don't create a login session. Set node-local paths for everyone, in /etc/enroot/enroot.conf.d/10-paths.conf on every node: After that, the same step worked on both nodes for alice. ENROOT DATA PATH holds unpacked container filesystems, so put it on a local disk with room for them. ---

secs.head: Read-only by default, and mounts
secs.body: Test Result --- --- touch /x in the container touch: /x: Read-only file system Same, with --container-writable wrote --container-mounts=/srv:/data:ro , then ls /data labimg.sqsh touch /data/y on that mount Read-only file system --container-remap-root , then id uid=0 gid=0 groups=0 (Pyxis's help: "Does not grant elevated system permissions, despite appearances") Read-only is the right default: a training job shouldn't write into its image. Datasets and checkpoints come in through --container-mounts ; give each mount :ro unless the job writes to it. In our lab the user's home directory was mounted by Enroot's home hook without asking; whether that happens on your cluster depends on ENROOT MOUNT HOME and the hooks installed, so check before users rely on it. ---

secs.head: Named containers outlive the job
secs.body: Unpacking a big image takes time. --container-name keeps the unpacked filesystem so the next step skips it: The second step reused the named container and found the file; the third, unnamed, got a fresh one. Then, after the job ended: Plugstack setting enroot list on cn001 after the job --- --- Default ( container scope=global , per Pyxis's config.c ) pyxis work container scope=job (empty) With the default, every named container stays on the node's disk until someone removes it. That's a feature for a user who runs the same image all week, and a disk-full drain waiting to happen on a shared cluster. To clean up at the end of each job: ---

secs.head: The PyTorch hook
secs.body: Enroot ships optional hooks in /usr/local/share/enroot/hooks.d/ . One, 50-slurm-pytorch.sh , sets PyTorch's variables from Slurm's. It only acts when the image's environment defines PYTORCH VERSION , which NVIDIA's PyTorch images do. We enabled it on the nodes and built a test image with that variable: Everything Way 1 of part 2 needed a wrapper for. The port is SLURM JOB ID % 4536 + 61000 (job 128 here), so two jobs sharing a node don't collide. The same srun with the plain image left RANK empty. The hook doesn't overwrite a variable the image already sets. ---

secs.head: Images from a registry
secs.body: Docs-only: the lab couldn't reach a registry. Pyxis also accepts registry images, as Enroot URIs: Pyxis imports a registry image on each node where the step runs (its README shows the pyxis: importing docker image line per step), so a 64-node job pulls from the registry 64 times at once. Our recommendation, not tested here: import once to a squashfs file on shared storage with enroot import -o , then point jobs at the file: Registry credentials go in $ENROOT CONFIG PATH/.credentials , in netrc format, per Enroot's import docs. Without curl on the node, the import fails as shown in the dependency table. ---

secs.head: Back to the two odd ranks
secs.body: The new node gets /etc/slurm/plugstack.conf from the same Ansible role as the others, with required , so a node without Pyxis now fails container steps loudly instead of running them on the host. Enroot's paths point at node-local directories, so it works for users who never logged in. container scope=job keeps named containers from filling the disks. And for a quick check that a node is ready, the GPU health check in part 4 can test for the plugin file too: The odd ranks weren't a PyTorch bug. They ran outside the container, because nothing on that node knew there was one. Takeaway: Pyxis must be loaded on every compute node, not just where you type srun , so mark it required ; set node-local Enroot paths, mount data read-only into read-only images, and scope named containers to the job. Next: Part 4, GPU Health Checks, keeps jobs off nodes whose GPUs aren't all there. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Pyxis README and wiki: Setup: --container- options, plugstack arguments such as container scope , installation. - Enroot documentation: enroot.conf paths, import / create / start , hooks, .credentials . - Enroot 50-slurm-pytorch.sh hook: the variables it sets and when. - Slurm: SPANK: plugstack.conf , required vs optional , where plugins are loaded. - Slurm: Containers Guide: Slurm's own OCI container support, the alternative to Pyxis.

label: 4. GPU health checks
title: When a GPU Falls Off the Bus: Health Checks That Drain the Node
desc: Part 4 of Slurm for AI Clusters GPUs fail in ways the scheduler can't see on its own. By the end you'll have a health ch

secs.head: When a GPU Falls Off the Bus: Health Checks That Drain the Node
secs.body: Part 4 of Slurm for AI Clusters GPUs fail in ways the scheduler can't see on its own. By the end you'll have a health check that takes a node with a missing GPU out of service within one interval, leaves running jobs alone, and doesn't trample a drain an admin set by hand. - The node that ate the queue - What Slurm does on its own - HealthCheckProgram in one paragraph - A GPU health check - Pulling a GPU out - The bug: it overwrote the admin's reason - What a real check should test - 26.11: drain one GPU, not the node - Back to the queue - References ---

secs.head: The node that ate the queue
secs.body: One GPU in an 8-GPU node drops off the PCIe bus overnight. The driver now sees seven. Slurm still thinks there are eight, because it read gres.conf when slurmd started. Every job that lands there with --gpus-per-node=8 dies in its first minute with a CUDA error. Each failure frees the node, so the scheduler gives it to the next job in the queue. By morning, forty jobs have failed on one node, and to the scheduler it looks like the healthiest node in the cluster, because it's always free. Nothing checked the GPUs between job starts. [!NOTE] Lab: Slurm 23.11.4 , gpu001 with four GPUs that are fake device files ( /dev/nvidia0 – 3 ). "A GPU falls off" is simulated by deleting one device file. On a real node you'd count GPUs with nvidia-smi ; the Slurm behaviour (drain, reasons, states) is the same and is what we tested. ---

secs.head: What Slurm does on its own
secs.body: We tried the obvious thing first: delete /dev/nvidia1 , restart slurmd on gpu001 . slurmd refused to start, and the node showed idle (not responding) until it would be marked DOWN . So Slurm notices a missing device at slurmd start . While slurmd keeps running, it doesn't look again. A GPU that disappears between restarts is invisible to it, which is the story above. ---

secs.head: HealthCheckProgram in one paragraph
secs.body: slurm.conf can name a HealthCheckProgram : a script that slurmd runs as root, every HealthCheckInterval seconds, on every node that is responding. The script decides what "healthy" means and takes any action itself, usually scontrol update ... state=drain . From slurm.conf(5) : it runs at the same time on all nodes, it's killed if it doesn't finish within 60 seconds, and it also runs when slurmd starts, before the node registers. HealthCheckNodeState limits which node states run it; the default is ANY . Drain , not down: a draining node finishes its running jobs and takes no new ones. Setting a node DOWN kills its jobs. ---

secs.head: A GPU health check
secs.body: The check compares the GPUs Slurm expects with the GPUs the node can see: That's the second version. The first didn't have the already drained line, and the bug it caused is below. Install it on every node, CPU nodes included (it exits at once when the node has no GPUs), then in slurm.conf : 30 seconds is a lab value to keep the test short. Production clusters usually check every few minutes; a check that runs nvidia-smi on 8 GPUs isn't free. ---

secs.head: Pulling a GPU out
secs.body: Alice had a 1-GPU job running on gpu001 . At 06:20:48 we deleted /dev/nvidia2 : Within one interval the node was draining ( drng ): alice's job kept running, and the reason says exactly what's wrong. A new 1-GPU job from bob waited: Then we put the device back. Forty seconds later the node was still drng with the same reason: the check drains, it never undrains. That's deliberate. A GPU that fell off once will fall off again; a person should look at it and run scontrol update nodename=gpu001 state=resume . After that, bob's job started. Notice that bob asked for one GPU, and three healthy ones sat idle the whole time. Drain works on whole nodes. That's what 26.11 changes, below. ---

secs.head: The bug: it overwrote the admin's reason
secs.body: Version 1 drained whenever GPUs were missing, whatever state the node was in. We drained gpu001 by hand for planned work, then removed a GPU: The change ticket's reason was gone, replaced by the health check's. The next admin to look sees a hardware problem and opens a hardware ticket for a node that's down for planned firmware work. Worse, when the firmware work ends and someone resumes the node, nothing records that it was ever drained for a change. Version 2 skips nodes that are already drained. Same test: The admin's reason survives. When the admin resumed the node with the GPU still missing, the next check drained it with gpu-health: 3/4 GPUs visible , which is the behaviour you want. [!TIP] If you run several checks (GPUs, disks, Pyxis, mounts), have one HealthCheckProgram call them all and drain once with the first failure as the reason. Several scripts racing to set a reason produce the same overwrite problem. ---

secs.head: What a real check should test
secs.body: The device count catches "the GPU is gone". It doesn't catch a GPU that's present but broken. On real hardware, sites usually add (docs-only here, no GPUs in the lab): Check Tool --- --- Expected GPU count nvidia-smi -L \ wc -l Uncorrectable ECC errors, retired or remapped pages nvidia-smi -q -d ECC,PAGE RETIREMENT (fields vary by GPU generation) A quick functional test NVIDIA DCGM: dcgmi diag -r 1 Everything else (mounts, disk, daemons) LBNL Node Health Check (NHC), a framework built for HealthCheckProgram Keep the periodic check short (it's killed after 60 seconds) and run the slow diagnostics from a prolog or epilog, or on demand. ---

secs.head: 26.11: drain one GPU, not the node
secs.body: Docs-only: Slurm 26.11 was at rc1 when this was written, and these come from its release notes and man pages. The 26.11 release notes list "per-device drain of GRES devices, CPUs, and memory with scontrol update TresName=... Action=Drain " and "the DEGRADED node state for nodes with drained TRES". From scontrol(1) : What changes for the story above: Through 26.05 26.11 --- --- --- One GPU bad Drain the whole node Drain that GPU; node becomes DEGRADED Other GPUs on the node Idle until resume sinfo(1) : "The rest of the node stays schedulable" A UUID-tracked GPU stops being reported slurmd won't start (our test) Its index is drained automatically, shown as gpu(IDX:1)(gres/gpu:not found) . The node is also marked INVAL unless SlurmctldParameters=drain absent gres is set, which keeps it up Return to service state=resume TresName=... Action=Resume ; state=RESUME KEEP TRES returns the node but keeps drained GPUs drained MaxDrainedTres on a NodeName line drains the whole node once too many of its parts are drained. With these, the check above would drain the missing index instead of the node, and bob's 1-GPU job would have run on one of the three good GPUs. ---

secs.head: Back to the queue
secs.body: With the check in place, the GPU falls off at 02:13, and at the next interval the node drains with gpu-health: 7/8 GPUs visible . The job running on it finishes or fails on its own; no new job lands there. The forty jobs that would have failed run elsewhere. In the morning there's one drained node with a precise reason, and a hardware ticket. Nothing changed in the GPU. Slurm got told to look. Takeaway: slurmd only checks GPU devices when it starts; a HealthCheckProgram that compares expected and visible GPUs and drains (never resumes, never overwrites an existing drain) keeps a broken node from eating the queue, and 26.11 can drain just the bad GPU. Next: Part 5, Metrics into VictoriaMetrics, puts drained nodes, idle CPUs and pending jobs on a graph. ---

secs.head: References

label: 5. Metrics into VictoriaMetrics
title: Slurm Metrics Without an Exporter: OpenMetrics into VictoriaMetrics
desc: Part 5 of Slurm for AI Clusters Since 25.11, slurmctld can serve its own metrics over HTTP. By the end you'll scrape the

secs.head: Slurm Metrics Without an Exporter: OpenMetrics into VictoriaMetrics
secs.body: Part 5 of Slurm for AI Clusters Since 25.11, slurmctld can serve its own metrics over HTTP. By the end you'll scrape them into VictoriaMetrics, read the two numbers that explained a half-empty cluster, and have a unit-tested alert that survives the metric change in 26.11. - Idle CPUs, pending jobs - Turning it on - Scraping it - The two numbers that explained it - bytes that are MiB - An alert, and the bug its test caught - Who can read it - Back to the half-empty cluster - References ---

secs.head: Idle CPUs, pending jobs
secs.body: The cluster dashboard shows a third of the CPUs idle. The queue has jobs pending with reason Resources . Users send screenshots of both side by side: "the cluster is half empty and my 1-CPU job can't start". The admin checks sinfo : every node is mix , nothing is down or drained. The scheduler isn't broken. Something else is full. [!NOTE] Lab: Slurm 26.05.6 built from source on s26a – s26c (2 CPUs and RealMemory=1000 each). VictoriaMetrics v1.156.0 single-node, and vmalert-tool from the same release, as set up in the VictoriaMetrics series. 23.11 doesn't have these endpoints; for older Slurm you need an external exporter. ---

secs.head: Turning it on
secs.body: One line in slurm.conf , then restart slurmctld : The metrics are served by slurmctld itself, on its normal port (default 6817). No exporter process, no extra port: A sample from each: ---

secs.head: Scraping it
secs.body: metrics path is one per scrape job, so one job per endpoint, all pointing at the controller: 146 series for three nodes. We left out /metrics/jobs-users-accts on purpose: the Slurm docs warn that per-user and per-account endpoints are "unbounded entities" that can "dramatically increase the amount of data stored". Add it only with a plan for its cardinality. The same docs note that every scrape takes locks inside slurmctld , so don't scrape it every second; the default 30 s or slower is fine. ---

secs.head: The two numbers that explained it
secs.body: We reproduced the dashboard: a 2-node job (1 CPU per node) and a 1-CPU job, then one more 1-CPU job. The last one pended with Resources while slurm node cpus idle said each node had a free CPU. The node metrics, side by side: CPUs free, memory fully allocated . Each 1-CPU job had been given all of its node's memory. That's the default: with memory as a consumable resource ( CR Core Memory ) and no DefMemPerCPU , DefMemPerGPU or DefMemPerNode , a job that doesn't ask for memory gets the whole node's. slurm.conf(5) says DefMemPerNode 's default is 0 (unlimited) , and the lab showed it: The fix is a default per CPU: After scontrol reconfigure , resubmitting the same three jobs (jobs already running keep their old allocation): All three running, s26c left completely free for a bigger job. Pick the value from your nodes: RealMemory divided by CPUs (or by GPUs, for DefMemPerGPU on GPU partitions), minus some room for the OS. ---

secs.head: bytes that are MiB
secs.body: Look at that sample again: slurm node memory bytes 1000 , on a node configured with RealMemory=1000 , which is in MiB. In 26.05 the node memory metrics carry a bytes name and a MiB value. slurm node memory free bytes read 4911 , the container host's free memory in MiB. The 26.11 release notes fix it: "Report node memory metrics in bytes in the openmetrics endpoint. They were in MiB." So on the upgrade from 26.05 to 26.11, every node memory series jumps by a factor of 1,048,576. A dashboard that shows them as "GB" by dividing by 1024 is wrong before the upgrade and wrong in a different way after. An alert like slurm node memory free bytes < 1024 (meant as "less than 1 GiB free") fires on every node before 26.11 and never after. Rule of thumb: write rules as ratios of two memory metrics. A ratio has no unit, so it's right on both versions. The alert below does that. ---

secs.head: An alert, and the bug its test caught
secs.body: The pattern from the story, as a rule: idle CPUs on a node whose memory is fully allocated. And a unit test for vmalert-tool , with one node in the trap and one fixed: That's the second version of the rule. The first had the two sides of and the other way round, and the test failed: and returns the left side's samples, so $value was the memory, not the CPU count. Swapping the sides fixed it. To check the test can fail, we changed for: 15m to for: 25m : got:[] at 20 minutes, FAILED . On the live data, the expression returned all three nodes at the minute of the trap, and nothing after the fix. ---

secs.head: Who can read it
secs.body: In our lab, curl with no credentials got HTTP 200 from every endpoint. That's the default. From the Slurm metrics guide: "By default, metrics endpoints do not require authentication. They are either accessible to everyone or to no one (with the exceptions of SlurmUser and root), depending on whether PrivateData is set." Setting Effect --- --- Nothing Open to anyone who can reach port 6817 PrivateData set Closed except to SlurmUser and root, unless MetricsParameters=ignore private data MetricsAuthUsers=<users Only those users (plus SlurmUser and root), with a JWT; overrides the other two The guide also points out that the metrics reveal job patterns and user activity. Port 6817 has to be reachable by every node and every client anyway, so a firewall rule doesn't fix it; decide who may read the metrics, and set MetricsAuthUsers for the scraper's user if the answer isn't "everyone". ---

secs.head: Back to the half-empty cluster
secs.body: With slurm node cpus idle and slurm node memory alloc bytes on the same graph, the answer to the screenshots takes one look: the CPUs were free, the memory wasn't, because every job without --mem got a whole node's worth. DefMemPerCPU fixed the default, the queue drained, and the SlurmStrandedCPUs alert now catches the next time it happens, for example a partition someone adds without a memory default. The cluster wasn't half empty. It was full of memory nobody was using. Takeaway: Slurm 25.11+ serves its own OpenMetrics from slurmctld , open by default; scrape one job per endpoint, look at idle CPUs and allocated memory together, write memory rules as ratios because the units change in 26.11, and unit-test the rules. Next: Part 6, Lab Build Cheatsheet, has every command used to build the lab behind this series. ---

secs.body: Part 6 of Slurm for AI Clusters , and the lab behind Why Is My Job Still Pending? too. Direct steps, in order, to build the same cluster on one Linux machine: one controller, four CPU nodes, one node with four fake GPUs, and a second small cluster on Slurm 26.05. - Lab Build Cheatsheet: A Slurm AI Cluster in Containers - What you get - 0. The host - 1. The node image - 2. Start the containers - 3. Munge, names and users - 4. Slurm 23.11 with accounting - 5. Accounts, QOS and limits - 5b. Preemption drill (optional) - 6. Topology variants - 7. PyTorch - 8. Containers: Enroot and Pyxis - 9. GPU health check - 10. Slurm 26.05 from source - 11. Metrics into VictoriaMetrics - When the lab breaks - References [!NOTE] Every command here was run while building the lab for these pages, on an Ubuntu 24.04 host. They're collected from several sessions into one order; the whole sequence was not re-run from an empty machine in one go. Lab-only shortcuts (privileged containers, a password in a config file, world-writable directories) are marked. Don't copy them into production. ---

secs.head: What you get
secs.body: Host IP Role --- --- --- head01 10.10.0.10 slurmctld, slurmdbd, MariaDB, login node cn001 – cn004 10.10.0.11–14 CPU nodes, partition cpu , 2 CPUs each gpu001 10.10.0.21 partition gpu , four fake GPUs ( /dev/nvidia0 – 3 ) s26a – s26c 10.10.0.31–33 Slurm 26.05.6 from source; s26a also runs slurmctld Versions: Slurm 23.11.4 (Ubuntu packages) and 26.05.6, MariaDB 10.11, PyTorch 2.15.0, Enroot v4.2.1 tag, Pyxis v0.24.0, VictoriaMetrics v1.156.0. ---

secs.head: 0. The host
secs.body: You need Docker, debootstrap , about 20 GB of free disk (PyTorch alone is 5.3 GB), and cgroup access for systemd in containers. Our host was cgroup v1 (hybrid); the nodes' cgroup.conf uses CgroupPlugin=autodetect . ---

secs.head: 1. The node image
secs.body: One Ubuntu 24.04 root filesystem with everything any node needs, imported as a Docker image that boots systemd: bsdextrautils is in the list because Enroot needs column for named containers; leaving it out cost us a failed test (part 3). ---

secs.head: 2. Start the containers
secs.body: ~/alab/lab.sh , which starts, stops or rebuilds the six main nodes: --privileged is a lab shortcut: systemd, cgroups and mknod for the fake GPUs need it. ---

secs.head: 3. Munge, names and users
secs.body: We distributed the key with the munge role from the Ansible series; docker cp does the same in a lab. ---

secs.head: 4. Slurm 23.11 with accounting
secs.body: The configuration is an Ansible project, ~/slurmlab , with the inventory groups head (head01) and nodes (cn001–cn004, gpu001): templates/slurm.conf.j2 : The QOS=gpu-normal on the gpu partition comes from part 3 of the pending series. The QOS doesn't exist yet on the first run: leave QOS=gpu-normal out until step 5 has created it, then add it back and run the playbook again. Note there's no DefMemPerCPU : this lab shows the default that part 5 fixes. templates/slurmdbd.conf.j2 (installed mode 0600, owner slurm): templates/cgroup.conf.j2 and templates/gres.conf.j2 : site.yml does, in order: start MariaDB and create the slurm acct db database and slurm user; install slurmdbd.conf and start slurmdbd , waiting for port 6819; on every host, create the fake GPU device files on gpu001 ( mknod -m 666 /dev/nvidia$i c 195 $i for 0–3), create /var/lib/slurm and /var/log/slurm , template the three config files, install topology.conf only when the topology conf variable is set (and remove it otherwise), restart what changed, then start slurmctld on the head and slurmd on the nodes. Expected: partitions cpu (4 nodes) and gpu (1 node), all idle . ---

secs.head: 5. Accounts, QOS and limits
secs.body: On head01 : The pending series' whypending script goes to /usr/local/bin/whypending on head01 ; it's printed in full in part 1. ---

secs.head: 5b. Preemption drill (optional)
secs.body: Want to see an urgent job evict a running one on this lab? This reuses the urgent QOS from step 5 as the preemptor and adds a requeueable scavenger victim. The same sequence was run, with low and high physics as the names, on a separate two-node test cluster (Slurm 23.11.4) and is explained step by step in The Guest List. It was not re-run on this container lab, so treat the names below as an adaptation. Add to the slurm.conf template (through extra slurm conf ), then restart slurmctld , because PreemptType is not picked up by a plain reconfigure: Then, on head01 : The drill: fill the cpu partition with scavenger jobs submitted with --requeue , then submit one urgent job from carol . The scavenger job should show PREEMPTED and then run again; sacct -X -D shows both lives (see Autopsy of a Job). If nothing happens, check that the victim has --requeue and that the urgent job really asked for the same nodes. ---

secs.head: 6. Topology variants
secs.body: Two variable files for site.yml . Tree ( /tmp/tree.yml ): Block ( /tmp/block.yml ): every block the same size, and gpu001 left out (a 1-node block next to 2-node blocks is fatal to slurmctld ): Run site.yml without -e @... to go back to no topology. extra slurm conf replaces the whole block, so repeat any line you still want, such as the health check from step 9. ---

secs.head: 7. PyTorch
secs.body: On the host, into the image's root filesystem (the shell there needs the proxy and CA settings if your network has them): The PyPI wheel pulls about 3 GB of NVIDIA libraries even for CPU use; import torch fails without them ( libcudart.so.13: cannot open shared object file ), so don't install with --no-deps . We added the venv to already-running containers; starting fresh, do this before the docker import in step 1, so /opt/torchenv is in the image. Then put the test program from part 2 on the CPU nodes: ---

secs.head: 8. Containers: Enroot and Pyxis
secs.body: Build in the image root (which has libslurm-dev 23.11.4 for Pyxis), then copy the results to the nodes that should have them. Enroot's musl submodule points at git.musl-libc.org ; if your network can't reach it, point it at a mirror of the same commit. Pass the same sysconfdir to the build and the install. We built without it, and Enroot looked for its hooks in /usr/local/etc/enroot instead of /etc/enroot (part 3); the lab fixed it with ln -s /etc/enroot /usr/local/etc/enroot on each node. The build line above is the corrected form, not re-run. On head01 , cn001 and cn002 (leave cn003 without, to reproduce part 3's story): The test images, a busybox root with an os-release , one with PYTORCH VERSION set for the hook: Expected: PRETTY NAME="acot lab image 1.0" twice. ---

secs.head: 9. GPU health check
secs.body: The script is in part 4. Copy it to every node, then add it to slurm.conf : Test: docker exec gpu001 rm /dev/nvidia2 , wait 30 s, sinfo -R . Put it back with docker exec gpu001 mknod -m 666 /dev/nvidia2 c 195 2 and scontrol update nodename=gpu001 state=resume . ---

secs.head: 10. Slurm 26.05 from source
secs.body: A separate build root, so the main image keeps its Ubuntu Slurm packages: --with-http-parser and --with-yaml matter: the OpenMetrics endpoints and topology.yaml need them. The runtime libraries ( libhttp-parser2.9 , libjwt2 ) were already in the node image. Image and containers: Copy /tmp/munge.key in and restart munge as in step 3, then on each: mkdir -p /var/lib/slurm26 /var/log/slurm26 && chown slurm:slurm /var/lib/slurm26 /var/log/slurm26 . /opt/slurm26/etc/slurm.conf on all three: (Add DefMemPerCPU=400 after reproducing the part 5 story.) Node names are listed one by one: s26[a-c] isn't a valid range, Slurm ranges are numeric. /opt/slurm26/etc/topology.yaml is in part 1. Start the daemons once munge is running. Use docker exec -d ; a background & inside docker exec bash -c died with the exec session: Expected: partitions all and nvl , and the index of five metrics endpoints. ---

secs.head: 11. Metrics into VictoriaMetrics
secs.body: VictoriaMetrics single-node as in its series, with the scrape file from part 5: Expected: three up series with value 1 , and SUCCESS . ---

secs.head: When the lab breaks
secs.body: Symptom Cause Fix --- --- --- docker commands hang or the daemon is gone dockerd was started from a shell that ended setsid -f dockerd /tmp/dockerd.log 2 &1 < /dev/null After a Docker restart, gpu001 is down /dev/nvidia don't survive a container restart Re-run site.yml (step 4) Ansible: UNREACHABLE /etc/hosts lost the node names Re-add the lines from step 3 Ansible: Attempting to decrypt but no vault secrets found The inventory has vault-encrypted vars vault password file in ansible.cfg 26.05 daemons: auth/munge fatal Started before munge systemctl restart munge , then start them again slurmctld exits after a topology change Unequal block sizes See step 6 scontrol reboot leaves nodes in reboot^ Containers report the host's boot time Lab artifact; scontrol update nodename=... state=resume (reboot order) scancel -u alice -u bob cancels only bob's jobs Only the last -u counts Loop: for u in alice bob; do scancel -u $u; done Teardown: ~/alab/lab.sh down , then docker rm -f s26a s26b s26c . Takeaway: the whole lab is one Ubuntu root filesystem imported as a systemd image, six plus three privileged containers on one Docker network, and an Ansible playbook for Slurm; everything after that is a few files copied onto the nodes. Series index: Slurm for AI Clusters. For what this lab was used to show about the queue, see Why Is My Job Still Pending?. ---
