secs.body: - free(1) man page, 2023 procps-ng ( used = total − available) - free(1) man page, 2016 procps-ng ( used = total − free − buffers − cache; column definitions) - free(1) man page, 2018 copy ( available description) - Linux kernel commit 34e431b0: add MemAvailable to /proc/meminfo - Rik van Riel's RFC patch: provide estimated available memory - Unix StackExchange: is cached memory de facto free (tmpfs and MemAvailable experiment) - Unix StackExchange: MemAvailable higher than expected (the estimate in practice) - Detailed explanation of /proc/meminfo fields (Shmem and Cached)

label: 1. How Linux reclaims memory
title: How Linux Reclaims Memory: Cache, Swap and the Two Kinds of Stall
desc: Part 1 of the Linux Memory Pressure series. A Linux machine with almost no free memory is usually healthy, and a machine

secs.head: How Linux Reclaims Memory: Cache, Swap and the Two Kinds of Stall
secs.body: Part 1 of the Linux Memory Pressure series. A Linux machine with almost no free memory is usually healthy, and a machine with plenty of free memory can still be in trouble. By the end of this page you'll know why, you'll be able to read /proc/meminfo without panic, and you'll know the exact moment a program starts to stall.

secs.head: The library with no empty desks
secs.body: A university library has a reading room with a fixed number of desks. Every desk holds something a student is working on right now. The rest of the collection lives in the basement stacks, which are slow to reach. A good librarian doesn't keep desks empty. An empty desk is wasted. She fills spare desks with books people might want again soon, because fetching from the basement costs ten minutes. When a student walks in and needs a desk, she clears one in seconds by sending the least-recently-touched book back down. Walk in at 3 p.m. and every desk is covered. Is the library overloaded? Not necessarily. Most of those desks hold books that can be swept away at no cost the moment someone needs the space. Library Linux machine --------- --------------- Reading-room desks RAM, in 4 KiB pages The basement stacks Disk (files, swap) Spare desks used as a shelf of "might want again" books The page cache The librarian clearing a desk Page reclaim The student who can't sit down until a desk is cleared A program waiting on an allocation Everything on this page is about how the librarian decides what to clear, and what happens when she can't keep up. ---

secs.head: Three kinds of page
secs.body: Not every page is equally cheap to take back. This is the fact that everything else follows from. Kind of page Library version What reclaim has to do Cost -------------- ----------------- ------------------------ ------ Clean file page A library book: the original is in the stacks Just drop it. Re-read it from the file if it is needed again Free now, a disk read later Dirty file page A book someone wrote notes in Write the changes back to the file first, then drop it One disk write Anonymous page Your own handwritten notes: no original exists Needs somewhere to go: swap . With no swap, these pages cannot be reclaimed A disk write now, a read later Anonymous means "not backed by a file": a program's heap, its stack, memory from malloc . That's the memory programs own. The kernel sorts pages onto four lists in /proc/meminfo : Active(file) , Inactive(file) , Active(anon) and Inactive(anon) . A page moves from active to inactive when it hasn't been touched for a while, and the inactive ends are where reclaim eats first. (Kernels with multi-gen LRU , on by default on Ubuntu 26.04, age pages through several generations instead. The four /proc/meminfo counters are still there, so the picture here still reads correctly. Check /sys/kernel/mm/lru gen/enabled .) This is the "least recently used" rule from the memory-locking page, made concrete. One consequence is worth saying out loud. A machine with no swap isn't safer, it just has fewer pages it is allowed to reclaim. All the anonymous memory is pinned by the lack of a place to put it, and only the file cache is left to squeeze. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Grab a pen. A 16 GiB server reports this: Is the server in trouble? Got your answer? Scroll on. Answer: no . 11 GB of the "used" memory is cache, mostly clean file pages the librarian can send back to the stacks in an instant. The 300 MB figure only says the desks are being used well. The number that matters is the next section's. One catch: Cached also counts shared memory ( tmpfs , /dev/shm , MPI shared segments), which is swap-backed like anonymous memory. With no swap those pages can't be dropped. Check the Shmem line in /proc/meminfo before you call all of Cached free. ---

secs.head: Free is not available
secs.body: MemFree is memory nobody is using at all. On a healthy, busy machine it is small on purpose , because the kernel spends the spare on cache. The number you want is MemAvailable : the kernel's estimate of how much it could hand to a new program without swapping , which is free memory plus the part of the cache it can drop, minus a safety margin. On the machine I wrote this page on (Ubuntu 26.04, Linux 7.0, 14.8 GiB of RAM): Field Value Meaning ------- ------- --------- MemTotal 14.8 GiB The desks MemFree 1.3 GiB Empty desks Cached 4.3 GiB Books kept on desks, mostly droppable MemAvailable 5.4 GiB What a new student could get without anyone being sent to swap free says 1.3, MemAvailable says 5.4. A script alerting on MemFree would have paged someone for nothing. A script alerting on MemAvailable is much closer to right, and PSI in the next page is closer still. ---

secs.head: Who does the clearing: kswapd and direct reclaim
secs.body: The librarian doesn't wait for a student to ask. She has two modes, and the difference between them is the most important idea on this page. The kernel tracks three watermarks on free memory: high , low and min . Think of them as three lines painted on the wall of the reading room. Free memory is... What happens Who waits ------------------- -------------- ----------- Above high Nothing. Everything is calm Nobody Below low A background thread, kswapd , wakes up and reclaims pages Nobody. It runs beside the programs Below min The program asking for memory has to reclaim pages itself , before its allocation can finish. This is direct reclaim The program While kswapd keeps up, memory pressure is invisible. When programs allocate faster than it can clear, free memory sinks to min , and now the program that wanted one page is made to do the clearing before it gets it . That wait is a stall: no CPU used, nothing wrong with the code, just a thread queued behind disk writes. This is exactly the trap behind the mlock page: allocating under pressure can block, which is why a rescuer must do its allocating before the trouble starts. The kernel counts both. On the same machine: Counter in /proc/vmstat Value Reading -------------------------- ------- --------- pgscan kswapd 5.39 million Pages scanned by the background thread pgscan direct 122 thousand Pages scanned by stalled programs themselves allocstall about 1,000 in total Times a program had to enter direct reclaim Roughly two scanned pages in a hundred were done by a program that was made to wait. A healthy machine has a small pgscan direct . When that line starts climbing fast, the stalls have begun. ---

secs.head: The knobs: swappiness, zram and zswap
secs.body: Three settings change how the librarian behaves. People often misread the first. vm.swappiness (default 60) is the balance between reclaiming file pages and anonymous pages . It is not "start swapping when memory is 60% full". Higher values make the kernel more willing to push anonymous pages to swap rather than shrink the cache. At 0 it strongly prefers dropping cache first. The range is 0 to 200 since Linux 5.8 (0 to 100 before). zram is a swap device that lives in RAM and compresses what is put into it. Swapping out a page costs a bit of CPU instead of a disk write, which is why zram-backed swap hurts far less. It is common on laptops and some servers. zswap is a compressed cache in front of a real swap device . Pages are compressed into a RAM pool first, and only pushed to disk when that pool fills. Where evicted pages go Cost to bring one back - ------------------------ ------------------------ Disk swap A swap file or partition Microseconds (SSD) to milliseconds (disk), worse when the disk is busy zram A compressed block in RAM A decompression: far faster than disk zswap Compressed RAM, spilling to disk when full Fast while the pool lasts None of these remove the stall. They make each swapped-in page cheaper, so the stall is shorter. ---

secs.head: Thrashing: when the clearing never ends
secs.body: One more word, because it names the worst case. If the pages programs are actively using (their working set ) don't fit in RAM, reclaim evicts a page, the program touches it a moment later, and it has to be read straight back in. The kernel counts these in workingset refault . The machine spends its time swapping the same pages in and out while no program makes progress. This is thrashing , and it feels like the machine froze, though nothing has crashed. Thrashing is also why the kernel's OOM killer, which only fires when it truly cannot find a page, can take minutes to act on a machine that is unusable long before. That gap is the subject of the OOM-killer page, and it is why something has to notice trouble earlier. ---

secs.head: See it on your own machine
secs.body: Run the /proc/vmstat line twice, a minute apart, during busy work, and subtract. A growing pgscan direct is the number that says programs are paying for the clearing themselves. Takeaway: the kernel keeps RAM full on purpose and takes it back as needed; a background thread does it quietly until free memory hits the minimum line, and from then on your program does the clearing and stalls. Watch MemAvailable and pgscan direct , not MemFree . So the machine is spending its time clearing desks. How do you notice that it's happening before anything breaks? That's part 2.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Linux kernel docs: Concepts overview (page cache, anonymous memory, reclaim) - Linux kernel docs: /proc/sys/vm (swappiness, min free kbytes, watermark scale factor) - Linux kernel docs: zram and zswap - proc(5): /proc/meminfo and /proc/vmstat

label: 2. Memory pressure (PSI)
title: Pressure Stall Information: Measuring Time Lost, Not Bytes Left
desc: Part 2 of the Linux Memory Pressure series. "How much memory is left?" is the wrong question, because Linux keeps it nea

secs.head: Pressure Stall Information: Measuring Time Lost, Not Bytes Left
secs.body: Part 2 of the Linux Memory Pressure series. "How much memory is left?" is the wrong question, because Linux keeps it nearly all in use on purpose. The right question is "how much time are programs losing waiting for memory?", and the kernel counts exactly that. By the end you'll read the three lines of /proc/pressure/memory at a glance and know how a rescuer program gets woken by them.

secs.head: The restaurant that watches the queue, not the pantry
secs.body: A restaurant manager wants to know when the kitchen is in trouble. She could watch the pantry: "how many eggs are left?" But a full pantry says nothing about whether customers are waiting, and an almost-empty one might be fine if a delivery is due. Pantry counts are a guess about trouble. What she really cares about is the queue : "what share of the evening are customers sitting at a table with no food, waiting?" That number is trouble itself. It does not need interpreting. Restaurant Linux machine ------------ --------------- The pantry stock Free or available memory Customers waiting with no food Tasks stalled on memory "Share of the evening someone was waiting" PSI , Pressure Stall Information PSI (kernel 4.20 and up) is that queue measurement. It turns the stalls from part 1 (direct reclaim, swap-ins, refaults) into a percentage of wall-clock time. ---

secs.head: Reading the file
secs.body: Two lines, each with the same four numbers. Field Meaning ------- --------- avg10 , avg60 , avg300 The percentage of time spent stalled, averaged over the last 10, 60 and 300 seconds total Stall time since boot, in microseconds . A raw counter you can diff yourself The three averages tell you the trend : if avg10 is much higher than avg300 , the pressure just started. If they're all high, it has been going on a while. The zeros above are a calm machine. The thing to remember: 0.00 here means no task lost any time to memory in that window, whatever MemFree says. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Two machines. - A: MemFree is 200 MB of 32 GB. PSI memory some avg60=0.00 . - B: MemFree is 8 GB of 32 GB. PSI memory some avg60=35.00 . Which one needs attention? Got your answer? Scroll on. Answer: B . A has a full cache and is losing no time at all. B has plenty of free memory and tasks are stalled a third of the time: perhaps one job is thrashing inside a small cgroup limit, or a burst of allocations just drained the free pool. The pantry looked fine; the queue was long. ---

secs.head: Some versus full
secs.body: There are two lines because "someone is waiting" and "everyone is waiting" are different emergencies. Line It counts the time when... Think of it as ------ --------------------------- ---------------- some At least one runnable task was stalled on memory A customer is waiting. Annoying full All non-idle tasks were stalled on memory at the same moment Every customer is waiting and nobody is being served. The kitchen has stopped some is the early warning, full is the "the machine is effectively down" signal. A single-threaded program that stalls shows up as some and full together, because its one thread is every non-idle task it has. ---

secs.head: Bytes versus time, with two examples
secs.body: Why is time a better alarm than bytes? Low free memory, no pressure. A file server reads a lot of files, and the cache fills RAM. MemFree is 2% and PSI is 0. The kernel is using the spare as it should. An alert on MemFree fires every night for nothing. Plenty free, high pressure. A container is limited to 2 GiB with memory.max while the host has 20 GiB free. The container's working set is 2.5 GiB. The host looks relaxed. The container is thrashing and its PSI is high. An alert on host MemFree never fires. In both cases the stall time was the thing that mattered, and bytes pointed the wrong way. PSI also measures the cost : how bad a given level of use feels to the programs running on it. That is why it is the right input for a rescuer. A threshold on bytes has to be tuned per machine, and a threshold on stalled time means the same thing everywhere. PSI also exists for cpu and io ( /proc/pressure/cpu , /proc/pressure/io ), with the same format. ---

secs.head: Getting woken up: triggers
secs.body: Polling a file every second is fine. The kernel also lets a program say "wake me when pressure crosses this line", with no polling at all. You write a threshold to the file, then wait on it with poll / epoll : The string means: stall time (150000 µs) within a window (1000000 µs) . If tasks lose 150 ms or more out of any second, the program is woken. Windows run from 500 ms to 10 s. Two notes, both tested in clean VMs on Ubuntu 22.04 (Linux 5.15) and Ubuntu 26.04 (Linux 7.0). A trigger keeps firing while the stall lasts. The kernel docs say notifications are rate-limited to one per tracking window. In a test, a 150 ms-in-1 s trigger on a cgroup under sustained pressure woke the program 14 times in 15 seconds on 5.15 and 15 times on 7.0, about once per window. Don't assume a single wake-up, and re-read the file after you act to decide from the numbers. Who may register a trigger depends on the kernel. The kernel docs say unprivileged users can create triggers if the window is a multiple of 2 seconds. On 7.0 that is what happened: an ordinary user registered a 2 s window on /proc/pressure/memory , and the 1 s window above was refused with EINVAL . On 5.15 the same user got EPERM for both. On both kernels a user's own user@1000.service cgroup file was owned by root and refused the write ( EACCES ), so a rescuer that watches a group needs a file it can write. If you must support older kernels, run the rescuer as root. This is how a lightweight rescuer can sleep at zero cost until it is needed. And because it sleeps in the kernel until it is woken, it fits the memory-locking idea: the program is idle until the worst moment , the exact profile that part 5 protects. ---

secs.head: Per group, and who uses it
secs.body: Every cgroup v2 group has its own memory.pressure (and cpu.pressure , io.pressure ), in the same format. So you can ask "is this container stalled?" while the rest of the machine is calm. That is the data a rescuer needs to decide which group to act on, not just whether to act. Tool What it watches Notes ------ ----------------- ------- systemd-oomd Per-cgroup memory PSI (plus swap use) Kills a whole cgroup when pressure stays above a limit for a set time. Defaults to 60% for 20 seconds earlyoom MemAvailable and swap free, in percent A simpler, older approach: bytes, not time A custom rescuer Anything you choose PSI triggers plus the per-group files give the finest control On the machine this page was written on (Ubuntu 26.04, Linux 7.0), systemd-oomd is running and earlyoom is not. ---

secs.head: Check it on your own machine
secs.body: If /proc/pressure/memory doesn't exist, the kernel was built without PSI, or booted with psi=0 . Some distribution kernels ship PSI switched off by default (they need psi=1 on the kernel command line), so check the file before you build on it. To watch it move, put a deliberately small memory limit on a throwaway group and run something greedy inside it (see the cgroup page). Its memory.pressure climbs while the host's stays near zero. Takeaway: don't alarm on how many bytes are free; alarm on the share of time tasks spend stalled on memory ( some for early warning, full for "the machine has stopped"), because that measures the trouble itself and means the same on every machine. You can now see pressure coming. If nothing relieves it, the kernel eventually loses patience and kills something: who, and when? That's part 3.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Linux kernel docs: PSI, Pressure Stall Information (trigger rate limit, window range, unprivileged monitors) - Facebook Engineering: PSI and cgroup2-based OOM handling (oomd) - systemd-oomd.service(8) - earlyoom

label: 3. The OOM killer
title: The OOM Killer: Who Gets Thrown Overboard, and Why So Late
desc: Part 3 of the Linux Memory Pressure series. When reclaim can't free another page, the kernel kills a process. It will te

secs.head: The OOM Killer: Who Gets Thrown Overboard, and Why So Late
secs.body: Part 3 of the Linux Memory Pressure series. When reclaim can't free another page, the kernel kills a process. It will tell you which one in dmesg , but never why that one, and rarely early enough. By the end you'll be able to predict the victim, protect or sacrifice a process on purpose, and explain why the kernel is the last line of defence, not the first.

secs.head: The overloaded ship
secs.body: A cargo ship is caught in a storm, riding too low. The captain will not throw cargo overboard while the ship is merely heavy. She waits until water is coming over the deck and nothing else can be done. Then she picks the crate that frees the most weight and sends it into the sea. Two things about this are true of the Linux OOM killer too: 1. It is a last resort . It only fires after everything else, including all the reclaim from the previous pages, has failed. 2. It picks the heaviest crate , with a way for the crates to wear labels like "medical supplies: do not throw". Ship Linux machine ------ --------------- Water over the deck An allocation that reclaim cannot satisfy The captain The kernel's OOM killer A crate A process Weight of the crate Memory the process holds (RSS plus swap and page tables) The label on the crate oom score adj ---

secs.head: When the kernel decides it is out of memory
secs.body: It does not trigger on "memory is low". It triggers on a failure : 1. A program asks for a page. 2. There isn't one, so the kernel tries direct reclaim (part 1), and compaction, repeating several times. 3. Still nothing. Only now it calls the OOM killer. Because of memory overcommit ( vm.overcommit memory , default 0), a program's malloc almost always succeeds : the kernel promises memory without handing over real pages until each page is first touched. The bill arrives at touch time, which is why a program can crash with an OOM kill in the middle of an ordinary loop, long after the allocation call that "worked". ---

secs.head: How the victim is chosen
secs.body: For every candidate process the kernel computes a badness score. The base is how much real memory it holds: $$\text{points} = \text{RSS} + \text{swap used} + \text{page-table pages}$$ and that is scaled to a number from 0 to 1000 by the share of the machine's memory it represents. A process holding half of all RAM scores about 500. Then the label is added: $$\text{oom\ score} = \frac{\text{points} \times 1000}{\text{total pages}} + \text{oom\ score\ adj}$$ "Total pages" is the memory the process is allowed to use: RAM plus swap on the whole machine, or the cgroup's limit inside a cgroup (so the same process scores higher in a small cgroup). The proc(5) man pages describe it as an estimate of memory and swap use relative to allowed memory. The process with the highest score is killed. Its memory is released quickly by a helper (the OOM reaper ), so the system recovers without waiting for the victim to finish exiting. Notes that explain real surprises: - It's the biggest , not the guilty . A small leaky service filled the machine, but a large database holding more RAM scores higher and gets killed instead. - Memory is counted per process . Ten workers at 1 GiB each score lower than one process at 8 GiB, even though together they use more. - You can read any process's current score in /proc/<pid /oom score . ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Grab a pen. On a 16 GiB machine that has run out of memory: Process RSS oom score adj --------- ----- ----------------- A: database 8 GiB 0 B: a rescue daemon 0.05 GiB -900 C: a build job 5 GiB 0 D: a browser 3 GiB +500 Which process is killed first? Got your answer? Scroll on. Answer: the browser (D) . The scores are roughly A: 500, B: -897, C: 312, D: about 690 (3 GiB is 188 on its own, plus 500). Even though it is the smallest of the big three, its label of +500 pushes it to the top. The rescue daemon, at -900, is nearly untouchable. Labels, not just size, decide. ---

secs.head: Shielding and sacrificing: oom score adj
secs.body: oom score adj is a number from -1000 to +1000 written to /proc/<pid /oom score adj . Value Effect ------- -------- -1000 Never kill. The process is exempt (its badness score is always 0). Use sparingly: if it leaks, the kernel has nothing else left to sacrifice -900 Very strongly protected, but not exempt. The usual choice for something that must survive 0 Default: judged on size alone +500 to +1000 Prefer to kill this first. Good for disposable batch work The rule that matters for permissions: an ordinary user can raise the value of their own processes . Lowering it below the value the process started with, which is what shields it, needs CAP SYS RESOURCE , which in practice means root. (This rule is from the kernel source, fs/proc/base.c , not from the man pages, which don't spell it out. Tested as an ordinary user on Linux 5.15: raising to 100, then lowering to 50 and back to the starting 0, worked; lowering to -100 failed with Permission denied .) This is the same shape as RLIMIT MEMLOCK from part 5: protection from the machine's limits is rationed to privileged code. In systemd you don't write the file yourself: Locking a program in RAM (part 5) keeps it from being slow under pressure. A low oom score adj keeps it from being killed . A rescuer needs both, and they are separate settings. ---

secs.head: A smaller ship: OOM inside a cgroup
secs.body: A cgroup with a hard memory.max has its own, smaller ship. When the group tries to go past its cap and reclaim inside it fails, the kernel runs an OOM kill within that cgroup only , and the rest of the machine is untouched. The kernel's log says so: Memory cgroup out of memory , and in the constraint line CONSTRAINT MEMCG . Two files in the group show what happened: File What it tells you ------ ------------------- memory.events Counters: how often max was hit, how many times oom fired, how many processes were killed ( oom kill ) memory.oom.group If set to 1 , an OOM kill takes down the whole group together, instead of one process. Right for a container that is useless once any part dies This is why a container is "OOM-killed" with the host looking healthy: its ship was small, and it sank on its own. The files are covered in part 4. ---

secs.head: Why the kernel is late, and who acts earlier
secs.body: The kernel OOM killer only runs when reclaim fails outright . But recall thrashing from part 1: a machine can spend minutes swapping the same pages in and out, where every allocation technically succeeds , slowly. The OOM killer never fires, and the machine is unusable. People then power-cycle it, which is worse than a kill. That gap, from "unusable" to "kernel notices", is why userspace killers exist. They watch pressure (part 2) and act early, on purpose, and on a chosen victim: Kernel OOM killer Userspace killer (systemd-oomd, earlyoom, your own rescuer) - ------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------- Trigger An allocation failed after reclaim Pressure stays high, or available memory is low Timing Last resort, can be minutes late Early, while the machine still works Victim Biggest score Chosen by policy: a whole cgroup, a low-priority job Gentler options None, it kills Can throttle, freeze or pause first Needs memory to act? It's the kernel Yes , which is the reason for memory locking Note the last row. The userspace killer is the program whose pages could have been swapped out. It is the tow truck from part 5. systemd adds a policy setting: OOMPolicy= decides what happens to a service when one of its processes is OOM-killed ( stop the whole service, kill it, or continue ), and ManagedOOMMemoryPressure=kill opts a cgroup into systemd-oomd . ---

secs.head: Read the crime scene
secs.body: When something was killed, the kernel writes a report. Read it with: You'll see lines like Out of memory: Killed process 1234 (python) ... anon-rss: ... , a table of every process's memory at that moment, and the constraint ( CONSTRAINT NONE for the whole machine, CONSTRAINT MEMCG for a cgroup). To see how exposed a process is right now: Takeaway: the kernel kills only after reclaim has failed, picks the process holding the most memory adjusted by oom score adj , and often acts long after the machine became unusable; so shield what must survive with a low oom score adj , and use a userspace killer on pressure for the early, gentler action. The kernel's tool is a blunt kill. The cgroup files give you gentler levers, such as throttling, asking a group to give memory back, freezing it. That's part 4.

secs.head: References

label: 4. cgroup v2 memory control
title: cgroup v2 Memory Control: The Levers Between Doing Nothing and Killing
desc: Part 4 of the Linux Memory Pressure series. Detection (part 2) is only half a rescuer. The other half is a set of levers

secs.head: cgroup v2 Memory Control: The Levers Between Doing Nothing and Killing
secs.body: Part 4 of the Linux Memory Pressure series. Detection (part 2) is only half a rescuer. The other half is a set of levers it can pull, and cgroups have a surprisingly fine one for every stage, from "slow this group down" to "remove it". By the end you'll know what each memory file does, in which order you'd pull them, and which ones an ordinary user can't touch.

secs.head: The hotel with a group booking
secs.body: A conference books a block of rooms in a busy hotel. The manager has a set of controls for that one group, and they escalate: 1. Guaranteed rooms : "these 20 are theirs; nobody else may be given them." 2. Preferred rooms : "we'll try to keep these 30 free for them, but in an emergency we may need them back." 3. Slow check-in : past 50 rooms, each extra guest is made to wait at the desk. 4. No more rooms : past 60, the desk turns people away, and if the group insists, someone is asked to leave. Beyond the booking, the manager can also act directly: ask the group to give some rooms back, send everyone to their rooms and shut the doors (nobody leaves or arrives), or clear the whole block. That list is the memory controller of cgroup v2, almost one for one. Hotel cgroup v2 file ------- ---------------- Guaranteed rooms memory.min Preferred rooms memory.low Slow check-in memory.high No more rooms memory.max Ask them to give rooms back memory.reclaim Shut the doors cgroup.freeze Clear the block cgroup.kill ---

secs.head: What a cgroup is, in one paragraph
secs.body: A control group is a set of processes that the kernel accounts for and limits together. On modern systems with cgroup v2 there's a single tree under /sys/fs/cgroup . Each systemd service, user session and container is a directory in it, and the files in that directory are both the measurements ( memory.current , memory.pressure ) and the controls. You change a limit by writing a number to a file. There is no special API. ---

secs.head: The four limit files
secs.body: All values are in bytes (or the word max for "no limit"). Think of them as four lines on a ruler, from protection to hard stop. File Name What the kernel does Never OOM-kills? ------ ------ ---------------------- ------------------ memory.min Hard protection Memory below this is not reclaimed , even under pressure n/a memory.low Soft protection Memory below this is reclaimed only if nothing unprotected is left n/a memory.high Throttle Above this, the group is put under heavy reclaim pressure and its tasks are slowed down Yes: it never kills memory.max Hard limit Above this, the group runs OOM handling and a process in it is killed No, this is the kill Two limits on that table. memory.min is not absolute: the kernel docs say that if there is no unprotected reclaimable memory left, the OOM killer is invoked anyway. And memory.low is capped by the memory.low of the group's ancestors , so protecting one service while its parent slice has none protects little. The distinction people trip on is high versus max : - memory.high is a speed limit. The group can go over it, but every allocation past the line turns into forced reclaim and sleeping, so it runs slower and slower. It cannot kill anything. - memory.max is a wall. There the OOM killer (part 3) is invoked inside the group. Setting memory.high a bit below memory.max gives a working group a warning zone: it slows down before it dies, and the cgroup's memory.pressure (part 2) rises as a signal that you could see. A catch worth knowing. memory.high works by making the group reclaim memory. If nothing in the group can be reclaimed (all anonymous pages and no swap), it can't get under the line, and the throttling just gets heavier. When I tried this by putting a small program in a scope with a 100 MiB memory.high and swap disabled for it, allocating 130 MiB, it had not finished after 40 seconds (Ubuntu 26.04, Linux 7.0). I repeated it in clean VMs with a 60-second cap. On Ubuntu 22.04 (Linux 5.15, systemd 249), touching 130 MiB did not finish, and neither did 105 MiB, only 5 MiB over the line. On Ubuntu 26.04 (Linux 7.0) 130 MiB still did not finish, but 105 MiB finished in 9 seconds, so a small overshoot is throttled hard on the old kernel and survivable on the new one. After 8 seconds the group sat at about 106 MiB, memory.events showed high at 997, and its memory.pressure read some avg10=43.67 . The throttle is real and can look like a hang. To reproduce it, use the throwaway-scope command at the end of this page with MemoryHigh=100M and MemorySwapMax=0 , and allocate and touch more than 100 MiB inside it. [!WARNING] A group throttled by memory.high that has nothing to reclaim looks hung, not dead, and it never gets OOM-killed for it. Watch memory.events ( high counting up) and the group's memory.pressure , or you'll wait on a job that can't finish. Writing memory.high is itself an action with a cost: the kernel docs say a normal write triggers synchronous reclaim, and that opening the file with O NONBLOCK bypasses it . A rescuer that lowers memory.high under pressure should open the file that way. Two companions: memory.swap.max caps how much of the group can go to swap (0 means none), and memory.events counts what has happened: times high and max were reached, oom and oom kill events. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Grab a pen. A container has memory.high = 4 GiB and memory.max = 6 GiB. It's growing steadily, and nothing in it can be swapped. 1. At 3 GiB, what happens? 2. At 5 GiB? 3. At 6 GiB? Got your answers? Scroll on. Answers: at 3 GiB, nothing : it is below every line. At 5 GiB it is throttled : it is still alive but slowed, with its pressure rising and memory.events high counting up. At 6 GiB it runs out of room and the kernel's OOM handling kills a process in it. And if it throttles so hard it can't grow, it may never reach 6 GiB. ---

secs.head: The active levers: reclaim, freeze, kill
secs.body: The limit files are standing rules . Three more files are actions a rescuer can take on demand. memory.reclaim . Writing an amount, such as echo 512M memory.reclaim , asks the kernel to reclaim that much from the group now , pushing its cold pages to swap or dropping its cache. It does not change any limit. It is a polite request that returns an error ( EAGAIN ) if the group couldn't give back the full amount. Since it is proactive, it is the gentlest way to free memory from a specific group. It needs Linux 5.19 or newer : on Ubuntu 22.04 (5.15) the file does not exist in a new cgroup, while cgroup.kill , cgroup.freeze , memory.high , memory.low and memory.min do. The docs don't say whether the write waits for the reclaim. On Linux 7.0 a request against a group holding 200 MiB of anonymous memory with no swap returned EAGAIN immediately (under a millisecond), so it did not block when nothing could be reclaimed; I did not time one where pages could be reclaimed, so time it on your kernel before you put it in a rescuer's hot path. On Linux 7.0 it also accepts a swappiness= argument that overrides vm.swappiness for that one request (0, 60 and max were accepted and 201 was refused; it is not available on 5.15, where the whole file is missing). cgroup.freeze . Writing 1 freezes every process in the group: they stop being scheduled, like a paused video. It does not release their memory; it only stops it growing. Writing 0 thaws them. This is how docker pause works. It is a good emergency brake: it buys time without destroying anyone's work. Frozen processes can still be killed. cgroup.kill . Writing 1 kills every process in the group and its child groups . No sequence of signals, no waiting for children. It is the clean "remove this entire container" action, and it frees the memory. It needs Linux 5.14 or newer ( cgroup.freeze needs 5.2). [!CAUTION] cgroup.kill is not reversible and takes down the whole subtree. Never point it at a group you picked by a name pattern without a dry run: log which group the rescuer would kill for a few days before you let it write 1 . Lever Frees memory? Loses work? Reversible? ------- --------------- ------------- ------------- memory.high lowered Gradually, by throttling No Yes memory.reclaim Some (cold pages) No Yes (pages come back on use) cgroup.freeze No : stops growth No Yes cgroup.kill Yes , all of it Yes No ---

secs.head: The escalation ladder
secs.body: Put them in order of how much damage each does, and you have the plan of a graduated rescuer. Lowest rung first, moving up only while pressure stays high: Two design points make this practical: - Choose the victim by priority. Because every service and container is a cgroup, a rescuer can act on the lowest-priority group first and leave the important ones alone, which the kernel's blunt per-process OOM killer cannot do. - Each rung is a single write . That is what makes it fit with the memory-locking page: open the files for the groups you might act on ahead of time , keep the handles, and the action under pressure becomes one pwrite on a handle you already hold, with nothing to open or allocate in your own program. The kernel may still do work inside that write: a normal memory.high write reclaims synchronously (open it with O NONBLOCK to skip that), and memory.reclaim may take time. See part 5. ---

secs.head: Who may pull the levers
secs.body: Writing these files requires ownership of the cgroup . A normal user typically owns only a delegated subtree, such as their own user session's slice, and only the controllers that systemd has enabled for it ( cat /sys/fs/cgroup/user.slice/user-1000.slice/user@1000.service/cgroup.controllers shows them; on my machine it lists cpu memory pids ). Ordinary user Root - --------------- ------ Groups it can control Only a delegated user subtree Every group, including other services and containers Container actions Through the Docker API, if in the docker group ( pause , stop ) Directly: freeze, throttle, reclaim and kill any container's cgroup Typical rescue ability Pause or stop the containers it can reach The full ladder above [!WARNING] Membership of the docker group is effectively root on that host: anyone in it can start a privileged container. Treat "an unprivileged rescuer that talks to Docker" as a root-equivalent service when you decide who may run it. This is the same split as in the memory-locking page: a rescuer without root is best effort and uses the few tools it can reach, while a root service has the whole ladder and the lock. ---

secs.head: Look at your own groups
secs.body: To set a limit safely, let systemd do it on a throwaway group, which cleans up after itself: Success: it prints Running scope as unit: run-<id .scope and then your command's output. Tested as an ordinary user on Ubuntu 22.04, where the user's cgroup.controllers was memory pids . Check that memory is in that listing first: a user session without a delegated memory controller can't apply these limits. To watch memory.events while it runs, find the scope's directory with cat /proc/<pid /cgroup for the command's PID. Do not point experiments at your login session's group. Create a new scope as above and watch it from a second terminal. Takeaway: cgroup v2 gives a rescuer a graduated ladder ( memory.high to slow a group, memory.reclaim to ask for pages back, cgroup.freeze to stop it growing, cgroup.kill to remove it), so it can take the gentlest step that works and choose the victim by priority; most of the ladder needs ownership of the group, which in practice means root. You now have pressure to see and levers to pull . What keeps the program that holds the levers alive and fast when the machine is at its worst? That's the memory-locking page, next, and part 6 ties everything into one checklist.

label: 5. Memory locking (mlockall)
title: Memory Locking: Keeping a Rescuer in RAM with mlockall
desc: Part 5 of the Linux Memory Pressure series. Some programs exist to act when the machine is out of memory: a watchdog tha

secs.head: Memory Locking: Keeping a Rescuer in RAM with mlockall
secs.body: Part 5 of the Linux Memory Pressure series. Some programs exist to act when the machine is out of memory: a watchdog that kills a runaway job, a daemon that pauses containers. Those programs have a trap waiting for them, and mlockall is the fix. By the end you'll know what the trap is, what the fix pins, what it costs, and why an ordinary user can only get half of it.

secs.head: The tow truck that got towed
secs.body: A city's parking lot is full. The council employs a tow truck whose whole job is to clear the lot when it gets too crowded. To make room, the rule is simple: the least recently used cars get towed to a faraway yard, and fetched back when their owner shows up. One busy afternoon the lot overflows. The tow truck driver walks out to start the clearing, and finds that her own car has been towed . It was parked there all day doing nothing, so it was the least recently used car in the lot. Now she has to wait for it to come back from the far yard, and the yard is busy hauling everyone else's cars. The lot stays jammed. The one person who could fix the jam is stuck waiting for transport. The fix is not a faster tow truck. The fix is a reserved parking spot that the towing rule is forbidden to touch, plus keys that are already in her hand . City Linux machine ------ --------------- The parking lot RAM The far yard Swap (a disk, or compressed RAM like zram) The towing rule The kernel's page reclaim, least recently used first The tow truck Your rescuer program (watchdog, governor, OOM helper) The reserved spot mlockall Keys already in hand Resources opened and allocated before trouble The rest of this page is that table, one row at a time. ---

secs.head: Step 1: what swapping really is
secs.body: Programs don't touch RAM directly. They see virtual memory : the kernel hands each process a big imaginary address space and chops it into pages (usually 4 KiB). Each page is either in RAM right now, or it isn't. When RAM gets short, the kernel needs free pages. It looks for pages nobody has used lately and evicts them: - A page backed by a file (a library, the program's own code) can simply be dropped, because it can be read from the file again. - A page that only exists in memory (heap, stack) has nowhere to go, so it is written to swap . Later, if the program touches an evicted page, the CPU raises a page fault , the kernel reads the page back in, and the program continues. The program never notices, except that the access took far longer. How much longer? A RAM access is around a hundred nanoseconds. Reading a page back from an SSD is around a hundred microseconds, a thousand times slower. From a spinning disk it is milliseconds. And when the machine is thrashing, the disk queue is full of everybody else's evictions, so your page waits in line. This is a fine trade for a text editor you left open overnight. It is a terrible one for the program whose job is to act right now . ---

secs.head: Step 2: the trap
secs.body: Put the two facts together: 1. Memory pressure is exactly when the kernel evicts pages. 2. A rescuer is exactly the program that sits idle until memory pressure arrives. An idle program is a perfect eviction candidate: its pages haven't been touched in hours. So by the time pressure hits, the rescuer's code and data have probably been pushed out to swap. The moment it wakes up to act, it page-faults on its own instructions , and each fault waits on a disk that is busy with the crisis it was supposed to stop. Nothing is broken here. The kernel is doing exactly what it should. The design is what's wrong: the program that handles emergencies is treated as just another idle program. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Grab a pen. Which of these should pin its memory in RAM? 1. A text editor with ten open files. 2. A watchdog that pauses containers when free memory drops below 5%. 3. A database buffer pool of 200 GiB. Got your answer? Scroll on. Answer: 2 . The editor can afford a slow page fault. The 200 GiB pool is far too big to pin (and the database has its own tools). The watchdog is tiny, idle most of the time, and needed at the worst possible moment: the textbook candidate. ---

secs.head: Step 3: the fix, mlockall
secs.body: Linux lets a program say "never evict these pages". The call is mlockall : The two flags are the whole trick: Flag Pins Why you need it ------ ------ ----------------- MCL CURRENT Every page the process has mapped right now : its code, libraries, heap, stack The rescuer's existing instructions and data can no longer be swapped out MCL FUTURE Every page the process maps from now on Memory it grows into later is born locked, not evictable After the call, the process is the tow truck with the reserved spot. The kernel's reclaim loop skips its pages, no matter how long they sit idle. A sibling call, mlock(addr, len) , pins just one range. mlockall is the blunt tool: "everything I have, and everything I'll get". For a small daemon that's what you want. ---

secs.head: Step 4: the second half of the fix, pre-allocation
secs.body: A locked car is no use if the driver has to hunt for her keys. The same holds here, and it is the subtler half. When the rescuer finally acts, it has to do something: open a file, write to a control file, start a helper. Each of those can need new memory : a fresh buffer, a new file handle, a new kernel structure. And asking for new memory under pressure means asking the kernel for a free page when there are none. The kernel has to reclaim one first (this is direct reclaim ), and the caller waits while it happens. Locking doesn't help with that. It protects pages you already have, not pages you're about to ask for. So the second half is: do all the asking before the crisis. - Open the files and sockets the rescue will write to, and keep the handles. - Allocate the buffers it will need, and touch them (write to them once) so the kernel really backs them with RAM instead of promising it for later. - Do this before calling mlockall , so those pages are included in the lock. When the crisis comes, the rescuer's work is a single write to a handle it already holds, using memory it already owns. No allocation, no waiting on reclaim. Without pre-allocation With pre-allocation ------------------------ --------------------- Opens the control file at the moment of need Handle was opened at startup Allocates a buffer under pressure Buffer was allocated and touched at startup May stall in reclaim Nothing left to wait for Two honest limits. If the rescue involves starting a new process (for example running a docker stop command), the kernel has to allocate for that process, and no pre-allocation inside your program can prevent it. Only plain writes to already-open handles avoid new allocations in your own code. And the examples on this page are Python, which allocates small objects on almost every call, even os.pwrite . A Python rescuer can shrink that (build the bytes to write once at startup and reuse them) but can't get to zero. If the rescuer has to be strict about it, write it in C, Go or Rust, and treat the Python here as the readable version of the idea. ---

secs.head: Step 5: the cost, and where 8 MiB comes from
secs.body: A locked page is a page the kernel can never reclaim. If every program did it, the kernel would run out of pages it's allowed to take back, and the whole machine would fall over. Locking is a privilege that has to be rationed. Linux rations it with a per-process limit, RLIMIT MEMLOCK : - It caps how many bytes one unprivileged process may lock. - Since Linux 5.16 the default is 8 MiB . (Before that it was 64 KiB.) - It has a soft limit (the one enforced) and a hard limit (the ceiling the soft one can be raised to). - An ordinary user can raise the soft limit up to the hard limit, but cannot raise the hard limit . Now the catch. mlockall(MCL CURRENT MCL FUTURE) locks everything mapped , not just the program's own few kilobytes. A Python interpreter with its libraries is easily tens of MiB. So against an 8 MiB limit, the call fails with ENOMEM , even though the program is tiny by any other measure. ---

secs.head: Root versus ordinary user
secs.body: This is why a rescuer often comes in two modes. Ordinary user Root service - --------------- -------------- Memory-lock limit 8 MiB default, hard limit can't be raised Not limited ( CAP IPC LOCK ), or LimitMEMLOCK=infinity in the service file mlockall Often fails with ENOMEM Succeeds Result Best effort : it still runs, but its pages may be swapped out The real guarantee Other powers Only what the user can do, e.g. talking to Docker Can also write cgroup control files: throttle a group, force reclaim So the lock isn't just a flag you switch on. It is tied to privilege: the same program gives a weaker guarantee when started as a normal user. That's a design tradeoff, not a bug. The unprivileged mode is easy to start and useful, and the privileged service is the upgrade you install when you need the full promise. A good program in the unprivileged mode tries the lock, logs that it failed, and carries on , rather than refusing to start. It also pairs well with OOMScoreAdjust=-900 in a systemd unit, which tells the kernel's OOM killer to prefer almost any other victim first (more on that below). ---

secs.head: Check it on your own machine
secs.body: For a systemd service, the limit comes from the unit file, not your shell: To see the failure for yourself, run the Python snippet from Step 3 as a normal user with an 8 MiB limit ( ulimit -l 8192 first). Expect OSError: [Errno 12] Cannot allocate memory . I confirmed that on Ubuntu 22.04 (Linux 5.15). The limit varies by distribution and systemd version: on that same VM ulimit -l was 251360 KiB out of the box, and the call succeeded for an ordinary user ( VmLck: 17564 kB ). On a clean Ubuntu 26.04 VM (Linux 7.0) ulimit -l was 8192 and the same call failed for an ordinary user with ENOMEM , so that is the default to expect on newer systems. Check ulimit -l before you assume you're limited to 8 MiB. Run it as root and it returns normally, and VmLck in /proc/self/status jumps from 0 kB to the size of the process. ---

secs.head: What locking does not do
secs.body: Pinning pages fixes one stall. It is not armor. - It doesn't stop the OOM killer. A locked process can still be chosen and killed when the machine truly runs out of memory. That's what OOMScoreAdjust is for, and it's a separate setting. - It doesn't give you CPU. If the machine is so loaded that your process isn't scheduled, being in RAM doesn't help. Real-time scheduling priority is another tool. - It doesn't make allocation free. Only memory you got before the lock is guaranteed. That's why Step 4 exists. - It isn't free for the machine. Locked pages are lost to everyone else. Keep the rescuer small, and never lock a big cache "just in case". - It counts inside cgroup limits. In a container with a memory cap, locked pages count against it and can't be reclaimed to get back under it. Slurm does this for its own node daemon: slurmd -M locks it into memory, as described in slurmstepd. The same call has a second, unrelated use: programs that hold secrets (keys, passwords) lock that memory so it never reaches a swap file on disk. Takeaway: a program meant to act under memory pressure is the first thing the kernel would evict, so it pins its own pages with mlockall and does its allocating before trouble starts; Linux rations that power, which is why the full guarantee needs root and an unprivileged run is best effort. The lock is one piece of survival. CPU priority, the OOM shield and a watchdog complete it in part 6.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - mlock(2), mlockall(2): Linux manual pages - getrlimit(2): RLIMIT MEMLOCK - systemd.exec: LimitMEMLOCK, OOMScoreAdjust - Linux kernel docs: Concepts overview (virtual memory, swapping)

label: 6. The rescuer checklist
title: Making a Rescuer Survive: CPU, Protection and a Checklist
desc: Part 6 of the Linux Memory Pressure series. Pinning a program in RAM stops one kind of stall. A machine in trouble has o

secs.head: Making a Rescuer Survive: CPU, Protection and a Checklist
secs.body: Part 6 of the Linux Memory Pressure series. Pinning a program in RAM stops one kind of stall. A machine in trouble has others: the program can be starved of CPU, killed by the OOM killer, or simply hung. This page covers the rest of what a rescuer needs, then gives one checklist for the whole series.

secs.head: The ambulance that is stuck in traffic
secs.body: A city gives its ambulance a reserved garage so it is never towed (that's memory locking), and keys always in the ignition (pre-allocation). On the day of the big traffic jam it is parked, intact, in its garage, and cannot get out. Three more things were needed: Gap What goes wrong The ambulance equivalent ----- ----------------- -------------------------- CPU The machine is so busy the rescuer isn't scheduled Stuck in the jam: needs lights and siren, the right to jump the queue Being killed The OOM killer picks it as the heaviest crate Someone impounds it for taking up space Hanging It's alive but stuck, and nobody notices The driver fell asleep at the wheel; no dispatcher is checking ---

secs.head: Gap 1: CPU time
secs.body: Under memory pressure the machine is busy: reclaim threads, a thrashing workload, a disk queue. A rescuer in RAM still has to be given the CPU . Linux has real-time scheduling classes , SCHED FIFO and SCHED RR , which always beat ordinary processes. A real-time task runs the moment it is ready, and keeps the CPU until it blocks. In a systemd unit: CPUSchedulingPolicy=fifo and CPUSchedulingPriority=50 . [!CAUTION] SCHED FIFO can freeze a machine. A real-time rescuer that loops without blocking starves everything, including the SSH session you'd use to stop it. Try it on one canary node first, and keep a second root shell open. The cost: this is a power that can freeze a machine. A real-time program that loops without blocking would starve everything, including the programs it was meant to rescue, which is why the kernel limits it: - A normal user needs CAP SYS NICE or an RLIMIT RTPRIO allowance to ask for it, so it is privileged , just like the memory lock. - Real-time tasks get at most 95% of each second by default ( sched rt runtime us is 950000 of 1000000 µs on my machine), leaving 5% for everyone else. That reserve is the safety net against a runaway. Rule of thumb: a rescuer should do a small amount of work and then block (wait on a PSI trigger or a timer). It uses real-time priority for latency , not for throughput. A softer version: a negative nice value ( Nice=-10 ) and a higher IO class ( IOSchedulingClass=realtime , which usually needs privilege too). ---

secs.head: Gap 2: being killed
secs.body: Even locked and prioritized, the rescuer is a process. When the kernel is out of memory, it is scored like any other (part 3). The shield is OOMScoreAdjust=-900 . Why -900 and not -1000 ? Because -1000 makes the process exempt from the OOM killer entirely . If the rescuer itself ever leaks, the kernel has no way to remove it, and the machine can wedge. -900 makes it a victim of last resort: almost any other process dies first, but a real bug in the rescuer is still correctable. One more shield sits in the cgroup. Giving the rescuer's service a MemoryLow= (or memory.low ) tells reclaim to take memory from other groups first when the machine is short. It's a cousin of the lock for pages that are not worth pinning individually. The kernel docs say the effective protection is limited by the memory.low of the ancestor groups, so also protect the parent slice, or the line may do little. ---

secs.head: Gap 3: hanging, and who watches the watcher
secs.body: A rescuer that crashes is bad. One that is alive but stuck is worse, because nothing restarts it. Two systemd settings handle this: - Restart=always brings it back after a crash or a kill. - WatchdogSec=30 makes the service send an "I'm alive" message (via sd notify ) at least that often. If it goes quiet, systemd treats it as hung and restarts it. This turns the rescuer's own failure into a short gap instead of a silent one. The sd notify call must itself be allocation-free, so the same rule from part 5 applies: open the notification socket at startup. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Grab a pen. A rescuer has mlockall and OOMScoreAdjust=-900 . During a memory spike it still reacts three seconds late. Name two things that could still be wrong. Got yours? Scroll on. Answers: (1) It isn't getting CPU quickly. It is a normal-priority process competing with a busy machine. (2) Its action allocates. If acting means starting a subprocess like docker stop , the child process needs new memory and can stall in direct reclaim, even though the parent is locked. A third: its trigger is slow. Polling once every few seconds is itself a three-second delay, which a PSI trigger would remove. ---

secs.head: The whole unit file
secs.body: Putting every gap together, a privileged rescuer's unit might look like this: Most lines here need privilege (everything except Restart= and WatchdogSec= ), which is the reason an unprivileged rescuer is "best effort" and a root service is "the real thing". WatchdogSec= works without Type=notify : systemd sets NotifyAccess=main for you when WatchdogSec= is set and NotifyAccess= isn't. Tested on Ubuntu 22.04 (systemd 249): systemctl show -p NotifyAccess printed main for a plain Type=simple unit that never set it. Roll it out safely. Install it on one canary node first, as a drop-in, so you can undo it: 1. Run it for a few days in log-only mode (it names the group it would act on and does nothing). 2. Turn on the real action on the canary node only, and keep a second root shell open. 3. Roll back with systemctl stop rescuer , delete the unit or drop-in, and systemctl daemon-reload . Prove the watchdog works. Freeze the process with kill -STOP $(pidof rescuer) . Within about WatchdogSec (30 seconds here) the journal should show a watchdog timeout and systemd restarting the service. If nothing happens, the service isn't sending its keep-alive pings. I ran this on Ubuntu 22.04 with WatchdogSec=6 and a small Python process sending WATCHDOG=1 every 2 seconds. Healthy for 14 seconds, it kept the same PID. After kill -STOP and 12 seconds it had a new PID, and the journal showed: ---

secs.head: The checklist
secs.body: One row per page of the series. Question What to do Page --- ---------- ------------ ------ 1 Am I looking at the right number? Alert on MemAvailable and pgscan direct , never MemFree How Linux reclaims memory 2 How will I know pressure is coming? Read PSI ( some early, full late), or use a PSI trigger to wake up Memory pressure (PSI) 3 What happens if I'm too late? Know the kernel OOM victim rule; shield what matters with oom score adj The OOM killer 4 What can I do, gentlest first? memory.high , then memory.reclaim , then cgroup.freeze , then cgroup.kill , chosen per group by priority cgroup v2 memory control 5 Will I be fast when it happens? mlockall , plus pre-open handles and pre-touch buffers before the lock Memory locking (mlockall) 6 Will I get CPU, survive and be noticed if I hang? Real-time priority, -900 OOM adjust, Restart= and WatchdogSec= This page And the one rule that holds them all: everything the rescuer needs under pressure must be acquired before the pressure. Memory, file handles, sockets, buffers, the decision about whom to act on. If any step opens, allocates or looks something up during the crisis, the crisis can delay it. The unprivileged fallback is a sensible product decision, not a failure: try each privileged step, log the ones that fail, and keep running with what worked. ---

secs.head: Other uses of locked memory
secs.body: Locking isn't only for rescuers. The same call shows up wherever the kernel moving a page would be a problem: - Secrets. Keys and passwords are locked so they never reach a swap file. Newer kernels also offer memfd secret , memory even the kernel cannot read directly. - Latency-critical programs. Audio, trading and packet-processing code lock memory so a page fault never interrupts a deadline. Often paired with huge pages and real-time priority, the same recipe as above. - Hardware access. Devices that read memory directly (RDMA, GPU transfers) need pages that cannot move, which is why this series is related to the GPU storage and fabric pages. Takeaway: a rescuer that is only locked in RAM can still be starved of CPU, killed by the OOM killer or hang unnoticed; give it real-time priority, a -900 OOM shield and a watchdog, and acquire every resource it will need before the pressure begins.

secs.body: - sched(7): real-time scheduling policies and chrt(1) - systemd.service(5): Restart, WatchdogSec and sd notify(3) - systemd.exec(5): CPUSchedulingPolicy, OOMScoreAdjust, LimitMEMLOCK - memfd secret(2)

secs.head: Node Health Check - Overview
secs.body: An eleven-part series on LBNL Node Health Check (NHC) , the small bash framework that big HPC clusters trust to decide whether a compute node deserves a job. Read it in order the first time; come back to the troubleshooting page and cheat sheet whenever a node misbehaves at 2 AM.

secs.head: Who this is for
secs.body: Cluster admins and HPC/AI platform engineers who run Slurm (or PBS, or Grid Engine, or even Kubernetes) and are tired of one sick node quietly eating a queue full of jobs. You should be comfortable with a root shell and slurm.conf . Bash wizardry is helpful for part 6, not required before it.

secs.head: The route
secs.body: Page You'll walk away with --- ------ ----------------------- 1 Why your cluster needs a bouncer The black-hole-node problem, what NHC is, and how it decides who gets in 2 Build and install NHC on your nodes from an RPM, a tarball or the Git tree, tested 3 Writing nhc.conf A real config for CPU, GPU and login nodes, plus match strings and contexts 4 Slurm integration The drain/resume handshake, HealthCheckNodeState , prolog/epilog and reboots 5 Rolling out to a fleet A dry-run → canary → enforce plan that won't drain your whole cluster on day one 6 Writing custom checks Your own .nhc module, with GPU examples and NHC-style fast bash 7 Auto-remediation A safe detect → drain → fix → verify → resume loop with guard rails 8 Troubleshooting Symptom-first fixes for the classic NHC headaches 9 Architecture-driven NHC NHC generated from one cluster definition, cross-checked with slurm.conf and tested with real NHC 10 Case study: build us an NHC A client engagement on DGX H100 + AMD EPYC hardware: discovery questions, proposal, validation, final answer 11 Cheat sheet Every command and knob from the series on one page

secs.body: File Description ------ ------------- why-node-health-check Black-hole nodes, what NHC is and how it works build-and-install Installing NHC from RPM, tarball or Git writing-nhc-conf Config syntax, match strings, contexts and starter configs slurm-integration Wiring NHC into Slurm, PBS and cron rollout-at-scale Deploying NHC safely across hundreds of nodes custom-checks Writing your own checks, GPU examples included architecture-driven-nhc Generating NHC configs from an architecture definition auto-remediation Automating fixes without automating disasters troubleshooting Symptom-first troubleshooting guide case-study-build-me-an-nhc Consulting case study: from a vague request to a validated proposal cheat-sheet Commands, options and variables at a glance Tools and inputs for parts 9-10: nhc gen.py , acme arch.nhc , nhc test harness.sh , cluster-example.yaml , case-study-delta-cluster.yaml , case-study-delta-expected.txt .

label: 1. Why NHC
title: Why Your Cluster Needs a Bouncer
desc: Part 1 of the Node Health Check series. No commands to run yet. Grab the tea, this one is the "why" and the mental model

secs.head: Why Your Cluster Needs a Bouncer
secs.body: Part 1 of the Node Health Check series. No commands to run yet. Grab the tea, this one is the "why" and the mental model everything else hangs on.

secs.head: The night one node ate 400 jobs
secs.body: Picture cn042 . Its /scratch Lustre mount dropped at 23:10. Everything else on the node is fine: slurmd is up, it answers pings, the scheduler sees it as IDLE . So the scheduler does exactly what it's built to do. It hands cn042 a job. The job dies in two seconds because /scratch/$USER doesn't exist. cn042 is now idle again, and it's the most available node in the partition, so it gets the next job. And the next. By morning, 400 jobs have "completed" in a few seconds each, users are filing tickets about their "broken code", and your job-failure dashboard looks like a heart monitor in a horror film. HPC folks call this a black-hole node : a node that fails fast and therefore looks permanently available, sucking in work like a drain. The faster your scheduler, the bigger the hole. The fix isn't a smarter scheduler. It's a bouncer at the door : something on every node that asks, every few minutes and before work lands, "are you actually fit to run a job?" , and if the answer is no, takes the node out of rotation with a reason a human can read. [!NOTE] Slurm, PBS/TORQUE and friends all have a hook for exactly this, usually called a node health check program . They provide the hook. You provide the program. NHC is the program almost everybody ends up using. ---

secs.head: Meet NHC
secs.body: LBNL Node Health Check (NHC) was started at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in late 2010 (it was called Warewulf NHC until 1.4.2) and has been running in production on clusters of every size since. It's maintained by Michael Jennings at github.com/mej/nhc, BSD-style licensed, and its latest release is 1.5 (October 2026). Why did it win over the thousand home-grown healthcheck.sh scripts out there? Its design goals, straight from the project: Goal What it means in practice ------ --------------------------- Reliable A watchdog timer kills hung checks, and NHC itself, so a dead NFS server can't wedge your node's health check forever. Fast Written almost entirely in native bash (4.3+), avoiding grep / awk / sed forks wherever possible. Less overhead, less OS jitter for your MPI jobs. Flexible Anything you can write as a shell function can be a check. Extensible Drop a .nhc file in the scripts directory, reference the check in the config, done. Reusable One config file for the whole cluster, with per-host targeting. Runs from the RM daemon, cron, or by hand via pdsh / clush . Big users publish their own extensions on top of it. Azure's AzNHC is NHC plus GPU, NVLink, InfiniBand and NCCL checks for their AI VMs, and LANL contributed GPU, Kubernetes and network modules upstream. ---

secs.head: How it works, in one picture
secs.body: A few things worth burning into memory: 1. One config for the whole cluster. Every line in nhc.conf looks like target check . Each node only runs the lines whose target matches its own hostname. More on this in part 3. 2. First failure wins (by default). NHC stops at the first failing check, reports it and exits non-zero. Use -a when you want to see every failure, which is exactly what you want while debugging. 3. Silence is golden. A healthy run prints nothing and exits 0 . Details go to /var/log/nhc.log . 4. NHC takes action itself. The scheduler only runs the program. Slurm's own docs say any action must be performed by the program, and NHC's helper scripts do the draining and resuming. ---

secs.head: The "NHC:" handshake
secs.body: This is the single most important idea in the series, so it gets its own section. When NHC drains a node, it writes a reason that starts with NHC: : When a later run passes, NHC only resumes the node if the current reason still starts with NHC: . If the node is drained with no reason, or with a reason someone else wrote, NHC leaves it alone. That one rule gives you a clean ownership contract: Who drained it Reason looks like Will NHC auto-resume it? ---------------- ------------------- -------------------------- NHC NHC: <failure message ✅ Yes, as soon as checks pass again You, for maintenance HW ticket 4711: DIMM swap ❌ No, it's yours until you resume it Anyone, no reason given (empty) ❌ No, by default [!TIP] Want NHC to keep its hands off a node it drained, say while you investigate? Just change the reason: scontrol update nodename=cn042 reason="ahmed: investigating lustre" . The node stays drained and NHC no longer considers it its own. ---

secs.head: Four moments to check a node
secs.body: Health checks aren't one thing. Mature sites check at several moments, each with a different budget: Moment Trigger Time budget Good for -------- --------- ------------- ---------- Boot / daemon start slurmd startup, before it registers Seconds to a minute "Did this node come up right?" Mounts, NICs, GPUs present, BIOS settings Periodic HealthCheckInterval timer Well under a minute, every few minutes Cheap, continuous checks: mounts, daemons, memory, link state Job boundaries Prolog / Epilog Seconds (it delays jobs!) "Is it safe to start?" / "Did the last job break something?" On demand / deep You, cron, after a drain Minutes are fine Stress tests, DCGM level 2-3 diagnostics, burn-in NHC can serve all four with contexts : separate configs for the same binary (see part 3). The golden rule: the more often a check runs, the cheaper it must be. ---

secs.head: What NHC is not
secs.body: Knowing the edges saves you from asking it to do things it was never built for: - Not a monitoring system. It answers a yes/no question about one node right now. Trends, graphs and capacity planning belong in Prometheus, Grafana and friends. - Not a hardware diagnostic suite. It can call dcgmi diag , memtester or vendor tools, but it doesn't replace them. - Not a cluster-wide performance validator. A single slow GPU or a degraded fabric path can pass every per-node check and still drag down a 512-GPU job. That takes multi-node tests (NCCL, MPI benchmarks). - Not magic. It only finds what you tell it to look for. Your config is your health policy. ---

secs.head: Where we go next
secs.body: Enough theory. In part 2 we get NHC built, installed and passing its own test suite on a node. Takeaway: a fast-failing node looks like the most available node in the cluster. NHC is the bouncer that drains it with a readable NHC: reason, and resumes it once it's healthy again, without touching nodes a human drained.
