secs.head: The answer back to the client
secs.body: Thursday, 16:40, two working days after the call as promised. The proposal, as sent: Delta Research Computing: Node Health Check proposal (v1.0) Summary. Your GPU job hangs match a known NVSwitch failure mode: on at least one DGX, the GPU fabric wasn't initialized although Fabric Manager was running, and CUDA can't start in that state. Your batches of CPU I/O failures match nodes that keep accepting jobs after losing a filesystem. We propose LBNL NHC 1.5, configured from a single description of your cluster, to take such nodes out of service automatically with a readable reason, and to return them once healthy. What gets checked Node type Every 5 minutes (staggered) After every job On demand / after repairs --- --- --- --- DGX H100 ×16 Mounts ( /home , /lustre/scratch , /raid ), 8 GPUs present, NVSwitch fabric ready, fatal GPU errors, Fabric Manager/munge/sshd running (auto-restart), CPU, NUMA, memory, 8 × NDR links at 400 Gb/s, GPU model Mounts, GPUs, fabric, fatal GPU errors Everything, plus DCGM diagnostics level 2 EPYC ×120 Mounts, services, CPU (SMT on), NUMA (NPS1), memory, HDR link Mounts Everything Login ×2 Mounts, services, CPU, memory, HDR link (alerts only) — — What changes in Slurm. Three slurm.conf lines ( HealthCheckProgram , HealthCheckInterval=300 , HealthCheckNodeState=ANY,CYCLE ), a short epilog, and ThreadsPerCore=2 for the EPYC nodes (already agreed). How we roll it out (no node is drained by NHC until week 3) Week Step Exit criterion --- --- --- 1 Install, dry run on all nodes, triage every finding with you Every failure explained: config fixed or node fixed 2 Canary: NHC may drain only dgx[01-02] and cpu[001-008] 5 working days, zero false drains 3 Enforce everywhere, with an alert if more than 5% of nodes are NHC-drained You sign off 4-5 Optional phase 2: automatic reboot for a short list of GPU and service failures, max 2 per node per day, then escalation to you Agreed list, dry-run log reviewed How you'll know it worked. Baseline from your last 60 days: GPU jobs failing in the first 5 minutes, CPU jobs failing on I/O, hours that drained nodes sit unexplained. We report the same numbers 30 days after week 3. New rules for your team (one-page runbook included): always drain with a reason; reasons starting with NHC: belong to NHC; NVSM and DCGM alert, only NHC drains; change node expectations only through the cluster description in Git, which is tested automatically before deployment. What we need from you. Root access to one node per type and to the Slurm controller; a 30-minute slot to apply slurm.conf changes; a decision on the 5 nodes currently drained without a reason. Deliverables. Cluster description, generated configs, check module, test harness and CI pipeline, all in your Git repository; packages for Rocky 9 and DGX OS; runbook; a handover session. Out of scope. Multi-node performance validation (NCCL/MPI benchmarks across nodes), which we recommend as a follow-up: a node can pass every check and still slow a 16-node job. Open questions. (1) Confirm /raid is ext4 on all 16 DGX (verified on dgx01 only). (2) Who should be emailed for escalations in phase 2? Notice what the answer does not contain: NHC syntax, bash, or the word "match string". The client asked for an outcome. The technical depth lives in the deliverables and the runbook. ---

secs.head: The reusable checklist
secs.body: For the next "build us an NHC" email: 1. Before replying: map each symptom to plausible causes and to what would detect it. Reply with understanding, a discovery call and a data bundle, not a config. 2. Discovery: problem and success criteria; scheduler version, drain habits, reboot habits; every hardware class, with BIOS settings; OS per class; compute vs storage HCAs; mounts; GPU platform (NVSwitch?), driver, Xid history; other health tools; deployment method; test nodes; who acts on drains. 3. Ask for data, not descriptions: sinfo -R , slurm.conf node lines, lscpu , ibdev2netdev , findmnt , nvidia-smi fabric state, dmesg Xids. Clients describe the cluster they designed; commands show the cluster they have. 4. First proposal: classes and contexts, Slurm settings, rollout phases, remediation as a separate phase. 5. Validate every assumption against vendor documentation and a real test run: device names, service names, what "healthy" looks like, error policies, timeouts, OS differences, overlapping tools. Expect the proposal to change. Ours changed in 9 places. 6. Answer in the client's language: what was wrong, what gets checked, what changes, how it rolls out, how success is measured, what you need from them, what's out of scope. Takeaway: "build us an NHC" is the client's chosen solution, not their problem. Ten minutes of thinking turns it into the right questions; data beats descriptions; and a coffee-separated validation pass, against vendor docs and real test runs, is what turns a plausible proposal into one that works on their hardware. ---

secs.head: The rules, in eight lines
secs.body: 1. A fast-failing node is a black hole; NHC is the bouncer. 2. NHC: -prefixed reasons are NHC's; everything else is a human's. 3. Cheap checks, often. Expensive checks, rarely and elsewhere. 4. NHC's timeout below Slurm's. 5. Dry run, canary, enforce, behind a circuit breaker. 6. Every custom check: namespaced, cached, timed out, proven to fail. 7. Automate cheap fixes; budget retries; escalate by dropping the NHC: prefix. 8. Read the reason, rerun with -a -v -l- MARK OFFLINE=0 .

label: **Predicting GPU Node Failures**
title: Predicting GPU Node Failures - Overview
desc: A five-part series on the "AIOps" half of a classic AI-infrastructure interview question: how do you see a GPU dying bef

secs.head: Predicting GPU Node Failures - Overview
secs.body: A five-part series on the "AIOps" half of a classic AI-infrastructure interview question: how do you see a GPU dying before it takes a training run down with it? It's about understanding, not tooling: by the end you'll be able to reason about GPU failures, judge any monitoring setup, and defend your design in a review or an interview.

secs.head: The question this series answers
secs.body: "How do you define and measure operational excellence and performance in an AI research cluster?" A strong answer has two halves. The first is the hardware "golden signals": GPU utilization, memory bandwidth, NVLink and InfiniBand traffic, thermal throttling, collected with tools like the NVIDIA DCGM exporter. That half tells you how well the cluster performs . The second half is what separates a senior answer: use the GPU's own error telemetry to predict which node will fail, and get it out of the way before it crashes a critical run. That half tells you how well the cluster survives . This series is about the second half. A 60-second version you can say in an interview: "GPU memory rarely dies in one step. It climbs a ladder: corrected errors, then rows swapped for spares, then spares running out, then uncorrectable errors. Each rung is visible in telemetry. I react instantly to the rungs NVIDIA documents as fatal, treat the trends as early warnings, and measure every warning by precision and lead time against real failures. I only move to a learned model once I have enough labeled failures to prove it beats simple rules." ---

secs.head: The five ideas, one per page
secs.body: Page The idea you'll take away --- ------ --------------------------- 1 How GPU memory fails Errors are mostly hard faults that repeat and cluster, which is exactly what makes them predictable 2 Reading the GPU's vital signs Counters, gauges and events lie in different ways; know which one you're looking at 3 From signals to decisions State, event and trend rules; baselines beat fixed thresholds; tiers map to actions 4 Acting without making it worse Automate only reversible steps, and cap the blast radius of your own automation 5 Is the prediction any good? Base rates, precision, recall and lead time, and when a model is worth it Read them in order the first time. Page 5 is the one to reread before any design review. [!TIP] Deploying it? The runbook is the deep-technical companion: the counters file, node checks, tested Prometheus rules and unit tests, Alertmanager routing, a guarded Slurm drain hook and a backtest script, step by step with expected output and rollbacks. ---

secs.head: Who this is for
secs.body: HPC and AI platform engineers who run NVIDIA data-center GPUs (A100, H100 or newer), usually under Slurm or Kubernetes, and who are tired of hearing about a bad GPU from a user whose job just died. You don't need a statistics background; page 5 builds what it needs. ---

secs.head: What the series assumes
secs.body: Topic Assumed Explained here ------- --------- ---------------- Prometheus-style metrics You've seen a dashboard Counter vs gauge vs event, and why it matters Slurm You know what draining a node means Why drain is the right first action GPU hardware You know what HBM is ECC, banks, rows, spares, containment Statistics None Base rates, precision, recall, lead time, overfitting Facts come from NVIDIA documentation and published field studies (Meta's Llama 3 paper, Google's DRAM study, NCSA's Delta GPU study), cited on each page. Where a page gives an opinion rather than a fact, it says so.

label: 1. How GPU memory fails
title: How GPU Memory Fails, and Why You Can See It Coming
desc: Part 1 of the Predicting GPU Node Failures series. Prediction only works if failure leaves footprints before it happens.

secs.head: How GPU Memory Fails, and Why You Can See It Coming
secs.body: Part 1 of the Predicting GPU Node Failures series. Prediction only works if failure leaves footprints before it happens. This page explains the hardware that leaves them: ECC, spare rows, error containment, and the field evidence that errors repeat. By the end you'll be able to draw the error ladder from memory and say which rungs are predictions and which are already failures.

secs.head: A Friday night on cn042
secs.body: Here's a story every GPU cluster admin has lived in some form. The host is invented; the events follow NVIDIA's documentation. On Tuesday, GPU 3 in cn042 logged an Xid 94 , a contained memory error. One user's job died; they resubmitted. Right behind it came an Xid 63 : the GPU had recorded a repair that would only take effect after a GPU reset. Nobody reset it. The node kept taking jobs. On Friday at 23:10 the same GPU logged Xid 79 , "GPU has fallen off the bus," and took a 512-GPU training run down with it. The run restarted from a checkpoint six hours old. Nothing about Friday was a surprise. The GPU had been talking since Tuesday. The point of this series is to understand what it was saying. ---

secs.head: Why one GPU stops a thousand
secs.body: Large training jobs are synchronous : every step waits for every GPU to finish its share. If one GPU disappears, the step never completes, and the whole job usually restarts from its last checkpoint. So the real cost of a failure is roughly: cost ≈ GPUs in the job × time since the last checkpoint Meta's Llama 3 paper shows how often this happens at scale. In a 54-day snapshot of pre-training on 16,384 H100 GPUs there were 466 job interruptions, 419 of them unexpected. Faulty GPUs caused 30.1% of the unexpected ones and GPU HBM3 memory another 17.2%. The paper notes that because training is synchronous, a single GPU failure may require restarting the entire job. That equation is also why prediction pays. Draining a suspect node on Tuesday afternoon costs one node's worth of idle time. The same failure on Friday night costs every GPU in the job, times six hours. ---

secs.head: Concept 1: ECC, the first line of defense
secs.body: Memory bits occasionally read back wrong. ECC (error-correcting code) stores a few extra check bits next to each memory word, so the hardware can notice and often repair a bad bit. The common scheme in servers is SECDED : single error correct, double error detect . Google's DRAM study describes it plainly: it can reliably detect and correct any single-bit error, but can only detect, not correct, multi-bit errors. That gives two kinds of event: Event Also called What happens Does the job notice? ------- ------------- -------------- ---------------------- Correctable error (CE) Single-bit error, SBE Hardware fixes the bit and counts it No Uncorrectable error (UE) Double-bit error, DBE Hardware knows the data is wrong but can't fix it Usually yes: the process or node is hit The key insight for prediction: a correctable error is free today, but it's information. It says a bit in this memory went wrong once. Whether that matters depends on the next concept. Two more ideas from the same study are worth knowing: - Scrubbing. Some memory systems scan memory in the background and rewrite corrected words, so single-bit errors don't pile up into double-bit ones. Without scrubbing, errors are only found when memory is read. - Detection depends on use. The study found correctable error rates 2 to 3 times higher under high utilization, even at the same temperature. A GPU that sat idle all month and reported no errors hasn't proven much. ---

secs.head: Concept 2: soft errors versus hard errors
secs.body: Not all bit flips are equal. - A soft error is a random flip, from a particle strike for example. The cell is fine; rewrite it and the problem is gone. Soft errors are random in time, so they don't predict anything. - A hard error comes from a physical defect: a weak or stuck cell. It will go wrong again, in the same place. Older thinking assumed most memory errors were soft. Google's large field study (2.5 years of its server fleet) found strong evidence for the opposite: errors are dominated by hard errors. The fingerprints: - Errors repeat. In more than 85% of cases a correctable error was followed by another in the same month. - Errors concentrate. For every platform, the top 20% of DIMMs with errors produced over 94% of all observed errors. - Errors persist. The month-to-month correlation of error counts stayed significant for up to about 7 months. This is the single most important idea in the series: Memory errors are not lightning strikes. They're mostly weak cells that keep failing. That's why the past predicts the future. The study was on host DIMMs, not GPU HBM, so treat the exact numbers as an illustration. The shape, a few bad parts producing most of the errors and repeating, is what the rest of this series builds on. ---

secs.head: Concept 3: banks, rows and spare rows
secs.body: GPU memory is organized in banks , and each bank in rows of cells. NVIDIA's documentation for Ampere and later GPUs describes a hardware repair built on that structure: row remapping. - Every bank has spare rows. When a row degrades, the GPU marks it to be replaced by a spare. Unlike older "page retirement," the swap happens in hardware and doesn't leave holes in the address space. - The swap waits for a reset. A remap is recorded immediately (that's Xid 63) but only takes effect at the next GPU reset . Until then it's pending . NVIDIA says that while a remap is pending, unaffected applications can keep running and new work can still launch. - Repairs are permanent. Once applied, a remap lasts for the life of the GPU. - The budget is finite. The frame buffer supports up to 512 remappings. Remaps caused by correctable errors can be replaced by remaps for uncorrectable errors when a bank's reserved rows run out. - Dynamic page offlining fills the gap: the page holding the bad memory is excluded from new allocations until the remap is applied. NVIDIA also exposes how full each bank is, as bucketized counts : how many banks still have their maximum number of spares, how many are "High," "Partial," "Low" (one spare left) or "None" (no spares). A healthy GPU has every bank in the top bucket. NVIDIA's own example shows 640 banks there. When the budget runs out, the GPU sets the row-remap failure flag , NVIDIA's RMA criterion. Per the RMA policy, the flag is set when a remap for an uncorrectable error hits a bank that already has eight uncorrectable rows remapped, hits a row that was already remapped, or when 512 uncorrectable remaps have happened in total. Think of spare rows like spare tires in a fleet of trucks. Using one isn't a failure. Running a truck with no spare left is a failure waiting for a pothole. ---

secs.head: Concept 4: containing the damage
secs.body: An uncorrectable error used to mean "the GPU is in an unknown state, reset everything." Ampere-generation GPUs add error containment : if the hardware can tell which process touched the bad memory, it kills only that process. Xid Name What it means ----- ------ --------------- 94 Contained ECC error Only the application that hit the error is affected; restart it 95 Uncontained ECC error Containment failed; NVIDIA says reboot immediately when MIG is off Containment is good news and bad news. Good, because one bad row no longer kills everything on the GPU. Bad, because the GPU looks fine afterwards. The neighbors keep running, the dashboards stay green, and the pending remap waits for a reset nobody schedules. That's Tuesday on cn042 . ---

secs.head: The error ladder
secs.body: Put the four concepts together and a failing GPU tends to climb a ladder. Every rung is visible. Read it as three zones: - Wear (correctable errors, remaps, shrinking spares): nothing is broken, but the trend is visible. This is where prediction lives. - Damage (uncorrectable errors, pending remap): something is already wrong, but there's time to act gracefully. This is where planned action lives. - Failure (remap failure, uncontained errors): act now. [!NOTE] Xid 79 isn't on the ladder. "Fallen off the bus" has several possible causes in NVIDIA's Xid catalog, spanning hardware, driver, bus and thermal problems. Sometimes a memory story ends there, often it doesn't. Treat it as an event to react to, not something memory counters will reliably predict. The rule of thumb for the whole series: predict wear, react to breaks. ---

secs.head: What the field studies say
secs.body: Two studies frame what to expect. Google, "DRAM Errors in the Wild" (Schroeder, Pinheiro, Weber, SIGMETRICS 2009). Host memory, millions of DIMM-days. - Correctable errors predict uncorrectable ones: 70-80% of uncorrectable errors were preceded by a correctable error in the same or previous month, and a correctable error raised the uncorrectable-error probability by factors between 9 and 400. - But the absolute risk stayed small: 0.1 to 2.3% per month. The authors concluded that replacing memory just because of correctable errors only pays off where downtime is very expensive. (AI training clusters are such a place. Part 5 explains why "9-400× more likely" and "probably still fine" are both true.) - A more sophisticated model (CART trees) did not predict significantly better than the simple correctable-error signal. NCSA Delta (Cui et al., "Characterizing GPU Resilience and Impact on AI/HPC Systems"). 2.5 years and 11.7 million GPU hours on A100 and H100. - H100 had 3.2× lower per-GPU mean time between errors than A100 for uncorrectable ECC memory errors, and memory errors were the main cause of job failures on H100. - Row remapping and error containment mitigated 92% of uncorrectable ECC memory errors on H100. - In one case an uncontained memory error persisted for 17 days because monitoring didn't trigger a timely GPU reset. The lesson from that last finding: the hardware did its job; the operations around it didn't. ---

secs.head: What's predictable and what isn't
secs.body: Signal Zone Predictable? Why -------- ------ ------------- ----- Rising correctable error rate Wear Weakly Hard faults repeat, but most never become fatal Spare rows nearly gone in a bank Wear Strongly The next uncorrectable error in that bank can't be repaired Remap pending Damage Not a prediction: a known-bad state with time to act Needs a reset, which needs an empty GPU Remap failure, Xid 64 Failure Already happened Spares exhausted or repair not recorded Xid 79, Xid 95 Failure Mostly no Sudden, several causes Xid 13 Usually not hardware No NVIDIA lists it as a graphics engine exception, often the application ---

secs.head: What this is not for
secs.body: - Not a replacement for health checks. Something still has to refuse a node that's broken right now . Prediction works on a longer horizon, alongside it. - Not for silent data corruption. A GPU that computes wrong answers without raising errors leaves nothing in these counters. - Not for software failures. Out-of-memory crashes, NCCL hangs and bad kernels aren't hardware wear. - Not for GPUs you aren't watching. No telemetry means no prediction. Takeaway: GPU memory errors are mostly weak cells that keep failing, and the hardware's repairs (ECC, spare rows, containment) leave a visible ladder, so prediction is really about reading how far up the ladder each GPU has climbed. Next: part 2, reading the GPU's vital signs.

secs.head: Reading the GPU's Vital Signs
secs.body: Part 2 of the Predicting GPU Node Failures series. Part 1 described the error ladder. This page is about how the ladder reaches you: what kind of number each signal is, where it comes from, and how it can mislead you. By the end you'll be able to look at any GPU dashboard and say what it can and can't tell you.

secs.head: A doctor's analogy
secs.body: A doctor uses three kinds of information. A chart of measurements taken regularly (blood pressure every visit). An alarm that goes off when something happens (a heart monitor beeping). And the patient's history , written down at the time. GPU monitoring has the same three: Doctor GPU Example -------- ----- --------- Chart Metrics scraped every 15-60 s ECC counters, remap counts Alarm Events Xid messages from the driver History Logs The kernel log, where every Xid is written Most monitoring mistakes come from treating one kind as if it were another: reading an alarm off a chart, or trusting a chart that started yesterday as if it were the full history. ---

secs.head: Concept 1: three shapes of signal
secs.body: Every number in GPU telemetry has one of three shapes. Knowing the shape tells you how to read it. Shape What it is Example How to read it Classic mistake ------- ----------- --------- ---------------- ----------------- Counter Only goes up (until it resets) Single-bit ECC errors so far Look at its rate or increase , not its value Alerting on "errors 100" on a GPU that's three years old Gauge Goes up and down; describes now Remap pending (0 or 1), temperature Read the value directly Expecting it to remember the past Event Something happened at a moment Xid 79 Count it, or keep the log Sampling it like a gauge and missing it A good example of shape confusion is in NVIDIA's dcgm-exporter. Its default configuration exports a field described as "Value of the last XID error encountered." That's an event squeezed into a gauge . If a GPU logs Xid 79 and then Xid 13 between two scrapes, the dashboard only ever sees 13. The exporter also offers a proper per-code counter of Xid events ( DCGM EXP XID ERRORS TOTAL ). Using the counter instead of the gauge is the difference between seeing the failure and not seeing it. [!TIP] When you meet a new metric, ask first: counter, gauge or event? It decides every query and alert you'll write on it. ---

secs.head: Concept 2: volatile versus persistent
secs.body: GPU error counters come in two lifetimes, and dcgm-exporter exposes both for ECC: - Volatile counts start from zero when the driver loads. They tell you about this session . A reboot or driver reload wipes them. - Aggregate (persistent) counts are stored on the GPU and survive reboots. They tell you about this GPU's life . Row-remap counts are a third kind: NVIDIA notes that the remapped-row numbers are the entries recorded in the GPU's InfoROM (a small non-volatile store on the board), not the rows remapped in hardware so far. A recorded remap can still be pending. Each lifetime answers a different question: Question Use ---------- ----- "Is something happening on this GPU right now ?" The rate of a volatile counter "Has this GPU been in trouble before?" Aggregate counts and recorded remaps "How much repair budget is left?" The bank buckets from part 1 A GPU that was moved from another node, or reset last night, can look brand new on volatile counters and tired on persistent ones. Both are true. ---

secs.head: Concept 3: where the numbers come from
secs.body: NVIDIA describes two paths for reading GPU health, and they fail differently. - In-band : software on the node asks the driver. Tools: NVML, nvidia-smi , DCGM and the DCGM exporter, plus the kernel log. Rich and detailed, but it depends on the driver and the OS being alive. - Out-of-band : the board's management controller reads the GPU over a side channel (NVIDIA calls the interface SMBPBI), usually reached through the server's BMC. It exposes the essentials, including remap counts and the pending and failure flags, and works even when the OS has hung. When a GPU falls off the bus, in-band tools on that node can't reach the GPU, or can't reach anything. Out-of-band telemetry is how you still learn what happened. For prediction, in-band is enough most of the time. For the post-mortem, you'll want both. There's also a matter of scope . dcgm-exporter only knows what happened since it started: its Xid counter begins at zero with the process. The kernel log is written by the driver regardless of whether any exporter is running. That makes the log the closest thing to ground truth for Xid events, and it's why NVIDIA's own triage guidance starts from log messages. ---

secs.head: Concept 4: the cost of looking
secs.body: Every check has a price: time, load on the GPU, and sometimes disruption to the job running on it. That gives a simple rule of thumb: The more often a check runs, the cheaper it must be. How often What fits Example ----------- ----------- --------- Every scrape (seconds) Reading counters the driver already keeps ECC, remaps, Xid counts Every job (prolog/epilog) Quick queries and short tests nvidia-smi queries, recent Xids in the log, a short DCGM diagnostic On a drained node Deep tests that stress the GPU NVIDIA's long DCGM diagnostic, about 30 minutes Before an RMA The authoritative test NVIDIA's field diagnostic NVIDIA's debug guidelines make the same split: they recommend checks at the start or end of jobs (recent Xid errors, a short dcgmi diag -r 2 ), and the long diagnostic for fully stressing a system. Prediction lives in the first row. Everything below it is what prediction tells you to do . ---

secs.head: The ladder, as telemetry
secs.body: Here's each rung from part 1 with the signal that shows it, as exposed by dcgm-exporter and nvidia-smi . Rung Signal Shape How you'd read it ------ -------- ------- ------------------- Correctable errors Single-bit ECC count Counter Rate, compared with this GPU's own past Row remapped Correctable / uncorrectable remapped rows; Xid 63 Counter, event Did it go up recently? Spares running out Banks in the "Low" and "None" buckets Gauge Above zero means a bank is nearly out of repairs Uncorrectable error Double-bit ECC count; Xid 48, 94 Counter, event Any increase matters Remap pending Pending flag Gauge 1 means a reset is owed Remap failure Failure flag; Xid 64 Gauge, event 1 means RMA candidate, latched Uncontained / off the bus Xid 95, 79 Event Any occurrence To see the remap state of a GPU by hand, nvidia-smi has a dedicated view. These field names are from its documentation; confirm them with nvidia-smi --help-query-remapped-rows on your driver. [!WARNING] The defaults don't show the ladder. In dcgm-exporter 4.8.4, the shipped counter list has the ECC counters and the per-code Xid counter commented out. The remap counts and failure flag are on; the pending flag and bank buckets are not listed at all. A stock install mostly shows temperatures and utilization. Check what yours exports before trusting any GPU-health dashboard built on it. ---

secs.head: Five ways the numbers lie
secs.body: What you see What's really happening Concept -------------- ------------------------ --------- A GPU logged Xid 79 but the dashboard shows only Xid 13 The "last Xid" gauge was overwritten between scrapes Event read as a gauge ECC errors dropped to zero overnight The driver reloaded and volatile counters reset Volatile lifetime A GPU with a long error history looks clean It was reset or moved; you're reading volatile counts Volatile vs persistent An idle GPU has a perfect record Errors are mostly found when memory is used Detection depends on use (part 1) Xid history vanished after maintenance The exporter restarted and its counter started over Scope: exporter vs log One more, which deserves its own name because it bites rules in part 3: counters that are born on their first event. The per-code Xid counter has no series for Xid 79 until the first Xid 79 happens. A rule that asks "did this counter increase?" can't see an increase from nothing to 1, so it misses exactly the first fatal event. [!WARNING] Metric names change. In the go-dcgm library behind dcgm-exporter 4.8.4, several remap field names in the default list are marked deprecated in favor of new ones. The exporter names each metric after the line in its config, so "modernizing" the config renames the metrics and every alert built on the old names silently stops matching. ---

secs.head: Silence is not health
secs.body: The most dangerous dashboard is the one with no data on it. An exporter that crashed, a node whose scrape target was removed, a GPU that fell off the bus and took the exporter's view with it: all of them produce no errors . No errors looks exactly like a healthy GPU. So a GPU monitoring design always needs a second question next to "is anything wrong?": "are we still able to see?" Missing telemetry is itself an alert. Part 3 builds it in. Takeaway: know each signal's shape (counter, gauge, event), its lifetime (volatile, persistent) and its source (exporter, log, out-of-band), because every misleading GPU dashboard gets one of those three wrong. Next: part 3, from signals to decisions.

label: 3. From signals to decisions
title: From Signals to Decisions
desc: Part 3 of the Predicting GPU Node Failures series. A signal is not a decision. This page is about the thinking between t

secs.head: From Signals to Decisions
secs.body: Part 3 of the Predicting GPU Node Failures series. A signal is not a decision. This page is about the thinking between the two: what kinds of rules exist, how to make a rule notice change without crying wolf, and how to tie each rule to a specific action. By the end you'll be able to design a GPU failure rule set on a whiteboard and explain every line of it.

secs.head: Concept 1: three kinds of rule
secs.body: Every useful GPU health rule is one of three kinds. They differ in what they look at and how certain they are. Kind Question it asks Example Certainty ------ ------------------ --------- ----------- State "Is the GPU in a known-bad condition right now?" Remap failure flag is set; a remap is pending High: NVIDIA defines the meaning Event "Did something bad just happen?" A new Xid 79, 95 or 64 High, but it's already happened Trend "Is this GPU getting worse?" Correctable error rate climbing; spare rows running out Lower: this is the actual prediction State and event rules are mostly reaction: fast, confident, and late. Trend rules are prediction: early, uncertain, and the only part that's truly "AIOps." A good rule set needs all three, and it must never let the uncertain kind trigger the drastic actions on its own. ---

secs.head: Concept 2: compare a GPU with itself
secs.body: The obvious trend rule is a fixed threshold: "alert when a GPU has more than N correctable errors per hour." It breaks in two ways. - What's normal differs. Part 1 showed that errors concentrate: a few parts produce almost all of them. A fleet-wide threshold is either too high for a GPU that just started failing, or too low for a GPU that has always produced a steady trickle and never got worse. - Nobody publishes the number. There's no NVIDIA figure for "a normal single-bit error rate for H100 HBM3." Any fixed threshold you pick is a guess. The better question is: "Is this GPU behaving differently from its own recent past?" Compare the last hour's error rate with the same GPU's rate over the last day. A GPU that always produces 1 error a minute stays quiet. A GPU that jumps from 1 to 30 a minute gets noticed, whatever the absolute numbers are. This is a personal baseline , and it's the core idea behind most anomaly detection: model what's normal for this thing , then look for departures. ---

secs.head: Concept 3: persistence and noise floors
secs.body: Two problems make baseline rules noisy, and each has a simple fix. Problem 1: blips. A single bad scrape or a momentary flag can flip a rule on and off. The fix is persistence : require the condition to hold for a while before acting. How long depends on what's at stake: Condition Sensible persistence Why ----------- --------------------- ----- Remap failure flag A couple of minutes It's latched; you're only guarding against a bad read Remap pending Longer, say 15 minutes NVIDIA says unaffected work keeps running; no rush Fatal Xid None The event already happened Rising error trend Tens of minutes Trends are noisy; you want it to hold Problem 2: ratios explode near zero. "3× its baseline" sounds sensible until a GPU with zero errors yesterday has one today: infinitely more than its baseline. The fix is a noise floor : a minimum absolute amount of activity before the ratio counts. "At least 3× the baseline and at least 10 errors in the hour." The second clause ignores a GPU going from silent to slightly less silent. When we tested a rule set like this, removing the noise floor did exactly that: a quiet GPU with 5 errors in an hour fired a "rate accelerating" alert. Ratios without floors page you about nothing. ---

secs.head: Concept 4: tiers that map to actions
secs.body: A rule that only says "something is wrong" pushes the hard part onto whoever reads it at 3 AM. Each rule should say what to do , and the doing should depend on how sure you are and how bad it is. Tier Meaning Action Rules in this tier ------ --------- -------- ------------------- 1. Broken Already failed Stop sending work now; evidence, diagnostics, likely RMA Remap failure; Xid 64, 79, 95 2. Will break jobs Damaged, still running Let current jobs finish, then reset the GPU Remap pending; uncorrectable errors; Xid 48, 94 3. Early warning Wearing out Plan, watch, prefer it for short jobs Spares nearly gone; error rate accelerating Blind spot Can't see Fix the monitoring Telemetry missing Tier 2 is worth a second look. Why not reset the GPU immediately? Because a reset needs an empty GPU, and NVIDIA's guidance for a pending remap and for "drain and reset" situations is to stop new work, let existing work finish or checkpoint, then reset. A scheduler drain does exactly that. A design trick that keeps this clean: give every alert an action label ( drain now , drain and reset , plan rma , watch ) and let the automation in part 4 look only at that label. The automation never has to know what Xid 95 means; the rule author decides once, in one place. ---

secs.head: The rule set, on one page
secs.body: Here's a complete rule set in plain words. Each line maps to one Prometheus alerting rule over dcgm-exporter metrics. Rule Kind Fires when Holds for Action ------ ------ ----------- ----------- -------- Remap failure State Failure flag is 1 2 min drain now Fatal Xid Event New Xid 64, 79 or 95 in the last 10 min - drain now Remap pending State Pending flag is 1 15 min drain and reset Uncorrectable error Event Double-bit count rose in the last hour, or new Xid 48 / 94 - drain and reset Spares nearly gone Trend Any bank in the "Low" or "None" bucket 1 h plan rma Errors accelerating Trend Last-hour SBE rate 3× its 24 h rate, and ≥ 10 SBEs in the hour 30 min watch Telemetry missing Blind spot Exporter down 10 min watch Notice what's not there: no rule drains on Xid 13, which NVIDIA lists as a graphics engine exception that is often the application's fault. And no trend rule drains anything. ---

secs.head: The first-event trap
secs.body: This trap is worth understanding because it hides the most important event in the whole series: the first time a GPU falls off the bus. Recall from part 2 that the per-code Xid counter is born on its first event: before the first Xid 79 there is no Xid 79 series at all, and then one appears with the value 1. The natural rule asks "did this counter increase in the last 10 minutes?" To answer, the monitoring system subtracts the old value from the new one. There is no old value, so it sees 1 → 1, which is no increase. The alert stays silent. We confirmed it with a rule unit test: we expected an increase of 1 and the test reported 0. The fix is to ask a second question alongside the first: "does this series exist now when it didn't 10 minutes ago?" In PromQL: The general lesson goes beyond Xids: any rule built on "change" must say what it does when there's no "before." Counters that appear on demand, nodes that just joined, exporters that just restarted all have no before. ---

secs.head: Rules are code: test them
secs.body: A rule that never fires looks exactly like a rule on a healthy cluster. That's why rules should be treated like code: written down, versioned, and tested with fake inputs where you know the right answer. A good test set for GPU rules covers four kinds of case: Case Example Why ------ --------- ----- Should fire A remap failure flag set for 10 minutes Proves the rule works Should not fire A steady, unchanging error rate; an application Xid 13 Proves it isn't noisy Edge The first-ever Xid 79; a GPU going from 0 to 5 errors Where rules actually break Silence Every counter flat on a healthy GPU Proves the quiet path stays quiet Then comes the step most people skip: prove the tests can fail. Deliberately break a rule (remove the "new series" branch, remove the noise floor) and check that a test goes red. When we did this, both breaks were caught. A test suite that can't fail tells you nothing. [!IMPORTANT] Run the rule tests whenever the telemetry configuration changes, not just when the rules do. Renaming one metric upstream silently disables every rule that used the old name, and only a test will notice. ---

secs.head: Knobs are opinions
secs.body: The numbers in the rule set (3× baseline, 10 errors, 15 minutes) are starting opinions, not facts about GPUs. They encode trade-offs: Knob Turn it up and you get Turn it down and you get ------ ------------------------ -------------------------- Baseline ratio Fewer, surer warnings, later Earlier warnings, more false alarms Noise floor Quiet GPUs never trip it Real but small degradations get noticed Persistence Fewer flapping alerts, slower reaction Faster reaction, more flapping The only honest way to set them is against your own failure history, which is what part 5 is about. Takeaway: combine state, event and trend rules; judge trends against each GPU's own baseline with persistence and a noise floor; give every rule an action tier; and test the rules, including the cases where they should stay silent and the case where there's no "before." Next: part 4, acting without making it worse.

label: 4. Acting safely
title: Acting Without Making It Worse
desc: Part 4 of the Predicting GPU Node Failures series. A prediction nobody acts on at 23:10 on a Friday is a log line. But a

secs.head: Acting Without Making It Worse
secs.body: Part 4 of the Predicting GPU Node Failures series. A prediction nobody acts on at 23:10 on a Friday is a log line. But automation that acts on predictions can do more damage than any single GPU. This page is about the principles that keep automated response safe. By the end you'll be able to say which actions to automate, how to limit the harm a bad rule can do, and how to roll it out without betting the cluster.

secs.head: The real risk is your own automation
secs.body: One failing GPU costs one job's worth of restart. One bad deploy of a monitoring config, a driver update that misreports a flag, or a renamed metric can make every GPU look sick at once. If your automation drains on every alert, it turns a monitoring bug into a cluster-wide outage, at machine speed. So the design question isn't "how do I act fast on predictions?" It's: "what's the worst my automation can do on its worst day, and is that acceptable?" Everything below answers that. ---

secs.head: Principle 1: automate the reversible, hand off the irreversible
secs.body: Sort the possible responses by how easy they are to undo: Action Reversible? Who should do it -------- ------------- ------------------ Drain the node (stop new jobs, let running ones finish) Yes: resume it Automation Reset the GPU Mostly, but it kills anything still running on it Automation after the node is empty, or a human Reboot the node Mostly, same caveat Human or a guarded remediation loop Open an RMA, pull the GPU No Human, after NVIDIA's field diagnostic A scheduler drain is the ideal automated response. It doesn't kill anything; it just stops feeding the node. Running jobs finish or reach their next checkpoint, which is exactly what NVIDIA's guidance asks for before a reset. The rule of thumb: automation may take capacity away; only humans give hardware back. Resuming a node whose GPU had a remap failure is a decision, not a cleanup step. One trade-off to accept up front: schedulers like Slurm drain nodes , not GPUs. On an 8-GPU node, draining for one bad GPU also idles seven healthy ones until the reset. Removing just the one GPU from the scheduler is more efficient and much easier to get wrong. Start with whole-node drains. ---

secs.head: Principle 2: lead time must beat drain time
secs.body: A drain is only useful if it finishes before the failure. That gives a simple test for whether a prediction is worth acting on: prediction lead time time for running jobs to finish or checkpoint If your long jobs checkpoint every six hours, a warning that arrives two hours before failure can't save the job that's running; it can only stop the next job from landing there. That's still worth a lot, but it's a different promise. Measure lead time (part 5), and be honest about which of the two you're buying. This is also why the action tiers from part 3 differ. Tier 1 (already broken) can't benefit from lead time; draining just stops the bleeding. Tier 2 (pending remap) has time on its side, because NVIDIA says unaffected work keeps running. Tier 3 (wear) has the most lead time and the least certainty, so it plans instead of draining. ---

secs.head: Principle 3: correlated alerts are rarely correlated hardware
secs.body: Real GPU failures are mostly independent: one weak HBM cell doesn't make the GPU in the next rack weaker. So when many GPUs alert at once, the likely cause is upstream: a driver change, an exporter upgrade, a metric rename, a firmware bug. That suggests a drain budget : a cap on how many nodes your automation may hold drained at any moment. When the budget is full, the automation stops and asks a human. This is a circuit breaker : it trips when behavior looks abnormal, so a fault can't spread. How to size it: - Size it to what you can lose without anyone noticing , not to how many GPUs you expect to fail. - Count only drains made by the automation , so a human's maintenance drains don't use it up. - Treat "budget full" as a page , never a log line. Either several GPUs really are failing together, which is rare and worth a human, or something upstream is lying. [!CAUTION] Never let a "resolved" alert un-drain a node. Alerts resolve for many reasons, including the exporter dying. A predictive system that drains on one signal and resumes on its absence will flap nodes in and out of service. ---

secs.head: Principle 4: earn trust in stages
secs.body: New automation has to earn the right to act. A standard ladder: Stage What happens Move on when ------- -------------- -------------- Dry run The automation logs "would drain X because Y" and touches nothing. You compare the log with what actually failed Every "would drain" points at a GPU you'd have drained by hand, for at least a week or two Canary Real drains, but only on a short list of nodes you're happy to lose Drains look right, running jobs finished normally Enforce Real drains everywhere, with a small budget A normal week passes without hitting the budget Raise the budget Only when the backtest in part 5 says the rules earn it - The dry-run stage has a second benefit: its log is the start of your label set . Part 5 needs a history of "we predicted X" next to "X actually failed," and the dry-run log is exactly that. ---

secs.head: Principle 5: every action must be findable and undoable
secs.body: Give every automated drain a recognizable signature , for example a reason that always starts with the same prefix. Then three things become one-liners: - Find everything the automation did: list drained nodes whose reason has the prefix. - Count it, which is how the drain budget works. - Undo it in bulk if the automation was wrong. In Slurm, the drain reason is that signature: Bulk rollback is "find every node drained with the prefix, resume it." But the rollback is for wrong drains. A node whose GPU had a remap failure or fell off the bus shouldn't be resumed just because undoing is easy. [!TIP] A good reason string answers "why is this node out?" without opening a dashboard: who drained it (the prefix), which rule, which GPU, and which action tier. ---

secs.head: Principle 6: humans hear about everything
secs.body: Automation should never act in silence. Every automated drain should also notify the team, through the same channel as everything else. The alert router has to send drain-tier alerts to both the automation and the people. This is easy to get wrong. With Prometheus Alertmanager, a route that sends drain alerts to the automation, marked to "continue" matching, does not automatically also reach the default human receiver: the default only catches alerts that matched no route. When we checked a config built that way with Alertmanager's own route tester, drain alerts went to the automation only. The fix is an explicit catch-all route for humans after the automation route. The general lesson: test your alert routing like you test your rules. "Who gets this alert?" should be a question with a checked answer. ---

secs.head: After the drain: reset, reboot or RMA
secs.body: The drain buys time. This is what the time is for, condensed from NVIDIA's triage guidance: What fired Once the node is empty Then ------------ ------------------------ ------ Remap pending, uncorrectable error (Xid 48, 94) Reset the GPU Confirm the remap is no longer pending, run a short diagnostic, resume Xid 64, or Xid 95 with MIG off Reboot the node If it repeats: collect a bug report, run field diagnostics, report Xid 79 Collect evidence, reboot Expect it to recur; report to the vendor Remap failure Keep it drained NVIDIA's field diagnostic validates the flag for RMA Reset limits depend on the platform. On Hopper and later systems with NVSwitch, GPUs can be reset individually; older NVSwitch systems may need the Fabric Manager running, or all connected GPUs reset together. Check NVIDIA's reset-capabilities table before automating resets. For the fix-and-verify loop itself, see NHC auto-remediation. Takeaway: automate only the reversible step (drain), cap your automation's blast radius with a budget, earn trust through dry run → canary → enforce, make every action findable and undoable, and make sure humans hear about all of it. Next: part 5, is the prediction any good?

secs.body: - NVIDIA GPU Debug Guidelines: GPU Node Triage (actions, reset capabilities) - NVIDIA GPU Memory Error Management: Error Recovery and Response Flags (drain and reset) - Slurm scontrol man page (DRAIN, RESUME, Reason) - Alertmanager configuration (routes, continue ) - Grattafiori et al., "The Llama 3 Herd of Models", arXiv:2407.21783

label: 5. Is the prediction any good?
title: Is the Prediction Any Good?
desc: Part 5 of the Predicting GPU Node Failures series, the last one. A prediction you never checked is a superstition. This

secs.head: Is the Prediction Any Good?
secs.body: Part 5 of the Predicting GPU Node Failures series, the last one. A prediction you never checked is a superstition. This page gives you the ideas to check one: why rare events fool intuition, the three numbers that describe a predictor, the mistakes that make those numbers lie, and when a machine-learning model is actually worth it. By the end you'll be able to defend (or demolish) any "we predict GPU failures" claim.

secs.head: Concept 1: the base-rate trap
secs.body: Part 1 quoted two facts from Google's DRAM study that sound contradictory: - A correctable error made an uncorrectable error in the same month between 9 and 400 times more likely. - Even so, the chance of an uncorrectable error after a correctable one was only 0.1 to 2.3% per month. Both are true because uncorrectable errors are rare to begin with . Multiply a tiny number by 400 and you can still get a small number. This is the base-rate trap : a signal can be enormously informative and still be wrong most of the time when it fires. Work it through with the study's own upper figure. If you replaced every part that showed a correctable error, at most 2.3% of those parts would have had an uncorrectable error that month. At least 97.7% of the replacements would, that month, have been unnecessary. That's why the authors said early replacement only makes sense where downtime is very costly. Two lessons follow: - "X makes failure N times more likely" is not a reason to act. Ask how likely failure is after X, in absolute terms. - Cheap actions tolerate weak signals; expensive actions don't. Flagging a GPU on a dashboard can follow a signal that's usually wrong. Draining a node, or worse, pulling a GPU, needs one that's usually right. ---

secs.head: Concept 2: four outcomes, three numbers
secs.body: Every time a rule could have fired, one of four things happened: GPU failed soon after GPU didn't fail --- --- --- Rule fired True positive: a real warning False positive: a false alarm Rule stayed quiet False negative: a missed failure True negative: correctly quiet From that table come the three numbers that describe any predictor: Number Question Plain meaning -------- ---------- --------------- Precision When it fires, how often is it right? "Should I trust this alert?" Recall Of all real failures, how many did it warn about? "How much does it catch?" Lead time How much warning did the right alerts give? "Is the warning early enough to use?" Precision and recall pull against each other. Make a rule more sensitive and it catches more failures (recall up) but raises more false alarms (precision down). Neither number alone means anything: a rule that fires on every GPU every day has perfect recall, and a rule that never fires has no false alarms. Different action tiers from part 3 need different balances: Tier Needs Because ------ ------- --------- Drain now Very high precision Every false alarm costs a node Drain and reset High precision, useful lead time Gentle, but still capacity Early warning Recall and long lead time; precision can be low A wrong warning costs a glance The rule of thumb: a rule earns its action with its precision. A warning rule gets promoted to a draining rule only when its measured precision says so. ---

secs.head: Concept 3: the horizon
secs.body: "Did the GPU fail after the alert?" needs a time limit, or every alert is eventually right: everything fails someday. That limit is the horizon . The horizon isn't a statistical choice; it's an operational one. It should be the window in which a warning is still useful , which ties back to part 4: long enough to drain and checkpoint, short enough that the warning is about this failure and not some later one. The same alerts can look excellent or useless depending on the horizon. In a small hand-made test of a backtest, alerts that came 13 to 36 hours before failures scored well with a 72-hour horizon and scored zero with a 12-hour one. Nothing about the alerts changed; only the question did. Always state the horizon next to any precision or recall number. ---

secs.head: Concept 4: what counts as a failure
secs.body: Every number above depends on the list of failures you compare against: your labels . Bad labels make every score meaningless, and they're the hardest part of the whole project. Good sources, roughly from most to least trustworthy: 1. RMA records with the GPU identified. 2. Drain reasons written by humans or node health checks. 3. Fatal Xids in the kernel log (64, 79, 95). 4. Job failures that users blamed on a GPU. Common label problems: Problem Effect --------- -------- Software crashes counted as GPU failures The predictor gets blamed for missing failures no hardware signal could see The GPU your automation drained "didn't fail" The early drain prevented the failure, so a good prediction scores as a false alarm GPUs that haven't failed yet treated as healthy forever Recent warnings look wrong just because there's been no time to be proven right The last two have names in statistics. Acting on a prediction changes the outcome you're trying to measure (an intervention problem). And a GPU that hasn't failed by the end of your data isn't "healthy," it's censored : you just don't know yet. Keep a list of drained GPUs and what happened to them after the reset, and leave the newest warnings out of the score until their horizon has passed. [!TIP] Start collecting labels on day one, before you trust any rule. The dry-run log from part 4 plus a spreadsheet of RMAs is already a usable label set. ---

secs.head: Concept 5: backtesting, and how it lies
secs.body: Backtesting means replaying history: take the alerts your rules would have fired, take the failures that actually happened, and compute precision, recall and lead time. It's the only way to tune the knobs from part 3 on evidence instead of taste. Three ways a backtest flatters you: - Tuning and grading on the same data. If you adjust the threshold until last quarter's failures are all caught, of course they're caught. Tune on older months, then grade on newer months you held back. This is a time-based split , and with time-ordered data it's the only honest one. - Leakage. A feature that is really the failure itself, such as "an Xid 79 happened," makes a predictor look perfect at predicting Xid 79. Ask of every input: "could I have known this before the failure?" - Drift. A driver or firmware update can change how often counters tick or how flags behave. A rule tuned before the update may be wrong after it. Re-run the backtest after every driver or exporter change, and compare. [!WARNING] A backtest score with no stated horizon, no time split and no description of the labels is not a score. Ask for all three whenever someone shows you one, including yourself. ---

secs.head: Rules or a model?
secs.body: "AIOps" often means a learned model that combines many weak signals into one risk score per GPU. In principle it can beat rules: a GPU with a slowly rising error rate, one bank low on spares and some PCIe retries might be risky even when no single rule fires. Two pieces of evidence argue for patience: - You probably don't have enough failures yet. For logistic regression, the simplest common model, Peduzzi et al. (1996) found that with fewer than about 10 outcome events per predictor variable, the estimates became biased and confidence intervals unreliable. A model with six inputs wants on the order of 60 real, labeled GPU failures. Many clusters don't have that many. - Simple signals are hard to beat. In Google's DRAM study, a classification-tree model using correctable-error counts and memory attributes did not predict uncorrectable errors significantly better than the simple correctable-error signal. That was host memory, not GPU HBM, but it's a reason to expect modest gains, not magic. The recommended path, and what each step costs: Step Gain Cost ------ ------ ------ Rules from NVIDIA's documented states and events Confident, explainable, available today Can't combine weak signals Trend rules with personal baselines Early warning Knobs to tune; lower precision Logistic regression on per-GPU-day features Combines signals; each weight is readable Needs dozens of labeled failures Gradient-boosted trees or similar Captures interactions Hard to explain; easy to overfit Every step up buys recall and costs explainability. At 3 AM, "drained because spare rows ran out" is an answer. "Drained because the risk score was 0.83" is a question. Whatever you build, judge it exactly like the rules: same labels, same horizon, same time split, same three numbers. If it doesn't beat the best rule on held-out months, keep the rule. ---

secs.head: What a model must never do
secs.body: - Skip the tiers. A model's score starts as a warning and earns the right to drain through backtests, exactly like a rule. - Decide an RMA. NVIDIA's field diagnostic decides that; the model only points at which GPU to test. - Overrule a documented flag. Remap failure and fatal Xids stay as rules. A model that disagrees with them is the one that's wrong. - Treat missing data as safe. No telemetry means "unknown," never "low risk." ---

secs.head: The interview answer, revisited
secs.body: You can now answer the original question with reasons, not buzzwords: "I define operational excellence in two halves: performance and survival. For survival I watch the GPU memory error ladder: corrected errors, row remaps, spare-row budget, pending remaps, and fatal Xids. I react immediately to the states NVIDIA defines as failures, drain gracefully on damage, and treat trends against each GPU's own baseline as early warnings. My automation only drains, never more, behind a budget and a staged rollout. And I measure every rule by precision, recall and lead time on held-out history, because failures are rare and rare events fool intuition. I'd only move to a learned model once I had enough labeled failures to prove it beats the rules." Takeaway: a GPU failure prediction is only as good as its measured precision, recall and lead time on honest, held-out history, so respect base rates, state your horizon, guard your labels, and let evidence decide when rules give way to a model. That's the end of the concepts. To deploy all of it, continue to the runbook, the deep-technical companion with every config, test and script. Or go back to the overview, or the reactive side in the Node Health Check series.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Schroeder, Pinheiro, Weber, "DRAM Errors in the Wild: A Large-Scale Field Study", SIGMETRICS 2009 - Peduzzi et al., "A simulation study of the number of events per variable in logistic regression analysis", J Clin Epidemiol 1996 - Cui et al., "Characterizing GPU Resilience and Impact on AI/HPC Systems", arXiv:2503.11901 - Grattafiori et al., "The Llama 3 Herd of Models", arXiv:2407.21783 - NVIDIA GPU Memory Error Management: RMA Policy - Prometheus: alerting rules and the ALERTS series (alert history for backtests)

secs.head: Runbook: Deploying GPU Failure Prediction End to End
secs.body: The deep-technical companion to the Predicting GPU Node Failures series. Parts 1-5 explain the why : how GPU memory fails, what telemetry means, how to design rules, act safely and measure predictions. This runbook is the how : every config, command and script you need to deploy it on a real cluster, in order, with expected output and a rollback for each risky step. Read the concept pages first; come back here with a root shell.

secs.head: What you need
secs.body: Component Version this runbook targets Role ----------- ----------------------------- ------ NVIDIA GPUs Ampere or later data-center parts (A100, H100, ...) Row remapping and bank buckets exist from Ampere on dcgm-exporter 4.8.4 (built on go-dcgm 1.4611.2) Exports GPU telemetry on :9400 Prometheus / promtool 3.15.1 Rule evaluation and rule unit tests Alertmanager / amtool 0.34.2 Routing alerts to people and to the drain hook Slurm client tools Any current release scontrol , sinfo on the Alertmanager host Python 3.12 (standard library only) Drain hook and backtest

secs.head: What was tested, and what wasn't
secs.body: Item Status ------ -------- Prometheus rules (13 rules) and 10 unit tests Tested with promtool 3.15.1, including two deliberate failure paths Alertmanager routing Tested with amtool check-config and amtool config routes test Drain hook Tested in all modes against fake scontrol / sinfo scripts, plus the HTTP path Backtest script Tested on a hand-made fixture checked by hand Xid log one-liners Tested on captured kernel-log text Counters file field names Checked against the dcgm-exporter 4.8.4 source and go-dcgm field table dcgm-exporter, nvidia-smi , journalctl on real GPUs; scontrol on a real cluster Not run (no GPU in the test environment). From NVIDIA and SchedMD docs [!IMPORTANT] Run every phase on one node first. The untested items above are standard tools used as documented, but your driver, exporter packaging and Slurm setup are the final judges. ---

secs.head: Phase 1: export the health signals
secs.body: Why: in dcgm-exporter 4.8.4 the shipped etc/default-counters.csv has the ECC counters and the per-code Xid counter commented out , and doesn't list the remap-pending flag or the bank buckets at all. Concepts: part 2. 1. Copy the default counters file from the dcgm-exporter release you run ( etc/default-counters.csv in the repo) and keep it in version control. Success: grep -c ROW REMAP FAILURE /etc/dcgm-exporter/health-counters.csv prints 1 . 2. Append the health fields. Format: DCGM field, Prometheus type, help text . Success: grep -c '^DCGM' /etc/dcgm-exporter/health-counters.csv is six higher than before. 3. Hopper only: add the NVLink error counters. Pre-Hopper and Blackwell use different NVLink fields; copy the commented lines for your generation from the default file rather than guessing. 4. Point the exporter at the file. Flag -f (long form --collectors , env DCGM EXPORTER COLLECTORS ); default listen address :9400 . In a container or the GPU Operator, mount the file and set DCGM EXPORTER COLLECTORS to its path. 5. Verify. Success: one line per GPU per field, with labels gpu , UUID , pci bus id , device , modelName , hostname (the 4.8.4 label set). DCGM EXP XID ERRORS TOTAL appears only after a GPU logs an Xid , labeled xid ; its absence on a healthy node is normal. [!WARNING] Pin the metric names. In go-dcgm 1.4611.2 several remap names in the default file are deprecated aliases (for example DCGM FI DEV UNCORRECTABLE REMAPPED ROWS → DCGM FI DEV ROW REMAP UNCORRECTABLE TOTAL , DCGM FI DEV ROW REMAP FAILURE → DCGM FI DEV ROW REMAP FAILED ). The exporter names each metric after its CSV line, so renaming lines renames metrics and silently breaks Phase 3. Keep the file as written here, and keep Phase 3's tests in CI. Rollback: restart the exporter without -f (or unset DCGM EXPORTER COLLECTORS ); it falls back to its default list. ---

secs.head: Phase 2: node-side checks
secs.body: Why: the exporter only knows what happened since it started; the kernel log is the ground truth for Xids. These checks fit a Slurm prolog or a manual triage. NVIDIA's debug guidelines recommend checking recent Xids at job start.

secs.head: Remap state with nvidia-smi
secs.body: From the nvidia-smi docs; confirm field names on your driver with nvidia-smi --help-query-remapped-rows . Healthy: pending and failure read No / 0 , all banks in the top bucket. On a misbehaving multi-GPU node, query one GPU at a time with -i N .

secs.head: Xid summary for the last 24 hours
secs.body: On our test log (Xid 13 on one GPU; 94, 63 and two 79s on another): No Xids: no output, exit 0. MIG lines ( PCI:0000:01:00 GPU-I:05 ) collapse to the same shape.

secs.head: Prolog gate on fatal Xids
secs.body: Tested: exit 1 on the log with Xid 79, exit 0 on a clean log.

secs.head: What each Xid means
secs.body: Condensed from NVIDIA's GPU Debug Guidelines, Table 1: Xid Meaning Action ----- --------- -------- 48 Double-bit ECC error Followed by 63/64: drain, wait, reset GPU. Otherwise field diagnostics 63 Row remap recorded With 94: restart that app; reset/reboot when convenient 64 Row remap recording failure Reboot immediately; if it continues, drain, triage, report 74 NVLink error Decode the first DWORD; repeated ECC/parity bits on one link: report 79 GPU fell off the bus Drain and report 92 High single-bit ECC rate Field diagnostics; check RMA guidance 94 Contained ECC error Restart the affected app; reset when convenient 95 Uncontained ECC error MIG off: reboot immediately. MIG on: drain other instances, reset [!CAUTION] Don't gate or drain on Xid 13 alone. NVIDIA classes it as a graphics engine exception and says to run diagnostics to separate hardware from application faults. ---

secs.head: Phase 3: the Prometheus rules
secs.body: Why: turns Phase 1 metrics into tiered alerts, each with an action label that Phase 4 routes on. Concepts: part 3.

secs.head: The rule file
secs.body: Save as gpu-health.rules.yml : [!NOTE] GpuTelemetryMissing assumes your scrape job is named dcgm-exporter . Change the job matcher to match your prometheus.yml .

secs.head: The unit tests
secs.body: Save as gpu-health.rules.test.yml next to the rules. Ten cases: the first-Xid trap, a repeat Xid, an application Xid that must stay quiet, pending and failed remaps, a double-bit error, accelerating SBEs with two GPUs that must stay quiet, nearly exhausted spares, a healthy GPU, and missing telemetry. <details <summary gpu-health.rules.test.yml (click to expand)</summary </details

secs.head: Lint, test, load
secs.body: 1. Lint. Expected, exit 0: 2. Test. Expected, exit 0: 3. Prove the tests can fail. Temporarily delete the or (... unless ... offset 10m) branch and rerun. Expected: exit 1 and Then delete the and gpu:ecc sbe:increase1h = 10 floor instead. Expected: exit 1, with an extra alert for the quiet GPU cn012 ( ... is 0.00/s, over 3x its 24h baseline ). Restore the file afterwards. 4. Load. Add to prometheus.yml and reload ( SIGHUP , or POST /-/reload with --web.enable-lifecycle ): Success: the rules appear on /rules with no evaluation errors; gpu:remap banks nearly full returns one series per GPU. [!IMPORTANT] Put step 2 in CI for both the rules repo and the counters file from Phase 1. A renamed metric upstream disables rules silently; only the tests notice. Rollback: remove the file from rule files and reload.

secs.head: Knobs to tune later
secs.body: Knob Starting value Raise if Lower if ------ ---------------- ---------- ---------- SBE ratio vs 24h baseline 3× Many watch alerts never precede failures Failures arrive unwarned SBE noise floor 10/hour Quiet GPUs keep tripping it Real degradations stay under it Pending-remap for: 15m Pending flags clear on their own Jobs die on pending GPUs within 15 min Spare-rows for: 1h Rarely needed You want earlier RMA planning Set them with Phase 6, not by feel. ---

secs.head: Phase 4: alert routing
secs.body: Why: acting tiers go to the drain hook and to people; everything else goes to people only. Concepts: part 4. Save as alertmanager.yml (or merge into yours): Replace the ops-chat URL with your real receiver (Slack, email, PagerDuty, ...). 1. Check the config. Expected: Checking 'alertmanager.yml' SUCCESS , exit 0. 2. Check who gets what. Expected: gpu-drain-hook,ops-chat , then ops-chat . [!WARNING] continue: true alone doesn't reach the root receiver. Our first version had only the drain route plus continue: true ; the route test returned just gpu-drain-hook , because the root receiver only catches alerts that match no child route. The explicit catch-all sibling fixes it. send resolved: false is deliberate: a resolved alert must never un-drain a node. ---

secs.head: Phase 5: the drain hook
secs.body: Why: turns drain now / drain and reset alerts into Slurm drains, with a mode switch, a canary list and a budget.

secs.head: The script
secs.body: Save as /usr/local/sbin/gpu drain hook.py on the Alertmanager host (which needs Slurm client tools and a user allowed to drain nodes): Design notes: - Listens on 127.0.0.1 only. Anything that can POST to it can drain nodes. Put authentication in front before widening the address. - instance → node name by stripping the port ( cn042:9400 → cn042 ). If your targets use IPs or FQDNs, map them here or relabel in Prometheus. - Whole-node drains. Slurm drains nodes, not GPUs; one bad GPU idles its node until the reset.

secs.head: Run it as a service
secs.body: An example systemd unit (standard systemd syntax; not run in our test environment): Save as /etc/systemd/system/gpu-drain-hook.service , then systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl enable --now gpu-drain-hook . Logs: journalctl -u gpu-drain-hook . Replace slurmops with a user your Slurm configuration allows to drain nodes.

secs.head: Test it offline before connecting Alertmanager
secs.body: Save this as payload.json : a fatal Xid on cn042 , a watch alert on cn011 , a pending remap on cn017 , a resolved fatal Xid on cn050 . Expected (dry run touches nothing): What our tests with fake scontrol / sinfo showed in each mode: Mode Output scontrol calls ------ -------- ------------------ dryrun WOULD DRAIN for cn042 and cn017 none canary , CANARY NODES=cn017 WOULD DRAIN (canary) cn042 , DRAINED cn017 one enforce DRAINED cn042 , DRAINED cn017 two enforce , MAX DRAINED=2 , two GPUPRED: drains active BUDGET 2/2 reached, NOT draining ... for both none cn011 ( watch ) and cn050 (resolved) were ignored in every mode, and a POST of the same payload returned HTTP 200 . The real command produced:

secs.head: Roll out: dry run → canary → enforce
secs.body: 1. Dry run, at least a week. MODE=dryrun . Each morning compare WOULD DRAIN lines with what actually failed. Move on when every line points at a GPU you'd have drained by hand. 2. Canary. MODE=canary CANARY NODES=cn201,cn202,cn203 (nodes you're happy to lose). Move on when canary drains carry the GPUPRED: reason and running jobs finished normally. 3. Enforce, small budget. MODE=enforce MAX DRAINED=4 . Size the budget to what you can lose unnoticed. Move on after a normal week with no BUDGET lines. 4. Raise the budget only when Phase 6 says the rules earn it. [!CAUTION] Alert on any BUDGET ... reached line from the hook's journal. It means either several GPUs are failing together (rare) or something upstream is lying (common).

secs.head: Rollback
secs.body: Undo every drain the hook made (tested against fake Slurm: it resumed only the GPUPRED: node and left others alone): Stop new drains without undoing old ones: set MODE=dryrun and restart the service. [!WARNING] Don't resume a node whose GPU had a remap failure or Xid 79 just because the rollback is easy. Roll back drains you believe were wrong.

secs.head: After the drain
secs.body: Alert Once the node is empty Then ------- ------------------------ ------ GpuRowRemapPending , GpuUncorrectableMemoryError nvidia-smi -r -i N (root, no processes on that GPU) Confirm remapped rows.pending is No, run dcgmi diag -r 2 , resume GpuFatalXid 64, or 95 with MIG off Reboot the node If repeated: nvidia-bug-report.sh , field diagnostics, report GpuFatalXid 79 Collect evidence, reboot Expect recurrence; report to the vendor GpuRowRemapFailure Keep it drained Field diagnostic validates the flag for RMA GPU reset limits depend on the platform (NVSwitch and Fabric Manager state); check NVIDIA's reset-capabilities table before automating resets. For the fix-and-verify loop, see NHC auto-remediation. ---

secs.head: Phase 6: backtesting
secs.body: Why: precision, recall and lead time per rule, on your own history, decide which knobs to turn and which rules may drain. Concepts: part 5.

secs.head: Inputs
secs.body: Two CSV files with ISO timestamps, a GPU identified by node and index: Alert history: Prometheus keeps firing alerts as the ALERTS series. Export ALERTS{alertstate="firing"} with the HTTP API's query range , keep the first sample of each firing run, and strip the :9400 port from instance . The hook's dry-run log is a second source.

secs.head: The script
secs.body: Save as backtest.py : Run with the horizon in hours as the last argument:

secs.head: What a run looks like
secs.body: On a hand-made fixture (four alerts, three failures; test input, not cluster data ): With a 12-hour horizon the same inputs score 0.00 everywhere: every warning came more than 12 hours early. Always report the horizon with the numbers.

secs.head: Using the results
secs.body: 1. Tune knobs on older months, grade on the most recent months you held back. 2. Change one knob at a time; keep before/after output in the commit that changes the rule. 3. Promote a watch rule to a drain tier only when its precision on held-out months justifies it. 4. Rerun after every driver, firmware or exporter upgrade (drift). ---

secs.head: Troubleshooting
secs.body: Symptom Likely cause Fix --------- -------------- ----- curl :9400/metrics shows no ECC or pending metrics Exporter still on the default counters file Check -f / DCGM EXPORTER COLLECTORS points at health-counters.csv DCGM EXP XID ERRORS TOTAL missing everywhere Normal until a GPU logs an Xid Verify with the Phase 2 log one-liner GpuFatalXid never fires for a first Xid 79 Naive increase() rule Use the unless ... offset branch; run test 1 All GPU alerts went quiet after an upgrade Metric names changed in the counters file or exporter Restore pinned names; run the rule tests Drains happen but nobody is told Routing without the catch-all sibling Phase 4, amtool config routes test Hook logs BUDGET ... reached Correlated alerts: probably upstream, not hardware Stop and investigate before raising the budget Hook says WOULD DRAIN in enforce MODE not set in the service environment systemctl show gpu-drain-hook -p Environment scontrol permission denied from the hook Service user not allowed to drain Run as a Slurm operator/admin user Pending remap stays after reset GPU still in use, or reset not supported in this topology Confirm no processes; check NVIDIA's reset table GpuTelemetryMissing never fires Scrape job name isn't dcgm-exporter Fix the job matcher ---

secs.head: Day-2 checklist
secs.body: How often Check ----------- ------- Every change promtool test rules and amtool check-config pass in CI Daily (during dry run) WOULD DRAIN lines vs actual failures Weekly Nodes drained with GPUPRED: and their outcome after reset Monthly Backtest on the latest month; review knobs Every driver / exporter upgrade Counters file still exports every field; backtest again Takeaway: deploy in order (signals, node checks, tested rules, routing, a dry-run drain hook, then backtests), and never skip the tests or the dry run, because every phase can fail silently. Back to the concepts: series overview.

secs.head: Storage and Fabric for AI Clusters - Overview
secs.body: A two-part series on the least glamorous way to waste a GPU: making it wait for data. By the end you'll know how parallel filesystems and RDMA fabrics keep 10,000 GPUs fed, and how to tell when they don't.

secs.head: The claim, and what's missing from it
secs.body: A common summary of AI infrastructure says: scaling to 10,000+ GPUs needs data ingestion built on high-performance distributed filesystems such as Lustre or GPFS, paired with InfiniBand or RDMA networks, to prevent GPU starvation. True, and incomplete in three useful ways: - Bandwidth isn't the usual bottleneck; metadata is. Millions of small files starve GPUs on storage with petabytes free. (Part 1) - Checkpoints, not datasets, set the peak. Meta's Llama 3 paper names bursty checkpoint writes as a major storage challenge. (Part 1) - "InfiniBand or RDMA" is not either/or. InfiniBand is one way to run RDMA; RoCE is another, and Llama 3 405B trained on RoCE. And the last hop into GPU memory needs GPUDirect. (Part 2) ---

secs.head: The route
secs.body: Page The question it answers --- ------ ------------------------- 1 Parallel filesystems Why can GPUs starve on storage with petabytes free and bandwidth to spare? 2 RDMA, InfiniBand and GPUDirect Why does a 400 Gb/s network still leave GPUs waiting, and how do you take the CPU out of the way?

secs.head: Contents
secs.body: File Description ------ ------------- parallel-filesystems-for-ai Lustre architecture, striping, the small-file trap, checkpoint storms rdma-infiniband-gpudirect Two fabrics, RDMA, InfiniBand vs RoCE, GPUDirect RDMA and Storage
