label: 1. Parallel filesystems
title: Parallel Filesystems: Why 10,000 GPUs Can Starve on a Full Disk
desc: Part 1 of the Storage and Fabric for AI Clusters series. A GPU that's waiting for data is the most expensive idle hardwa

secs.head: Parallel Filesystems: Why 10,000 GPUs Can Starve on a Full Disk
secs.body: Part 1 of the Storage and Fabric for AI Clusters series. A GPU that's waiting for data is the most expensive idle hardware in your building. This page explains how parallel filesystems like Lustre keep thousands of GPUs fed, the two workloads that break them (small files and checkpoints), and what to do about each. By the end you'll be able to diagnose a data-starved training job and explain the fix.

secs.head: The training run with a heartbeat
secs.body: A team trains an image model on 512 GPUs. The GPU utilization graph has a heartbeat: long stretches near 100%, then a sharp dip to 30% at the start of every epoch, and smaller dips every few minutes in between. The model is fine. The GPUs are fine. The network is fine. The dataset is 40 million JPEG files in one directory tree, and every epoch begins with 512 GPUs' worth of data loaders asking the filesystem to open millions of tiny files at once. The storage system has petabytes free and hundreds of gigabytes per second of bandwidth. It's starving the GPUs anyway, because the bottleneck isn't bytes . It's opens . To see why, you need to know how a parallel filesystem is built. ---

secs.head: Why a normal file server can't do this
secs.body: A single NFS server is one machine with one set of disks and one network link. Every client goes through it. Ten clients are fine. Ten thousand GPUs reading training data are not: the server's network port and CPU become the ceiling for the whole cluster. A parallel filesystem spreads one shared namespace (one /data , visible identically everywhere) across many servers, so clients read from many servers at once. Total bandwidth grows as you add servers. The two classic examples in HPC are Lustre and IBM Storage Scale (formerly Spectrum Scale, originally GPFS). ---

secs.head: Lustre in one picture: the librarian and the shelves
secs.body: Lustre's design splits the filesystem in two, and the split explains almost everything about its behavior. Component Role Stores ----------- ------ -------- MGS (management server) Holds configuration for one or more filesystems Its config, on an MGT MDS (metadata server) Manages the namespace: names, directories, permissions, where each file's data lives Metadata, on MDTs OSS (object storage server) Serves file contents Data objects, on OSTs Clients Mount the filesystem with a normal POSIX interface Nothing The key behavior, from the Lustre project's architecture guide: metadata operations go to the MDS, data operations go directly to the OSSs. The MDS is never in the data path for reads and writes. That's what makes Lustre scale. Think of a library. The MDS is the librarian with the catalog: "where is train/000123.jpg , and may I read it?" The OSSs are the shelves . Once the librarian tells you which shelves hold your book, you walk to the shelves yourself, and thousands of readers can do that in parallel without queuing at the desk. Two operational facts from the same guide worth knowing: Lustre supports up to 256 MDTs, and if the MGS is down, running filesystems keep working, but new mounts and configuration changes fail. Hold onto the library picture. It tells you which workloads Lustre loves (big files: one trip to the librarian, then lots of shelf reading) and which it hates (tiny files: a trip to the librarian for every few kilobytes). ---

secs.head: Striping: one file, many servers
secs.body: Lustre can split one file across several OSTs. That's striping , controlled by two settings: Setting Meaning Default (per the Lustre architecture guide) --------- --------- --------------------------------------------- stripe count How many OSTs the file is spread across 1 (the whole file on one OST) stripe size How big each chunk is before moving to the next OST 4 MiB With stripe count=1 , a file lives on one OST, so one OSS's bandwidth caps how fast anyone can read it. With a wider stripe, many clients reading different parts of one big file hit different servers at once. The rule of thumb: stripe big shared files wide; leave small files at 1. A 2 TB dataset shard read by hundreds of nodes wants many OSTs. A 100 KB file gains nothing from striping, and every extra stripe is extra bookkeeping. You set striping per directory, so new files inherit it: (Standard lfs commands from the Lustre documentation; not run for this page.) ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Two datasets, the same 10 TB of images: - A: 50 million individual JPEG files of about 200 KB. - B: 5,000 archive files ("shards") of about 2 GB, each containing 10,000 images. Same bytes. Which one starves 512 GPUs, and why? A. Every image is a separate open, permission check and layout lookup at the MDS: 50 million trips to the librarian per epoch. B needs 5,000 trips, then long sequential reads straight from the OSSs, which is exactly what Lustre is built for. ---

secs.head: The small-file trap
secs.body: That puzzle is the most common cause of data-starved GPUs. The bandwidth number on the storage system's spec sheet is about bytes ; small files are limited by metadata operations , a completely different resource, and usually the scarcer one. Fixes, roughly from most to least effective: Fix How it helps ----- ------------- Pack samples into large shards (tar-based or record formats, a few hundred MB to a few GB each) Turns millions of metadata operations into thousands, and random reads into sequential ones Stage data to local NVMe on each node before or during training Each epoch after the first reads from local disk, not the shared filesystem Spread metadata load (multiple MDTs, directories distributed across them) More librarians; helps but doesn't remove the per-file cost Raise data-loader parallelism and prefetching Hides latency, but multiplies the load on a struggling MDS if files are tiny The opinionated default: shard first. It's a one-time data preparation step that fixes the problem at its source, and it works on every filesystem, not just Lustre. ---

secs.head: The checkpoint storm
secs.body: Reading data is a steady stream. Writing checkpoints is a flash flood. Every so often, a training job saves its full state so a failure doesn't cost days. For a large run, every GPU writes its share at the same moment. Meta's Llama 3 paper describes exactly this: its storage system offered 240 PB across 7,500 SSD servers, with 2 TB/s of sustainable throughput and 7 TB/s peak, and a major challenge was highly bursty checkpoint writes that saturated the storage fabric for short durations. Each GPU's saved state ranged from 1 MB to 4 GB. Why checkpoints matter so much: while a synchronous job checkpoints, training typically pauses. And at scale, failures are frequent: the same paper reports 419 unexpected interruptions in 54 days (see the GPU failure series). Checkpoint too rarely and each failure costs hours. Checkpoint too often and the storms eat your training time. So the peak your storage must survive is usually set by checkpoints, not by dataset reads. Size for the storm, not the stream. Common mitigations: write checkpoints asynchronously (copy to host memory, keep training, flush in the background), stagger writes, and write to a fast tier first. ---

secs.head: Lustre, GPFS, or something else?
secs.body: The common advice is "use Lustre or GPFS." Those are proven choices for HPC-style AI clusters, especially with InfiniBand. But it's worth knowing the real options: Option Strengths Watch out for -------- ----------- --------------- Lustre Open source, very high aggregate bandwidth, widely used in large HPC systems Metadata limits with small files; needs expertise to run IBM Storage Scale (GPFS) Mature, enterprise support, flexible metadata handling Commercial licensing Other distributed or object storage with caching Scales capacity cheaply; cloud-native Not POSIX by default; needs a fast cache tier for training reads Meta's Llama 3 training didn't use either of the classic two: the paper describes Tectonic , Meta's own distributed filesystem. The underlying principle is the same everywhere: separate metadata from data, spread data across many servers, and connect it over a fast fabric. That fabric is part 2. ---

secs.head: Symptom, cause, fix
secs.body: Symptom Likely cause Fix --------- -------------- ----- GPU utilization dips at each epoch start Data loaders opening millions of small files Shard the dataset; stage to local NVMe Steady low GPU utilization, storage bandwidth far from its limit Metadata-bound (opens and stats), or too few loader workers Shard; check MDS load before adding workers Throughput capped near one server's bandwidth Big files with stripe count=1 Stripe large shared files across more OSTs Training stalls for minutes at regular intervals Synchronous checkpoint writes saturating storage Asynchronous checkpoints, staggered writes, a fast tier One slow node drags the whole job That node's storage path is degraded (link errors, a bad mount) Health-check storage mounts and links per node (NHC series) Takeaway: a parallel filesystem scales by keeping the metadata librarian out of the data path, so feed it few large files instead of millions of small ones, stripe what's big, and size the storage for checkpoint storms, not steady reads. Next: part 2, RDMA, InfiniBand and GPUDirect.

secs.body: - Lustre wiki: Lustre Architecture for Admins (MGS, MDS, OSS, data path, striping defaults) - Lustre wiki: Understanding Lustre Internals - Grattafiori et al., "The Llama 3 Herd of Models", arXiv:2407.21783 (section 3.3.1, storage and network) - IBM Storage Scale documentation

label: 2. RDMA and GPUDirect
title: RDMA, InfiniBand and GPUDirect: Taking the CPU Out of the Way
desc: Part 2 of the Storage and Fabric for AI Clusters series. Part 1 built the storage. This page is the road between storage

secs.head: RDMA, InfiniBand and GPUDirect: Taking the CPU Out of the Way
secs.body: Part 2 of the Storage and Fabric for AI Clusters series. Part 1 built the storage. This page is the road between storage, GPUs and other GPUs. By the end you'll know why AI clusters use RDMA instead of ordinary networking, what InfiniBand and RoCE are, and how GPUDirect lets data skip the CPU entirely.

secs.head: The fast network with a slow middleman
secs.body: A team upgrades to 400 Gb/s network cards. Their data loading barely improves. Profiling shows the network links half idle and the CPUs on each node busy at 80%. The network wasn't the bottleneck. The CPU was the middleman. With ordinary TCP networking, every packet is handled by the operating system kernel: copied from the network card into kernel memory, processed, copied again into the application's memory, and, for a GPU workload, copied once more into GPU memory. At hundreds of gigabits per second, all that copying and interrupt handling eats the CPU alive, and the CPU becomes the speed limit of a network that could go much faster. AI clusters fix this by taking the CPU out of the data path. Twice. ---

secs.head: Two fabrics, two jobs
secs.body: A large GPU cluster usually has at least two kinds of network traffic, often on separate physical networks: Fabric Carries Traffic shape What breaks if it's slow -------- --------- --------------- -------------------------- Compute fabric (east-west) GPU-to-GPU traffic between nodes: gradient all-reduces, tensor and pipeline parallel exchanges Huge, synchronized bursts; everyone waits for the slowest link Every training step (the rowing boat rule) Storage fabric Dataset reads, checkpoint writes Steady streams, plus checkpoint storms Data loading and checkpoints (part 1) Keeping them separate means a checkpoint storm can't slow down the all-reduces, and vice versa. Many clusters also have a third, ordinary Ethernet network for management, logins and monitoring. ---

secs.head: RDMA: three things the CPU stops doing
secs.body: RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) lets one machine's network card read or write another machine's memory directly. Three things change: Without RDMA With RDMA -------------- ----------- The kernel handles every send and receive Kernel bypass : the application hands work straight to the network card Data is copied between kernel and application buffers Zero-copy : the card moves data directly to and from application memory The CPU runs the network protocol Offload : the network card runs the transport itself The result is lower latency, higher bandwidth, and CPUs left free for actual work, like decoding the images part 1's data loaders just read. The analogy: ordinary networking is sending a package through a mailroom, where a clerk opens it, logs it and repackages it at each end. RDMA is a courier with a key to the recipient's office who puts the package straight on their desk. ---

secs.head: InfiniBand or RoCE?
secs.body: RDMA runs on two main families of network: InfiniBand RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet) --- --- --- What it is A network designed around RDMA from the start RDMA carried over Ethernet Strengths Built-in lossless behavior and congestion handling; long HPC track record Uses Ethernet switches and skills many organizations already have Watch out for A separate technology and toolset to run Needs careful configuration to stay lossless and avoid congestion problems Both work at the largest scales. Meta's Llama 3 paper is a nice proof: the 405B model trained on a RoCE fabric, while smaller Llama 3 models trained on NVIDIA Quantum-2 InfiniBand , both with 400 Gb/s links between GPUs. So the opinionated answer isn't "InfiniBand always." It's: InfiniBand if you want the most mature path with the least tuning; RoCE if your team is strong on Ethernet and wants one network technology everywhere. Either way, it must be RDMA. ---

secs.head: GPUDirect: skipping one more stop
secs.body: RDMA took the kernel out. But on a GPU node there's one more stop: the data still usually lands in CPU memory first, then gets copied to GPU memory. NVIDIA's GPUDirect technologies remove that stop too. GPUDirect RDMA lets the network card read and write GPU memory directly. When NCCL sends gradients from a GPU on one node to a GPU on another, the bytes can go GPU memory → network card → network → network card → GPU memory, without a detour through either node's CPU memory. GPUDirect Storage (GDS) does the same for storage. NVIDIA's overview describes it as a direct DMA data path between storage and GPU memory that avoids a bounce buffer through the CPU . Without it, a read goes storage → CPU memory → GPU memory, two trips. With it, one. What GDS needs and gives, per NVIDIA's overview guide: - It's explicit. Applications use the cuFile API, whose reads and writes work with GPU memory buffers, closely mimicking POSIX pread and pwrite . - It needs O DIRECT , which bypasses the filesystem page cache, for direct transfers (newer releases can take the direct path for aligned buffers even without it). - It needs GDS-enabled filesystem drivers. The direct path depends on the filesystem's driver supporting it, which is why "does our parallel filesystem support GDS?" is a real procurement question. - It suits big streaming transfers better than fine-grained random access. - The gain can be large on the right hardware. NVIDIA notes that on some systems, a direct path through a PCIe switch offers at least twice the peak bandwidth of a path through the CPU. Notice the pattern across this whole page: every layer removes a middleman. RDMA removes the kernel. GPUDirect removes the CPU memory hop. The goal is the same each time: let the data go where the GPUs are, as directly as the hardware allows. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ A training job loads large dataset shards from a parallel filesystem over RDMA, but GPU utilization is still low, and each node's CPUs are busy. Which of these would you check first? 1. Upgrade the network to faster links. 2. Check whether data takes a CPU-memory detour and whether the CPU is busy decoding or copying. 3. Add more storage servers. 2. Busy CPUs plus underused links point at the middleman, not the road. Check whether GPUDirect Storage is available and used, and whether data preprocessing (like image decoding) is running on the CPU when it could move to the GPU. Options 1 and 3 add capacity to resources that aren't the bottleneck, the roofline lesson all over again. ---

secs.head: How to know if the fabric is starving your GPUs
secs.body: Symptom Likely cause First check --------- -------------- ------------- All-reduce time grows with node count far more than expected Compute fabric congestion or a bad link Run NCCL tests across nodes (NCCL benchmark guide) One node makes every step slower A degraded link or misconfigured port on that node Point-to-point bandwidth tests (OSU benchmarks); link error counters High CPU, low network and GPU use during data loading CPU copying and processing data GPUDirect Storage support; move preprocessing to the GPU Checkpoint stalls also slow other jobs' communication Storage and compute traffic sharing one fabric Separate fabrics, or traffic classes on a shared one Good bandwidth in tests, poor in training Small messages, latency-bound collectives, or topology-unaware placement Rank placement and affinity (affinity guide) Takeaway: at AI scale the CPU is the slowest thing between your data and your GPUs, so use RDMA (InfiniBand or RoCE) to remove the kernel, GPUDirect to remove the CPU memory hop, and separate fabrics so checkpoints don't trample gradients. Back to the series overview.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - NVIDIA Magnum IO GPUDirect Storage Overview Guide - NVIDIA GPUDirect RDMA documentation - Grattafiori et al., "The Llama 3 Herd of Models", arXiv:2407.21783 (section 3.3.1, network) - NVIDIA AI Enterprise: GPUDirect Storage overview

label: **OpenMP and Open MPI**
title: OpenMP and Open MPI - Overview
desc: An eight-part series for anyone whose brain blue-screens when two names differ by one space. By the end you'll know what

secs.head: OpenMP and Open MPI - Overview
secs.body: An eight-part series for anyone whose brain blue-screens when two names differ by one space. By the end you'll know what each name means, why they exist, how to spot their code at a glance, and how the two end up in the same job script, arguing over the same CPU, and who starts them on Slurm and Kubernetes. The cast, so you can keep score: OpenMP is one kitchen with several chefs sharing a counter. MPI is the rulebook for kitchens that pass notes through a delivery window. Open MPI is one courier company that follows that rulebook. Nobody here is a twin. Several of them are, however, very good at stepping on each other's toes.

secs.head: The route
secs.body: Page The question it answers --- ------ ------------------------- 1 Not twins, not even cousins Are OpenMP and Open MPI twins? What is MPI, then? 2 Where they came from Why do two parallel standards exist, and who wrote each? 3 Threads and ranks What does each style look like when it runs, and what bug does each invite? 4 Spotting the code How do I tell OpenMP, MPI or both from the source, the build and the job script? 5 Hybrid and the binding trap Why does mixing them silently halve my speed, and how do I fix it? 6 Where they're going What did OpenMP 6.0 and MPI 5.0 add, and what never changes? 7 Under Slurm Who starts the ranks on a cluster, and which job-script lines decide the binding trap? 8 On Kubernetes How does an MPIJob give mpirun its address book, and which three numbers must agree? Each page ends with the question the next one answers. The story: name the things (1, 2), see them run (3), recognize them anywhere (4), combine them safely (5), know what is stable (6), and run it on Slurm (7) and Kubernetes (8) .

secs.head: Versions
secs.body: Parts 1 to 6 ran on Ubuntu 26.04.1 (Linux 7.0), gcc 15.2.0 and Open MPI 5.0.10 in a throwaway 4-CPU VM, destroyed afterwards. Ubuntu 22.04 and Open MPI 4.x were not tested; where a page leans on older behaviour it says so. Parts 7 and 8 were not run : they are written from the Slurm, Kubernetes, MPI Operator and Open MPI documentation (Slurm 26.05 docs, MPI Operator v2beta1) and say so on the page. The history and version facts come from the OpenMP and MPI Forum sites linked at the end of each page.

label: 1. The name mix-up
title: Not Twins, Not Even Cousins: OpenMP, MPI and Open MPI
desc: Part 1 of 8. Two names that differ by one space, and one that is not even a program. By the end of this page you'll be a

secs.head: Not Twins, Not Even Cousins: OpenMP, MPI and Open MPI
secs.body: Part 1 of 8. Two names that differ by one space, and one that is not even a program. By the end of this page you'll be able to say, without hesitation, what each of the three is, and you'll know which one to blame when the ticket comes back.

secs.head: Contents
secs.body: - The meeting where nobody understood anybody - Three names, three jobs - The kitchen analogy - Try it before you scroll - Proof that Open MPI is not OpenMP - The cheat table ---

secs.head: The ticket that came back
secs.body: Monday, a ticket lands in the cluster team's queue: Ticket 1: "Please install Open MPI so my OpenMP code runs on more nodes." A junior engineer types apt install openmpi-bin , writes "done", and closes it. Friday, the same user is back: Ticket 2: "Still one node. Still slow. Did the install even work?" The install worked perfectly. It also did nothing for this user, because the ticket asked for the wrong thing in a way that sounds exactly right. To see why, you need to pull apart three names. The names are the problem. OpenMP and Open MPI differ by one space. Say them aloud and they differ by nothing, like "affect" and "effect", except with a job queue attached. Pull them apart and the confusion goes away, because they are not related the way the names suggest. If they were on a family-DNA website, the result would read: "Relationship: none. Both parents are called Open, which is probably how this started." ---

secs.head: Three names, three jobs
secs.body: Name What it is Kind of thing Where your program's pieces live ------ ----------- --------------- ---------------------------------- OpenMP An API (an agreed set of directives, functions and variables) for sharing work between threads A specification, built into compilers One process, one shared memory MPI The M essage P assing I nterface: an agreed set of functions for processes to send each other messages A specification (a document) Many processes, each with its own memory, possibly on many machines Open MPI One program that implements the MPI specification Software you install Same as MPI: it is MPI Read that table twice. The only name that is software you install is Open MPI . The other two are rulebooks. Ticket 1 asked for the one name that is software, to fix a problem in the rulebook that isn't. - OpenMP describes itself as an API that "supports multi-platform shared-memory parallel programming in C/C++ and Fortran" (OpenMP FAQ). - The Open MPI project calls itself "an open source, freely available implementation of the MPI specifications" (Open MPI FAQ). So: Open MPI is to MPI what a browser is to the HTML spec. Nobody says "I installed HTML to open this page", and nobody should say "I installed OpenMP so my cluster can talk". Chrome and Firefox both implement HTML. Open MPI and MPICH both implement MPI. OpenMP is a different rulebook altogether. That is the theory. The kitchen version is easier to remember. [!NOTE] "Open" in both names is a coincidence of branding, not a family tie. The two projects have different authors, different goals and different release schedules. The next part tells where each one came from. ---

secs.head: The kitchen analogy
secs.body: Keep one picture and every later page gets easier. OpenMP MPI --- --- --- Picture One kitchen , several cooks sharing one counter Several kitchens , one cook each, passing notes through a delivery window Sharing Everyone sees the same ingredients. Fast, and easy to trip over each other Nobody sees anyone else's ingredients. You must send them Scale As many cooks as the kitchen has stove burners (the cores of one machine) As many kitchens as you can build, in one building or across a city Classic mistake Two cooks grab the same egg (a data race) A cook waits for a note that never comes (a deadlock) OpenMP stops at the kitchen wall: the chefs can shout at each other all day, but they cannot shout across town. MPI is what lets kitchens cooperate, with all the paperwork that implies. Big jobs use both: several kitchens (MPI), each with several cooks (OpenMP). That is part 5. So where do those chefs and kitchens come from in software? Hold that thought for one pause. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Ten seconds. A colleague installs Open MPI on a fresh machine, then compiles an OpenMP program with mpicc and runs it. Will it run with threads? Hint: what did mpicc get installed to do, and who turns on OpenMP? ---

secs.head: Proof that Open MPI is not OpenMP
secs.body: The answer is no, and here is the evidence, from a throwaway Ubuntu 26.04 VM with Open MPI 5.0.10 installed from the distribution's packages ( openmpi-bin , libopenmpi-dev ) and gcc 15.2. 1. mpicc is just gcc with extra flags. It adds the MPI headers and library and nothing about threads: 2. OpenMP comes from a different place. Thread support is turned on by your compiler's own flag, -fopenmp in gcc, and its runtime is the compiler's library ( libgomp for gcc). Compile an OpenMP program through mpicc without that flag and the OpenMP functions are not found: Installing Open MPI gave that program no OpenMP at all. The two are installed, switched on and versioned separately. That is Ticket 1: the install had nothing to do with the user's real problem (threads can't leave one machine), so the user was still on one node on Friday. 3. An MPI program does not even need a cluster. Started without mpirun , an MPI program just runs as a team of one: ---

secs.head: The cheat table
secs.body: If you hear... Think... You need... ---------------- ---------- ------------- "OpenMP" Threads inside one machine A compiler with OpenMP support ( gcc -fopenmp ) "MPI" Messages between processes, maybe across machines An MPI implementation: Open MPI, MPICH or a vendor one "Open MPI" One implementation of MPI The openmpi-bin / libopenmpi-dev packages, or a module on your cluster "Hybrid MPI+OpenMP" Both, at once Both. Part 5 Takeaway: OpenMP shares work between threads, MPI passes messages between processes, and Open MPI is merely one program that implements MPI. So here's the question this raises: if both rulebooks solve "make a program parallel", why did anyone write two? The answer is in part 2: where they came from, and it starts in the early 1990s with a very annoying hotel. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - OpenMP FAQ (openmp.org): what OpenMP is - Open MPI FAQ, general category: what MPI and Open MPI are - About Open MPI (open-mpi.org) - Evidence on this page: run on Ubuntu 26.04.1, Linux 7.0, gcc 15.2.0, Open MPI 5.0.10, in a throwaway VM.

label: 2. Where they came from
title: Two Tribes, One Problem: Where OpenMP and MPI Came From
desc: Part 2 of 8. Two committees, one headache, and a standard that nearly died on the way in. By the end of this page you'll

secs.head: Two Tribes, One Problem: Where OpenMP and MPI Came From
secs.body: Part 2 of 8. Two committees, one headache, and a standard that nearly died on the way in. By the end of this page you'll know why two parallel standards exist, who wrote each, and where Open MPI fits in the family tree.

secs.head: Contents
secs.body: - The problem: every vendor spoke its own dialect - Tribe 1: the message passers (MPI) - Try it before you scroll - Tribe 2: the shared-memory crowd (OpenMP) - Where Open MPI was born - The whole timeline on one screen ---

secs.head: The problem: every vendor spoke its own dialect
secs.body: Picture the early 1990s. You spent a year writing a clever parallel program for one vendor's supercomputer. Then the machine was retired, and the replacement came from another vendor. Your year of work did not move. It had to be rewritten, because every vendor had invented its own way to say "split this work up". It was like a hotel chain where every hotel makes you learn a different way to switch on the light. There were two kinds of machines, and so two kinds of dialect: Machine How the processors see memory How you program it --------- ------------------------------- -------------------- Shared-memory All processors see one memory Mark loops for parallel execution; the compiler splits them Distributed-memory Each processor has its own memory Send messages between processors Both tribes arrived at the same cure: stop inventing light switches, write the dialects down once as a standard, and let every vendor build to it. Then they went off and did it separately, which is the whole reason you are reading two stories. Who went first, and who went at all? ---

secs.head: Tribe 1: the message passers (MPI)
secs.body: The distributed-memory tribe moved first, and in the open. The MPI-1.1 standard tells the story itself: - April 29-30, 1992: a workshop on standards for message passing in a distributed-memory environment is held in Williamsburg, Virginia. It agrees that a standard is worth writing and sets up a working group. - November 1992: Dongarra, Hempel, Hey and Walker put forward a first draft called MPI1, then a revised one in February 1993. The same month, in Minneapolis, the group decides to run itself by the procedures of the High Performance Fortran Forum. That group becomes the MPI Forum . - 1993: the Forum meets every six weeks for two days and shows its draft at Supercomputing 93 in November. - Who: about 60 people from 40 organizations, spread over vendors, universities, government labs and industry. MPI-1.0 was published in 1994 (per the Open MPI FAQ); MPI-1.1 followed on June 12, 1995. Notice what MPI is: a document , finished by a committee of about 60 people who still managed to agree. The Forum writes the rules and, then, anyone may build software that follows them. That is the whole reason there is more than one MPI program (part 1). Meanwhile, the shared-memory tribe tried the same trick in 1994, three years before OpenMP. It did not go well. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Ten seconds. In 1994 a committee drafted a standard for shared-memory directives (it was called ANSI X3H5 ), and then nobody adopted it . Why do you think it was abandoned? Hint: what was happening, at that exact moment, to the other kind of machine? ---

secs.head: Tribe 2: the shared-memory crowd (OpenMP)
secs.body: The answer is in the sources. The shared-memory tribe had a false start. Per the LLNL OpenMP tutorial, makers of shared-memory machines had each offered "comparable Fortran extensions based on compiler directives", where you mark a loop and the compiler spreads it over the processors. In 1994 a draft from ANSI X3H5 tried to standardize them. It was "never adopted, largely due to waning interest as distributed memory machines became popular". Read that again: the rise of MPI-style machines is part of why the first shared-memory standard stalled. In short, the message-passing tribe accidentally knocked over the shared-memory tribe's first standard on the way in, and the shared-memory tribe came back three years later with a better plan. It came back in spring 1997 , when work on the OpenMP standard began, "continuing where X3H5 left off", led by the OpenMP Architecture Review Board (ARB). The first spec, OpenMP Fortran 1.0, came out in October 1997 . The C/C++ version followed in October 1998 (OpenMP specifications list). MPI OpenMP --- --- --- Written by The MPI Forum: vendors, universities, labs The OpenMP ARB: a board of vendors and research bodies First finished MPI-1.0, 1994 Fortran 1.0, October 1997 Language it lives in A library you call (C, Fortran) Directives your compiler understands (C, C++, Fortran) Failed predecessor None needed: it started from a workshop ANSI X3H5 (1994 draft, never adopted) [!NOTE] The sources say the ARB led the 1997 work. They do not give an exact date for the board's founding, so this page doesn't either. ---

secs.head: Where Open MPI was born
secs.body: MPI was a document, so implementations followed. By the Open MPI FAQ, Open MPI "began as a merger" of three existing MPI implementations, with ideas from a fourth: Ancestor From ---------- ------ FT-MPI University of Tennessee LA-MPI Los Alamos National Laboratory LAM/MPI Indiana University PACX-MPI (contributed) University of Stuttgart The project's copyright notice starts in 2004. Open MPI is therefore a descendant of MPI implementations , not of OpenMP. The name is "Open" because it is open source, the same way a hundred other projects are. Open MPI is not alone. MPICH is another implementation, and vendors ship their own. Which is why, in part 1, installing "Open MPI" and "MPI" was never the same sentence. ---

secs.head: The whole timeline on one screen
secs.body: Year Shared memory (OpenMP) Message passing (MPI) ------ ------------------------ ----------------------- 1992 Williamsburg workshop (April); first draft (November) 1994 ANSI X3H5 draft, never adopted MPI-1.0 published 1995 MPI-1.1 (June 12) 1997 Fortran 1.0 (October) MPI-2.0 (July 18) 1998 C/C++ 1.0 (October) 2004 Open MPI project's copyright begins Takeaway: MPI and OpenMP are two answers from two tribes to the same 1990s headache, and Open MPI is a later, separate program that implements MPI. You now know the cast and the history. Time to stop reading about them and run them: in part 3 four threads count to 100 million, and two out of three times they get it wrong. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - MPI-1.1 standard, introduction: history of the MPI effort - MPI Forum: standards and release dates - Open MPI FAQ: MPI release history and Open MPI's ancestors - LLNL OpenMP tutorial: history of OpenMP - OpenMP specifications: release dates

label: 3. Threads and ranks
title: Cooks and Kitchens: Threads, Ranks and the One Mental Model
desc: Part 3 of 8. By the end you'll know what a thread and a rank are, you'll have seen both run, and you'll understand the o

secs.head: Cooks and Kitchens: Threads, Ranks and the One Mental Model
secs.body: Part 3 of 8. By the end you'll know what a thread and a rank are, you'll have seen both run, and you'll understand the one bug each style invites. The case file: I asked four threads to count to 100 million. Two out of three times they proudly reported 75 million . Nobody lied. Nobody crashed. Twenty-five million counts simply vanished, without a single error message. This page is about how that happens.

secs.head: Contents
secs.body: - The mental model in two sentences - OpenMP: one process, many threads - Try it before you scroll - The bug OpenMP invites: a data race - MPI: many processes, many ranks - The bug MPI invites: not enough slots, and waiting forever - Side by side ---

secs.head: The mental model in two sentences
secs.body: An OpenMP program is one process that, at marked spots, splits into a team of threads which all see the same memory, then joins back into one. An MPI program is a team of separate processes , called ranks , started together, each with its own private memory, which cooperate only by sending messages. Everything else in both worlds is detail on top of that. Here are the two shapes: OpenMP: the process forks into a team, the team shares memory, the team joins. MPI: separate processes, each with its own number, combined only because they sent it. [!NOTE] Written against Ubuntu 26.04.1 (Linux 7.0), gcc 15.2.0 and Open MPI 5.0.10, run in a throwaway 4-CPU VM. Output order and exact numbers will differ on your machine. That is the point of parallel code: nothing promises the order. ---

secs.head: OpenMP: one process, many threads
secs.body: pragma omp parallel is the whole trick: the next block runs once per thread . critical lets only one thread print at a time so lines don't get mixed up. Two knobs to remember: - -fopenmp tells gcc to honour the pragmas. Other compilers have their own spelling. - OMP NUM THREADS sets the team size. Unset, it printed 4 lines on this 4-CPU VM, but the standard leaves the default to the implementation, so set it yourself. [!WARNING] Forget -fopenmp and the pragmas are silently ignored . A program with only pragmas builds clean (gcc warns only with -Wall ) and runs on one thread. I tested a four-thread printf region: with the flag it printed 4 lines, without it, 1. If your OpenMP program is mysteriously slow, check the flag first. That's the happy path. Now let's give four threads a job they can get wrong. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Ten seconds. Four threads share one variable, racy , and each one runs racy += 1 twenty-five million times. What is racy at the end? Hint: += is not one step for a CPU. It is three: read the old value, add one, write the new value back. What happens if two threads do the reading before either does the writing? ---

secs.head: The bug OpenMP invites: a data race
secs.body: Threads share memory, so two threads can touch the same variable at once. Count to 100 million with four threads, the wrong way and the right way: Three runs, four threads, expected 100000000 every time (the program prints the three lines expected , racy , reduction ; condensed here): The racy total was wrong in two runs out of three, and right in the third by luck. That is the nasty part: the program that is wrong sometimes will happily pass the one test you ran before shipping it. I did not dig into why it landed on those exact numbers. The lesson stands: a race gives wrong answers that change from run to run , so a pass proves nothing. reduction(+:var) is the standard fix for "everyone adds to one total". That's the threads' signature bug. The other kitchens have their own way to go wrong, but first they need to run at all. ---

secs.head: MPI: many processes, many ranks
secs.body: Everything between Init and Finalize runs in every rank at once. That is why the one printed sum of ranks line is wrapped in if (rank == 0) : without it, all four ranks would print it. - MPI COMM WORLD is "everyone who was started together". - MPI Get processor name just reports which machine the rank runs on (here the VM is called twins ). - rank is your number in that group (0 to size-1); size is how many there are. - MPI Reduce is a collective : every rank calls it, and rank 0 receives the sum of everyone's value. 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. Four separate processes each held one number in private memory, and the library carried the numbers together, like four kitchens each handing a single note through the window to rank 0. No rank could simply read another's rank variable. That is the "separate kitchens" rule. Both programs run. So what is the first thing that goes wrong when you ask for more kitchens than the building has? ---

secs.head: The bug MPI invites: not enough slots, and waiting forever
secs.body: Ask for more ranks than the machine has slots and Open MPI refuses to start (exit code 1): --oversubscribe means "yes, I know there are only 4 slots, and I would like to seat eight guests anyway". Use it for testing, not for speed. [!WARNING] On this Ubuntu 26.04 install, the refusal message is hidden behind Sorry! You were supposed to get help about: prte-rmaps-base:alloc-error plus "couldn't open the help file". The packages looked for the help text under /usr/lib/x86 64-linux-gnu/prrte3/share/prte/ , and I found one such file only under /usr/share/doc/libprrte-dev/ . On such a system, alloc-error means "not enough slots". The same missing file also breaks mpirun --version ; ompi info --version works. The other classic MPI bug I did not run here, because it hangs by design: a deadlock , where two ranks each wait for a message the other has not sent. It is the mirror of the data race: instead of a wrong answer, you get no answer. Think of two people at a door, each insisting "after you", forever. ---

secs.head: Side by side
secs.body: OpenMP threads MPI ranks --- ---------------- ----------- What runs in parallel Threads inside one process Separate processes Memory Shared Private to each rank How they cooperate By reading and writing shared variables By calling library functions to send and receive How you start it ./prog (set OMP NUM THREADS ) mpirun -np N ./prog How you build it gcc -fopenmp mpicc (a gcc wrapper) Reach One machine One machine or many Signature bug Data race: wrong, changing answers Deadlock or too few slots: no answer Takeaway: a thread shares memory and needs care about who writes what; a rank owns its memory and needs messages to cooperate. You've now seen both models run and both models break. The next skill is the one you'll use every week: someone hands you a repo or a job script, and in thirty seconds you have to say which kitchen you're standing in. That's part 4. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - OpenMP API specification: parallel construct, reduction clause, OMP NUM THREADS - MPI standard (MPI Forum): MPI Init, communicators, MPI Reduce - Open MPI mpirun manual (v5.0.x): slots and --oversubscribe - Every output block on this page: run on Ubuntu 26.04.1, Linux 7.0, gcc 15.2.0, Open MPI 5.0.10, 4 vCPUs.

label: 4. Spotting the code
title: Know It on Sight: Reading OpenMP and MPI Code, Builds and Job Scripts
desc: Part 4 of 8. By the end, you'll be able to open an unfamiliar source tree, Makefile or job script and say "this uses Ope

secs.head: Know It on Sight: Reading OpenMP and MPI Code, Builds and Job Scripts
secs.body: Part 4 of 8. By the end, you'll be able to open an unfamiliar source tree, Makefile or job script and say "this uses OpenMP", "this uses MPI" or "this uses both", and know what each line is asking of the machine. Think of this page as a detective's pocket guide. Every suspect leaves fingerprints: an include line here, a function prefix there, a launch command at the scene. Learn the five fingerprints and you can name the culprit before you've finished your tea.

secs.head: Contents
secs.body: - The 30-second triage - Spotting OpenMP - Spotting MPI - Spotting both: the hybrid fingerprint - Reading a job script - Try it before you scroll - Three look-alikes that fool people ---

secs.head: The 30-second triage
secs.body: Someone hands you a project. Before reading a line of logic, run three searches: Then follow the trail: I ran the three searches on the test programs from part 3: the first listed the five OpenMP files, the second listed the three MPI ones, the third listed the two files that use both. ( !$omp is how OpenMP is written in Fortran; I did not run Fortran here.) Got a hit? Then it's time to read the fingerprints. ---

secs.head: Spotting OpenMP
secs.body: OpenMP is hints written into ordinary code . Strip the hints and what remains is a normal serial program, which is by design. You see It means --------- ---------- include <omp.h The program calls OpenMP functions pragma omp parallel (C/C++) or !$omp parallel (Fortran) "Run this block on a team of threads" pragma omp parallel for "Split this loop's iterations among the threads" reduction(+:total) Each thread keeps a private total ; they are added at the end private(x) / shared(y) Which variables each thread copies, and which all threads share critical , atomic Only one thread at a time may run this (or update this) barrier Everyone waits here until all have arrived omp get thread num() , omp get num threads() "Which thread am I?" and "how many are there?" -fopenmp in a Makefile or build log The compiler is told to honour all of the above OMP NUM THREADS=8 in a script Team size OMP PLACES , OMP PROC BIND Where threads may run: part of the thread-affinity controls added in OpenMP 4.0 pragma omp target Offload this region to an accelerator such as a GPU (device support arrived in OpenMP 4.0) The marker for "OpenMP and nothing else": no MPI anywhere, started as a plain ./prog . A chef with no delivery window. [!WARNING] Pragmas are only comments to a compiler that doesn't know them. No -fopenmp , no error, no speed-up (part 3). ---

secs.head: Spotting MPI
secs.body: MPI is a library you call . Everything is a function whose name starts with MPI . Strip them out and the program stops working, because the communication is the program. You see It means --------- ---------- include <mpi.h The program calls MPI MPI Init / MPI Init thread , MPI Finalize The brackets around every MPI program MPI Comm rank , MPI Comm size , MPI COMM WORLD "Who am I?", "how many of us?", "everyone started together" if (rank == 0) { ... } One rank does a special job, usually reading input or printing MPI Send , MPI Recv One rank sends a message to another (point to point) MPI Isend , MPI Irecv , MPI Wait The same, but non-blocking: start now, finish later MPI Bcast , MPI Scatter , MPI Gather One rank hands out, or collects, data from all MPI Reduce , MPI Allreduce Combine one value from every rank (sum, max, ...); Allreduce gives everyone the result MPI Barrier Everyone waits here mpicc , mpicxx , mpifort Compiler wrappers that add the MPI headers and libraries ( mpicc --showme prints what they add) mpirun -np 16 ./prog or mpiexec ... Start 16 ranks srun ./prog inside a Slurm job Slurm starts the ranks instead of mpirun Two reading habits pay off, and they have saved me from more than one afternoon of staring: 1. Everything between MPI Init and MPI Finalize runs in every rank , unless an if (rank == ...) fences it off. 2. A collective call must be made by every rank in the communicator. If a collective sits inside an if that only some ranks enter, the others wait forever: a deadlock. ---

secs.head: Spotting both: the hybrid fingerprint
secs.body: The rarest sighting, and the one that makes people hold their coffee more tightly. A hybrid program has both includes, usually MPI Init thread instead of MPI Init , and pragmas inside functions that also call MPI . The ask for thread support is a one-line fingerprint: The MPI standard defines four levels you may request: SINGLE , FUNNELED (only the main thread calls MPI), SERIALIZED (any thread, one at a time) and MULTIPLE (any thread, any time). The library tells you what it will actually give in provided . On my Open MPI 5.0.10 install, asking for FUNNELED returned provided=1 , which is the value MPI THREAD FUNNELED has there (the program printed both to compare). [!TIP] FUNNELED is the common choice: OpenMP threads compute, the main thread talks. If you see MPI THREAD MULTIPLE , the code lets many threads call MPI at once, which is harder to get right. ---

secs.head: Reading a job script
secs.body: A Slurm script tells you the shape of the job. Pattern, not run here , so check it against your site's Slurm settings: Decode it: ntasks = ranks , cpus-per-task = threads per rank . Here that is 2 × 4 = 8 ranks, each with 8 threads, 64 cores in total. Slurm's manual says SLURM CPUS PER TASK is "only set if either the --cpus-per-task option or the --tres-per-task=cpu= option is specified", so a script that uses it without the option exports an empty value. If --cpus-per-task is missing but OMP NUM THREADS is large, every thread competes for one core. Part 5 shows that trap on a real machine, and part 7 explains what Slurm does with these lines. Script says Reading ------------- --------- Only --ntasks=N , no OMP NUM THREADS Pure MPI --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=N plus OMP NUM THREADS Pure OpenMP --ntasks=N --cpus-per-task=M plus OMP NUM THREADS Hybrid ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Three scripts land in your inbox. For each, say OpenMP, MPI or hybrid before you read the answers. Hint: look for who starts the processes, and for who sets a thread count. Answers. A is MPI only : eight ranks, no thread setting. B is OpenMP only : one plain process with 16 threads, no launcher. C is hybrid : 4 ranks, each with 8 threads, 32 cores in all. If you got C right, you can already read most real-world job scripts. ---

secs.head: Three look-alikes that fool people
secs.body: Looks like Actually ------------ ---------- OpenMP and Open MPI Different things (part 1). openmpi-bin installs MPI, not OpenMP libgomp gcc's OpenMP runtime. A binary that loads it uses OpenMP, with or without MPI mpicc gcc with extra flags, not a different compiler. It does not add -fopenmp Takeaway: pragma omp and OMP mean threads in one process; MPI and mpirun mean separate ranks; MPI Init thread plus pragmas means both. Script C above is the interesting one. It runs both models at once, and it is the one that quietly goes slow without telling you why. Part 5 catches it on camera. ---

secs.body: - OpenMP API specifications (directives, clauses, environment variables) - OpenMP 4.0 press release: devices, SIMD, task dependencies, thread affinity - MPI standard (function names, thread levels) - Slurm sbatch manual: --ntasks, --cpus-per-task - Tested on this page: the three grep commands and the provided value, on Ubuntu 26.04.1 with Open MPI 5.0.10. The Slurm script is a pattern, not run.

label: 5. Hybrid and the binding trap
title: Kitchens With Cooks: Hybrid MPI+OpenMP and the Binding Trap
desc: Part 5 of 8. By the end you'll know why the two models are combined, what "binding" means, how to see it, and the one-li

secs.head: Kitchens With Cooks: Hybrid MPI+OpenMP and the Binding Trap
secs.body: Part 5 of 8. By the end you'll know why the two models are combined, what "binding" means, how to see it, and the one-line fix for the most common hybrid mistake. The scene: you reserve a nice 4-core node, start 2 ranks with 4 threads each, and the job runs. No error. No warning. It is just a bit slow, and slow is the one thing a cluster never complains about. Meanwhile half your cores are doing a very good impression of a break room.

secs.head: Contents
secs.body: - Why combine them - Binding in one paragraph - The trap, caught on camera - Try it before you scroll - The fix - Proof it matters - A surprise on the way - The safe path ---

secs.head: Why combine them
secs.body: Back to the kitchens (part 1). A real cluster is many machines (kitchens), each with many cores (cooks). - All MPI means one rank per core. It works, but every cook has private ingredients and every shared fact must be sent as a message. Memory gets copied and message counts grow. - All OpenMP is impossible past one machine. - Hybrid puts one rank per machine (or per socket) and OpenMP threads across the cores that rank owns. Fewer messages, shared data inside each kitchen, MPI only between kitchens. Hybrid is not always faster. It is one more thing to get right, and the thing most people get wrong is binding . [!NOTE] Written against Ubuntu 26.04.1 (Linux 7.0), gcc 15.2.0, Open MPI 5.0.10, in a throwaway VM with 1 socket and 4 cores. Binding defaults come from the Open MPI 5.0.x manual and may differ in other versions. ---

secs.head: Binding in one paragraph
secs.body: Binding (also called pinning or affinity) tells the operating system "this process may only run on these CPUs". Open MPI binds each rank by default, so ranks don't wander between cores. Good for MPI. But a rank's OpenMP threads inherit its allowed CPUs, so if a rank is bound to one core, all its threads share one core. Open MPI's defaults, from its mpirun manual: Number of processes Default binding --------------------- ----------------- 2 or fewer to a core more than 2 to a package (a socket) oversubscribed no binding So the trap bites hardest on small test runs of one or two ranks, which is exactly what you do while debugging. ---

secs.head: The trap, caught on camera
secs.body: A hybrid hello. Each thread reports the CPU it is on, and each rank reports how many CPUs it is allowed to use ( sched getaffinity ): Read the last column: "rank may use 1 cpus" . Four threads per rank, all on cpu 0 (rank 0) or cpu 1 (rank 1). Four chefs, one stove burner, and two other stoves sitting cold. The program runs without a single error message. This is the whole trap. You can also see the pinning without writing code, through --report-bindings on the plain MPI hello: Each rank bound to one core ( core:L0 , core:L1 ). Four threads, two ranks, and "rank may use 1 cpus". So how do you get the second CPU? ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Ten seconds. Each rank is allowed one CPU and needs two. What would you tell mpirun to change? Hint: the manual describes a qualifier that means "reserve n CPUs for each process". Its name is a pair of letters. ---

secs.head: The fix
secs.body: The answer is PE . Tell Open MPI to give each rank as many CPUs as it has threads: PE=2 ("processing elements") means "reserve 2 CPUs per rank". The manual describes it as binding n CPUs to each process. Now the output reads "may use 2 cpus", and the four threads sit on four different CPUs (0, 1, 2, 3). The rule of thumb: ranks × threads per rank = cores you reserved, and each rank's binding must hold its threads. Fixed on paper. But does it matter in practice, or is this a purist's complaint? Let's put a stopwatch on it. ---

secs.head: Proof it matters
secs.body: A busy loop of 400 million iterations, 2 ranks × 2 threads. This is a demonstration of the effect, not a benchmark: the machine is a small VM and the loop is trivial. Launch Time per rank -------- --------------- default binding (1 core per rank) 0.38 s and 0.41 s in two runs --map-by slot:PE=2 --bind-to core 0.19 s --bind-to none 0.19 s Same work, same threads, twice as long under the default, because two threads shared one core. Same chefs, same recipe, half the stove. --bind-to none also recovered the time, but it lets the operating system move processes around, and on real multi-socket nodes you usually want the explicit binding. ---

secs.head: A surprise on the way
secs.body: My first attempt at the PE=2 run failed (of course it did) with exit code 213. The error text was hidden behind the missing-help-file message (part 3), and only its topic name survived: span-packages-multiple . That first VM had libvirt's default CPU layout, which I did not record. I changed the VM to present 1 socket with 4 cores and the same command worked. My reading, from the topic name only: Open MPI would not give a rank two CPUs that straddle two sockets. Treat that as a guess, but the lesson is real: on a VM whose CPU layout is odd, binding can fail where bare metal works , so check lscpu first. I also found --report-bindings working on 5.0.10, although the manual lists it as deprecated in favour of --display bindings . I ran the latter once and saw no binding lines in that run, and did not investigate further. ---

secs.head: The safe path
secs.body: 1. Dry run. Start tiny: 2 ranks, 2 threads, --report-bindings , and a program that prints how many CPUs each rank may use (the hybrid.c above). 2. Check the numbers. "may use N cpus" must be at least your thread count, and the CPUs should differ between ranks. 3. Canary. Run the real program on one node for a minute, watch top -H or your monitoring, and confirm every core you reserved is busy. 4. Scale up. Only then run across nodes. 5. Rollback. If binding misbehaves, --bind-to none is the escape hatch. It works, but check the thread placement afterwards. OpenMP has its own placement controls ( OMP PLACES , OMP PROC BIND ). I did not test them here. Binding that MPI sets first limits what OpenMP can choose from, which is why this page starts with the MPI side. Takeaway: In a hybrid job, check "rank may use N cpus" before you trust any timing, because the default can quietly give every rank one core. One last question. Both standards just shipped a big new version, OpenMP 6.0 and MPI 5.0. Do you have to rewrite everything you've seen in this series? Two Monday tickets say otherwise, in part 6. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Open MPI mpirun manual, v5.0.x: default binding, --map-by , PE=n , --bind-to - MPI standard: MPI Init thread and thread levels - Parallel Execution and Affinity (this repo): the wider affinity picture, Slurm and NUMA - Every output block on this page: Ubuntu 26.04.1, Linux 7.0, gcc 15.2.0, Open MPI 5.0.10, 1 socket × 4 cores.

label: 6. Where they're going
title: Two Tickets About the Future: OpenMP 6, MPI 5 and What Never Expires
desc: Part 6 of 8. Both standards shipped a big new version. By the end of this page you'll know what each one added, why the

secs.head: Two Tickets About the Future: OpenMP 6, MPI 5 and What Never Expires
secs.body: Part 6 of 8. Both standards shipped a big new version. By the end of this page you'll know what each one added, why the answer to "do we have to rewrite everything?" is mostly no, and the one caveat hiding in it.

secs.head: Contents
secs.body: - Two tickets in the Monday queue - OpenMP: the kitchen gets a loading dock - MPI: the delivery box gets a standard size - Try it before you scroll - Open MPI today - The tickets, answered - The whole series in six lines ---

secs.head: Two tickets in the Monday queue
secs.body: Monday morning, two tickets land in the platform team's queue. Ticket 1: "OpenMP 6.0 is out. Our code is full of parallel for loops from years ago. Do we have to rewrite everything?" Ticket 2: "MPI 5.0 is out and the news keeps saying 'ABI'. What is that, and do we have to recompile?" A junior engineer reads both, writes "yes, upgrade everything, it's a new major version", and closes them. They're wrong, and not in the same way twice. One answer is "mostly no, with a caveat". The other is "no, and here's what you get if you want it". To see why, look at what each version actually added, using the two kitchens from part 1. First, the trail, with dates from the official lists (OpenMP, MPI): OpenMP MPI --- -------- ----- The pilot Fortran 1.0, October 1997 MPI-1.0, 1994 The big widening 4.0, July 2013 3.0, September 2012 The recent big one 5.0 (2018), 5.1 (2020), 5.2 (2021) 4.0, June 2021 , then 4.1 (November 2023) Latest 6.0, November 14, 2024 5.0, June 5, 2025 A rule for reading version numbers: a jump in the first digit is a bigger storyline; a jump in the second is mostly tidying. Ticket 1 first. What did OpenMP learn? ---

secs.head: OpenMP: the kitchen gets a loading dock
secs.body: For years, OpenMP's whole plot was "several chefs share one kitchen". Then, in 4.0 (July 2013) , the kitchen got a loading dock. Per the 4.0 announcement: New in 4.0 In kitchen terms ------------ ------------------ Accelerator devices ( pragma omp target ) The head chef can send a dish to an annex kitchen next door, the GPU SIMD One chef, one knife stroke, eight carrots chopped Task dependencies "Dice the onions before you fry them", written down Thread affinity Which stove each chef stands at (you met the trouble with that in part 5) User-defined reductions, cancellation Custom ways to combine results, and a way to say "stop, the order was cancelled" Then came 6.0 (November 14, 2024) , which per the release page brought easier tasks, finer control over memory, loop transformations such as fusion, reversal and interchange, support for recent C, C++ and Fortran standards, and a clean-out: features that were deprecated in 5.0, 5.1 and 5.2 were removed . The OpenMP blog says Intel and GCC compilers already ship first implementations of some 6.0 features. There is also a 6.1 public comment draft dated July 2026. That is a trailer, not a release. So Ticket 1 isn't a "yes". It's a "mostly no, with one caveat": your plain parallel for loops are the heart of OpenMP and were never the target. What 6.0 removed is the stuff that had been deprecated , meaning already marked "please stop using this". If your old code used only the basics, you have nothing to do. If it used something that was flagged along the way, that's where to look. [!NOTE] A spec version is not a compiler version. What matters for you is what your cluster's compiler supports, so check its documentation before leaning on a brand-new directive. That settles the threads. But the other ticket mentions an acronym that sounds suspiciously like a new bug. ---

secs.head: MPI: the delivery box gets a standard size
secs.body: Before 5.0, here's a thing nobody tells beginners. A compiled MPI program was quietly married to one specific MPI implementation . Small details, such as how a communicator looks inside memory, differed between Open MPI and MPICH. Compile against one, and the binary only really worked with that one. Switch implementations and you recompiled. Picture a delivery window where every courier company has its own box size. To change courier, you repack every parcel. MPI 5.0 (June 5, 2025) adds the standard ABI (Application Binary Interface): one agreed box size. In its own words it "exists in parallel with existing implementation ABIs", so nothing that already works breaks, and the standard promises "any valid MPI-4.1 program is a valid MPI-5.0 program". There's a catch, and it's the same catch as OpenMP's compilers: a standard is a promise, and an implementation has to keep it. At ISC25, MPICH was described as already supporting the ABI, and Open MPI's support as work in progress (MPI 5.0 announcement, ISC25 slides). The season before that, MPI 4.0 (June 2021) had added, per the MPI-4.1 document: large counts (message sizes no longer limited by what a plain int can hold), persistent collectives (set up a repeating operation once, run it many times), partitioned communication , and sessions , a new way to start MPI. So Ticket 2 is a "no". The ABI is something you may use once your MPI supports it, not something you must do on Monday. Time to see if it stuck. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Ten seconds. A colleague upgrades from Open MPI 4.1 to 5.0 and says: "The MPI standard promises compatibility, so my job script will run unchanged." What part of that sentence could still bite? Hint: think about what the standard actually promises, and what a job script contains. Answer: the standard promises that your program stays valid. It says nothing about your launch line : mpirun flags, binding defaults, and error messages belong to the implementation, not to MPI. I tested 5.0.10 only: its mpirun shipped with PMIx and PRRTE packages, and on Ubuntu 26.04 hid its error text behind a missing help file (part 3). I did not test 4.1, so I can't tell you which flags differ. The right move is the oldest one in the book: read the version's manual before you reuse the script. ---

secs.head: Open MPI today
secs.body: Per its downloads page when I wrote this: Series Status -------- -------- v6.0 Upcoming, no date listed v5.0 Current stable; latest 5.0.11 (September 16, 2026) v4.1 Still supported v4.0 and older Retired Its about page says it offers full MPI-3.1 conformance with many MPI-4.0 elements. Remember the cast from part 1: MPI is the script, and Open MPI is one of the actors reading it, so the script's version and the actor's version are different questions. ---

secs.head: The tickets, answered
secs.body: Back to Monday's queue. Ticket Verdict Why -------- --------- ----- "OpenMP 6.0: rewrite everything?" Mostly no. Check anything that was deprecated Basic loops are the core and stay. 6.0 removed features that were already deprecated in 5.0 to 5.2 "MPI 5.0 ABI: recompile?" No. The ABI is optional Valid 4.1 programs are valid 5.0 programs; the ABI runs alongside the old ones, and not every implementation has it yet Notice what neither verdict needed: knowing the new features. It needed the models from this series. Threads share memory and need care about who writes what. Ranks own their memory and need messages. Binding decides where the work lands. Those storylines have run since the 1990s and no version number cancels them. ---

secs.head: The whole series in six lines
secs.body: Part One line ------ ---------- 1 OpenMP = threads, MPI = messages, Open MPI = one implementation of MPI 2 Two tribes in the 1990s solved the same headache from opposite sides 3 One kitchen with many chefs vs many kitchens passing notes; race vs deadlock 4 omp.h + pragma omp + -fopenmp vs mpi.h + MPI + mpirun ; both = hybrid 5 Check "rank may use N cpus": the default can pin each rank to one core 6 OpenMP 6.0 and MPI 5.0 are current, and the core ideas are the stable part Takeaway: a new version number adds vocabulary, but the two ideas underneath, share memory between threads or send messages between processes, are the part that doesn't expire. The standards are the stable part. The next question is about where your job actually runs: on a cluster someone else manages. Next time a Slurm script says --ntasks=4 and your program prints rank 0 of 1 four times, can you say who forgot to introduce the ranks? That's part 7: who starts the ranks under Slurm, and Kubernetes follows in part 8. ---
