secs.head: Software Tool: AWS Services for HPC Systems
secs.body: The AWS services that support High-Performance Computing (HPC) systems, plus Kubernetes and AWS ParallelCluster in more detail. By the end you'll know which service does which job, and have answers to common interview questions on the topic. In this Chapter, we are interested in introducing the AWS services that support the High-Performance Computing (HPC) Systems. HPC means running big computing jobs, such as machine learning or simulations, on many machines working together. AWS sells the pieces for that as separate services: compute, fast network, storage, scheduling. This page maps them out so you can tell which one to reach for. Who this is for: engineers who need to run HPC or ML workloads on AWS, or who are preparing for an HPC systems engineer interview.

secs.head: AWS Services for HPC Systems
secs.body: The following AWS services can be used in HPC systems: Service Details - - Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) Amazon EC2 provides scalable computing capacity in the cloud. You can use Amazon EC2 to create instances of the latest-generation high-performance computing (HPC) processors, such as the Intel Xeon Scalable processors and the AMD EPYC processors. Amazon EC2 also offers a variety of instance types that are optimized for specific HPC workloads, such as machine learning, computational fluid dynamics, and seismic processing. Amazon Elastic Fabric Adapter (Amazon EFA) Amazon EFA is a high-performance network interface that is designed for HPC applications. Amazon EFA provides low latency and high throughput communication between Amazon EC2 instances. Amazon FSx for Lustre Amazon FSx for Lustre is a fully managed, high-performance file system that is designed for HPC workloads. Amazon FSx for Lustre provides scalable storage capacity and high-performance throughput. AWS Batch AWS Batch is a job scheduler that can be used to manage and scale HPC workloads. AWS Batch can automatically scale your HPC workload based on demand, and it can optimize your costs by using Spot Instances. AWS ParallelCluster AWS ParallelCluster is a managed service that makes it easy to set up and manage HPC clusters on AWS. AWS ParallelCluster provides a variety of cluster templates that are optimized for specific HPC workloads, and it makes it easy to scale your cluster up or down as needed. Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) Amazon S3 is a highly scalable object storage service that can be used to store and access large datasets for HPC workloads. Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Amazon EBS is a block storage service that can be used to store and access persistent data for HPC workloads. Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) Amazon EKS is a managed service that makes it easy to run Kubernetes on AWS. You can use Amazon EKS to run Kubernetes-based HPC applications. You can choose the AWS services that are right for your HPC needs based on the specific requirements of your applications and workloads.

secs.head: What is Kubernetes?
secs.body: Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestration platform. It automates the deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. Kubernetes makes it easy to deploy applications across multiple hosts, and it provides a number of features that make it easy to manage and scale applications. Kubernetes is based on the concept of a cluster. A cluster is a group of machines that work together to run containerized applications. Kubernetes uses a master node to manage the cluster. The master node is responsible for scheduling containers to the worker nodes, and it also monitors the health of the cluster. The worker nodes are the machines that run the containers. Kubernetes automatically distributes the containers to the worker nodes based on a number of factors, such as the availability of resources and the load on the nodes.

secs.head: Provided Features
secs.body: Kubernetes provides a number of features that make it easy to manage and scale containerized applications. These features include: Feature Description - - Deployment Kubernetes makes it easy to deploy containerized applications to a cluster. You can use Kubernetes to deploy a single container or a group of containers. Scaling Kubernetes makes it easy to scale containerized applications up or down. You can scale applications manually or automatically based on demand. Health monitoring Kubernetes monitors the health of the containers in a cluster. If a container fails, Kubernetes will automatically restart it. Service discovery Kubernetes makes it easy for containers to discover each other. This makes it easy to build distributed applications. Load balancing Kubernetes can load balance traffic across the containers in a cluster. This makes it easy to ensure that traffic is distributed evenly across the cluster. Kubernetes is a powerful tool that can be used to manage and scale containerized applications. It is a popular choice for organizations that are looking to build and deploy scalable applications.

secs.head: Benefits of Using
secs.body: Here are some of the benefits of using Kubernetes: Benefit Details - - Scalability Kubernetes makes it easy to scale your applications up or down based on demand. This can save you money on infrastructure costs. Availability Kubernetes automatically restarts failed containers, which helps to improve the availability of your applications. Manageability Kubernetes provides a number of features that make it easy to manage your applications, such as deployment, scaling, and health monitoring. Portability Kubernetes can be used to deploy applications on a variety of platforms, including on-premises, in the cloud, and in hybrid environments.

secs.head: AWS ParallelCluster
secs.body: AWS ParallelCluster is a managed service that makes it easy to set up and manage High Performance Computing (HPC) clusters on AWS. It provides a variety of cluster templates that are optimized for specific HPC workloads, and it makes it easy to scale your cluster up or down as needed. AWS ParallelCluster is built on top of the following AWS services: - Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) - Amazon Elastic Fabric Adapter (Amazon EFA) - Amazon FSx for Lustre - AWS Batch AWS ParallelCluster is a good choice for organizations that need to run HPC workloads on AWS. It is easy to use and manage, and it provides a variety of features that are optimized for HPC workloads.

secs.head: Benefits
secs.body: Here are some of the benefits of using AWS ParallelCluster: Benefit Details - - Easy to use AWS ParallelCluster provides a simple user interface and command line interface for managing your HPC clusters. Managed service AWS ParallelCluster is a managed service, which means that AWS takes care of the underlying infrastructure and software. Scalable AWS ParallelCluster makes it easy to scale your HPC clusters up or down as needed. High performance AWS ParallelCluster is optimized for HPC workloads, and it provides low latency and high throughput communication between Amazon EC2 instances. If you are looking for a way to run HPC workloads on AWS, AWS ParallelCluster is a good option to consider.

secs.head: Supported HPC Workloads
secs.body: Here are some examples of HPC workloads that can be run on AWS ParallelCluster: - Machine learning - Computational fluid dynamics - Seismic processing - Financial modeling - Scientific research - Engineering simulations AWS ParallelCluster is a flexible and powerful tool that can be used to run a wide variety of HPC workloads.

secs.head: Version Control - Overview
secs.body: Git and GitHub, from the idea to the command line. By the end you'll know what version control gives you, how to work with Git day to day, and which page to open when a situation gets messy.

secs.head: Introduction
secs.body: Imagine you’re working on a project — maybe writing some code, editing a document, or building something cool. A few days later, you realize something broke, and you wish you could go back to the version that worked perfectly. That’s exactly where version control comes to the rescue!

secs.head: Version Control in a Nutshell
secs.body: Version control is like a time machine for your projects. It keeps track of every change you make — what was added, what was deleted, and when it happened. You can jump back to any point in history, compare versions, or even experiment safely without breaking the main work.

secs.head: Meet Git
secs.body: Then comes Git, the superhero behind it all. Git lets you create “checkpoints” of your project (/called commits) and experiment on new ideas (/branches) without fear. If something doesn’t work out, you can always go back — no panic, no mess. It’s fast, it’s flexible, and it works right on your machine — even without an internet connection.

secs.head: Enter GitHub
secs.body: Now imagine you want to share your work with the world, collaborate with friends, or just back it up safely online — that’s what GitHub does! It’s like a social network for developers. You can store your Git projects, work with others through pull requests, track issues, and even showcase your portfolio.

secs.head: Why It Matters
secs.body: Learning Git and GitHub isn’t just about managing code — it’s about building confidence as a developer. You’ll collaborate better, take more risks safely, and understand your own workflow more deeply. So, let’s dive in and start mastering version control — one commit at a time!

secs.head: Git CLI
secs.body: In the context of Git, "gh" refers to the GitHub CLI tool, which is a command-line interface for interacting with GitHub repositories. It provides a convenient way to manage GitHub-specific features, such as issues, pull requests, and releases, directly from your terminal. The GitHub CLI is available for macOS, Windows, and Linux, and it can be installed using a package manager or by downloading the binary from the GitHub CLI website.

secs.head: CLI Benefits
secs.body: Here are some of the benefits of using the GitHub CLI: Benefit Details - - Efficiency It allows you to perform GitHub tasks without having to switch between the terminal and a web browser. Automation You can use scripts to automate repetitive tasks, such as creating issues or updating pull requests. Customization You can create custom aliases and extensions to personalize your GitHub CLI experience.

secs.head: HTTP vs CLI Cloning
secs.body: Normal HTTP cloning and gh clone are both methods for cloning a Git repository, but there are some key differences between the two. Normal HTTP cloning involves downloading the contents of the repository directly from the Git server using the HTTP protocol. This method is simple to use, but it can be slow and unreliable, especially for large repositories. gh clone is a command provided by the GitHub CLI tool that uses GitHub-specific APIs to clone repositories. This method is more efficient and reliable than normal HTTP cloning, and it also supports additional features, such as cloning private repositories and using SSH authentication. Here is a table summarizing the key differences between normal HTTP cloning and gh clone: Feature Normal HTTP cloning gh clone - - - Protocol HTTP GitHub-specific APIs Speed Slow Efficient Reliability Unreliable Reliable Supported features Cloning public repositories Cloning public and private repositories, using SSH authentication In general, it is recommended to use gh clone for cloning Git repositories whenever possible. It is a more efficient, reliable, and feature-rich method than normal HTTP cloning.

secs.body: Here are the general steps on how to use the GitHub CLI: 1. Install the GitHub CLI: - For macOS, download the binary from the GitHub CLI website or use Homebrew to install it. - For Windows, download the installer from the GitHub CLI website or use Chocolatey to install it. - For Linux, use your distribution's package manager to install the GitHub CLI package. 2. Authenticate with GitHub: - Open a terminal window and run the command gh auth login. - Follow the on-screen instructions to sign in to your GitHub account. - GitHub CLI will store your credentials securely. 3. secs.head: Local App Accounts: Six Tea Talks on Teaching an App Who Is Who
secs.body: A six-part series on adding accounts to a desktop app that used to trust everyone at the keyboard. By the end you'll know what accounts should promise, how to handle passwords and sessions, and where this kind of design tends to go wrong. Two people share one laptop and one desktop app. Ahmed runs training jobs, Abdelrahman babysits the storage, and until now the app showed them the same clusters, the same notes and the same saved passwords. This series follows how that app learns to tell them apart, one locked door at a time. Each talk is short enough to finish before the tea goes cold, and each stands on its own. Read them in order, or jump to the one you need.

label: Threat Model and First Launch
title: Two People, One Laptop: What Accounts Should (and Shouldn't) Promise
desc: Local App Accounts, tea talk 1 of 6. Next: Sign-In Hygiene. Picture a shared workstation in a lab. Ahmed runs training j

secs.head: Two People, One Laptop: What Accounts Should (and Shouldn't) Promise
secs.body: Local App Accounts, tea talk 1 of 6. Next: Sign-In Hygiene. Picture a shared workstation in a lab. Ahmed runs training jobs. Abdelrahman babysits the storage. Both use the same desktop app, and before accounts existed they opened the same window and saw the same clusters, the same notes and the same saved passwords. Comfortable, right up to the moment Abdelrahman's reminder to "delete the scratch data" pops up on Ahmed's screen while he is sharing it in a meeting. This series follows what happens when that app learns to tell the two of them apart. This first talk is about the part that comes before any code: deciding what the feature is for. ---

secs.head: The one-sentence version
secs.body: Accounts in a local app are a gate and a separator, not a vault: they keep each person's workspace out of the other person's view, and give you a lock for when you step away. ---

secs.head: Words you'll meet
secs.body: Term Plain meaning --- --- Threat model A short answer to "who am I defending against, and who am I not?" Authentication Proving who you are ("it's really Ahmed") Authorization Deciding what that person may do ("Ahmed may edit his clusters") ---

secs.head: The honest disclaimer
secs.body: The most useful sentence in the whole design is a negative one. Accounts here: - Do keep Ahmed's workspace out of Abdelrahman's view and out of his way. - Do not stop anyone who can read your files as you on the operating system. Saved secrets are sealed by the computer's keychain, and the keychain belongs to the computer user, not the app user. So the app protects who sees what inside the app , plus a lock for the moment you step away . That is the whole contract. The threat model is "the other person using this app", not "an attacker with full control of the computer." Lesson. Write the threat model before the feature. A modest, honest promise is much easier to keep than an ambitious, vague one, and every later decision gets judged against it. ---

secs.head: The cast
secs.body: Every responsibility gets a character, which makes the design easy to hold in your head. They'll keep turning up in the next five talks: Character Their job Appears in --- --- --- The Doorman Decides which screen you get: sign-up, sign-in, claim, or the app This talk The Clerk Checks who you say you are Talk 2 The Slow Clerk Makes password guessing expensive Talk 2 The Memory Knows who's signed in, in memory only Talk 3 The Bouncer Inspects every request and asks "is that yours?" Talk 3 The Cartographer Draws the map of what you may see, down in the database Talk 3 The Night Watch Runs background monitors, but only while somebody is home Talk 4 The Curtain The lock screen Talk 5 The Locksmith Gets you back in when you forget your password Talk 5 ---

secs.head: The very first launch
secs.body: Scene. Fresh install, no accounts. The Doorman sees an empty list of people, so the first thing you get is Create your account . Two small decisions are worth a second look. The password is optional. Plenty of single-user laptops don't want one. An account without a password simply opens with an empty one. The login is a gate for people who chose to have one, not a requirement the app imposes on everyone. The first account adopts the empty profile. A fresh install already has one empty profile the app made for itself. Asking a brand-new user to "claim" an empty profile would be silly, so the first account just takes it. The rules stay tiny: a username is 3 to 32 characters (letters, digits, dot, underscore, dash, starting and ending with a letter or digit), and a password, if you set one, is 8 to 256 characters. The rules live behind an info icon so the form stays calm. Lesson. Don't make the common case (one person, one laptop) pay for a feature built for the uncommon one. ---

secs.head: Recap
secs.body: - State the threat model first, including what you are not protecting. - Keep the first-run path frictionless: optional password, and the first account adopts the empty profile. Next tea talk: Sign-In Hygiene, where the Clerk learns to say "no" without giving anything away.

desc: Local App Accounts, tea talk 2 of 6. Previous: Threat Model and First Launch. Next: Sessions and Two Walls. Ahmed comes

secs.head: Sign-In Hygiene: How the Clerk Says "No" Without Giving Anything Away
secs.body: Local App Accounts, tea talk 2 of 6. Previous: Threat Model and First Launch. Next: Sessions and Two Walls. Ahmed comes back the next morning, types his password and presses Enter. In the fraction of a second that follows, the Clerk does four things he never notices, and each one closes a small leak. This talk is about those four things. ---

secs.head: The one-sentence version
secs.body: Most of sign-in hygiene is making different failures look identical: in text, in timing and in counting. ---

secs.head: Words you'll meet
secs.body: Term Plain meaning --- --- Hash A one-way scramble of a password. You can check a guess against it, but you can't run it backwards Salt Random extra data mixed into each hash, so two identical passwords don't produce identical hashes Memory-hard hash A hash (scrypt, Argon2id) that is deliberately slow and RAM-hungry, so guessing millions of passwords gets expensive Timing attack Learning a secret from how long something takes, not from what it says User enumeration Using differences in errors or timing to learn which usernames exist Throttling vs lockout Throttling only slows repeated attempts; lockout blocks the account after N failures ---

secs.head: Detail 1: slow, self-describing hashes
secs.body: Passwords are scrambled with scrypt , taking about a tenth of a second per check. The stored result records its own settings, so the app can raise the cost later and quietly upgrade an entry the next time its owner signs in. (A sketch of the idea, not production code.) Why slow? A normal hash is fast, which is exactly what a password cracker wants. scrypt and Argon2id are built to be slow and to need a lot of RAM per guess, so an attacker can't simply buy more cheap chips. How slow is slow enough? OWASP's Password Storage Cheat Sheet recommends Argon2id first. If it isn't available, it says to use scrypt with a cost of at least 2^17, a block size of 8 and parallelism of 1. A tenth of a second usually means defaults well below that. The original design says it tuned for comfort, because the login protects a door that encrypts nothing. That is defensible, and because each record stores its own settings, raising them later costs one line of code. (Your runtime's default memory ceiling may need raising to use the larger setting, so check its docs.) ---

secs.head: Detail 2: unknown usernames cost the same
secs.body: Type a name that doesn't exist and the Clerk still checks your password, against a decoy. Otherwise a faster "no" would reveal which accounts exist. If "no such user" returns in 1 ms and "wrong password" takes 100 ms, an attacker can stopwatch their way to a list of valid usernames. Doing the same work either way closes that leak. OWASP's Authentication Cheat Sheet describes the same defence: the code should go through the same process whatever the user or password is. ---

secs.head: Detail 3: one message for every failure
secs.body: Wrong password or no such user, the answer is identical: "Wrong username or password." The red ring and the little shake on the password field are the same too. For screen reader users, the sentence is announced from a visually hidden alert, so nobody is left in silence. OWASP's guidance is the same: respond with a generic message whether or not the account exists, for login, password reset and recovery alike. ---

secs.head: Detail 4: the Slow Clerk
secs.body: After four wrong passwords you start waiting: one second, then two, four, eight, doubling up to a cap of fifteen minutes. Two clever choices make this interesting: - It counts per username whether or not the account exists , so the waiting message can't be used to discover accounts either. - It lives in memory on purpose . Restart the app and it's a fresh start. The honest trade-off: someone at the keyboard could keep a username waiting for fifteen minutes, but nobody can lock Ahmed out forever . Why not a hard lockout? OWASP lists the lockout threshold, the observation window and the duration as the parameters to weigh. A fixed, long lockout is easy to abuse against a victim. A capped, doubling delay is a common compromise: it slows guessing without giving an attacker a way to lock someone out for good. (That last comparison is design reasoning, not an OWASP quote.) ---

secs.head: Recap
secs.body: Leak Plug --- --- Fast hashes are cheap to guess Slow, memory-hard hash with self-describing settings Timing reveals which usernames exist Decoy check for unknown users Error text reveals which usernames exist One identical message Waiting message reveals which usernames exist Throttle counted per username, existing or not Next tea talk: Sessions and Two Walls, where the password is right and the real separation begins. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, Password Storage Cheat Sheet: Argon2id first, then scrypt at N of at least 2^17, r of 8 and p of 1 - OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, Authentication Cheat Sheet: generic error messages, equal processing for known and unknown accounts, lockout parameters

label: Sessions and Two Walls
title: Who's Home, and What May They Touch? Sessions and Two Walls
desc: Local App Accounts, tea talk 3 of 6. Previous: Sign-In Hygiene. Next: Old Data and Background Work. The password was rig

secs.head: Who's Home, and What May They Touch? Sessions and Two Walls
secs.body: Local App Accounts, tea talk 3 of 6. Previous: Sign-In Hygiene. Next: Old Data and Background Work. The password was right, and the app now knows Ahmed is home. This talk covers what "home" means in memory, how the app can remember him tomorrow without storing his password, and the part that actually keeps Abdelrahman out of Ahmed's clusters. ---

secs.head: The one-sentence version
secs.body: Authorize at the door and again at the data, and make the build fail when someone forgets the door. ---

secs.head: Words you'll meet
secs.body: Term Plain meaning --- --- Session The app's memory of "this person is signed in right now" Token A random secret that stands in for a password after sign-in Fingerprint A hash of the token, stored instead of the token itself Keychain The operating system's protected store for secrets, tied to the computer user Main process / UI process In many desktop apps: the part that does privileged work, and the part that draws the window. The UI process is treated as less trusted IDOR Insecure direct object reference : a request names a resource ("cluster 42") and the app serves it without checking that the asker owns it Deny by default If no rule explicitly allows a request, it is refused ---

secs.head: The Memory
secs.body: Once the password is right, the main process notes that Ahmed is home. That note lives in memory in the app's main process. Not a cookie, not a file. The screen is told his name and nothing else. The note can announce changes , and three things listen: 1. The Cartographer, who redraws the map of what's visible 2. The Curtain, which lifts (a new sign-in never starts locked) 3. The app itself, which starts or stops all its background work (talk 4)

secs.head: "Keep me signed in on this computer"
secs.body: If Ahmed ticks the box, the app does not remember his password. It makes a random token , seals it with the computer's keychain, and stores only a fingerprint of that token beside his account. On the next launch it unseals the token, fingerprints it and compares. If anything is off (keychain unavailable, token revoked, account gone), you simply get the sign-in screen. - One slot per computer. Remembering Abdelrahman replaces Ahmed. - Sign-out or reset deletes the fingerprint , revoking the token at once. - Changing the password revokes the old token , and if the box was ticked, a fresh one is sealed so Ahmed stays signed in. - No keychain, no promise. Where there isn't a usable keychain, the box is switched off and says why, instead of promising something it can't deliver. Why a fingerprint? If someone copies the database, a stored fingerprint can verify a token but can't be turned back into one. Storing the token itself would hand over a working key. ---

secs.head: Wall one: the Bouncer
secs.body: Everything the screen asks of the engine goes past the Bouncer, who asks two questions: 1. Did this come from the app's own page? 2. Is this person allowed to ask this? With nobody signed in, refuse everything except a short list of public doors (the sign-in screens and the window's own buttons). He also carries a list of what each request is about . If a request says "edit cluster 42," he checks that cluster 42 belongs to a profile the signed-in person owns. Abdelrahman asking for Ahmed's cluster gets exactly the same answer as asking for one that doesn't exist. And here's the detail worth stealing: the build has a check that fails if anyone adds a request that names a cluster, profile, note or rule and forgets to put it on the Bouncer's list. The easiest mistake in this design is also the one the tooling refuses to let through. ---

secs.head: Wall two: the Cartographer
secs.body: Checking at the door is good; checking at the shelves is better. Every question the app asks the database about profiles, clusters, notifications, reminders or watches passes through one ownership rule. A feature that forgets to filter cannot , because the filter is part of how the database answers. The map, short enough to memorise: Situation What you see --- --- No accounts exist yet Everything, as it always was (so upgrades behave) Accounts exist, nobody signed in Nothing Signed in as Ahmed Ahmed's profiles, and through them his clusters, notes and so on A profile nobody owns Nothing, for anybody, and nothing runs for it Ownership is a single label, the owner , on each profile. Clusters, notes and the rest belong to a profile or a cluster, so they inherit it. Anything new that gets stored must say how it reaches an owner.

secs.head: One click, both walls
secs.body: Abdelrahman clicks Edit on a cluster. The Bouncer checks the request is from the app's page and that this cluster is one of his . If not, it's refused like "no such cluster." If it passes, the database applies the ownership rule again . A mistake in one wall isn't an open door. ---

secs.head: What the references recommend
secs.body: IDOR sits under OWASP's top-ranked web risk, Broken Access Control. OWASP's Authorization Cheat Sheet says to deny by default , to validate permissions on every request (checking most of them is not enough), and to write tests proving the permissions work. Its Developer Guide checklist adds: send all requests through access checks unless they're public, and use a single component to make authorization decisions. The Bouncer is that single component, and the build check is the test. Lesson. Authorize at the door and again at the data. Make "no access" and "doesn't exist" the same answer, so refusals don't leak what exists. Store a fingerprint of the token, never the token. ---

secs.head: Recap
secs.body: - The session lives in the main process's memory, and announces changes to whoever cares. - "Keep me signed in" stores a fingerprint of a random, keychain-sealed token, with one slot per computer. - Two walls: a request-level check with a build guard, and an ownership rule inside the database. Next tea talk: Old Data and Background Work, where a year of pre-account data finds its owner and two nasty bugs teach a lesson. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, Authorization Cheat Sheet: deny by default, validate permissions on every request, test the permissions - OWASP Developer Guide, Enforce Access Controls checklist: route requests through access checks, use a single component for authorization decisions - OWASP Top 10, A01 Broken Access Control: where IDOR sits

label: Old Data and Background Work
title: The Orphans Come Home: Old Data and Background Work
desc: Local App Accounts, tea talk 4 of 6. Previous: Sessions and Two Walls. Next: Lock, Recovery and Going Online. Two awkwar

secs.head: The Orphans Come Home: Old Data and Background Work
secs.body: Local App Accounts, tea talk 4 of 6. Previous: Sessions and Two Walls. Next: Lock, Recovery and Going Online. Two awkward questions arrive the moment accounts exist. What happens to the data created before anyone had an account? And what happens to everything the app does in the background when the person who started it signs out? This talk answers both, and the second answer comes with two bugs worth framing. ---

secs.head: The one-sentence version
secs.body: A data migration is a trust event, and background work is part of the session: when the person leaves, both the work and its cached results must go with them. ---

secs.head: Words you'll meet
secs.body: Term Plain meaning --- --- Atomic Two related meanings. In concurrent code: indivisible , so nobody can observe it half-done. In databases (ACID): all or nothing , so if a fault hits partway through, every write is rolled back Isolation Overlapping operations don't see or disturb each other's half-finished work. It's the ACID letter that handles concurrency Race condition Two actions overlap and the result depends on who got there first Derived data Data computed from other data, such as a cache or a "last known status." It goes stale when its source changes Idempotent Safe to do more than once: doing it again changes nothing further ---

secs.head: Part 1: the orphans
secs.body: Scene. Ahmed has used the app for a year, before accounts. His profiles have no owner. On his first sign-in they appear on a claim screen : each profile with its cluster and note counts, nothing ticked until he chooses. Four rules make that screen safe: 1. Nothing is claimed silently. Skipping leaves the profiles unowned and hidden. A small banner and an "Unclaimed data (N)" menu entry show how many are waiting, by count only. 2. A safety copy first. Before ownership changes, the data is backed up. If the backup fails, nothing changes. 3. All or nothing. The change is applied as one step. If someone else claimed one in between, everything is undone, not half of it. 4. A confirmation, and no undo. Nothing is pre-selected, and a second step says what will be taken and that there is no undo. And the question every new user asks: "How do I know these clusters are mine?" Each row has a small arrow that opens the names of the clusters inside. Those names are shown only to the first account on the computer, the person who owned everything before accounts existed. Later accounts see counts only, so a second person who signs up can't read the first person's cluster names before they're claimed. Unclaimed profiles are paused: no monitoring, no reminders, no alerts, because nobody is there to receive them.

secs.head: Two different problems hiding in rule 3
secs.body: Atomic (the database sense) covers a failure partway through : if something breaks halfway, every change is rolled back, so you never end up with half the profiles claimed. A race condition is two claimers reaching the same profile at the same moment. That one is about isolation , not atomicity: the claim must check "is it still unowned?" inside the same transaction as the write, so only one claimer wins. The word "atomic" is also used in concurrent code to mean indivisible (nobody can see the operation half-done). It's related, but it is not the same promise. Lesson. Make consent explicit, the change atomic, a backup first, and show people proof of what they're taking. ---

secs.head: Part 2: the Night Watch
secs.body: Scene. The app does a lot while you aren't looking: checking that clusters are reachable, polling the job scheduler, watching a ticket tracker, tracking storage, firing reminders. Before accounts, all of that started with the app. Now it starts when someone signs in and stops when they sign out . Sign-out also shows a short list of what it's about to close. So when Ahmed signs out and Abdelrahman signs in, nothing of Ahmed's is still running behind his back, and Abdelrahman's monitors watch only Abdelrahman's clusters.

secs.head: Bug one: the ghost reading
secs.body: A tester signed out, switched a test VM off, signed back in, and the card still said the VM was up for a moment before flipping to down. The monitors had stopped, but their last answers were still in memory . The fix: clear those cached readings on sign-out too, so each card says checking until it has really been probed. A "last known status" is derived data : a copy computed from reality, so it goes stale the moment reality changes. Anything derived (caches, snapshots, indexes) needs a rule for when it's thrown away.

secs.head: Bug two: the late arrival
secs.body: A tester on a Mac opened the app after an update and found the overview stuck on grey placeholder cards. The cause is only visible in the real app: a remembered sign-in happens while the app is still starting up, before some monitors have registered. The system considered itself "on duty", but a monitor that showed up late was never told to start. The fix was one rule: a monitor that turns up while the system is on duty starts at once. That's an idempotent start : make "start" safe to call at any time, in any order, any number of times. "Start everything when X happens" is fragile whenever a component can register after X. Lessons. (1) Cached and derived state is part of what a sign-out must clear. (2) Don't assume startup order; make start safe to call late. ---

secs.head: Recap
secs.body: - Old data gets an owner only by explicit choice, with a backup, an all-or-nothing change and a confirmation. - Atomicity handles failures partway through; isolation handles two actors colliding. - Background work starts on sign-in and stops on sign-out, and cached readings are cleared with it. - A component that registers late must still start. Next tea talk: Lock, Recovery and Going Online, covering the lock screen, forgotten passwords, and the door already built for online sign-in.

label: Lock, Recovery and Going Online
title: The Curtain, the Locksmith and the Door Already Built
desc: Local App Accounts, tea talk 5 of 6. Previous: Old Data and Background Work. Next: Reviewing the Design. Three things ar

secs.head: The Curtain, the Locksmith and the Door Already Built
secs.body: Local App Accounts, tea talk 5 of 6. Previous: Old Data and Background Work. Next: Reviewing the Design. Three things are left to design, and each one is where good intentions usually leak: what happens when someone walks away, what happens when someone forgets their password, and what happens when the app one day needs a real sign-in service. ---

secs.head: The one-sentence version
secs.body: A lock protects the screen while work continues, a recovery path must destroy the thing worth stealing, and the rest of the app should depend on a role , not on any one way of signing in. ---

secs.head: The Curtain (lock screen)
secs.body: Scene. Ahmed goes to get tea. The window locks. This is not a sign-out: terminals keep running, jobs keep being watched, reminders still fire. A curtain is drawn over the window and the app underneath is made inert, so Tab can't wander into it. It falls three ways: - By hand: a keyboard shortcut, or the account menu. - When idle: after a stretch with no activity in the app's own windows. The default is 15 minutes, with options from 1 minute to 60, or never. Only activity inside the app counts, not system-wide idle, which is unreliable on some Linux setups and lets work in other apps keep the lock open. - By the computer: when the operating system suspends or locks the screen, the app locks too (a per-account setting, on by default). The "locked" state is held by the engine, not the page, so reloading the window doesn't undo it. To unlock, type the password again. It is a screen lock for someone walking past. It is not a barrier against a person who can run programs as you, and the guide says so plainly. Lesson. Lock and sign-out are different tools. A lock protects the screen while work continues; a sign-out ends the session . Keep the lock state somewhere a page reload can't reset. ---

secs.head: The Locksmith (forgot my password)
secs.body: Scene. There's no email to send a reset link to; everything is local. The way back is a command run once from a terminal that names the account. It needs access to the computer, which is also what it would take to read the data, so it's no weaker than the login. The account loses its password and the secrets saved on its clusters (SSH passwords, passphrases, API tokens), because those were guarded by that identity. Clusters, notes and settings stay. Ahmed signs in with no password and sets a new one, and a remembered sign-in is revoked at the same moment. The clever part is what reset doesn't give you: it wipes the secrets instead of exposing them, so the recovery path can't be turned into a way to steal them. Lesson. A recovery path is part of the attack surface. Design it so that using it destroys the thing worth stealing. ---

secs.head: What this design does not do
secs.body: Being honest is part of the design. According to the write-up: - Not a vault. The keychain belongs to the computer user, so two app users sharing one computer login could, with effort, read each other's sealed secrets. - Some settings are shared: panel layout, cluster order, sidebar width, notification preferences and known SSH hosts. - Not built yet: a password reset without a terminal, disabling or removing an account, an admin role, online sign-in, and database-level links between tables. - Password hashing is tuned for a local gate , not for resisting a leaked password database. ---

secs.head: The door that's already built: going online
secs.body: The rest of the app never talks to the Clerk by name. It talks to a role : "someone who can create an account, sign someone in and change a password." The local Clerk, with a username and optional password, is simply the first to fill that role. Each account also records which kind of Clerk vouched for it, with room for the identity that Clerk knows it by. So an online sign-in (say, through the browser with a company login) is a second Clerk filling the same role, while the screens, the Bouncer, the Cartographer, the Night Watch and the Curtain stay exactly as they are. Lesson. Depend on the role, not the implementation, and record who vouched for each identity. ---

secs.head: Recap
secs.body: - Lock is not sign-out, and its state lives in the engine. - Recovery wipes the secrets instead of exposing them. - The honest limits are written down. - Sign-in is a role, so a second provider can fill it later. Next tea talk: Reviewing the Design, where we stop admiring it and start poking holes.

label: Reviewing the Design
title: Reviewing the Design: Where Would You Push Back?
desc: Local App Accounts, tea talk 6 of 6. Previous: Lock, Recovery and Going Online. A good design is not one with no open qu

secs.head: Reviewing the Design: Where Would You Push Back?
secs.body: Local App Accounts, tea talk 6 of 6. Previous: Lock, Recovery and Going Online. A good design is not one with no open questions. It is one where the open questions are written down. This last talk puts the design on the review table: six questions it leaves open, the common mistakes it avoids, the book chapters that explain why it works, and a few exercises so the ideas stick. ---

secs.head: The one-sentence version
secs.body: Every design makes implicit promises, and reviewing is the skill of spotting them and deciding which ones you'd write down. ---

secs.head: Six questions to push back on
secs.body: Think about each before reading on. There are no single right answers. 1. Remember-me on a shared login. The token is sealed by a keychain that belongs to the computer user. So when Abdelrahman opens the app from the same computer login, whose account does he land in? Should the checkbox say so? 2. Claiming old data. If any account can claim any unowned profile, could a second account created during the migration window take the first person's data without ever seeing the names? Who should be allowed to claim? 3. The locked state. The screen is covered, but does the engine also refuse requests while locked? A covered page and a refusing engine are different guarantees. 4. Shared settings that leak. If the known-SSH-hosts list is shared between accounts, can it reveal hostnames that the pre-claim hiding was meant to protect? 5. The backup copy. The claim flow writes a safety copy of the very data you're protecting. Where does it live, with what file permissions, and when is it deleted? 6. Hash cost. Given the stated trade-off, what would you raise the scrypt settings to, and what would it do to sign-in time on a slow laptop? ---

secs.head: Mistakes this design avoids
secs.body: Common mistake What the design does instead --- --- Overpromising ("secure accounts!") States the threat model, including what it doesn't do Different errors for "no such user" and "wrong password" One message, one look, same timing via a decoy Storing a "remember me" password or a raw token Stores a fingerprint of a random token Authorization only in the UI Checks at the door and at the data Forgetting to guard a new endpoint The build fails until it's on the list Background tasks outliving the session Stops them all, then clears their cached readings Silent data migration Explicit consent, backup, atomic change Treating lock like sign-out Two separate states with different effects Recovery that leaks secrets Recovery wipes them ---

secs.head: Go deeper: Designing Data-Intensive Applications
secs.body: Martin Kleppmann's Designing Data-Intensive Applications (O'Reilly, 2017) is about data systems at scale, but several of its chapters explain why the small decisions in this series are right. The mapping below is my own reading of how the book's ideas apply, not claims the book makes about this design. Chapter numbers refer to the first edition; if you have a newer edition, check its table of contents, because the numbering may differ. Idea in this series Where to read more What it teaches --- --- --- The self-describing password record, upgraded at the next sign-in Ch. 4, Encoding and Evolution Backward and forward compatibility: new code must read old records, and formats need room to change The all-or-nothing claim, and "what if someone claimed one in between?" Ch. 7, Transactions Atomicity, isolation, and preventing lost updates when two writers collide Cached "last readings" going stale, and the change announcement Ch. 11, Stream Processing , and the book's derived data theme Keeping caches and other derived data in step with their source The build check that stops a forgotten guard Ch. 1, Reliable, Scalable, and Maintainable Applications Human error is a major cause of failures, so design to make mistakes hard What changes when the app goes online Chs. 5, 6, 8 and 9 (replication, partitioning, distributed-systems trouble, consistency and consensus) Everything in this series assumed one computer . A shared server brings these problems in ---

secs.head: Try it yourself
secs.body: 1. Threat model in five lines. Pick an app you use. Write what accounts would protect against and what they wouldn't, then compare with talk 1. 2. Self-describing hash. Implement the record format from talk 2 in your language, with a function that verifies a password and says whether the record needs upgrading. 3. Make it identical. Write a sign-in whose response is the same text, and takes about the same time, for an unknown user and a wrong password. Then measure both. 4. Break the door guard. Add an endpoint that takes a resource id, forget the ownership check, and write the test or build step that catches it (talk 3). 5. Late arrival. Build a tiny "start all monitors on sign-in" loop, register one monitor after sign-in, watch it never start, then fix it (talk 4). 6. Review the review. Pick two of the six questions above, decide your answers, and write the one sentence each would add to the threat model. ---

secs.head: Cheat sheet
secs.body: - Who's signed in? One note in the engine's memory. - What may they see? Profiles they own, and everything under them. - Where is it enforced? At the door (Bouncer) and again in the database (Cartographer). - A new request names a resource? The build fails until it's on the Bouncer's list. - What stops on sign-out? Sessions, tunnels, pop-outs and every monitor, plus their cached readings. - What does the lock do? Covers the window; changes nothing underneath. - Forgot the password? A terminal command resets it and wipes the saved secrets. - Going online? Add a second Clerk. ---

secs.head: The one-paragraph takeaway
secs.body: Adding accounts to a local app is mostly honesty plus plumbing. Be honest about what the feature protects, then do the plumbing so the promise holds everywhere: identical failures at sign-in, two independent walls around data, background work that follows the signed-in person, migrations that never surprise, and a lock that isn't a sign-out. Where the design leaves questions open, write them down. ---

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications , O'Reilly, 2017: chapters on encoding and evolution, transactions, stream processing and derived data - OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, Password Storage Cheat Sheet - OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, Authentication Cheat Sheet - OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, Authorization Cheat Sheet - OWASP Developer Guide, Enforce Access Controls checklist - OWASP Top 10, A01 Broken Access Control The "Where would you push back?" questions, the DDIA mapping and the lessons are reviewer commentary, not part of the original design.

label: Customer Segmentation
title: Customer Segmentation
desc: Customer segmentation is a crucial marketing strategy that involves dividing a company's customer base into distinct gro

secs.head: Customer Segmentation
secs.body: Customer segmentation is a crucial marketing strategy that involves dividing a company's customer base into distinct groups or segments based on certain shared characteristics, behaviors, or preferences. The goal of customer segmentation is to understand your customers better and tailor your marketing efforts, products, and services to meet the unique needs and preferences of each segment. This approach allows businesses to be more efficient and effective in their marketing efforts, ultimately leading to increased customer satisfaction and profitability.

secs.head: Key Points to Consider when Exploring Customer Segmentation
secs.body: Key Point Description -- -- Segmentation Criteria Customer segments can be defined based on various criteria such as demographics (age, gender, income), psychographics (lifestyle, values, interests), geographic location, behavior (purchase history, online activity), and more. The choice of criteria depends on your business and its goals. Benefits Customer segmentation provides several advantages, including improved targeting, personalized marketing messages, higher conversion rates, reduced marketing costs, and better customer retention. Types of Segmentation There are different approaches to segmentation, including:</br Demographic segmentation : Dividing customers based on demographic factors like age, gender, income, and education.</br Psychographic segmentation : Grouping customers based on their lifestyles, attitudes, values, and interests.</br Behavioral segmentation : Segmenting based on customer behavior, such as purchase history, frequency of purchases, and brand loyalty.</br Geographic segmentation : Dividing customers by their geographical location or region. Segmentation Process The process typically involves data collection and analysis, segmentation criteria selection, segment identification, and the development of targeted marketing strategies for each segment. Implementation Once segments are identified, businesses can tailor their marketing campaigns, product offerings, pricing strategies, and customer service to cater to the unique needs and preferences of each segment. Monitoring and Adaptation Customer segments may evolve over time, so it's essential to continuously monitor and adapt your segmentation strategy to stay relevant and effective.

secs.head: Aspects in Customer Segmentation
secs.body: Customer segmentation can be approached from various aspects, and there are numerous project ideas to explore. Here are some key aspects of customer segmentation and corresponding project ideas: Segmentation Aspect Brief Description Project Idea -- -- -- Demographic Segmentation Divide customers based on demographics like age, gender, income, etc. Create customer personas for targeted marketing. Psychographic Segmentation Segment based on interests, values, and lifestyle choices. Conduct surveys for personalized content and offers. Behavioral Segmentation Segment by purchase history, behavior, and engagement. Implement a recommendation system for product suggestions. Geographic Segmentation Divide customers by location or region. Craft location-specific promotions and inventory. RFM Analysis Categorize customers by Recency, Frequency, Monetary value. Develop loyalty programs and promotions for high-value customers. Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) Segmentation Calculate CLV for each segment and tailor strategies. Create retention plans for high CLV segments. Segmentation by Purchase Channel Segment based on where customers make purchases. Tailor marketing efforts for each channel. Churn Prediction Predict customers at risk of leaving and apply retention strategies. Develop a churn prediction model and retention campaigns. Market Basket Analysis Analyze frequently purchased product combinations. Create product bundles and cross-selling strategies. Sentiment Analysis Gauge customer sentiment through reviews and feedback. Address customer concerns and improve products/services. Multi-Channel Segmentation Segment customers based on multiple touchpoints. Develop omnichannel marketing strategies. Seasonal Segmentation Segment based on buying behavior during different seasons or holidays. Create seasonal marketing campaigns. Competitor Comparison Compare customer segments with competitors. Identify gaps and target untapped segments. AI-Driven Segmentation Use machine learning for automatic segmentation. Continuously refine and optimize the model. Segmentation for New Product Launch Identify early adopters and target segments. Plan targeted marketing for new product launches.

secs.head: Key Concepts & Consideration
secs.body: To effectively address a customer segmentation problem, there are several key concepts and considerations you should be aware of: Key Concept Descriptio -- -- Data Quality and Collection Ensure that your data is accurate, complete, and up-to-date. Clean and preprocess the data to remove outliers and handle missing values.</br Collect relevant data sources, which may include customer profiles, purchase history, website behavior, survey responses, and more. Segmentation Criteria Selection Carefully choose the criteria or variables for segmentation based on your business objectives. Consider both demographic and behavioral factors that align with your goals. Segmentation Methods Understand different segmentation methods, such as clustering algorithms (e.g., K-means, hierarchical clustering), decision trees, and regression analysis. Choose the appropriate method for your data and objectives. Sample Size and Representativeness Ensure that your sample size is large enough to produce statistically significant results for each segment.</br Aim for a sample that is representative of your entire customer base to avoid bias in segment creation. Validation and Testing Validate your segmentation by assessing how well it aligns with real-world customer behavior and preferences. Use techniques like cross-validation to test the stability and validity of your segments. Overfitting and Generalization Be cautious about overfitting, where segments are too tailored to your current data and may not generalize well to new customers. Strike a balance between specificity and generalizability. Segment Interpretation After creating segments, interpret the characteristics and behaviors of each group. What defines them, and how can you differentiate marketing strategies for each segment? Marketing Personalization Develop tailored marketing strategies, content, and offers for each segment based on their unique preferences and needs. Measurement and KPIs Define key performance indicators (KPIs) to track the success of your segmentation strategy. These could include conversion rates, customer retention, and revenue growth. Dynamic Segmentation Recognize that customer segments may change over time. Continuously update and adapt your segmentation strategy as customer behaviors evolve. Ethical Considerations Be mindful of privacy and ethical considerations when collecting and using customer data. Ensure compliance with relevant regulations (e.g., GDPR, CCPA) and prioritize customer consent and data protection. Technology and Tools Utilize appropriate tools and technology, such as data analytics platforms, machine learning libraries, and customer relationship management (CRM) systems, to facilitate the segmentation process. Customer Feedback Incorporate feedback from customers to refine and improve your segmentation strategy. Regularly solicit input from different segments to ensure their needs are being met. Collaboration Collaboration between marketing, sales, and data analytics teams is essential for the successful implementation of customer segmentation strategies. Long-Term Strategy View customer segmentation as a long-term strategy rather than a one-time effort. Continuously monitor and adapt your approach to stay competitive. Remember that customer segmentation is not a static process but an ongoing effort to better understand and serve your customers. Staying informed about emerging trends in data analytics, machine learning, and customer behavior will also be beneficial in refining your segmentation strategies over time.

secs.head: Question - Cheapest Flats per city using SQL
secs.body: You are given a table of flats with the following structure: </br create table flats(</br id integer primary key,</br city varchar(40) not null,</br price integer not null</br )</br Each row of table flats represents a flat located in a city available for sale for a given price. The result table should contain three columns: id, city, and price and should be sorted by id column. If the city has less than three flats for sale, the result table should contain all of them. Please use an OVER clause to simplify your solution. Example:</br 1.Given:</br id city price -- -- -- 25 London 200000 5 Cairo 90000 7 London 200000 18 Warsaw 150000 2 London 170000 3 Cairo 300000 21 London 500000 9 London 200000 One of the possible outputs is:</br id city price -- -- -- 2 London 170000 3 Cairo 300000 5 Cairo 90000 7 London 200000 9 London 200000 18 Warsaw 150000 There are only two flats available in Cairo and one in Warsaw, so they are all selected. The cheapest flat in London has ID 2, then there are three flats with the same price (with IDs: 7, 9, 25). Any two of them may be selected. Assume that: - The flast table has at most 100 rows. - Price column can only contains from 1000 to 100000000 inclusive.

secs.head: Question - Machine Learning Classifier
secs.body: An interview ML problem: build a logistic regression and a random forest on bank customer data, and report what drives term-deposit subscriptions. Implement a function, identify customers, which will build two classifier models based on financial data. The identify customers functions accepts two arguments: - data train - a Pandas DataFrame consisting of a binary column 'label' (1 means that the client subscribed to a term deposite, 0 otherwise), three integer columns describing the customer, including their age, account (account balance), and duration (time of being a bank customer) and 17 binary columns (with 'yes' and 'no' values) that also describe the customers. - data test - a Pandas DataFrame with the same structure as data train. In the identify customers function, you should perform the following steps: 1. Prepare the 17 binary variables in data train and data test by replacing 'yes' with 1, and 'no' with 0. Retain the rest of the variables without any changes. After this step, you will have two new data frames 'onehot train' and 'onehot test'. 2. Find the proportion (prep) of clients that have subscribed to a term deposit in onehot train (use the 'label' variable) and round the value to 3 decimal places. This will be necessary to set weights in the classifier models. 3. build a LogisticRegression Classifier on onehot train. Set the parameters: class weight={0:prep, 1:1-prep}, random state=0, max inter=50. 4. Build a RandomForest Classifier on onehot train. Set the parameters: max depth=10, random state=0, n estimators=30, class weight={0:prep, 1:1-prep}. 5. Do a prediction on onehot test. After these steps you should return, in identify customers, a dictionary with the following keys: - onehot train - data train DataFrame after replacing 'yes' and 'no' values with 1 and 0 (without 'label' column). - onehot test - data test DataFrame after replacing 'yes' and 'no' values with 1 and 0 (without 'label' column). - prep - propotion from point 2, above. - negative impact - list of column names which reduce the probability of subscribing term deposit (when this variables increases). Use properities of the LogisticRegression classifier to obtain this point. - feature importance - list of tuples with the five most important varialbes based on feature importances from the RandomForest classifier in the form (column names, feature importance). - lr recall - tupple of recall scores from onehot train and onehot test after training with the LogisticRegression Classifier. - rf recall - tupple of recall scores from onehot train and onehot test after training with the RandomForest Classifier. - lr obs - the probabilty of varialbes from LogisticRegression Classifier. - rf obs - the probabilty of varialbes from RandomForest Classifier.
